text:
Progenies Caesarum in Nerone defecit: Nero left no son of his own,
nor had he adopted a son who might have been chosen as his successor.
Dio Cassius (ap. Xiphilinum), lxiii 29, describes him as ἔσχατος τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ
Αἰνείου καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ Αὐγούστου γεγονότων and in lxii 18 mentions a
"Sibylline" verse quoted by the angry populace against Nero after the
great fire at Rome in his reign: ἔσχατος Αἰνεαδῶν μητροκτόνος ἡγεμονεύσει
(imitated in Auson. Caes. vi, Aeneadum generis qui sextus et ultimus
heres, polluit et clausit Iulia sacra Nero). Cf. also Eutrop. vii 15, in eo
omnis Augusti familia consumpta est: Tac. Ann. xiv 17, (Nero) qui unus
superesset e familia summum ad fastigium genita. In Tac. Hist. i 16.
Galba says in his speech when adopting Piso: sub Tiberio et Gaio et Claudio
unius familiae quasi hereditas fuimus: loco libertatis erit quod eligi
coepimus, et finita Iuliorum Claudiorumque domo optimum quemque adoptio
inveniet. The house of the Julian Caesars came to an end on the death of
the emperor Gaius (Caligula), son of Germanicus. When his successor
Claudius took the name "Caesar," it was no longer a family name but an
imperial title, as Claudius, son of Drusus, had not been transferred into the
Julian gens like his uncle Tiberius and his brother Germanicus. See Bury
(Student's Roman Empire c. 15, 1), who points out that the Julian and
Claudian families had been so closely connected since the marriage of
Augustus and Livia that they were almost regarded as a single house.

Liviae: Livia Drusilla, daughter of Livius Drusus Claudianus, was
first married to Tiberius Claudius Nero to whom she bore a son Tiberius,
afterwards emperor. Octavian became enamoured of her beauty, and in
38 B.C. her husband was forced to surrender her to the triumvir, though she
was with child (Drusus) at the time. Suetonius says that Augustus
esteemed and loved her faithfully to the end: dilexit et probavit unice ac
perseveranter (Aug. 62, 2). She outlived Augustus and died in 29 A.D.

Veientanum: sc. praedium, an estate about nine miles from Rome at
Veii a town in Etruria on the site of the mod. Isola Farnese.
..

aquila gallinam demisit: the same story is told by Pliny, N.H.
xv 136: Sunt et circa divom Augustum eventa eius digna memoratu;
namque Liviae Drusillae quae postea Augusta matrimoni nomen accepit,
cum pacta esset illa Caesari, gallinam conspicui candoris sedenti aquila ex
alto abiecit in gremium inlaesam, intrepideque miranti accessit miraculum,
quoniam tenentem rostro laureum ramum onustum suis bacis; conservari
alitem et subolem iussere haruspices ramumque eum seri ac rite custodiri.
Quod factum est in villa Caesarum fluvio Tiberi imposita iuxta nonum
lapidem Flaminia via, quae ob id vocatur ad Gallinas, mireque silva provenit; ex ea triumphans postea Caesar laurum in manu tenuit coronamque
capite gessit ac deinde Caesares cuncti; traditusque mos est ramos quos
tenuerunt serendi et durant silvae nominibus suis discretae, fortassis ideo
mutatis triumphalibus. This story is regarded by some as the origin of
the expression gallinae filius albae (Juv. xiii 141), which others explain by
the statement of Columella (viii 2, 7) that white hens are delicate and unprolific.

pangi: Fest., p. 213 Müll., pangere, figere; unde plantae pangi dicuntur,
cum in terram demittantur. This verb (connected with πήγνυμι) is sometimes used with the acc. of the place and the abl. of the plant, e.g. Colum.
xi 2, 18, vitiaria malleolis pangere; Prop. iii 17, 15, ipse seram vites
pangamque ex ordine colles.

placuisset: Pliny (l.c.) says that it was the haruspices who ordered this
to be done. Dio (xlviii 52) mentions that Livia herself took care of the
hen and planted the laurel: τήν τε ὄρνιθα ἐν ἐπιμελείᾳ ἦγε (ἡ Λιουία) καὶ τὴν
δάφνην ἐφύτευσε.

hodieque: = hodie quoque (hodie etiam, usque adhuc, etiam nunc); cf.
Tit. 2, Claud. 19, Tib. 14, 3.
This use of hodieque is post-Aug.; first in
Velleius, then in Val. Max., Sen., Plin. N.H., and isolated instances in Quint.
and Tac. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarbarus, I 597.

ad Gallinas: see on Dom. 1, 1, ad Malum Punicum. At Rome one of
the side-streets on the Viminal bore the name of "gallinae albae” (Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom I, 3, 374). The interesting ruins at Prima Porta
which have been identified with the villa of Livia, and the excavations which
have been made there, are described by Burn, Rome and the Campagna,
c. xiv; see also J.R.S. xi 145.

'illas: a correction by Burman (followed by Wolf, Baumg.-Crus., Roth,
Preud'homme) of alias (which is retained by Ihm). Lipsius suggested eas.
Pliny states definitely that the Caesars planted the same laurel branches
which they had carried in their hands during the triumph.
institutam: "planted"; cf. Suet. Gramm. 23, vitem manu eius institutam: Cic. Agr. ii 25, 67, iugera trecenta, ubi institui vineae possunt.
novissimo Neronis anno: 68 A.D.

exaruit interiit: Dio lxiii 29, καθάπερ που σαφῶς καὶ αἱ δάφναι αἱ ὑπὸ
τῆς Λιουίας φυτευθεῖσαι τό τε γένος τῶν λευκῶν ὀρνίθων προδιαφθαρέντα αὐτοῦ
(Νέρωνος) ἐσήμανεν: Aur. Vict. Caes. 5, 17, Hic finis Caesarum genti fuit;
quem fore prodigiorum multa denuntiavere, praecipueque eorum praediis
arescens lauri nemus dicatum triumphantibus; atque interitus gallinarum,
quae adeo multae albaeque aptiores erant religionibus, ut iis Romae habeatur
hodie locus. The withering of laurel trees is mentioned among the omens
of the fall of Troy in Quint. Smyrn. xii 517, ἀπαυαίνοντο δὲ δάφναι | πὰρ νηὸν
Φοίβοιο, πάρος θαλεραί περ ἐοῦσαι.

quidquid gallinarum erat: Suetonius is very fond of this use of quidquid c. gen. either of persons or things; e.g. Oth. 10, 2, quidquid epistularum
erat: Vitell. 10, 1, quidquid cohortium fuit. See Kühner-Stegmann, Lat.
Gramm. I 429.

subinde: this adv. is not ante-Aug.; Livy is the first prose writer to use
it. Suetonius has it in its two senses: (a) = mox, statim, as here and in
Galb. 10, 4: Vitell. 9: Tit. 5, 2; (b) identidem, saepius (Fr. souvent
from subinde), as in Galb. 3, 4; 16, 1.
=

Caesarum aede: the Templum Divi Augusti on the Palatine, begun by
Livia, continued by Tiberius, and completed by Caligula. Since in the
course of time all the deified members of the Julio-Claudian house were
worshipped there, it was known at the end of the first dynasty as the aedes
Caesarum. It was destroyed by fire under Vespasian, and restored by
Domitian; there was another restoration of it on a large scale by Antoninus
Pius. See Jordan-Huelsen, op. cit. I 3, 80 sq.; Marquardt, Röm. Staatsverwaltung iii² 468; Platner and Ashby, Topogr. Dict. of Ancient Rome
62 sqq.

sceptrum: the statue represented Augustus in triumphal garb bearing
the sceptre and wearing the tunica palmata and the toga picta; an ivory
sceptre crowned with an eagle was carried by the triumphator in his left
hand, and a laurel branch in his right (Dion. Hal. iii 61; Val. Max. iv 4, 5;
Juv. x 43; Mommsen, Röm. Staatsrecht is 425). In Aug. 94, 6 Suetonius
describes a vision, which Octavius, father of Augustus, had of the future
greatness of his son: sequenti nocte videre visus est filium mortali specie
ampliorem, cum fulmine et sceptro exuviisque Iovis Optimi Maximi ac
radiata corona, super laureatum currum bis senis equis candore eximio
trahentibus.

excussum est: cf. Dom. 15, 2 (on the portents of Domitian's death):
e basi statuae triumphalis titulus excussus vi procellae.

nullo gradu contingens Caesarum domum: Plutarch, Galb. 3, says that
Galba was related to Livia, wife of Augustus, and owed to her his consulship. Plutarch may be referring to the fact that Livia Ocellina, stepmother of Galba (see c. 3, 3), and Livia Drusilla, wife of Augustus, belonged
to the same gens; Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) thinks that Plutarch confused
Livia Ocellina with Livia Augusta.
For contingere used of family connexions cf. Aug. 4, 1, a matre Magnum
Pompeium artissimo contingebat gradu: Ner. 32, 2, ullae familiae quas
ipse contingeret: Juv. viii 7, multa contingere virga | fumosos equitum
cum dictatore magistros: id. xi 62, contingens sanguine caelum: Liv. xlv 7,
quos sanguine ac genere contingebat.
...

nobilissimus: cf. Tac. H. i 49 (of Galba), vetus in familia nobilitas,
magnae opes. claritas natalium: Aur. Vict. Caes. 6, 1, Galba haud secus
nobilis a gente clarissima Sulpiciorum: Eutrop. vii 16, Servius Galba
antiquissimae nobilitatis senator. Galba himself is represented by Tacitus
(i 15) as speaking proudly of his descent from the gens Sulpicia on his
father's side and the gens Lutatia on his mother's. Juvenal (viii 5) uses
the family of Galba as typical of the old noble families of Rome: pictos
ostendere vultus | maiorum et stantes in curribus Aemilianos | et Curios iam
dimidios umerosque minorem | Corvinum et Galbam auriculis nasoque
carentem.

prosapia:
an archaic word found in Plaut. Curc. 393, Merc. 626.
Sallust, who uses it in Iug. 85, 10, homo veteris prosapiae, is said to have
borrowed it from Cato's Origines (cf. Nonius p. 94 Lindsay). Cicero uses
it apologetically, Tim. 11, et eorum, ut utamur veteri verbo, prosapiam.
Quintilian (i 6, 40) mentions it as a specimen of the words "ab ultimis
et iam oblitteratis repetita temporibus" which are to be avoided, and later
(viii 3, 26) says that the use of it denotes a lack of taste: prosapiam
dicere insulsum est. The word has been variously connected with satus,
supare (dissipare), the Old Eng. sib "relationship," etc. Walde, Lat.
Etym. Wörterb., would connect it with the subst. sopio (see R. Ellis on
Catull. 37, 10).

ut qui statuarum titulis .. ascripserit: there is no other mention of
these statues of Galba, and in none of the extant inscriptions referring to
him is he thus described. A statua triumphalis would be included in the
triumphalia ornamenta which were bestowed on him for his victories in
Africa and Germany (c. 8, 1), and when he became emperor, numerous
statues would be erected in his honour (cf. Vitell. 9).

Quinti Catuli Capitolini: Galba's mother, Mummia Achaica, was the
granddaughter of Catulus. Galba's pride in this illustrious ancestor is
described in Plut. Galb. 3, μέγα δὲ ἔχων εὐγενείας ἀξίωμα τὸν Σερουΐων (i.e. the
Servii Sulpicii) οἶκον αὐτὸς ἐφρόνει μεῖζον ἐπὶ τῇ Κάτλου συγγενείᾳ, πρωτεύσαντος
ἀνδρὸς ἀρετῇ καὶ δόξῃ τῶν καθ᾽ ἑαυτόν, εἰ καὶ τὸ δύνασθαι μᾶλλον ἑκὼν ἑτέροις παρῆκεν.
Catulus, one of the leading optimates, was consul in 78 B.C., and when his
colleague Lepidus tried to overthrow the Sullan constitution he defeated
him in arms at the Mulvian Bridge in 77. He was one of the iudices who
condemned Verres (70). He opposed the Gabinian and Manilian Laws
(67, 66). He urged Cicero to include Caesar in the list of Catilinarian
conspirators, and in '62 Caesar as praetor tried in vain to deprive him of
the commissionership for the restoration of the Capitol (burned in 83), a
post which he had held since 78, and from which he got the cognomen
"Capitolinus"; his name remained inscribed on the temple till it was
again burned under Vitellius (Vitell. 15, 3). Cicero speaks in the most
glowing terms of Catulus, who is one of the interlocutors in the Academica
(see Reid, Introd. p. 73); he calls him one of the pillars of the state
(Brut. 222) and classes him with the ancient worthies of Rome (Verr. ii 3,
210). Catulus alone had the courage to rebuke equally the follies of the
mob and of the senate (Sest. 122); he was not only glorious in his life, but
fortunate in his death (Att. ii 24, 4). He died in 60 в.с.

stemma in atrio: in the atrium of the noble families at Rome were
placed the imagines, or waxen masks fitted to busts, kept in small cases
(armaria) under which were inscriptions (tituli) of the distinctions of the
various ancestors; the imagines were connected by painted lines (lineae)
and the imagines and lineae together made up the stemma or genealogical,
tree. Cf. Ner. 37, 1, obiectum est Cassio Longino quod in vetere gentili
stemmate C. Cassii percussoris Caesaris imagines retinuisset: Plin. N. H.
xxxv 6, aliter apud maiores in atriis haec erant quae spectarentur; non
..
signa exterorum artificum nec aera aut marmora: expressi cera vultus
singulis disponebantur armariis, ut essent imagines quae comitarentur
gentilicia funera... stemmata vero lineis discurrebant ad pictas imagines:
Sen. Ben. iii 28, 2, qui imagines in atrio exponunt et nomina familiae suae
longo ordine ex multis stemmatum illigata flexuris in parte prima aedium
collocant: Mart. iv 40, 1, atria Pisonum stabant cum stemmate toto.

originem ad Iovem referret: for such genealogical pretensions see
on Vesp. 12.

Pasiphaam: daughter of Helios and wife of Minos king of Crete; she
was a sister of Circe and of Aeetes the father of Medea. Pasiphaë is
notorious in legend as the mother of Minotaurus, and Galba must have
claimed descent from her merely because she was a daughter of the Sungod. Silius Italicus (Pun. viii 468 sqq.) attributes a similar mythical
pedigree to a Galba who commanded the Etruscan contingent at Cannae:
Iamque per Etruscos legio completa maniplos | rectorem magno spectabat
nomine Galbam. Huic genus orditur Minos, inlusaque tauro | Pasiphae.

Minonis: this form, and not the more usual Minois (Roth, Preud 'homme),
has the support of M here and in Tib. 70. Priscian (vi 13, 70) notices its
use in Sallust (Hist. ii frag. 5 Kritz): Daedalum ex Sicilia profectum, quo
Minonis fugerat iram atque opes.
Priscian says that similarly the
Syracusans used ἥρων, ἥρωνος for ἥρως, ἥρωος, and he also mentions “Athos
(Athon), Athonis” in Cicero, Rep. iii.
imagines: see on c. 2 and Vesp. 1, 1.

elogia: the inscriptions (tituli) under the imagines, giving the names,
honours, and achievements of each ancestor. elogium (connected by Curtius
with ἐλεγεῖον, cf. oliva ἐλαία, lopas λεπάς) is used by Cicero for an epitaph,
and for a clause in a will. Suetonius has it in both these senses (Claud. 1,5:
vit. Horat. 1); also for an inscription on a votive tablet (Calig. 24, 3),
and for an abstract or précis of a criminal case (Calig. 27, 1).
exequi: cf. Dom. 1, 3, n.

familiae attingam: the particular family of the gens Sulpicia
which bore the surname of Galba; other family names of the Sulpicii
under the Republic were Camerinus, Cornutus, Gallus, Longus, Paterculus,
Peticus, Praetextatus, Quirinus, Rufus.
"familiae” (sc. imagines et elogia) seems certainly to be the gen.,
though Dalmasso (p. 54) takes it as dat. The dat. with attingere only
occurs a few times (Apul. Apol. 100, C.I.L. ix 5438; see Thesaurus Ling.
Lat.). Suetonius uses the verb in twelve other passages, and always with
the accusative.

galbano: galbanum (χαλβάνη) was a resinous gum from a Syrian
plant; it was used for the purpose of smoking away serpents (Plin. N.H. xii
126; Verg. G. iii 415; Luc. ix 916; Nicand. Ther. 51, βαρύοδμος ἐπὶ φλογὶ
ζωγρηθεῖσα | χαλβάνη).
0
..
succenderit... uteretur.. visus sit: Suetonius frequently couples
the impf, and perf. subj. in this way, and seems to use these two tenses
quite indifferently; e.g. Vitell. 7, 2, ut domum
ablocaret, utque
unionem pigneraverit: Vesp. 4, 3, ut qui obligaret et descenderit:
Iul. 22; 39: Tib. 52: Claud. 4: Ner. 25, etc. See Draeger, Hist. Synt. i
270 sqq.; Roth, praef. p. xxxv; Bagge, p. 94; Dalmasso, p. 84.
..

galbeo: galbeus (calbeus) or galbeum was a kind of armlet or bracelet
according to the notices in Festus, p. 46 Müll., calbeos armillas dicebant,
quibus triumphantes utebantur; p. 96, galbeum ornamenti genus; p. 265
(quoting from Cato's Origines), mulieres opertae auro purpuraque
coronas aureas, rusceas fascias, galbeos, lineas, pelles, etc. Suetonius uses
it here for a bandage (= fascia, Dom, 17, 1) put round the arm like an
armlet, consisting of wool in which were wrapped healing medicines or,
at times, amulets; cf. Plin. N.H. xxx 143, stellionis ("newt'') cinerem
linamento (‘‘lint’”) involutum in sinistra manu venerem stimulare; xx 155,
Xenocrates pulei (“pennyroyal'') ramum lana involutum in tertianis ante
accessionem olefactandum dari tradit; Cels. vii 26, 5, inducendus hapsus
(i.e. a lock of wool used in bandaging) lanae mollis tepido oleo repletus;
id. iv '6, 9, circumdare oportet latus hapso lanae sulphuratae.
..

praepinguis quem galbam Galli vocent: this is probably the right
derivation of the name Galba (a Celtic word = venter obesus), so many
Roman cognomina denoted physical peculiarities. Cf. the Germ. Kalb (calf)
used for a fat person. For the numerous words cognate to Kalb, e.g. Sanser.
gárbhas (= uterus), Goth. kalbo, see Walde Etym. Wörterb. s.v. galba;
the root meaning is "swelling." We find mention of a king of the
Suessiones, a Gallic tribe, who bore the name of Galba (Caes. B.G. ii 4, 13),
and Galbus is a variant for Chalbus as a name of a Spanish chieftain
in Liv. xxiii 26. One of the Sulpicii may have got the nickname when
serving abroad. Hofstee compares the cognomen ‘“Arvina" ("fat"
"suet'") in the family of the Cornelii Cossi.
..
visus: Bentley would substitute for this either et obesus or ut vitulus.

animalia galbae: this "galba" is defined by Lewis and Short as
"a small worm, the ash-borer, or the larva of the ash-spinner, Bombyx
aesculi, Linn."; it does not seem to be mentioned elsewhere. An interesting parallel to this derivation of the name "Galba" would be "Cossus,''
as cossus is used frequently in Pliny for a kind of larva under the bark of
trees.

§ 2. familiam illustravit: Suetonius makes no reference to the ancestor
who first brought distinction to the family, viz. P. Sulpicius Ser. f. P. n.
Galba Maximus, who was elected consul in 211 B.C. without having filled
any curule office previously, and was consul again in 204 (Liv. xxv 41,
xxvi 1). Other ancestors who held office at Rome were C. Sulpicius Galba,
pontifex 201 B.C. (Liv. xxx 39, xxxii 7): Ser. Sulpicius Galba, curule aedile
in 188, urban praetor in 187 (Liv. xxxviii 35, etc.): C. Sulpicius Galba,
urban praetor in 171 (Liv. xlii 28, 31).

Servius Galba consularis: he was consul in 144 B.с., his colleague being
L. Aurelius Cotta.

vel: this is Bentley's correction of et, the reading of all MSS. except
I which omits the word. Casaubon proposed ditissimus et eloquentissimus,
introducing ditissimus from Appian Hisp. 60, where this Galba is called
πλουσιώτατος ῾Ρωμαίων, and this suggestion is approved by Burman.
Preud'homme keeps et; Ihm marks it as corrupt.

eloquentissimus: Cicero describes him as “eloquentissimus’(Brut. 33,
127) and “divinus homo in dicendo” (de or. i 10, 40); cf. also Brut. 21, 82,
sine controversia Ser. Galba eloquentia praestitit; et nimirum is princeps
ex Latinis illa oratorum propria et quasi legitima opera tractavit, ut egrederetur a proposito ornandi causa, ut delectaret animos, ut permoveret, ut
augeret rem, ut miserationibus, ut communibus locis uteretur. Sed nescio
quo modo huius, quem constat eloquentia praestitisse, exiliores orationes
sunt et redolentes magis antiquitatem quam aut Laelii aut Scipionis, aut
etiam ipsius Catonis; itaque exaruerunt, vix iam ut appareant.

Hispaniam ex praetura optinentem: he was praetor in 151, and in 150
was allotted the province of Hispania Ulterior where war was being waged
with the Celtiberians. He invaded Lusitania to relieve some Roman subjects there, and routed the Lusitanian forces, but pursuing them incautiously
met with a severe reverse and lost 7000 men. On his next invasion of
Lusitania the Lusitanians sent an embassy promising to resume the
observance of a treaty previously made with Rome. Galba treated them
with despicable treachery, pretending to sympathize with their poverty
which had led to their revolt, and promising to assign them fertile lands if
they assembled in three bodies, together with their women and children,
at three specified places. Each of the three bodies when it assembled was
ordered to surrender arms and being surrounded by a ditch, to prevent
escape, was massacred by Galba's troops. Viriathus was one of the few
who managed to escape. In 149 Galba was impeached for this outrage
and Cato, aged 85, denounced him in a speech of great vehemence, but by
bribery and by appearing as a suppliant along with his children and the
orphan child of a relative he succeeded in securing an acquittal. Appian
Hisp. 58-60; Cic. de or. i 53, 227; Val. Max. viii 1, 2; 7, 1; Plut. Cat. mai.
15; Nep. Cat. 3; Oros. iv 21.)

triginta milibus: Val. Max. (ix 6, 2) says 7000: septem milia, in
quibus flos iuventutis consistebat, electa et armis exuta, partim trucidavit,
partim vendidit. Quo facinore maximam cladem barbarorum magnitudine
criminis (Galba) antecessit.

Viriathini belli: after his escape from the massacre of the Lusitanians
by Galba, Viriathus organised a guerilla warfare against the Romans with
such success that in 145 and the following years a consul and consular army
had to be sent against him. These efforts to subdue him were ineffective,
and in 141 he entrapped the Roman army in a pass like the Caudine Forks
and forced the proconsul Fabius Servilianus to make peace. Servilius
Caepio, who commanded in Further Spain, renewed the war on some pretext
in 140, and bribed three envoys of Viriathus to assassinate him. After his
death (139 в.с.) the Lusitanians were driven to submit.

nepos: Servius Sulpicius Galba, who was a cousin of Decimus Brutus
(Cic. Fam. xi 7) and a friend of Cicero. A letter from him to Cicero is
still extant (Fam. x 30) giving an account of the battle at Forum Gallorum
02
in which M. Antonius was defeated during the siege of Mutina in 43 B.C.,
Galba commanding the legio Martia on the victorious side.

ob repulsam consulatus: Galba, urban praetor in 54, was a candidate
for the consulship in 49, but was defeated, as being an intimate friend and
officer of Caesar, by the party opposed to Caesar; cf. Hirt. Bell. Gall. viii
50, propterea quod insolenter adversarii sui (i.e. of Caesar) gloriarentur
L. Lentulum et C. Marcellum consules creatos, qui omnem honorem et
dignitatem Caesaris spoliarent, ereptum. Ser. Galbae consulatum, cum is
multo plus gratia suffragiisque valuisset, quod sibi coniunctus et familiaritate et necessitudine legationis esset. This defeat, however, could not have
been the cause of the bitter estrangement between Galba and Caesar, and
we must assume that at a subsequent date Caesar, when dictator, refused
Galba's claim to the consulship. For repulsam see on Vesp. 2, 3.

infensus Iulio Caesari: an instance of Galba's presumption and Caesar's
forbearance is given in Val. Max. vi 2, 11, Iam Ser. Galbae temeritatis
plena postulatio, qui Divum Iulium consummatis victoriis in foro ius
dicentem in hunc modum interpellare sustinuit: “C. Iuli Caesar, pro Cn.
Pompeio Magno, quondam genero tuo, in tertio eius consulatu (52 B.C.)
pecuniam spopondi, quo nomine nunc appellor. Quid agam? dependam?”
Palam atque aperte ei bonorum Pompei venditionem exprobrando ut a
tribunali summoveretur meruerat. Sed illud ipsa mansuetudine mitius
pectus (i.e. Caesar) aes alienum Pompei ex suo fisco solvi iussit. Cf. Cic.
Fam. vi 18.

legatus in Gallia: in 57 B.C. Caesar sent Galba as legatus to subdue the
Nantuates, Veragri, and Seduni; he defeated them and later resisted successfully a strong counter attack which they made on his camp at
Octodurus. (Caes. B.G. iii 1-6, Dio Cass. xxxvii 48, xxix 5.)

conspiravit: Galba's participation in the conspiracy against Caesar is
mentioned also by Appian (Bell. Civ. ii 113). Cicero (Phil. xiii 16) threatens
M. Antonius that Galba (“fortissimus et constantissimus civis’”) would use
on him the same dagger (pugio) as he had used to kill Caesar.

Pedia lege: a law proposed in 43 B.c. by the consul Q. Pedius, interdicting from fire and water all those who had taken part in the murder of
Julius Caesar: Vell. Pat. ii 69, 5, lege Pedia, quam consul Pedius, collega
Caesaris tulerat, omnibus qui Caesarem patrem interfecerant, aqua ignique
damnatis interdictum erat; cf. Monum. Ancyr. i 2, Qui parentem meum
[interfecer]un[t, eo]s in exilium expuli iudiciis legitimis ultus eorum
[fa]cin[us]. See Mommsen, Röm. Strafrecht 159, 199. Suetonius, Ner.
3, 1, says of Nero's great-grandfather: ‘“inter conscios Caesarianae necis
quanquam insons damnatus lege Pedia ... solusque omnium ex iis, qui
pari lege damnati erant, restitutus in patriam.'”

§ 3. avus: this C. Sulpicius Galba, the historian, is mentioned as one of
the authorities of the elder Pliny (N.H., index in lib. xxxvi). Peter (Hist.
Rom. Frag., p. 238) cites two references to his history: Plut. Rom. 17,
Ἑάλω δὲ καὶ (cum filia Tarpeia) Ταρπήϊος προδοσίας ὑπὸ ῾Ρωμύλου διωχθείς, ὡς
Ιόβας φησὶ Γάλβαν Σουλπίκιον ἱστορεῖν: Oros. v 23, 6, fuisse tunc Pompeio
triginta milia peditum, mille equites Galba scribit, Sertorium autem sexaginta milia peditum octo milia equitum habuisse commemorat.

non egressus praeturae gradum: cf. Oth. 1, 1, nec praeturae gradum
excessit. This use of egredi is found first in Velleius, and often in later
writers, e.g. Tac. A. iii 30, vetus familia neque tamen praeturam egressa.

incuriosam: an adjective used freely in post-Aug. Latin of persons,
either absolutely or with the gen., abl., or in (e.g. Aug. 79, 1, in capite
comendo incuriosus); its use in a passive sense of things, as here, is found
in Tac. A. vi 17, acribus, ut ferme talia, initiis, incurioso fine, and earlier
in a frag. of Sall. (H. iv 66, Kritz), infrequentem stationem nostram incuriosamque ab armis (= milites in statione positos, neque arma in promptu
habentes).

consulatu functus: in what year is uncertain, but he is probably the
"Ser. Sulpicius C. f. Galba" mentioned as consul suffectus in 5 B.C.
(C.I.L. i², p. 69).
quanquam: see on Tit. 7, 2.

gibber: "hunch-backed"; see on “gibba,” Dom. 23, 2. A witticism
of Augustus on Galba's deformity is quoted in Macrob. Sat. ii 4, 8:
Galbae, cuius informe gibbo erat corpus, agenti apud se causam et
frequenter dicenti: “Corrige, in me si quid reprehendis,” respondit: “Ego
te monere possum, corrigere non possum” (“corrigere" meaning "to make
straight the crooked"). The schoolmaster Orbilius also jested sarcastically
on the same subject; Macrob. ii 6, 4, In eundem Galbam Orbilius grammaticus acerbius inrisit. Prodierat Orbilius in reum testis. Quem Galba, ut
confunderet, dissimulata professione eius interrogavit: “Quid artium
facis?" Respondit: “In sole gibbos soleo fricare." In Suet. Gramm.
9, 2 (quoted on Dom. 23, 2) the repartee of Orbilius is given in a different
form and is directed against A. Terentius Varro Murena, not against Galba.
modicae in dicendo facultatis: Macrobius (ii 6, 3) rates his eloquence
more highly: In Galbam eloquentia clarum, sed quem habitus
corporis
destruebat, M. Lollii vox circumferebatur: Ingenium Galbae male habitat.

§ 4. Mummiam Achaicam: she may, as Borghesi says, be a daughter
of the Mummius who is mentioned as legatus of M. Crassus in the Servile
war against Spartacus in 71 B.с. (Plut. Crass. 10). See Dessau, Prosopographia Imperii Romani ii p. 389. The family of Mummius continued the
use of the cognomen ‘‘Achaicus" won by the consul L. Mummius in 146 в.с.
for the destruction of Corinth and the conquest of Greece, which was
transformed into the Roman province of Achaia.
Catuli: Q. Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus (see on c. 2).

Liviam Ocellinam: her father may have been the Lucius Livius Ocella
who was honoured with an inscription by two peoples of Hither Spain;
C.I.L. vi 246, L. Livio L. f. Ocellae quaestori) Segobrigenses. L. Livio
L. f. Ocellae Suessetanei (Dessau, Prosop. ii 290). The meaning of the
name "Ocella" is given in Plin. N.H. xi 150, qui altero lumine orbi
nascerentur Coclites vocabantur, qui parvis utrisque Ocellae; Luscini
iniuriae cognomen habuerunt.
subinde: see on c. 1.
quasi: causal; see on Tit. 5, 1.

Gaius: consul in 22 A.D. along with D.
C. Sulpicius D. Haterius consules sequuntur).
Haterius (Tac. A. iii 52,
The same account of his
death is given in Tac. A. vi 40, C. Galba consularis et duo Blaesi voluntario
exitu cecidere, Galba tristibus Caesaris litteris provinciam sortiri prohibitus.
He died in 36 A.D., fourteen years after his consulship.

anno suo: i.e. the year in which he became senior ex-consul (consularis).
Augustus enforced anew a rule of Pompeius that five years must elapse
between the tenure of magistracy and the sortitio provinciae; but a much
longer interval usually did elapse in the case of consular provinces owing
to the increase in the number of ex-consuls caused by the practice of
appointing consules suffecti (see on Dom. 2, 1). The consequent slowness
in succession to proconsulships was relieved to some extent by the fact
that some consulares were disqualified, or rejected by the emperor or by
the senate, or like Agricola declined the sortitio. See Furneaux, Tac. Ann.
vol. i², Introd. c. vii; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 251.

proconsulatum: either of Asia or Africa which were reserved for consulares, the other provinces being usually given to praetorii, though both
classes of governors are properly styled proconsuls (Furneaux, l.c.).

M. Valerio Messala: this is M. Valerius Corvinus Messala Messalinus,
son of M. Valerius Messala Corvinus (cons. 31 B.C.) who was the literary
patron of Ovid and Tibullus. The appointment of the son as one of the
Quindecimviri sacris faciundis was the occasion of an extant poem of
Tibullus (ii 5); cf. also Ov. Pont. i 7, ii 2. For his military achievements
as governor of Dalmatia and Pannonia see Dio lv 29 sqq., Vell. Pat. ii 112.

Cn. Lentulo: in the Index to Dio lv the names of the consuls for
3 B.c. are given as Λ. Κορνήλιος Λ. υἱ. Λεντοῦλος, καὶ Μ. Οὐαλέριος Μ. υἱ. Μεσσαλᾶς,
ἢ Μεσσαλίνοs (L. Cornelius L. f. Lentulus, et M. Valerius M. f. Messala
vel Messalinus); and in Monum. Ancyr. iii 16 the names appear as
L. Lentulus and M. Messala. The praenomen “Gnaeus" in our text is
probably due to a confusion by Suetonius or the copyists with Cn. Cornelius
Cn. f. Lentulus, consul in 14 B.c.; another Cn. Lentulus was consul in
18 в.с.

VIIII Kal. Ian: Dec. 24, 3 в.с.
date of Galba's birth and reconciling
see on c. 23.
For the difficulty of determining the
the conflicting statements of Suetonius

Terracinam: Terracina (usually "Tarracina Carracina'") is the mod. Terracina
in Latium, 62 miles from Rome, at the point where the Appia Via first
touches the sea coast. Latin poets preferred to use the Volscian name
Anxur as metrically more convenient than Tarrăcina. That Tarracina was
the home of the Galbae is confirmed by an inscription found there,
C.I.L. i 576, [Ser. Sulpic]ius Ser. f. Galba cos. pavimentum [faciendum
locavi]t eisdemque probavit (see Mommsen ad loc.).

Fundos: mod. Fondi, in Latium, 12 miles from Tarracina; mentioned
by Horace (S. i 5, 34) as the next stopping-place after Anxur (Tarracina)
on the journey to Brundusium.

petentibus: for this use of the dat. see on Vesp. 1, 3, a Nursia
Spoletium euntibus.
adoptatus a noverca: she must have adopted him by her will; a
similar instance of adoptio in nomen et familiam is mentioned in Cic.
Att. vii 8, Dolabellam video Liviae testamento cum duobus coheredibus
esse in triente, sed iuberi mutare nomen. Est πολιτικὸν σκέμμα rectumne
sit nobili adulescenti mutare nomen mulieris testamento. (Dolabella did
not accept the legacy at least he did not change his name; see Tyrrell
and Purser ad loc.). Under Roman law no woman could adopt during her
life, since she was not the head of a family and did not possess the patria
potestas; in 291 A.D. Diocletian and Maximian by a special rescript allowed
a woman to adopt her stepson to console her for the loss of her own children
(Cod. Iust. xlviii 8 Inst. Iust. i 11, 10). See Roby, Roman Private Law i
59 n.; Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 40.

Livi nomen: the stepmother's name was Livia Ocellina (c. 3, 4). The
reading Livii (Livi Roth, Preud'homme) is only found in later MSS.; the
earlier have Livia (read by Ihm), but this leaves nomen very bare. Heinsius
conjectured Livium; Bentley Livianum, which may well be right (-num
being lost before nomen).

Ocellare cognomen: i.e. the cognomen “Ocella”; cf. Hor. S. ii 3, 25,
Mercuriale cognomen: Ov. Pont. ii 5, 49, surgit Iuleo iuvenis cognomine
dignus. The ed. Basil. (1533 A.D.) reads Ocellae; so too Roth. This
cognomen of Galba's is not found in inscriptions or on coins.

mutato praenomine: the praenomen ‘"Lucius” assumed by Galba on
adoption was that of Lucius Livius Ocella, father of Livia Ocellina
(c. 3, 4, n.). As a praenomen of Galba it appears on gladiatorial tesseraė
(C.I.L. i 770, 771) where the consuls for 33 A.D. are given as L. Sulp. and
L. Sull.

usque ad tempus imperii: Dessau (Inscr. Lat. Sel. 237 n.) points out
that the title which Galba chose as emperor was "Ser. Galba imp. Caesar
Augustus," as is shown by the military diplomata issued by him to the
veterans of the First legion (Adiutrix); see Dessau 1988, C.I.L. x 770, 771.
But in Greek inscriptions in Egypt during his reign we find his adoptive
praenomen and nomen still appearing along with the nomen “Sulpicius”
and the cognomen ‘“Galba," e.g. in C.I.G. iii 4957 he is styled Λούκιος Λίβιος
Σεβαστός (= Augustus) Σουλπίκιος Γάλβα(ς) αὐτοκράτωρ (= imperator); so too on
Alexandrian coins, Λουκ. Λιβ. Σουλπ. Γάλβα(ς) Καισ. Σεβ. αὐτ. (see Prosop.
Imp. Rom. iii p. 285). Hofstee suggests that these inscriptions may have
been cut and the coins struck before it was known that the emperor had
discarded his adoptive names.

Augustum puero adhuc dixisse: Suetonius differs from Tacitus, Dio,
and Josephus in attributing this prophecy to Augustus and not to Tiberius.
Tacitus (A. vi 20) says: Non omiserim praesagium Tiberii de Servio Galba
tum (33 A.D.) consule; quem accitum et diversis sermonibus pertemptatum
postremo Graecis verbis in hanc sententiam adlocutus est: "et tu, Galba,
quandoque degustabis imperium,” seram ac brevem potentiam significans,
scientia Chaldaeorum artis, cuius apiscendae otium apud Rhodum, magistrum Thrasullum habuit. Dio (lvii 19) relates the prediction as made by
Tiberius to Galba at the time of his betrothal: οὕτω δ᾽ οὖν τὸ πεπρωμένον
ἑκάστῳ τῶν πρώτων καὶ ἐξήταζε καὶ ἠπίστατο ὥστε καὶ τῷ Γάλβα τῷ μετὰ ταῦτα
αὐταρχήσαντι ἀπαντήσας, γυναῖκα ἐγγεγυημένῳ, εἰπεῖν ὅτι “καὶ σύ ποτες τῆς
ἡγεμονίας γεύσῃ." Josephus (Antiq. xviii 6) cites it as a remark of Tiberius to
his intimates when he saw Galba come in to him: Γάλβαν οὖν ποτὲ θεασάμενος
ὡς αὐτὸν εἰσιόντα, φησὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιτηδειοτάτους αὐτῷ, ὡς παραγίνοιτο ἀνὴρ τῇ
῾Ῥωμαίων ποτὲ προτιμησόμενος ἡγεμονίᾳ.
salutanti: for the imperial receptions (salutationes) see on Vesp. 4, 4.

apprehensa buccula: this may mean merely that Augustus took hold of
his cheek; cf. Ap. Rhod. Arg. iii 128 (where Aphrodite is coaxing her young
son Eros), γναθμοῖο κατασχομένη προσέειπε. Most commentators think that
there is a reference to the peculiar method of kissing children by placing
one's fingers on their lips or on their cheek and then withdrawing the
fingers and placing them on one's own lips; cf. Apul. Met. vi 22, Iuppiter
prehensa Cupidinis buccula manuque ad os suum relata consaviat: Suet.
Aug. 94, 8, quasi Iuppiter
eius (pueri) osculum delibatum digitis ad
os suum rettulisset: Serv. on Aen. i 260 (oscula libavit natae), Sane multi
nolunt ita intellegi, ut summum osculum filiae dederit, id est, non pressum,
sed summa labella contingens; sed ita aiunt: tum hilaris Iuppiter vultus
natae libavit, id est, contigit, scilicet ut nos solemus cum blandimentis quibusdam sinistram maxillam contingere liberorum et deinde ad os nostrum
referre.
παρατρώξῃ : = degustabis. παρατρώγειν means "to nibble at the side," "take a
bite of" (Aristoph. Ran. 988, Pax 415); used metaph. in Philostrat. 595, παρατρώγειν δικῶν τε καὶ δικαστηρίων. Aristophanes also uses περιτρώγειν (e.g. Vesp. 672,
σὺ δὲ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἀγαπᾶς τῆς σῆς τοὺς ἀργελόφους περιτρώγων) and ἀποτρώγειν
(Ran. 367, τοὺς μισθοὺς τῶν ποιητῶν . . ἀποτρώγει).

sed et: as sed et is used after non modo, non solum, etc., so it is used
fairly frequently in Silver and late Lat. with a cumulative or intensive
force ("and what is more,” “aye, and") even when non modo, etc., are
omitted. See the examples cited by Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii² 109. Suetonius
is fond of this use; e.g. Aug. 31, 3, sacerdotum et numerum et dignitatem,
sed et commoda auxit. He several times (as here) begins a sentence or
clause with sed et when introducing a further instance or confirmation in
development of what he has previously said; cf. Vitell. 14, 3: Vesp. 19, 1:
19, 2: Dom. 13, 1.
Cicero uses sed etiam with an ellipse of non solum,
e.g. Att. iii 15, 5, hic mihi primum meum consilium defuit, sed etiam
ob fuit.

Vivat ad nos nihil pertinet: a very similar utterance is attributed
to Caracallus by Capitolinus (Maxim. Iun. c. 4): Nec defuerunt qui
cavendum infantem (Maximinum) dicerent Caracallo. Tum ille dixit
"longe est ut mihi iste succedat." Dio (lvii 17) conjectures that Tiberius
spared Galba because Galba's fate had so ordained it, but adds that
Tiberius' own explanation was that Galba would reign only in old age
and long after his own death.
§2. Avo: C. Sulpicius Galba, the historian (c. 3, 3).

fulgur procuranti: procurare was a technical term for averting by
prayer, sacrifice, etc., the evil effects of portents of all kinds, especially
lightning and thunderbolts; cf. Val. Max. i 1, 1, sacrificio ostentorum ac
fulgurum denuntiationes procurantur. The ars fulminum, derived by the
Romans from the Etruscans and their libri fulgurales, was divided into
exploratio, interpretatio, and exoratio (Sen. N.Q. ii 32, 2). procuratio
and expiatio are often used as synonyms of exoratio. Part of the procuratio
carried out by the fulgurator, or lightning-interpreter, was to encircle the
place which had been struck by lightning with a stone curb (puteal) and
to make sacrifices of sheep (bidentes; hence bidental = puteal).

frugiferam quercum: the portent probably occurred in the autumn;
the eagle flew to the top of the oak, showing the height to which Galba
would attain; the oak was already bearing acorns, which foretold that
Galba would only obtain the empire in his old age (he was in his 73rd year
when he became emperor).

cum mula pepererit: a proverbial expression, like our "when pigs fly";
cf. Plin. N.H. viii 173, Observatum
mulas non parere. Est in annalibus
nostris peperisse saepe, verum prodigii loco habitum: Cic. Div. ii 22, 49,
mulae partus prolatus a te: res mirabilis, quia non saepe fit; ii 28, 61,
saepius enim mulam peperisse arbitror quam sapientem fuisse: Juv. xiii 64,
egregium sanctumque virum si cerno, ... fetae comparo mulae. In Hdt. iii
151 a Babylonian says jeeringly that the Persians would take Babylon
“ ἐπεὰν ἡμίονοι τέκωσι” (cf. Hdt. vii 57; Arist. H.A. vi 24; ausc. mirab. 70).

confirmavit mulae partus: Dio lxiv 1, ἡμίονός τε ἔτεκεν, ὅπερ αὐτῷ
(i.e. Galba) σύμβολον τοῦ κράτους ἔσεσθαι ἐτεθέσπιστο.

ut obscaenum ostentum: Livy (xxvi 23, xxxvii 3) mentions “mulam
peperisse" among "prodigia maioribus hostiis procurata." Walde derives
obscaenus from *obs- (ob) and caenum "filth"; it was regularly used in
the sense of "inauspicious," cf. Paulus (Fest. p. 201 Müll.), apud antiquos
omnes fere obscaena dicta sunt, quae mali ominis habebantur: Cic. dom. 55,
140, obscaenum omen: Verg. Aen. xii 876, obscaenae volucres.

abhorrentibus: here c. acc., as in Aug. 83, Vitell. 10, 3; Suetonius is
the first to use this constr. (Cic. Cluent. 14, 41 is not an example, see
Peterson's note). Suetonius also uses abhorrere a re (Ner. 43, 1: Dom. 9, 1),
and employs the verb impersonally in Tib. 62, 3, Calig. 12, 3, abhorret a
vero, a veritate.

§ 3. sumpta virili toga: see on Vesp. 2, 2. Dio (lvi 29) says that it
was on Jan. 1, 14 A.D. that Galba assumed the toga virilis (ἐς τοὺς ἐφήβους
ἐνεγράφη), and that some afterwards regarded it as a remarkable coincidence
that Augustus died in this year and that Galba was the first to become
emperor after the family of Augustus died out with Nero.
See

somniavit Fortunam dicentem: Suetonius here extends to somniare
the same construction (predicative pres. part.) as is commonly found with
“verba videndi, audiendi, fingendi, etc." (Kühner-Stegmann, i 703). Не
varies the constr. in c. 18, 2, somniavit speciem Fortunae querentis.
also on Dom. 15, 3, Minervam
somniavit excedere negantemque. The
same dream of Galba's is narrated in Dio lxiv 1, την τε γὰρ Τύχην ἔδοξεν
αὐτῷ λέγειν ὅτι χρόνον ἤδη συχνὸν αὐτῷ παραμένοι καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς αὐτὴν ἐς τὴν οἰκίαν
αὐτοῦ ἐσδέχοιτο, καὶ δὴ ἐὰν ἐπὶ πλεῖον εἰρχθῇ, πρὸς ἕτερόν τινα μεταστήσεται,

stare defessam: prob. "tired of standing"; for the infin. instead of
the abl. ger. cf. Plaut. Epid. 719, ego sum defessus reperire, vos defessi
quaerere: Lucr. v 1145, genus humanum defessum vi colere aevom.

ocius: "at once,'' cf. Iul. 68, 2, ocius amoveri; in Cic. ocius has always
a comparative sense "more quickly," but the meaning "at once" is
common in colloquial Lat. and in poetry.

cuicumque: the use of quicumque in the sense of quivis, quilibet (cf,
Vitell. 14, 1; Vesp. 8, 5) is frequent in Livy (see Riemann, La Langue de
Tite-Live 178 sq.) and post-Aug. writers. Cic. and Caes. nearly always use
quicumque as a rel. with a verb expressed, except in the abl., e.g. quacumque ratione, quocumque modo; there are only a couple of examples in Cic.
of the indefinite use in cases other than the abl. (Madvig, Cic. Fin.,
Excursus vi p. 834).
evigilavit: in the sense of expergisci this verb is post-Aug.

simulacrum: this image is mentioned again in c. 18, 2, in connexion
with the omens of Galba's downfall.

cubitali: sc. simulacro; cf. Plin. N.H. viii 73, maiora cubitalibus
cornua habens: xxii 86, frutex est nunquam cubitali altior.

Tusculum: in Latium, about 15 miles from Rome on the Via Latina,
mod. Frascati and Il Tuscolo; a favourite site for the villas of the wealthy
Romans, e.g. Cicero, Julius Caesar, and Tiberius.
aestivare: see on Vesp. 24.

in parte aedium: this use of parte without a defining adjective is
strange, and Boissevain suggested in <prima > parte (i.e. atrio), comparing Nep. praef. 6, Sen. Bem. iii 28, Val. Max. v 8, 3. Under subsequent
emperors we find a golden statue of Fortuna which was kept in the
imperial bedchamber and was transferred by each emperor to his successor;
cf. Capitol. Anton. Pius 12, cum se gravari videret, Marco Antonino rem
publicam commendavit, Fortunamque auream, quae in cubiculo principum poni solebat, transferri ad eum iussit: Capitol. Marc. Anton.
Philos. 7: Spartian. Sev. 23. The goddess Fortuna figures on the coins of
Galba (Cohen, Méd. Imp. i² pp. 323, 343).

pervigilio: these all-night vigils (παννυχίδες) for religious purposes
were unknown to the primitive worship of the Romans but were introduced
along with the Greek and oriental religions of which they were so prominent
a feature, and they came to be celebrated in Italy with no less licentiousness
than in Greece. The nightly ceremonies which formed part of such rites
as those of the Bona Dea, Bacchus, Isis, Ceres, Adonis, and Sabazius often.
developed into mere orgies and were the occasion of grave scandals (Cic.
Leg. ii 14 sq.). Cf. Vitell. 10, 3.
§ 4. quanquam: see on Tit. 7, 2.

aetate constanti: settled age" "middle age," ἡ καθεστηκυία ἡλικία:
cf. Cic. Sen. 20, 76, ea constans iam aetas, quae media dicitur.
exoletum: cf. Claud. 22, aut exoleta revocavit, aut etiam nova instituit:
Aug. 86, 2, exoletas et reconditas voces aucupari. Cicero prefers obsoletus.
See also on c. 22. The custom mentioned here is not referred to by other
writers.

salvere.. valere: the ordinary morning salutation was either salve or
ave (= χαῖρε); the farewell at the end of day was vale (= ὑγίαινε or ἔρρωσο).
The person so addressed replied salve et tu (καὶ σὺ χαῖρε) or vale et tu
(καὶ σὺ ὑγίαινε).

liberales disciplinas: cf. Ner. 52, liberales disciplinas omnes fere puer
attigit: Calig. 53, 1, ex disciplinis liberalibus minimum eruditioni,
eloquentiae plurimum attendit: Claud. 3, 1, disciplinis liberalibus ab aetate
prima non mediocrem operam dedit: Dom. 20, liberalia studia imperii
initio neglexit: Aug. 84, 1, eloquentiam studiaque liberalia ab aetate prima
et cupide et laboriosissime exercuit. Under liberales disciplinae were included rhetoric, philosophy, music, poetry, jurisprudence, etc.; cf. Cic. de
or. iii 32, 127, has artes, quibus liberales doctrinae atque ingenuae continerentur, geometriam, musicam, litterarum cognitionem et poetarum.

attendit iuri: attendere (προσέχειν), when used absolutely (without
animum), takes the acc. in class. Lat., but Vitruvius and later writers use
it also with the dat. This is the only construction found in Suetonius;
cf. Calig. 53, 1 (quoted above), Ner. 56, attendit et extispicio.

dedit matrimonio operam: in the general laxity of morals which
prevailed at Rome matrimony was regarded as a troublesome business, an
onerous duty to be undertaken by loyal citizens in the interest of the state.

Lepida: not mentioned by name elsewhere, but she was probably
the daughter of Manius Aemilius Lepidus, proconsul of Asia in 26-7 A.D.
(Tac. A. iv 56), who excused himself from accepting the proconsulship of
Africa in 21 A.D. on the ground that he had to arrange for the marriage
of a "nubilis filia” (Tac. A. iii 35).
quatenus sibi

remansit in caelibatu: cf. Claud. 26, 2, confirmavit
matrimonia male cederent, permansurum se in caelibatu. Widowers, as
well as bachelors, were described as “caelibes.”

condicione: condicio (uxoria) was used for a marriage-proposal and the
attendant negotiations, an alliance or match, and sometimes (by metonymy)
for the person to be married; cf. Iul. 27, 1, Octaviam condicionem ei
detulit: Aug. 63, 2, multis ac diu, etiam ex equestri ordine, circumspectis
condicionibus, Tiberium privignum suum legit: Cic. Lael. 34, dirimi
(amores) tamen interdum contentione vel uxoriae condicionis vel commodi
alicuius: Plin. Ep. i 10, inter altissimas condiciones, generum non honoribus
principem, sed sapientia, elegit.

Agrippinae: daughter of Germanicus, married first (in 28 A.D.) to
Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus to whom she bore a son Nero, afterwards
emperor; immediately after the death of Domitius in 40 A.D. she was
banished by her own brother Caligula (Ner. 6), but was recalled from
exile on the accession of Claudius in 41; shortly afterwards she married
Crispus Passienus and was believed to have murdered him; later (in 51)
she married her uncle, the emperor Claudius, such a union being legalised
by a special senatus-consultum. For her death see on Oth. 3,1. Dalmasso
takes Agrippinae here as dative of the agent, but it is the gen. after
condicione; cf. Claud. 26, 3, nec durare valuit quin de condicionibus continuo tractaret, etiam de Paetinae, quam olim exegerat, deque Lolliae
Paulinae, quae C. Caesari nupta fuerat.

viduatae: M and G have viduata, which is read by Ihm who follows
Becker in inserting quae before viduata. The relative, which in n and Q
comes after Domitii, is omitted in the other MSS.
Domitii: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus; see on Oth. 2, 1.

conventu matronarum: at Rome from ancient times there was a conventus matronarum, apparently a guild of religious origin, of which little
is known. Assemblies of matrons are mentioned in Liv. v 25, xxvii 37.
Seneca (De Matrimon. ed. Haase iii p. 428) describes how a husband has
to listen to his wife's nightlong reproaches: per noctes totas garrulae
conquestiones “illa ornatior procedit in publicum, haec honoratur ab
omnibus, ego in conventu feminarum misella despicior." The guild had
its curia or meeting-place on the Quirinal and perhaps another in Trajan's
Forum. It met for certain festivals, also when a bride through her
marriage entered the class of consulares feminae. Elagabalus built a
senate-house (senaculum) for it on the Quirinal, and this feminine senate
decided a number of points of etiquette: “quae quo vestitu incederet,
quae cui cederet, etc." (Lamprid. Heliogab. 4). Aurelian seems to have
restored its old religious character by assigning the highest position in it
to those who had been priestesses (Vopisc. Aurel. 49). See Friedlaender,
Sittengeschichte i¹º 282: Daremberg-Saglio, Dict. Antiq. iii 1660.
observant.

§ 2. observavit: for observare “to show respect to” (θεραπεύειν) cf.
Tib. 70, 1, quem senem adulescens observaverat: Cic. Att. ii 19, Caecilium
colimus et observamus diligenter: Verg. G. iv 210, regem
The reverence of Galba for Livia Augusta is shown by his coins with her
image and the legend Augusta or Diva Augusta (Eckhel, Doctrina numorum
veterum, vi pp. 292-3).

Liviam Augustam: i.e. Livia Drusilla, wife of Augustus; see on c. 1, 1.
By the will of Augustus she was adopted into the Julian family and
received the title of Augusta: Tac. A. i 8, Livia in familiam Iuliam nomenque Augustum adsumebatur. After this adoption Tacitus always speaks
of her as "Augusta” or “Iulia Augusta"; Suetonius has "Iulia Augusta"
in Calig. 16, 3, and "Augusta" in Claud. 3, 2, but inaccurately styles
her "Livia Augusta'' here and in Oth. 1, 1; Calig. 10, 1; 15, 2; 23, 2.

plurimum valuit: according to Plutarch (Galb. 3) he owed to her his
consulship (see on c. 2, 1), but this is doubtful, since Livia died in 29 A.D.
and Galba was not consul till 33 (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii p. 285).

namque: this is the only instance in Suetonius of namque occupying
the second place, as in Varro ap. Gell. iii 10, is namque numerus, and
frequently in Livy and Quintilian; in Cic. and Caes. it always begins the
sentence (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 109).

quingenties: sc. centena milia, 50,000,000 sesterces, about £425,000.
Casaubon regarded this sum as incredibly large, and would read quinquagies,
i.e. 5,000,000.

praecipuum: here used as a subst. denoting a first charge on an estate,
what is taken from it before the general distribution of the assets, the
adj. being often used in this sense in legal writers, e.g. praecipua dos (Ulp.
Dig. xxxiii 4, 2); cf. Sidon. Apoll. Ep. vi 12, illud autem deberi tibi
quodam, ut iurisconsulti dicunt, praecipui titulo. In Plin. Ep. v 7 we find
praecipere 'to take preferentially and praeceptio “a preferential legacy."

legatarios: "legatees"; a word apparently first used here but common
in the later legal writers.
=
500,000 sesterces and

notata: i.e. merely marked in figures or symbols and not written fully
in words; the difference between HS D
HSD = 50,000,000 sesterces is very slight.
quingenta: sc. sestertia; 500,000 sesterces.

revocante: this use of revocare in the sense of reducing is remarkable,
and no other example is cited; Suetonius elsewhere uses the normal redigere
ad or recidere ad. For the aoristic use of the present participle (= cum
revocasset) see Appendix I. § 10. b.

ne haec quidem accepit: Tiberius suppressed the will of his mother
Livia and paid none of the legacies; cf. Dio lix 1, οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνης
διαθηκῶν ἀπήλλαξεν. Suetonius (Calig. 16, 3) says that Caligula paid these
legacies and those under Tiberius' own will (though it had been set aside)
faithfully and without dispute: legata ex testamento Tiberi quanquam.
abolito, sed et Iuliae Augustae, quod Tiberius suppresserat, cum fide ac
sine calumnia repraesentata persolvit.

ante legitimum tempus: Augustus issued an ordinance determining the
conditions and sequence of the magistracies in the cursus honorum.
The young Roman, before holding the first of these magistracies, the
quaestorship, had to qualify himself by a term in one of the departments
of the vigintivirate (decemviri stlitibus iudicandis, quattuorviri viarum
curandarum, triumviri capitales, triumviri monetales) and by some brief
military experience, generally as tribunus militum; the earliest age for the
quaestorship was 25; a year must elapse between this and the next magistracy, the tribuneship of the plebs (or the curule aedileship), and between
either of these offices and the praetorship, and a period of two years
between the praetorship (minimum age 30 years) and the consulship (minimum age 32). The restriction of attaining a certain age for an office or
waiting for a certain period between offices could be removed by the candidate being father of three children (ius trium liberorum) or by special grace
of the emperor. See Mommsen, Staatsr. I³ 572 sqq.

praetor
edidit: under the Republic the aediles (first appointed in
366 в.с.) were gradually given control of all the games except the Ludi
Apollinares and Piscatorii which were in the charge of the praetors. In
22 B.C. Augustus transferred the cura ludorum to the praetors, assigning
to them the management of all games and spectacles (Dio liv 2, τοῖς μὲν·
στρατηγοῖς τὰς πανηγύρεις πάσας προσέταξεν). We find references to the
praetors administering the Ludi Megalenses (Juv. xi 193), Florales (Dio
lxxviii 3), the Augustalia (Tac. A. i 15), gladiatorial shows (Dio lv 31), etc..
See Mommsen, op. cit. ii³ 237.
comcommissione: the regular word for the opening of the games.
mittere (like συμβάλλειν, συνιέναι) meant to bring men together (in a hostile
sense), to set them to fight; it was used primarily of pitting or matching
gladiators in the arena, and then more widely of starting a contest or games
of any kind; cf. Ner. 23, 1, commisit musicum agona: Claud. 21, 1, ludos
dedicationis Pompeiani theatri e tribunali posito in orchestra commisit.

ludorum Floralium: the Floralia or Ludi Florales were a festival first
celebrated in 238 B.c., when in consequence of a dearth a temple was dedicated to Flora ad Circum Maximum; it was made an annual festival
(Apr. 28-May 3) under the charge of the aediles in 173 B.c., and consisted
mainly of theatrical performances, especially by mimi, accompanied by
drinking and licentious merrymaking; cf. Cic. Verr. v 14, 36: Val. Max.
ii 10, 8: Sen. Ep. 97: Mart. i 35. The games concluded with the coursing
of hares and roes in the Circus Maximus (Ov. Fast. v 371). See Warde
Fowler, Roman Festivals 92 sqq.

elephantos funambulos: an elephant on tight ropes was a feature of
the spectacles of Nero; cf. Ner. 11, 2, notissimus eques Romanus elephanto
supersidens per catadromum decucurrit (a performance more clearly described by Dio, lxi 17, who says that an elephant which had been brought
up to the top of the theatre ran down stretched ropes with a rider on its
back: ἐλέφας ἀνήχθη ἐς τὴν ἀνωτάτω τοῦ θεάτρου ἁψίδα καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐπὶ σχοινίων
κατέδραμεν ἀναβάτην φέρων). Pliny (N.H. viii 3) marvels at such elephants:
mirum maxime et adversis quidem funibus subire, sed regredi magis utique
pronis; Seneca also mentions them (Ερ. 85, 41): elephantem minimus
Aethiops iubet subsidere in genua et ambulare per funem. Numerous references to the rope-walker (funambulus, schoenobates, σχοινοβάτης) are
collected by Mayor on Juv. xiv 272.

provinciae Aquitaniae
praefuit: as a legatus Augusti pro praetore,
probably in 31 or 32 A.D. (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 285). Augustus divided
Gallia into four provinces: Narbonensis, Aquitania, Lugdunensis, and
Belgica. In 22 B.c. he assigned Narbonensis to the senate, while the others
remained under imperial legati. Aquitania was in Southern Gaul, between
the Loire and the Pyrenees.
anno: for the ablative of duration of time see App. I § 3. D. b.

consulatum ordinarium: for the distinction between consules ordinarii
and consules suffecti and the period for which the office was held see note
on Dom. 2, 1. Galba was consul in 33 A.D.

L. Domitio: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus; see on c. 5, 1: Oth. 2, 1. The
praenomen “Lucius" instead of "Gnaeus" is a slip on the part of
Suetonius or the copyists. "Lucius" was the praenomen of his father
(cons. 16 в.с.). Torrentius corrected L. to Cn.; Ihm suggests as an alternative the deletion of L.
Salvius Otho pater Othonis: see Oth. 1, 2; as consul suffectus he succeeded Galba in the consulship on the Kalends of July, 33 A.D.

§ 2. Gaio Caesare: i.e. Caligula, who reigned from 37 to 41. Galba's
appointment was made in 39.
८

<in locum Gaetulici substitutus: a conjectural restoration by Roth,
which is adopted by Preud'homme; in the MSS. there is a lacuna between
in locum
Caesare and lici (al, licio, licis, liciis, lice). Ihm reads <.....
Gaetulici, suggesting legatus Germaniae superioris in locum Gaetu>lici.
Madvig, who regarded Roth's method of filling the gap as inadequate, proposed <in administratione exercitus Germanici in locum Gaetulici. Earlier
readings are Gartulico (Stephanus, Turnebus) and Gaetulici vice (Heinsius).

Gaetulici: Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus, who inherited the cognomen "Gaetulicus" received by his father Cossus Cornelius Lentulus
Gaetulicus for victories over the Gaetuli in Africa in 6 A.D. He was consul
in 26 A.D., and afterwards commanded the legions in Upper Germany for
ten years, the mildness of his discipline making him immensely popular:
mirum amorem adsecutus erat, effusae clementiae, modicus severitate (Tac.
A. vi. 30). His daughter was betrothed to Sejanus, and it was generally
believed that Tiberius would have had him condemned along with the other
connexions of Sejanus at the latter's downfall, had he not feared a revolt
of the legions in Germany (Tac. l.c.). Caligula put him to death in 39 A.D.,
charging him with conspiracy and currying favour with the army (Dio lix
22, Suet. Claud. 9). As an epigrammatist he is mentioned in Mart. i praef.;
Plin. Εp. v 3, 5. From the fact that in Suet. Calig. 8 he is cited as an
authority on the birthplace of Caligula he is supposed to have written
history (see Peter, Hist. Rom. Frag. p. 291).

tessera: the tessera militaris (σύμβολον) had two uses: (1) to make
known to the soldiers the password; (2) to circulate any orders of the
general as to intended movements, etc.; for this latter use cf. Liv. ix 32
quod postquam consuli nuntiatum est, extemplo tesseram dari iubet, ut
prandeat miles firmatisque cibo viribus arma capiat: Liv. vii 35, xxvii 46:
Sil. Ital. vii 347, discurrit tessera castris | intentique docent quae sint
properanda, monentque | quisque suos: xv 475.

ut manus paenula continerent: a reading introduced by Salmasius, the
MSS. varying between manus paenulas, manus paenulis, and manu paenulas.
The paenula was a sleeveless cloak of frieze or leather drawn on over the
head and worn by all classes in bad weather or when travelling; its use
by soldiers is mentioned in Ner. 49: Sen. Ben. v 24, 1. In its ordinary
form it prevented any free movement of the arms (cf. paenulatus = paenula
irretitus, Cic. Mil. 10) and in a couple of the very few representations on
monuments of soldiers wearing the paenula (and not the sagum) there are
openings for one or both arms. See Baumeister, Denkmäler p. 1836:
Marquardt, Privatl.2 564 sqq.: Smith, Dict. Ant. ii³ 308.
Disce
...

Gaetulicus: a trochaic tetrameter catalectic or trochaic
septenarius (IC/II/IC/IC/II/II/IC/C), which was a favourite
metre for the soldier's ditties; cf. the very free lines on Caesar's immorality
which were shouted by his soldiers in the licence of his Gallic triumph,
Iul. 51: “Urbani, servate uxores; moechum calvum adducimus. | Aurum
in Gallia effutuisti, hic sumpsisti mutuum"; ib. 49, "Gallias Caesar
subegit, Nicomedes Caesarem: | ecce Caesar nunc triumphat qui subegit
Gallias, | Nicomedes non triumphat qui subegit Caesarem.”

§ 3. interdixit peti: the infin. for the usual ne c. subj.; the dat.
and infin. are found in Sen. Vit. Beat. 18, 3, cum sibi interdixerit habere,
interdixit et poscere. (Ter. Phorm. 708 is wrongly cited by L. and S. as
an example of interdicere with infin.).

commeatus: among the abuses in the army at this period was the
improper granting of furlough, the soldiers being able to purchase from
the centurions exemption from duties (vacatio munerum) and leave of
absence (see Tac. H. i 46, A. i 17); weak commanders allowed the legions
to be depleted by grants of furlough and this at times led to disaster, e.g.
the defeat of Paetus by the Parthians in 62 A.D. (legiones promiscis militum
commeatibus infirmaverat, Tac. A. xv 9).

barbaris
coercitis: Galba was victorious over the Chatti (see on
Dom. 6, 1) in 41 A.D.; Dio lx 8, τούτῳ τῷ ἔτει ὁ Γάλβας ὁ Σουλπίκιος Χάττους
ἐκράτησε. His distinguished command of the army in Germany is mentioned in Plut. Galb. 3, λέγεται δὲ καὶ στρατεύματος ἐν Γερμανίᾳ καλῶς ἄρξαι :
Tac. H. i 49, dum vigebat aetas, militari laude apud Germanias floruit.

praesenti Gaio approbavit: for Caligula's expedition to Germany
in 39 A.D. see on Vesp. 2, 3. On that campaign the emperor posed as a
stern disciplinarian; cf. Calig. 44, 1, postquam castra attigit, ut se acrem
et severum ducem ostenderet, legatos, qui auxilia serius ex diversis locis
adduxerant, cum ignominia dimisit. At in exercitu recensendo, plerisque
centurionum maturis iam, et nonnullis ante paucissimos, quam consummaturi
essent, dies, primos pilos ademit, causatus senium cuiusque et imbecillitatem:
ceterorum increpita cupiditate, commoda emeritae militiae ad sex milium
summam recidit.
..

innumeras copias: Calig. 43, legionibus et auxiliis undique excitis,
dilectibus ubique acerbissime actis, contracto et omnis generis commeatu,
quanto numquam antea, iter ingressus est. Dio (lix 22) gives the number
as 200,000 or 250,000.

campestrem decursionem: decursus and decursio were terms applied
sometimes to a defile of soldiers under arms on ceremonial occasions
(funerals, etc.), sometimes, as here, to manoeuvres designed to accustom
the soldiers to carry out rapidly long marches in full armour and to keep
their ranks. Vegetius (de arte mil. i 9) says that recruits were trained
to cover in five summer hours (almost 6t of our hours) at an ordinary
marching pace (militari gradu) a distance of 20 milia passuum, and in
the same time at an accelerated pace (pleno gradu, qui citatior est) 24 milia
passuum. Scipio Africanus made his troops execute on every fourth day
a decursio of 4 milia passuum (Liv. xxvi 51); cf. also Liv. xxiii 35, xxiv 48,
xl 6, 47, xlii 52; Tac. A. ii 55). Vegetius calls such manoeuvres campicursio,
See Daremberg-Saglio,
which is the same as campestris decursio here.
ii p. 41.

scuto moderatus: Galba controlled the manoeuvres, marching in front
and bearing the heavy scutum with which he directed the various movements;
cf. Ner. 7, 2, where Nero at the beginning of his public career personally
headed the praetorians at a special command display of manoeuvres: indicta decursione praetorianis scutum sua manu praetulit.

etiam: even after the fatiguing decursio he had energy enough leït
to run for such a long distance by the emperor's chariot.

ad essedum cucurrit: Caligula also made senators in their togas run
by his chariot; Calig. 27, nihilo reverentior leniorve erga senatum: quosdam summis honoribus functos ad essedum sibi currere togatos per aliquot
passuum milia
.. passus est. In 297 A.D. Diocletian treated in the same
humiliating way his son-in-law Galerius, in anger at his defeat by the
Persians; Amm. Marc. xiv 11: Eutrop. ix 15, Galerius pulsus (a Persis)
et ad Diocletianum profectus, cum ei in itinere occurrisset, tanta insolentia
a Diocletiano fertur exceptus, ut per aliquot passuum milia purpuratus
tradatur ad vehiculum cucurrisse. It is mentioned as an indignity inflicted
by Eastern kings in Plut. Lucull. 21.

viginti passuum milia: 20 Roman miles, the Roman mile being 1618
yds., or about 1 of an English mile; the passus was 4 ft. 101 in.

caede Gai: on Jan. 24, 41 A.D. the emperor Gaius (Caligula) was
assassinated by Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus, tribunes of the
praetorian guards, in the vaulted corridor through which he was passing
from the Palace to see the Ludi Palatini (Calig. 58).

ad occasionem: sc. capiendi imperii. Becker proposed ad occasionem
<captandam >.

cohortem amicorum: = comites (Vesp. 4, 4, n.), the companions of the
emperor on a journey or campaign. Horace (Ep. i 3, 6, 8, 14) uses cohors
for the suite of Tiberius who was sent by Augustus to the East in 20 B.c.,
also (Sat. i 7, 23) for the staff of a commander or provincial governor (cf.
cohors praetoria, Cic. Verr. ii 1, 14). The poet Lucan was admitted to
Nero's cohors amicorum (Suet. vit. Lucani). Domitius, father of Nero,
was expelled by Caligula from his cohors amicorum for an outrage committed by him when a comes of Caligula on a journey to the East (Ner. 5).
At one of his pageants Caligula was attended by his cohors amicorum
driving in Gallic chariots (Calig. 19). The amici of the emperor were those
admitted to his receptions (salutationes, see on Vesp. 4, 4); from them
were chosen his judicial and administrative advisers (consilium) as well
as his comites. See also on Tit. 7, 2.

dignationis: dignatio (ἀξίωσις, ἀξίωμα) is used by Suetonius either
passively (as here, Dom. 2, 1 Vesp. 4, 3) or actively (Calig. 24, 3, reliquas
sorores nec cupiditate tanta, nec dignatione dilexit).
nec adeo: see on Oth. 5, 2.

expeditionis Britannicae: see on Vesp. 4, 1. The words of Suetonius
imply that Galba took part in the expedition, though there is no other
evidence of it.

Africam optinuit: his successful administration of Africa is mentioned in Plut. Galb. 3, λέγεται καὶ Λιβύης ἀνθύπατος (proconsul)
γενόμενος σὺν ὀλίγοις ἐπαινεθῆναι: cf. Tac. H. i 49, pro consule Africam
moderate, iam senior citeriorem Hispaniam pari iustitia continuit.
Vespasian and Vitellius also were proconsuls of Africa (Vesp. 4, 3;
Vitell. 5).

biennio: 45 and 46 A.D.; the normal tenure of the governorship of
senatorial provinces was for one year. Julius Caesar had fixed the period
in consular provinces as two years, in praetorian provinces as one (Cic.
Phil. i 8, 19). Augustus restored the period of one year (Suet. Aug. 47,
Dio liii 13, Tac. A. iii 58), but a special appointment like that of Galba
might be renewed for the following year (see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 250 n.,
254 sq.). Dio (lx 25) mentions that Claudius allowed some of the proconsuls
to govern for two years: ἐπὶ δύο ἔτη τινὰς ἐῶν αὐτῶν ἄρχειν, αἱρετούς τε ἔστιν οὓς
πέμπων (αἱρετοí means extra sortem electi, opp. to κληρωτοί). For the tenure
of governorships in imperial provinces see on c. 9, 1.

extra sortem electus: the provinces of Africa and Asia were usually
assigned by lot to the senior consulares; see on c. 3, 4. Galba was specially
appointed to Africa by Claudius, just as the younger Pliny was specially
chosen by Trajan for the administration of Bithynia in 111 A.D. Tiberius
on an earlier occasion had nominated a proconsul for Africa on the outbreak of war with Tacfarinas in 21 A.D.; Tac. A. iii 35, Tiberius.. Manium
Lepidum et Iunium Blaesum nominavit, ex quis pro consule Africae
legeretur; Blaesus was appointed by the senate and continued in office for
a second year (ib. 58).

ordinandam: ordinare = turbatum ordinem restituere; cf. Iul. 40, 1,
ad ordinandum rei publicae statum: Aug. 13, 3, cum Antonius Orientem
ordinandum recepisset: Flor. ii 16: Plin. Ep. viii 24. See also on Vesp.
23, 2.

intestina dissensione: such conflicts as that described by Tacitus (H.
iv 50) between Oea (Tripoli) and Leptis in 70 A.D. See Mommsen, Prov.
Rom. Emp. (trans. Dickson) ii 316.

barbarorum tumultu: the Mussulamii, who earlier had carried on
warfare for eight years (17-24), were again defeated in the reign of
Claudius; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 4, caesa Mussulamiorum manus. Other tribes
which constantly menaced the peace of the Roman province of Africa were
the Garamantes and Gaetuli (genus insuperabile bello, Verg. A. iv 40).
Augustus stationed a legion in Africa, and it was the only senatorial
province with an army. Caligula changed this by putting Numidia and the
Roman legion under an imperial legatus and confining the proconsul's
power to the civil administration of Africa Vetus. If Claudius adhered to
this arrangement, Galba when sent as proconsul to Africa must have been
specially empowered to take command of the army.

§ 2. artissima annona: for arta annona (arta “tight" in the sense of
"scarce'") cf. Tib. 8, cura
annonae, quae artior inciderat: Claud. 18, 2,
artiore annona ob assiduas sterilitates: Liv. xxvi 20; so arti commeatus,
Liv. ii 34: Tac. H. iv 26.

modium centum denariis vendidisse: the modius ( of a medimnus)
was nearly our “peck” (1 of a bushel); the denarius was worth about
9d. Similar avariciousness on the part of starving soldiers is described in
Luc. iv 93 sqq. (where Caesar's army surrounded by floods near Ilerda in
Spain was suffering from famine): iamque comes semper magnorum prima
malorum | saeva fames aderat: nulloque obsessus ab hoste | miles eget; toto
censu non prodigus emit | exiguam Cererem. Pro lucri pallida tabes! | non
deest prolato ieiunus venditor auro. A famous example of the same thing
was the sale of a mouse for 200 denarii during the siege of Casilinum (near
Capua) by Hannibal in 215 в.с.; Plin. N.H. viii 222, venisse murem ducentis
denariis, Casilinum obsidente Hannibale, eumque qui vendiderat fame interiisse, emptorem vixisse annales tradunt (cf. Val. Max. vii 6, 3;
Frontin. Strateg. iv 5, 20; Strab. v 248).

extabuit: cf. the iambic senarius quoted by Cicero (Tusc. iii 12):
Refugere oculi, corpus macie extabuit.
at: see on Vesp. 5, 5.
in iure dicendo: see on c. 9, 2, conventum agens.

proprietate: this seems to be the earliest instance of the use of proprietas in the sense of ownership" (dominium). In Cic. it means "id
quod proprium alicuius rei est," a peculiar property or special quality.

adaquari: adaquare (ποτίζειν) is a post-Aug. verb, used of watering
plants in Plin. N.H. xvii 63, etc. A deponent adaquari "to fetch water"
is given by the MSS. in Caes. B.C. i 66, but the reading is very doubtful,
as in six other passages in that work (and in Sall., Liv., etc.) the simple
aquari is the form used of soldiers getting water.
ornamenta triumphalia: see on Vesp. 4, 2.

sacerdotium triplex: Vitellius was honoured in the same way, Vitell. 5,
non solum honoribus verum et sacerdotiis amplissimis auctus; Vespasian
received a duplex sacerdotium in addition to the ornamenta triumphalia
for his services in Britain (Vesp. 4, 2).

quindecimviros: the care of the Sibylline books was originally entrusted
to duumviri under the kings; in 367 B.C. the number of priests was increased to 10, five patrician and five plebeian, later to 15 (quindecimviri
sacris faciundis) probably by Sulla; in addition to consulting the Sibylline
books as directed by the senate, they also had charge of the games of
Apollo (Liv. x 8) and the Secular games (Hor. C.S. 70, Tac. A. xi 11), and
as priests of Apollo each of them kept in his house a bronze tripod
dedicated to the god (Val. Fl. Arg. i 6).
sodales Titios: the origin of this ancient confraternity is obscure.
Tacitus (H. ii 95) says that Romulus founded it in honour of the Sabine
king Titus Tatius: Augustales,
quod sacerdotium, ut Romulus Tatio
regi, ita Caesar Tiberius Iuliae genti sacravit. In A. i 54 Tac. gives
another version: idem annus (14 A.D.) novas caerimonias accepit addito
sodalium Augustalium sacerdotio, ut quondam Titus Tatius retinendis
Sabinorum sacris sodales Titios instituit. The view that Tatius founded
this priesthood at Rome to preserve his native Sabine rites is supported
by Varr. L.L. v 85, sodales Titii dicti ab Titiis avibus, quas in auguriis
certis observare solent, the priests preserving the ancient Sabine auguries,
as distinct from those of other Italian peoples, when the Sabines as the
Tities or Titienses were united with the other two tribes, the Ramnes and
Luceres, under Romulus. Augustus revived this priesthood and invested
it with great dignity; in the Monum. Ancyr. (i 7) he mentions that he
was ἑταῖρος Τίτιος. Nero Caesar (son of Germanicus) and the emperor
Claudius were among the sodales Titii. See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 446 sq.;
Daremberg-Saglio, v 347.

item: often used by Suetonius merely in the sense of et or etiam, and
in enumerations he has it alternating with et, e.g. Iul. 43, 1, lecticarum
usum item conchyliatae vestis et margaritarum
ademit: Aug. 4, 1,
superstitibus liberis Octavia maiore et Octavia minore item Augusto.

Augustales: a sacerdotium instituted by Tiberius for the worship of
Augustus and the Gens Iulia; see Tac. A. i 54, H. ii 95 (quoted above).
Originally there were 21 members “e primoribus civitatis" and Tiberius,
Drusus, Claudius, and Germanicus were added ‘“supra numerum” as honorary
members; afterwards the number rose to 28. When the cultus of Claudius
(after his deification) was added, they are called at times sodales Augustales
Claudiales. For similar priesthoods in honour of other emperors see note
on “collegium Flavialium,” Dom. 4, 4.

cooptatus: the great priestly bodies, such as the Augures and Pontifices,
at first filled vacancies in their number by cooptatio, but by the Lex Domitia
(103 в.с.) the comitia sacerdotum (17 out of the 35 tribes, chosen by lot)
were given the election from a list of nominees supplied by the colleges;
the candidates elected were then coopted by the colleges, this cooptatio,
though now a mere formality, being necessary to complete the election.
From the time of Tiberius these elections, like those of magistrates, were
transferred to the senate. In 29 B.C. Augustus was given the right of
choosing as many priests as he pleased even beyond the statutory number.
As a member of the various colleges the emperor had the right of nominatio,
and also exercised the right of commendatio which was tantamount to
appointment, the candidate recommended by the emperor being elected by
the senate and then coopted by the priestly bodies, e.g. Pliny was recommended by Trajan for the augurship (Plin. Εp. iv 8).

in secessu vixit: Vespasian passed a like period of retirement, through
fear of Agrippina, between his consulship (51 A.D.) and proconsulship
(63 A.D.); Vesp. 4, 2, medium tempus ad proconsulatum usque in otio
secessuque egit.
=

ne ad gestandum quidem: ne gestationis quidem causâ; for the
passive use of gestandum see on Dom. 11, 1, and for the gestatio see on
Vesp. 21.

umquam iter ingressus, quam ut efferret: it is perhaps possible
with Hofstee to defend the ellipse of aliter here by the ellipse of aliud
in Claud. 10, commilitones fluctuantes nec quicquam adhuc quam frementes.
Torrentius inserted aliter before iter, where it would easily have fallen
out; Casaubon would read aliter ingressus (omitting iter), and Lipsius
suggested aliter egressus (sc. domo).
lemma: umquam iter ingressus, quam ut efferret

text: decies: sc. centena milia, 1,000,000 sesterces, about £8,500.

in auro: for this use of in cf. Tib. 49, 2, quod partem rei familiaris
in pecunia haberent. In case of sudden flight Galba had provided himself
with 10,000 aurei (aureus = 100 sestertii, see on c. 20, 2).

Fundis: see on c. 4, 1.
Hispania Tarraconensis: under Augustus Spain was formed into three
provinces, Hispania Ulterior being divided into the two provinces of Baetica
and Lusitania, and Hispania Citerior receiving the name of Tarraconensis
from Tarraco (mod. Tarragona), which was made the capital instead of
New Carthage. Baetica was a senatorial province, Lusitania and Tarraconensis imperial provinces.

oblata est: Plutarch (Galb. 3) says that Nero anticipated no danger
to himself in appointing Galba to Spain: ἐπέμφθη δὲ ὑπὸ Νέρωνος Ιβηρίας
ἄρχων, οὔπω δεδιδαγμένου φοβεῖσθαι τοὺς ἐν ἀξιώμασι μεγάλους τῶν πολιτῶν. ἐκείνῳ
δὲ καὶ φύσει δοκοῦντι πράῳ γεγονέναι προσετίθει πίστιν εὐλαβείας τὸ γῆρας. Galba
was 65 years old when he received this appointment in 60 A.D.
§ 2. rerum mutationem: cf. Dom. 16, 1, n.

iuveni senem: Nero died in his 32nd year, and Galba succeeded him
in his 73rd. Dio (lxiv 1) mentions the same prodigy and gives the same
interpretation: παῖς λιβανωτὸν αὐτῷ θύοντι προσφέρων πολιὰς ἐξαίφνης ἔφυσεν, καὶ
οἱ μάντεις τὴν τοῦ νεωτέρου ἀρχὴν πρὸς τὸ γῆρας αὐτοῦ μεταστήσεσθαι ἔφησαν.

hoc est ipsum Neroni: Bentley suspected the genuineness of these
words; see on Vesp. 11, Dom. 17, 1.

Cantabriae: a mountainous district about midway on the N. coast of
Spain, forming part of the province of Tarraconensis.

lacum: Torrentius conjectured lucum; so, too, Bentley.
.

duodecim secures imperii signum: the duodecim lictores cum
fascibus were among the regia insignia marking the imperium of the old
Roman kings; cf. Cic. Rep. ii 17, 31, Liv. i 8, Dion. Hal. ii 29, iii 61, 62.
In later days these 12 lictors, bearing rods and axes, were granted to the
consuls and proconsuls, Augustus limiting the privilege to those proconsuls
who as ex-consuls governed the provinces of Asia and Africa (Mommsen,
Staatsr. i 382, ii³ 5). For the lictors who attended on the emperors themselves see on Dom. 14, 3.

octo annos: 60-68 A.D. The tenure of office by a legatus in an imperial
province depended on the emperor's pleasure (Dio liii 13, Tac. A. i 80);
Tiberius kept Sabinus as governor of Moesia for 24 yrs. and Silius as
governor of Upper Germany for 7 yrs. (Tac. A. vi 39, iv 18); Otho was
legatus in Lusitania for 10 yrs. (Suet. Oth. 3, 2). See Mommsen Staatsr. ii
259, Greenidge, Roman Public Life 434.

varie et inaequabiliter
rexit: Tacitus (H. i 49) praises Galba's
administration: pro consule Africam moderate, iam senior citeriorem
Hispaniam pari iustitia continuit. Plutarch (Galb. 4) says that Nero's
unscrupulous “receivers” (ἐπίτροποι, procuratores) harassed the provincials
in the most cruel manner; Galba could not assist them against the persecutors, but his concern for their misfortunes, a concern as great as if
he had been a sufferer himself, afforded them some consolation even while
they were condemned and sold as slaves. Lampooning verses were written
against Nero and sung everywhere; and as Galba did not try to suppress
them and did not share the resentment of the receivers of the revenue,
this endeared him still more to the natives.

primo acer: cf. the remark of Paetus Thrasea on Roman provincial
administration, Tac. A. xv 21, initia magistratuum nostrorum meliora ferme,
finis inclinat.

nummulario: a post-Aug. word for mensarius, argentarius, a money-changer or money-broker; cf. Petron. Satyr. 56, Mart. xii 57, 18; the
nummularius also conducted auctions and did banking business, e.g.
receiving deposits; cf. Ulp. Dig. xvi 3, 7, quotiens foro cedunt ("become
bankrupt'") nummularii, solet primo loco ratio haberi depositariorum, hoc
est eorum qui depositas pecunias habuerunt, non quas faenore apud nummularios vel cum nummulariis vel per ipsos exercebant.

ex fide: cf. Iul. 74, 2, quamvis omnia ex fide rettulissent; this use
of ex fide in the sense of cum fide is found in writers from Tacitus onwards.

versanti pecunias: “handling'" "dealing with" = tractanti; cf. Cic.
Div. in Caecil. 10, pecuniam publicam tu tractabas. Torrentius explains
versanti as contrectanti et exploranti, thus limiting it to the actual handling
and testing of the coins exchanged, such as is referred to in Aug. 4, 2;
Apul. Met. x 9, ne forte aliquis istorum quos offers aureorum nequam vel
adulter repperiatur nummulario praesente comprobentur. Casaubon
would omit pecunias or read in pecuniis.

manus amputavit: cf. Dom. 10, 5. Claudius on one occasion had this
punishment inflicted in court; Claud. 15, 2, proclamante quodam praecidendas falsario (“a forger," cf. Tit. 3, 2) manus, carnificem statim acciri
cum machaera mensaque lanonia flagitavit.

cui substitutus heres erat: substituere heredem (alicui) was a lega!
phrase for a testator naming a person as secundus heres in the event of
the primus heres refusing to accept the inheritance or dying before reaching
puberty; similarly a tertius heres could be named to succeed the secundus
in a like event: cf. Dig. xxviii 6, 1, Heredes aut instituti dicuntur aut
substituti: instituti primo gradu, substituti secundo vel tertio. Heredis
substitutio duplex est aut simplex, veluti: “Lucius Titius heres esto: si
mihi Lucius Titius heres non erit, tunc Seius heres mihi esto: si heres
non erit, sive erit et intra pubertatem decesserit, tunc Gaius Seius
heres mihi esto." Cf. Tib. 76, heredes aequis partibus reliquit Gaium et
Tiberium, substituitque invicem (i.e. should either die, the other was to
succeed): Quint. vii 6, 9, substitutus heres erat, si postumus ante tutelae
