annos decessisset. To appoint the tutor of the primus heres as secundus
heres showed an implicit confidence on the part of the testator; Cicero
enjoyed such confidence, as he tells us in Fam. xiii '61: T. Pinnio familiarissime me usum esse scire te arbitror: quod quidem ille testamento declaravit,
qui me cum tutorem tum etiam secundum heredem instituit.

cruce adfecit: Cic. Verr. i 9, cum cives Romanos morte, cruciatu, cruce
adfecerit; so adficere exilio, verberibus, etc. More usual expressions for
crucifying are cruci figere (and compounds); cf. Dom. 10, 1, n.
imploranti leges: the laws invoked by Cicero in his passionate
denunciation of Verres for scourging and crucifying Gavius, a Roman
citizen, at Messana, Verr. v 63, O nomen dulce libertatis! O ius eximium
nostrae civitatis! O lex Porcia legesque Semproniae! The lex Porcia
(с. 197 в.с.) exacted penalties for scourging or killing a Roman citizen
(Liv. x 9); the lex Sempronia of Gaius Sempronius Gracchus (123 в.с.)
confirmed and widened the right of appeal (provocatio) for the condemned
man to the people (Cic. Rab. 12). Under the provisions of the lex Iulia
de vi (46 B.с.) Galba's victim was entitled to appeal to the emperor
against the sentence of the legatus; Paul. Sent. v 26, 1, lege Iulia de vi
publica damnatur qui aliqua potestate praeditus civem Romanum antea ad
populum, nunc ad imperatorem appellantem necarit necarive iusserit torserit
verberaverit condemnaverit inve publica vincula duci iusserit. See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii³ 269.

civem Romanum se testificanti: cf. Cic. Verr. v 62, nulla vox alia illius
miseri inter dolorem crepitumque plagarum audiebatur nisi haec: “civis
Romanus sum." Asinius Pollio (Cic. Fam. x 32), describing how his
quaestor Balbus burned Fadius alive, says: et illi misero quiritanti
('crying out'"): “civis Romanus natus sum,” responderet “Abi nunc,
populi fidem implora." St. Paul used the plea of Roman citizenship to
escape scourging (Acts 22, 25).
•

quasi solacio iussit: Galba's response to the privilege claimed by
a Roman citizen was as contemptuous as that of Verres who ordered the
cross of Gavius to be set up facing the Straits of Messina, "ut ille quoniam
se civem Romanum esse diceret, ex cruce Italiam cernere ac domum suam
prospicere posset."
multo praeter ceteras altiorem: for the pleonasm cf. Vitell. 13, 1,
famosissima super ceteras: Dom. 12, 2, praeter ceteros acerbissime.
Bentley needlessly conjectured prae ceteris here.

in desidiam segnitiamque conversus est: cf. Tac. H. i 49 (of Galba),
sed claritas natalium et metus temporum obtentui, ut quod segnitia erat
sapientia vocaretur: Tac. Agr. 6 (of Agricola), mox inter quaesturam ac
tribunatum plebis atque ipsum etiam tribunatus annum quiete et otio
transiit, gnarus sub Nerone temporum, quibus inertia pro sapientia fuit:
Tac. Ann. xiv 47 (of Memmius Regulus in Nero's reign), vixit . quiete
defensus: Plin. Ep. viii 14, at nos iuvenes fuimus quidem in castris, sed
cum suspecta virtus, inertia in pretio.

ne quid materiae praeberet Neroni: sc. invidiae; cf. Cic. Phil. xi 9,
21, ut aut suspicioni crimen aut invidiae materiam dedisse videamur: Liv.
iii 46, non praebiturum se illi eo die materiam (seditionis): Suet. Aug. 16,
2, praebitam materiam exprobrandi: Claud. 4, 2, praebenda materia deridendi et illum et nos non est hominibus.

rationem otii reddere: referring to the famous maxim of Cato the
censor cited by Cicero, Planc. 27, 66, M. Catonis illud, quod in principio
scripsit Originum suarum, semper magnificum et praeclarum putavi,
clarorum virorum atque magnorum non minus otii quam negotii rationem
exstare oportere; cf. Colum. ii 22, tam otii quam negotii rationem reddere
oportere maiores nostri censuerunt: Justin (Hist. Philip. praef.), ut otii
mei, cuius et Cato reddendam putat, apud te ratio constaret.

§ 2. Carthagine nova: mod. Cartagena in Hispania Tarraconensis at
the S.E. extremity; founded by Hasdrubal in 242 B.c.; captured by Scipio
in 210; a Roman colony under the Empire with the title of Colonia Victrix
Iulia Nova Carthago.

conventum agens: for judicial purposes the province was divided into
districts called conventus iuridici, the courts being held in the chief town
of each district; "agere conventum" was the phrase for "to hold the
assizes" and the circuit judge was said “circumire conventus" (e.g. Iul.
7, 1, cum iure dicundo conventus circumiret). Pliny (N. H. iii 18) enumerates the 7 conventus of Tarraconensis as those of Carthago Nova,
Tarraco, Caesaraugusta, Clunia, Lucus Augusti, Bracara Augusta, Asturica
Augusta; these contained 472 towns and villages.

tumultuari Gallias: C. Julius Vindex, a descendant of a royal Celtic
family and governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, revolted against Nero in
68 A.D. As Lugdunum would take no part, Vienna on the Rhone was made
the centre of the rebellion. Some of the Gallic tribes, such as the Arverni,
Aedui, and Sequani, joined Vindex; but others, such as the Lingones,
Treviri, and generally all that "pars Galliarum quae Rhenum accolit”
(Tac. H. i 51) refused their aid. The revolt was crushed by the army
from Germany which remained loyal in spite of the solicitations of Vindex;
see on c. 11, 1.

Aquitaniae: see on c. 6, 1; its legatus would have no army under his
control. Tacitus (H. i 76) mentions Julius Cordus as governor of
Aquitania at the beginning of 69 A.D.

Vindicis litterae: Plutarch (Galb. 4) says that before the rebellion
broke out Galba had intimations of it in letters from Vindex; but he
neither countenanced it nor disclosed it to Nero as the governors of other
provinces did. After Vindex commenced hostilities he wrote to Galba
inviting him to accept the imperial dignity and to give a head to the
strong Gallic body which needed one (παρασχεῖν ἑαυτὸν ἰσχυρῷ σώματι
ζητοῦντι κεφαλήν); already there were 100,000 Gauls in arms, and further
forces could be raised. Dio (lxiii 23) gives a speech of Vindex to the
Gauls in which, after denouncing the villanies of Nero, he calls upon them
to rid the world of such a monster.

assertorem: "liberator"; cf. Iul. 80, 1, populo detrectante dominationem atque assertores flagitante: Ov. Rem. Am. 73, publicus assertor
dominis suppressa levabo | pectora; also used for "a champion of," e.g.
Tib. 2, 4, assertores unicos dignitatis ac potentiae patriciorum. See further
on "asserere,” Oth. 9,3, Vesp. 3; "assertio," Dom. 8,1. On some of the
coins of Galba are found the words salus gen. humani (Eckhel, vi 297;
Cohen, i² 334).

nec diu cunctatus: according to Plutarch (Galb. 4), he held a council
of his friends, and while some advised him to await developments, he was
influenced in his decision by the argument of T. Vinius, his lieutenant, who
pointed out that having once entertained the idea of revolt they were
already committed to it (cf. Tac. H. ii 77, nam qui deliberant, desciverunt).

condicionem recepit: recipere instead of the usual accipere is found
also in Vell. Pat. i 48, 5, condiciones pacis

recepit: Tac. A. ii 81, non
receptae condiciones.

mandata Neronis de nece sua: cf. Ner. 43, 1, Initio statim tumultus
(the revolt of Vindex and Galba) multa et immania, verum non abhorrentia
a natura sua creditur destinasse; successores percussoresque summittere
exercitus et provincias regentibus, quasi conspiratis idemque et unnım
sentientibus.
с, 9, 2-с. 10, 1.]
..

procuratores: Plutarch's description of the strained relations between
Galba and the procurators has been already referred to (see above, note on
"varie
rexit'"). In the senatorial provinces there were procurators to
look after the interests of the fiscus and the emperor's private affairs, but
it was in the imperial provinces (like Tarraconensis) that they held a most
important position independent of the governor, and often at variance
with him. In Britain the legatus Suetonius Paulinus was thwarted by the
procurator Classicianus, and the quarrel between them was so bitter that
Nero sent Polyclitus to compose it (Tac. A. xiv 38); the feeling of the
Britons under their oppressors is described in Tac. Agr. 15, binos reges
imponi, e quibus legatus in sanguinem, procurator in bona saeviret.
Agricola avoided such feuds when he was in Britain: ib. 9, procul a contentione adversus procuratores.

honestae: = honesto genere ortae (Vesp. 1, 3); so honeste natus (Aug.
43, 3).

Cluniae: a Celtiberian town, at this time the seat of a conventus
iuridicus in Tarraconensis (see above on “conventum agens''). After the
death of Vindex, Galba remained inactive at Clunia till news arrived that
he had been made emperor at Rome (see c. 11, 1); he continued to be a
patron of the town (C.I.L. ii 2339) and on coins of his reign Clunia bears
the additional name of Sulpicia (Eckhel, i 46, vi 294; Cohen, i² 324, 86).

fatidica puella: cf. Tac. H. iv 61, (Germani) plerasque feminarum
fatidicas arbitrantur; Cic. N.D. i 18, anus fatidica; Verg. Aen. viii 340,
vates fatidica.

carminum: oracula, sortes, and prophecies in general took the form of
verse; e.g. Liv. i 45, cecinere vates . fore ., idque carmen pervenerat ad
antistitem: Prop. iv 1, 51, Pergameae sero rata carmina vatis (i.e.
Cassandra). Cf. θεσπιῳδός, Carmenta, Camena.

oriturum ex Hispania principem: Galba, though merely a Roman
governor in Spain, took these prophecies as referring to himself; they were
more literally fulfilled when Spaniards by birth or descent, like Trajan,
Hadrian, and Theodosius, became emperors. Similarly the prophecies that
men from Judaea would rule the world were supposed to be fulfilled when
Vespasian, the Roman commander in Judaea, made himself emperor (see
Vesp. 4, 5).

manumissioni: Plut. Galb. 5, ἐκ τούτου προγράμματι ("by edict'')
μὲν ἐδήλωσεν ὁ Γάλβας ἡμέραν ἐν ᾗἢ τὰς κατὰ μέρος ἐλευθερώσεις ἀποδώσει τοῖς
δεομένοις. Galba chose the day on which in the normal course the
court would have requests for manumission to make public his intention of
"emancipating" the empire from the despotism of Nero. The usual
process of manumission was per vindictam, i.e. by the touch of the wand of
the lictor who acted as assertor libertatis, accompanied by the words
"Hunc ego hominem ex iure Quiritium liberum esse aio" and by the
master turning the slave round and releasing his hold on him. This proceeding required the presence of a consul, praetor, or provincial governor.
Pliny (Ep. vii 16) offers to get a friend of his, who is going to Baetica as
proconsul, to stop at Ticinum to perform the ceremony of manumission
(vindicta liberare). For other modes of manumission see on Vesp. 3, Latinae
condicionis.

vacaturus: vacare c. dat., used of a judge, meant that he was free to
hear certain cases on a certain day; cf. Plin. Ep. vii 33, cum explorasset
consules postulationibus vacaturos (“would be free to hear claims for restitution'"); so sedere c. dat. "to sit to hear certain cases," e.g. Ulp.
Dig. xxxviii 17, 2, 43, ubi primum potuit, id est, praetoris copiam habuit
huic rei sedentis.

proxima Baliari insula: i.e. Baliaris Maior. The Balearic islands
(Baliaris Maior and Minor, mod. Majorca and Minorca) are off the E. of
Spain; under the Empire they formed part of Hispania Tarraconensis and
belonged to the conventus of Carthago Nova (c. 9, 2); they served as one
of the places of exile for those banished by the Roman emperors (cf.
Tac. A. iv 42, xiii 43, and see note on Tit. 8, 5).
consalutatus imperator: Plutarch (Galb. 5) says that he was thus
saluted the moment he appeared on the tribunal: Οὐκ ἔφθη γοῦν φανερὸς ἐπὶ
τοῦ βήματος γενόμενος καὶ πάντες αὐτὸν ὁμοφώνως αὐτοκράτορα (imperatorem) προσεῖπον.
Ὁ δὲ ταύτην μὲν εὐθὺς οὐ προσεδέξατο τὴν προσηγορίαν, κατηγορήσας δὲ τοῦ
Νέρωνος καὶ τῶν ἀνῃρημένων (occisorum) ἀνδρῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοὺς ἐπιφανεστάτους
ὀλοφυράμενος ὡμολόγησεν ἐπιδώσειν τῇ πατρίδι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ πρόνοιαν, οὔτε Καῖσαρ οὔτ᾽
αὐτοκράτωρ, στρατηγὸς δὲ συγκλήτου καὶ δήμου ῾Ρωμαίων (senatus populique R.)
ὀνομαζόμενος. Dio calculates the duration of Galba's reign from the day
(April 2, 68) on which he was thus acclaimed emperor in Spain (see
on c. 23 infr.); similarly Vespasian's reign was reckoned from the day
on which he was saluted as emperor by his soldiers (see Vesp. 6, 3).
On
imperator as a title of the princeps see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 781.
Dio (lii 41) says of Augustus: καὶ τὴν τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος ἐπίκλησιν ἐπέθετο.
λέγω δὲ οὐ τὴν ἐπὶ ταῖς νίκαις κατὰ τὸ ἀρχαῖον διδομένην τισίν (see on Tit. 5, 2)...
ἀλλὰ τὴν ἑτέραν τὴν τὸ κράτος διασημαίνουσαν, ὥσπερ τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ τῷ Καίσαρι..
ἐψήφιστο.
..

legatum se senatus professus est: thus renouncing his allegiance
to Nero who had appointed him as legatus Augusti pro praetore in the
imperial province of Tarraconensis. A similar recognition of the supreme
authority of "the senate and the Roman people" was professed by
Verginius Rufus who crushed the revolt of Vindex (c. 9, 2, Dio lxiii 25)
and by Clodius Macer in Africa (see c. 11 infr.). Mommsen (Hermes xiii
90 sqq.) argues that a return to a senatorial or republican government was
seriously contemplated at this period. The exultation of the senate in its
brief freedom after Nero's death finds expression on the coins it issued
inscribed with Libertas P.R., Libertas restituta or renascens, Roma
renascens, Mars or Hercules Adsertor, etc. (Eckhel vi 293 sqq.). See Schiller,
Geschichte der röm. Kaiserzeit i 366.

§ 2. iustitio indicto: a iustitium (= iuris quasi interstitio quaedam et
cessatio, Gell. xx 1) was a suspension of legal and other business at Rome
on occasions of national danger; it was proclaimed (indicere, Calig. 24, 2,
Liv. ix 7; edicere, Liv. iii 27) by a dictator, consul, or praetor; under the
Empire we find a iustitium ordered on account of religious festivals, a
famine, a funus publicum, and (most frequently) the death of a member
of the imperial house.
..
..

e plebe legiones conscripsit: legiones may be a mistake or a
corruption (as Heraeus, on Tac. H. i 6, suggests) for legionem, as there
is no evidence that Galba enrolled from his province more than the one
legion, viz. vii Galbiana, which is mentioned by Tacitus (e.g. H. iii 25,
Iulius Mansuetus ex Hispania inter septimanos a Galba conscriptus). The
theory of Grotefend that Legio prima Adiutrix (see on c. 12, 2) was enrolled
by Galba and not by Nero is rightly rejected by Mommsen (C.I.L. iii
p. 907); see also Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa xii 1380 sqq., Parker Roman
Legions 99 sq.

auxilia: in the Roman army “auxilia” were auxiliaries from the provinces (also, at times, from allied states and princes, and even from
independent nations), corresponding in number approximately with the
legionaries; cf. Tib. 16, bellum . per quindecim legiones paremque auxiliorum copiam gessit: Tac. A. iv 5.

exercitum veterem: under Augustus and Tiberius there were three
legions quartered in Spain: iv Macedonica, vi Victrix, x Gemina; Galba
as legatus of Hispania Tarraconensis had one legion, vi Victrix (Tac. H.
i 16, v 16), by which he was proclaimed emperor.

alarum: auxiliary cavalry, divided into alae miliariae of 960 men each
(24 turmae of 40 each) and alae quingenariae of 480 (16 turmae of 30).

cohortium: these are cohortes auxiliariae, sociae, and might be infantry
(cohortes peditatae) or include a certain proportion of cavalry (cohortes
equitatae); the cohors miliaria equitata had 240 cavalry and 760 infantry,
the cohors quingenaria equitata had 120 cavalry and 360-380 infantry.
Sometimes these cohortes were equipped with their native weapons, and are
described as sagittarii, funditores, contarii, cataphracti, etc. See Marquardt,
Staatsv. ii² 468 sqq.

velut instar senatus: i.e. a copy of the Roman senate whose legatus
and champion he now professed to be. For the uses of instar in Suet. see
on Vesp. 5, 2. The MSS. vary between velut (read by Preud'homme) and
vel (read by Ihm); velut is supported by the equally pleonastic use of
quasi in Cic. Tusc. i 17, 40, terra ad universi caeli complexum quasi puncti
instar obtinet.

quotiens opus esset: Suetonius uses quotiens more often than any
other particle in introducing iterative clauses; it occurs 30 times in the
Lives, 29 times with the subjunctive (imperf. or pluperf.) and once (Aug.
88) with pres. indicative. In class. Lat. quotiens takes the indic.; post-Aug. writers frequently use the subjunct. (Draeger, ii² 584). Suetonius
also uses quotiensque (not quotienscunque): Aug. 37, quotiensque opus

esset: Calig. 7, quotiensque introiret. (Düpow, De Suet. consuetudine
sermonis 19 sq.)

$ 3. manente anulorum aureorum usu: i.e. without sacrificing their
rank as equites; an eques who became a centurion in a legion lost his rank
as eques (see Mommsen Staatsr. iii³ 504 n. where our passage is cited).
The gold ring had come to be a badge of the equestrian order (cf. Iul. 33;
39, 2; Galb. 14, 2; Vitell. 12). Originally it was given at public expense
(de publico) to those senators who were sent as ambassadors (legati):
then it came to be worn by the nobiles, by the equites equo publico, and
later by all the knights. The gift of the anulus aureus, e.g. by Sulla to
the actor Roscius, conferred equestrian status. Under the early Empire
it was freely bestowed; so many wealthy freedmen obtained it that in
23 A.D. a decree of the senate was passed: “ne cui ius anulorum esset nisi
cui ingenuo ipsi, patri avoque paterno sestertia cccc census fuisset" (Plin.
N.H. xxxiii 8; cf. Daremberg-Saglio, i 296 sqq.). Six months' service as
tribunus legionis carried with it the rank of eques and the ius anuli aurei
(Juv. vii 88, with Mayor's note).

evocati: Galba gave to this special bodyguard the title of "evocati”
or volunteer veterans (see on Vesp. 1, 2) because the evocati in the Roman
army formed at times the personal guard (cohors praetoria, Cic. Fam. x 30)
of the general, as in the case of the evocati of Octavian before the battle
of Mutina (Appian Bell. Civ. iii 40); sometimes this personal guard was
composed of Roman equites (Polyb. vi 31, 2).
excubias agerent: they were to act as excubitores, a name specially
given to the cohort of praetorians which guarded the emperor in his
palace and accompanied him to entertainments at other houses (cf. Oth.
4,2; 6, 1; Ner. 8; 21, 1; Tac. 4. xii 69, H. i 29; 38); their officer
(tribunus excubitor) received the password (tessera) from the emperor
(Calig. 56, 2; Claud. 42, 1; Ner. 9; Tac. A. i 7, xiii 3).

per provincias: Otho, in Lusitania, was the first of the provincial
governors to declare for Galba (Oth. 4, 1; Plut. Galb. 20); then all the
others, except Clodius Macer in Africa and Verginius Rufus in Germany,
sided with him (Plut. c. 6). A coin of Galba's bears the words concordia
provinciarum (Eckhel, vi p. 293).

auctor conspirandi et ut.. iuvarent: for a similar change of
construction cf. Iul. 88, placuit Idus Martias Parricidium nominari, ac ne
umquam eo die senatus ageretur. Such changes are common in poetry and
are found at times in Cicero, e.g. Deiot. 10, quibus ille studiis se imbuerat, non saltandi, sed bene ut armis, optime ut equis uteretur.

singulis: in all the MSS. except IQ the reading is in singulis which
is adopted by Ihm but not by Preud'homme, Roth, or the early editors.
communem causam = causam rei publicae.

§ 4. oppidi: its name is unknown; Galba made it the headquarters for
the assembly of men and munitions for the campaign, and fortified it in
case of attack.

sedem bello: cf. Tac. H. i 65, where Vienna (in Gallia Narbonensis)
is spoken of as "sedes Gallici belli."

scalptura exprimente: the wonderful skill of ancient lapidaries
(gemmarii scalptores) enabled them to depict a great variety of designs
on signet rings; Pompey's ring, like the ring mentioned here, represented.
three trophies (Dio xlii 18); the seal of Galba's family was a dog looking
from the prow of a ship (Dio li 3); Pliny (N.H. xxxvii 8, 10) tells us that
the gem on Sulla's ring showed the surrender of Jugurtha, and that
Augustus had as a signet first the figure of a Sphinx, later a portrait of
Alexander the Great, and finally a faithful likeness of himself which subsequent emperors also used. Cf. Aug. 50.

navis: Dio (lxiv 1) says that there were more than one of these
miraculous ships: καὶ πλοῖα ὅπλων μεστὰ πρὸς Ἰβηρίαν
ἀνθρώπων ἄγοντος αὐτά, προσωρμίσθη.
αὐτόματα, μηδενὸς

Dertosam: in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the left bank of the Hiberus
(Ebro) and near its mouth; mod. Tortosa. Livy (xxiii 28) calls it "Hibera
urbs"; Strabo (iii 160, 195) mentions it as a Roman colony. Some of
the coins of Dertosa show the figure of a ship, it being an important
trading port. See Pauly-Wissowa, v 246 sq.
..

cum repente turbata sunt: for this use of “cum inversum” (= tum,
a relative form of proposition being substituted for a demonstrative) see
Draeger, ii² 569; it is used principally by the historians to introduce something unexpected and surprising; Cicero also is fond of it, e.g. Verr. 2, 29,
non dubitabat Minucius quin iste quaesiturus non esset, cum repente
iubetur dicere: Sest. 37, 79, venit
obnuntiavit consuli, cum subito
manus illa Clodiana exclamat.
§ 5. alarum: see c. 10, 2.

paene interemerunt, nisi
esset: for paene with perf. ind. in the
..
apodosis of an unreal condition in past time, cf. Iul. 52, 1, paene
Aegyptum penetravit, nisi exercitus sequi recusasset: Plaut. Pers. 594,
paene in foveam decidi, ni hic adesses: Cic. Att. xv 26, 4, paene fecit,
nisi tua malitia adfuisset: Liv. ii 10, 2, pons sublicius iter paene hostibus
dedit, ni unus vir fuisset, Horatius Cocles. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 171,
174.

cohortantibus: the pres. ptc. is here used in a perf. or aorist sense;
see on c. 5, 2.

mors Vindicis: Vindex (c. 9, 2) was defeated at Vesontio (Besançon)
in Gallia Belgica by Verginius Rufus, the legatus of Upper Germany
(Тас. Н. і, 51, iv 57); it is doubtful whether he was slain ("caeso cum
omnibus copiis Vindice," Tac.) or committed suicide (Plut. Galb. 6, and
Dio lxiii 24). The victorious legions offered the empire to Rufus but he
declined it and in his epitaph which he wrote he prides himself on his
refusal: "Hic situs est Rufus pulso qui Vindice quondam | imperium
asseruit non sibi sed patriae" (Plin. Ep. vi 10). Juvenal (viii 221) says
that of all the crimes of which Nero was guilty his poetic and musical
efforts called most for the vengeance of Verginius, Vindex, and Galba:
Quid enim Verginius armis | debuit ulcisci magis aut cum Vindice Galba
quod Nero tam saeva crudaque tyrannide fecit?

consternatus: Plutarch (Galb. 6) describes the panic of Galba and his
subsequent inactivity at Clunia: τότε δὴ περίφοβος γενόμενος ὁ Γάλβας ἔγραψε
τῷ Οὐεργινίῳ παρακαλῶν κοινοπραγεῖν καὶ διαφυλάσσειν ἅμα τὴν ἡγεμονίαν καὶ τὴν
ἐλευθερίαν τοῖς ῾Ρωμαίοις· αὖθις δὲ μετὰ τῶν φίλων εἰς Κλουνίαν, Ἰβηρικὴν πόλιν,
ἀναχωρήσας ἐν τῷ μετανοεῖν περὶ τῶν γεγονότων καὶ ποθεῖν τὴν συνήθη καὶ σύντροφον
απραγμοσύνην μᾶλλον ἢ πράττειν τι τῶν ἀναγκαίων διέτριβεν.

vitae renuntiaret: in Cic. renuntiare in the sense of cancelling an
agreement or breaking off relations usually takes the acc. of the thing
cancelled and the dat. of the person notified, e.g. Verr. 2, 2, 89, incensus
hospitium ei renuntiat (so amicitiam alicui renuntiare, Suet. Calig. 2, 3,
Liv., Tac., etc.): Verr. 2, 1, 141, renuntiat Habonius illam decisionem
tutoribus told the guardians the offer was withdrawn"; in post-Aug.
Lat. the dat. is used of the thing abandoned as though it were a person
receiving notice (see Summers on Sen. Ep. 108, 15, inde ostreis boletisque
in omnem vitam renuntiatum est), so we find such phrases as renuntiare
civilibus officiis (Plin. Ep. ii 1, Quint. x 7), foro (Suet. Rhet. 6), inertiae
(Plin. Pan. 59, 2), Naturae (Sen. Prov. 6, 8).

nuntiis: according to Plutarch (Galb. 7) it was Icelus, a freedman of
Galba, who first brought the news of Nero's death and Galba's appointment (see c. 22 infr.); two days later Titus Vinius and others brought
full details.

occisum Neronem: for Nero's death see on Dom. 11, 2, more maiorum
puniendi.

in verba sua iurasse: cf. c. 16, 1; Oth. 8, 1; Vitell. 15, 1; Tac. A. i 7,
consules primi in verba Tiberii Caesaris iuravere, apudque eos Seius Strabo
et C. Turranius, ille praetoriarum cohortium praefectus, hic annonae; mox
senatus milesque et populus. So also in nomen principis iurare'” (Claud.
10, 4, etc.). This oath taken by the whole people and provinces was a
recognition of Caesar's sole proconsulare imperium (Furneaux on Tac. l.c.),
and was an extension of the old military oath (sacramentum) by which
the soldier was said “iurare in verba consulum, etc." The oath of fealty
to the emperor was taken afresh every New Year's day (cf. c. 16. 2) and
on the anniversary of the day on which it had first been taken (Plin. Ep. x
52; Tac. A. i 8, H. i 55). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 792 sq.

Caesaris appellationem: cf. Dio ap. Zonar. xi 14, Γάλβας δ', ἐπεὶ ὁ Νέρων
διέφθαρτο καὶ ἡ βουλὴ τὴν ἀρχήν οἱ ἐψηφίσατο καὶ ὁ ῾Ῥοῦφος αὐτῷ προσεχώρησεν,
ἀνεθάρσησεν, οὐ μέντοι καὶ τὸ Καίσαρος ἀνέλαβεν ὄνομα πρὶν τοὺς τῆς βουλῆς
πρεσβευτὰς πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐλθεῖν. ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ τὸ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος (imperatoris) πρότερον
εἰς οὐδὲν γράμμα ἐνεγεγράφει. “Caesar” is now adopted as a mere title for
the Roman emperor since "progenies Caesarum in Nerone defecit” (Galb. 1).
See further on Dom. 1, 3.
iter ingressus est: Galba left Hispania Tarraconensis in June 68 A.D.
and did not reach Rome till September (Tac. H. i 6, tardum iter Galbae).

paludatus: wearing the paludamentum or general's cloak, usually of
purple or scarlet (cf. Vitell. 11, 1, n.).
Under the Empire, when the
military imperium was concentrated in the emperor, the paludamentum became one of the insignia of his power. Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 432.
..

dependente pugione: the dagger of military officers was worn either
on a bandolier round the neck or on a girdle by the side (Mommsen, i³
p. 434, n. 1); the pugio (less frequently called gladius, ξίφος) was an
emblem of the proconsular power of the princeps, the assumption of
empire being described as the taking of the dagger in the hand, and the
surrender of the empire as the giving back of the dagger; cf. Vitell. 8, 1;
15, 4; Tac. H. iii 68 (of Vitellius' abdication) adsistenti consuli
exsolutum a latere pugionem velut ius necis vitaeque civium reddebat:
Sen. Clem. i 11, 3 (of Nero), nulli umquam citius gladius commissus est.
The right of wearing the pugio as a symbol of military command was
granted by the emperor, especially to the praefectus praetorio who is
often described as the bearer and custodian of the imperial dagger, e.g.
Aurel. Vict. Caes. 13, 9 (of Trajan appointing Suburanus as praefectus
praetorio), cum insigne potestatis, uti mos erat, pugionem daret; cf. Plin.
Pan. 67, Plut. Galb. 8, Philostr. Apoll. iv 42, viii 16, Lamprid. Comm. 6,
tunc primum tres praefecti praetorio fuere, inter quos libertinus, qui a
pugione appellatus est. Dio (Xiph.), lxiv 3, says that the wearing of a
"large sword" by Galba (a feeble old man of 73) on his march from
Spain excited great ridicule : ὅτι δὲ ξίφος μέγα διὰ πάσης τῆς ὁδοῦ ἐξηρτᾶτο, καὶ
γέρων καὶ ἀσθενὴς τὰ νεῦρα ὤν, καὶ πάνυ πολὺν γέλωτα ὠφλίσκανε.
..

prius quam oppressis: Suetonius in his fondness for participial constructions sometimes uses prius .. quam and ante.. quam in neg. sentences
(1) with the ptc., e.g. Vesp. 6, 1, nec.. ante temptavit
quam sollicitatus:
Vesp. 15: Iul. 58, 2: Aug. 53, 3: Calig. 27, 4: (so in Cic. Phil. i 25,
Tusc. i 13, Fin. i 49, N.D. i 68, Liv. vii 35, etc.); (2) with the ptc. in
the abl. abs., as here: Vitell. 8, 2, nec ante
rediit quam flagrante
triclinio: Tib. 22 and 37, 3: (earlier in Livy, e.g. xxiv 18, non ante quam
bello confecto: Plin. N.H. viii 144).

usum togae reciperavit: this use of reciperare in the sense of repetere
"to resume" does not seem to occur earlier.

Nymphidio Sabino: son of Nymphidia, a freedwoman, and Martianus,
a gladiator (Plut. Galb. 9); though he himself alleged that he was a son
of Caligula (Tac. A. xv 72). He was made praefectus praetorio by Nero
in 65 after the conspiracy of Piso. When Nero's affairs were in a desperate
state, Nymphidius persuaded the praetorian guards to declare Galba emperor,
hoping to exercise the real authority himself; but finding that Galba preferred his own officers Vinius and Laco (who was appointed praefectus
praetorio in his stead), he tried to induce the praetorians to proclaim him
as emperor; they refused, and when he tried to force an entrance to their
camp he was slain by them (Tac. H. i 5, 25, 37).

Fonteio Capitone: consul in 67, legatus of Lower Germany in 68;
according to Plutarch (Galb. 13) and Suetonius he entertained treasonable
designs against Galba who had him put to death, but from the account
in Tac. H. i 7 it appears that his guilt was doubtful: Forte congruerat ut
Clodii Macri et Fontei Capitonis caedes nuntiarentur. Macrum in Africa
haud dubie turbantem Trebonius Garutianus procurator iussu Galbae,
Capitonem in Germania, cum similia coeptaret, Cornelius Aquinus et
Fabius Valens legati legionum interfecerant, antequam iuberentur. Fuere
qui crederent Capitonem ut avaritia et libidine foedum ac maculosum, ita
cogitatione rerum novarum abstinuisse; sed a legatis bellum suadentibus
postquam impellere nequiverint, crimen ac dolum ultro compositum; et
Galbam mobilitate ingenii, an ne altius scrutaretur, quoquo modo acta,
quia mutari non poterant, comprobasse. Tacitus also mentions (i 58) that
when Vitellius became emperor, Capito's soldiers, who held his memory
dear, demanded the death of his accuser. Dio (lxiv 2) says that Nymphidius
and Capito were so wantonly arrogant that on one occasion when an accused
person appealed from Capito to Caesar, Capito at once leaped into a
higher chair and invited him to plead his cause before Caesar, and having
heard his appeal put him to death.

Clodio Macro: appointed legatus of Africa by Nero and guilty of
much extortion and bloodshed as governor. On Nero's death he revolted
and laid claim to the throne, being instigated by Crispinilla (magistra
libidinum Neronis, Tac. H. i 73) who crossed to Africa and advised him
to starve Rome by cutting off the African corn supply. He aimed at
restoring the Republic, and on coins which he had struck he put his own
image and the inscription s(enatus) c(onsulto) pro praetore Africae, instead
of leg. Aug. pr. pr. prov. Africae (Eckhel vi p. 289, Cohen i² p. 316). He
also enrolled a new legion in Africa which he called “Legio I Liberatrix
Macriana." When Galba had secured the empire, he caused Macer to be
put to death by the procurator Trebonius Garutianus (Tac. H. i 7, 37, 73;
ii 97; Plut. Galb. 6, 15). The legio Macriana was disbanded by Galba
but was again pressed into service by Vitellius and finally disappeared
on his death (Parker, Rom. Legions 106).

saevitiae atque avaritiae: vices masquerading under the guise of
severitas and parsimonia, according to Otho in his speech denouncing Galba
to the soldiers, Tac. H. i 37: quae usquam provincia, quae castra sunt
nisi cruenta et maculata aut, ut ipse (Galba) praedicat, emendata et
correcta? nam quae alii scelera hic remedia vocat, dum falsis nominibus
severitatem pro saevitia, parsimoniam pro avaritia, supplicia et contumelias
vestras disciplinam appellat. The "saevitia Galbae” is mentioned also in
Тас. Н. і 87; cf. Oros. vii 8, 1, cumque omnes avaritia saevitia segnitiaque
offenderet.

civitates Hispaniarum Galliarumque punisset: we have no details
of the particular Spanish civitates which were treated vindictively by
Galba, but he punished those cities and communities in Gaul (such as
Lugdunum, the Treveri and the Lingones) which had remained loyal to
Nero during the revolt of Vindex (c. 9, 2), and he rewarded those which
had supported that abortive rising (such as Vienna, the Sequani, Aedui,
and Arverni); cf. Tac. H. i 65, Galba reditus (“revenues'') Lugdunensium
occasione irae in fiscum verterat; multus contra in Viennenses honor: i 53,
Treveri ac Lingones quasque alias civitates atrocibus edictis aut damno
finium Galba perculerat. The plurals Hispaniae and Galliae denote the
various provinces mentioned in the notes on c. 8, 1 (‘‘Hispania Tarraconensis'') and c. 6, 1 (“Aquitania’”).

sibi: for the use of the reflexive see on Vesp. 15, 1, qui se
salutaverat.

murorum destructione: cf. Liv. viii 14, in Veliternos, quod totiens rebellassent, graviter saevitum; et muri deiecti, etc. The subst. destructio
occurs first in Quintilian (x, 5, 12) as a rhetorical term, sententiarum
destructio (= ἀνασκευή, refutatio; opp. to confirmatio, κατασκευή.)

praepositos: a vague title which has been variously interpreted. Ernesti
and Bremi explain it of the provincial governors put to death by Galba,
such as Clodius Macer in Africa and Fonteius Capito in Germany (c. 11),
but Suetonius is speaking of executions connected with Spain and Gaul.
Stahr takes it as higher officials, and La Harpe as Gallic and Spanish
chieftains. Baumg.-Crus. is probably right in understanding by it "militiae
praefecti (so Hofstee “duces militares"), as the word is used for
military officers in c. 16, 1: Oth. 1, 2: Tac. H. i 36, etc. Tacitus (H. i 37)
mentions Obultronius Sabinus and Cornelius Marcellus as slain by Galba
in Spain, and Betuus Chilo as slain in Gaul, but does not state what
positions they held there; again (H. i 6) he says: tardum Galbae iter et
cruentum interfectis Cingonio Varrone consule designato et Petronio
Turpiliano consulari: ille ut Nymphidii (see Galb. 11, n.) socius, hic ut
dux Neronis, where Ritter takes "dux Neronis" to mean that Turpilianus
was selected by Nero to command against Vindex and Galba.
procuratores: for these and their hostility to Galba see on c. 9, 2.

Tarraconensibus: the citizens of Tarraco, the capital of Hispania
Tarraconensis (c. 8, 1).
confiasset: ''melted down" to coin into money; cf. Aug. 52, argenteas
statuas conflavit exque iis (i.e. with the money coined from them)
aureas cortinas ("tripods'') Apollini Palatino dedicavit. Suetonius also
uses conftare in the fig. sense, Ner. 36, 1, coniuratio Beneventi conflata.

§2. classiarios: the classiarii or classici were the marines (ἐπιβάται),
either libertini or peregrini, thousands of whom had been brought by Nero
to Rome to support his waning power. Much controversy has arisen with
regard to the formation of the first legion of classiarii and whether the
classiarii mentioned here as so severely dealt with by Galba were those
already formed into that legion; the accounts given by Tacitus, Suetonius,
Plutarch, and Dio being difficult to reconcile. Heraeus and Spooner on
Tac. H. i 6 hold that Nero had formed the best of the classiarii into a
legion "prima Adiutrix classicorum” (cf. Tac. i 31, 36: ii 43, 67: iii 44:
Dio, lv 24, says that Galba created this legion); the rest wished to be
regularised in the same way as legionaries; Galba did not interfere with
Nero's legio classica, but dealt drastically with the other classiarii who
came out to claim similar privileges; his slaughter of them alienated the
legio classica, which consequently supported Otho against him, Tac. i 31,
legioni classicae diffidebatur infestae ob caedem commilitonum, quos primo
statim introitu trucidaverat Galba: i 36, universa classicorum legio sacramentum eius (i.e. Otho) accepit; Otho on his accession released the classiarii
who had escaped the slaughter, and had been imprisoned by Galba; he
gave them the organisation of a legion and held out hopes of a more
honourable service (i.e. in the legions) to other classiarii for the future,
thus securing the loyalty of the fleet (Tac. i 87). If Tacitus were our
only authority, these are certainly the most natural conclusions to draw
from his statements. On the other hand, Suetonius here seems to agree
with Plutarch (Galb. 15) who says that those who met Galba with their
demands were the ἐρέται (remiges or classiarii) whom Nero had formed
into a legion and declared to be legionary soldiers (οὺς εἰς ἓν τάγμα ὁ Νέρων
συλλοχίσας ἀπέφηνε στρατιώτας), and most modern writers accept this as
correct, assuming that the legion had not been fully organised at the time
of Nero's death and had not yet received its aquila and signa. (See
Dessau, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1, 307; Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa xii
1382; Parker, Rom. Legions 100.) Dio, lxiv 3, erroneously states that it
was the bodyguard (δορυφόροι, praetoriani) of Nero who met Galba and
claimed to be kept on in the same service.

cum redire ad pristinum statum cogeret: Suetonius is alone in stating
that Galba had already ordered them to resume their former position and
that they had refused. Plutarch says that when they made their demand
Galba was for postponing the matter, and that they, taking this postponement as a refusal, followed him with shouts and some of them even drew
their swords; whereupon he ordered the cavalry to charge. Dio agrees
with Plutarch.
lemma: cum redire ad pristinum statum cogeret

text:
aquilam et signa: Marius made the aquila the standard of the legion;
the 30 signa were the ensigns of the legionary maniples (the maniple consisting of two centuries). In form, a signum was a silver-plated pole
with a cross-bar near the top; below the bar were silver discs (phalerae)
along the pole, and from the bar hung ribands, often with silver ornaments
at their ends. The aquila was generally made of silver, sometimes of gold
(Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 438).

inmisso equite disiecit : so Plut., ἐκέλευσε τοὺς ἱππεῖς ἐμβαλεῖν αὐτοῖς.
Dio says that Galba attacked them with his army: ἐφῆκέ (inmisit) σφισι
τὸ στράτευμα. This happened at the Pons Mulvius, on the Tiber two
miles above Rome (Tac. H. i 87). Dio asserts that 7000 were slain, and
Tacitus (i 6) talks of many thousands: introitus in urbem trucidatis tot
milibus inermium militum infaustus omine atque ipsis etiam qui occiderant
formidolosus. Plutarch says that some were knocked down immediately
and others were cut down as they fled, and that it was a bad omen for
Galba that his entry into Rome should be through streams of blood and
over heaps of corpses. Any previous contempt for his age and weakness
was now changed into a universal horror and apprehension (πᾶσι φρικώδης
καὶ φοβερὸς ἐγένετο.)

decimavit: cf. Tac. i 37, where Otho says: Horror animum subit,
quotiens recordor feralem introitum et hanc solam Galbae victoriam, cum
in oculis urbis decumari deditos iuberet, quos deprecantes in fidem acceperat.
Polybius (vi 38) describes decimatio (δεκάτευσις), which was the penalty
when whole companies had failed in their duty. The tribune assembles
the legion, calls the defaulters to the front and after severely censuring
them selects about a tenth of them by lot. Those selected are punished
without mercy either by the fustuarium or by military execution; the
rest are put on rations of barley instead of wheat and quartered outside
the protection of the vallum. Appius Claudius thus dealt with his mutinous
army in 471 в.с. (Liv. ii 59); decimatio was also used by Crassus (Plut.
Crass. 10), Caesar (Dio xli 35), Octavian (Suet. Aug. 24, 2; Dio xlix 38),
etc.

Germanorum cohortem: Augustus at first had a bodyguard of
Calagurritani from Hispania Tarraconensis until he had defeated
M. Antonius, and then of Germans (prob. Batavi, cf. Dio lv 24) until the
clades Variana in 10 A.D. when Varus lost his legions in the Saltus
Teutoburgiensis and was himself slain (Aug. 49). The German bodyguard
was restored by Tiberius (Tac. A. i 24); Caligula also had Germans (Batavi)
as "corporis custodes," and they slew several of his assassins (Calig. 43;
58, 3). From numerous inscriptions (C.I.L. vi 4337-4345, 4716, 8802-8812)
we see that the bodyguards of Tiberius, Claudius, and Nero were drawn
from various German tribes subject to Rome, the Batavi, Frisii, Ubii, Suebi,
etc. They were legally slaves and not organised as soldiers into centuriae
or turmae but as a collegium divided into decuriae (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii
471; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 808). The dismissal of the Germans by Galba
seems to have been final, as they are not mentioned later. Julius Caesar
had a bodyguard of Spaniards which he had dispensed with before his
assassination (Iul. 86); M. Antonius was guarded by Ityraeans (Cic. Phil.
ii 112).
=
multis experimentis fidelissimam :
quae saepe se fidelissimam probaverat; cf. Sall. Iug. 46, sed Metello iam antea experimentis cognitum
erat genus Numidarum infidum.

sine commodo ullo: commodum was the regular word for the "bounty"
of money or land granted to time-expired soldiers (veterani, emeriti) on
their discharge (missio); Aug. 24, 2; 49, 2: Calig. 44, 1: Ner. 32, 1:
Vitell. 15, 1, n.: Cic. Phil. v 53, etc.

Cn. Dolabellae: probably a son of P. Dolabella (cons. 10 A.D.); his
wife Petronia had been earlier wedded to Vitellius before he became
emperor (Vitell. 6, Tac. H. ii 64); he was a relative of Galba (Tac. H. і 88),
and when Galba at the beginning of 69 was thinking of adopting a
successor, some of his friends recommended Dolabella (Plut. Galb. 23);
Otho banished him to Aquinum (Tac. l.c., Plut. Oth. 5); on Otho's death
(Apr. 69) he returned to Rome, but was put to death by Vitellius on a
charge of tampering with the troops (Tac. H. ii '63).

hortos: the horti Dolabellae, according to Gilbert (Topogr. Rom iii
377), extended from the Mons Pincius to the Campus Agrippae in which
was the castra of the cohors Germanorum. The Mons Pincius was known
as the Collis hortorum; on it, or close to it, were the horti Sallustii, Variani,
Lucullani, etc.

tendebat: tendere properly meant to stretch tents (tentoria)," and
then was used in the general sense "to be quartered or stationed,"
whether the troops were under canvas or in buildings; cf. c. 19, 1; Tac.
H. i 31, 55, 59: ii 66, etc.
..
§3. verene an falso: see note on Oth. 1, 1, incertum an ingenua.

ordinario: a “servus ordinarius” was a servant who was duly appointed
to a definite permanent position (officium ordinarium) and exercised
authority over those under him; the verb “ordinare” being used of
appointing to an "officium ordinarium,” e.g. Vesp. 23, dispensatorem
ordinavit. Cf. Sen. Ben. iii 28, Quo tandem ab istis gerulis raperis?
ad ostium alicuius ostiarii, ad hortos alicuius ne ordinarium quidem habentis
officium: id. Ep. 110, 1, unicuique nostrum paedagogum dari deum non
quidem ordinarium, sed hunc inferioris notae, ex eorum numero quos Ovidius
ait "de plebe deos": Ep. 53, 9, exercet philosophia regnum suum; dat
tempus, non accipit; non est res subsiciva; ordinaria est, domina est;
adest et iubet (see Summers ad loc.): Ulp. Dig. xiv 4, 5, si vicarius servi
mei negotietur, ordinario sciente.
dispensatori: see on Vesp. 22.

breviarium rationum: "abstract of accounts” (= “breviariae
rationes," Scaev. Dig. xxxiii 8, 26); see on Vesp. 21. In some of the
MSS., including M, rationem is read, and Bücheler would delete the word
or write breviariam rationem.

paropsidem: restored by Stephanus; M has par obsidem and the other
MSS. give parabsidem, parapsidem, per obsidem. παροψίς (ὄψον) was used
by the Gr. comic writers either for a dainty side-dish or entrée or for the
actual dish on which the dainty was served, though this latter use was
condemned by the Atticists (Phryn. παροψὶς τὸ ὄψον, οὐχὶ δὲ τὸ ἀγγεῖον.
Rutherford New Phrynichus p. 265).
In Latin writers it is always used
for the actual dish; see Mayor on Juv. iii 142, quam multa magmaque
paropside cenat?

Cano: this famous flute-player is mentioned by Martial (iv 5, 8;
x 3, 8). Philostratus (vit. Apoll. v 21) describes an interview at Rhodes
between Canus and Apollonius of Tyana on the subject of flute-playing,
and Plutarch (an seni res p. ger. sit, c. 5 p. 786c) quotes a dictum of his
that his audience never knew how much more pleasure he was getting from
his playing than they, otherwise they would demand payment from him
instead of paying to hear him.

choraulae: the choraules (χοραύλης) accompanied a chorus, generally
on double pipes. Martial (v 56) mentions the profession of a choraules as
a lucrative one, but (ix 77) would exclude such choral performances from
dinners, as drowning conversation: Quod optimum sit quaeritis convivium?
In quo choraules non erit.

denarios quinque: Plutarch (Galb. 16) says that Galba gave Canus
some gold pieces, and emphasized the fact that he was giving them out of
his own purse and not out of state funds: βουλόμενος δὲ τῆς περὶ τὰς δωρεὰς
ἀμετρίας καὶ πολυτελείας τοῦ Νέρωνος ἀποδεικνύναι μεγάλην μεταβολὴν ἀστοχεῖν ἐδόκει
τοῦ πρέποντος ("to miss the mark of propriety"). Κάνου γὰρ αὐλήσαντος αὐτῷ παρὰ
δεῖπνον (ἀκρόαμα δὲ ἦν ὁ Κάνος εὐδοκιμούμενον) ἐπαινέσας καὶ ἀποδεξάμενος ἐκέλευσεν
αὑτῷ κομισθῆναι τὸ γλωσσόκομον (“purse"), καὶ λαβὼν χρυσοῦς τινας ἐπέδωκε τῷ
Κάνῳ, φήσας ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων, οὐκ ἐκ τῶν δημοσίων χαρίζεσθαι. Dio (lxiv 2) says that
Galba was so penurious that on occasions he would not even give denarii
when making presents, but only sestertii: χρήματα ἀπλήστως, ἅτε καὶ πολλῶν
δεόμενος, ἤθροιζε, καὶ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐλάχιστα ἀνήλισκεν, ὥστε μηδὲ δραχμὰς ἔστιν οἷς,
ἀλλ᾽ ὀβολοὺς χαρίζεσθαι. Contrast the lavish sums which Vespasian gave to
musicians (Vesp. 19, 1).

peculiaribus: = propriis, ἰδίοις, denoting what was his own private
property; cf. Iul. 76, 3, peculiares servi (opp. to publici): Aug. 5, quasi
proprio suo ac peculiari deo. This adj. (from peculium "a slave's
savings'') is used in another sense in Vitell. 4.

loculis: loculi (always plur.) was used of any kind of a casket or case
with compartments for holding keys, jewels, etc.; in the sense of money-box
or purse it occurs in Hor. S. i 3, 17 ii 3, 146, Ер. ің 1, 175; Juv. i 89 (see
Mayor), x 46, xi 33; Mart. v 39, 7; etc.

non perinde gratus: this elliptical use of perinde with the implied
comparison omitted is frequent in Silver Latin; the meaning may often be
expressed in full by non perinde ac facile crederes, "not so much as you
might expect" and so "not very much"; e.g. Tib. 52, 1, itaque ne mortuo
quidem perinde adfectus est "not moved by his death in the way you would
expect'": Tac. A. ii 88, Romanis haud perinde celebris "not so famous as
he should have been": id. Agr. 10, mare perhibent ne ventis quidem
perinde attolli: id. H. ii 84, Vespasiano
haud perinde obstinante. See
also on "non adeo,” Oth. 5, 2.
.

spectaculo: the spectacles or shows were divided into the Circus, the
Amphitheatre, the Theatre, and the Stadium; theatrical performances being,
as Friedlaender says, the most frequent, the least costly and troublesome,
and the least appreciated.

Atellanis: the Atellani were the actors in the Atellanae (fabulae), a
burlesque popular comedy (transplanted from Atella in Campania to Rome),
which at first was an improvisation, but in Sulla's time had become literary.
It was generally a one-act piece with four stock characters: Pappus (the
dotard or pantaloon), Dossennus (the wise man, the dottore, the cunning
sharper), Bucco (the glutton), and Maccus (the booby). The Atellanae
were full of broad humour and indecent allusions. See Friedlaender,
Sitteng. ii¹º 112 sq., where a list of the subjects of the Atellanae is given.

canticum: this word was used in two senses: (a) a canticum proper was
a lyrical monody accompanied by a flute and sung with appropriate gesture;
(b) in a wider sense cantica included all the parts of a play which were
*written in trochaic septenarii and declaimed with musical accompaniment
as a kind of recitative. Livius Andronicus (c. 284-204) introduced the
custom of having the words of the lyrical canticum sung by a young slave
standing beside the flute-player, thus leaving the actor free to perform the
accompanying gestures. Such cantica formed part of the Atellanae and
Mimi as well as of the ordinary tragedies and comedies. The words and
airs of some of the cantica became so familiar to the public that they were
often sung separately like our operatic airs; cf. Suet. Iul. 84, where
cantica are sung at the funeral of Caesar and move the people by the
allusions which they find in them to the fate of the dictator. In Vitell. 11,
2, "cantica Neroniana” composed or sung by Nero are mentioned; in Tac.
A. xiii 15 we read of Britannicus singing a canticum from the Andromache
of Ennius which fitly described his own treatment by Nero. The licence of
actors in conveying political allusions by lines in the Atellanae and the keen
appreciation of such "hits" by the audience are often referred to by
Suetonius; see the passages cited on Vesp. 19, 2.
...

"Venit Onesimus a villa": the reading is uncertain: venit onesimus
is found only in a late MS., the others give venitione (or veditione) simus
(or simul). The name "Onesimus" had been conjectured by Augustinus
and is accepted by Oudendorp, Roth, and the recent editors. Lachmann
suggested "Dorsennus" (adopted by Ribbeck Com. Rom. frag. p. 274),
Dorsennus or Dossennus being a standing character in the Atellan plays
(see note above, and Wilkins on Hor. Ep. ii 1, 173). Other conjectures are
venit io Simus (Turnebus) and venit ohe Simus (Iac. Gronovius), Simus
"snub-nosed" being a rustic in comedy (cf. Pollux iv 19, τῷ ἀγροίκῳ
ἡ ῥὶς σιμή) and Galba being described as "adunco naso" in c. 21 infr. It
seems however from the context that the allusion must rather be to the
niggardly grasping nature of Galba, and Hofstee finds a special appropriateness in the name Onesimus: “nomen Onesimi a verbo quod est ὀνινάναι,
aptissimum est ad designandum hominem avarum.” This canticum was
probably a lament of the familia on the unwelcome arrival of the old master
from the country. Galba had been long absent from Rome, having lived
for many years in secessu before the governorship in Spain was offered to
him in 60; see c. 8, 1.

egerunt: they went through all the gestures appropriate to the singing
of the canticum; for the use of agere cf. Liv. vii 2, 9, (Livius Andronicus)
suorum carminum actor dicitur, cum
vocem obtudisset, puerum ad
canendum cum statuisset, canticum egisse aliquanto magis vigente motu,
quia nihil vocis usus impediebat.
..
...

maiore imperium: the truth of the maxim ἀρχὴ δείξει ἄνδρα was
illustrated in the case of Galba; cf. Tac. H. i 49, maior privato visus dum
privatus fuit, et omnium consensu capax imperii nisi imperasset: Auson.
Caes. vii, Spe frustrate ("deceptive in thy promise'") senex, privatus
sceptra mereri visus et (es, Peiper) imperio proditus inferior, fama tibi
melior iuveni; sed iustior ordo est | complacuisse dehinc, displicuisse prius.
...

adeo: of this use of adeo “ad augendas singulas voces, quibus postponitur sicut ye" there are numerous instances (including this) collected in
the Thes. Ling. Lat. i col. 614 sq., e.g. Claud. 37, 1, nulla adeo suspicio
tam levis exstitit: Ner. 35, 4, nullum adeo genus est: Iul. 14, 2, obtinuissetque adeo: Plaut. Amph. 1133, multo adeo melius (where see Palmer's
note): Verg. G. i 94, multum adeo iuvat: Cic. de or. ii 15, magis adeo
id facilitate quam alia ulla culpa mea contigit.

quanquam: used by Suetonius 15 times with the subjunctive (never
with the indicative). The few apparent instances of this constr. in Cicero
are to be explained either by the potential force of the subjunctive or by
assimilation of moods (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 442). A few examples are
found in Varr., Nep., the poets (e.g. Verg. Aen. vi 394, Ov. Met. xiv 465),
Liv., Colum., Sen., etc. The subjunctive is more frequent than the indicative
in Tacitus (Draeger, Synt. Tac. 201) and in the younger Pliny (Merrill on
Plin. Ep. i 12, 3).

documenta egregii principis daret: cf. Claud. 15, 1, proprio negotio
documentum daturus, quam aequus iudex in alieno negotio futurus sit.; for
the personal genitive following documentum cf. Vell. Pat. ii 42, documentum
tanti mox evasuri viri.

invisa: Tac. H. i 7, ceterum utraque caedes (i.e. the killing of Clodius
Macer and Fonteius Capito, see c. 11 supr.) sinistre accepta, et inviso semel
principi seu bene seu male facta parem invidiam adferebant. Dio (lxiv 2)
says that Galba, however guiltless himself, was held responsible for the
outrages committed by his freedmen, because he either permitted them or
was culpably ignorant of them.

§ 2. regebatur trium arbitrio: the same statement is made in Tac. H. i
13, potentia principatus divisa in Titum Vinium consulem, Cornelium
Laconem praetorii praefectum; nec minor gratia Icelo Galbae liberto.
Corneille (Othon i 1) makes Otho say of them: Je les voyais tous trois se
hâter sous un maître, Qui, chargé d'un long âge, a peu de temps à l'être;
Et tous trois à l'envi s'empresser ardemment A qui dévorerait ce règne
d'un moment.
paedagagos: (Aur. Vict.] Epit. 6, trium amicorum consilio, id est
Vinii, Cornelii, et Iceli cuncta disponens, adeo ut intra Palatinas aedes
pariter habitarent, et vulgo paedagogi dicerentur. So Tigellinus, the infamous minister of Nero, was denounced by the people as “τὸν διδάσκαλον·
καὶ παιδαγωγὸν τῆς τυραννίδος” (Plut. Galb. 17). The παιδαγωγός (whence
our "pedagogue" and "page'') was the slave-tutor who looked after the
manners and morals of children and conducted them to and from school;
his qualifications and his duties in a Roman house are described by Wilkins,
Roman Education, p. 40 sq.
The word came to be used in an extended
sense for a leader or guide, e.g. Sen. Ep. 110 unicuique nostrum paedagogum
dari deum inferioris notae.

T. Vinius: his career is sketched in Tac. H. i 48. His father was of
a praetorian family and his maternal (paternal, Dio xlvii 7) grandfather
was proscribed by the triumvirs in 43 в.с. He was born in 12 A.D. and
served as military tribune under Calvisius Sabinus, legatus of Pannonia
in Caligula's reign, but was disgraced and imprisoned for an intrigue with
his general's wife. Liberated under Claudius, he passed through the
cursus honorum and after his praetorship was appointed legatus legionis.
Though suspected of having stolen a gold cup from the table of Claudius,
he was made proconsul of Gallia Narbonensis and administered the province
strictly. Later he served in Spain as legatus of Galba, and when Galba
was made emperor, held the consulship with him in 69 A.D.; he was the
next victim of Otho's soldiers after they had slain Galba. Tacitus (l.c.)
says that he was "audax, callidus, promptus, et, prout animum intendisset,
pravus aut industrius eadem vi," but in i 6 (quoted below) he tersely
stigmatizes him as "deterrimus mortalium."

legatus: sc. legionis; cf. Plut. Galb. 4, Τίτος Οὐίνιος ὁ τοῦ στρατιωτικοῦ
τάγματος ἡγεμών (where see Hardy). Galba as governor of Hispania
Tarraconensis had one legion, vi Victrix (c. 10, 2). Vinius persuaded
Galba to aid the designs of Vindex; see on c. 9, 2.

cupiditatis immensae: Plut. Galb. 12, ἦν δὲ Οὐίνιος ἀργυρίου ἐσχάτως καὶ
παρ᾿ ὁντινοῦν (praeter omnes) ἥττων. Plutarch also tells how the notorious
Tigellinus bought his life by vast presents to Vinius, a striking proof
that there was nothing he would not do for money (μέγα δίδαγμα τοῦ μηδὲν
ἄπρακτον εἶναι παρὰ Οὐινίῳ μηδὲ ἀνέλπιστον τοῖς διδοῦσιν, Galb. 17). For cupiditas
see on Vesp. 1, 1.

Cornelius Laco: nothing is known as to his previous history; Tacitus
(H. i 6) describes his character: invalidum senem (i.e. Galba) Titus
Vinius et Cornelius Laco, alter deterrimus mortalium, alter ignavissimus,
odio flagitiorum oneratum contemptu inertiae destruebant (i.e. the
flagitia of Vinius and the inertia of Laco). The three "paedagogi”
quarrelled over the nomination of a colleague and successor to Galba,
Vinius supporting the adoption of Otho, Laco and Icelus that of
Piso (ib. 13); Laco refused to be sent by Galba to appease the
discontent of the Germanic legions under Vitellius (ib. 19); he concealed
from Galba the murmurings of his soldiers (ib. 26, multa erumpentis
seditionis indicia per conscios suppressa: quaedam apud Galbae aures praefectus Laco elusit, ignarus militarium animorum consiliique quamvis egregii,
quod non ipse afferret, inimicus et adversus peritos pervicax); he persuaded
Galba to adopt his fatal advice that he should present himself to the
angry soldiers who had declared for Otho (ib. 33); on Otho's accession he
was sentenced to be deported, but Otho secretly commissioned his guard to
assassinate him (ib. 46); Plutarch (Galb. 27) says, however, that he was
slain at the same time as Galba.
"conassessore: "assessores” (πάρεδροι), also called in later writers
siliarii,””‘“iuris studiosi,” were men versed in the law who sat as legal
advisers to various civil and military functionaries when administering
justice, assisting by their technical knowledge consuls, praetors, governors
of provinces, iudices, the praefectus praetorio, the praefectus urbi, etc.
The emperors appointed salaried assessores (consiliarii) to act with the
legati provinciarum (Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 318, ii³ 245). Paulus, who wrote
a work De Officio Adsessoris, specifies the matters with which they dealt:
Dig. i 22, 1, Omne iudicium adsessoris, quo iuris studiosi partibus suis
funguntur, in his fere causis constat: in cognitionibus, postulationibus,
libellis, edictis, decretis, epistulis. The famous jurisconsult Ulpian, like
Laco, held the position of assessor before becoming praefectus praetorio
under Alexander Severus (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 31).
praefectus praetorii: see on Tit. 4, 2 and 6, 1.

Icelus: this freedman of Galba was imprisoned at Rome by Nero when
he learnt of Galba's revolt in Spain, but he was released on Nero's death,
and allowed Nero's body to be cremated: Ner. 49, 4, permisit hoc Icelus,
Galbae libertus, non multo ante vinculis exsolutus in quae primo tumultu
coniectus fuerat. He conveyed to Galba the news of Nero's death and of
Galba's acclamation as emperor (Galb. 11 and 22), and Galba rewarded him
with the rank and insignia of an eques. He supported Laco against Vinius
(Tac. H. i 13) and opposed the adoption of Otho by Galba. On Galba's
death Otho had him executed as a “libertus,” ignoring the ingenuitas conferred by his rank as "eques”: Tac. i 46, in Marcianum Icelum ut in
libertum palam animadversum.

anulis aureis ornatus: the sign of equestrian dignity; see on c. 10, 3.
Plutarch says he became the most influential of the freedmen: Galb. 7,
τῷ δ᾽ ἀπελευθέρῳ (liberto) δακτυλίους τε χρυσοῦς ἔδωκε καὶ Μαρκιανὸς ὁ Ἴκελος ἤδη
καλούμενος εἶχε τὴν πρώτην ἐ ντοῖς ἀπελευθέροις δύναμιν : cf. Tac. H. i 13, пес
minor gratia Icelo Galbae liberto, quem anulis donatum equestri nomine
Marcianum vocitabant. Other instances of the bestowal of equestrian rank
on unworthy freedmen were by Nero on Pallas (Plin. Ep. viii 6), by
Vitellius on Asiaticus (Suet. Vitell. 12), and by Vespasian on Hormus (Tac.
Η. iv 39).

Marciani cognomine: his new name would be Servius Sulpicius
Marcianus, as he would assume the gentile nomen (Sulpicius) and praenomen
(Servius) of his patronus Galba. See Hardy on Plut. Galb. 7.

summae equestris gradus: the “summa equestris," i.e. the highest
office attainable by equites, was the praefectura praetorii (see on Tit. 4, 2).
Under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, an eques, according to the office he
held, was designated as (1) vir eminentissimus (ἐξοχώτατος), a prefect of
the praetorian guard; (2) vir perfectissimus (διασημότατος), any other
prefect, from the praefectus classis to the praefectus annonae, or a head
of the secretariate or of the finance department; (3) vir egregius (κράτιστος),
a holder of any of the lesser offices open to equites. Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr.
iii³ 565.

grassantibus: see on Vesp. 6, 2, omni rapinarum genere grassati.
Tacitus (H. i 37) uses the same word in Otho's speech denouncing the
rapacious outrages of Galba's ministers: Septem a Neronis fine menses
sunt et iam plus rapuit Icelus quam Polycliti et Vatinii et Aegiali (extortionate freedmen of Nero) quoad perierunt. Minore avaritia ac licentia
grassatus esset T. Vinius, si ipse imperasset: nunc et subiectos nos habuit
tanquam suos et viles ut alienos.

adeo se abutendum permisit: cf. the words of Nymphidius Sabinus in
Plut. Galb. 13, ἔφη Γάλβαν μὲν αὐτὸν εἶναι πρεσβύτην ἐπιεικῆ καὶ μέτριον, ἐλάχιστα
δὲ τοῖς αὑτοῦ χρώμενον λογισμοῖς ὑπὸ Οὐινίου καὶ Λάκωνος οὐκ εὖ διοικεῖσθαι. abutor
was used with the acc. in early Lat., hence the gerundive; Cicero has
utendus, fruendus, perfruendus, fungendus (Kühner-Stegmann, i 733).

ut vix ipse sibi constaret: he had shown the same inconsistency in his
administration of Hispania Tarraconensis; see c. 9, 1.
parcior: Tacitus (H. i 49) describes Galba as "pecuniae alienae non
appetens, suae parcus, publicaė avarus.”

principi electo: the emperors before him had succeeded to the empire
as a kind of inheritance: cf. Galba's own words in the speech attributed to
him in Tac. H. i 16, Sub Tiberio et Gaio et Claudio unius familiae quasi
hereditas fuimus: loco libertatus erit, quod eligi coepimus.

illud aetatis: 73 years of age. For the adverbial accusative cf. Cic.
Phil. viii 5, cum illud esset aetatis; similarly id (hoc, istuc) aetatis, id
temporis, hoc noctis, illud horae (Ner. 26, 2, numquam publico se illud horae
commisit); in Tac. A. xii 18 we find nemo id auctoritatis aderat. See
Kühner-Stegmann, i 306.
8, 3.
§ 3. ex utroque ordine: senatorio et equestri; cf. Vesp. 9, 2: Dom.

inauditos: = indictâ (incognita) causâ, re inoratâ, a post-Aug. use found
in Tac., Plin. Ep., etc.; cf. Vitell. 14, 4: Claud. 38, 2. In class. Lat.
inauditus means 'unheard of,” “strange," in which sense it is used in
Calig. 19, 1; 40: Ner. 42, 1.

civitates R. raro dedit: Galba granted the franchise to the Gallic communities of the Sequani, Aedui, and Arverni, who had supported Vindex
(Tac. H. i 8, 51); it is doubtful whether it was bestowed on these people
at large or only on a certain number of their leading men (see Heraeus
and Spooner on Tac. l.c. and Hardy on Plut. Galb. 18). The ius civitatis
was very charily conferred by Augustus (Aug. 40, 3, civitates R. parcissime
dedit); so too by Tiberius and Caligula; Claudius was very lavish (Dio lx
17, τὴν πολιτείαν πάνυ ἀνέδην, τοῖς μὲν κατ' ἄνδρα, τοῖς δὲ καὶ ἀθρόοις, ἐδίδου), and
Nero also gave it indiscriminately (cf. Ner. 12, 1, where he bestows
“diplomata civitatis R.'' on Greek dancers).

iura trium liberorum: under the Lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus
(18 B.c.) and an amplification of it, the Lex Papia Poppaea (9 A.D.),
Augustus rewarded those with three or more children and penalised the
unmarried and those who were married but childless. The unmarried were
taxed and could not inherit by will, and the childless could only take
half a hereditas or legatum, the remainder going to the Treasury as a
caducum. A fictitious ius liberorum, however, was granted by the senate
in several cases and later by the emperors from Claudius on (Dio lv 2,
Suet. Claud. 19). Martial obtained it from Domitian (Epigr. ii 91, 92)
and Statius (Silv. iv 8, 20) mentions another grant by him; Pliny the
Younger was granted it by Trajan (Plin. Ep. x 2) and also obtained it
for some of his friends including Suetonius (Ep. x 94, 95). A preference
in election to offices and choice of provinces was given to persons having
children (Tac. A. ii 51 xv 19 Plin. Ep. vii 16). See Roby, Roman Private
Law i 381; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 888.

uni atque alteri: "one or two," "a few"; cf. Vesp. 4, 6, uno atque
altero proelio: Iul. 20, 5, uno atque altero frustra nominatis: Tib. 63, 2:
Claud. 12, 3. Suetonius has only unus et (or atque) alter; Tacitus uses
unus et alter, unus alterque, unus aut alter, unus alterve to denote "indefinitum numerum eumque non magnum” (Gerber and Greef, Lex. Tас.).

sextam decuriam: three decuriae of iudices were formed by the Lex
Aurelia (70 B.C.) which enacted that the iudices should be chosen from
the three classes of senatores, equites, and tribuni aerarii. Julius Caesar
by a Lex Iulia iudiciaria (46 B.c.) did away with the decuria of the
tribuni aerarii, but a third decuria was restored by M. Antonius (44 в.с.),
the property qualification being removed and service as a centurion or
in the cavalry or in the legio Alauda substituted. Augustus added to the
three existing decuriae (which, according to Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 535,
he composed entirely of equites) a fourth of ducenarii, i.e. those whose
census reached 200,000 sesterces (half that of an eques), this fourth decuria
adjudicating in cases involving smaller amounts ("de levioribus summis,”
Aug. 32, 3). Caligula added a fifth decuria to lighten the labours of the
jurymen ("ut levior labor iudicantibus foret," Calig. 16, 2).

concessum a Claudio beneficium: Claud. 23, 1, Rerum actum divisum
antea in hibernos aestivosque menses coniunxit (“actus rerum" denotes
the legal term-time during which the courts sat). Augustus, to expedite
legal business, added to the law-term thirty extra days which had previously
been given over to ludi honorarii, and as the jurymen tried to shirk their
onerous duties, he reluctantly granted each decuria, in its turn, exemption
for one year, and gave all four decuriae vacation in November and
December (Aug. 32). By the time of Claudius this had come to be altered,
and there were legal vacations in spring and autumn; Claudius apparently
arranged that the iudices should serve continuously from spring to the
beginning of winter (see Smilda on Claud. 23, 1). For "beneficium” see
note on Tit. 8, 1.

senatoria et equestria officia: the positions held by senators under the
Principate included the offices of state at Rome, provincial governorships,
the command of the legions, the prefectship of the city, and commissionerships (curationes) of the water-supply, roads, public works, etc. See
Greenidge, Rom. Publ. Life p. 401. On the other hand, the knights (equites)
held a number of administrative and financial positions from which senators
were excluded: the government of Egypt was reserved to them, and the
smaller provinces to the north of Italy were under equestrian governors;
the commanders of the fleet were equites, as were many of the prefects
appointed by Augustus, e.g. the praefectus annonae, pr. praetorii, pr.
vigilum; most important of all were the financial offices entrusted to them:
the imperial tax-officers (procuratores Augusti) in the provinces were chosen
from the equites alone. Presumably the officia which Galba wished to circumscribe were more especially the provincial governorships and fiscal
procuratorships.

nisi invitis ac recusantibus: Galba may have hoped by this novel.
method of appointment to secure provincial governors and commanders of
legions, who, being free from any desire of self-aggrandisement, would not
endanger the emperor's position; also fiscal procurators who would not
oppress by merciless exactions the wretched provincials as those in Galba's
own province had done (see on c. 9, 1). Vespasian promoted the most
rapacious procurators, that they might be the richer when he condemned
them later (Vesp. 16, 2). Galba's mode of appointing to public offices was
adopted by Alexander Severus: praefectum praetorii fecit, qui ne fieret
etiam fugerat, dicens invitos non ambientes in re publica conlocandos
(Lamprid. Alex. 19).

liberalitates Neronis: liberalitates = dona (abstract for concrete, see
on "custodias" Dom. 14, 4) as in Claud. 29, 1, revocatas liberalitates eius;
so in sing., Tib. 46, una modo liberalitate milites prosecutus. Tacitus is the
first to use liberalitas in this way. The enormous sum of 2200 million
sesterces (nearly £20,000,000) is said to have been lavished by Nero (Tac.
H. i 20); cf. Ner. 30, 2, Quare nec largiendi nec absumendi modum tenuit.
In Tiridatem, quod vix credibile videatur, octingena nummum milia diurna
erogavit abeuntique super sestertium milies contulit. Menecraten citharoedum et Spiculum murmillonem triumphalium virorum patrimoniis aedibusque donavit.

revocandas curavit: the efforts made by Galba to recover Nero's
bounties from the recipients are described also in Tac. H. i 20: Appellari
("to be sued") singulos iussit, decuma parte liberalitatis apud quemque
corum relicta. At illis vix decumae super portiones erant, isdem erga aliena
sumptibus, quibus sua prodegerant, cum rapacissimo cuique ac perditissimo
non agri aut faenus (“capital'') sed sola instrumentà vitiorum manerent.
Exactioni triginta (Suet. says 50) equites R. praepositi, novum officii genus
et ambitu ac numero onerosum. Ubique hasta et sector ("sales and
brokers'") et inquieta urbs actionibus ("trials"; auctionibus, Ritter and
Orelli). Dio (lxiii 14) mentions that the sum of a million sesterces given
by Nero to the Ἑλλανοδίκαι (judges at the Olympic games) was recovered
by Galba, and also 400,000 sesterces given to the Pythian prophetess for
favourable oracles. In 24 A.D. Tiberius wrested from the estate of C. Silius
the bounty granted him by Augustus (Tac. A. iv 20, liberalitas Augusti
avulsa).

scaenici: stage-players, actors (histriones); cf. Cic. Off. i 31, 114;
Planc. 30; Verr. iii 184. Nero himself is spoken of contemptuously as “ille
scaenicus" in Tac. A. xv 59; in his mania for the stage he even thought of
appearing as a professional actor (inter scaenicos) when one of the praetors
offered him a million sesterces to perform at one of his shows (Ner. 21, 2).

xystici: athletes"; Aид. 45, 4, xysticorum certationes: Tertull.
Spect. 30, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasio sed in igne iaculati;
ib. 20, atrocitas harenae, vanitas xysti: Ulp. Dig. iii 2, 4, omnes opinantur
ignoet utile videtur ut neque thymelici neque xystici neque agitatores
miniosi habeantur. The xystus was a covered colonnade where athletes
exercised in winter (Vitruv. v 11); it is the Gr. ξυστός (from ξύειν το
scrape, make smooth) and may originally have denoted the part of the
gymnasium where the athletes scraped off the oil and dust with the strigilis,
though some think that the name came from the smooth polished floor.
xystus was also used for an open colonnade, a garden-walk or terrace
adorned with flowers and shrubs, as in Aug. 72, 3, xystis et nemoribus
excoluit praetoria ("country mansions'') sua, and in Pliny's description
of his villas (Ep. ii 17, v 6). Nero's passion for Greek athletics is mentioned in Ner. 12, 3: Instituit et quinquennale certamen primus omnium
Romae, more Graeco triplex, musicum, gymnicum, equestre, quod appellavit Neronia; dedicatisque thermis atque gymnasio senatui quoque et equiti
oleum praebuit; Tac. A. xiv 47, etc.

auferretur emptoribus: this is omitted by Tacitus (H. i 20) but
mentioned in Plut. Galb. 16, τοὺς πριαμένους παρ' αὐτῶν ἢ λαβόντας ὁτιοῦν
ἀνεζήτει καὶ παρ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐξέπραττε.

quando nequirent: quando is used here in a temporal and not in a
causal sense; see on Vesp. 16, 3.
§2. comites: see on Vesp. 4, 4.

libertos: Tac. H. i 7, venalia cuncta, praepotentes liberti, servorum
(used contemptuously for libertorum) manus subitis avidae et tanquam
apud senem festinantes; eademque (i.e. the same as in Nero's court) novae
auiae mala, aeque gravia, non aeque excusata. The freedmen are Icelus
and Halotus (Spooner on Tac. l.c. adds Tigellinus, but he was not a freedman). Plutarch (Galb. 16) blames Vinius for bringing Galba into disrepute by the attempt to recover the bounties of Nero and for his own
shameless trafficking: φθόνον δὲ καὶ μῖσος εἶχεν Οὐίνιος, ὡς τοῖς μὲν ἄλλοις ἅπασιν
ἀνελεύθερον παρέχων τὸν ἡγεμόνα καὶ μικρολόγον, αὐτὸς δὲ χρώμενος ἀσώτως καὶ
λαμβάνων πάντα καὶ πιπράσκων. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ησίοδος ἀρχομένου τε πίθου καὶ λήγοντος
κορέσασθαι φησὶ δεῖν, ὁ δὲ Οὐίνιος ὁρῶν ἀσθενῆ καὶ γέροντα τὸν Γάλβαν ἐνεπίμπλατο
τῆς τύχης, ὡς ἅμα μὲν ἀρχομένης, ἅμα δὲ φθινούσης.

addici: the regular word for knocking a thing down at an auction; e.g.
Aug. 24, 1, equitem Romanum bonaque subiecit hastae ("auction''), quem
tamen liberto suo addixit: Calig. 38, 4, nec licendi ('bidding'") finem
factum quoad tredecim gladiatores sestertio nonagies addicerentur.

vectigalia: see on Vesp. 16, 1, omissa sub Galba vectigalia. Cf. Plut.
Galb. 18, ἐδόκουν γὰρ οὐ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος, ἀλλ᾽ ὠνούμενοι παρὰ Οὐινίου
τυγχάνειν ἀνέσεώς τε δασμῶν καὶ πολιτείας.
impunitates: the pl. is not found earlier, but Cicero has immunitates.

populo deposcente supplicium: in the circus and in the theatre the
people clamoured for the death of Tigellinus; cf. Plut. Galb. 17, οὐδένος
γὰρ οὕτω θεάματος ἐρασθεὶς ὁ ῾Ῥωμαίων δῆμος ὡς τοῦ Τιγελλῖνον ἰδεῖν ἀπαγόμενον,
οὐδὲ παυσάμενος ἐν πᾶσι θεάτροις καὶ σταδίοις αἰτούμενος ἐκεῖνον : Tac. Η. i 72, non
alium pertinacius ad poenam flagitaverunt Eo infensior populus, addita
ad vetus Tigellini odium recenti Titi Vinii invidia, concurrere ex tota urbe
in Palatium ac fora, et ubi plurima vulgi licentia, in circum ac theatra effusi
seditiosis vocibus strepere. See also Dio lxiv 3, cited below.
...

Haloti: a eunuch who held the position of "food taster” (“praegustator," Claud. 44) at the court of Claudius. He was one of the agents
used by Agrippina to administer to Claudius the poison prepared by Locusta
(Тас. 4. xii 66), and he continued his infamous career under Nero.

Tigillini: “Tigillinus'" (not "Tigellinus'') is the form attested by our
MSS. here, by those of Martial (iii 20, 16), and by the Schol. on Juv. i 155;
the Medicean MS. of Tacitus also gives "Tigillinus" except in Ann. xiv 48,
xv 37. On the other hand, "Tigellinus" is found in the text of Juvenal
(l.c.) and in most of the MSS. of Plutarch, Dio, and Josephus; see Prosop.
Imp. Rom. iii 250. There is also doubt with regard to the first part of his
name, whether it was "Sophonius" or "C. Ofonius"; the best MSS, in
Tac. H. i 72 (see Heraeus) and inscriptions give "Ofonius." He was a
son of a native of Agrigentum, and early became notorious for his beauty
and immorality. He was banished by Caligula for intriguing with the
emperor's sisters. Favoured by Agrippina he was made praetorian prefect
by Nero in 63 and encouraged Nero in his licentious career (intimis libidinibus adsumptus, Tac. A. xiv 51). He and the empress Poppaea formed
Nero's privy council (intimum consiliorum, A. xv '61); to them was largely
due the number of executions after Piso's conspiracy in 65. He deserted
Nero at his downfall and helped to win the soldiers for Galba. On Otho's
accession he was forced to commit suicide (Tac. H. i 72, infamem vitam
foedavit etiam exitu sero et inhonesto). See Mayor's note on Juv. i 155,
Pone Tigellinum: taeda lucebis in illa | qua stant ardentes qui fixo gutture
fumant.
emissariis: see on Dom. 11, 1.

incolumes praestitit: Dio (lxiv 3) says that Galba, true to his principle
that an emperor should not act under compulsion, refused to yield to the
popular clamour, though, had it not been for this clamour, he would probably have executed Tigellinus and his fellows, as he executed Narcissus,
Locusta the poisoner, and others. According to Tacitus (H. i 72) it was
the influence of Vinius which protected Tigellinus: Apud Galbam Titi
Vinii potentia defensus (Tigellinus) praetexentis servatam ab eo filiam.
Haud dubie servaverat non clementia, quippe tot interfectis, sed effugium
in futurum, quia pessimus quisque diffidentia praesentium mutationem
pavens adversus publicum odium privatam gratiam praeparat. Plutarch
(Galb. 17) adds that Tigellinus had secured the protection of Vinius by
large sums of money.

procuratione: the particular procuratorship is nowhere specified; he
may be the same Halotus as is mentioned in C.I.L. vi 8833, Halotus
Aug(usti) l(ibertus) proc(urator).

saevitiae increpuit: cf. Calig. 39, 2, avaritiae singulos increpans:
Apul. Apol. 77, levitatis et inconstantiae increpitus. For the wide use of
the Genitive of the Charge in non-class. Latin see Kühner-Stegmann, i 463.

edicto: Plutarch (l.c.) says that the edict alleged that Tigellinus was'
dying of a wasting disease, and it asked the people not to stain the rule of
Galba by needless bloodshed: ὁ ῾Ῥωμαίων δῆμος ἐπεπλήχθη (increpitus est)
διαγράμματι (edicto) τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος Τιγελλῖνον μὲν οὐ πολὺν ἔτι βιώσεσθαι
φάσκοντος χρόνον ὑπὸ φθινάδος νόσου δαπανώμενον, ἐκείνους δὲ παραιτουμένου μὴ
διαγριαίνειν μηδὲ τυραννικὴν ποιεῖν τὴν ἡγεμονίαν.

prope: propere, a variant in the later MSS., was approved by Burman
and read by Oudendorp.

offensis: in all the other passages (Iul. 19, 2; Tib. 13, 2: 34, 2;
Calig. 27, 4; Ner. 2, 1:38, 1) where Suetonius uses offensus it means
"offended," and so the reading offensis here is preferable to the variant
offensus (XN) "offensive," which is adopted by Roth.
vel praecipua: see on Dom. 19.

flagrabat invidia: "was in a blaze of unpopularity"; cf. Aug. 27, 3,
multiplici flagravit invidia: Tib. 44, 1, maiore adhuc et turpiore infamia
flagravit. The phrases flagrare invidia, infamia, etc. are common in Cicero.
Wickham on Hor. S. i 4, 125, cum flagret rumore malo, explains flagrare
as meaning "to be in the full glow of," i.e. to be the conspicuous victim
of.

in verba eius
iurantibus: see on c. 11.

donativum grandius solito: Plutarch (Galb. 2) says it was 7500
drachmae (= 30,000 sesterces) to each of the praetorians, and 1250 drachmae
(= 5000 sesterces) to each of the other soldiers. Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) calculates the total sum thus promised as 900 million sesterces, and suggests
that Nymphidius, when making the promise, probably knew that Galba
would refuse to pay the sum and hoped to gain by the consequent dissatisfaction of the troops. For the practice of granting such donativa to
the soldiers, and the amounts given by other emperors see on Dom. 2, 3.

praepositi: Nymphidius Sabinus (see on c. 11) and the other officers
who repeated his promises to their men.

pronuntiassent: = promisissent; cf. Dom. 4, 5: Calig. 46: Iul. 19, 1:
26, 2. So in Cicero, e.g. Att. i 16, 13, P. Clodium pronuntiare solitum esse
et non dare.
..

legere se militem consuesse: Tacitus (H. i 5) says that these were
noble words from the point of view of the commonwealth but dangerous
for Galba himself: accessit Galbae vox pro re publica honesta, ipsi anceps,
legi a se militem, non emi. Dio (lxiv 3) mentions the incident as an
example of Galba's strength of will in refusing to submit to dictation:
εἰ καὶ τῇ ἡλικίᾳ τῇ τε νόσῳ ἐκεκμήκει, ἀλλὰ τῇ διανοίᾳ ἤκμαζεν, οὐδ᾽ ἠξίου τὸν
αὐτοκράτορα ἀναγκαζόμενόν τι ποιεῖν· ἀμέλει καὶ τοῖς δορυφόροις (praetorianis)
αὐτοῦσι χρήματα οὐκ ἔδωκε, καὶ ἔφη γε ὅτι “καταλέγειν στρατιώτας ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἀγοράζειν
εἴωθα.” Plutarch characterizes this utterance of Galba as “ φωνὴ ἡγεμόνι
μεγάλῳ πρέπουσα” (Galb. 18).
eo nomine: eâ causâ; see on Vesp. 4, 3.

exacerbavit: Plut. (l.c.), πυθομένοις τοῦτο δεινὸν εἰσῆλθε μίσος καὶ ἄγριον πρὸς
αὐτόν. Tacitus (H. i 25) says that the soldiers were turned against Galba
"ira et desperatione dilati toties donativi.”

indignitate: indignitas is used here in its subjective sense of "indignation"; cf. Cic. Att. x 8, 3, tacita esse poterit indignitas nostra?: Liv.
vii 7, 2, plenus irae et indignitatis. The objective sense of "indignity"
is much more frequent, and Baumg.-Cr. explains indignitas in our passage
by contumelia. In Calig. 23, 2, indignitates means "indignities," but in
the only other place where Suetonius uses the word, Claud. 36, Messalinae
amorem flagrantissimum non tam indignitate contumeliarum quam periculi
metu abiecit, it seems to mean "indignation" (cf. Liv. viii 28, 6, ingens
vis hominum cum aetatis miseratione tum indignitate iniuriae accensa
concurrit); Rolfe and Pike, however, explain indignitate contumeliarum as
"her unseemly and insulting conduct."

removens
plerosque: Tacitus (H. i 20) gives the names of some of
the officers cashiered by Galba when he heard of the revolt of the legions
in Germany: exauctorati per eas dies tribuni, e praetorio Antonius Taurus
et Antonius Naso, ex urbanis cohortibus Aemilius Pacensis, e vigilibus
Iulius Fronto.

ut suspectos et Nymphidi socios: those who owed their promotion to
Nymphidius incurred the suspicion of Galba; cf. Tac. H. i 25, stimulant
primores militum per beneficia Nymphidii ut suspectos. For the attempts of
Nymphidius to seduce the praetorians from their allegiance to Galba see
note on c. 11. His favourites, after their humiliation by Galba, flocked to
support Otho; Plut. Galb. 23, πλεῖστοι δὲ τῶν περὶ Τιγελλῖνον καὶ Νυμφίδιον ἐν
τιμῇ γεγονότων ἀπερριμμένοι καὶ ταπεινὰ πράττοντες ἐφθείροντο (“rushed headlong")
