πρὸς αὐτὸν (i.e. Otho) καὶ συνηγανάκτουν καὶ παρώξυνον.

§ 2. superioris Germaniae exercitus: the army of Upper Germany
consisted of the following legions: iv Macedonica, xxi Rapax, xxii Primigenia (ii Augusta, which originally belonged to it, had been sent to Britain
by Claudius, Tac. A. xiv 37). Tacitus (H. i 8) describes the dangerous
temper of the armies in Germany at this time: Germanici exercitus, quod
periculosissimum in tantis viribus (7 legions in all), solliciti et irati, superbia
recentis victoriae (over Vindex) et metu tanquam alias partes (i.e. the side
of Verginius Rufus) fovissent. Tarde a Nerone desciverant; nec statim
pro Galba Verginius: an imperare noluisset dubium: delatum ei a milite
imperium conveniebat. Fonteium Capitonem occisum (note on c. 11)
etiam qui queri non poterant, tamen indignabantur. Dux deerat, abducto
Verginio per simulationem amicitiae; quem non remitti atque etiam reum
esse tanquam suum crimen ("an accusation against themselves'') accipiebant. Galba replaced Verginius by Hordeonius Flaccus, a feeble old man
incapable of maintaining discipline, and sent Aulus Vitellius to command in
Lower Germany (Vitell. 7, 1). Cf. also Dio lxiv 4, and Plut. Galb. 18
where an example is given of the mutinous spirit of the army under
Hordeonius Flaccus: one day when games were being held and the officers
according to custom made vows for the happiness of the emperor, the
soldiers turbulently added the words "If he deserves it." For the
boundaries, etc., of the two Germanies (superior and inferior) see on
Vitell. 7, 1.

Gallos et Vindicem: see on c. 9, 2, and c. 11. Plut. (l.c.), οἱ ὑπὸ
Φλάκκῳ, μεγάλων μὲν ἀξιοῦντες αὑτοὺς διὰ τὴν μάχην, ἣν ἐμαχέσαντο πρὸς Οὐΐνδικα,
μηδένος δὲ τυγχάνοντες, ἀπαρηγόρητοι τοῖς ἄρχουσιν ἦσαν.
Kal. Ian. adigi

recusarunt: Tac. H. i 12, Paucis post kalendas
Ianuarias diebus Pompeii Propinqui procuratoris e Belgica litterae
adferuntur, superioris Germaniae legiones rupta sacramenti reverentia
imperatorem alium flagitare et senatui ac populo Romano arbitrium eligendi
permittere, quo seditio mollius acciperetur. Tacitus (c. 55) says further
that the army of Lower Germany did take the oath to Galba, though not
without a turbulent display on the part of some, whereas in Upper Germany
the two legions (iv and xxii) which were quartered at Moguntiacum (Mainz)
broke in pieces the images of Galba; cf. Plut. Galb. 22, τὰς μὲν εἰκόνας τοῦ
Γάλβα προσελθόντες ἀνέτρεψαν καὶ κατέσπασαν, αὐτοὶ δ᾽ ὀμόσαντες ὑπὲρ συγκλήτου
(senatus) καὶ δήμου ῾Ῥωμαίων διελύθησαν.

sacramento: for the oath of fealty to the emperor and its renewal
at certain times see on c. 11.

in nomen senatus: cf. c. 10, 1. Tacitus (i 55) observes that such a
form of words was so long disused that it had become meaningless: ac ne
reverentiam imperii exuere viderentur, senatus populique Romani oblitterata
iam nomina sacramento advocabant: c. 56, in senatus ac populi Romani
verba iurasse, id sacramentum inane visum.

praetorianos: the various occasions on which the praetorians played
the part of "king-makers" are collected by Cagnat (Daremberg-Saglio, iv
632 sqq.). Caligula's death was due to them, and on the next day they
saluted Claudius as emperor; Nero was recognised by them, and the
senate conformed to their decision; they support Galba, and then desert
him for Otho; they overthrow Domitian and choose Nerva; Marcus Aurelius
and Verus on their adoption hasten to secure the support of the praetorians
by a largess of 20,000 sesterces to each; they plot the death of Commodus;
they elevate Pertinax to the throne, and in 87 days put him to death;
they auction the Roman empire to Didius Julianus, who promised to each
of them 6,250 denarii. Septimius Severus (193-211 A.D.) dealt sternly
with them and reorganised them, but they soon recovered their dominant
influence in state affairs. They put to death Maximus and Balbinus, and
hailed Gordian III as emperor (238 A.D.); to them Maxentius, the predecessor of Constantine, applied to be saluted as Augustus. They were
finally disbanded by Constantine in 312 A.D.

displicere imperatorem in Hispania factum: the jealousy felt by the
troops in Germany at the elevation of Galba by those in Spain is illustrated
by the words of one of the mutineers in Upper Germany urging the selection
of Vitellius, the commander in the Lower province: “φέρε, τοῦτον ἑλόμενοι
δείξωμεν ἀνθρώποις πᾶσιν ὡς Ἰβήρων καὶ Λυσιτανῶν ἀμείνους ἐσμὲν αὐτοκράτορα
αἱρεῖσθαι.” (Plut. Galb. 22). Galba's proclamation as emperor by the 6th
legion in Spain disclosed what Tacitus calls a "constitutional secret," that
an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome (H. i 4, evolgato imperii
arcano, posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri).

eligerent: Tacitus (H. i 12) says that the Germanic legions left the
““arbitrium eligendi" to the senate and Roman people; but the senate, of
course, could merely ratify the choice made by the praetorians.

nuntiatum est: by a despatch from Pompeius Propinquus, procurator
of Gallia Belgica; see Tac. H. i 12 quoted on c. 16, 2.

despectui esse: despectus in Caesar (and Lucretius) is used in the
sense of a "view downwards"; it is once used for an "object of con-
tempt' in Rhet. Her. 1v 39, 51, filii parvi
ludibrio et despectui paternis
inimicis erunt oppositi; in post-Aug. prose it is used both for "contempt"
and "object of contempt" (in this latter sense only in dat., as here and
Tac. H. iv 57, non adeo turbatam rem Romanam ut Treveris etiam
despectui sit). Cf. contemptui, despicatui, esse, habere, ducere. Cicero
has despicientia despising," "contempt."

orbitatem: Plut. Galb. 19, ὁ δὲ (Γάλβας) φοβηθείς, ὡς μὴ μόνον διὰ τὸ γῆρας,
ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὴν ἀπαιδίαν καταφρονούμενος, ἐβουλεύετο παῖδα θέσθαι (“adopt ") τῶν
ἐπιφανῶν τινα νεανίσκον καὶ διάδοχον ἀποδεῖξαι τῆς ἀρχῆς: Tac. H. ii 1 materia
sermonibus senium et orbitas principis et intemperantia civitatis, donec
unus eligatur, multos destinandi.

Pisonem Frugi Licinianum: the full name was Lucius Calpurnius Piso
Frugi Licinianus. He was son of M. Licinius Crassus Frugi (cons. 27 A.D.)
and Scribonia, a granddaughter of Sex. Pompeius. Of his three brothers
one was put to death by Claudius, one by Nero, and the third, Licinius
Crassus Scribonianus, refused the empire when it was offered to him by
Antonius Primus (Tac. H. iv 39). Born in 38, he was for long exiled by
Nero (Tac. i 48) and so held no magistracies at Rome. He only survived
his adoption by Galba for four days, as he was dragged from the temple
of Vesta and murdered by Otho's soldiers at the time when Galba was
slain.
egregium iuvenem: Plutarch (Galb. 23) describes him as “veavíaς ἐν τῇ
πρὸς πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν εὐφυΐᾳ τὸ κόσμιον καὶ αὐστηρὸν ἐμφανέστατα ἔχων,” “a young
man whose self-control and austerity were the most conspicuous traits in
a character naturally inclined to every virtue"; cf. Tac. H. i 14, vultu
habituque moris antiqui et aestimatione recta severus, deterius interpretantibus tristior habebatur: Dio lxiv 5, νεανίσκος εὐγενής, ἐπιεικής, φρόνιμος.
testamento: Tacitus and Plutarch make no mention of Piso's having
been named as heir in Galba's will. Dessau (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1,
313) regards Suetonius' statement here as quite unreliable.

semper: Bentley's insuper may be right; Cornelissen suggested nuper.
If genuine, semper means that Galba never altered his will in the way, for
example, that Julius Caesar did; cf. Iul. 83, where we learn that Caesar,
from his first consulship to the beginning of the civil war, was wont to
write down Cn. Pompeius as his heir and to read this to the assembled
soldiers; in his last will, however, he named three other heirs, and at the
end of the will adopted Gaius Octavius into his family and gave him his
name (in familiam nomenque adoptavit).
..

in bona et nomen adscitum: cf. Claud. 39, 2, (Claudius) adsciturus in
nomen Neronem; Tac. H. i 15, Crassi subolem (i.e. Piso Licinianus) in
penates meos adsciscere: A. iii 30, Crispum C. Sallustius
in nomen
adscivit. For the so-called adoption by will, which was really appointment
of heir with direction to bear testator's name, see Roby, Roman Private
Law, i 59 n. After his adoption as Galba's successor, Piso's name seems
to have been Servius Sulpicius Galba Caesar; on Jan. 10, the day of his
adoption, the Fratres Arvales sacrificed "[ob adoptione[m Ser. Sulpici
Gal]bae C[aesaris]'' (Henzen, Acta Fratr. Arv. xci).

repente adprehendit: this account differs from that in Tac. H. i 14
where we are told that Galba, having decided to adopt a successor, held a
"council for the election of an emperor (comitia imperii)" at which were
present Vinius, Laco, Marius Celsus (consul designate) and Ducenius
Geminus (prefect of the city). Galba, after a few remarks on his advanced
years, ordered Piso to be summoned "seu propria electione sive, ut quidam
crediderunt, Lacone instigante." Galba knew that some of his friends
would have preferred Otho or Dolabella (for whom see c. 12, 2) to Piso;
Vinius was for Otho; Laco and Icelus were agreed, not in supporting any
particular individual, but in opposing the nominee of Vinius (Tac., c. 13).
Plutarch, Galb. 23, says that Galba without a word beforehand suddenly
sent for Piso (ἄφνω μηδὲν προειπὼν μετεπέμψατο Πείσωνα) and went down with
him to the camp to announce him as "Caesar" and as his successor.

pro contione adoptavit: in presence of the assembled soldiers in the
praetorian camp; Tac. H. i 18, apud frequentem militum contionem imperatoria brevitate adoptari a se Pisonem exemplo divi Augusti et more
militari quo vir virum legeret, pronuntiat. Galba had previously discussed
the advisability of making the announcement in this way or from the
Rostra to the assembled people or in the Curia to the senate: Tас. с. 17,
consultatum inde, pro Rostris an in senatu an in castris adoptio nuncuparetur. Iri in castra placuit: honorificum id militibus fore, quorum
favorem ut largitione et ambitu male adquiri, ita per bonas artes haud
spernendum. Augustus adopted Gaius and Lucius (Suet. Aug. 64, 65) and
Claudius adopted Nero (Tac. A. xii 26) in the ordinary method prescribed
by law, but Galba adopted Piso, not "lege curiata apud pontifices, ut moris
est" (Tac. H. i 15), but by mere public declaration (nuncupatio pro
contione); Nerva did the same in the case of Trajan (Dio lxviii 3), and
this method was probably continued by later emperors (Mommsen, Staatsr.
if³ 1137 sq.).

ne donativi mentione facta: Plutarch (Galb. 23) describes the
"festering" discontent of the sullen soldiers when no largess was given:
ἦν δὲ καὶ τὰ τῶν στρατιωτῶν ὕπουλα καὶ σκυθρωπὰ μηδὲ τότε δωρεᾶς αὐτοῖς δοθείσης.
Tacitus too says that a little liberality on Galba's part would have gained
for him the soldiers: constat potuisse conciliari animos quantulacumque
parci senis liberalitate; nocuit antiquus rigor et nimia severitas, cui iam
pares non sumus. It was usual to distribute a donativum when the emperor
made an adoption, e.g. when Hadrian adopted Verus (Spart. Hadr. 23).

faciliorem occasionem praebuit: see Plut. c. 24 for the ease with which
the agents of Otho by bribes and promises won over the soldiers who were
already rotten" with disaffection and only looking for a pretext (ἤδη
σαθροὺς ὄντας καὶ δεομένους προφάσεως).

intra sextum adoptionis diem: Piso was adopted on Jan. 10 and Galba
was slain on Jan. 15, which was the sixth day after, according to the
Roman inclusive method of reckoning; so Plut. (l.c.) ἕκτῃ γὰρ ἀνῃρέθησαν (i.e.
Galba and Piso were slain), ἣν ἄγουσι Ῥωμαῖοι πρὸ δεκαοκτὼ καλανδῶν Φεβρουαρίων
(= ante diem octavum decimum kalendas Februarias). Tacitus says that
Piso was 'quadriduo Caesar'" (H. i 48).
Instead of a clause with quam after ante, post, intra, we find at times
in post-Aug. authors a genitive depending on the accusative after these
prepositions; e.g. Claud. 27, 1, ante quintum mensem divortii: Tac. A. i 62,
sextum post cladis annum: id. H. ii 70, intra quadragesimum pugnae diem:
Vell. Pat. i 10, 5, ante paucos triumphi dies. Already in class. Lat. we
have post diem tertium eius diei, Cic. Att. iii 7, 1, Tusc. i 114 (see KühnerStegmann, i 405). Suetonius also uses quam, e.g. Iul. 35, 2, intra quintum
quam adfuerat diem (so in Liv., etc.).

monstra exitum portenderant: an enumeration of the omens and
prodigies foreboding the death of a Caesar is characteristic of the Lives;
cf. Iul. 81, Aug. 97, Tib. 74, Calig. 57, Claud. 46, Ner. 46, Oth. 8, Vitell. 9,
Vesp. 23, Tit. 10, Dom. 15. See Introd. c. ii.

per omne iter: the whole length of his march from Spain to Rome to
assume the empire.

dextra sinistraque
victimae caederentur: cf. Calig. 13 (Caligula's
journey from Misenum to Rom, on his accession), inter altaria et victimas
ardentesque taedas densissimo et laetissimo obviorum agmine incessit:
Curt. v 1, 20 (Alexander's entry into Babylon), Plures obviam egressi sunt
inter quos Bagophanes, arcis et regiae pecuniae custos,
totum iter
floribus coronisque constraverat, argenteis altaribus utroque latere dispositis,
quae non ture modo, sed omnibus odoribus cumulaverat : Tac. H. ii 70
(Vitellius visits the battlefield of Betriacum), Nec minus inhumana pars
viae quam Cremonenses lauru rosaque constraverant, extructis altaribus
caesisque victimis regium in morem: Appian Bell. Civ. v 24 (the coming
to Rome of Octavian and Antonius after peace had been made between
them), παροδεύουσιν αὐτοῖς, οἷα σωτῆρσιν, ἐγίγνοντο θυσίαι. See also Hirt. Bell.
Gall. viii 51. Such honours, as Casaubon says, were originally paid to the
gods when their statues were moved from one place to another (cf. Cic.
Verr. iv 35).
=

oppidatim:
per oppida, κατὰ πόλεις. This adv., used also in Aug. 59,
is not cited from any other author. For the remarkable number of adverbs
in -im used by Suetonius see App. I. § 1. f.

securis: the larger victims were usually slain by an axe (securis,
dolabra) or hammer (malleus); sheep, pigs, and birds had their throats cut
with a knife (culter).

rupto vinculo: a victim's breaking away from the altar was a sure
portent of disaster; see on Tit. 10, 1. Cf. Amm. Marc. xxiv 6, 17 (describing a portent of Julian's approaching end), conplures hostias Marti
parabat ultori, et ex tauris pulcherrimis decem ad hoc perductis, nondum
aris admoti voluntate sua novem procubuere tristissimi, decimus vero, qui
diffractis vinculis lapsus aegre reductus est, mactatus ominosa signa
monstravit.

speculator: these speculatores were picked soldiers (lancers) of the
praetorian cohorts who formed a special bodyguard for the emperor at
Rome, on journeys, and on military expeditions; cf. Claud. 35, 1, neque
convivia inire ausus est (Claudius) nisi ut speculatores cum lanceis circumstarent: Tac. H. ii 11, ipsum Othonem comitabantur speculatorum lecta
corpora cum ceteris praetoriis cohortibus, etc. They are distinct from the
speculatores legionum of whom each legion had ten, acting as despatchbearers, etc. Marquardt (Staatsv. ii² 547) and Cauer (Eph. Epigr. iv 464)
hold that they were, at least during the first cent., formed into a special
corps, a mounted corps, under special officers, and distinct from the rest of
the praetorians. On the other hand, von Domaszewski (Die Religion des
röm. Heeres p. 94) thinks that the speculatores always formed an integral
part of the praetorian cohorts; each cohort contained 24 of them (Tac.
H. i 27, 31, 35), and as the cohorts were 12 in number, the total number of
speculatores was 288, or roughly 300. See Daremberg-Saglio, iv 637;
Smilda on Suet. Claud. 35.
Palatium: see on Vesp. 25.

terrae tremor: cf. Ner. 48, 2 (describing Nero's last flight from Rome),
statim tremore terrae et fulgure adverso pavefactus. ‘“terrae tremor” for
“terrae motus" (Vesp. 17) is a poetical expression used in post-Aug. prose.

assimilis mugitui sonus: cf. Amm. Marc. xvii 7, 14, inter haec tria
genera terrae motuum mycematiae (mycematias, μυκηματιάς, is a rumbling
earthquake) sonitu audiuntur minaci, cum dissolutis elementa compagibus
ultro absiliunt vel relabuntur concidentibus terris; tunc enim necesse est
velut taurinis reboare mugitibus fragores fremitusque terrenos: Sen.
N.Q. vi 13, 4, antequam terra moveatur, solet mugitus audiri ventis in
abdito tumultuantibus; nec enim aliter posset, ut ait noster Vergilius
(Aen. vì 256), “sub pedibus mugire solum et iuga celsa moveri,” nisi hoc
esset ventorum opus.

§ 2. monile margaritis gemmisque consertum: among the presents
lavished by Caligula on the pampered horse Incitatus (which he once
thought of making consul) were “monilia e gemmis” (Calig. 55, 3). For
the adornment of the statues of goddesses with jewelry cf. Plin. N.H. ix
121, where we are told that the second of the two famous pearls from the
earrings of Cleopatra (the companion to that which she dissolved in vinegar
and drank) was cut in two to serve as pendants for the ears of Venus in the
Pantheon at Rome. Julius Caesar dedicated to Venus Genetrix (in the
temple which he built for her in the Forum Iulium) a breastplate (thorax)
made of British pearls (Plin. N.H. ix 116, Solin. 54).

Fortunam suam Tusculanam: for the story of this image of Fortune,
which he treasured in his villa at Tusculum, see c. 4, 3.
quasi: causal, see on Tit. 8, 1.

Capitolinae Veneri: Suetonius mentions a temple of the Capitoline
Venus in Calig. 7, where he says that Livia dedicated there a statue of a
son of Germanicus in the guise of Cupid (effigiem habitu Cupidinis in aede
Capitolinae Veneris Livia dedicavit). There is no other reference to this
temple, which some would identify with the shrine (or altar) of Venus
Victrix on the Capitol (C.I.L. i² p. 245). Jordan (Topogr. Rom і 2, 42)
says that there is nothing definite known of any other temple of Venus on
the Capitol besides that of Venus Eryciną, vowed in 217 B.C. by Q. Fabius
Maximus after the battle of Trasimenus and dedicated by him in 215.
Platner and Ashby, Topogr. Dict. Rome p. 551, regard it as "altogether
probable" that this is the aedes Capitolina Veneris.
somniavit: see on c. 4, 3.

speciem: phantom" (= simulacrum, εἴδωλον) cf. Ner. 34, 4, saepe
confessus exagitari se materna specie: Calig. 50, inter ceteras (imagines
noctis) pelagi quondam speciem colloquentem secum videre visus: Claud.
1, 2; 37, 2: Aug. 96, 1. This poetical use of species is found in prose
from Livy on.
quae dedisset: sc. imperium.

ad expiandum somnium: cf. Petron. Satyr. 114, ut Lycas Tryphaenae
somnium expiavit; Mart. xi 50, 8, expiet ut somnos garrula saga tuos.
Sacrifice was one method adopted to avert the evil portended by bad dreams;
the offering of salted cakes (salsae molae) and incense (tus) is often
mentioned, e.g. Plaut. Amph. 740, sed, mulier, postquam experrecta es, te
prodigiali Iovi | aut mola salsa hodie aut ture conprecatam oportuit;
Tibull. i 5, 14, Ipse procuravi ne possent saeva nocere | somnia ter sancta
deveneranda mola. Another method was lustration in running water, e.g.
Pers. ii 16, noctem flumine purgas; Sil. Ital. viii 124, sub lucem ut visa
secundent | oro caelicolas ac vivo purgor in amni.

nihil invenit merum: everything was the direct opposite of what
it should have been for a successful sacrifice: the fire should have been
blazing; the attendants on the sacrificing priest should have been young
(like the camilli) and robed in white; the incense should have been carried
in an ornate incense box (acerra); the wine should have been poured from
a patera, which at this period was usually of silver or gold and richly
wrought.

catino: from this glass dish or bowl the grains of incense would be
thrown on to the fire-pan or brasier (cf. Rich 125, where a similar vessel of
agate is illustrated). A catinus (or catinum) of black earthenware (like
the black Etruscan pottery) was used at primitive sacrifices in the days
of Numa; cf. Juv. vi 343, simpuvium (“libation-ladle'") ridere Numae
nigrumque catinum: Apul. Mag. 18, eadem paupertas etiam populo Romano
imperium a primordio fundavit, proque eo in hodiernum diis immortalibus
simpulo et catino fictili sacrificat. For the various uses of the catinus see
Pauly-Wissowa, iii 1790.

tus: the MSS. give thus, but in the other three passages where the
word occurs they give the forms ture and tura, and Ihm restores tus here.

$ 3. coronam de capite excidisse: another portent of dire disaster; cf.
Sil. Ital. xvi 268 (when Syphax was sacrificing), Vittaque, maiorum decoramen, fronte sine ullo | delapsa adtactu, nudavit tempora regis. | Talia
caelicolae casuro tristia regno | signa dabant, saevique aderant gravia
omina fati; Sen. Thyest. 701 (when Atreus, like a sacrificing priest, slays
the children of Thyestes), regium capiti decus (i.e. his diadem) | bis terque
lapsum est. When Vitellius set out from Germany on his march to Rome,
the laurel wreath which he had donned fell into a stream (Vitell. 9);
Alexander's death was foreshadowed by his diadem being blown from his
head by the wind near Babylon (App. Syr. 56).

auspicanti pullos avolasse: omens were derived from the appetite of
birds, generally chickens (pulli, hence auspicia pullaria used for such omens).
The chickens were kept in a coop (cavea), and if a general or magistrate
wished to get omens from them, they were let out and food was thrown to
them, the pullarii drawing various conclusions from the degree of eagerness
which they showed in eating, the most favourable sign (solistimum tripudium) being when they ate so greedily that some of the grain fell from
their bills to the ground. Any attempt on the part of the birds to fly away
was most inauspicious, and this was among the warning signs given to
C. Hostilius Mancinus (cons. 137 B.C.) when starting on his disastrous
campaign in the Numantine war in Spain: Val. Max. i 6, 7, cum Lavinii
sacrificium facere vellet (Mancinus), pulli cavea emissi in proximam silvam
fugerunt, summaque diligentia quaesiti reperiri nequiverunt. Claudius
Pulcher began a sea-fight off Sicily (249 B.C.) though the sacred chickens
would not eat, throwing them into the sea in defiance of the omen, and
saying that they might drink since they would not eat (Suet. Tib. 2, 2).

adoptionis die: the adoption of Piso (c. 17) on Jan. 10, 69 A.D.
Suetonius says nothing of the boding storm of rain and thunder accompanying the adoption, which is described in Tac. H. i 18 and Plut. Galb.
23. Tacitus adds 'observatum id antiquitus comitiis dirimendis non terruit
Galbam, quo minus in castra pergeret, contemptorem talium, ut fortuitorum,
seu, quae fato manent, quamvis significata, non vitantur.” Plutarch says
it was manifest that heaven disapproved of the ill-omened adoption.

castrensem sellam: the "campstool” placed for the commander-inchief on the tribunal from which he delivered his harangue to the troops;
it resembled the ordinary sella curulis but was less elaborate; the sella
curulis was a folding chair without back or arms and with legs curved like
pincers, while the sella castrensis had straight legs; the seat was of
straps covered with a cushion (see the illustrations in Daremberg-Saglio
iv 1180; Smith Dict. Ant. ii³ 620). Like modern campstools, the sella
curulis gave way at times and the occupant came ignominiously to the
ground; this happened to Augustus at the games on the dedication of the
theatre of Marcellus: evenit ut laxatis sellae curulis compagibus caderet
supinus (Aug. 43, 5).

curulem: when the emperor appeared in the senate he sat between the
consuls and, like them, on a raised sella curulis; see Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³
936. This seat was first assigned to Augustus in 19 B.с. (Dio liv 10).
The adj. curulis is for * currulis from currus a chariot, this explanation
being given in Gell. iii 18 on the authority of Gavius Bassus, “senatores
enim dicit in veterum aetate, qui curulem magistratum gessissent, curru
solitos honoris gratia in curiam vehi, in quo curru sella esset, super quam
considerent, quae ob eam causam‘curulis' appellatur.”

perverse: this perhaps means “back to the front," though there is no
means of determining what difference there was between the back and the
front of a sella curulis; another possible meaning is "askew” “sideways,"
and so La Harpe renders it "de travers.”

sacrificantem: this was the sacrifice at which Otho was present (see
Oth. 6) and, as Plutarch says, was almost delivered up to Galba by the
hand of the gods: Galb. 24, ἐκείνῃ (τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) γὰρ ἕωθεν εὐθὺς ὁ μὲν Γάλβας ἔθυεν
ἐν Παλατίῳ τῶν φίλων παρόντων, ὁ δὲ θύτης Ὀμβρίκιος ἅμα τῷ λαβεῖν εἰς τὰς χεῖρας
τοῦ ἱερείου τὰ σπλάγχνα καὶ προσιδεῖν οὐ δι' αἰνιγμῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἄντικρυς ἔφη σημεῖα
μεγάλης ταραχῆς καὶ μετὰ δόλου κίνδυνον ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἐπικείμενον τῷ αὐτοκράτορι,
μονονουχὶ τὸν Ὄθωνα τοῦ θεοῦ χειρὶ ληπτὸν παραδιδόντος. Cf. also Dio lxiv 5; Tac.
H. i 27, Octavo decimo kalendas Februarias (i.e. Jan. 15) sacrificanti
pro aede Apollinis Galbae haruspex Umbricius tristia exta et instantes
insidias ac domesticum hostem praedicit, audiente Othone (nam proximus
adstiterat) idque ut laetum e contrario et suis cogitationibus prosperum
interpretante. The way in which Otho escaped from his dangerous predicament and was carried off to the camp to be proclaimed emperor is described
in Oth. 6.

haruspex: 'soothsayer," lit. 'entrail-observer" (root ghar, cf. hirae,
hillae, ilia, χόλιξ), one who foretold the future from the appearance of the
entrails of the sacrifice. This was an Etruscan form of divination.
Victims sacrificed for this purpose were called hostiae consultatoriae;
ordinary sacrificial victims were called hostiae animales.

haud multo post: Tacitus says that it was while Galba was still
keeping on sacrificing and importuning the gods of an empire no longer his:
ignarus interim Galba et sacris intentus fatigabat alieni iam imperii deos,
cum affertur rumor rapi in castra incertum quem senatorem, mox Othonem
esse qui raperetur; simul ex tota urbe, ut quisque obvius fuerat, alii formidine augentes, quidam minora vero, ne tum quidem obliti adulationis (H.
i 29). So too Plutarch (Galb. 25) says that the soothsayer still held the
entrails in his hands when the news arrived which dumbfounded even those
who had been sceptical of the truth of such presages.

cognoscit: this is one of the few instances of the historic present in
Suetonius: see Appendix I. § 9. a.

castra: the castra praetoria (praetoriana Suet.) or permanent camp for
the praetorian cohorts was an institution of Tiberius on the advice of
Sejanus in 23 A.D.; cf. Tib. 37, 1, Romae castra constituit, quibus praetorianae cohortes, vagae ante id tempus et per hospitia dispersae, continerentur: Aug. 49, 1, numquam plures quam tres cohortes in urbe passus
est (Augustus), easque sine castris. It lay to the N.E. of Rome, outside
the Servian agger, between the Viminal and Colline gates, and so commanded the important roads (Salaria, Nomentana, Tiburtina) leading
eastward. For a description of it see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Romi
3, 385 sqq. and the plan in Daremberg-Saglio iv 634. It figures largely in
the history of the Empire from Claudius to Vespasian, and is mentioned in
Tac. A. iv 2, xi 31, xii 69, xiii 14, xv 53, 59; H. i 31, ii 93, iii 84, etc.
1

ut eodem pergeret suadentibus: Tacitus (H. i 32 sq.) mentions the two
courses of action suggested to Galba, one advocated by Vinius, the other
by Laco and Icelus: Interim Galbam duae sententiae distinebant. Titus
Vinius manendum intra domum, opponenda servitia, firmandos aditus, non
eundum ad iratos censebat
Festinandum ceteris videbatur, antequam
cresceret invalida adhuc coniuratio paucorum
Vel si cadere necesse sit,
occurrendum discrimini; id Othoni invidiosius et ipsis honestum.
...
nihil amplius quam: see on ‘“nihil aliud quam,” Dom. 21.

continere se statuit: Suetonius here differs from Tacitus (H. i 34)
who says that Galba decided to follow the advice of his more plausible
supporters to go out and face the mutinous soldiery, and that he sent Piso
(his adopted son) in advance to the praetorian camp, as being likely to
gain the favour of the cohorts by his great name and popularity, and by
his hostility to Vinius whom the soldiers hated. Plutarch (Galb. 25) agrees
in the main with the account of Tacitus.

legionariorum: Nero's legion “prima Adiutrix classicorum” (see on
c. 12, 2) was at Rome; also chosen contingents from the armies of Germany,
Britain, and Illyricum, which Nero had prepared to send against the
Albani but had recalled on the revolt of Vindex (Tac. H. i 6). The legion
which Galba had recruited in Spain (“septima Galbiana," see c. 10, 2),
and which had accompanied him to Rome, had been despatched to Pannonia
(Тас. Н. ii 11).
multifariam: see on "plurifariam,” Vitell. 9.

tendebant: "were quartered" (c. 12, 2, n.). The contingent of the
Illyrian army was quartered at this time in the Porticus Vipsania (in the
Campus Martius), and the contingent of the German army in the Atrium
Libertatis (near the Circus Flaminius ?); see Tac. H. i 31.

loricam linteam induit: sumpto thorace, Tac. c. 35; τεθωρακισμένος,
Plut. c. 27. A cuirass or corselet of linen is frequently mentioned in Greek
writers. In Homer the epithet λινοθώρηξ is applied to the Locrian Ajax
and the Mysian Amphios (Il. ii 529, 830), and a linen cuirass was worn
by the Persians (Xen. Cyrop. vi 4, 2), Egyptians (Hdt. ii 182), Phoenicians
(Paus. vi 19, 4), and Chalybes (Xen. Anab. iv 7, 15); cf. also Arr. Tact. 14.
Nepos (Iphicr. 1) says of Iphicrates: genus loricarum mutavit, et pro
sertis atque aeneis linteas dedit; quo facto expeditiores milites reddidit:
nam, pondere detracto, quod aeque corpus tegeret et leve esset, curavit.
Pausanias (i 21, 8) says that these cuirasses made of folds of linen were
of little use in war, though a protection in hunting: οἱ δὲ θώρακες οἱ λινοῖ
μαχομένοις μὲν οὐχ ὁμοίως εἰσὶ χρήσιμοι, διϊᾶσι γὰρ καὶ βιαζόμενοι τὸν σίδηρον,
θηρεύοντας δὲ ὠφελοῦσιν, ἐναποκλῶνται γάρ σφισι καὶ λεόντων ὀδόντες καὶ παρδάλεων.
Casaubon cites from the Byzantine historian Nicetas Acominatus (c. 1190
A.D.) a description of a linen cuirass worn by Conrad; it was made with
eighteen folds and stiffened by steeping in vinegar and salt so as to be
impenetrable by any weapon.
quanquam: see on Tit. 7, 2.

§ 2. rumoribus falsis: there was a widespread rumour that Otho had
been slain: Tac. H. i 34, vixdum egresso Pisone occisum in castris
Othonem vagus primum et incertus rumor: mox, ut in magnis mendaciis,
interfuisse se quidam et vidisse adfirmabant, credula fama inter gaudentes
et incuriosos: Plut. Galb. 26, θροῦς διῆλθε πολύς, ὡς ἀνῃρημένου τοῦ Οθωνος.

conspirati: the use of conspirati as a subst. (= coniurati) is first found
in Suetonius; cf. Iul. 82, 1: Dom. 17, 1.

de industria dissiparant: Tac. (l.c.), Multi arbitrabantur compositum
auctumque rumorem mixtis iam Othonianis, qui ad evocandum Galbam laeta
falso volgaverint.
..

paucis affirmantibus: Tacitus says that everyone kept making
positive assertions, though no one knew anything definite: nemo scire et
omnes adfirmare.

gratulabundos: this rare adj. occurs first in Liv. vii 33; see on
“osculabundus,” Vitell. 2, 5. Tacitus (c. 35) describes the crowd of
all classes flocking to the Palace to congratulate Galba on the reported
death of Otho: Tum vero non populus tantum et imperita plebs in plausus
et inmodica studia, sed equitum plerique et senatorum, posito metu incauti,
refractis Palatii foribus ruere intus ac se Galbae ostentare, praereptam
sibi ultionem querentes, ignavissimus quisque et, ut res docuit, in periculo
non ausurus, nimii verbis, linguae feroces.
prodiit: he was carried in a sella (φορεῖor) on account of the throng.

Quo auctore?: this question was a proof of Galba's intrepidity in
checking indiscipline; cf. Tac. (l. c.): Obvius in Palatio Iulius Atticus
speculator (see note on c. 18, 1) cruentum gladium ostentans occisum a se
Othonem exclamavit; et Galba “commilito,” inquit, “quis iussit?”
insigni animo ad coercendam militarem licentiam, minitantibus intrepidus,
adversus blandientes incorruptus. Dio (lxiv 6) supplies a version of the
soldier's words as he showed the bloodstained sword: “Θάρσει, αὐτοκράτορ,
Οθωνα γὰρ ἀπέκτεινα, καὶ ἔστι σοι δεινὸν ἔτι οὐδέν.” πιστεύσας οὖν ὁ Γάλβας πρὸς
μὲν ἐκεῖνον εἶπε “Καὶ τίς σοι τοῦτο ποιῆσαι ἐκέλευσεν;” Plutarch (Galb. 26)
adds that the soldier, a distinguished praetorian, replied to Galba that
it was his oath of allegiance which bade him do the deed (τοῦ δὲ ἀνθρώπου
τὴν πίστιν εἰπόντος καὶ τὸν ὅρκον, κ.τ.λ.).
processit: Bentley needlessly conjectured processerit.

equites equos adegissent: Tacitus (c. 40) gives a vivid account
of the charge into the Forum which was ordered by Otho when he heard
that Galba's supporters were arming the mob: Othoni tamen armari
plebem nuntiabatur. Ire praecipites et occupare ("forestall'') pericula
iubet. Igitur milites Romani, quasi Vologaesum aut Pacorum avito
Arsacidarum solio depulsuri ac non imperatorem suum inermem et senem
trucidare pergerent, disiecta plebe, proculcato senatu, truces armis, rapidi
equis Forum irrumpunt. Nec illos Capitolii aspectus et imminentium
templorum religio et priores et futuri principes terruere, quo minus facerent
scelus, cuius ultor est quisquis successit.

paganorum: paganus (“rustic" or "peasant") is used at times in
Silver Latin for a "civilian"; cf. Aug. 27, 3, concionante se, admissa
turba paganorum, apud milites: Juv. xvi 32, citius falsum producere
testem | contra paganum possis, quam vera loquentem | contra fortunam
armati contraque pudorem: Tac. H. iii 24 (Antonius Primus rouses the
praetorians with the taunt "vos, nisi vincitis, pagani"): i 53, inter
paganos corruptior miles.

restiterunt: this momentary halt on the part of Otho's attacking
force is not mentioned by other writers. Plutarch (c. 26) says that the
standard-bearer of the cohort accompanying Galba dashed to the ground
the medallion of the emperor which was attached to the standard of the
cohort, and at once the litter of Galba was attacked, first with javelins
and then with swords; cf. Tac. (c. 41): Viso comminus armatorum agmine
(i.e. Otho's troops) vexillarius comitatae Galbam cohortis dereptam
Galbae imaginem solo adflixit. Eo signo manifesta in Othonem omnium
militum studia, desertum fuga populi Forum, destricta adversus dubitantes
tela.

desertum a suis: see on c. 20, 1, neque praesentium quemquam opem
imperatori ferre conatum.

sunt qui tradant: there were various reports, friendly or otherwise,
of the last words of Galba; cf. Tac. H. i 41, Extremam eius vocem, ut
cuique odium aut admiratio fuit, varie prodidere: alii suppliciter interrogasse quid mali meruisset, paucos dies exsolvendo donativo deprecatum;
plures obtulisse ultro percussoribus iugulum: agerent ac ferirent, si ita e
re publica videretur (Tacitus cynically adds "Non interfuit occidentium
quid diceret"): Dio lxiv 6, τοῦτο μόνον εἰπών, “ Καὶ τί κακὸν ἐποίησα;”:
Plut. Galb. 27, ὁ δὲ τὴν σφαγὴν (iugulum) προτείνας ‘“ Δρᾶτε” εἶπεν “εἰ τοῦτο τῷ
δήμῳ ῾Ῥωμαίων ἄμεινόν ἐστι."

Quid agitis
mei: these words form a trochaic septenarius
(CCC-II-IC-II-CCI-II-I( - -) and seem to be a poetical
quotation.

donativum etiam pollicitum: Tacitus (l.c.) mentions this reported
offer, but Plutarch and Dio say nothing of it. Galba had persistently
refused to grant a donativum; see c. 16, 1, and c. 17.

ut hoc agerent: “agere" in the ritual of Roman sacrifice meant to
slay the victim; the slayer (popa) before striking the blow asked the
priest "Agone?”, “Shall I do it?", and he replied "Age” or “Hoc
age"; cf. Ov. F. i 321, qui calido strictos tincturus sanguine cultros |
semper agatne rogat, nec nisi iussus agit. This reply of the priest to the
popa was a warning to the assembled people to keep silence and give
attention to the solemn act; hence "hoc age" came to be used colloquially
meaning "give attention." Suetonius uses it again in the sacrificial
sense in Calig. 58, 2 (describing the assassination of Caligula by Chaerea):
tradunt Chaeream cervicem gladio caesim graviter perculisse praemissa
voce "Hoc age!”
..

neque quemquam opem ferre conatum: both Plutarch and Dio
mention with great praise a centurion Sempronius Densus, who singlehanded made a gallant effort to protect Galba: Plut. Galb. 26, ῎Ημυνε δὲ οὐδεὶς
οὐδὲ ὑπέστη πλὴν ἑνὸς ἀνδρός, ὃν μόνον ἥλιος ἐπεῖδεν ἐν μυριάσι τοσαύταις ἄξιον τῆς
Ῥωμαίων ἡγεμονίας· Σεμπρώνιος ἦν Δῆνσος ἑκατοντάρχης, οὐδὲν ἰδίᾳ χρηστὸν ὑπὸ
Γάλβᾳ πεπονθώς, τῷ δὲ καλῷ καὶ τῷ νόμῳ βοηθῶν προέστη τοῦ φορείου (“litter"). Καὶ
τὸ κλῆμα (i.e. the vitis, or vine-switch carried by centurions) πρῶτον . . ἐπαράμενος
τοῖς ἐπιφερομένοις ἐβόα καὶ διεκελεύετο φείδεσθαι τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος. Ἔπειτα συμπλεκ
ομένων αὐτῷ σπασάμενος τὸ ξίφος ἠμύνατο πολὺν χρόνον, ἕως τυφθεὶς τὰς ἰγνύας
("knee-joints") ἔπεσε: Dio lxiv 6, καὶ αὐτῷ Σεμπρώνιος Δῆνσος ἑκατόνταρχος ἐπαμύνας
ἐς ὅσον ἠδυνήθη, τέλος, ὡς οὐδὲν ἤνυσεν, ἐπεσφάγη. καὶ διὰ τοῦτό γε καὶ τὸ ὄνομα
αὐτοῦ ἐνέγραψα, ὅτι ἀξιώτατός ἐστι μνημονεύεσθαι. Tacitus, however, says that
Sempronius showed this gallantry in defending Piso (Galba's adopted
son), to whom he had been attached as a guard by Galba: Insignem illa
die virum Sempronium Densum aetas nostra vidit. Centurio is praetoriae
cohortis, a Galba custodiae Pisonis additus, stricto pugione occurrens
armatis et scelus exprobrans ac modo manu modo voce vertendo in se percussores quanquam vulnerato Pisoni effugium dedit. Piso sought sanctuary
in the temple of Vesta, but Otho's soldiers dragged him out and slew him.

omnes qui arcesserentur: Galba had sent Celsus Marius to try and
bring to his support the contingent of the Illyrian army quartered in the
Porticus Agrippa; two centurions of the first rank (primipilares) were
ordered to bring up the German soldiers quartered in the Atrium Libertatis
(see on c. 19, 1). No confidence could be placed in Nero's legion "prima
Adiutrix classicorum” which was incensed by Galba's massacre of their
comrades (see on c. 12, 2). Three military tribunes were sent to the
camp of the praetorians in a vain effort to recall them from the side of
Otho. The Illyrian detachments drove Celsus away with a shower of
javelins, and the legio classica joined the seditious praetorians who
rejected with defiance the overtures of the tribunes sent by Galba. See
Тас. с. 31.

Germanicianorum: a correction by Turnebus of Germaniciorum; for
the form "Germanicianus" see on Vesp. 6, 2.

vexillatione: the vexillum, as distinct from the aquila and the
signum (c. 12, 2, n.), was a special ensign reserved for a corps of temporary
formation and for detachments; the name of such a detachment was
vexillatio (first found in Suetonius); vexillum denoted both the ensign
and the detachment, and vexillarius both the ensign-bearer and the soldier
who formed part of the detachment. Another meaning of vexillarius was
a time-expired soldier serving in the reserve company attached to each
legion, such a company having a special vexillum or ensign.

ob recens meritum
advolaverunt: Tacitus says that the detachments from the German army wavered for a long while between Otho and
Galba, being slow to desert Galba on account of his recent kindness:
Germanica vexilla diu nutavere, invalidis adhuc corporibus et placatis
animis, quod eos a Nerone Alexandriam praemissos atque inde rursus longa
navigatione aegros impensiore cura Galba refovebat. Mommsen (Prov.
Rom. Emp. ii 61) thinks that the sending of troops to Alexandria was in
connexion with an Ethiopian war which Nero had planned inter reliqua
bella (Plin. N.H. vi 29, 184), wishing to extend the imperial frontier in
Africa. These plans were upset by the revolt of Vindex, and any troops
which had been despatched were recalled.

magno opere: though the MSS. here and in Vesp. 21 give magnopere,
their evidence in other passages is decisively in favour of the uncontracted
forms magno (quanto, tanto) opere; see Ihm, p. liv.

fovisset: Wölfflin suggested refovisset (re- being lost after opere), as
Tacitus (l.c.) has refovebat.

§ 2. iugulatus est: “iugulum haurire" is the Virgilian mode of
expression which Tacitus (c. 41) uses of the murder: De percussore non
satis constat. Quidam Terentium evocatum (“one of the reserve" or
"one of the select bodyguard" of Galba, see c. 10, 3), alii Laecanium;
crebrior fama tradidit Camurium quintae decimae legionis militem impresso
gladio iugulum eius hausisse. Ceteri crura brachiaque (nam pectus tegebatur) foede laniavere; pleraque volnera feritate et saevitia trunco iam
corpori adiecta.

ad lacum Curti: Tac. (l.c.), iuxta Curti lacum trepidatione ferentium
Galba proiectus e sella ac provolutus est: Plut. Galb. 27, τὸν δὲ Γάλβαν .
περὶ τὸν Κουρτίου καλούμενον λάκκον ἐκκυλισθέντα. . ἔτυπτον ἐπιδραμόντες. The
“lacus Curtius" was originally a pool or swamp in the centre of the site
of the Roman Forum. It disappeared through being drained by the
cloacae of Tarquin. Varro (L.L. v 148-150) mentions three traditions of
the origin of the name: (1) the Sabine leader Mettius Curtius, hard
pressed by the soldiers of Romulus, galloped his horse safely across the
marsh (cf. Liv. i 12, Dion. Hal. ii 43); (2) in 362 B.C. a gulf opened in
the Forum and the haruspices declared that the gods demanded that one
of the courageous citizens whom Rome held dear should cast himself in
and it would be closed; Marcus Curtius fully armed mounted his horse
and plunged into the abyss (cf. Liv. vii 6); (3) the lacus was simply a
puteal erected by the consul C. Curtius (445 в.C.) round a spot in the
Forum struck by a thunder-bolt. Whatever the origin of the name, the
place was surrounded by some kind of an ornamental structure, and altars
were raised in the centre; cf. Ov. F. vi 397, Curtius ille lacus, siccas qui
sustinet aras, nunc solida est tellus, sed lacus ante fuit. Every year, on
the anniversary of the birth of Augustus, people of all classes came and
cast in a small votive coin for the safety of the emperor; cf. Suet. Aug.
57, 1, Omnes ordines in lacum Curtii quotannis ex voto pro salute eius
stipem iaciebant. As the lacus was connected with the underworld, these
coins were probably offerings to the gods below; see Wissowa, Religion
und Kultus der Römer² 235.

relictus ita uti erat: "quia, ut reperi in commentariis Graecorum,
adstiterit illi canis, quo vivo caput Galbae amputari non potuerit. Historia
id sit, an fabula, nihil pronuntio.” (Casaubon.) What commentarii
Graecorum" Casaubon is referring to I have not been able to ascertain.
•

gregarius miles caput amputavit: Plutarch (Galb. 27) mentions
those who were variously reported to have slain Galba, viz. Camurius (of
the 15th legion), Terentius, Laecanius, and Fabius Fabullus, the last named
being said to have also cut off his head and carried it away: οἱ δὲ (λέγουσι)
Φάβιον Φάβουλον, ὃν καί φασιν ἀποκόψαντα τὴν κεφαλὴν κομίζειν τῷ ἱματίῳ συλλαβόντα διὰ τὴν ψιλότητα (calvitiem) δυσπερίληπτον οὖσαν· ἔπειτα τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ κρύπτειν
οὐκ ἐώντων, ἀλλ᾿ ἐμφανῆ πᾶσιν ποιεῖν τὴν ἀνδραγαθίαν, περιπείραντα περὶ λόγχην καὶ
ἀναπήλαντα... δρόμῳ χωρεῖν, ὥσπερ αἱ βάκχαι, πολλάκις μεταστρεφόμενον καὶ
κραδαίνοντα τὴν λόγχην αἵματι καταρρεομένην. Tacitus (H. i 41, quoted above on
“iugulatus est'") mentions Terentius, Laecanius, and Camurius, but not
Fabius Fabullus. Groag (in Pauly-Wissowa vi 1769) infers (1) that
Plutarch does not reproduce his original quite accurately; (2) that Fabius
Fabullus was the gregarius miles who cut off Galba's head; (3) that he
was not one of those who actually slew Galba, and so is not included by
Tacitus among the reputed percussores.

inserto per os pollice: these unpleasant details are given even more
fully by Suetonius than by Plutarch (l.c.); Tacitus omits them; presumably they were given by the common authority (most probably Pliny the
Elder, see Introd. c. iii) followed by the three writers.

ad Othonem detulit: Otho, according to Plut. (l.c.), when Galba's
head was brought, said "This is nothing, my fellow-soldiers; show me the
head of Piso” (“ οὐδέν ἐστι τοῦτο, ὦ συστρατιῶται, τὴν Πείσωνός μοι κεφαλὴν
δείξατε"). The head of Piso, who had been adopted as son and successor
by Galba, was shortly afterwards brought to him. Otho's ghoulish joy at
seeing the head of Piso is described in Tac. H. i 44.

lixis calonibusque: Tac., c. 49, caput per lixas calonesque suffixum.
"lixae” are defined by Festus as "qui exercitum sequuntur quaestus
gratia"; they formed no part of the army (extra ordinem sunt militiae),
but supplied the soldiers with supplementary provisions, etc., and so
corresponded to sutlers or vivandiers.
"Calones" were servants of the
soldiers, discharging various menial duties; they were slaves, while lixae’”
were freeborn or, more rarely, freedmen.
..

hasta suffixum portarunt: Dio lxiv 6, καὶ τά τε ἄλλα τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ
ἐλυμήναντο, καὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀποκόψαντες περὶ κοντὸν ἀνέπειραν: Tac. c. 44, praefixa
contis capita (of Galba and Piso) gestabantur inter signa cohortium iuxta
aquilam legionis, certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus qui occiderant,
qui interfuerant, qui vere, qui falso ut pulchrum et memorabile facinus
iactabant. Such outrageous treatment of fallen foes was common in
antiquity; cf. Justin xxiv 5 (describing the fate of Ptolemaeus Ceraunus,
king of Macedon, slain by the Gauls c. 280 в.с.), Ptolemaeus multis
vulneribus saucius capitur; caput eius amputatum, et lancea fixum, tota
acie ad terrorem hostium circumfertur.
Cupido: the variant cupide (GX) is much less forcible..

fruaris aetate tua: cf. Sen. Phaedr. 446, aetate fruere: mobili cursu
fugit; Liv. xxvi 50, 5, frui ludo aetatis; Cic. Verr. 2, 5, 33, multa eius
in stipendiis damna proferentur, quae ab isto aetatis fructu dissoluta et
compensata sunt. The use of aetas in the sense of adulescentia, iuventus,
ὥρα, is fairly frequent, e.g. Cic. Off. ii 13, 45, tua aetas incidit in id
bellum; Hor. Ep. i 20, 10, carus eris Romae donec te deserat aetas. So
too the diminutive aetatula, Suet. Claud. 16, 1, invenem corruptelis
adulteriisque famosum nihil amplius quam monuit ut aut parcius aetatulae
indulgeret aut certe cautius.
..

exierat in vulgus respondisse eum: for the subject-clause expressing
the report that had got out cf. Nep. Dat. 6, si in turbam exisset, ab
homine tam necessario se relictum. Suetonius has an object-clause with
“exiit opinio” in Ner. 53, exiit opinio descensurum eum ad Olympia inter
athletas.
ἔτι . . ἐστιν : words used by Diomedes (Il. v 254) and by Odysseus
(Od. xxi 426).

Patrobii Neroniani: Tac. H. i 49, caput ante Patrobii tumulum
(libertus is Neronis punitus a Galba fuerat) postera demum die repertum..
Tacitus (ii 95) couples him with Polyclitus as among the most hated of
Nero's freedmen: nondum quartus a victoria mensis, et libertus Vitelli
Asiaticus Polyclitos Patrobios et vetera odiorum nomina aequabat. Dio
(lxiv 3) describes how, when Galba became emperor, Patrobius was
punished along with Narcissus, Locusta, and others by being led in chains
through the city and then put to death. The cognomen ‘“Neronianus”
denotes a freedman of Nero.

aureis: the aureus (sc. denarius), as standardised by Augustus, was
equivalent to 25 silver denarii or 100 sestertii. It was a little heavier
than a sovereign and in relation to English gold would be worth about a
guinea. For the subsequent fluctuations in its weight (and value) see
Mattingly, Roman Coins 123 sqq.

redemptum: Plutarch (Galb. 28) says that the head of Galba was
given to the slaves of Patrobius; the head of Vinius was sold to his
daughter for 2500 drachmae (= 10,000 sestertii); that of Piso was given
to his wife Verania at her entreaty. Cf. Tac. i 47, Pisonem Verania uxor
ac frater Scribonianus, Titum Vinium Crispina filia composuere, quaesitis
redemptisque capitibus, quae venalia interfectores servaverant. Tacitus
says nothing of the sale of Galba's head.

eo loco: apparently near the building called "Sessorium"; cf. Plut.
1.c., λαβόντες δ' ἐκεῖνοι (i.e. the slaves of Patrobius) καὶ πάντα τρόπον αἰκισάμενοι καὶ καθυβρίσαντες ἔρριψαν ᾗ τοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν Καισάρων κολαζομένους θανατοῦσιν.
ὁ δὲ τόπος Σεσσώριον (so Bekker, Σηστέρτιον MSS.) καλεῖται. The meaning
and derivation of "Sessorium" are very obscure; see Jordan-Huelsen
Topogr. Rom i 3, 250, Hardy on Plut. l.c. A place of execution outside
the Esquiline gate is mentioned in Tac. A. ii 32, extra portam Esquilinam
more prisco advertere: Suet. Claud. 25, civitatem Romanam usurpantes
in campo Esquilino securi percussit: Comm. Cruq. on Hor. S. i 8, 11, in
Esquiliis publicis sepulti sunt extra portam in qua est Sessorium:
Epod. 5, 100, Esquilina porta Romae dicitur, ubi certus erat locus sepulcrorum ad corpora pauperum aut sceleratorum viliumque comburenda aut
canibus proicienda. Platner and Ashby (Topogr. Dict. Rome p. 488) point
out, with reference to these statements of Cruquius, that the "Sessorium"
was at least 1400 metres from the Esquiline gate.

animadversum
acting in accordance with the ancient belief that the vengeance which
brought most comfort to the slain was that his slayer should be slain
either at the same spot or at the tomb of his victim; cf. Soph. El. 1494:
Val. Max. ix 2, 2: Flor. iii 21, 26: Sen. Troad. 1152: Curt. vii 5, 43:
Justin xi 2, 1.
fuerat: the freedman of Patrobius was
dispensator: cf. c. 12, 3; Vesp. c. 22, n.

Argivus: Tac. H. i 49, Caibae corpus diu neglectum, et licentia tencbrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum, dispensator Argius (= ᾿Αργεῖος, Plut.),
e prioribus servis, humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis contexit; caput
postera demum die repertum et cremato iam corpori admixtum est.
Plutarch (c. 28) says that Argeius was a freedman of Galba's; that he
buried the body by night; and that the body, in the first instance, was
lifted up and carried away by Helvidius Priscus, with Otho's permission.
For Helvidius Priscus see on Dom. 10, 3.

ceterum truncum: the use of the sing. ceterus, which is rare in class.
Lat. (5 exx. in Cic.), occurs 8 times in Suetonius.
•

in hortis sepulturae dedit: cf. Eutrop. vii 16, iugulatus (Galba) in
foro Romae sepultusque in hortis suis, qui sunt Aurelia via non longe ab
urbe Roma.

Aurelia via: this road, dating at least from the second cent. B.C.,
led northwards from Rome; it touched the sea at Alsium in Etruria, and
then ran along the coast of Etruria up to Pisa; the name was extended
to the continuation of this road from Pisa to Arelate (Arles) in Gaul.

statura fuit iusta: 'iusta statura aestimatione Romana senûm pedum
circiter fuit" (Casaubon). The Roman pes = 11.65 inches. In Liv. vii 10
we find the expression "media militaris statura," which is to be explained
in the light of Veget. Mil. i 5, proceritatem tironum scio semper exactam
ita ut senos pedes, vel certe quinos et denas uncias habentes inter alares
equites, vel in primis legionum cohortibus probarentur. The "statura”
of the other Caesars is thus described by Suetonius: -Julius, “excelsa'';
Augustus, "brevis”; Tiberius, "quae iustam excederet"; Caligula,
“eminens”; Nero, “prope iusta"; Otho, "modica"; Vespasian, "quadrata"; Titus, "non procera"; Domitian, “procera." The abl. of quality
is usual in these descriptions, but the gen. is found in Oth. 12, 1.

praecalvo: cf. c. 20, 2; Plut. Galb. 13, ἐπισκώπτων τὴν φαλακρότητα
("baldness") καὶ ῥυσότητα (“wrinkledness'") τοῦ Γάλβα.
The compound
praecalvus (found only here) most probably means "very bald” (valde
calvus), though some explain it as 'bald in front.” Other compounds with
intensive prae- used by Suetonius are praeclarus, praecupidus, praedives,
praedurus, praeferox, praegrandis, praelautus, praepinguis, praetrepidus,
praevalidus. He also has praeacutus sharp-pointed,” praemortuus “prematurely dead." The epithet praecanus which Horace applies to himself
(Ep. i 20, 24) may mean "very grey," "grey before his time," or "grey
in front" (see Wilkins ad loc.).

oculis caeruleis: similar descriptions are given in Iul. 45, nigris
vegetisque oculis fuit; Aug. 79, oculos habuit claros ac nitidos, quibus
etiam existimari volebat inesse quiddam divini vigoris; Tib. 68, cum praegrandibus oculis et qui, quod mirum esset, noctu etiam et in tenebris
viderent, sed ad breve et cum primum e somno patuissent: deinde rursus
hebescebant; Calig. 50, oculis et temporibus (“temples") concavis fuit;
Ner. 51, oculis caesiis ("bluish-grey'") et hebetioribus fuit; Dom. 18,
grandibus oculis, verum acie hebetiore fuit.

adunco naso: to judge from his coins and busts (e.g. that in the
Capitoline Museum) Galba had a very pronounced aquiline or hooked nose,
and that presumably is the meaning here, though aduncus nasus is always
explained as a "turned-up nose" in Hor. S. i 6, 5, naso suspendis adunco
(cf. Pers. i 40, nimis uncis Naribus indulges), and in Ter. Heaut. 1062,
virginem sparso ore, adunco naso. Suetonius describes the aquiline
nose of Augustus, Aug. 79, habuit nasum et a summo eminentiorem et ab
imo deductiorem (“bent inwards" i.e. a “Roman" nose).

articulari morbo: arthritis, inflammation of the joints due to gout
in the hands or feet (cheragra, podagra); cf. Scrib. Larg. 101, ad articularem morbum quem ἀρθρίτιν vocant: Hor. S. ii 7, 15, iusta cheragra Contudit articulos: Pers. v 58, cum lapidosa cheragra Fregerit articulos:
Plin. N.H. xx 195, anesum
lenit articulares morbos (in Ser. Samm.
695 sqq. a number of cures for articularis morbus are given). The emperor
Septimius Severus was crippled by this disease: Spart. Sept. Sev. 16, 6,
quod consistere in curru adfectus articulari morbo non posset.

distortissimis: cf. Apul. Met. v 10, ego vero maritum articulari morbo
complicatum curvatumque
sustineo, plerumque detortos et duratos in
lapidem digitos eius perfricans.

evolvere:
ἀναπτύσσειν, ἀνελίττειν, to unroll, to open for reading;
cf. Aug. 89, 2, in evolvendis (= legendis) utriusque linguae auctoribus:
Cic. Tusc. i 12, 24, evolvo diligenter eius eum librum, qui est de animo:
Hor. S. i 3, 112, fastos evolvere mundi.
=

valeret: valere c. inf. is a poetical construction; Livy is the first prose
writer to use it, and he has it only once (xxxviii 23, 4); Krebs-Schmalz,
Antibarb. ii 647.
dexteriore: for the comparative see on ‘‘sinisteriore,” Dom. 17, 1.
caro: there is a variant gibbus, for which see on Dom. 23, 2.

fascia: cf. Dom. 17, 1; Ov. A.A. iii 274, inflatum circa fascia pectus
eat; Capit. Anton. Pius c. 13, tiliaceis tabulis in pectore positis fasciabatur, ut rectus incederet.

cibi plurimi: cf. Aug. 76, 1, cibi minimi erat: Cic. Fam. ix 26, 4,
non multi cibi hospitem accipies, multi ioci: Hor. C. i 36, 13, multi
Damalis meri: iii 9, 7, multi Lydia nominis: Cic. Rosc. Am. 6, plurimarum
palmarum gladiator: Cic. Att. xiii 28, Cornificia multarum nuptiarum.
The descriptive genitive was preferred by Latin writers to express Greek
compounds like πολυφάγος, πολυπότης, πολυώνυμος, πολυστεφής, πολύγαμος;
in popular Latin we find compounds, e.g. multibibus (Plaut.), multiscius
(Apul.).

traditur: sc. fuisse; cf. Caes. B.G. v 6, quod eum magni animi, magnae
inter Gallos auctoritatis cognoverat.

inter cenam vero: vero is used intensively, with a special emphasis
on the preceding word.

abundantis: sc. cibi. This is Graevius' correction for abundanti or
abundans. In the Milan ed. of 1475 the reading is abundantem; Gruter
suggested abundanter; Guyetus abutens (with subter for super).
=

congestas super manus reliquias, etc.: a most obscure passage, which
may mean that Galba ordered the leavings of the huge portions served to
him to be carried round in handfuls and distributed (spargi dividi)
among the servi a pedibus. It was customary to give the attendants
what was left when dinner was over; cf. Sen. Ep. 77, 8, Marcellinum
admonuit non esse inhumanum, quemadmodum cena peracta reliquiae
circumstantibus dividuntur, sic peracta vita aliquid porrigi his qui totius
vitae ministri fuissent: Plut. Quaest. Rom. 64. Hofstee and Rolfe follow
Baumg.-Cr. in explaining super manus as = ante se (in mensa). Baumg..
Cr. is peculiar in taking stantibus as dat. of the agent, his interpretation
being as follows:-‘“Inter cenam usque eo abundantis cibi fuit, ut congestas super manus, h.e. ante se, ante locum ubi sumserat cibum, reliquias
circumferri iuberet, scil. circum mensam et convivas, ostentandi causa,
quantum fauces et venter valerent, spargique (quod dicitur de rebus
solidis, ut fundi de fluidis), sive in unum locum colligi, ad admirationem
convivarum, et ut ipse acto labore delectaretur, ad pedes stantibus, h.e.
a servis, ad lectum sive pedes ministrantibus, dativo, ut saepius, posito pro
ablativo cum praepositione “a”, adeoque hoc loco, ne auris offenderetur
excipientibus se verbis ab ad pedes stantibus.” D. C. Grimm (Dissert.
on Galb. c. 22, Leipzig 1798) took super manus as = per manus and altered
circumferri to circum se ferri, thinking that Galba was so gluttonous that
he had the remains left by each diner passed along from hand to hand
and set before him, and then having satisfied his appetite he gave anything that was over to the attendants. Stahr also takes super manus as
=
per manus, but interprets the passage differently:- "Bei Tafel nun
gar häufte er eine solche Masse Speisen vor sich auf, dass er die Reste
derselben von Hand zu Hand umherreichen und (zuletzt) unter die aufwartende Dienerschaft verteilen liess." The difficulty in extracting any
satisfactory meaning makes it highly probable that the text is unsound.

ad pedes stantibus: slaves who stood behind the diners as they
reclined on couches at table; cf. Sen. Ben. iii 27, servus qui cenanti ad
pedes steterat: Petron. Satyr. 58, Giton, qui ad pedes stabat.
Caligula
loved to humiliate senators by making them act in this capacity: Calig.
26, 2, quosdam summis honoribus functos . sibi cenanti modo ad pluteum
modo ad pedes stare succinctos linteo passus est. For these servi a pedibus
see Marquardt, Privatl.2 148, 322. Such slaves might be provided by the
host (Daremberg-Saglio, iv 1276 n.), but at ordinary private dinner-parties they usually came with their masters, took charge of their shoes
(soleae), stood behind them during dinner, and carried home any presents
(apophoreta) made by the host to their masters.
..

libidinis pronior: a very rare constr.; cf. Luc. i 461, ruendi mens
prona viris: Claud. Ruf. ii 400, pronior audendi. Suetonius also uses
pronus with the dat., with ad, and with in. R. Stephanus conjectured
libidinis pronioris; Torrentius libidini . pronior; Boxhorn libidinibus
pronior. In the Augustan poets and in later prose (isolated instances
in old Lat. but not in class. Lat.) the genitive is used with a great number
of adjectives of the most varied signification in order to define the sphere
or respect in which the adj. is applicable; see the list in Kühner-Stegmann,
i 443 sq. Suetonius has the gen. with certus, parcus, tenax, etc.; see
Appendix I. § 3. B. g.

in mares: contrast Claud. 33, 2, libidinis in feminas profusissimae,
marum omnino expers.

praeduros: "well hardened", poetical and in late prose; cf. Verg.
Aen. x 748, homo praedurus viribus: id. G. ii 531, corporaque agresti
nudant praedura palaestrae: Columell. vi 2, 1, praedura aetas (opp. to
tenera aetas). See on praecalvus, c. 21.
exoletus: Festus defines exoletus as "qui adolescere, id est crescere,
desiit.'' The word was used in the special sense of “adolescens alienae
libidini inserviens”; cf. Tit. 7, 1: Calig. 24, 3: Tib. 43, 1: Iul. 49, 2:
76, 3: Tac. A. xv 37: Cic. Mil. 21, ille qui semper secum scorta, semper
exoletos, semper lupas duceret. Suetonius also uses exoletus simply in the
sense of obsoletus; see Galb. 4, 4 (n.): Aug. 86, 2: Claud. 22.
Icelum: see on c. 14, 2.

concubinis: for concubinus (= delicatus, a favourite slave) see R. Ellis
on Catull. lxi 121-123, Nec nuces pueris neget Desertum domini audiens
Concubinus amorem.

nuntiantem: Plutarch (Galb. 7) describes the arrival of Icelus in Spain
bearing to Galba the news of Nero's death: Ἦν δὲ θέρος ἤδη, καὶ βραχὺ πρὸ
δείλης ἧκεν ἀπὸ ῾Ρώμης Ικελος ἀνὴρ ἀπελεύθερος ἑβδομαῖος (i.e. in 6 days). Πυθόμενος
δὲ τὸν Γάλβαν ἀναπαύεσθαι καθ' ἑαυτὸν ἐβάδιζε συντόνως ἐπὶ τὸ δωμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ
βίᾳ τῶν θαλαμηπόλων (cubiculariorum) ἀνοίξας καὶ παρελθὼν ἀπήγγειλεν, κ.τ.λ.

artissimis osculis: cf. Apul. Met. ii 13, eum amplexus exosculatur

artissime.
