non modo sed: this use of sed for sed etiam occurs also in Tit. 7, 2,
Aug. 88, Claud. 16, 2; the second clause in every case being stronger than
the first. In Cicero when non modo is followed by sed, the second clause
may be either stronger or weaker. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii '60.

velleretur: cf. Iul. 45, circa corporis curam morosior, ut non solum
tonderetur diligenter ac raderetur, sed velleretur etiam, ut quidam exprobraverunt: Quintil. ii 5, 12, vulsi levatique et inustas comas acu comentes.
Mayor (on Juv. viii 16 and 114, xi 157) has collected a number of passages
on this practice and the contempt in which in it was held by Romans of
the old type.

tertio et septuagesimo aetatis anno: cf. [Aurel. Vict.] Epit. 6, cum
septuagesimum tertium aetatis annum ageret
caesus est: Tac. H. i 49,
hunc exitum habuit Servius Galba, tribus et septuaginta annis quinque
principes (i.e. Aug., Tib., Calig., Claud., Ner.) prospera fortuna emensus
et alieno imperio felicior quam suo: Dio (Xiphilinus) Ixiv 6, ἔζησε δὲ
Γάλβας ἔτη δύο καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα (Zonaras adds καὶ ἡμέρας τρεῖς καὶ εἴκοσιν).
Thus, according to Dio (Zonaras), Galba must have been born on Dec. 24,
5 B.C., for he died on Jan. 15, 69 A.D. It is impossible to reconcile
Suetonius' statement here that Galba was in his 73rd year at the time of
his death with the statement in c. 4 supr. that he was born on Dec. 24,
3 B.C., in which case he would only have been in his 71st year when he
died. We must assume therefore that Suetonius has made a slip with
regard to the year of Galba's birth which was 5 B.C. and not 3 B.C.
further complication, however, arises from the fact that both Plutarch
(Galb. 8) and Eutropius (vii 16) say that Galba was in his 73rd year
when he became emperor in June 68 A.D. (and so must have been born
in 6 B.C.); their statement is supported by what Suetonius tells us in
Ner. 40 about the warning of the Delphic oracle to Nero to beware of the
73rd year; Nero understood this to mean that he would live to be 73,
and never took into account Galba's age. For other chronological inconsistencies in Suetonius see on Oth. 11, 2; Vitell. 18; Tit. 11.
A

imperii mense septimo: he reigned from June 9, '68 A.D. (the date
of Nero's death) to Jan. 15, 69; cf. Eutrop. vii 16, insidiis Othonis occisus

est imperii mense septimo: [Aurel. Vict.] Epit. 6, imperavit menses septem
diesque totidem: Joseph. Bell. Iud. iv 9, 2, φθάνει Γάλβας ἀναιρεθεὶς μετὰ
μῆνας ἑπτὰ καὶ ἴσας ἡμέρας: Tac. H. i 37 (Otho addressing the soldiers just
before the murder of Galba), septem a Neronis fine menses sunt, etc. Dio
(Xiph. Zon.), lxiv 6, says he reigned nine months and thirteen days (ἦρξε
μῆνας ἐννέα καὶ ἡμέρας δεκατρεῖς), counting from the 2nd of April, 68 A.D.,
when he was proclaimed emperor by the soldiers in Spain (cf. c. 10, 1).

ut primum licitum est: this may have been, as Hofstee suggests,
after the defeat of Otho by the Flavianists. When Antonius Primus,
Vespasian's general, advanced from Pannonia into upper Italy, he ordered
the images of Galba to be set up again in all the towns; Tac. H. iii 7,
Desiderata. diu res interpretatione gloriaque in maius accipitur, postquam
Galbae imagines discordia temporum subversas in omnibus municipiis recoli
iussit Antonius, decorum pro causa (Flaviana) ratus, si placere Galbae
principatus et partes revirescere crederentur. The decree which Suetonius
mentions may have been passed between the occupation of Rome by the
Flavian forces (about Dec. 20, 69 A.D.) and the arrival of Vespasian in
person at Rome in the summer of 70.

senatus
statuam.. decreverat: in 158 B.C. the censors ordered the
removal of all statues from the Forum and Capitol unless they had been
decreed by the people or by the senate. The right of granting them came
to be confined to the senate, but the restriction was often evaded, and
Claudius had to issue an edict that no statue was to be erected at Rome
without the order of the senate unless by an individual who had built
or restored some public building (Dio lx 25). We read of the emperor's
sanction being obtained for the erection of a statue, e.g. Plin. Ep. i 17,
Titinius Capito ab imperatore nostro (i.e. Trajan) impetravit ut sibi liceret
statuam L. Silani in foro ponere; but the emperors did not directly
authorize the erection, they asked the senate to decree the honour; cf.
Capitol. Marc. c. 2, cui (Frontoni) et statuam in senatu petiit: c. 3, cui
(Iunio Rustico) post obitum a senatu statuas postulavit. See Mommsen,
Staatsr. iii 1184 sqq. The most famous of the monuments decreed by
the senate to Roman emperors was the Column of Trajan.

rostratae columnae superstantem: columns adorned with the beaks
(rostra) of ships were erected at Rome originally to celebrate naval
victories, the best known being that in honour of C. Duilius for his defeat
of the Carthaginians in 260 в.с. A columna rostrata formed the support
of a triumphal statue decreed by the senate to Octavius in celebration of
his naval victory over Sextus Pompeius at Naulochus in 36 в.с.; cf.
Appian Bell. Civ. v 130, καὶ ἐπινίκιος ἐν ἀγορᾷ (Foro) χρύσεος ἑστάναι μετὰ
σχήματος οὗπερ ἔχων ἐσῆλθε, περικειμένων τῷ κίονι νεῶν ἐμβολῶν (rostrorum):
Servius on Verg. G. iii 29, navali surgentes aere columnas. Statues on a
columna rostrata are depicted not only on coins of Augustus but also on
those of Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian (Eckhel vii p. 85;
Cohen i pp. 82, 396).

in parte Fori qua trucidatus est: i.e. beside the lacus Curtius, see
c. 20. The people paid honours to the same spot in their exultation at
Otho's death; cf. Tac. H. ii 55, populus cum laura ac floribus Galbae
imagines circum templa tulit, congestis in modum tumuli coronis, iuxta
lacum Curtii, quem locum Galba moriens sanguine infecerat.
lemma: in parte Fori qua trucidatus est

text:
decretum abolevit: cf. Claud. 6, 2, quod decretum abolitum est:
Tac. A. iii 28, quae triumviratu iusserat abolevit (Augustus): Spart. Sev.
17, 5, Salvii Iuliani decreta iussit aboleri. The verb used of the senate
cancelling a decree already passed is inducere (διαγράφειν); e.g. Suet. Iul.
16, inducto priore decreto: Cic. de domo 4, 10, coeptum est referri de
inducendo senatus consulto. When the senate of itself or at the direction
of the emperor wished to cancel a decree already completed and registered
(ad aerarium delatum), some one moved a resolution “ut senatusconsultum
antea factum induceretur, tabulaque in qua perscriptum erat deleretur.”
See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 1014.

percussores summisisse: if the allegation is true (no other author
mentions it), Galba was trying to remove a dangerous rival who was in
command of a large army in Judaea (see Vesp. 4, 5), and he was using
the same means as Nero had adopted to try to remove Galba himself
when governor of Hispania Tarraconensis (see Galb. 9, 2). For summittere
cf. Tit. 6, 1.

orti sunt oppido Ferentio: in class. Lat. when urbs or oppidum precedes the name of the place a prep. is used in preference to the simple
local ablative (Kühner-Stegmann, i 480). Suetonius uses ortus (a) with
ex, e.g. Tib. 1, 1, gens Claudia orta est ex Regillis oppido Sabinorum;
(b) with a, e.g. Iul. 6, 1, maternum genus a regibus ortum; (c) with
simple abl., e.g. Ner. 28, 1, regio genere ortam: Aug. 2, 3, equestri familia
ortum se.

Ferentio: cf. Tac. H. ii 50, origo illi e municipio Ferentio. Ferentium,
or Ferentinum, was an Etruscan city on the site of the modern ruins of
Ferento. It is mentioned again in Vesp. 3, and is to be distinguished
from Ferentinum in the territory of the Hernici in Latium. It was
probably a dependency of Volsinii in Etruscan times (Dennis, Cities and
Cemeteries of Etruria, i³ 156 sqq.). We first hear of it in the time of
Augustus as a Roman colony of small importance (Strab. v 226; Frontin.
de colon.); Vitruvius (ii 7), like Tacitus, calls it a municipium.
possessed a temple of Fortuna (Tac. A. xv 53), probably the Etruscan
goddess Nurtia. There are the remains of a magnificent theatre at Ferento.
The connexion of the family of Otho with Ferentium is confirmed by an
inscription found there: M. Sal[vio Othoni Aug.] tribu[nic(ia) potest(ate)]
municipe[s
...
See Pauly-Wissowa, i A. 2035.
It

ex principibus Etruriae: cf. Hor. C. iii 29, 1, where Maecenas is
addressed as “Tyrrhena regum progenies," his ancestors on his father's
side, the Cilnii, being Lucumones or chieftains at Arretium. Etruria in
ancient times was a confederation of twelve states or cities, each with
an aristocratic form of government, the chief rulers, who combined political
and ecclesiastical functions, being called Lucumones; see Dennis, op. cit. i³
Introd. p. li.

Salvius: restored by Stephanus for “Silvius." Salvius, which is
often found as a praenomen in the contracted form Sa. or Sal., did not
become widespread as a gentile name till a late period. Those who bore
it as a single name in Republican times were persons of no great distinction,
often slaves e.g. the leader of the Sicilian slave war in 104: the influential
freedman of Caesar often mentioned in Cicero's Letters: the literary slave
or freedman of Atticus. The Salvius who as trib. pleb. in 43 B.C. vetoed
the decree of the senate declaring Antony a public enemy and who later
sided with Cicero against Antony and perished in the proscription may
have been a kinsman of the M. Salvius Otho whom Suetonius mentions
here; see Münzer in Pauly-Wissowa, i A. 2023.

incertum an ingenua: Suetonius is fond of introducing disjunctive
questions depending on incertum or dubium, or with incertum and dubium
omitted; e.g. Iul. 18, 1, profectus est incertum metune iudicii an quo
maturius sociis subveniret: Iul. 58, 1, dubium cautior an audentior:
Galb. 12, 3, illa quoque verene an falso per ludibrium iactabantur:
Vesp. 1, 2, Flavius Petro bello civili Pompeianarum partium centurio
an evocatus profugit. In our passage the first part of the interrogation
is omitted.
..

Liviae Augustae: wife of Augustus; see on Galb. 1 and 5, 2. Galba
was said to have owed his consulship to her (Galb. 2, 1, n.).

in cuius domo creverat: similarly Titus was brought up along with
Britannicus son of the emperor Claudius (Tit. 2, n.).

senator est factus: by imperial favour a person of equestrian rank
could become a senator in two ways: (1) the emperor could exercise his
right of adlectio and admit him directly to the senate, assigning him a
definite place on the roll, usually inter tribunicios, occasionally inter praetorios, and in the 3rd cent. even inter consulares, entitling him to the
privileges of those who had actually filled these offices; (2) the emperor
could bestow on him the latus clavus qualifying him to start with the
vigintivirate (see on Galb. 6, 1) and then proceed to the quaestorship and
the successive magistracies in the cursus honorum; sometimes the latus
clavus cum quaestura was granted and then the imperial favourite could
begin his career with the quaestorship, an office carrying with it admission
to the senate. Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 938 sqq.

nec praeturae gradum excessit: this fact is mentioned by Tacitus
also, who says that the emperor Otho had an “avus praetorius” (H. ii 50).
By a curious coincidence the grandfather of Galba never went beyond
being praetor; cf. Galb. 3, 3, avus non egressus praeturae gradum.
On coins with the head of Augustus (Eckhel, v 289) this M. Salvius Otho
is named as IIIvir A.A.A.F.F. (i.e. triumvir auro argento aere flando
feriundo, one of the triumviri monetales, directors of the mint). For nec
(= neque vero, neque tamen) cf. Oth. 5, 2 sollicitati reliqui, nec adeo
multi; Dom. 7, 2, edixit, nec exsequi rem perseveravit.

§2. pater: Tac. H. ii 50, (Othoni) pater consularis; he was consul
suffectus in 33 A.D., Galba being consul ordinarius during the first six
months of that year (Galb. 6, 1). In the acta Arvalia (Henzen p. xlviii)
this Lucius Otho is mentioned as "flamen et pro magistro" of the Fratres
Arvales in 39 A.D. (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 166).

materno genere praeclaro: Hofstee conjectures that the mother belonged to the gens Titia and that her grandson Titianus (see below) derived
his name from his grandmother, after the fashion of the period.

propinquitatium: “connexions"; cf. Nep. Dion 1, 2, Dion autem,
praeter nobilem propinquitatem, generosamque maiorum famam, multa
alia ab natura habuit bona; for the pl. cf. Cic. Fin. v 23, si propinquitates summo bono non continentur. Suetonius uses the word only
here and in Ner. 35, 4; elsewhere necessitudo and necessitudines, the latter
frequently in a concrete sense (= necessarii, ἀναγκαῖοι).

non absimilis : absimilis (ἀνόμοιος, late Gr. ἀφόμοιος) is found once in
class. Lat., Caes. B.G. iii 14, falces .. non absimili forma muralium falcium
(sc. formae); it is always used with a negative (by litotes) and it takes
the dative, as in Dom. 10, 1, arte formaque non absimilis magistro.
..

ut plerique crederent: there was a similar scandal current about
Drusus (father of the emperor Claudius), who was borne by Livia three
months after her marriage to Augustus, and it was said that Augustus
had begotten him in adulterous intercourse with her while she was the
wife of Tib. Claudius Nero (Claud. 1, fuit suspicio ex vitrico per adulterii
consuetudinem procreatum). Suetonius uses plerique not merely in the
sense of plurimi but also in that of multi or permulti (e.g. Galb. 16, 1;
Dom. 6, 2:8, 2:10,5:19; so in Nep., Liv., Tac.); sometimes, as here,
it is impossible to determine in which sense he is using it. The same
difficulty presents itself in Tacitus; see Gerber and Greef, Lex. Tac.

urbanos honores: i.e. the offices included in the regular cursus honorum,
the quaestorship, aedileship or tribuneship, praetorship, and consulship.

proconsulatum Africae: held also by Galba (Galb. 7, 1), Vitellius
(Vitell. 5), and Vespasian (Vesp. 4, 3). The provinces of Africa and
Asia were reserved for consulares (see on “proconsulatum,” Galb. 3, 4).
Lucius Otho probably succeeded Galba as proconsul and, like Galba, may
have been invested with special military powers (see on Galb. 7, 1).

extraordinaria imperia: we have no information as to the precise
nature of these, or the province or provinces in which Lucius Otho held
them. For an example of a provincial governor who was given an
‘“ extraordinarium imperium” see on Vitell. 2, 4, Lucius Syriae praepositus.

Illyrico: in the division of provinces in 27 B.c. Illyricum was made
a senatorial province, but in consequence of continual rebellions and the
necessity of keeping a military force there it was transferred to the
emperor (c. 10 B.c.) and divided into two provinces, Pannonia and Dalmatia.
In a wider sense Illyricum included Noricum and Moesia.

motu Camilli: the name of this Camillus is variously recorded as
Furius Camillus Scribonianus, L. Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus,
Camillus Arruntius, Camillus Scribonianus, etc. Mommsen (Hermes iii
133 sqq.) shows that he was a son of M. Furius Camillus (cons. '8 A.D.);
and was adopted by L. Arruntius (cons. 6 A.D.); his mother was the daughter
of Scribonia and Sextus Pompeius, hence he was called Scribonianus. He
was consul in 32 A.D. (see Oth. 2, 1), and was appointed governor (legatus
Aug. pro. pr. consularis) of Dalmatia under Caligula. He was continued
in this office under Claudius, but in 42 A.D. revolted against the emperor and
announced that he would restore the republic. Many senators and knights
flocked to him, but his soldiers refused to follow him and he was forced to
flee to the island of Issa in the Adriatic where he killed himself according
to Dio (lx 15, ἑκούσιος ἀπέθανε), but Tacitus (H. ii 75) says he was slain by a
private soldier. See also Tac. H. i 89, A. xii 52; Plin. Ep. iii 16;
Oros. vii 6.

ex paenitentia: cf. Claud. 13, 2, bellum civile movit Furius Camillus
Scribonianus Dalmatiae legatus, verum intra quintum diem oppressus est,
legionibus quae sacramentum mutaverant in paenitentiam religione
('superstition'") conversis, postquam, denuntiato ad novum imperatorem
itinere, casu quodam ac divinitus neque aquila ornari neque signa convelli
moverique potuerunt.
quasi: causal, see on Tit. 5, 1.

defectionis adversus: no example of this construction (for the usual
defectio ab) is given in the Thesaur. Ling. Lat.

ante principia: the use of the prep. ante shows that principia (= ἀρχεῖα,
cf. Plut. Galb. 12, ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείοις, ἃ πριγκίπια καλοῦσι ῾Ρωμαῖοι) is here
used for the officers' quarters themselves; it was also used in a wider
sense for the large open space in the centre of the camp containing the
general's tent (praetorium) and those of the higher officers, the eagle and
standards of the legion, and the raised platform (tribunal) where the
general administered justice and addressed the troops. The exact meaning
of principia and the precise relation between principia and praetorium
have been much disputed, some identifying principia with the via principalis or main street (E. and W.) of the camp or at least with that part
of it which the officers' tents or quarters adjoined. See Daremberg-Saglio,
i 945, iv '640; Smith, Dict. Ant. i3 374. The principia and praetorium are
often mentioned in connexion with military punishments of a merely
degrading kind (see on Vitell. 8, 1), but executions usually took place outside the porta decumana of the camp and were supervised by the tribunes
or centurions, so the procedure of Lucius Otho was quite exceptional.

promotos in ampliorem gradum: cf. Tac. H. ii 75, sic Scribonianum
sub Claudio interfectum, sic percussorem eius Volaginium e gregario ad
summa militiae provectum. The use of promovere aliquem in the sense
of perducere, producere, provehere is post-Aug.

§3. detecta equitis R. fraude: this was presumably one (though we
know not which) of the conspiracies by equites against Claudius which
are mentioned by Suetonius, Tacitus, and Dio; cf. Suet. Claud. 13, reperti
et equestris ordinis duo in publico cum dolone (“sword-cane'') ac venatorio
cultro praestolantes, alter ut egressum theatro, alter ut sacrificantem apud
Martis aedem adoreretur: Tac. A. xi 22 (47 A.D.), interea Romae, nullis
palam neque cognitis mox causis, Cn. Nonius eques Romanus ferro accinctus
reperitur in coetu salutantium principem; nam postquam tormentis
dilaniabatur, de se non infitiatus conscios non edidit, incertum an occultans :
Dio lx 18 (43 A.D.), καί τις ἐν τούτῳ τῶν ἱππέων, ὡς καὶ ἐπιβουλεύσας τῷ Κλαυδίῳ,
κατὰ τοῦ Καπιτωλίου ὑπό τε τῶν δημάρχων (‘tribunes '') καὶ τῶν ὑπάτων
(“consuls") κατεκρημνίσθη. Hofstee is probably right in assuming that
Suetonius in the present passage is referring to the design against the
life of Claudius which is mentioned by Tacitus as frustrated in 47 A.D.,
as L. Otho was ‘“inter patricios adlectus” when Claudius was censor in 48,
and thus Otho's reward would come shortly after his service to the emperor.
Dessau (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 168) thinks that the reference is to the
attempt in 43 which is mentioned by Dio.

statua in Palatio posita: cf. Tit. 2. Nero conferred a like honour
on Tigellinus and Nerva; Tac. A. xv 72, tum, quasi gesta bello expositurus,
vocat senatum et triumphale decus Petronio Turpiliano consulari, Cocceio
Nervae praetori designato, Tigellino praefecto praetorii tribuit, Tigellinum
et Nervam ita extollens ut super triumphales in foro imagines apud
Palatium quoque effigies eorum sisteret. In our passage and in Tac. l.c.
Friedlaender (Sitteng. iii¹º 75) takes Palatium as the Palatine hill, not
the imperial Palace; so too Hofstee, on the ground that in both cases the
senate decrees the honour, and the senate had nothing to do with the
Palace. But the erection of statues required the authorisation of the
senate (Galb. 23 n.), and the emperors went through the formality of
asking the senate to decree the statues.

adlectum inter patricios: the creation of a large number of patricians
by Claudius as censor in 48 A.D. is mentioned in Tac. A. xi 25, Isdem diebus,
in numerum patriciorum adscivit Caesar vetustissimum quemque e senatu
aut quibus clari parentes fuerant, paucis iam reliquis familiarum, quas
Romulus maiorum et L. Brutus minorum gentium appellaverant, exhaustis
etiam quas dictator Caesar lege Cassia et princeps Augustus lege Saenia
sublegere; laetaque haec in rem publicam munia multo gaudio censoris
inibantur. Under the Republic new patrician gentes were coopted by the
patrician curiae in the comitia curiata; the dictator Caesar and Augustus
created them under special law; Claudius created them in virtue of his
powers as censor, so too Vespasian and Titus (see note on Vesp. 9, 2);
when the censorship fell into abeyance, the emperors, beginning with
Trajan, created them in virtue of their general powers. See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii³ 1100 sq., iii 29 sq.
Vir, quo meliores, etc.: a similar eulogy was bestowed by Augustus
on Drusus (father of the emperor Claudius) after his death: Claud. 1, 5,
defunctum ita laudaverit, ut deos precatus sit, similes ei Caesares (i.e.
Gaius and Lucius) suos facerent.

ne opto quidem: Reid, on Cic. Balb. 9, points out the difference between
“sperare” to look forward to what is practicable and “optare” to look
forward to what can happen only by an extraordinary stroke of good
fortune; optare is used of the wild dreams of philosophers, e.g. Cic. Acad.
ii 121, somnia censet haec esse Democriti non docentis sed optantis.

Albia Terentia: Tacitus does not mention her name, but he says of
Otho, "pater consularis, avus praetorius; maternum genus inpar nec tamen
indecorum” (H. ii 50). Eutropius (vii 17) says that the family of Otho's
mother was more noble than that of his father: Otho materno genere
nobilior quam paterno, neutro tamen obscuro (some would transpose
paterno and materno, to make Eutropius accord with Tacitus). The notice
of Otho in Suidas begins: ὁ μετὰ Γάλβαν βασιλεύσας, γένους ἀσήμου καὶ
ἀφανοῦς ὤν (Barth proposed γένους μὴ ἀσήμου : cf. Plut. Galb. 19,
Μάρκος Ὄθων, ἀνὴρ γένει μὲν οὐκ ἀφανής).

splendida femina: it is generally assumed that she was of an
equestrian family, the epithet splendidus being applied to an eques of
high position and great wealth who had held no magisterial office at Rome
(Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 565); but more probably the adj. here means
simply "of distinguished family," the precise rank of the family being
unspecified; cf. Tit. 4, 2, duxit uxorem Marciam Furnillam splendidi
generis: Tac. Agr. 6, Domitiam Decidianam, splendidis natalibus ortam,
sibi iunxit.
filios tulit: for this expression see on Vesp. 3.

L. Titianum: his full name was Lucius Salvius Otho Titianus.
Tacitus (A. xii 52), mentioning him as consul under Claudius in 52 A.D.,
calls him Salvius Otho, but in H. i 90 ii 60, Agr. 6 gives his name as
Salvius Titianus. He is mentioned very often in the records of the Fratres
Arvales from 57 to 69 A.D. (C.I.L. vi 2038-2051). He was proconsul of
Asia ("in omnem aviditatem pronus," Tac. Agr. 6) with Agricola as his
quaestor in 63-64, and became consul for a second time in 69 along with
his brother the emperor. When Otho set out to meet Vitellius he left
Titianus in charge of the city, but soon sent for him to take command
of the army; he was defeated at Betriacum, where his army surrendered,
but he was pardoned by the enemy, "pietate et ignavia excusatus" (Tac.
H. ii 60).
minorem: the future emperor, Marcus Salvius Otho.

cognominem sibi: having the same cognomen Otho; in Vitell. 2, 2
“cognominis” means having the same nomen.

vixdum nubilem: Roman maidens might be betrothed when mere
children; they were regarded as marriageable from the beginning of the
thirteenth year, and were usually married between the ages of thirteen and
sixteen, fourteen being the average age, though there were instances of
girls being married when under twelve, e.g. Messalina was only eleven
when she married the sixteen-year-old Nero; see the statistics on the
subject given in Friedlaender, Sitteng. iv¹º 133 sqq.

Druso: this son of Germanicus and Agrippina assumed the toga
virilis in 23 A.D.; he and his elder brother Nero were designated as heirs
and successors of Tiberius, but Sejanus, who was ambitious to reign, used
Drusus as a tool to secure the banishment and death of Nero, and then
worked the downfall of Drusus, who was accused of treason to the emperor
and sentenced to death by the senate.
Tiberius did not execute him at
once, but kept him a prisoner in a vault of the palace for some years, and
finally in 33 A.D. had him starved to death (Suet. Tib. 54, 65; Calig. 12;
Tac. A. iv 4, 60; vi 23: Dio lviii 22).

despondit: it is not known whether Drusus married this daughter
of Lucius Otho, but we are told that in 30 A.D. he was already married to
Aemilia Lepida (Dio lviii 3; Tac. A. vi 40, Aemilia Lepida, iuveni Druso
nupta), who was a shameless character driven to suicide through her profligacy; she was amongst those who accused her husband to Tiberius.
IIII. Kal. Mai.: April 28 (32 A.D.).
Camillo Arruntio: see on c. 1, 2.

Domitio Ahenobarbo: father of the emperor Nero, and husband of
Agrippina daughter of Germanicus (see on Galb. 5, 1); after his consulship (32 A.D., see Vitell. 2, 2) he was proconsul of Sicily; accused of many
crimes, adultery, incest, murder, he only escaped execution through the
death of Tiberius; he died of dropsy (aqua intercus) in 37. Suetonius
(Ner. 5) speaks of him as “omni parte vitae detestabilis," and says that
when his friends congratulated him on the birth of Nero he replied that
nothing that was not abominable and a public bane could be born of
Agrippina and himself.

a prima adulescentia prodigus: Tac. H. i 13, Otho pueritiam incuriose,
adulescentiam petulanter egerat: Plut. Galb. 19, Μάρκος Ὄθων .. τρυφῇ καὶ
φιληδονίαις εὐθὺς ἐκ παίδων ἐν ὀλίγοις ῾Ῥωμαίων (“as few even of the Romans
were") διεφθαρμένος.

flagris: the flagrum or flagellum was a "knout" or "cat" of
knotted cord or wire, the thongs being often loaded with pieces of metal
or knuckle-bones. It was used for the punishment of slaves (Marquardt,
Privatl.2 182).

obiurgaretur: in post-Aug. writers obiurgare is often used of corporal
chastisement; e.g. Suet. Calig. 20, ferulis obiurgari: Pers. v 169, nugaris;
solea puer obiurgabere rubra: Petron. Satyr. 34, colaphis obiurgare puerum
iussit: Sen. Ira iii 12, 6, servulum istum verberibus obiurga.

vagari noctibus solitus: assaults committed by revelling young
"Mohocks" in the streets at night are often referred to by Plautus; e.g.
Stich. 606, Non tu scis, quam adflictentur homines noctu hic in via: Trin.
315, ne noctu irem obambulatum, neu suum adimerem alteri: Amph. 153,
Qui me alter est audacior homo aut quis confidentior, Iuventutis mores
qui sciam, qui hoc noctis solus ambulem? Cf. Juv. iii 278 sqq. Nero was
notorious for his nightly escapades (Ner. 26, Tac. A. xiii 25), as were also
Caligula and Vitellius; cf. Capitol. L. Veri c. 4, in tantum vitiorum
Gaianorum et Neronianorum ac Vitellianorum fuisse aemulum ut vagaretur
nocte per tabernas ac lupanaria
et comissaretur cum triconibus, committeret rixas, etc.
...

potulentum: “drunken"; cf. Apul. Met. iii 5, cum a cena me serius
aliquanto reciperem potulentus. In Cicero potulenta means "drinkables."
N.D. ii 56, 141, gustatus in ea parte oris, qua esculentis et potulentis iter
natura patefecit; cf. Scaevola's definition of “penus," Gell. iv 1, 17,
penus est quod esculentum et potulentum est. The termination -lentus
denotes "full of" (e.g. fraudulentus, vinolentus, opulentus), and so
potulentus more naturally means “full of drink" than "drinkable," and
in Plin. N.H. viii 90 we find "esculentum os” where the meaning is 'filled
with food."

sago iactare: sagatio (Gr. παλμός) was the Roman parallel to our
"tossing in a blanket" (Fr. berner, Germ. prellen, Fuchsprellen). Cf.
Mart. i 3, 8, ibis ab excusso missus in astra sago; Libanius, orat. 58, 18.
The use of the word sagum (a soldier's cloak, see Marquardt, Privatl.2
561, 565) shows that it was originally an amusement of the soldiers (cf.
Friedlaender on Mart. l.c.).
§2. aulicam: see on Dom. 4, 1.

quo coleret, diligere simulavit: colere "to court the favour of,
by showing deference to" is frequently distinguished from diligere “to
love", e.g. Cic. Lael. 53, quis enim aut eum diligat, quem metuat, aut eum,
a quo se metui putet? coluntur tamen simulatione dumtaxat ad tempus:
Plin. Ep. ii 9, 6, diligeris, coleris, frequentaris: Sidon. Ep. iv 4, ipse
hinc amplius capiebatur, quod se diligi magis quam quasi coli intelligebat:
Mart. ii 55, Vis te, Sexte, coli: volebam amare. | Parendum est tibi: quod
iubes, colere: | Sed si te colo, Sexte, non amabo.

anum: used adjectivally as in Ner. 11, 1, anus matronas.
With the
possible exception of Cic. Scaur. 8, uxorem, anum et locupletem et molestam,
this adjectival use is limited to poetry and post-Aug. prose.

per hanc summum locum tenuit: this passage is quoted with a
number of others by Mayor to illustrate Juv. i 38, in caelum quos evehit
optima summi | nunc via processus, vetulae vesica beatae.

insinuatus Neroni: Suetonius always uses insinuare in the passive
(middle) and c. dat.; cf. Calig. 12, 2, insinuatus Macroni: Gramm. 21,
Augusto insinuatus est Melissus: vit. Horat. 3, ac primo Maecenati, deinde
Augusto insinuatus. In earlier writers, from Plautus onward, we find such
phrases as insinuare se in familiaritatem (amicitiam) alicuius; insinuare
se ad aliquem or alicui; and with the reflexive omitted insinuare alicui
(e.g. Cic. de or. i 20, 90, blandiri suppliciter et subtiliter insinuare eis, a
quibus, etc.).

congruentia morum: the friendship of Nero and Otho was a case of
ὁ ὅμοιος τῷ ὁμοίῳ, pares cum paribus. Tacitus says the same thing, H. i 13,
Otho gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus; cf. id. A. xiii 45, Otho pellexit
(Poppaeam) iuventa ac luxu et quia flagrantissimus in amicitia Neronis
habebatur: Dio lxi 11, ἦν δέ τις Μάρκος Σαλούιος ῎Οθων, ὃς οὕτως ἔκ τε τῆς
ὁμοιότητος τῶν τρόπων καὶ τῆς κοινωνίας τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων τῷ Νέρωνι ᾠκείωτο ὥστε,
κ.τ.λ.: Plut. Galb. 19, φίλῳ δὲ τῷ ῎Οθωνι καὶ συμβιωτῇ διὰ τὴν ἀσωτίαν ἐχρῆτο
(ὁ Νέρων).
..

consuetudine stupri: consuetudo (consuetio, Plaut. Amph. 490) is
used in Terence and later writers for intercourse in love (generally illicit
love); cf. Calig. 24, 1, cum omnibus sororibus suis stupri consuetudinem
fecit: Tit. 10, 2, consuetudinem recordatum, quam cum fratris uxore
habuerit: Ner. 35, Octaviae consuetudinem cito aspernatus. The improper
relations between Otho and Nero are often referred to; e.g. Aurel. Vict.
Caes. 7, Neroni quoque quondam criminose familiaris: Juv. ii 99, pathicus
Otho: Mart. vi 32, 2, mollis Otho: Eutrop. vii 17, Otho in privata vita
mollis et Neronis familiaris.

damnatum repetundis: repetundae (sc. pecuniae) denoted the sums of
money claimed as a refund from magistrates or officials who had illegally
extorted it in Rome or the provinces, and so came to denote the illegal
extortion itself. The Lex Calpurnia (149 в.с.) established a perpetua
quaestio to try cases of extortion, the penalty being the payment of the
amount assessed (litis aestimatio) as illegally taken and the forfeit to the
state of the summa sacramenti; the relationship between the Lex Acilia
(c. 123 в.с.) and the Lex Servilia (c. 111 в.с.) is obscure, but between them
the penalty was raised to double the amount and also included exilium;
the Lex Cornelia (of Sulla, 81 B.c.) seems to have made the pecuniary
penalty four times the amount and defined the exilium as aquae et ignis
interdictio; the Lex Iulia (of Caesar, 59 B.c.) repealed the exilium,
retained the litis aestimatio, and ordained that those convicted should lose
their rank and be debarred from being senators, judges, witnesses, etc.;
cf. Suet. Iul. 43, repetundarum convictos etiam ordine senatorio movit.
The Lex Iulia, with some modifications in detail, continued to govern these
prosecutions under the empire, the cases being usually tried by the senate.
This is the only example of damnatus with the simple abl. of the
particular offence, and Ursinus introduced de before repetundis. There is
a similar use of the simple abl. in Tac. A. iii 38, Cordum postulaverat
repetundis, where Nipperdey inserts de. A general term such as crimine
is found with postulare (e.g. Apul. Met. iii 6, vii 3) and Kühner-Stegmann
(i 465) cite Cic. Ph. xiii 27, quo scelere damnatus: id. Cael. 78, absolutus
ambitu: Sen. Controv. i 5, 1, stupro (al. stupri) accusatur: Suet. Ner. 31,
scelere convictos: Sen. Herc. O. 898, scelere (al. sceleris) te misera arguis.

restitutionem: the tech. term for the restoration of rights which have
been forfeited by law: cf. Cic. Agr. ii 4, iudiciorum perturbationes, rerum
iudicatarum infirmationes, restitutio damnatorum; so “restituere," e.g.
Suet. Iul. 41, Caliy. 15, restituere aliquem (damnatum): Claud. 12, restituere
exulem; see also Digest iv 1, 3, “De in integrum restitutionibus.”
Tacitus (H. i 77) mentions that Otho as emperor restored to their places
in the senate some of those convicted of extortion under Claudius and
Nero: redditus Cadio Rufo, Pedio Blaeso, Saevinio Proculo senatorius
locus; repetundarum criminibus sub Claudio ac Nerone ceciderant; and
it is the restitutio of the senatorius locus which is referred to in our
passage.
ad agendas gratias: see on Vesp. 2, 3.

secretorum particeps: cf. Tac. A. i 6, quod postquam Sallustius Crispus
particeps secretorum comperit; so “secretorum conscius,' e.g. Suet.
Tib. 14, 4. In post-Aug. writers secretum is freely used as a subst.
Suetonius has it in the following senses: (a) res secreta "a secret,”
here and in Aug. 66, 3, Tib. 14, 4; (b) = secessus “retirement, seclusion,"
Dom. 3, 1, Tib. 42, 1: 60, Ner. 20, 2, Claud. 10, 1; (c) = locus secretus,
Oth. 10, 2 Vesp. 21; (d) = colloquium secretum, Calig. 23, 2, Tib. 25, 3;
(e) secreta = litterae secretae “private papers," Calig. 49, 3, in secretis
eius reperti sunt duo libelli.
..

die quem Nero destinarat: Nero's various efforts to murder his
mother Agrippina are described in Ner. 34. Having thrice failed to poison
her, he introduced a mechanical device in the ceiling of her bedroom by
which the panels would fall on her as she slept, but this design leaked
out. He then invited her to Baiae during the festival of the Quinquatrus
(March 19-23), and arranged that the vessel on which she came should be
run into after her arrival so that it could not be used on her return. In
the evening she was entertained to dinner (Suetonius here says by Otho)
and when the time came for her to return to Bauli, Nero put her on
board a collapsible vessel which would cause her death either by its
breaking in pieces or by the falling in of its cabin (solutilis navis, cuius
vel naufragio vel camerae ruina periret); she managed, however, to swim
ashore. Finally, in the same year 59 A.D., he had her stabbed to death,
everything being arranged to make it appear that she had committed
suicide in consequence of the failure of a plot of hers to assassinate Nero.
See also Tac. 4. xiv 1-9, where the details are given somewhat differently.

necandae matri: the use of the dative of the gerundive to express
end or object, which is comparatively infrequent in pre-class. and class.
Lat., is increasingly common from Livy on, especially in Tacitus. For
other examples in Suetonius see Dom. 8,2; Vesp. 5, 3:8,5:10; Tit. 8, 4.
Kühner-Stegmann (i 746 sqq.) give numerous instances of this dat. with
such phrases as comitia edico, indico, habeo; diem dico, indico, statuo;
dies venit; tempus do; locum eligo, do, relinquo; finem facio.

ad avertendas suspiciones: according to Tacitus (A. xiv 4) Agrippina
had heard of the plot and in doubt whether she was to believe it she
went by litter and not by boat from Bauli to Baiae. There some soothing
words from Nero allayed her fears. Dio (lxi 12) says that Nero had
brought her with him by sea from Antium to Bauli, using the ship which
had been prepared for the murder, in order to accustom her to it.

cenam dedit: in the narrative in Ner. 34 Suetonius does not mention
that the banquet was given by Otho, and it is not in Tacitus or Dio;
moreover, this account of Otho acting as host to Nero and Agrippina in
59 A.D. contradicts Tacitus (A. xiii 46) who records the sending of Otho
to Lusitania among the events of 58, and it is also irreconcilable with
what Suetonius says below of the duration of Otho's governorship of
Lusitania per decem annos ending in the summer of 68. Furneaux (on
Tac. A. xiv 4) suggests that the story about Otho, if true at all, is to be
referred to some previous attempt on Agrippina's life.

exquisitissimae comitatis: Dio (lxi 13), τὴν μητέρα . . φιλοφρόνως εἰστίασεν
(ὁ Νέρων): Tac. (l.c.), comiter excepta (Agrippina) superque ipsum
(Neronem) collocata. Iam pluribus sermonibus, modo familiaritate iuvenili
Nero et rursus adductus ("grave"), quasi seria consociaret, tracto in
longum convictu, etc. Comitas was a characteristic of the dinners given
by Augustus; cf. Aug. 74, cenam ternis ferculis ("courses'") aut cum
abundissime senis praebebat, ut non nimio sumptu, ita summa comitate.

Poppaeam Sabinam: a daughter of T. Ollius, who perished with
Sejanus, but she took the name of her maternal grandfather Poppaeus
Sabinus (cons. 9 A.D.). Married first to Rufrius Crispinus, she became the
mistress and wife of Otho and mistress and wife of Nero. She induced
Nero to murder his mother Agrippina, and to divorce and put to death
his wife Octavia. In 63 A.D. she bore to him a son who only lived four
months, and when she was again with child in 65 she met her death through
Nero kicking her in a fit of rage. Tacitus (A. xiii 45) gives a well-known
description of her: Huic mulieri cuncta alia fuere praeter honestum
animum. Quippe mater eius, aetatis suae feminas pulchritudine supergressa, gloriam pariter et formam dederat; opes claritudini generis sufficiebant. Sermo comis nec absurdum ingenium: modestiam praeferre et
lascivia uti. Rarus in publicum egressus, idque velata parte oris, ne
satiaret adspectum, vel quia sic decebat. Famae numquam pepercit,
maritos et adulteros non distinguens; neque adfectui suo aut alieno
obnoxia, unde utilitas ostenderetur, illuc libidinem transferebat.

tunc adhuc amicam eius: conflicting accounts are given of the exact
relationship which existed between Poppaea, Nero, and Otho.
In his.
earlier work, the Histories (i 13), Tacitus calls her "the imperial
mistress," whom Nero had entrusted to Otho until he himself could get
rid of his wife Octavia and marry again: Otho pueritiam incuriose,
adulescentiam petulanter egerat, gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus. Eoque
Poppaeam Sabinam, principale scortum, ut apud conscium libidinum,
deposuerat, donec Octaviam uxorem amoliretur. In the Annals (xiii 45-6),
however, he says that while her husband Crispinus was still alive she was
attracted to Otho by his youth and extravagance and by the fact that he
was such an ardent friend of Nero (whom she may have hoped to captivate).
This intrigue with Otho was followed at once by their marriage.
Nero,.
inflamed by Otho's praises of his wife's beauty, sent for Poppaea and
fell a complete victim to her charm. She in coquettish fashion pretended
that she could not be his, as she was a married woman, and so Nero, to
get rid of Otho and have sole possession of her, sent him as governor to
Lusitania. (See Fabia, “L'adultère de Néron et de Poppée," Rev. de
Phil. 1896 p. 12 sqq., who thinks the account in the Annals is based on
more accurate information). Dio (lxi 11) agrees fairly closely with
Suetonius and Tacitus in the Histories, saying that Poppaea was taken
from her first husband (Crispinus) by Nero and given to Otho and that
thus she became the joint mistress of them both (αὐτῇ ἀμφότεροι ἅμα ἐχρῶντο).
So too Plutarch (Galb. 19) states that Nero fell in love with her while she was
wife to Crispinus, but retaining as yet some respect for his own wife-
(Octavia) and fearing his mother (Agrippina) he employed Otho to solicit
her. Otho seduced her, promising her that through him she would have Nero
as a lover, and persuaded her to leave her husband and marry him. Having
married her, he became so jealously fond of her that he would not brook
even the emperor as a sharer of her affection, and he was in imminent
danger of his life through thwarting Nero's desires; his appointment to
Lusitania saved him from death.

marito: Rufrius Crispinus, a prefect of the praetorians in the reign
of Claudius, who was rewarded with “sestertium quindecies et insignia
praeturae" for the arrest of Valerius Asiaticus (Tac. A. xi 1 and 4). He
was banished by Nero after the conspiracy of Piso in 65, occasione coniurationis, sed Neroni invisus, quod Poppaeam quondam matrimonio
tenuerat (A. xv 71). He committed suicide in Sardinia when Nero sent
orders for his death (A. xvi 17).
demandatam: demandare (= committere, tradere, παρακατατιθέναι) is
first found in the title of a play of Caecilius “Demandati''; Livy is the
next writer in whom it occurs, e.g. v 27, plures pueri
unius curae
demandabantur. Suetonius uses it more frequently than any other author;
e.g. Ner. 35, 5, privignum mergendum mari. servis ipsius demandavit:
Tib. 51, 2, quibus ea funeris sui curam moriens demandarat: Calig. 9,
ablegari eum.. et in proximam civitatem demandari (= servandum tradi).
..

nuptiarum specie: this version of the story makes Nero arrange
that Otho was to go through a form of marriage with Poppaea, and was
then merely to hold her in trust and inviolate until Nero, freed from
Octavia and Agrippina, was ready to take her over.

nec corrupisse contentus: poets and post-Aug. prose writers use the
infinitive with contentus (= satis habens).
In Aug. 82 Suetonius has
contentus hoc erat ut. Here, as frequently, corrumpere is used in the
sense of διαφθείρειν γυναῖκα.

adeo dilexit, ut: Plutarch describes how Otho chafed at the thought
of sharing his loved one with any other, and how Poppaea was pleased
with this jealous love: ἐλθούσης δὲ παρ᾽ αὐτὸν ὡς γαμετῆς οὐκ ἠγάπα μετέχων, ἀλλ᾽
ἤσγαλλε μεταδιδούς, οὐδὲ αὐτῆς ἀχθομένης, ὥς φασι, τῇ ζηλοτυπίᾳ τῆς Ποππαίας.
When emperor, Otho still cherished the memory of Poppaea; cf. Tac. H. i
78, ne tum quidem immemor amorum statuas Poppaeae per senatus consultum reposuit.

§2. creditur non recepisse: according to Plutarch it was Poppaea
who refused to admit Nero when Otho was absent: καὶ γὰρ ἀποκλεῖσαι τὸν
Νέρωνα λέγεται μὴ παρόντος τοῦ Ὄθωνος, εἴτε τῆς ἡδονῆς ἀφαιροῦσα τὸ πλήσιμον,
εἴτε, ὥς φασιν ἔνιοι, βαρυνομένη τὸν Καίσαρος γάμον, ἐραστῇ δὲ μὴ φεύγουσα χρῆσθαι
διὰ τὸ φιλακόλαστον. Plutarch's account agrees with what Tacitus says
in his later version (A. xiii 46) of Poppaea discouraging Nero ‘‘nuptam
esse se dictitans nec posse matrimonium amittere." See Hardy on Plut.
l.c.

depositum: cf. Tac. H. i 13, Sabinam (apud Othonem) deposuerat
(Nero). "depositum” was used of persons as well as things; e.g. in
Luc. ii 71 (of Marius hiding in the marshes of Minturnae) stagna avidi
texere soli laxaeque paludes | depositum, Fortuna, tuum: Sen. Controv. ii
4, 1, accede huc, puer, depositum, crimen meum: Stat. Ach. i 385 (of the
young Achilles entrusted to Lycomedes king of Scyros), depositumque
ingens timido commisimus astu.

reposcentem: so "poscere," Hor. C. i 24, 10, tu frustra pius heu non
ita creditum | poscis Quintilium deos. One who denied or refused to return
a deposit was called infitiator, e.g. Mart. i 103, 11, In ius, o fallax atque
infitiator, eamus; cf. Juv. xiii '60, si depositum non infitietur amicus.

diducto matrimonio: cf. Sen. Controv. ii 5, 1, nuptias tyrannicidium
diduxit, quas non diduxit tyrannus: Hor. C. iii 9, 18, quid si prisca redit
Venus diductosque iugo cogit aeneo?: Prop. ii 7, 3, diducere amantes |
non queat invitos Iuppiter.
sepositus est: for this use of seponere see on Tit. 9, 3.

per causam legationis: cf. Tac. H. i 13, mox suspectum (Othonem) in
eadem Poppaea in provinciam Lusitaniam specie legationis seposuit. For
“per causam” see on Vesp. i. Plutarch (Galb. 20) says that it was Seneca
who saved Otho from the jealous Nero by getting him appointed governor:
Σενέκαν δὲ εἶχεν εὔνουν, κἀκείνου τὸν Νέρωνα πείσαντος καὶ παραινέσαντος ἐξεπέμφθη
Λυσιτανῶν στρατηγός (legatus) ἐπὶ τὸν ᾿Ωκεανόν. Tacitus (A. xiii 46) describes
how Otho was cut off from Nero's familiar intercourse, and later excluded
from interviews or levées and from the imperial suite, and finally was
made governor of Lusitania that he might not be the emperor's rival at
Rome: deicitur familiaritate sueta, post congressu et comitatu Otho, et ad
postremum, ne in urbe aemulatus ageret, provinciae Lusitaniae praeficitur.

Lusitaniam: Lusitania, which earlier was included in Hispania
Ulterior, was made into a separate imperial province by Augustus. It
comprised nearly all Portugal and a part of Spain (Salamanca and
northern Estremadura). The capital was Emerita Augusta (Merida), a
colony of veterans founded by Augustus; and Olisipo (Lisbon) and Pax
Iulia (Beja) were important towns.
id: a correction by Casaubon of et (which is kept by Ihm).

poena acrior: i.e. death, cf. Plut. Galb. 19, ἐκινδύνευσεν οὖν ὁ Ὄθων
ἀποθανεῖν· καὶ παράλογον ἦν, ὅτι τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ ἀδελφὴν ἀποκτείνας διὰ τὸν
Ποππαίας γάμον ἐφείσατο τοῦ Ὄθωνος.

mimum omnem divulgaret: mimus is used occasionally in post-Aug.
writers for farcical proceedings or shams of any kind; e.g. Calig. 45 (of
Caligula's pretended military triumphs), in hoc quoque mimo praeter modum
intemperans: Tib. 24, principatum, quamvis neque occupare confestim
neque agere dubitasset, et statione militum, hoc est vi et specie dominationis assumpta, diu tamen recusavit impudentissimo mimo (so Gronovius,
animo MSS): Plin. N.H. vii 53, Antiocho regi Syriae e plebe nomine
Artemon in tantum similis fuit, ut Laodice coniux regia, necato iam
Antiocho, mimum per eum commendationis regnique successionis peregerit:
Flor. ii 14, Pseudophilippus regiam formam regium nomen mimo (so
Gronov., animo MSS.) quoque regio implevit.

disticho: the subst. distichon (distichum), δίστιχον, was used by
Martial, Suetonius, Ausonius, etc. for a couplet of any kind of verse (not
merely an elegiac couplet, as Lewis and Short say); e.g. in Suet. Iul. 51
of two trochaic septenarii: Suet. (?) vit. Verg. 58 of two hexameters. The
adj. distichos (-us), δίστιχοs, occurs in Varro Men. 398, etiam distichon
epigrammation vocant pоета. These lines on Otho seem modelled on
Ov. R.A. 161 sq.: Quaeritis Aegisthus quare sit factus adulter?
promptu causa est: desidiosus erat.
In
..

mentito exul honore: Plutarch (Galb. 20) says that Otho quite
realised that his governorship was only a specious name and a mere disguise
for banishment, and so took care not to make himself disagreeable or
oppressive to the provincials: παρέσχεν ἑαυτὸν οὐκ ἄχαριν οὐδὲ ἐπαχθῆ τοῖς
ὑπηκόοις, εἰδὼς φυγῆς ὑποκόρισμα καὶ παρακάλυμμα τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτῷ διδομένην. Cf.
Tac. H. i 21 (considerations which influenced Otho in making a bid for
empire), praegravem se Neroni fuisse nec Lusitaniam rursus et alterius
exilii honorem expectandum.
provinciam administravit
moderatione: his administration is
praised by Tacitus also; H. i 13, comiter administrata provincia; A. xiii 46,
provinciae Lusitaniae praeficitur, ubi usque ad civilia arma non ex ("in
accordance with'") priore infamia sed integre sancteque egit, procax otii et
potestatis temperantior ("a wanton in respect of his hours of idleness,
more self-controlled in respect of his official life." Furneaux).
quaestorius: Lusitania was an imperial province of the second class,
and as such its governor was normally a man of praetorian rank (legatus
Augusti propraetore); Otho had held nothing higher than the quaestorship,
and was only 26 years of age when appointed.
per decem annos: 58-68 A.D. For lengthy tenures of governorships of
imperial provinces see on Galb. 9, 1. Nero, of course, had a special reason
for keeping Otho away from Rome.
abstinentia: opp. to avaritia; see on Tit. 7, 3, abstinuit alieno.

conatibus Galbae primus accessit: Tac. H. i 13, primus in partes
(Galbae) transgressus nec, donec (“as long as") bellum fuit, segnis et
inter praesentes splendidissimus (i.e. most conspicuous of Galba's
followers): Plut. Galb. 20, ἀποστάντος δὲ Γάλβα πρῶτος αὐτὸς προσεχώρησε
τῶν ἡγεμόνων (“provincial governors''). Plutarch adds that Otho brought
with him all his gold and silver vessels to be melted down and coined for
Galba's use, and presented him with such of his servants as knew best
how to wait upon an emperor; his fidelity and experience were invaluable
to Galba, and he accompanied him during all his journey from Spain,
driving in the same carriage with him for many days.

et ex condicione: et (= etiam or vel) is omitted in some of the MSS.
and of the older editions.

Seleuci: the name of this astrologer is given as Ptolemaeus by
Tacitus and Plutarch. Seleucus was the name of Vespasian's trusty
astrologer (Tac. H. ii 78), and Suetonius may have confused the two.
Juvenal (vi 557 sqq.) refers to Otho's astrologer without mentioning his
name: Praecipuus tamen est horum (sc. astrologorum), qui saepius exul, [
cuius amicitia conducendaque tabella | magnus civis obit et formidatus
Othoni, “by whose friendship and by whose venal horoscope a great citizen
(i.e. Galba) died, one whom Otho dreaded." Duff. The great influence
of the mathematici, or astrologers, in persuading Otho to seize the empire
is described in Tac. H. i 22: urgentibus etiam mathematicis, dum novos
motus et clarum Othoni annum observatione siderum adfirmant, genus
hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax, quod in civitate nostra
et vetabitur semper et retinebitur. Multos secreta Poppaeae mathematicos,
pessimum principalis matrimonii instrumentum, habuerant; e quibus
Ptolemaeus Othoni in Hispania comes, cum superfuturum eum Neroni promisisset, postquam ex eventu fides, coniectura iam et rumore senium Galbae
et iuventam Othonis computantium persuaserat fore ut in imperium
ascisceretur. Sed Otho tamquam peritia et monitu fatorum praedicta
accipiebat, cupidine ingenii humani libentius obscura credendi.
Plutarch
(Galb. 23) also mentions the two predictions of Ptolemaeus that Otho
would survive Nero and that he would become emperor.
mathematici: see on Vitell. 14, 4.

superstitem Neroni: for the dat. cf. Calig. 7, liberi superstites patri;
Suetonius also uses the gen. in Tib. 62, 3, superstes omnium suorum.
Cicero and Tacitus have both constructions; see Kühner-Stegmann, i
448 sq.

repromittens: Baumg.-Cr. explains this as insuper promittens or novo
promisso spondens, a meaning which the word does not seem to bear elsewhere. repromittere was properly a mercantile term for binding oneself
to do something in return for a certain consideration; e.g. Plaut. Asin.
453, verum istuc argentum tamen mihi si vis denumerare, | repromittam
istoc nomine solutam rem futuram: Cic. Rosc. Com. 13, 37; Suet. Claud.
20, 2, cum quidam privato sumptu emissuros (i.e. that they would drain
the Fucine Lake) se repromitterent, si sibi siccati agri concederentur. It
was also used merely as a more emphatic form of promittere, e.g. Plin.
Εp. iv 27, ad hunc gustum totum librum repromitto (“I guarantee that
the whole book is up to the level of this extract'"), and this may be the
meaning here and in Tib. 17, 2, eo (cognomine) contentum repromittens
quod se defuncto suscepturus esset (i.e. Augustus promised that Tiberius
would be satisfied with the title which he would receive on Augustus'
death), though there Rolfe translates repromittens ‘‘reiterating the promise," while Bentley and Madvig would read contentum fore promittens;
similarly in the present passage Madvig proposed imperatorem
promittens.
fore

§ 2. nullo
genere omisso: Tacitus describes the sedulous efforts of
Otho to make himself popular with the army, H. i 23, studia militum iam
pridem spe successionis aut paratu facinoris adfectaverat, in itinere (from
Spain), in agmine, in stationibus vetustissimum quemque militum nomine
vocans ac memoria Neroniani comitatus (their companionship under Nero's
régime) contubernales appellando; alios agnoscere, quosdam requirere et
pecunia aut gratia iuvare, inserendo saepius querellas et ambiguos de Galba
sermones, quaeque alia turbamenta volgi: ib. 36, nec deerat Otho protendens manus adorare volgum, iacere oscula, et omnia serviliter pro
dominatione. So Plutarch (Galb. 20) tells how Otho was affable and
obliging to everyone (παρέχων ἑαυτὸι· εὐπροσήγορον καὶ φιλάνθρωπον ἅπασιν), and
how he specially courted the favour (ἐξεθεράπευσεν) of Vinius (see Suet.
Galb. 14, 2) and got preferment for the soldiers from Vinius and the
influential freedmen Icelus and Asiaticus.

officii: 'attentiveness,” attentions"; cf. Iul. 26,2, nullum officiorum
in quemquam genus omisit: ib. 19, 2, omnibus officiis Pompeium assectatus
est: Aug. 61, 2, cum praecipua officia vivae praestitisset.

ambitionis: “favour-seeking,” “popularity-hunting"; cf. Aug. 25, 3,
murales coronas quam parcissime et sine ambitione tribuit: Iul. 28, 3,
quod per ambitionem data esset (civitas): Tib. 21, 2, ambitione tractus,
ut tali successore desiderabilior ipse quandoque fieret.

quotiens cena principem acciperet: cf. Plut. Galb. 20, ὁσάκις δὲ τὸν Γάλβαν
εἱστία, τὴν παραφυλάττουσαν ἀεὶ σπεῖραν (“cohort") ἐδέκαζε ("bribed") χρυσοῦν
ἑκάστῳ διανέμων, οἷς τιμᾶν αὐτὸν (i.e. Galba) ἐδόκει καταπολιτευόμενος καὶ δημαγωγῶν
τὸ στρατιωτικόν. Tacitus (H. i 24) says this bribery was done through the
agency of Maevius Pudens, an associate of Tigellinus: Flagrantibus iam
militum animis velut faces addiderat Maevius Pudens, e proximis Tigellini.
Is mobilissimum quemque ingenio aut pecuniae indigum et in novas cupiditates praecipitem alliciendo eo paulatim progressus est, ut per speciem
convivii, quotiens Galba apud Othonem epularetur, cohorti excubias agenti
viritim centenos nummos divideret; quam velut publicam largitionem
Otho secretioribus apud singulos praemiis intendebat. For quotiens see
on Galb. 10, 2.

aureos: see on Galb. 20, 2; an aureus was equivalent to centeni nummi,
100 sesterces, the amount stated by Tac. l.c.

excubanti cohorti: sc. praetoriae; one praetorian cohort at a time
acting as a guard for the emperor at his palace (c. 6, 1) and accompanying
him to other houses. The emperors gave to their guards the sportula, or
allowance for food, given to clients by patrons (Dom. 7, 1); and Otho,
when he was entertaining Galba, took upon himself to play the patron's
part towards the guards in attendance on the emperor by bestowing upon
them an extravagantly lavish allowance; cf. the words of Tacitus quoted
above, “per speciem convivii" (= titulo sportularum).

cuidam litiganti: Tacitus (H. i 24) gives his name and says that
he was one of the imperial bodyguard: adeo animosus corruptor (Otho)
ut Cocceio Proculo speculatori de parte finium cum vicino ambigenti universum vicini agrum sua pecunia emptum dono dederit, per socordiam praefecti (i.e. Laco, see on Galb. 14, 2), quem nota pariter et occulta fallebant.

arbiter: an “arbiter ex compromisso” to whom the parties agree to
leave the decision of the dispute; a magistrate could also refer a case to
one arbiter or to more than one, to have it decided in accordance with
the principles of bona fides.
emancipavit: Torrentius, ingeniously but needlessly, conjectured eique
mancipavit. The compound emancipare is used here of the conveyance of
land, as in Quintil. vi 3, 44, omnes autem illas (possessiones) Brutus
vendiderat; et tum paterna emancipare praedia turpius habebatur: Plin.
Ep. x 4, fundos emancipavit et cetera quae in emancipatione implenda
solent exigi consummavit, i.e. he went through all the formalities of a
fictitious sale (mancipatio per aes et libram) which required the presence
of the vendor (qui mancipio dat) and the purchaser (qui mancipio accipit),
five witnesses, and a libripens with the scales; the "purchaser" placed a
sesterce in the scales held by the libripens and said "hanc ego rem ex
iure Quiritium meam esse aio, eaque mihi empta est hoc aere aeneaque
libra." See Hardy on Plin. loc. cit. The various senses of emancipare
are illustrated in Roby, Rom. Priv. Law, i 75 sqq.
..

qui non sentiret dignum: this was also the universal opinion with
regard to Galba before he became emperor; cf. the familiar words of
Tacitus (H. i 49), maior privato visus, dum privatus fuit, et omnium consensu capax imperii, nisi imperasset.

speraverat ut adoptaretur: Galba's choice of an adopted son and
successor is described in Galb. 17, where see notes. Otho's hopes were
based on Vinius (Galb. 14, 2), whose daughter Crispina was betrothed to
him (Tac. H. i 13, Plut. Galb. 21), and on the support of the soldiers and
of Nero's courtiers who recognised in him a kindred nature to Nero, cf.
Tac. (l.c.), Otho
spem adoptionis statim conceptam acrius in dies
rapiebat, faventibus plerisque militum, prona in eum aula Neronis ut
similem.

Pisone praelato: Plutarch (Galb. 21) says that in preferring him
Galba was actuated, as always, by the consideration of what was best for
the state: ὁ δὲ Γάλβας ἀεὶ μὲν ἦν δῆλος πρὸ τοῦ ἰδίου τὸ κοινὸν τιθέμενος καὶ ζητῶν

decidit.

πολλὰ σημεῖα τῇ μορφῇ πικρῶς καὶ σὺν ὀργῇ τῆς ἐλπίδος τὴν ἀπότευξιν φέροντος, ἧς

in Foro: in the Forum the bankers (mensarii, argentarii) and merchants

mersus “bankrupt" (Plaut. Epid. 118), and the common phrase cedere
Foro "to become bankrupt."

truth of the dream were being proved at once); Ner. 21, 1, (Nero) repraesentaturum se pollicitus est (i.e. promised that he would sing at once);
Vitell. 10, 12, verbera et plagas, saepe vulnera, nonnunquam necem repraesentantes adversantibus.
quinquagena: sc. sestertia, 50,000 sesterces, about £425.

nec adeo multi: "but not so very many"; cf. Aug. 65, 2, C. Lucique
casu non adeo fractus: ib. 88, orthographiam
non adeo custodit: Galb.
7, 1, valitudo neque adeo gravis. The use of non perinde is similar (see

fiducia plures adfuturos: Gruter aptly quotes Tac. A. iv 7, primas
dominandi spes in arduo: ubi sis ingressus, adesse studia et ministros;
cf. also Tac. H. i 55, insita mortalibus natura propere sequi quae piget
inchoare. The acc. c. inf. depending on fiducia occurs earlier in Ov.
A.A. i 269, prima tuae menti veniat fiducia cunctas | posse capi: ib. ii 349:

Tac. A. xi 28, ipsa facilitas imperatoris fiduciam dabat posse opprimi
damnatam ante quam ream. Suetonius uses the same constr. with fides,
persuasio, suspicio, rumor, opinio, spes, metus, mos, religio, etc.

tulerat animus occupare: the expression animus fert (only here in
Suet.) is mainly poetical, though found a few times in Sall. and Liv.; cf.
Ov. Her. xiii 85, volui revocare animusque ferebat: Hor. E. i 14, 8: Sall.
Cat. 58, 6, diutius in his locis esse, si maxime animus ferat, frumenti ..
egestas prohiberet: Sall. Iug. 54, 4: Liv. xxiii 15, xxx 12, xl 4. It is
used with the inf., as here, in Ov. Met. i 1, In nova fert animus mutatas
dicere formas | corpora: Luc. i 67: Pers. iv 7. Some of our MSS. have
erat for tulerat, and Ursinus read fuerat (cf. Iul. 82, 4, fuerat animus
coniuratis corpus occisi in Tiberim trahere).

post adoptionem statim: Piso was adopted by Galba on Jan. 10,
69 A.D., and on Jan. 15 Galba was slain and Otho was proclaimed emperor
by the soldiers. The design which Suetonius here attributes to Otho of
attacking Galba immediately after the adoption is not mentioned elsewhere; Tacitus (H. i 26) says that the conspirators had thoughts of
carrying off Otho to the camp on the evening of Jan. 14, but refrained:
adeoque parata apud malos seditio, etiam apud integros dissimulata fuit,
ut postero iduum die redeuntem a cena Othonem rapturi fuerint, ni incerta
noctis et tota urbe sparsa militum castra nec facilem inter temulentos
consensum timuissent.
castra: i.e. the castra praetoria; see on Galb. 19, 1.
excubabat: cf. c. 4, 2.

statione: used here for the period of duty during which one out of
the twelve praetorian cohorts acted as guard at the imperial palace. Other
meanings of statio in Suet. are: (1) posts where soldiers are stationed as
guards; e.g. Iul. 32, cum plurimi etiam ex stationibus milites concucurrissent: (2) the soldiers stationed as guards; e.g. Aug. 32, 1, dispositis
per opportuna loca stationibus: (3) more especially the soldiers stationed
as guards at the palace, e.g. Tib. 24, 1, statione militum, hoc est vi et
specie dominationis, assumpta: Ner. 21, 1, adiuvante vulgi preces etiam

Gaius fuerat occisus: the two conspirators who took the leading
part in the assassination of Gaius Caligula were Cassius Chaerea and
Cornelius Sabinus, who were both tribunes of a cohort of the praetorian
guard. The two prefects of the praetorian guard had been accused of
complicity in an earlier conspiracy against that emperor (Calig. 56 and 58).

desertus Nero: Nero tried to induce the tribunes and centurions of
the praetorian guard to accompany him in a last despairing flight from
Rome, but they either openly refused or gave evasive answers; one even
exclaimed in the words of Virgil "Usque adeone mori miserum est?”
Waking at midnight, he found that his guard had left (comperit stationem
recessisse), and he fled from the city with only four faithful attendants
(Ner. 47).

medium tempus: between Jan. 10 and Jan. 15; see on Galb. 17, intra
sextum adoptionis diem.

religio: portents, evil omens; cf. Ner. 19, 1, turbatus religione simul

religionis (''in defiance of the portent'"): Oth. 8, 3. It is not necessary
to assume a reference to “dies religiosi” (Claud. 14, Tib. 61, 2), i.e. days
in the Roman year which were unfavourable for any undertaking, generally
because they were dedicated to the worship of the gods of the underworld
or were associated with some historical disaster to the Roman people and
so were dies atri or vitiosi, e.g. the day of the battle of the Allia, July 18
(Vitell. 11, 2); other dies religiosi were the dies postriduani (Vitell. '8, 1, n.).
See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 295.
Seleucus: the astrologer; see c. 4, 1.

exemit: eximere diem, tempus, etc., meant to take away a day, etc.,
from a purpose for which it might have been used, and so to waste it;
cf. Liv. i 50, 8, quia ea res exemisset illum diem: Cic. Q. Fr. ii 4, Lentulus
dies comitiales exemit omnes: Cic. Phil. vi 3, 7, horam eximere ullam in
tali cive liberando sine scelere non possumus: Sen. N. Q. iii 1, damna
aetatis male exemptae labor sarciat. To "talk out" a bill in the senate
was “diem dicendo eximere” (Cic. Att. iv 3, Q. Fr. ii 1).

§ 2. sub aede Saturni: this temple of Saturn was dedicated in 497 B.c.
(Liv. ii 21, Dion. Hal. vi 1); it was situated “sub clivo Capitolino” (Serv.
on Aen. ii 115, viii 319: Varr. L.L. v 42: Fest. p. 322 Müll.: Dion. Hal. i
34, παρὰ τῇ ῥίζῃ τοῦ λόφου κατὰ τὴν ἄνοδον τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς (Fori) φέρουσαν εἰς
τὸ Καπιτώλιον). Munatius Plancus restored it under Augustus (Suet. Aug.
29). See Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 360 sqq.

miliarium aureum: cf. Tac. H. i 27, Otho .. ad miliarium aureum sub
aedem Saturni pergit. This miliarium or milepost of bronze gilt was
erected at the upper end of the Forum by Augustus as curator viarum
in 20 B.C.; cf. Dio liv 8, προστάτης τῶν περὶ τὴν ῾Ρώμην ὁδῶν αἱρεθεὶς τὸ
χρυσοῦν μίλιον κεκλημένον ἔστησε. Plutarch (Galb. 24) describes it as the
centre at which all the roads of Italy terminated; the mileposts, however,
on these roads marked the distances, not from the miliarium aureum, but
from the gates of the city. Pliny (N.H. iii 66) mentions it as the
starting-point in the survey of Rome under Vespasian: mensura currente
a miliario in capite Romani Fori statuto.

salutavit: at the emperor's morning reception or levée (salutatio); see
on Vesp. 4, 4.

osculo exceptus: cf. Tib. 10, 2, paucos .. in digressu exosculatus: Ner.
37, 3, neque adveniens neque proficiscens quemquam osculo impertiit, ac
ne resalutatione quidem. The amici principis of the first order, and
senators as the emperor's peers received the honour of the imperial kiss;
cf. Plin. Pan. 23 (on Trajan's entry into Rome as emperor), gratum erat
cunctis, quod senatum osculo exciperes, ut dimissus osculo fueras; Pliny
also praises Trajan for not requiring his fellow-citizens to kiss his feet
and for not returning their kiss with his hand: ib. 24, non tu civium
amplexus ad pedes tuos deprimis nec osculum manu reddis. Caligula,
according to Dio lix 27 (cf. Sen. Ben. ii 12), kissed very few; to most,
even to senators, he gave his hand or foot to kiss. Nero showed his
animosity against the senate by refusing to kiss them when he set out for
Greece and on his return from his tour (Ner. 37, 3, quoted above).
Agricola on his return from Britain visited Domitian and was greeted
with a hasty kiss, but the emperor held no converse with him (Tac. Agr. 40,
exceptus brevi osculo et nullo sermone). The custom of the imperial kiss,
which was probably introduced from the East, is discussed at length by
Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 95 sq.; see also Marquardt, Privatl.2 260.

sacrificanti interfuit: this use of interesse c. dat. pers. (= adesse) is
very remarkable; the normal expression would be sacrificio eius interfuit;
there does not seem to be any parallel passage (Freund, De Suet. genere
dicendi, cites Sen. Prov. i 1, cum probaremus interesse nobis Deum, which
is quite different). Ernesti conjectured superfuit, for which see on Tit. 1.
This sacrifice and the soothsayer's warnings of the danger threatening
Galba are mentioned in Galb. 19, 1. Otho was the only senator present
at the sacrifice; cf. Dio lxiv 5, οὕτως ὑπ' αὐτοῦ (i.e. Galba) ἐτιμᾶτο ὥστε καὶ
ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, ἐν ᾗ ἀπέθανε, θυομένῳ αὐτῷ μόνος τῶν βουλευτῶν παρέστη.

liberto nuntiante: this freedman was Onomastus; Tac. H. і 27,
nec multo post libertus Onomastus nuntiat exspectari eum ab architecto et
redemptoribus (“contractors'"); quae significatio coeuntium iam militum
et paratae coniurationis convenerat.

quasi venalem domum inspecturus: Tac. (l.c.), Otho causam digressus
requirentibus cum emi sibi praedia (“country-house") vetustate suspecta
eoque prius exploranda finxisset, innixus liberto per Tiberianam domum
in Velabrum, inde ad miliarium aureum pergit. So too Plutarch (Galb.
24) says that Otho's pretext was that he had bought an old house and
wanted to point out to the vendors any defects (τὰ ὕποπτα δεῖξαι τοῖς
πωληταῖς). Under Roman law such defects had to be pointed out before
the contract was actually made, for after that time the thing bought was
at the buyer's risk (Hardy on Plut. l.c.).

postica parte Palati: = per Tiberianam domum (Tac.); διὰ τῆς Τιβερίου

the N.W. corner of the Palatine hill was at the back of the palace of
Augustus (domus Augustana) and connected with it. It looked down on
the Velabrum. From the Velabrum Otho entered the Forum through the
vicus Tuscus.

ad constitutum: the appointed place of meeting, viz. the miliarium
aureum in the Forum. "constitutum'' is often used as a subst. for an
appointed time and place of meeting, a tryst: e.g. Varr. R.R. ii 5, 1, qui
tum sero venisset ad constitutum: Cic. Caecin. 33, qui ad constitutum
experiundi iuris gratia venissent: Cic. Att. xii 1, 1, v Kalend, igitur ad
constitutum ("on the 26th, then, to our tryst'').

febrem simulasse: this feigned illness is implied in the account of
Tacitus (H. i 27), who says that Otho leant on a freedman (innixus liberto)
when leaving the palace (cf. id. Ann. ii 29, Libo aegritudine fessus seu
simulato morbo innisus fratri). Suetonius, on the other hand, says that
Otho rushed (proripuit se) from the Palace.

§3. abditus: "hidden away in" the closed sedan; cf. Vitell. 16,
abstrusus gestatoria sella. For the abl. with abdere see on Vitell. 7, 2.

muliebri sella: this was probably a cathedra, a sedan-chair fashioned
like the cathedra or chair ordinarily used by women (Marquardt, Privatl.”
726, 737), and differing in shape from the usual sedan-chair (sella gestatoria,
for which see Vitell. 16, and Dom. 2, 1, where it is distinguished from the
lectica). The cathedra is mentioned in Juv. i 65, cum iam sexta cervice
feratur | hinc atque inde patens ac nuda paene cathedra. These sedanchairs were roofed over and the openings at the side could be shut close
with curtains; cf. Juv. i 124, ostendens vacuam et clausam pro coniuge
sellam: Mart. xi 98, 11, lectica nec te tuta pelle veloque, | nec vindicabit
sella saepius clausa. Modest women had the sedan-chair closed; cf. Sen.
de Remed. 16, 7: Ben. i 9.

lecticariis: lecticarii (φορειαφόροι Plut.) was the general term for bearers
of either the lectica or sella. Sidonius (Ep. i 11, 9) has cathedrarii for
the bearers of the cathedra.

laxato calceo: the calcei were fastened with leather straps (corrigiae,
lora); see Marquardt, op. cit. 590: Daremberg-Saglio, i 816.

succollatus: "taken up on their shoulders.” succollare is first used
in Varr. R.R. iii 16, 8, of bees carrying the king-bee: apes fessum (regem)
sublevant, et si nequit volare, succollant (in Verg. G. iv 217 this is expressed by regem attollunt umeris). It was the regular word for the
lecticarii taking on their shoulders the poles (asseres) of the lectica; e.g.
Suet. Claud. 10, 2, ab his (militibus) lecticae impositus est et, quia sui
diffugerant, vicissim succollantibus in castra delatus est (cf. Catull. 10, 21,
fractum qui veteris pedem grabati | in collo sibi collocare posset).
The account given here by Suetonius differs in details from that in
Plutarch and Tacitus. According to Plut., Galb. 25, when Otho reached
the miliarium aureum in the Forum, he was saluted as emperor by 23
soldiers. Frightened at the fewness of his supporters he began to waver,
but these soldiers would not let him recede; they drew their swords and
surrounding his litter ordered the bearers to proceed, while Otho kept
ejaculating that he was ruined and urged the bearers to make haste.
Tacitus (H. i 27) says: Ibi tres et viginti speculatores consalutatum imperatorem ac paucitate salutantium trepidum et sellae festinanter impositum
strictis mucronibus rapiunt.
imperator consalutatus: cf. Galb. 10, 1.

principia: see on Oth. 1, 2. Plutarch (l.c.) describes how on Otho's
arrival at the camp the tribune on duty, Martialis, in the confusion of
the moment opened the gate, and then there was no more opposition, for
those who were ignorant of the plot, finding themselves in the midst of its
supporters, at once came over; so too Tac. (c. 28): stationem in castris
agebat Iulius Martialis tribunus; is magnitudine subiti sceleris, an corrupta
latius castra, et, si contra tenderet, exitium metuens, praebuit plerisque
suspicionem conscientiae. Anteposuere ceteri quoque tribuni centurionesque
praesentia dubiis et honestis, isque habitus animorum fuit, ut pessimum
facinus auderent pauci, plures vellent, omnes paterentur.

obvio quoque adhaerente: Plutarch says that while Otho was being
borne through the Forum, his 23 original supporters were increased by 23
more, and that on the way from the Forum to the camp others kept joining
by threes and fours at a time. Tacitus merely states that the original 23
were joined by about the same number on the way to the camp: totidem
fere milites in itinere adgregantur, alii conscientia, plerique miraculo
("curiosity"), pars clamore et caudiis, pars silentio, animum ex eventu
sumpturi.

id. reliquissent: there is nothing corresponding to these words in
the elaborate speech which Tacitus (cc. 37, 38) puts into the mouth of

of Galba, and an appeal to the soldiers to champion the rights of the
people and the senate. Dio (lxiv 5), like Suetonius, attributes to Otho
no long discourse; he simply says that Otho persuaded or rather bought

suggests that Suetonius here is indirectly criticizing Tacitus: “En racontant
vivement ces événements rapides, Suétone, qui n'embellit point la réalité,
ne fait prononcer à Othon qu'une phrase fort courte: 'J'aurai ce que
vous me laissez!' dit-il aux soldats. Et le biographe ajoute: 'Il ne leur
fit point de plus longue harangue, ni plus de promesses, ni plus de protestations. Cette allusion ne serait-elle point une critique discrètement
adressée par le modeste biographe à l'éloquent historien?" There can be
little doubt that Fabia (Sources de Tacite p. 140) is right in saying "Tacite
a fabriqué le beau discours d'Othon de toutes pièces.”

καθάπερ ἄλλοι γεγονότες ἢ θεῶν ἄλλων γεγονότων συνελθόντες ὤμνυον ὅρκον ὑπὲρ τοῦ
Οθωνος, ὃν αὐτὸς ὀμόσας οὐκ ἐτήρησε, κ.τ.λ.

praeter urbanus, as both consuls, Galba and Vinius, were dead.

positaque brevi ratione: ratione is a correction by Erasmus of oratione.
Elsewhere ponere rationem is used in the literal sense of making a reckoning or furnishing an account; e.g. Digest xlvi 3, 89, ratione posita eius
pecuniae: xlvii 4, 1, ponere rationem actus quem servus administravit :
Sen. Ep. 87, cum ad patrimonium ventum est, diligentissimi computatores
sic rationem ponitis singulorum quibus aut pecuniam credituri estis aut
beneficia (= rationem initis facultatum eorum quibus "you make calculations concerning'"). This reading is accepted by Roth and Preud 'homme,
but not by Ihm. Oudendorp preferred propositaque
ratione. Ernesti
tried to defend ponere orationem as equivalent to habere orationem.
Burman proposed expositoque brevi oratione, explaining exposito as an
abl. abs. like cognito, intellecto, perspecto, etc., while the clause with quasi
gives the gist of the speech. Similarly Walther suggested positoque
oratione, citing Cic. Orat. 4, positum sit in primis
sine philosophia non
posse effici eloquentem: id. Cael. 7, posuistis enim coniurationis hunc
participem fuisse: id. Verr. ii 38, tantum verbo posuit. There is not,
however, any instance in Suet. of such a use of the abl. abs. Bentley
wildly conjectured perfunctusque or professusque brevi oratione. Erasmus'
correction is strongly supported by Spart. Sev. 7, where Septimius Severus
tries to justify to the senate his seizing the imperial power: in curia reddidit rationem suscepti imperii causatusque est, quod ad se occidendum
Iulianus notos ducum caedibus misisset.

coactus: Otho's defence, that he had acted under compulsion of the soldiers and that he had endangered his life by trying to
oppose their wishes, is mentioned in Dio lxiv 8, βεβιάσθαι μὲν γάρ, καὶ ἐς τὸ
τεῖχος (murum castrorum) ἄκων ἐσῆχθαι, κἀνταῦθα ἀντιλέγων κεκινδυνευκέναι ἔλεγε.

raptus: Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 791 n. 6) notices that from the practice
of the soldiers hurrying away the newly acclaimed emperor in a lectica
or sella to the camp (Suet. Claud. 10, Ner. 8; Tac. A. xii 69, H. і 27)
the verb rapi came to be used by metonymy for the elevation to the throne;
e.g. Capitolin. Max. et Balb. 3, qui statim raptus est et novo genere senatus
consulti, cum eodem die senatus consultum factum esset, inductus in curiam
Caesar est appellatus.

Palatium petit: Tac. H. i 47, Otho cruento adhuc foro per stragem
iacentium in Capitolium atque inde in Palatium vectus. For the Palatium
or domus Palatina see on Vesp. 25.

2,5; 16; Vesp. 24; Tit. 10, 1.
