super: praeter; see on Vesp. 24.

appellatus Nero: cf. Plut. Oth. 3, τοῖς δὲ πολλοῖς χαριζόμενος οὐκ ἔφευγε
τὸ πρῶτον ἐν τοῖς θεάτροις Νέρων προσαγορεύεσθαι: Dio lxiv 8, τὸ γοῦν ὄνομα αὐτοῦ
(i.e. Nero) αὑτῷ εὐθὺς ἐπέθετο: Tac. H. i 78, Creditus est etiam de celebranda
Neronis memoria agitavisse spe volgum alliciendi. Et fuere qui imagines
Neronis proponerent; atque etiam Othoni quibusdam diebus populus et
miles, tanquam nobilitatem et decus adstruerent, Neroni Othoni acclamavit
(greeted him with shouts of "Nero Otho"). Ipse in suspenso tenuit
(i.e. he left it undecided whether he would accept the title) vetandi metu
vel agnoscendi pudore. The populace in their first exultation at Nero 's
death put on caps of freedom (Ner. 57, 1, tantum gaudium publice praebuit
ut plebs pilleata tota urbe discurreret), but they soon longed for a revival
of his lavish expenditure on food and spectacles provided for their entertainment.

nullum indicium recusantis dedit: a favourite form of expression
with Suetonius; cf. Claud. 43, signa quaedam nec obscura paenitentis
dederat: Calig. 12, 2, suspicionem retinentis dabat: Ner. 40, 4, ut
gaudentis etiam suspicionem praeberet: Iul. 2, non sine rumore prostratae
pudicitiae.

ut quidam tradiderunt: Plutarch (Oth. 3) cites Cluvius Rufus as
authority for the statement that the name of Nero was added to that of
Otho on the imperial passports sent to Spain for use in the postal service:
Κλούβιος δὲ ῾Ροῦφος εἰς ᾿Ιβηρίαν φησὶ κομισθῆναι διπλώματα, οἷς ἐκπέμπουσι τοὺς γραμματηφόρους, τὸ τοῦ Νέρωνος θετὸν ὄνομα προσγεγραμμένον ἔχοντα τῷ τοῦ ῎Οθωνος.
Plutarch adds that Otho discontinued this when he observed the irritation
it caused to the aristocracy. The historian Cluvius Rufus was already
an ex-consul at the time of Caligula's death (41 A.D.); he accompanied
Nero on his musical tour in Greece (Ner. 21); Galba appointed him as his
successor in the governorship of Hispania Tarraconensis (Tac. H. і 8),
and he retained this post under Vitellius (H. ii '65). He is described as
“perinde dives et eloquentia clarus'” (H. iv 43). As a historian he wrote
on the reigns of Nero, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius (cf. Tac. A. xiii 20,
xiv 2). See also Introd. c. iii.

diplomatibus: a diploma (δίπλωμα) consisted of two folding tablets;
such tablets were used to convey official authorisations and answered to
our permits and passports. They were issued to couriers carrying public
despatches, and also to those who were given the privilege of using the
State means of conveyance, the cursus publicus established by Augustus.
They were granted by the emperor or a provincial governor, and the holder
was entitled to have his journey expedited in every way by the provision
of fresh horses, etc.; cf. Tac. H. ii 54 where the diplomata Othonis are
mentioned as ensuring rapid travelling. Such diplomata were inscribed
with the name of the reigning emperor, the name of the authorised person,
and the period for which they were available: they became invalid on the
emperor's death. For a full description and illustrations of these and
of military diplomata (conferring such rights as civitas and connubium
on time-expired soldiers) see the articles by Thédenat in Daremberg-Saglio ii 266 sqq., and by Purser in Smith's Dict. Ant. i3 641 sqq.; cf.
also Marquardt Staatsv. i² 561.
provinciarum praesides: see on Vesp. 6, 4.

imagines reponi passus est: cf. Plut. Oth. 3, καί τινων εἰκόνας
Νέρωνος εἰς τοὐμφανὲς προθεμένων οὐκ ἐκώλυσε: Tac. H. i 78, et fuere qui
imagines Neronis proponerent. The statues of hated emperors were overthrown after their death; cf. Dom. 23, 1, and the instances given by
Friedlaender, Sitteng. iii¹º 59.

procuratores atque libertos
revocavit: we are not told who these
were or when they were deprived of their positions by Galba. In Galb. 20,
2 Patrobius, a freedman of Nero, is mentioned as having been executed
by Galba. Dio (lxiv 8) says that Otho was intimate with Nero's infamous
freedman Sporus, and that he frightened the people by making use of
the other favourites of that emperor. Tacitus (H. i 76) states that
Crescens, a freedman of Nero, ingratiated himself with Otho by giving a
banquet to the people of Africa in honour of Otho's accession. Most of
the notorious freedmen of Nero, such as Polyclitus, Doryphorus, and
Helius, were already dead, but Epaphroditus, Nero's a libellis (“receiver
of petitions''), was also a libellis to Domitian (see Dom. 14, 4); it is
not known whether he was reappointed under Otho and continued in office
down to Domitian's reign.

subscripsit: Otho signed the order authorising the (procurator) a
rationibus, or chief controller of the fiscus, to pay the amount. The fiscus
was the emperor's own treasury; see on Vesp. 16, 3. The cost of building
palaces was defrayed from it (Stat. Silv. iii 3, 103; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³
950, 1003). The emperor's signature to official documents is mentioned
also in Ner. 10, 2, cum de supplicio cuiusdam capite damnati, ut ex more
subscriberet, admoneretur: Calig. 29, 2, numerum puniendorum subscribens.

quingenties sestertium:
quingenties centena milia sestertium,
50,000,000 sesterces, about £425,000.

Auream Domum: for the first of his two palaces, the Domus Transitoria
or House of Passage (so called as connecting the Palatine with the
Esquiline), Nero took the whole of the Palatine, the Velia, the valley
of the Colosseum, the S.-E. portion of the Esquiline, including the gardens
of Maecenas, and up to the Servian agger. This palace was destroyed in
the great fire of 64 A.D., and he then began the even more wildly extravagant
Aurea Domus with a vestibule big enough to contain his colossal statue,
120 ft. high (see on Vesp. 18), and with a triple colonnade a mile long.
All the parts of the palace were overlaid with gold and adorned with gems
and mother-of-pearl. He dedicated it, though not finished, and said that
he was at last beginning to be housed like a human being (Ner. 31, 2,
hactenus comprobavit, ut se diceret quasi hominem tandem habitare
coepisse). Though Otho continued the building during his brief reign, it
was never completed. Vespasian stopped the work and restored the ground
to the public, confining the limits of the imperial residence to the Palatine
itself.

§ 2. dicitur obmurmurasse: the construction of this sentence is twofold: first dicitur is used personally with the nom. and inf. (pave factus
edidisse), but later we have the acc. and inf. (prolapsum obmurmurasse)
depending on dicitur in an impersonal sense. In c. 12 infr. there is the
same variation with traditur followed by fuisse scambus and later by linere
consuetum. Similar mixed constructions are found in Cic., Liv., etc.;
e.g. Cic. de or. ii 299, ad Themistoclem quidam doctus homo accessisse
dicitur eique artem memoriae pollicitus esse se traditurum; cum ille quaesisset, quidnam illa ars efficere posset, dixisse illum doctorem, ut omnia
meminisset, etc.; Liv. v 41, M. Papirius dicitur Gallo barbam suam permulcenti scipione eburno in caput incusso iram movisse; atque ab eo
initium caedis ortum, ceteros in sedibus suis trucidatos. See KühnerStegmann, i 710.

per quietem:
=
per somnum; cf. Vesp. 7,2; 25.

pavefactus: cf. the troubled dreams of Caligula, Calig. 50, 3, neque
enim plus quam tribus nocturnis horis quiescebat ac ne iis quidem placida
quiete, sed pavida miris rerum imaginibus. Nero's sleep was broken by
frightful visions after he had murdered his mother Agrippina and his
wife Octavia (Ner. 46).
repertus humi: Dio lxiv 7, καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο τῆς νυκτὸς οὕτω δή τι ἐν
τοῖς ὕπνοις ἐταράχθη, ὥστε καὶ ἐκ τῆς εὐνῆς ἐκπεσεῖν, τοὺς δὲ προκοιτοῦντας (ante
cubiculum excubantes) ἐκπλῆξαι. ἐσπηδήσαντες οὖν εὗρον αὐτὸν χαμαὶ κείμενον.

Manes propitiare: the Manes of one whose death was due to outrage did not rest till the guilty paid the penalty or made fitting atonement;
cf. Liv. iii 58, manes Verginiae
per tot domos ad petendas poenas
vagati nullo relicto sonte tandem quieverunt. When the survivor of the
three Horatii, after vanquishing the three Curiatii, slew his sister Horatia
for bewailing their death, though he was acquitted by the people as having
slain her justly, yet his father had to offer expiatory sacrifices (“piacularia
sacrificia") for the bloodshed, and these sacrifices were continued every
year by the Horatian family to the Manes of Horatia (Liv. i 26, Тас. А.
xii 8). Agrippina invokes against Nero the shades of the Silani whom he
had murdered (Tac. A. xiii 14, infernos Silanorum manes invocare). There
is a remarkable story in Apul. Met. viii 9 sqq. of the vengeance exacted
by a wife, in obedience to the Manes of her murdered husband, from a
would-be lover of hers who had been his murderer.

postridie: Dio (l.c.) says that it was after his unsuccessful sacrifice
on the first day.

prolapsum: a most unlucky omen; cf. Iul. 59, cum immolanti aufugisset hostia, profectionem adversus Scipionem et Iubam non distulit.
Prolapsus (πεσὼν ἐπὶ στόμα, Dio xlii 58) etiam in egressu navis verso ad
melius omine: “Teneo te,” inquit, ‘“Africa.” The Crassi, father and son,
both fell at the doors of the temple of Astarte at Hierapolis in Syria, an
omen of the disaster they were to meet with at Carrhae (Plut. Crass. 17).

obmurmurasse: in the few other passages where this compound is
found it means to murmur or mutter against; e.g. Ov. Her. xviii 47 (Leander
complaining of Boreas), Vana peto; precibusque meis obmurmurat ipse:
Frontin. Strat. iv 6, 2 (of the mutterings of soldiers against their general),
cum unus ex eis obmurmurando diceret. In our passage the ob- seems to
have little force, though it may be intensive as in obverberare, etc. Roby
(Lat. Gram. ii p. 415) gives a list of compound verbs in which ob- is
"almost pleonastic.”
Τί γάρ μοι καὶ μακροῖς αὐλοῖς;: SC. κοινόν ἐστι, ‘“What have I to do
with long pipes?” Dio (lxiv 7) gives the words in a slightly different form:
θύοντί τε γὰρ αὐτῷ τὴν θυσίαν τὴν πρώτην τὰ ἱερὰ πονηρὰ ὤφθη, ὥστ᾽ αὐτὸν
μεταγνόντα ἐπὶ τοῖς πεπραγμένοις εἰπεῖν “τί γάρ με ἔδει μακροῖς αὐλοῖς αὐλεῖν;” ἔστι
δὲ τοῦτο δημῶδες, ἐς παροιμίαν φέρον, ἐπὶ τῶν ἔξω τι τοῦ προσφόρου σφισι ποιούντων.
The expression which Dio thus describes as proverbially used of unfitting
and unprofitable effort is not found elsewhere; the meaning as applied to
Otho would be that given by Torrentius, "Non omnibus buccis longas
tibias, quae difficilius inflentur quo longiores sint, pariter convenire, ut
neque Othoni imperium.” Burman cites as parallel the lines of Soph.
(frag. 701, Nauck) which Cicero (Att. ii 16) applies to Pompey: φυσᾷ γὰρ
οὐ σμικροῖσιν αὐλίσκοις ἔτι, | ἀλλ' ἀγρίαις φύσαισι, φορβειᾶς ἄτερ ‘“He blows no
more upon a tiny pipe, But with a fierce unmodulated blast." Were it
not for the statement of Dio, it would be easy with some of the early
commentators to take Otho's words as meaning "What use is there in my
trying to sacrifice or to make atonement?'"; long pipes being used especially
in connexion with sacrifices (see Daremberg-Saglio, v 304). Cedrenus (11
cent.) differs from other authors in stating (p. 216 C) that the words were
the dying words of Otho: θύων δέ ποτε ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τὰ τῆς ᾿Αφροδίτης ᾄσματα τοῖς
ἱεροῖς παρέμιξε· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο, Οὐιτελίου (Vitellius) αὐτῷ ἐπαναστάντος, ξιφιδίῳ
ἑαυτὸν διεχρήσατο, εἰπών “ Τί γάρ με ἔδει μακροῖς αὐλοῖς ἄδειν καὶ αὐλεῖν;”

sub idem tempus: on January 1, 69 A.D., the oath of fealty to Galba
was taken by the army of Lower Germany; but in Upper Germany the 4th
and 22nd legions took the oath to the senate and people of Rome. News
of this was brought to Vitellius at Cologne and he communicated it to the
officers of the army of Lower Germany of which he was legatus. On
January 3 Vitellius was proclaimed emperor by the troops of both armies
(Vitell. 8, Tac. H. i 52 sqq.). Galba was deliberating about the adoption
of a son and successor when the revolt occurred; cf. Plut. Galb. 22,
καταλαμβάνει δ' αὐτὸν ἔτι μέλλοντα καὶ βουλευόμενον ἐκραγέντα τὰ Γερμανικά.
When the tidings reached him, he proceeded at once to adopt Piso on
January 10 (Suet. Galb. 17, Oth. 5, 1; Plut. Galb. 23). On January 15
Galba and Piso were slain, and Otho was made emperor.

Germaniciani: for this adj. see on Vesp. 6, 2. The legions composing
the armies in Upper and Lower Germany are mentioned in the notes on
Galb. 16, 2 and Vitell. 8, 1.

in. verba iurarant: the usual expression for swearing allegiance;
see on Galb. 11.

Vitelli: Vitellius was appointed by Galba to the command in Lower
Germany (Vitell. 7, Tac. H. i 9). He arrived there about December 1,
68 A.D.; so that he had been just a month in command when both armies
declared him emperor.
auctor senatui fuit: see on Vesp. 11, auctor senatui fuit decernendi.

mittendae legationis: Galba had already sent envoys to the mutinous
German armies on the occasion of his adoption of Piso, but these envoys
were recalled by Otho who sent others to replace them; cf. Tac. H. i 74,
Otho, revocatis quos Galba miserat legatis, rursus ad utrumque Germanicum
exercitum et ad legionem Italicam easque, quae Lugduni agebant, copias
specie senatus (“nominally from the senate'') misit. Legati apud Vitellium
remansere promptius quam ut retenti viderentur; praetoriani, quos per
simulationem officii legatis Otho adiunxerat, remissi, antequam legionibus
miscerentur.

per internuntios ac litteras optulit: Tac. (l.c.), Crebrae interim et
muliebribus blandimentis infectae ab Othone ad Vitellium epistulae offerebant pecuniam et gratiam et quemcumque quietis locum prodigae vitae
legisset. Plutarch (Oth. 4) says that when Otho's confidence was restored
by the receipt of friendly despatches from Mucianus and Vespasian, who
were in command of large forces in Syria and Judaea, he wrote to
Vitellius advising him to remember his position as a soldier (παραινῶν
στρατιωτικὰ φρονεῖν) and offering him large sums of money and a city
where he could live in luxurious ease. Vitellius at first replied in a hypocritical strain, but soon both he and Otho grew heated and wrote in most
abusive terms, charging each other with disgraceful vices of which they
were both equally guilty according to Plutarch and Tacitus.

consortem imperii: Otho's offer to share the empire with Vitellius is
mentioned also in Dio lxiv 10: ὁ δὲ Ὄθων, ἐπειδὴ καὶ μὴ ἔπειθε τὸν Οὐιτέλλιον,
ἐς κοινωνίαν αὐτὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς πολλάκις παρακαλῶν, εἰς πόλεμον λοιπὸν φανερὸν
καθίστατο. For the position of the consors imperii in relation to the
princeps see on Tit. 9, 3.

generumque: Suetonius alone states that Otho proposed to become
the son-in-law of Vitellius. The daughter of Vitellius is mentioned in
Vitell. 6; for her marriage to D. Valerius Asiaticus and her subsequent
marriage in Vespasian's reign see on Vesp. 14, 1.

copiis quas Vitellius praemiserat: Vitellius, having been proclaimed
emperor by the armies in Germany, was joined by various commanders in
Gaul and by the troops in Britain. He sent Fabius Valens and Aulus
Caecina in advance with two forces to invade Italy by different routes;
see Vitell. 9 and the notes there.

paene internecione: Tacitus (H. i 80) says that this outbreak of the
praetorians nearly brought about the destruction of the whole city: Parvo
initio, unde nihil timebatur, orta seditio prope urbi excidio fuit.
amplissimi ordinis: = senatorii ordinis; see on Vesp. 2, 3.

§ 2. placuerat per classiarios arma transferri remittique navibus: a
most obscure passage, and it is possible that some words have been lost,
since in all the better MSS. et is found before placuerat, though it has
been generally deleted by editors as being due merely to the preceding est.
Lipsius suggested etenim for et, Oudendorp Ostiam, Bücheler ei. The
military riot which Suetonius mentions is described by Tacitus (H. i 80)
and Plutarch (Oth. 3), but it is very difficult to reconcile the three accounts.
The account given by Tac. is as follows:-Septumam decumam cohortem
e colonia Ostiensi in urbem acciri Otho iusserat; armandae eius cura Vario
Crispino tribuno e praetorianis data. Is quo magis vacuus quietis castris
iussa exequeretur, vehicula cohortis incipiente nocte onerari aperto armamentario iubet. Tempus in suspicionem, causa in crimen, adfectatio quietis
in tumultum evaluit, et visa inter temulentos arma cupidinem sui movere.
Fremit miles et tribunos centurionesque 'proditionis arguit, tamquam
familiae senatorum ad perniciem Othonis armarentur, pars ignari et vino
graves, pessimus quisque in occasionem praedarum, volgus, ut mos est,
cuiuscumque motus novi cupidum; et obsequia meliorum nox abstulerat.
Resistentem seditioni tribunum et severissimos centurionum obtruncant,
rapta arma, nudati gladii, insidentes equis urbem ac Palatium petunt.
Plutarch says: Κρισπῖνον δὲ πέμψαντος αὐτοῦ τὴν ἑπτακαιδεκάτην σπεῖραν
Ωστίας ἀπάξοντα, κἀκείνου νυκτός ἔτι συσκευαζομένου καὶ τὰ ὅπλα ταῖς ἁμάξαις
ἐπιτιθέντος, οἱ θρασύτατοι πάντες ἐβόων οὐδὲν ὑγιὲς τὸν Κρισπῖνον ἥκειν διανοούμενον, ἀλλὰ τὴν σύγκλητον (senatum) ἐπιχειρεῖν πράγμασι νεωτέροις καὶ τὰ
ὅπλα κατὰ Καίσαρος, οὐ Καίσαρι παρακομίζεσθαι. Τοῦ δὲ λόγου πολλῶν ἁπτομένου
καὶ παροξύνοντος οἱ μὲν ἐπελαμβάνοντο τῶν ἁμαξῶν, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἐνισταμένους
ἑκατοντάρχας δύο καὶ τὸν Κρισπῖνον αὐτὸν ἀπέκτειναν, πάντες δὲ διασκευασάμενοι καὶ παρακαλέσαντες ἀλλήλους Καίσαρι βοηθεῖν ἤλαυνον εἰς τὴν ῾Ῥώμην.
From Plutarch's account it appears that Crispinus had been sent to Ostia
to bring the 17th cohort to Rome; that the disturbance began in the camp at
Ostia; and that the rioters rode from Ostia to Rome. It is not clear whether
Tac. means that the mutiny began at Ostia, and that the mutineers on
their arrival at Rome were joined by the praetorians, or that the outbreak
occurred in the praetorian camp outside the gates of Rome, from which the
praetorians rode into the city to the Palace. Most probably Tac. is in
agreement with Suet. that the mutiny took place in the praetorian camp,
and that the mutineers were praetorians. Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) understands
Tac. to mean that the 17th cohort had already arrived in the city, having
been brought from Ostia to be converted into a praetorian cohort, and
that while Crispinus was taking the arms for its equipment out of the
armoury in the praetorian camp, the praetorians, suspecting some treachery,
mutinied. Hardy accepts Mommsen's view that this 17th cohort, stationed
at Ostia, was one of the cohortes urbanae, while others hold that it was
one of the cohortes civium Romanorum or that it consisted of marines
(classiarii); see note on Vesp. 8, 3. The account given by Suet. here of
the cause of the disorder is so condensed as to be almost unintelligible.
The best explanation of his words is that given by Krauss (De vitarum
imperatoris Othonis fide quaestiones, p. 27): “Ut septima decima cohors
classiariorum Ostiae collocata iustis ad bellum armis instrueretur, classiarii
cum vehiculis in castra praetoriana, ubi armamentarium publicum erat,
praemissi et inde arma vehiculis imposita ad Tiberim transportare impositaque navibus Ostiam transferre iussi erant. Vocabulum "Remittere"
significare videtur, armamentarium praetorianorum omnibus cohortibus circa
Romam tendentibus commune fuisse illamque cohortem, ut in pace, arma
sua habuisse in illo deposita et reservata, unde bello exorto cohortibus
singulis reddebantur.” Hofstee infers from Tac. H. ii 63 that the 17th
cohort returned to Ostia from Rome during Otho's reign, and thinks that
Suet. is describing the trouble as happening in the praetorian camp at
the time when the arms were being taken out to be sent back to Ostia
on the cohort's return. Both Tac. and Plut., however, definitely connect
the disorder with the bringing of the cohort from Ostia to Rome, and not
with its return.
remitti: Stephanus suggested praemitti, which is approved of by
Burman and Ernesti; Oudendorp (followed by Wolf and Bremi)
demitti (= secundo flumine devehi Ostiam).
lemma: placuerat per classiarios arma transferri remittique navibus

text:
castris: the praetorian camp; for its origin and situation see on
Galb. 19, 1.

promerentur: i.e. given out of the armoury (armamentarium) in the
praetorian camp which served also as a depot for the cohorts in the
neighbourhood of Rome and contained arms for every class of troops (cf.
Tac. H. i 38). By an oversight Howard and Jackson in their Index
verborum to Suetonius take promerentur here from promereor.

in Palatium: where Otho was entertaining at dinner eighty of the
senators with their wives; Plut. (l.c.), πυθόμενοι παρ' αὐτῷ δειπνεῖν ὀγδοήκοντα
συγκλητικοὺς ἐφέροντο πρὸς τὰ βασίλεια: Tac. (c. 81), erat Othoni celebre
convivium primoribus feminis virisque.

cucurrerunt: Plutarch says that the rioters rode from Ostia to Rome
(ἤλαυνον εἰς τὴν Ρώμην), a distance of 16 miles, but if the 17th cohort at
Ostia was one of the cohortes urbanae (Mommsen, Hermes xvi 645), the
difficulty is that there were no cavalry attached to the cohortes urbanae
(Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1067); if the trouble began in the praetorian camp,
then the words of Tacitus “insidentes equis urbem ac Palatium petunt”
are to be explained by the fact that the praetorian camp lay outside the
city of Rome, and there was a squadron of 24 cavalry attached to each
praetorian cohort (Heraeus on Tac. l.c.; Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 477).

caedem senatus flagitantes: Tac. (c. 82), undique arma et minae,
modo in centuriones tribunosque, modo in senatum universum, lymphatis
caeco pavore animis, et quia neminem unum destinare irae poterant,
licentiam in omnes poscentibus: Plut. (l.c.), νῦν καιρὸν εἶναι λέγοντες ἐν
ταὐτῷ πάντας ἀνελεῖν τοὺς Καίσαρος πολεμίους.

repulsis tribunorum qui inhibere temptabant: Tac. (l.c.), volnerato
Iulio Martiale tribuno et Vitellio Saturnino praefecto legionis, dum
ruentibus obsistunt. Both Tac. and Plut. say that Otho sent out the
prefects of the praetorians to try to appease the soldiers, while the senatorial
guests made their escape from the Palace by another door.

nonnullis et occisis: neither Tac. nor Plut. mentions any officers slain
at the Palace, though some had been slain earlier at the praetorian camp.

sic ut erant cruenti: ut, sic ut (sicut), erat, etc., like the Gr. ὡς εἶχεν,
denote the state or condition in which a person or thing was when an action
took place (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 451); cf. Calig. 45, 2, sic ut erant
loricatos ad discumbendum adhortatus est: Claud. 9, 1, sic ut vestitus
advenerat : Claud. 34, 2, induxit unum (in arenam), sic ut erat togatus.

perruperunt in triclinium: Tac. (l.c.), militum impetus ne foribus
quidem Palatii coercitus, quo minus convivium inrumperent, ostendi sibi
Othonem expostulantes. Plut. says that they forced their way in, asking
what had become of the enemies of Caesar (i.e. the senators).

nec nisi viso destiterunt: Otho stood up on a couch and succeeded in
quieting them with entreaties and tears; cf. Tac. (l.c), donec Otho contra
decus imperii toro insistens precibus et lacrimis aegre cohibuit, redieruntque in castra inviti neque innocentes: Plut. (l.c.) ὀρθὸς ἀπὸ τῆς κλίνης πολλὰ
παρηγορήσας καὶ δεηθεὶς καὶ μηδὲ δακρύων φεισάμενος μόλις ἀπέπεμψεν αὐτούς. Οn
the following day the prefects harangued them and paid 5000 sesterces to
each man. Then Otho ventured to enter the camp and was surrounded by
the tribunes and centurions wishing to resign command of such mutinous
troops. The soldiers were shamed by this and returned to their duty,
even demanding the punishment of the ringleaders, two of whom were
executed.

§ 3. praepropere: Tacitus (c. 89) mentions two reasons for his
haste: aspernatus est omnem cunctationem ut Neroni quoque exitiosam; et
Caecina iam Alpes transgressus extimulabat. Bentley's praepostere is
needless.

incohavit: owing to the express testimony of the grammarian
Diomedes (Keil, i 365) that Suetonius in one of his writings defended the
form incohare against inchoare, Ihm restores incohare everywhere in the
Lives of the Caesars, though the MSS. give inchoare, which is retained
by Preud'homme.

religionum: see on c. 6, 1.
The

motis necdum conditis ancilibus: cf. Tac. (l.c.), fuere qui proficiscenti
Othoni moras religionemque nondum conditorum ancilium afferrent. The
ancilia, or sacred shields, were 12 in number, 11 being copies of the original
shield which fell from heaven on March 1 in the reign of Numa.
name ancile is for ancidile (am-caedere "to cut on both sides''), the shield
being an oval with incisions at both sides, so that it roughly resembled the
figure 8. On March 1, the opening of the campaigning season, the ancilia
were brought out (moveri, cf. κινεῖν τὰ ὅπλα) from the sacrarium Martis
(or curia Saliorum in Palatio) by the Salii, or priests of Mars, who in a
warlike dance (tripudium; hence their name Salii, a saliendo) and with
special chants (axamenta) bore them round various halting-places
(mansiones) where the ancilia were deposited for one night while the Salii
feasted, and not until the end of March were the ancilia put back (condi)
into the sacrarium Martis. There was a minor festival (Armilustrium)
on Oct. 19 (the campaigning season, in theory, ending in Oct.), when the
ancilia were again brought out and put back.

quod antiquitus infaustum habetur: it was inauspicious to make a
march “ancilibus nondum conditis,” as we see from Liv. xxxvii 33 where
Scipio is retarded by this consideration: stativa deinde ad Hellespontum
aliquamdiu habuerunt, quia dies forte, quibus ancilia moventur, religiosi
ad iter inciderant (for dies religiosi see on “religio,” Oth. 6, 1). It was
also an inauspicious time for marriage; cf. Ov. Fast. iii 393, Nubere si
qua voles, quamvis properabitis ambo, | differ; habent parvae commoda
magna morae. | Arma movent pugnam, pugna est aliena maritis. | Condita
cum fuerint, aptius omen erit.
.....

die: Otho set out on March 24 according to Suetonius, but on March
14 according to Tacitus (H. i 90). The date given by Tac. is apparently
confirmed by the Acta Fratr. Arval. for 69 A.D. (Henzen p. xciii = Dessau
Inscr. Lat. 241): pri(die) idus Martias vota nuncupata pro s[al]ute et
reditu... (Vitelli has been erased) Germanici imp(eratoris). In his
note on this Dessau says: “Pridie idus Martias, quo die Othonem ab urbe
profectum esse narrat Tac. H. i 90, pro huius sine dubio salute et reditu
vota nuncupata sunt ab Arvalibus; sed devicto Othone, cum nondum acta
huius diei perscripta essent, pro Othonis nomine, Vitellii positum; id
ipsum postea erasum. De nomine Germanico Vitellio indito cf. Tac. H. i 62,
ii 64.'"

cultores deum Matris: in 205 B.c., during the second Punic war, the
worship of the Magna Mater (Cybele) was introduced to Rome from
Pessinus in Galatia, and the festival of the Megalesia (Μεγάλη = Magna)
was held annually from April 4 to April 10. Under the emperor Claudius
(41-54 A.D.) another religious celebration was instituted to commemorate
the grief of Cybele at the loss of Attis, and her joy when he was restored.
This celebration was held from March 22 to March 27. The first day,
March 22, was the day of Arbor intrat, when the priests (Dendrophoroi)
carried a pine-tree, on which hung an image of Attis, to the temple of
Cybele on the Palatine. On March 23 there was a sounding of trumpets
(περισαλπισμός, tubilustrium). March 24 (the day on which Suet. says
Otho set out) was the day of blood (dies sanguinis) on which the chief
priest (Archigallus) gashed his arm and sprinkled the blood. March 25
was a day of rejoicing (Hilaria) for the restoration of the body of Attis
to Cybele. March 26 was a day of rest (requietio), and on March 27 the
celebration concluded with the lavatio or bathing of the image of the
goddess in the Almo where it joins the Tiber. See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii
367 sqq.; R. Ellis, Introd. to Catull. lxiii.

adversissimis auspiciis: in addition to the unfavourable auspices
which Suetonius mentions here, most alarming prodigies were reported;
cf. Tac. H. i 86, Prodigia insuper terrebant diversis auctoribus volgata:
in vestibulo Capitolii omissas habenas bigae, cui Victoria institerat;
erupisse cella Iunonis maiorem humana speciem; statuam divi Iulii in
insula Tiberini amnis sereno et immoto die ab Occidente in Orientem conversam; prolocutum in Etruria bovem, insolitos animalium partus et plura
alia rudibus saeculis etiam in pace observata, quae nunc tantum in metu
audiuntur. The omission of these prodigies by the superstitious Suetonius
is one of the proofs that he did not follow Tacitus as his authority.

Diti patri: Dis pater was the Italian equivalent of the Greek Pluto,
god of the underworld. The name is traditionally explained as di(ve)s
"rich” (cf. Πλούτων from πλοῦτος “riches''), but some philologists derive
it from the stem div (in divus, divinus, Dialis, etc.). Dis pater was a son
of Saturn and Ops, and brother of Jupiter and Neptune. His oldest
shrine at Rome was connected with the temple of Saturn at the foot of
the Capitol. The worship of Dis first comes into prominence at Rome in
249 B.C., while the issue of the first Punic war was uncertain; alarming
portents occurred, such as the destruction of part of the walls of Rome
by lightning, and the Sibylline books ordained that ludi Tarentini were
to be celebrated in honour of Dis and Proserpina in the Campus Martius
for three successive nights, and that black victims (hostiae furvae) were
to be offered, and that these ceremonies were to be renewed every hundred
years (see on the “ludi saeculares,” Dom. 4, 3). Except in this connexion
we hear little of the worship of Dis at Rome either in the state religion
or in private cults. For the offering of black cattle to the gods of the
underworld, as of white victims to the di superi, cf. Verg. Aen. vi 153,
243 sqq.; Serv. on Verg. G. ii 380.
..

victima. caesa litavit : litare (καλλιερεῖν) is probably used here of
the victim itself (= felicem esse); cf. Aug. 96, 2, sacrificio non litanti:
Mart. x 73, 6, non quacumque manu victima caesa litat. Suetonius also
has litare in the more usual sense of the sacrificer obtaining favourable
omens: Iul. 81, 4, pluribus hostiis caesis, cum litare non posset: Ner. 56,
attendit et extispicio, nec unquam litavit.

contraria exta potiora sint: this peculiarity of the litatio in the case
of sacrifices to Dis is not mentioned elsewhere, and seems a mere
generalisation from the fate of Otho. Bouché-Leclercq (in Daremberg-Saglio iii 1268), commenting on this statement of Suetonius, says: “Cette
casuistique suspecte est contraire à l'essence même du sacrifice expiatoire
ou propitiatoire, qui est la substitution de la victime à la personne menacée,
laquelle se rachète par cette rançon acceptée. A. ce compte, les nombreux
sacrifices offerts aux divinités souterraines, durant les Jeux Séculaires
(Tellus, Dis Pater, Proserpine, les Moeres) auraient dû, pour être heureux,
présenter des entrailles défavorables, ce qui est absurde.”

inundationibus Tiberis: described more fully in Tac. H. i 86, Sed
praecipuus et cum praesenti exitio etiam futuri pavor subita inundatione
Tiberis, qui immenso auctu, proruto ponte sublicio (i.e. the old wooden
U 2
bridge) ac strage obstantis molis refusus, non modo iacentia et plana urbis
loca, sed secura eiusmodi casuum implevit. Rapti e publico plerique,
plures in tabernis et cubilibus intercepti. Fames in volgus inopia quaestus
et penuria alimentorum. Corrupta stagnantibus aquis insularum ("tenement houses”) fundamenta, dein remeante flumine dilapsa. Plutarch
(Oth. 4) says that the river rose to an unprecedented height: Καὶ τὸ περὶ τὸν
Θύμβριν σύμπτωμα σημεῖον ἐποιοῦντο οἱ πολλοὶ μοχθηρόν. Ἦν μὲν γὰρ ὥρα περὶ ἦν
μάλιστα οἱ ποταμοὶ πλήθουσιν, ἀλλ᾽ οὔπω τοσοῦτος ἤρθη πρότερον οὐδὲ ἀπώλεσε
τοσαῦτα καὶ διέφθειρεν ὑπερχυθεὶς καὶ κατακλύσας πολὺ μέρος τῆς πόλεως, πλεῖστον δὲ
ἐν ᾧ τὸν ἐπὶ πράσει διαπωλοῦσι σῖτον (i. e. the corn-market), ὡς δεινὴν ἀπορίαν ἡμερῶν
συχνῶν κατασχεῖν. Pliny (N.H. iii 55) says that the inundations of the
Tiber were prophetic of impending dangers: quin immo vates intelligitur
potius ac monitor, auctu semper religiosus verius quam saevus. We hear
of disastrous inundations in B.c. 241, 215, 202, 193-2, 189, 54, 44 (cf. Hor.
C. i 2), 27, 23, 22. Augustus tried to protect Rome by appointing
“Curatores alvei (“bed”) Tibéris et riparum,” but the inundations still
continued, and in 15 A.D. we find the senate considering (and rejecting) a
scheme to lessen the volume of the river by diverting some of its main
tributaries, the Nar, Velinus, and Clanis (Dio lvii 14, Tac. A. i 76).

vicensimum lapidem: the 20th milestone on the Via Flaminia which
ran up the valley of the Tiber through Etruria and continued through
Umbria and over the Apennines to Ariminum (Rimini) on the Adriatic.
A station "Ad Vicesimum" on the Via Flaminia is mentioned in the
Jerusalem Itinerary and the Peutinger Table; Bunbury (Smith's Dict.
Geogr. ii 1300) says that it must have been a little beyond the Monte di
Guardia, but was evidently a mere Mutatio, or station for changing horses,
and no ruins mark the site.

praeclusam viam: cf. Tас. Н. і 86, utque primum vacuus a periculo
animus fuit, id ipsum, quod paranti expeditionem Othoni campus Martius
et via Flaminia iter belli esset obstructum, a (“without regard to'")
fortuitis vel naturalibus causis in prodigium et omen imminentium cladium
vertebatur.

trahi bellum oporteret: cf. Tac. H. ii 30, Otho consultavit, trahi
bellum an fortunam experiri placeret. When the armies of Valens and
Caecina, the generals of Vitellius, had effected a junction, the combined
force in their fortified camp outside Cremona was nearly 100,000 men,
and they were ready to give battle. At the council of Otho's commanders,
which Otho himself attended, Suetonius Paulinus and Marius Celsus were
strongly in favour of delay, Otho was inclined to risk a decisive battle
(pronus ad certandum), and his brother Titianus along with Proculus,
prefect of the praetorian guard, with the rashness of ignorance (imperitia
properantes) advocated this course, which was adopted with disastrous
results.
quando: see on Vesp. 16, 3. Kraffert would read quoad.

fame urgeretur hostis: one of the arguments for delay used by
Suetonius Paulinus, the most skilful of Otho's officers (nemo illa tempestate
militaris rei callidior habebatur, Tac. c. 32). He urged that the full
forces of Vitellius had already come: that no troops from Britain or
Spain could reach him: that Gaul was ready to rise, and that Vitellius
could withdraw no more men from the Rhine: that Gallia Narbonensis
had been cowed by Otho's fleet and by his land forces: that Italy
beyond the Padus was shut in by the Alps and could not be relieved by
sea and was already exhausted by the passage of the Vitellian forces who
now lacked corn and supplies: that Otho had behind him all the resources
of the state and vast reserves of money "stronger than the sword in civil
war"; and by delaying he would allow of the arrival of reinforcements
from Pannonia, Moesia, Dalmatia, and the East.

impatiens longioris sollicitudinis: this is the view of Tacitus (c. 40),
who describes how Titianus and Proculus had recourse to their rights as
commanders-in-chief (in ius imperii transeunt) to overrule Paulinus and
Celsus, and ordered the attack which was angrily demanded in a despatch
from Otho: Aderat citus equo Numida cum atrocibus mandatis, quibus
Otho increpita ducum segnitia, rem in discrimen mitti iubebat, aeger mora
et spei impatiens. So too Plutarch (Oth. 9) says on the authority of
Secundus, Otho's secretary, that Otho was no longer able to endure the
suspense; his inexperience and effeminacy made him incapable of a
rational consideration of the dangers; overburdened by his cares, he
hurried on, and, with head veiled, like a man who leaps from a precipice,
he committed the fortunes of his party to the accidents of chance: δοκεῖ
δὲ μηδὲ αὐτὸς Ὄθων ἐξαναφέρειν ἔτι πρὸς τὴν ἀδηλότητα μηδὲ ὑπομένειν ἀηθείᾳ καὶ
μαλακότητι τοὺς περὶ τῶν δεινῶν λογισμούς, ἐκπονούμενος δὲ ταῖς φροντίσι σπεύδειν
ἐγκαλυψάμενος, ὥσπερ ἀπὸ κρημνοῦ, μεθεῖναι τὰ πράγματα πρὸς τὸ συντυχόν. Both
Plut. and Tac. mention another account that the two armies, considering
neither Otho nor Vitellius worth fighting for, were inclined to come to
terms and either give the empire to one of their own generals (Paulinus
having the best chance, according to Tac.) or leave the choice to the senate.
Plut. adds that some suspect that this design was one reason why Celsus
and Paulinus advised delay, while the adherents of Otho (Proculus and
Titianus) wished for immediate action. Tac. (c. 37) rejects this version
as improbable.

ante Vitelli adventum: Vitellius had just set out from Lower
Germany bringing up the remaining strength of the army of Germany
and 8000 men levied in Britain, when news reached him of his victory at
Betriacum and the death of Otho. See Tac., c. 57.

profligari plurimum posse: "that victory could be gained to a very
large extent." The expression is peculiar, as profligari must be taken
impersonally, plurimum being adverbial (cf. Galb. 5, 2; 8, 1; Dom. 4, 2;
so "plus,” Galb. 15, 1). In all the other passages where Suetonius uses
profligare, it means "to conquer": Iul. 30, 4, Pharsalica acie caesos profligatosque adversarios prospiciens; ib. 35, 2, Mithridatis filium una acie
profligavit; Ner. 3, 1, nec nisi partibus ubique profligatis M. Antonio.
tradidit classem. Gellius (xv 5) says that profligare means “ad perniciem
deducere,” “deperdere,” and that it was often wrongly used in the sense
of "prope absolvi" "to be almost completed” (Cicero, however, uses it
in this latter sense, Tusc. v 6, 15, profligata iam haec et paene ad exitum
adducta quaestio est, and the phrase profligare bellum, “to break the back
of the war," occurs in Cic., Liv., Tac., etc.). In our passage profligari
is usually explained as prope absolvi, but the use of plurimum seems
=
fatal to this; it would be a meaningless pleonasm to say "the matter
could be almost decided to a very large extent." For the impersonal use
of the passive see on Vitell. 1, 1, variatum esset.

impar militum ardori: Plutarch includes in the reasons for Otho's
decision for immediate action the indisputable fact that the praetorian
cohorts, now coming to taste what real campaigning was, longed to return
to the luxurious life of Rome, and therefore could not be restrained in
their eagerness for a battle, for they imagined that they would sweep the
enemy at the first charge (οὐκ ἦσαν καθεκτοὶ σπεύδοντες ἐπὶ τὴν μάχην, ὡς εὐθὺς
ἐξ ἐπιδρομῆς ἀναρπασόμενοι τοὺς ἐναντίους).
substitit Brixelli: Brixellum (mod. Brescello) was a town of Cisalpine
Gaul on the south side of the Padus (Po). When the council of Otho
and his commanders decided on a battle, Titianus and Proculus prevailed
on Otho to retire to Brixellum, while Paulinus and Celsus did not oppose
this for fear of being thought to expose the emperor to peril. This
mistake gave the death-blow to the party of Otho; cf. Tac. H. ii 33, Is
primus dies Othonianas partes afflixit; namque et cum ipso praetorianarum
cohortium et speculatorum (see on Galb. 18, 1) equitumque valida manus
discessit, et remanentium fractus animus, quando suspecti duces et Otho,
cui uni apud militem fides, dum et ipse non nisi militibus credit, imperia
ducum in incerto reliquerat. Similarly Plutarch (Oth. 10) characterizes
Otho's withdrawal as a blunder, not merely because it removed the respect
and emulation which his presence would have inspired, but also because he
took away with him the keenest and most efficient of the troops as his
bodyguard (ὡσπερεὶ στόμωμα τῆς δυνάμεως ἀπέκοψε). Dio (lxiv 10) says that
Otho withdrew from the battle, declaring that he could not bear to witness
a battle between kindred; just as if he himself had become emperor in
any legal fashion and not by butchering the consuls and the Caesar (i.e.
Piso) and the emperor (Galba) in Rome itself.

§ 2. apud Alpes: this victory seems to have been a very paltry affair.
Some of Otho's troops were sent up to seize the province of the Maritime
Alps and then attack Gallia Narbonensis which had declared for Vitellius.
The province of the Maritime Alps was on the borders of Italy and
Narbonensis. Augustus had made it a separate province under a procurator.
Tacitus (ii 12) describes how Otho's troops on their march devastated Italy
like a foreign land, and how Marius Maturus, the procurator of the
Maritime Alps, hastily raised a levy of the natives to resist the invasion
of his province; but these raw forces were speedily routed by Otho's
trained soldiers, who took vengeance by burning Albintimilium (Ventimiglia). In Gallia Narbonensis the troops of Otho, supported by his fleet,
twice defeated the detachments sent by Fabius Valens for the protection
of the province; but they withdrew after their victories to Albigaunum
(Albenga) in Liguria.

Placentiam: mod. Piacenza, on the south bank of the Padus, near
where that river is joined by the Trebia. It was defended by Othonian
troops under Vestricius Spurinna, and Caecina, crossing the Padus,
assaulted it unsuccessfully and had to retreat across the river to his camp
at Cremona. A corps of gladiators who fought for Otho made their way
over to the northern bank and routed the Vitellian auxiliaries near Cremona.
When Otho's generals (Paulinus, Celsus, and Gallus) would not follow up
this success, they were accused of treason by their own men, and Otho
summoned his brother Titianus, who was prefect at Rome, to act as
generalissimo of his army (Tac. ii 17-23).

ad Castoris: sc. aedes, the place being named from the temple of
Castor and Pollux there; Tacitus (ii 24) calls it “locus Castorum,” Orosius
(vii 8, 6) more briefly "Castores” (Pliny, N.H. vii 86, x 121, similarly
calls the temple of the twins Castor and Pollux at Rome, “aedes
Castorum''). Lucien Herr (Revue de Philol. xvii, 1893, p. 208 sqq.) argues
that locus castorum (not Castorum) should be read in Tac. (l.c.), the
meaning being "the place of beavers (fibrorum)” which were numerous
in the rivers of that region.
He thinks that Suetonius misunderstood
“castorum” and wrote "ad Castoris" as if the god were referred to.
Tacitus defines the position of the place as 12 miles E. of Cremona on
the Via Postumia in the direction of Betriacum and Mantua. The
Othonian forces under Paulinus, Celsus, and Gallus were now concentrated
at Betriacum. Caecina with the Vitellians at Cremona, eager to wipe out
his defeat at Placentia, arranged an ambush on the Via Postumia to
ensnare the Othonians at Locus Castorum, but Celsus and Paulinus skilfully planted a counter-ambuscade and encircled the forces of Caecina;
Paulinus, however, for some mysterious reason (treachery was freely hinted
at) did not press his advantage, though it seems that he might have utterly
routed the Vitellians and captured their camp at Cremona. See Tac. ii
24-26, Plut. Oth. 7, and the excellent description (with plan) of the battle
of Locus Castorum in Bury's Student's Roman Empire c. 19.

Betriacum: the name of this village appears with different spellings:
the best MSS. of Suetonius give the form with "t" (corruptly here
bretiacum, in Vitell. 10 betriacensi, in Vesp. 5 bretiacensi); Βητριακόν
occurs in Plut. Oth. 8; Betricum in Eutrop. vii 17; Tacitus (H. ii 42, etc.)
uses Bedriacum, so too Pliny (N.H. x 135) Bedriacensibus bellis; in
Juvenal ii 106 the MSS. give Bebriacis campis, and the adj. Bebriacus is
found in the Schol. on that line and also on line 99, as well as in Priscian ii
43. Lucien Herr (see preceding note) thinks the true form is Bebriacum,
a Celtic name from the same root bebr or bibr as appears in Bebronna,
Bibrax, Bibracte, Bibroci, etc., so that the meaning of Bebriacum is
“pagus fibrorum” i.e. "district of beavers," and “locus castorum” in
Tac. H. ii 24 is a translation of it. See Friedlaender on Juv. ii 106, and
Hofstee on our passage. Tacitus (ii 23) describes the position of

Betriacum: inter Veronam Cremonamque situs est vicus, duabus iam
Romanis cladibus notus infaustusque (i.e. the defeat of Otho's forces on
Apr. 14 (?), 69 A.D. by Caecina and Valens, and the defeat of Caecina and
Valens towards the end of Oct. in the same year by Antonius Primus the
lieutenant of Vespasian). Neither of the two battles of Betriacum was
fought at Betriacum itself, but on the road from it to Cremona and much
nearer to Cremona, the attacking forces advancing from Betriacum. The
battle which proved so disastrous to Otho was fought partly on the high
road and partly in the groves and vineyards at either side; cf. Tac. ii 42,
Et per locos arboribus ac vineis impeditos non una pugnae facies: comminus eminus, catervis et cuneis concurrebant. In aggere viae (i.e. the
raised causeway of the Via Postumia) conlato gradu corporibus et umbonibus niti, omisso pilorum iactu gladiis et securibus galeas loricasque perrumpere:
noscentes inter se, ceteris conspicui, in eventum totius belli
certabant. The army of Otho broke and fled to Betriacum and capitulated
on the following morning. For a discussion of Otho's strategy see
Henderson, Civil War and Rebellion in the Rom. Emp. 92 sqq., and the
criticism of Henderson's views by Hardy, J. Ph. xxxi 123 sqq.

spe conloquii: cf. Tac. ii 41, where we are told that two of Otho's
officers came asking for a parley with Caecina, and before he could reply
scouts reported that Otho's forces were already advancing to attack:
Eodem die ad Caecinam operi pontis intentum duo praetorianarum cohortium
tribuni conloquium eius postulantes venerunt. Audire condiciones ac
reddere parabat, cum praecipites exploratores adesse hostem nuntiavere.
Interruptus tribunorum sermo, eoque incertum fuit, insidias an proditionem
vel aliquod honestum consilium coeptaverint. Tacitus goes on to tell how
when Otho's army came near to the enemy a sudden rumour spread among
them that the army (Plut., Oth. 12, says the generals) of Vitellius had
deserted. Whether this rumour was spread by the spies of Vitellius or
originated through treachery or by chance among the partizans of Otho,
was never known. The Othonians took the initiative in peaceful overtures
by greeting the foe (ultro salutavere), but were answered by angry shouts,
while several on their own side, hearing and not understanding the greeting,
thought they were being betrayed. Any further misunderstanding was
prevented by the Vitellians making a fierce onslaught. Plutarch gives the
same account and says that the van of Otho's army greeted their adversaries
in friendly fashion as fellow-soldiers (ἠσπάσαντο φιλίως συστρατιώτας προσαγορεύσαντες).

consalutatione: this is the reading of Q.; the other MSS., including
M, have consultatione (‘“'nescio an rectius" Ihm). consalutatio is used
in the same way of soldiers' mutual greetings in Tac. H. iv 72, nulla inter
coeuntes exercitus consalutatio; id. A. xv 16, maesti manipuli
prae fletu usurpata consalutatio.
,
vix

§ 3. impetum capit: "came to a quick decision," "formed a sudden
resolve (subitum consilium)" on the analogy of capere consilium; cf.
Calig. 43, expeditionis Germanicae impetum cepit: Aug. 42, 3, impetum se
cepisse scribit frumentationes abolendi: Ner. 48, 1, revocato rursus impetu
"changing his hasty resolve”: Curt. v 12, 1, Bessus occidendi protinus
regis impetum ceperat.

dominationem sibi asserere: cf. the epitaph written by Verginius
Rufus for his own tomb: Hic situs est Rufus, pulso qui Vindice quondam |
imperium asseruit non sibi sed patriae (Plin. Ep. vi 10).

quippe: Trachmann (De conjunctionum causalium ap. Suet. usu, p. 41)
says, "Verba 'quippe
subirent' ad praecedentia 'desperatione ulla
aut diffidentia' ita spectant, ut 'quippe residuis integrisque
venientibus aliis' referenda sint ad vocem 'desperatione, verba
victis quidem adeo afflictis (sc. et quippe ne quidem)' ad vocem
‘diffidentia.' Itaque duo membra enuntiati ex 'quippe' suspensi
ἀσυνδετικῶς posita sunt.”
et super-
'ne
residuis integrisque (copiis): the strong force which he had taken
with him when he withdrew to Brixellum before the battle of Betriacum.

ad secundos casus: the meaning seems to be that given by Beroaldus,
“Noluit Otho primo discrimini casuique bellico committere copias omnes,
sed partem militum sibi reservaverat ad fortunam bellicam, casumque
secundo tentandum.” Baumg.-Cr. and the Thes. Ling. Lat. cite this as
an example of secundus = felix, which is unsatisfactory. Bentley would
alter either secundos to adversos or casus to iactus.

aliis e Dalmatia Pannoniaque et Moesia: cf. Tac. ii 44, Praetorianus
miles non virtute se sed proditione victum fremebat. Ne Vitellianis quidem
incruentam fuisse victoriam, pulso equite, rapta legionis aquila; superesse
cum ipso Othone militum quod trans Padum fuerit; venire Moesiacas
legiones; magnam exercitus partem Bedriaci remansisse: hos certe nondum
victos, et si ita ferret, honestius in acie perituros: ib. c. 46, Nec praetoriani
tantum, proprius Othonis miles, sed praemissi e Moesia eandem obstinationem
adventantis exercitus, legiones Aquileiam ingressas nuntiabant, ut nemo
dubitet potuisse renovari bellum atrox, lugubre, incertum victis et victoribus. We are told in Tac. ii 11 that two legions (vii Galbiana and xiii
Gemina) from Pannonia and two (xi Claudia and xiv Gemina Martia
Victrix) from Dalmatia were moving to the support of Otho, and that
2000 men from each of them had been sent on in advance. It is not clear
what portion of these forces had arrived in time to take part in the
battle of Betriacum (Spooner, Tac. Hist. Introd. pp. 75, 79). From Moesia
three legions (iii Gallica, vii Claudia, viii Augusta) or three detachments
of them (see Vesp. 6, 2 and notes) had come by the passes of the Julian
Alps and had reached (or were approaching) Aquileia, when they received
news of the defeat and death of Otho.
lemma: aliis e Dalmatia Pannoniaque et Moesia

text:
ne victis quidem
subirent: the eagerness of Otho's defeated
forces for another encounter is described in Tac. ii 46, Non expectavit
militum ardor vocem imperatoris. Bonum haberet animum iubebant:
superesse adhuc novas vires et ipsos extrema passuros ausurosque. Neque
erat adulatio: ire in aciem, excitare partium fortunam furore quodam et
instinctu flagrabant. Plutarch (Oth. 15) says that it was not wonderful
that Otho's friends should have done their best to encourage him, but
the passionate affection of his soldiers passed all belief (τὸ δὲ τῶν στρατιωτῶν
πάθος ἅπασαν ὑπερέβαλε πίστιν); not one of them deserted him to go over
to the victors.

Laetus: all the MSS., except M, have the reading “Lenis." Macé
(Essai sur Suétone, p. 31 sq.) points out that if "Lenis” were what
Suetonius wrote, the origin of "Laetus” would be inexplicable;
"Laetus,” on the other hand, would easily be corrupted into "Lenis," the
successive stages being LAETVS, LETVS, LENS, LENIS; it would also be felt
that "Lenis," as a cognomen for the father, corresponded with "Tranquillus," the cognomen of the son.

tertiae decimae legionis: Mommsen's view that the 13th legion
(Gemina) was created by Augustus in 6 A.D. is rejected by Parker (Roman
Legions p. 78 sqq.) and Ritterling (in Pauly-Wissowa xii 1711).
After
the disaster to Varus in 9 A.D. it was brought (perhaps from Illyricum)
to Vindonissa (Windisch) in Upper Germany. Under Claudius (in 45 or
46) it was transferred to Pannonia, whence it came to support Otho (see
on c. 9, 3). It was defeated at Betriacum by the 5th legion (Alaudae),
the legionaries attributing their defeat to their legatus Vedius Aquila
(Tac. H. ii 43 sq.). Vitellius, after his victory, put it to the forced labour
of building amphitheatres at Cremona and Bononia (Tac. ii 67, iii 32).
It was then sent back to its quarters at Poetovio in Pannonia, but was
immediately recalled to support Vespasian, and took part in the victory
at Cremona over the Vitellians (Tac. iii 1, 21, 27, 32), after which it was
sent back to Pannonia.

tribunus angusticlavius: i.e. a tribune of equestrian birth; see on
''tribunus laticlavius,'' Dom. 10, 5.
..
deinde
..

mox: here, as frequently, = post, postea; used in this sense in enumerations also, e.g. Iul. 22, 1, initio. mox: Aug. 19, 1, prima
тох exin.. ac praeter has item.. ad extremum: Vitell. 12, тох
et rursus iterum deinde: 15, 4, primum..dein. ac mox (cf. Tac. A. xi
22, primum deinde mox post). The generally accepted view that
mox for postea is merely post-class. is contested by H. J. Rose, Class.
Quart. xxi 2.

de Cassi Brutique exitu: both these leaders of the conspiracy against
Julius Caesar perished by the sword. In the first engagement at Philippi
(42 в.с.) С. СCassius, hard-pressed and isolated, mistaking for the pursuing
foe a force of cavalry which M. Brutus had sent to his support, laid bare
his neck and commanded his freedman Pindarus to cut off his head (Plut.
Brut. 43); twenty days afterwards, at the second encounter on the same
ground, Brutus, routed by Octavius and Antonius, threw himself on his
own sword (ib. 52).

nec concursurum cum Galba fuisse: concurrere must be used here in
the general sense of opposing, or disputing another's title (certamen de
imperio suscipere, Baumg.-Cr.); Burman points out that it cannot bear its
more usual meaning of committere proelium, for (1) the statement of
Suetonius would be a contradiction, being equivalent to non gesturum
fuisse bellum nisi confideret sine bello rem transigi posse; and (2) Otho
never did join battle with Galba, he merely won over the praetorians, who
gave him the empire and slew Galba. Bentley conjectured occisurum eum
Galbam.

exemplo manipularis militis: Dio (lxiv 11) tells this story in the
same form as Suetonius: ἐπεὶ δὲ οἱ τοῦ ῎Οθωνος ἐκρατήθησαν, ἤγγειλε μὲν ἱππεύς
τις τὸ πάθος τῷ Ὄθωνι˙ καὶ ἐπειδή γε ἠπιστεῖτο πρὸς τῶν παρόντων (ἔτυχον γὰρ πολλοὶ
κατὰ τύχην ἠθροισμένοι) καὶ οἱ μὲν δραπέτην (fugitivum) οἱ δὲ καὶ πολέμιον αὐτὸν
ἀπεκάλουν, “ εἴθε γάρ” ἔφη “ ψευδῆ ταῦτα, Καῖσαρ, ἦν· ἥδιστα γὰρ ἂν νικῶντός σου
ἐτελεύτησα. νῦν δὲ ἐγὼ μὲν πάντως οἰχήσομαι, ἵνα μή μέ τις ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ καταπεφευγέναι δόξῃ, σὺ δὲ βουλεύου, ὡς τῶν πολεμίων οὐκ ἐς μακρὰν ἡξόντων, ὅ τι χρὴ
πρᾶξαι.” καὶ ὁ μὲν ταῦτ᾽ εἰπὼν ἑαυτὸν διεχρήσατο. Plutarch (Oth. 15) says that
the incident occurred when the soldiers after the defeat at Betriacum were
imploring Otho not to leave them but to use, as long as there was life in
them, their souls and bodies in his service: Εἷς δὲ τῶν ἀφανεστέρων ἀνατείνας
τὸ ξίφος καὶ εἰπών “Ἴσθι, Καῖσαρ, οὕτως ὑπὲρ σοῦ παρατεταγμένους (prepared
to die) ἅπαντας” ἀπέσφαξεν ἑαυτόν. Tacitus (H. iii 54) tells a similar story
of Julius Agrestis, a centurion in the army of Vitellius, who persuaded
Vitellius to allow him to go and ascertain the extent of the disaster which
their army had sustained at Cremona against Vespasian's forces, and
when he brought back his report of the losses incurred, Vitellius refused
to believe him and charged him with having been bribed, whereupon
Agrestis: quandoquidem” inquit “magno documento opus est, nec alius
iam tibi aut vitae aut mortis meae usus, dabo cui credas." Atque ita
digressus voluntaria morte dicta firmavit.
..

non amplius. coniecturum: cf Tac. ii 47, hunc animum, hanc virtutem
vestram ultra periculis obicere nimis grande vitae meae pretium puto:
Eutrop. vii 17, petentibus militibus, ne tam cito de belli desperaret eventu,
cum tanti se non esse dixisset, ut propter eum bellum civile moveretur, etc.
Tacitus (l.c.), Plutarch (Oth. 15), and Dio (lxiv 13) all put into the
mouth of Otho a last speech in which he refuses to yield to the entreaties
of his soldiers who implored him to continue the struggle; he points out
to them that by dying he will benefit the State more than by continuing
to live, and that his death will be a glorious death, if by it are ended the
horrors of civil strife. Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) says "No doubt all these
speeches are inventions of the authors themselves"; but we may be sure
that Otho took leave of his men in a speech on some such lines as these.

§ 2. fratrem: Lucius Salvius Otho Titianus; see on c. 1, 3.
fratris filium: Lucius Salvius Otho Cocceianus (or Cocceius, Κοκκήϊος
Plut.), who was spared by Vitellius, but was put to death by Domitian,
nearly 20 years afterwards, for keeping the birthday of his uncle the
emperor Otho; see Dom. 10, 3. Plutarch (Oth. 16) describes how Otho
bade his nephew have no fear of Vitellius whose family he himself had
preserved unhurt; he tells him that he had intended to adopt him as his
son but postponed it from considerations of his safety, and he gives him
a last warning neither to forget nor to be too mindful of the fact that
his uncle had been a Caesar (μήτε ἐπιλαθέσθαι παντάπασι μήτε ἄγαν μνημονεύειν, ὅτι Καίσαρα θεῖον ἔσχες). Cf. Tac. ii 48, Mox Salvium Cocceianum,
fratris filium prima iuventa, trepidum et maerentem ultro solatus est,
laudando pietatem eius, castigando formidinem: an Vitellium tam inmitis
animi fore, ut pro incolumi tota domo ne hanc quidem sibi gratiam
redderet? Mereri se festinato exitu clementiam victoris: non enim ultima
desperatione, sed poscente proelium exercitu, remisisse rei publicae novissimum casum. Satis sibi nominis, satis posteris suis nobilitatis quaesitum.
Post Iulios Claudios Servios se primum in familiam novam imperium intulisse. Proinde erecto animo capesseret vitam, neu patruum sibi Othonem
fuisse aut oblivisceretur umquam aut nimium meminisset.

singulos amicorum cohortatus: Tac. (l.c.), Talia locutus, ut cuique
aetas aut dignitas, comiter appellatos, irent propere neu remanendo iram
victoris asperarent, iuvenes auctoritate, senes precibus movebat, placidus
ore, intrepidus verbis, intempestivas suorum lacrimas coercens. Dari naves
ac vehicula abeuntibus iubet.

osculo: see on c. 6, 2.
secreto: see on c. 3, 1.

binos: the distributive numeral, because codicilli is one of the words
regularly used in the plural only.

codicillos: thin tablets of wood (codices, caudices) covered with wax,
used for notes or hasty jottings with a stilus. The word can denote either
the tablets or the writing on them; e.g. Cic. Fam. ix 26, harum (litterarum)
exemplum in codicillos exaravi: Sen. Ep. 55, adeo tecum sum, ut dubitem,
an incipiam non epistulas sed codicillos tibi scribere. See also Marquardt,
Privatl. p. 804.

exaravit: exarare, “to plough up," was used metaph. of the furrows
traced in the wax by the stilus. Cicero uses it freely, but only in his
Letters; Suetonius uses it also in Ner. 52, versus quasi a cogitante atque
generante exaratas: vit. Lucan., codicillos ad patrem exaravit.
..
..

sororem: see c. 1, 3, where she is mentioned as betrothed to Drusus,
son of Germanicus.
His

Messalinam: Statilia Messalina, granddaughter of T. Statilius Taurus
(cons. 11 A.D.), and probably daughter of T. Statilius Taurus (cons. 44 A.D.)
who was a grandson of the orator Messala (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 266).
She was the third of Nero's wives, being married to him c. 66 A.D.
previous wives were Octavia and Poppaea. After Poppaea's death, caused
by his own brutality (see on c. 3, 1), he wished to marry Antonia, daughter
of the emperor Claudius, and when she refused he put her to death. He
then selected Messalina, and as she was already married to Atticus
Vestinus (cons. 65 A.D.) he had her husband put to death merely for having
knowingly married one who numbered Nero among her paramours (Tac.
A. xv 68 sq., Suet. Ner. 35). The Schol. on Juv. vi 434, where the poet
satirizes literary ladies, says that the accomplished Messalina is aimed at:
“Statiliam Messalinam significat, quae post quattuor matrimonia diverso
exitu soluta postremo Neroni nupsit; post quem interemptum et opibus et
forma et ingenio plurimum viguit. Consectata est usum eloquentiae usque
ad studium declamandi.
Illo tempore duae Messalinae fuerunt, haec et
Valeria de qua Claudius Britannicum filium sustulit." For coins with her
name and image see Cohen, i² p. 316; Eckhel, vi 287 sq.

Neronis: sc. uxorem. In expressing relationship the appellative nouns
(uxor, filius, etc.) are at times omitted as in Greek. This is most frequent
in poetry and post-Aug. prose, but there are a few instances in Cicero
(Kühner-Stegmann, i 414).

quicquid epistularum erat
concremavit: Tac. ii 48, libellos
("petitions'') epistulasque studio erga se aut in Vitellium contumeliis insignes abolet (= concremat): Zonar. xi 15, τά τε γράμματα ὅσα τινὲς αὐτῷ
κατ᾿ ἐκείνου ἐγεγράφεσαν ἔκαυσεν, ὥστε μηδένα ἐξ αὐτῶν φωραθέντα κινδυνεῦσαι, καὶ
καλῶν ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν παρόντων ἠσπάζετο αὐτοὺς καὶ ἐδίδου σφίσι χρήματα. For
quicquid c. gen. see on Galb. 1.

divisit pecunias domesticis: Tacitus (who does not specify to whom
the money was given) says that he distributed it sparingly and not like a
man about to die: pecunias distribuit parce nec ut periturus. Plutarch
(Oth. 17) states that he carefully rewarded each servant according to his
deserts, not squandering the money lavishly merely because he knew that
it would soon be another's: τοὺς οἰκέτας προσεκαλεῖτο, καὶ φιλοφρονούμενος
διένεμε τῶν χρημάτων τῷ μὲν πλέον, τῷ δὲ ἔλαττον, οὐχ ὥσπερ ἀλλοτρίων ἀφειδῶν,
ἀλλὰ τὸ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν καὶ τὸ μέτριον ἐπιμελῶς φυλάττων. According to Plut. it was
not till later in the evening, after he had chosen the dagger with which
to slay himself (see Suet. c. 11, 2), that he made this distribution of money
to his servants.

tumultu exorto: Tac. ii 49, Post quae, dimotis omnibus, paulum
requievit. Atque illum, supremas iam curas animo volutantem, repens
tumultus avertit, nuntiata consternatione ac licentia militum: namque
abeuntibus exitium minitabantur: Plut. (Oth. 16), Γενόμενος δὲ ἀπὸ τούτων
μετὰ μικρὸν ἤκουσε θορύβου καὶ βοῆς ἐπὶ θύραις. Οἱ γὰρ στρατιῶται τῶν συγκλητικῶν
(senatorum) τοῖς ἀπιοῦσι διηπείλουν ἀποσφάξειν, εἰ μὴ παραμενοῦσιν, ἀλλ᾽ οἰχήσονται
τὸν αὐτοκράτορα (Imperatorem) καταλιπόντες.

inter moras: the same phrase is used in Ner. 49, 2, where Nero is
hesitating to slay himself and a letter arrives stating that he has been
proclaimed a public enemy: inter moras perlatos a cursore Phaonti codicillos
praeripuit legitque se hostem a senatu iudicatum.

coeptabant: this verb only here in Suet.; twice in Cic. (Fin. v 24,
Arat. 131); most frequent in poets and Tac. For the use of "frequentative forms by Suet. see App. I § 7. b.
detineri: the soldiers were extreme in their violence against
Verginius Rufus, whose house they blockaded and besieged: Tac. ii 49,
atrocissima in Verginium vi, quem clausa domo obsidebant. Verginius,
the conqueror of Vindex (Galb. 9, 2), had been appointed by Otho to be
consul suffectus for the year. After Otho's death the soldiers tumultuously
demanded that he should undertake the empire, but he managed to slip
away from them: Tac. ii 51, per aversam domus partem furtim digressus
inrumpentes frustratus est.

Adiciamus noctem: these words, in which Otho announced the
postponement of his death for a few hours, are not mentioned by Tacitus
or Plutarch. Cf. Hor. C. iv 7, 17, Quis scit an adiciant hodiernae crastina
summae (al. vitae) Tempora di superi?
his ipsis totidemque verbis: totidem verbis is often used of copies
or translations "word for word"; e.g. Cic. Att. vi 2, istum ego locum
totidem verbis a Dicaearcho transtuli: Fin. ii 100, totidem verbis interpretari. The emphasis which Suetonius lays on the accuracy of his statement of Otho's words may be due to a desire to correct some current
misrepresentation of them.
vetuit vim cuiquam fieri: cf. Tac. c. 49, increpitis seditionis auctoribus
regressus vacavit abeuntium adloquiis, donec omnes inviolati discederent.
Plutarch (Oth. 16) describes how Otho sternly quelled the disorder: πάλιν
οὖν προῆλθεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀνδρῶν φοβηθείς, καὶ τοὺς στρατιώτας οὐκέτι δεητικὸς οὐδὲ
πρᾷος, ἀλλὰ τραχὺς ὀφθεὶς καὶ μετ᾿ ὀργῆς εἰς τὸ θορυβοῦν μάλιστα διαβλέψας ἀπελθεῖν
ἐποίησεν εἴξαντας καὶ διατρέσαντας.

potestatem sui praebuit: cf. Tib. 40, potestatem omnibus adeundi sui
fecit: ib. 34, 2, qui potestatem sui die festo non habuissent: Cic. Q.
Fratr. i 2, cum neque praetores diebus aliquot adiri possent vel potestatem
sui facerent.
•

§2. sedata siti potione: Tac. c. 49, vesperascente die sitim haustu
gelidae aquae sedavit: Plut. c. 17, ἤδη δὲ ἑσπέρας οὔσης ἐδίψησε, καὶ πιὼν
ὀλίγον ὕδατος, κ.τ.λ.

explorata utriusque acie: Tac. (l.c.), tum adlatis pugionibus < duobus >,
cum utrumque pertemptassset, alterum capiti subdidit. Plutarch says the
test took some time: δυεῖν ὄντων αὐτῷ ξιφῶν, ἑκατέρου κατεμάνθανε τὸ σπάσμα
(i.e. the blade drawn from the scabbard) πολὺν χρόνον. Similarly Nero,
when he heard that he was to be punished "more maiorum,” tested the
edges of two daggers: Ner. 49, 2, conterritus duos pugiones, quos secum
extulerat, arripuit temptataque utriusque acie rursus condidit, causatus
nondum adesse fatalem horam.

cum alterum pulvino subdidisset: cf. Dom. 17, 2, pugionem subditum
pulvino.

foribus adopertis: this use of adopertus in the sense of clausus (its
normal meaning being tectus, obvolutus velamine quodam) is found earlier
only in Ov. Met. i 713, vidit succubuisse oculos adopertaque lumina.
somno.

artissimo somno: cf. Aug. 16, 1, arto repente somno devinctus: Cic.
Rep. 6, 10, те artior, quam solebat, somnus complexus est. Tacitus (c.
49) puts it less strongly: noctem quietam, utque adfirmatur, non insomnem
egit; Plutarch (c. 17) agrees with Suet.: ἀποπέμψας δὲ τούτους ἤδη τὸ
λοιπὸν ἀνεπαύετο τῆς νυκτός, ὥστε τοὺς κατευναστὰς (cubicularios) αἰσθάνεσθαι
βαθέως αὐτοῦ καθεύδοντος. Cf. the description given by Pliny (Ep. vi 16, 13)
of the deep sleep of his uncle, Pliny the Elder, during the eruption of
Vesuvius in 79 A.D.: Tum se quieti dedit, et quievit verissimo quidem
somno. Nam meatus animae (‘his snoring'")
ab iis qui limini obversabantur (i.e. the cubicularii) audiebatur.
..

circa lucem: circa is used only of place (and that rarely) in Cic. and
Caes.; from Livy onwards it is used of time as well, e.g. Suet. Claud. 7,
circa initia imperii: Iul. 88, circa undecimam horam; also of number
"about" (= ad, circiter), e.g. Claud. 6, 2, circa sestertium vicies. For
other uses see on Tit. 4, 3; Dom. 3, 2.

uno se traiecit ictu: Dio lxiv 15, ξιφίδιον λαβὼν ἑαυτὸν διεχρήσατο :
Mart. vi 32, 4, et fodit certa pectora tota manu. Tacitus (c. 49) says that
he fell with his breast upon the steel: Luce prima in ferrum pectore incubuit. Plutarch (c. 17) gives fuller details. He describes how when
Otho awoke he sent a freedman to enquire about the senators, and when
he returned and said that they had all departed safely, Otho bade him go
and show himself to the soldiers that they might not afterwards slay him
for having helped to cause his death (as Epaphroditus aided Nero in his
suicide, see on Dom. 14, 4). As soon as the freedman had gone, Otho
placed his sword upright, and holding it with both hands threw himself
upon it and died with a single groan.
irrumpentibus ad primum gemitum: Tac. (l.c.) ad gemitum morientis
ingressi liberti servique et Plotius Firmus praetorii praefectus unum volnus
invenere.
...

celeriter funeratus: funerare meaning "to give funeral rites to"
is post-Aug. funeratus means "done to death" in Hor. C. iii 8, 7, prope
funeratus Arboris ictu. Otho had given orders for his hasty burial to
prevent his body being mutilated and made a mock of: cf. Tac. (l.c.),
Funus maturatum: ambitiosis ("earnest") id precibus petierat, ne
amputaretur caput ludibrio futurum (an indignity inflicted on the corpse
of Galba, see Galb. 20, 2). For the simple monument erected over his
grave see Vitell. 10, 3.

tricensimo et octavo aetatis anno: this erroneous statement is
repeated (as usual) by Eutropius (vii 17): voluntaria morte obiit, trigesimo
octavo aetatis anno. Otho was born on Apr. 28, 32 A.D. (see c. 2) and
died on Apr. 16 or 17, 69 A.D., so that he lived 37 years, all but 12 or 11
days, as Dio (lxiv 15) accurately states: τοῦτο τὸ τέλος τῷ Ὄθωνι ἐγένετο,
ζήσαντι ἑπτὰ καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη, ἕνδεκα ἡμερῶν δέοντα. Tacitus (ii 49) and
[Aurelius Victor] Epit. 7 say that he died in his 37th year; Plutarch
(Oth. 18) says more loosely: ἔτη ἑπτὰ καὶ τριάκοντα βιώσας. According to
Oudendorp and Baumg.-Cr. the inaccurate statement of Suetonius, that
Otho died in his 38th year, is due to a method of calculation by which
the year of birth and year of death are both included. There are similar
difficulties in the statements of Suetonius with regard to the length of
life or length of rule in the case of Galba (see on Galb. 23), Vitellius (see
on Vitell. 18), and of Titus (see on Tit. 11).

nonagensimo et quinto imperii die: this too is accepted by Eutropius
(l.c.); Dio (l.c.) says that he reigned 90 days; Plutarch (l.c.) 3 months;
Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 9,9) 92 days. Galba was slain on Jan. 15 and
Otho's reign began on that day, but there is no means of fixing definitely
the day in April on which he died. Opinion is divided between the 15th
(so Schiller, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit), the 16th (so Krauss, De vitarum imp.
Othonis fide quaestiones), and the 17th (so Puhl, De Oth. et Vit. imp.
quaest.). Nagl (in Pauly-Wissowa, i A. 2053) strongly favours the 16th,
and points out in support of this date that Tacitus (H. ii 55) says that
news of Otho's death was brought into the theatre at Rome during the
celebration of the Ludi Cereales (Apr. 13-19). On the last day (Apr. 19)
of the Ludi Cereales there were games in the Circus, and if the news
arrived on that day it would have been brought to the Circus, not to the
theatre. The news probably reached Rome late on the 18th, and it was
not till the following day that the senate formally appointed Vitellius as
emperor (cf. Henzen Act. Fratr. Arv. p. xciv, “ob diem imperi [Vitelli]
Germanici imp. quod xiii K. Mai. statutum est"). Allowing 2 days for
the message to arrive from Brixellum (367 Roman miles from Rome), Otho
died on the 16th, and the battle of Betriacum took place on the 14th (cf.
Holzapfel, Klio xiii 289 sqq.). If we assume then that Otho died on
Apr. 16, he died on the 92nd day of his reign; Suetonius, who says that
he died on the 95th, apparently reckoned from Jan. 15 (date of Otho's
accession) to Apr. 19 (date of Vitellius' accession).

animo nequaquam corpus competit: competit is a contracted perf.,
like petit, c. 7, 1. Suetonius uses competere absolutely in Aug. 31, 3, si
cuiusquam neptium suarum competeret aetas (i.e. if any of them were of
eligible age for the post of Vestal); in Iul. 40, 1, it takes the abl. (according
to the best MSS.): fastos.. adeo turbatos, ut neque messium feriae aestate
(v.l. aestati) neque vindemiarum autumno competerent. The dat. is the
normal constr. with competere in the sense of "congruere, consentire, convenire, aptum esse"; cf. Nonius (276 M., 424 Lindsay), conpetere, par
esse vel simile. unde et in aestimatione rerum “hoc illi conpetit” dicimus.
modicae staturae: see on Galb. 21.

male pedatus: "ill-set on his feet" ("splay-footed," Clarke). pedatus
(ὑπόπους) is not applied to persons elsewhere; the verb is used metaph. of
vines in the sense of suffulcire; Colum. iv 12, vineae pedandae cura:
Plin. N.H. xvii 164, vineae pedatae simplici iugo.
scambus: i.e. with the legs bent out and the feet bent in, bow-legged,
bandy-legged. This seems to be the only place where the late Gr. word
σκαμβός is found in Latin. The usual word is varus; cf. Varr. R.R. ii 9,
(canes) debent esse cruribus rectis et potius varis quam vatiis, which is
rendered by the compiler of the Geoponica (xix 2): σκαμβότερα μᾶλλον ἢ
βλαισά. In our passage the MSS. have cambus, which Turnebus altered
to scambus. Bonnet (Archiv Lat. Lex. 13, 579) defends cambus as the
more correct form. He says it is a Gallic word which became completely
Latinised, since it serves as a cognomen of different persons, of whom
one is mentioned in an African inscription of 329 A.D. (Ephem. epigr. v
p. 179).

munditiarum muliebrium: cf. Liv. xxxiv 7, munditiae et ornatus et
cultus, haec feminarum insignia sunt, his gaudent et gloriantur, hunc
mundum muliebrem appellarunt maiores nostri: Ulp. Dig. xxxiv 2, 25, 10,
mundus muliebris est, quo mulier mundior fit; continentur eo specula,
matulae, unguenta, etc.: Sall. Iug. 85 (Marius speaking), ex parente meo
et ex aliis sanctis viris ita accepi, munditias mulieribus, viris laborem convenire: Claud. Eutrop. ii 336, minimeque viriles | munditiae, compti voltus,
onerique vel ipsa | serica (“silken garments"). Juvenal (ii 99) ridicules
the mirror (speculum) which Otho carried with him on his campaigns: Ille
tenet speculum, pathici gestamen Othonis, | Actoris Aurunci spolium, quo
se ille videbat | armatum cum iam tolli vexilla iuberet- | res memoranda
novis annalibus atque recenti | historia, speculum civilis sarcina belli (the
allusions are to the shield described as “magni gestamen Abantis,” Aen.
iii 286, and the spear which Turnus was so proud of having taken from
Actor, “Actoris Aurunci spolium,” Aen. xii 94). Seneca (N.Q. i 17) is
equally severe on the “sarcinae militares" carried by effeminate Romans:
Adeoque omnia indiscreta sunt perversissimis artibus, ut quicquid mundus
muliebris vocabatur, sarcinae viriles sint: minus dico, etiam militares.
Iam speculum ornatus tantum causa adhibitum, nulli non vitio necessarium
factum est.
vulso corpore: cf. Galb. 22, n.

galericulo: "peruke.” galericulum is a dimin. of galerum (also
galerus and galera) which, like κυνέη, was used for a cap made from an
animal's skin with the fur or hair left on it; such caps were worn by
country labourers, and rustic warriors (e.g. Aen. vii 688; in Frontin.
Strateg. iv 7, 29 galericulum is used for the leather headgear of the
velites); they were also worn by athletes to save their hair from the
unguents used in wrestling, e.g. Mart. xiv 50 (entitled “Galericulum''),
Ne lutet immundum nitidos ceroma capillos, | hac poteris madidas condere
pelle comas. Then galerum and galericulum came to mean a peruke or
wig made of fine skin with human hair attached; Martial (xii 45) mentions
one made of kid, Haedina tibi pelle contegenti | nudae tempora (“brows'')
verticemque calvae ("skull") | festive tibi, Phoebe, dixit ille | qui dixit
caput esse calceatum (“well-shod"). Such wigs were worn at times as
disguises, e.g. by Nero on his nightly escapades, Ner. 26, 1, adrepto pilleo
vel galero popinas inibat, and by the notorious Messalina in her debauchery,
Juv. vi 120, nigrum flavo crinem abscondente galero. See Marquardt,
Privatl.2 603 sq.; Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1452 sq.

raritatem capillorum: cf. Plin. N.H. xxviii 163, ursinus adeps
emendat raritatem superciliorum: Suet. Calig. 50, 1, capillo raro ac circa
verticem nullo.
..

rasitare: this frequentative is post-Aug.; cf. Gell. iii 4, comperimus
viros barbam in eiusmodi aetate rasitavisse. With the introduction of
barbers from Sicily to Italy in 300 B.с. (Varr. R.R. ii 11, 10) the use of
the razor (novacula) became common.
been the first who was shaved daily;
radi cotidie instituit Africanus.
Scipio Africanus was said to have
Plin. N.H. vii 59, primus omnium

pane madido linere: Otho's use of bread-poultices for the face is
mentioned as one of his effeminacies by Juvenal (ii 103): Nimirum
summi ducis est occidere Galbam | et curare cutem, summi constantia
civis | Bebriacis campis spolium adfectare Palati | et pressum in
facie digitis extendere panem, | quod nec in Assyrio pharetrata Semiramis orbe, | maesta nec Actiaca fecit Cleopatra carina. Again in Sat. vi
461 sqq. Juvenal ridicules the use of these poultices (cataplasmata) by
women to beautify their complexions: Interea foeda aspectu ridendaque
multo | pane tumet facies aut pinguia Poppaeana | spirat, etc.
[“Рорраеапа" were cosmetics called after Poppaea, wife of Otho and
Nero (see Oth. 3), who was so careful of her beauty that she always
bathed in asses' milk; some of Otho's effeminate habits may have been
due to association with her.] Juvenal compares the removal of the
poultices to removing stucco: Tandem aperit vultum et tectoria prima
reponit. According to the Schol. on Juv. such poultices served two
purposes: (1) ad excandendam (‘brightening, whitening'') cutem; (2) ad
tendendam faciem aut cutem magis (a medicamen used to tighten the
skin and remove wrinkles was called tentipellium, Fest. p. 364 Müll.).
..
..

consuetum: for the irregular consecution of nom. and acc. in "fuisse
traditur. male pedatus.. rasitare. consuetum" see note on "dicitur
obmurmurasse,” c. 7, 2. Bentley would read consuetus.

a prima lanugine: lanugo was the first down of manhood; cf. Aen. x
324, flaventem prima lanugine malas: Juv. xiii 59, primaque par sacrae
lanugo senectae. The day on which the lanugo or first beard was shaved
was celebrated with sacrifices and rejoicings and the lanugo was dedicated
to some god; Nero dedicated his in a box adorned with costly pearls to
Jupiter Capitolinus (Ner. 12; cf. Juv. iii 186, Petron. Satyr. 29); Caligula
was exceptional: uno atque eodem die togam sumpsit barbamque posuit
sine ullo honore (Calig. 10, 1).

ne barbatus umquam esset: the usual practice was to allow the hair
on the face to grow again after the first ceremonial shaving (depositio
barbae). The young men at Rome (barbatuli iuvenes, bene barbati) wore
whiskers either without a beard or with a beard trimmed short; after the
age of 40 it was customary to be clean-shaven. See Daremberg-Saglio, i
669 sq.
sacra Isidis in lintea veste celebrasse: see on Dom. 1, 2, Isiaci habitu.
lemma: sacra Isidis in lintea veste celebrasse

text:
§ 2. putem: Suetonius frequently uses the potential subjunctive in
modest affirmations; e.g. Aug. 7, 1, satis certa probatione tradiderim:
16, 2, unde praebitam Antonio materiam putem: Vesp. 1, 4, non negaverim:
Gramm. 7, quod equidem non temere crediderim. See Madvig, L.G. § 350 b.

mors minime congruens vitae: the fact that "nothing in his life
became him like the leaving it" is noticed by several writers; cf. Dio lxiv
15, κάκιστά γε μὴν ἀνθρώπων ζήσας, κάλλιστα ἀπέθανε· καὶ κακουργότατα τὴν ἀρχὴν
(imperium) ἁρπάσας, ἄριστα αὐτῆς ἀπηλλάγη: Plut. Oth. 18, βιώσας γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐπιεικέστερον Νέρωνος ἀπέθανεν εὐγενέστερον: Mart. vi 32, Cum dubitaret adhuc
belli civilis Enyo | forsitan et posset vincere mollis Otho, | damnavit multo
staturum sanguine Martem | et fodit certa pectora tota manu. | Sit Cato,
dum vivit, sane vel Caesare maior: | dum moritur, numquid maior Othone
fuit: Auson. Caes. vii, Aemula polluto gesturus sceptra Neroni | obruitur
celeri raptus Otho exitio. | Fine tamen laudandus erit, qui morte decora |
hoc solum fecit nobile, quod periit: Tac. H. ii 31, Sane ante utriusque (i.e.
Otho and Vitellius) exitum, quo egregiam Otho famam, Vitellius flagitiosissimam meruere, minus Vitellii ignavae voluptates quam Othonis flagrantissimae libidines timebantur.

maiore miraculo fuerit: the dative maiori (Gr) appears in all the
early editions; maiore (MX) is read by Roth, Preud'homme, and Ihm.
It is questionable whether the ablative is defensible; the only parallel
seems to be a doubtful passage, Flor. ii 11, 6, alligati (the chained
captives) miraculo quodam (quidam, Lipsius) fuere, cum catenas morsibus
et ore tentassent. In Plin. N.H. xxvii 11, nec quicquam inter herbas
maiore equidem miraculo adspexi, the meaning is prob. "with greater
wonderment"; cf. xxxii 4, hoc est maioris miraculi (= hoc magis homines
admirantur): xii 1, arbor digna miraculo (= quam admiremur).
phrase miraculo esse often occurs, but in it miraculo is clearly the dative.
In Cic. Att. v 1, 4, multa mihi maiori stomacho quam ipsi Quinto fuerunt,
the MSS. give maiore; Orelli restored maiori, which is now the accepted
reading.
•
The

multi manus exosculati: Tac. H. ii 49, tulere corpus praetoriae
cohortes cum laudibus et lacrimis volnus manusque eius exosculantes. The
compound exosculari is stronger than the simple verb and denotes passionate
kissing. Plutarch (Oth. 17) describes the wild grief of the soldiers at
Otho's death and their self-reproaches for not having guarded him more
closely and hindered his dying for them. They took no thought for themselves, though the enemy was close at hand. They arrayed the body in
state, and in full armour bore it to the pyre: happy were those fortunate
