enough to support the bier! Some kissed his wound, some clasped his
hand, while others, afar off, prostrated themselves.

vim suae vitae attulerunt: Tac. (l.c.), Quidam militum iuxta rogum
interfecere se, non noxa neque ob metum, sed aemulatione decoris et caritate
principis: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 7, (Otho) adeo amabilis militibus propriis,
ut plerique, corpore eius viso, suis manibus interierint: Dio lxiv 15, καί
τινες ἑαυτοὺς ἐπέσφαξαν αὐτῷ: Plut. (l.c.), ἔνιοι δὲ τῇ πυρᾷ λαμπάδας ὑφέντες
ἑαυτοὺς ἀπέσφαξαν. Plut. adds that it was not because they had received
any special favour from Otho, or that they feared the victor's vengeance;
it would seem that no king or tyrant was ever so passionately fond of
ruling as they were of being ruled by Otho. Even after his death their
affection for him continued and developed into an ineradicable hatred of
Vitellius.

multi et absentium: Tac. (l.c.), ac postea promisce ("among all
ranks'') Bedriaci Placentiae aliisque in castris celebratum (= saepius
adhibitum) id genus mortis.

prae dolore: this ante-class. and post-class. use of prae (= propter)
in a positive sentence occurs also in Iul. 39, 4; Aug. 65, 2; Tib. 66;
Calig. 4; Claud. 10, 2:32. In class. writers prae is used in this sense
only with an expressed or implied negative or with vix (Kühner-Stegmann,
i 513).

incolumem detestata: Plutarch (c. 18) says that those who praised
Otho's death were not less in number or in worth than those who blamed
his life: ἀπέθανε δὲ Ὄθων... ἀπολιπὼν μὴ χείρονας μήδ᾽ ἐλάττους τῶν τὸν βίον
αὐτοῦ ψεγόντων τοὺς ἐπαινοῦντας τὸν θάνατον.

laudibus tulit: this poetical use of ferre for effere is found in prose
from Livy on.

Galbam.. interemptum: the slaying of Galba, which was ordered by
Otho (see Oth. 6, 3), is characterised as a "facinus flagitiosissimum” by
Tacitus, H. ii 50: Duobus facinoribus, altero flagitiosissimo, altero egregio
(i.e. Otho's noble death), tantundem apud posteros meruit bonae famae
quantum malae.
rei publicae

restituendae: under the early Empire there was constant talk of the restoration of the old republican form of government,
especially after Nero's death (see on Galb. 10, 1). Augustus himself,
according to Suet. Aug. 28, twice thought of restoring the republic (de
reddenda re publica bis cogitavit) in 27 and 23 B.c.; but, as Shuckburgh
says in his note on that passage, all Augustus did in reality was to
elaborate the restitution of the forms of the republic so far as was consistent with his own supremacy. Cf. also Claud. 1, 4, where Suetonius
says that Drusus Germanicus (brother of Tiberius) made no secret of his
intention to revive the republic if ever he should have the power:
dissimulasse umquam pristinum se rei p. statum, quandoque posset,
restituturum.
nec

nobilem: so [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 8, 1, Vitellius ortus familia nobili;
contrast Eutrop. vii 18, 1, Vitellius . . familia honorata magis quam nobili.

adulatores obtrectatoresque: two classes who distort the truth; cf.
the words of Tacitus (H. i 1) describing how the history of the early
emperors was biassed by partizan views: Simul veritas pluribus modis
infracta, primum inscitia rei publicae ut alienae, mox libidine adsentandi
aut rursus odio adversus dominantes: ita neutris cura posteritatis inter
offensos vel obnoxios. Sed ambitionem ("servility'') scriptoris facile
averseris, obtrectatio et livor pronis auribus accipiuntur: quippe adulationi
foedum crimen servitutis, malignitati falsa species libertatis inest.

variatum esset: other examples of the use of the impersonal
passive by Suetonius are Aug. 56, 2, assurrectum ab universis in theatro
et a stantibus plausum: Claud. 11, 1, de mutando rei p. statu haesitatum
erat: Ner. 26, 2, cum lapidibus et subselliorum fragminibus decerneretur: ib. 38, 2, ea clade saevitum est: Oth. 9, 1, plurimum profligari
posse.

§2. extat Q. Elogi.. libellus: the correct reading is quite uncertain.
The MSS. give extatq. elogi (-ii, -ium) and M. Hertz would write this as
extatque elogi (Bentley, extaretque elogi), presumably understanding elogi
libellus to be a genealogical monograph such as was written for the family
of the Junii by Atticus (Nep. Attic. 18, 3; see also on Suet. Galb. 3, 1).
It seems more probable that some proper name should be read: Muretus
suggested "Q. Clodii"; Lipsius "Q. Longini"; Casaubon "Q. Eulogii
(or Eclogii)"; Roth kept to the letters of the MSS. and read "Q. Elogi"
(so Preud'homme; Ihm prints "Q. † Elogi'"). Casaubon's conjecture
"Q. Eulogii" is perhaps more satisfactory than any other; he assumes that
Eulogius was a freedman of Quintus Vitellius and after his manumission
took the name of Q. Vitellius Eulogius; to please his patronus, he drew
up a stemma or family-tree of the Vitellian gens and dedicated the work
to him; in the same way Julius Marathus, a freedman of Augustus,
published records of Augustus (Aug. 79, 2:94, 3). There is no evidence
for "Elogius'' as a name; there are a few instances of "Eulogius" (see
Pauly-Wissowa).
Quintum Vitellium: uncle of the emperor; see c. 2, 2.

Divi Augusti quaestorem: he was probably one of the special
quaestors assigned to the emperor in virtue of his proconsular power; they
were known as quaestores principis, quaestores Caesaris, quaestores Augusti.
These imperial quaestors were employed to read to the senate the letters
and the orationes of the emperor; cf. Tit. 6, 1. Sometimes they are
referred to as quaestores candidati principis, being chosen from, and
usually coextensive with, the candidates for the quaestorship who were
recommended by the emperor and elected as a matter of course.
Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 529. The younger Pliny was an imperial quaestor,
as he mentions in Ep. vii 16, simul quaestores Caesaris (i.e. Domitian)
fuimus.
See

Fauno: Faunus was an old rural divinity, in whose honour the
Faunalia were celebrated by the country people on Dec. 5 (cf. Hor. C. iii
18). His worship was introduced into the city of Rome in 196 в.с. The
Roman annalists seem to have invented the legend that he was a Rex
Aboriginum (Dion. Hal. i 31, ἐτύγχανε δὲ τότε τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ᾿Αβοριγίνων
παρειληφὼς Φαῦνος), the third amongst the mythical kings of Latium (viz.
Saturnus, Picus, Faunus, Latinus). He was also identified with the Greek
Pan, whose cult was said to have been brought to Rome by the Arcadian
Evander, and Wissowa (Relig. u. Kult. Röm. p. 174) holds that the multiplication of Fauni was due to assimilation to the Pans and Satyrs. As a
prophetic god he was believed to reveal the future by oracles (in Saturnian
verse), dreams, and voices of unknown origin (Aen. vii 81 sqq., Cic. N.D.
ii 2, iii 6, etc.); hence the name Faunus was explained as the "speaker,
foreteller (fari)" by Isidorus, and Nettleship (Essays in Lat. Lit. p. 52)
says "Once imagine Faunus as a 'speaker,' and all becomes clear. He
is not only the composer and reciter of verses, but generally the seer or
wise man, whose superior knowledge entitles him to the admiration and
dread of the country folk who consult him. But as his real nature and
functions are superseded, his character is misconceived: he becomes a
divinity, the earliest king of Latium, the god of prophecy, the god of
agriculture." (Quoted by Warde Fowler, Rom. Fest. p. 259, who examines
critically the various theories with regard to Faunus and his cult.)

Aboriginum: the Aborigines (in Gr., with long penult., ᾿Αβοριγίνες)
who are connected in legend with Aeneas, Latinus, and Evander, were said
to have been the oldest inhabitants of Latium, having been driven down
by the Sabines from the mountain country about Reate. They are first
mentioned in Lycophron's Alexandra (v. 1253) where Cassandra prophesies
that Aeneas will colonize χώραν ἐν τόποις Βορειγόνων (cf. Sall. Cat. 6, Urbem
Romam condidere atque habuere initio Troiani . cumque eis Aborigines).
The traditional derivation of their name is “ab origine,” i.e. original
inhabitants, αὐτόχθονες; some regarded it as a corruption of “aberrigines”
i.e. nomads (Fest. p. 266, Dion. Hal. i 10); others explained it as
"mountain dwellers," connecting it with ὄpos (Dion. Hal. i 13).

Vitellia, quae pro numine coleretur: the worship of a goddess Vitellia
is not mentioned elsewhere. The name Vitellia, like Italia, is from ἰταλός
vitulus (Tusc. vitlu = bos), and would mean "the goddess of calves."
Servius (on Aen. viii 328) gives ‘“Vitalia'' as the old name of Italy, the
land of cattle. A female head, representing the personified Italia, with
the inscription “Italia” or “viteliu" is found on several coins; see
Roscher, Lex. Myth. iii 558 sqq., Eckhel i 103 sqq.

toto Latio imperasse: it is doubtful whether toto Latio is dat. or abl.;
in Ner. 12, 3 all the better MSS. give magistros toto certamini praeposuit
consulares, and the dat. toto occurs in Caes. B.G. vii 89, Hirt. B.G. viii 34,
Prop. iii 11, 57, Ov. Am. iii 3, 41, and other passages collected by Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii 529.

inter patricios adlectam: see on Oth. i, 3. The Vitellii were patricii
at Rome at the time of the last Tarquin. Livy (ii 4) mentions two of
the Vitellii as leaders of the "nobiles adulescentes” who conspired to
restore Tarquin; the plot failed, and they paid the penalty. Livy also
mentions a sister of these Vitellii who was married to the consul Brutus;
two of their sons were implicated in the conspiracy and were executed
by order of their father Brutus. Plutarch (Poplic. 3), in his account of
this plot, describes the Οὐιτέλλιοι as patricians (καλοὶ κἀγαθοί) and senators
(βουλευταί). The patrician family of the Vitellii may have become extinct
at that time, as we do not hear of them again under the Republic.

§3. viam Vitelliam: there is no other reference to this road.
Witzschel would identify it with the via Ianiculensis as a name for the
beginning of the via Aurelia (see Galb. 20, 2) which ran from the Porta
Ianiculensis.

Ianiculo: a long and almost continuous hill on the right bank of
the Tiber, east of Rome and outside the limits of the city.

coloniam eiusdem nominis: Vitellia was a town on the borders of
Latium and the territory of the Aequi. Its name occurs in Liv. ii 39
among the towns captured by Coriolanus (c. 490 в.с.). In Liv. v 29 it is
mentioned as a colonia Romana founded in the territory of the Aequi,
which was taken in a surprise night attack by the Aequi in 393 в.с.; we
are not told whether the Romans recovered it. Livy does not state directly
when it was founded, but in v 24 he mentions the foundation of a colony
of 3000 Roman citizens in the territory of the Volsci in 395 B.с., which
(if "Volsci" is used in its broader sense including "Aequi'") may be
Vitellia, as Niebuhr and Mommsen conjectured; see Weissenborn ad loc.
Pliny (N.H. iii 69) includes Vitellia among the cities of Latium which
were utterly extinct in his time.

gentili copia tutandam: there is no historical evidence of the
truth of this family tradition.
The most famous example of a family
furnishing a military force is that of the Fabii who asked the senate to
be allowed to conduct the war against Veii (Liv. ii 48). In 479 B.c. the
Fabii marched from Rome and founded a fortified post on the Cremera,
but two years later the whole Fabian gens (save one survivor) were
slaughtered by the Veientes.

Aequiculos: the Aequiculi, or Aequi, were mountain dwellers in
central Italy between the Latins, Marsi, and Hernici, in the valley of the
upper Anio and on the western shore of the Fucine lake. Their rugged
land bred hardy warriors; cf. Aen. vii 746 (describing the warrior Ufens),
Horrida praecipue cui gens adsuetaque multo | venatu nemorum, duris
Aequicula glebis: Ov. F. iii 93, Aequiculus asper ("rugged''): Sil. Ital.
viii 368, quique Anienis habent ripas, gelidoque rigantur | Simbruvio,
rastrisque domant Aequicula rura. The Aequi (and Volsci) were constantly
at war with Rome, their power being greatest in the first half of the fifth
cent. B.C. In 389 they were defeated by Camillus, and in 304 they were
completely subjugated, forty of their towns being captured in fifty days
(Diod. Sic. xx 101, Liv. ix 45); the vanquished were granted the civitas
sine suffragio (Cic. Off. i 35).

tempore Samnitici belli: this was the second of Rome's three Samnite
wars: (1) 343-341 в.с., (2) 327-304, (3) 298-290.

subsedisse: 'settled at"; cf. Vesp. 1, 4, subsedisse in oppido Reatino:
Cic. Fam. vi 8, in Sicilia ut subsidas.

Nuceriae: one of the principal cities of Apulia. It is better known
as Luceria, and is to be distinguished from the cities in Campania and
Umbria which bore the name of Nuceria. In Ptol. iii 1 it is called Νουκερία
᾿Απουλῶν, and in App. B.C. ii 38 simply Νουκερία; Livy, Strabo, and
Diodorus call it Luceria, Λουκερία (mod. Lucera); cf. Tac. H. iii 86, Patria
illi (i.e. the emperor Vitellius) Luceria. In the second Samnite war, while
the other Apulian cities broke the alliance which they had made with Rome
in 326, Luceria remained loyal and was besieged by the Samnites. In the
attempt to relieve it the Roman army suffered humiliation at the Caudine
Forks (321), and Luceria fell, but was recovered by the Romans in the
following year (Liv. ix 12-15). In 314 it was betrayed into the hands
of the Samnites, but once again the Romans made themselves masters of
it, slaughtering most of the inhabitants and replacing them by 2500 Roman
colonists (Liv. ix 26, Vell. Pat. i 14, Diod. Sic. xix 72).

Cassius Severus: notorious as a defamatory writer under Augustus
and Tiberius. Tacitus (A. iv 21) describes him as “sordidae originis,
maleficae vitae, sed orandi validus.” He was banished to Crete by
Augustus "commotus Cassii Severi libidine, qua viros feminasque inlustres
procacibus scriptis diffamaverat” (Tac. A. i 72); later, under Tiberius,
as he continued his attacks, he was removed to Seriphos where he died
in 34 A.D. after 25 years of exile. His writings were suppressed by
decree of the senate, but Caligula allowed them to be circulated again
(Suet. Calig. 16). He introduced a new style of oratory, bitter and
abusive (Tac. Dial. 26); Quintilian (x 1, 116) says of him: ingenii
plurimum est in eo et acerbitas mira et urbanitas ("wit") et fervor;
sed plus stomacho quam consilio dedit.
sutorem veteramentarium: a cobbler, repairer of old shoes. The
adj. veteramentarius seems to occur only here; it corresponds to the Gr.
παλαιουργός “cobbler” (Poll. vii 82); "sutor cerdo" was also used in
this sense (Mart. iii 16 and 59). These cobblers were distinct from the
various classes of shoemakers (e.g. calcearius, solearius, sandaliarius,
crepidarius, caligarius); see Marquardt, Privatl.2 596 sq.
=

sectionibus:
auctionibus bonorum publicatorum, auction sales of
confiscated goods; cf. Tac. H. i 90, Neronianae sectiones: id. A. xiii 23
(quoted below on “cognituris''): Cic. Phil. ii '64, illud scelus sectionis:
Caes. B.G. ii 33, sectionem eius oppidi universam Caesar vendidit. So
"sector'" was used for a purchaser at such sales; cf. Gaius iv 146,
sectores vocantur qui publica bona mercantur. The derivation from
secare (not sequi) is confirmed by Cicero's jest in Rosc. Amer. 80, sectores
bonorum et collorum. Rejecting the theory that sectores were so called
from "cutting up" the property to resell it, Mommsen explains their
name as "cutters off," referring to the deduction (sometimes very large)
from the price of a property in consideration of the debts and liabilities
attaching to it. See Halm, Introd. to Cic. Rosc. Amer. p. 4; Mayor on
Cic. Phil. ii 39.
=

cognituris: cognitor was used of one who appeared in place of
another or represented his interests in court, and so cognitura munus
defensoris in iudicio (cf. Gaius iv 124). In relation to the State a
cognitor was one who represented and defended the interests of the
State, especially the Treasury, not merely by informing about debts due
to the Treasury, but also by buying such debts from the Treasury as a
speculation, and then recovering them from the debtors. The conjunction
of sectiones and cogniturae in our passage is illustrated by Tac. A. xiii 23,
where Paetus “exercendis apud aerarium sectionibus famosus” is
sentenced to exile, and the records, by which he was reviving forgotten
debts due to the Treasury, were burnt (tabulae exustae sunt, quibus oblitterata aerarii nomina retrahebat). Cf. also Manil. v 319, non illo coram
digitos (i.e. "bidders'") quaesiverit hasta ("auction"), | defueritque
bonis sector, poenamque lucretur | noxius, et patriam fraudarit debitor
aeris; | cognitor est urbis.
=

muliere vulgari:
meretrice; cf. Ov. F. iv 865, numina vulgares
Veneris celebrate puellae: Suet. Dom. 22, inter vulgatissimas meretrices
(where Baumg.-Cr. would read vulgarissimas); in Cic. Phil. ii 18, 44
Antonius is called "vulgare scortum.”
Antiochi: not mentioned elsewhere.

furnariam exercentis: furnaria (post-class.) sc. ars et negotiatio;
cf. Plin. N.H. vii 135, castrensis furnaria "a camp bakery." The word
furnus denoted especially a baker's oven (see Daremberg-Saglio, ii
1420); hence panis furnaceus, bread baked in an oven, as distinct from
panis subcinericius, p. testicius, p. clibanicius. Wolf (followed by
Baumg.-Cr.) strangely explains furnariam exercere as meaning “ex furnis
vulgo locandis quaestum facere, ut moris erat Romae"; but, as Hofstee
points out, this view rests apparently on a doubtful inference from
Juv. vii 4, balneolum Gabiis, Romae conducere furnos. The enemies of
Augustus, like those of Vitellius, gave a disparaging account of his
ancestors, and said that his great-grandfather had carried on a bakery
(pistrinum exercuisse) at Aricia; see Aug. 4.

quod discrepat: cf. Liv. ix 46 id, quod haud discrepat: Claudius'
speech "de iure honorum,” col. i 1. 16, nam et hoc inter auctores discrepat.
The impers. use of "discrepat" (opp. "convenit") also occurs in Suet.
Claud. 44, 2, veneno occisum convenit; ubi autem et per quem dato, discrepat; this is frequent in Livy, e.g. iii 31, cum de legibus conveniret, de
latore tantum discreparet.

sit in medio: cf. in medio relinquere, "to leave it to every man's
judgment, leave it an open question," Cic. Cael. 20, 48, Sall. Cat. 19, 8.
Tacitus has in medium relinquere (cf. θεῖναι εἰς μέσον), Germ. 46, quod ego
ut incompertum in medium (medio, Halm) relinquam.

P. Vitellius: Dessau (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 453) suggests that there
may be a mistake in the praenomen (“Publius'' instead of "Aulus") as
his eldest son was called "Aulus" and only his third son "Publius."

domo Nuceria: abl. of origin, "whose home was Nuceria," Nuceria
being in app. with domo; cf. Aen. x 183, Qui Caerete (abl. of Caere) domo
sunt. A common phrase in asking a person's native place was "unde
domo?" lit. "whence from home?” “from what home?" e.g. Aen. viii
114, Qui genus? unde domo? (Conington, however, citing Plaut. Cist. iv 1, 6,
haec cistella numnam hinc ab nobis domo est?, says the abl. means “in
respect of domicile'"). For Nuceria see on c. 1, 3.

pudendis parentibus: cf. Hor. C. ii 4, 20, crede non illam potuisse
nasci Matre pudenda.

rerum Augusti procurator: Hirschfeld (Kais. Verwaltungsb., 3 sqq.)
shows that apparently under the early Empire the official expression for
the emperor's income was res Caesaris or res familiaris Caesaris; it is
from the time of Claudius that we find the term fiscus or fiscus Caesaris
definitely used in contrast to aerarium (see on Vesp. 16, 3); the imperial
revenues previously grouped as res or res familiaris (-es) of the emperor
were now divided into fiscus and patrimonium, the emperor's public and
private income, and a procurator patrimonii was appointed; under Septimius
Severus the patrimonium as crown property was divided from the patrimonium privatum (called res privata), the emperor's personal property,
and a procuratio rerum privatarum was established as distinct from the
procuratio patrimonii principis. See Mattingly, Imp. Civ. Serv. p. 14 sqq.

amplissimae dignitatis: though the father was only an eques, the sons
filled curule offices (which are called “amplissimi honores,” Iul. 72,
Ner. 3, 2, etc.) and so gained admission to the senate ("amplissimus ordo,”
Calig. 49, 1: Oth. 8, 1: Vesp. 2, 3).

cognomines: bearing the same nomen (gentilicium) of "Vitellius."
See on Oth. 1, 3. The cognomen is not found in the case of the Vitellii,
only the praenomen and nomen.

in consulatu obiit: in 32 A.D. he was consul suffectus from the Kalends
of July (C.I.L. i² p. 71, x 1233).

Domitio: i.e. Domitius Ahenobarbus (see on Oth. 2, 1).
..

quem inierat: strictly speaking, the expression ‘“consulatum cum
Domitio inierat could only be used of Camillus Scribonianus (Oth. 2, 1)
who was consul for the first half of the year 32 A.D. along with Domitius;
cf. Tac. A. vi 1, Cn. Domitius et Camillus Scribonianus consulatum inierant.
Suetonius (if not guilty of an inaccuracy) uses it loosely of A. Vitellius,
meaning that when he entered on office as consul suffectus his colleague
(the existing consul) was Domitius. Being related to the house of Caesar,
Domitius was allowed to hold the consulship for the whole year, and so
was an exception to Tiberius' practice of appointing as many successive
consuls as he pleased each year (Dio lviii 20).

praelautus: the MSS. have praelatus, but praelautus was correctly read
in the Basle ed. of 1533. Cf. Ner. 30, 1, sordidos ac deparcos esse putabat
quibus ratio impensarum constaret ("who could balance their accounts'');
praelautos, vereque magnificos, qui abuterentur ac perderent. This compound is not cited from any other author. For other adjs. strengthened
by prae- which are used by Suetonius see on Galb. 21.

alioqui: "in other respects” (τὰ μὲν ἄλλα); cf. Tib. 71, sermone Graeco
quamquam alioqui promptus et facilis, non tamen usque quaque usus est
abstinuitque maxime in senatu. It is a post-Aug. word and is used also
in the sense of "besides" (praeterea), and "otherwise" "in the opposite
case"; see Peterson, Introd. to Quintil. x, p. li. Cicero uses ceteroqui “in
other respects."

Quintus: see c. 1, 2, where he is described as “Divi Augusti quaestor.”
If Hirschfeld is right in his ingenious restoration of Q. Vitellii in Tac. A. i
10 († que tedii † et Vedii Pollionis luxus), Augustus was censured by some
for having such a luxurious spendthrift as a friend. He is mentioned
among the senators impoverished by extravagance, whom Tiberius in virtue
of his censorial powers expelled from the senate or allowed to resign; Tac.
A. ii 48, prodigos et ob flagitia egentes, Vibidium Varronem, Marium
Nepotem, Appium Appianum, Cornelium Sullam, Q. Vitellium movit senatu
aut sponte cedere passus est. Dio (li 22) refers to a certain Quintus
Vitellius who, though a senator, fought as a gladiator at games given by
Augustus in 29 B.c.; he was probably an uncle of the Q. Vitellius mentioned
here.

caruit ordine: this unusual phrase, instead of motus est ordine senatorio
or senatu, suggests that Q. Vitellius may have been one of those whom
Tiberius allowed “sponte cedere senatu.” The simple ordo is used in
the sense of ordo senatorius; cf. Tac. A. xiii 11, Lateranum ordine demotum
reddidit senatui.

auctore Tiberio: cf. Vesp. 11, auctor senatui fuit decernendi (where
see note): Oth. 8, 1, auctor senatui fuit mittendae legationis: Dom. 8, 2,
auctor tribunis plebis fuit aedilem .. accusandi.

§3. Publius: P. Vitellius served as legatus of Germanicus in Germany
and in 15 A.D. amid great difficulties succeeded in leading back in safety
the 2nd and 14th legions from the attack on the Chatti and other German
tribes (Tac. A. i 70). In the next year he was sent to take the census of
the Gauls (A. ii 6). He accompanied Germanicus to the East and was
proconsul of Bithynia in 18 A.D. On the death (attributed to poison) of
Germanicus in Syria in 19, Vitellius was one of those who aided in the
prosecution of Cn. Piso as the author of his death. Tacitus (A. iii 13)
says that Vitellius spoke "multa eloquentia.” Piso slew himself before
the investigation by the senate was finished; some maintained that he
was slain by an emissary of Tiberius, who feared the revelations which Piso
might make of the emperor's machinations against Germanicus. The
accusers of Piso, including Vitellius, were rewarded with a sacerdotium by
the senate on the proposal of Tiberius (A. iii 19).

Germanici: Germanicus was son of Nero Claudius Drusus and brother
of the emperor Claudius. He was adopted by his uncle Tiberius, who
afterwards became madly jealous of his popularity and military success.
Among his children were the emperor Gaius Caligula and Agrippina the
mother of the emperor Nero.

Cn. Pisonem: consul in 7 B.C., along with Tiberius the future emperor;
sent by Augustus as legatus to Hispania Tarraconensis, where he incurred
the hatred of the provincials; appointed by Tiberius as governor of Syria.
in 18 A.D. with secret instructions to thwart in every way the plans of
Germanicus who had been given the command of all the eastern provinces
(Tac. A. ii 43 sqq.).

inimicum: the bitter relations between Piso and Germanicus are
described by Tacitus. When Germanicus suspected that Piso was slowly
poisoning him, he sent him a letter in which he formally renounced his
friendship (amicitiam ei renuntiabat, Tac. ii 70).

interfectorem: it is doubtful whether Piso did poison Germanicus:
Tacitus (iii 14) admits that the evidence was in no way conclusive; but,
rightly or wrongly, the people were convinced of his guilt (cf. Suet. Tib. 52,.
Calig. 2 sq.; Dio lvii 18; Joseph. Ant. Iud. xviii 2, 5).
condemnavit: "secured the condemnation of." For condemnare used.
of a prosecutor cf. Tib. 8, Caepionem. reum maiestatis apud iudices fecit
et condemnavit: Plaut. Most. 1098, apud iudicem hunc argenti condemnabo:
Cic. Div. in Caec. 10, 30; id. Verr. ii 5, 69, 177, etc.

post praeturae honorem: Suetonius is inaccurate here in saying that
the arrest of P. Vitellius in 31 A.D. followed his praetorship, for he must
have been praetor before 14 A.D., as he is mentioned as proconsul of
Bithynia (18 A.D.) on a coin of Germanicus (Eckhel, ii p. 400). See Prosop.
Imp. Rom. iii 453.

inter Seiani conscios arreptus: in 31 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. v 8 where we
are told the precise charge that was made against him: Relatum inde de
P. Vitellio
illum indices ("informers'') arguebant claustra (“keys'")
aerarii (sc. militaris), cui praefectus erat, et militarem pecuniam rebus
novis obtulisse. The notorious Aelius Sejanus succeeded his father as
prefect of the praetorian guard in the reign of Tiberius with whom he
became all-powerful. Ambitious of empire, he contrived to remove the
members of the imperial house who stood in his path. At length Tiberius
became suspicious of his designs and sent a letter from Capreae (where
he was living in seclusion) to the senate denouncing Sejanus as a danger
to the State. The senate decreed his death, which was carried out at once,
his body being dragged through the streets and flung into the Tiber.
Juvenal (x 56 sqq.) cites Sejanus as an instance of the vanity of human
ambitions.

in custodiam fratri datus: as was done also in the case of Pomponius
Secundus who was accused along with P. Vitellius; Tac. (l.c.), neque aliud
periclitantibus auxilii quam in fratrum constantia fuit, qui vades exstitere
(i.e. gave surety and undertook their custody, till their appeal should be
heard by Caesar; see Furneaux ad loc.). The custodia mentioned by
Suetonius is that known as libera custodia by which accused persons instead of being kept in prison were held by the consuls or other magistrates
in their own houses, or consigned to relatives or others who became responsible as securities for their safe-keeping; cf. Sall. Cat. 47; Cic. Verr. v 29,
73; Liv. xxiv 45; Vell. Pat. i 11; Ulp. Dig. xlviii 3, 1; Dio lviii 3, 5.
The brother to whose safe-keeping Publius Vitellius was entrusted was
probably Aulus.

scalpro librario venas
incidit: cf. Tac. (l.c.): mox crebris prolationibus ("postponements") spem ac metum iuxta gravatus Vitellius
petito per speciem studiorum scalpro levem ictum venis intulit vitamque
aegritudine animi finivit (these words of Tac. seem naturally to imply
that the self-inflicted wound caused his death; if so, Tac. differs from
Suet.). The scalprum librarium was a pen-knife used by writers in cutting
and shaping the calamus. P. Vitellius edited his speech against Piso (cf.
Plin. N.H. xi 187; Teuffel-Schwabe, Röm. Lit. 276, 4).

§ 4. Lucius Syriae praepositus: Lucius Vitellius was consul in
34 A.D., and in the following year Tiberius appointed him proconsul of
Syria and gave to him the general control of the campaign against the
Parthians (Tac. A. vi 32, cunctis quae apud orientem parabantur L. Vitellium
praefecit). For such extraordinary commands (imperia) which raised the
holder over the governors of other provinces see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 853.
Tacitus (l.c.) praises L. Vitellius highly as a provincial governor:
regendis provinciis prisca virtute egit; cf. Dio lix 27, ὁ δ᾽ οὖν Οὐιτέλλιος
ὁ Λούκιος οὔτ᾽ ἀγεννὴς οὔτ᾽ ἄφρων ὤν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἐν τῇ Συρίᾳ ἀρχῆς ὀνομαστὸς
γενόμενος, τά τε γὰρ ἄλλα λαμπρῶς ἡγεμόνευσε, καὶ τὸν ᾿Αρτάβανον . . κατέπληξε
ἀπαντήσας αὐτῷ ἐξαπιναίως περὶ τὸν Εὐφράτην ἤδη ὄντι, κ.τ.λ.
in

Artabanum: Artabanus III was a descendant of the Arsacidae on his
mother's side, and in 16 A.D. he supplanted Vonones as king of Parthia.
In 35 A.D. Artabanus tried to make his son king of Armenia, and sent insulting letters to Tiberius at Rome. Tiberius thereupon appointed
Mithridates to be king of Armenia, and Tiridates to be king of Parthia.
To enforce these arrangements, Tiberius conferred on L. Vitellius, governor
of Syria, the same large powers in the East as he had previously conferred
on Germanicus. Vitellius established Tiridates, but in the following
year when Vitellius had withdrawn his forces, the Parthians recalled
Artabanus, and Tiridates had to flee into Syria. Vitellius again advanced
against Artabanus, but an agreement was entered into by which Artabanus
recognised Mithridates as king of Armenia, while the Romans discontinued
their support of Tiridates. Artabanus also paid homage as Suetonius
describes, and sent his son Darius as a hostage to Rome (Tac. A. vi 31-37,
41-44; Dio lviii 26; Joseph. Ant. Iud. xviii 4, 5).

conloquium: Dio (lix 27) and Suetonius (Calig. 14) say that this
conference took place in the reign of Caligula, but Josephus (l.c.) puts it
in the reign of Tiberius. Schiller (Gesch. röm. Kaiserz. i 278, n. 2)
proposes to reconcile these statements by assuming that negotiations began
in the last months of Tiberius (ob. 37 A.D.) and were concluded at the
beginning of the reign of his successor Caligula.

ad veneranda legionum signa: in the principia (see Oth. 1, 2, n.) of
a Roman camp there was a portable shrine in which were kept the standards
and the images of the emperors; medallion portraits of the emperors were
also affixed to the standards. For the sanctity of the standards cf. Tac.
A. i 39, illic signa et aquilam amplexus religione sese tutabatur: A. xv 16,
iure iurando Paeti cautum apud signa: Liv. xxvi 48, obstringere periurio
non se solum suumque caput, sed signa militaria et aquilas sacramentique
religionem. Dio (l.c.) says that Artabanus made offerings to the images
of Augustus and Caligula: ἔς τε λόγους (conloquium) αὐτὸν ὑπηγάγετο (pellexit)
καὶ θῦσαι ταῖς τοῦ Αὐγούστου τοῦ τε Γαΐου εἰκόσιν ἠνάγκασε, σπονδάς τε αὐτῷ πρὸς
τὸ τῶν Ῥωμαίων σύμφορον δοὺς καὶ προσέτι καὶ παῖδας αὐτοῦ ὁμήρους λαβών.
..

duos insuper consulatus: in 43 and 47 A.D.; he had been consul
earlier under Tiberius in 34. Eutropius (vii 18) says of the emperor
Vitellius: pater eius non admodum clare natus tres tamen ordinarios gesserat
consulatus. For “ordinarios” see on Dom. 2, 1.
censuram: L. Vitellius was censor along with the emperor Claudius
in 47-48 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. xii 4, Silanus repente per edictum Vitellii
ordine senatorio movetur: A. xi 13, Claudius munia censoria usurpans
theatralem populi lasciviam severis edictis increpuit: Suet. Claud. 16, 1,
gessit et censuram intermissam diu post Plancum Paulumque censores (in
22 B.C.). For the censorship under the Empire see Mommsen Staatsr. ii³
336 sqq. Vespasian and Titus held it in 73-74 (Tit. 6, 1), and Domitian
assumed it for life in 84 (Dom. 8, 3).

curam imperii sustinuit: cf. Plut. Galb. 22, where L. Vitellius is
described as τιμητής (censor) καὶ τρὶς ὕπατος (consul) γενόμενος καὶ Κλαυδίῳ
Καίσαρι τρόπον τινα συνάρξας (consors imperii). Mommsen (op. cit. ii³ 1114)
gives other examples of persons entrusted with the “cura imperii" during
the absence of the emperor from Rome, viz. Maecenas under Augustus,
Seneca under Nero, Mucianus under Vespasian. These all occupied a
position for which there is no official title and no formal recognition under
the constitution of the principate; it was a personal appointment of the
emperor. Mommsen also corrects the statement in Dio lx 21 (of the
events in 43 A.D.), ὁ Κλαύδιος τὰ μὲν οἴκοι τῷ Οὐιτελλίῳ τῷ συνάρχοντι (i.e. joint
consul) τά τε ἄλλα καὶ τοὺς στρατιώτας ἐνεχείρισε· καὶ γὰρ ἐξ ἴσου αὐτὸν ἑαυτῷ
ἑξάμηνον ὅλον ὑπατεῦσαι ἐποίησεν. Dio's attempt to connect the appointment
of Vitellius as deputy of Claudius with his position as consul breaks down
because both Claudius and Vitellius had laid down their consulships before
March 1, 43 A.D., and the emperor did not leave Rome for Britain till
the latter part of that year.

expeditione Britannica: for the expedition sent under A. Plautius to
Britain see notes on Vesp. 4, 1.

innocens: honest" "disinterested"; cf. Sall. Cat. 54, cum strenuo
virtute, cum modesto pudore, cum innocente abstinentia certabat: Cic.
..
Verr. i 4, 12, Sicilia, quam iste per triennium ita vastavit vexavit ac perdidit, ut vix per multos annos innocentesque praetores aliqua ex parte
recreari aliquando posse videatur: Plin. Pan. 28, 3, quodque (sc. congiarium)
antea principes, ad odium sui leniendum, tumentibus plebis animis obiectabant, id tu tam innocens populo dedisti, quam populus accepit. The subst.
innocentia is used in the same way for probity in money matters in c. 5
infr.; the “iustitia et aequitas et innocentia” of Aristides are mentioned
in Nep. Arist. 2.

amore
perinfamis: Tacitus (A. vi 32) refers to the unsavoury
reputation of L. Vitellius at Rome: eo de homine haud sum ignarus
sinistram in urbe famam, pleraque foeda memorari, ceterum <in > regendis
provinciis prisca virtute egit. The compound perinfamis occurs again in
Apul. Met. iii 16 where it takes the 'gen.: publicitus maleficae disciplinae
perinfames sumus. Other adjs. with intensive per- in Suet. are percivilis,
peridoneus, permodicus, perparvus, perpauci, persenex; also the advs.
perindigne, persaepe, persancte.

arterias: arteria meant the "windpipe," and as this divides at the
base into the two bronchial tubes, the pl. arteriae was also used (so in
Gr., ἀρτηρία and ἀρτηρίαι): cf. Ner. 25, 3, ut conservandae vocis gratia
neque milites umquam, nisi absens aut alio verba pronuntiante, appellaret
neque quicquam serio iocoque egerit, nisi astante phonasco (“a voicetrainer'') qui moneret parceret arteriis ac sudarium ("handkerchief'') ad
os applicaret.

fauces: 'throat"; often joined with arteria (-ae), e.g. Pallad. ii 15,
19, ut ex eo (melle) facta potio arterias curet et fauces.

pro remedio: cf. Ner. 35, 5, Burro praefecto remedium ad fauces
pollicitus toxicum misit.

fovebat: fovere, which is used very freely of medical applications,
here means to gargle or to soothe an irritated throat; cf. Novius, Atell.
109, fauces fovi (= gargarissavi): Fronto, p. 69, 14 N., aqua mulsa sorbenda
usque ad gulam et reiectanda fauces fovi potius quam dicerem gargarissavi: Verg. G. ii 135, animas (“breath'") et olentia Medi | ora fovent illo
(flore) et senibus medicantur anhelis. The disgusting practice of Vitellius,
which Suetonius describes here, may be referred to in Tac. A. xi 3 where
Asiaticus, accused by Vitellius, speaks of the "os impudicum” of his
accuser.

§5. miri in adulando ingenii: cf. Tac. A. vi 32, unde (i.e. from Syria)
regressus et formidine Gai Caesaris (i.e. Caligula), familiaritate Claudii
turpe in servitium mutatus exemplar apud posteros adulatorii dedecoris
habetur, cesseruntque prima postremis et bona iuventae senectus flagitiosa
oblitteravit: Dio lix 27, Οὐιτέλλιος .. πάντας . . τοὺς ἄλλους κολακείᾳ ὑπερεβάλετο. Dio tells how on one occasion Caligula claimed to be enjoying
converse with the Moon, and asked Vitellius if he could see the goddess
with him; Vitellius with downcast eyes replied in awe-struck accents:
"Only you gods, master, may behold one another."

reversus ex Syria: Caligula, jealous of the success of L. Vitellius
against Artabanus, and fearing that he might aspire to empire, recalled
him in 40 A.D. to put him to death. Vitellius managed to save his life by
throwing himself at the emperor's feet with tears and lamentations, calling
him by many divine titles and paying him worship, and by promising that
if he were spared he would offer sacrifice to him. Caligula not merely
granted him his life, but admitted him among his most intimate friends
(Dio l.c.).

capite velato: the Greeks worshipped "capite aperto," but the Romans
(except at the rites of Saturn) "capite velato (operto)," a custom said
to be derived from Aeneas; cf. Aen. iii 405, purpureo velare (imper.) comas
adopertus amictu, | ne qua inter sanctos ignes in honore deorum | hostilis
facies occurrat et omina turbet. Plutarch (Quaest. Rom. x sq.) suggests
various explanations: (1) it is a sign of humility, (2) it prevents the
hearing of ill-omened words, (3) it signifies that the soul which worships
is covered and concealed in the body. See the discussion in Daremberg-Saglio, iv 977; Rose on Plut. l.c.
circumvertens se, deinde procumbens: the Roman worshipper did not
approach the image of the god directly, but advanced to the left of it and
after prayer turned to the right and fell down before it in adoration; see
Munro on Lucr. v 1198, nec pietas ullast velatum saepe videri | vertier ad
lapidem atque omnes accedere ad aras, | nec procumbere humi prostratum,
etc. The custom is often referred to; e.g. Plaut. Curc. 69, quo me vortam
nescio. Si deos salutas, dextrovorsum censeo: Liv. v 21, convertentem
se inter hanc venerationem traditur memoriae prolapsum cecidisse,
idque ómen pertinuisse postea eventu rem coniectantibus visum ad
damnationem ipsius Camilli: Plin. N.H. xxviii 25, in adorando totum
corpus circumagimus, quod in laevum fecisse Galliae religiosius credunt (in
the temple of Aesculapius at Rome they also turned to the left, C. I. G.
5980); Val. Fl. Arg. viii 246, precari Incipiunt . . dextrum pariter vertuntur
in orbem. Plutarch (Num. 14) attempts several explanations of Numa's
religious ordinance “ τὸ προσκυνεῖν περιστρεφομένους.”

Claudium uxoribus libertisque addictum: cf. Claud. 29, His (libertis)
uxoribusque addictus non principem sed ministrum egit, compendio
("according to the interest of'") cuiusque horum vel etiam studio aut
libidine honores exercitus impunitates supplicia largitus est, et quidem
insciens plerumque et ignarus: ib. 25, Sed et haec et cetera totumque adeo
ex parte magna principatum non tam suo quam uxorum libertorumque
arbitrio administravit, talis ubique plerumque qualem esse eum aut expediret
illis aut liberet. Claudius, who had previously divorced two wives (Plautia
Urgulanilla and Aelia Paetina), was at the time of his accession (41 A.D.)
married to the infamous Valeria Messalina. She was put to death in 48
for publicly marrying a handsome Roman youth C. Silius while Claudius
was away at Ostia (Tac. A. xi 26-38). After her downfall he married
his niece Agrippina (see on Galb. 5, 1), who poisoned him in 54. For the
influence of Messalina cf. [Sen.] Octavia 950, rexit principis aulam cara
marito partuque (her son Britannicus) potens. Tacitus (A. xii 7) describes
the domination of Agrippina: Versa ex eo civitas, et cuncta feminae
oboediebant, non per lasciviam, ut Messalina, rebus Romanis illudenti;
adductum (‘stringent") et quasi virile servitium: palam severitas ac
saepius superbia; nihil domi inpudicum, nisi dominationi expediret.
Suetonius (Claud. 28) enumerates the freedmen who controlled the emperor:
the eunuch Posides, Felix, Harpocras, Polybius his literary adviser (a
studiis), and especially Narcissus his secretary (ab epistulis) and Pallas
his treasurer (a rationibus).
For ‘addictus" "a slave to" (properly of a bondsman debtor) cf.
Prop. iii 11, 1, Quid mirare, meam si versat femina vitam | Et trahit
addictum sub sua iura virum?: Amm. Marc. xxi 16, 16, addictus uxoribus
et palatinis: Suet. Calig. 55, 2, prasinae factioni ita addictus et deditus:
Tib. 69, addictus mathematicae ("astrology'').
ne qua non arte demereretur: cf. Vesp. 2, 3, Gaium ne quo non genere

demereretur: Oth. 4, 2, alium alia via militem demerebatur: Claud. 40, 3,
nihil habere se, quare eos demereatur. Suetonius also uses the form
"demereo," Aug. 8, 1, avunculum magno opere demeruit. In this sense
(= aliquem sibi obligare, devincire) the verb is not found earlier than
Ovid and Livy.

pro maximo munere: "as a supreme favour." Ihm adopts the reading
proximo munere (MGLP), but this yields no satisfactory sense ("at the
next gladiatorial spectacle''?). Iac. Gronovius proposed pro suтто.

a Messalina petit: the intimacy of Messalina and Vitellius is seen in
Tac. A. xi 2 sq., where she uses her influence with him to secure the condemnation of Asiaticus in 47 A.D., when Vitellius (who was consul and
censor with Claudius in that year) was sitting as assessor with the emperor
at that trial. For petit = petiit cf. Oth. 7, 1.

excalciandos: see on Vesp. 8, 3. Ovid (A.A. ii 211) describes the lover,
like a slave, removing or putting on the shoes of his mistress: Nec dubita
tereti scamnum producere lecto, | et tenero soleam deme, vel adde, pedi.

socculum: a shoe or slipper worn by women, which fitted the heel
but left the instep open; it was often adorned with gold and pearls
(Sen. Ben. ii 12, Plin. N.H. ix 114). The soccus muliebris affected by
Caligula (Calig. 52) was a socculus of this kind. See Daremberg-Saglio iv
1366 for probable illustrations of socculi.
tunicas: two tunicae were regularly worn, the inner shirt being called
tunica interior or subucula; cf. Varr. ap. Non. 542, 24, Posteaquam binas
tunicas habere coeperunt, instituerunt vocare subuculam et indusium.
Augustus in winter wore four tunicae besides a subucula and a thorax
laneus or “chest protector” (Aug. 82). See Marquardt, Privatl.2 552.

gestavit assidue: this expression shows the way in which so-called
"frequentative" verbs like gestare had lost their special meaning. See
App. I. § 7. b.

osculabundus: a verbal adj. found first here and later in Apul. Met. xi
6, Apol. 94, where it takes the acc. (cf. Suet. Tib. 65, 2, speculabundus
signa; Draeger, Hist. Synt. i² 357). Similar adjs. used by Suetonius are
errabundus (Iul. 31, 2), gratulabundus (Galb. 19, 2), indignabundus (Aug.
40, 5, Calig. 35, 3), ludibundus (Ner. 26, 1), venerabundus (Calig. 15, 1).

Narcissi: for this freedman and secretary of Claudius see on Vesp. 4, 1,
Tit. 2.

Pallantis: another freedman, who was treasurer of Claudius and
exercised an immense influence during his reign, especially when Agrippina,
aided by his support, became the wife of the emperor in 50 A.D. He was
deposed from office by Nero in 55 and died in 62, having been poisoned
by order of Nero who was covetous of his enormous wealth. His intolerable arrogance is described in Tac. A. xii 53; Plin. Εp. vii 29.
inter Lares coluit: see on Dom. 17, 2.

Saepe facias!: the same expression occurs in a birthday wish in
Censorin. De die natali c. 2, Nunc quoniam liber de die natali inscribitur,
a votis auspicia sumantur. Itaque “hunc diem,” quod ait Persius,
“numera meliore lapillo,” idque quam saepissime facias exopto.

saeculares ludos: celebrated by Claudius in 47 A.D. An interval of 100
or 110 years was supposed to elapse between successive celebrations. See
on Dom. 4, 3.
؟

paralysi: cf. Celsus iii 27, Resolutio (= παράλυσις) nervorum frequens
ubique morbus est. Sed interdum tota corpora, interdum partes infestat.
Veteres auctores illud ἀποπληξίαν, hoc παράλυσιν nominaverunt.
utrumque παράλυσιν appellari video.
Nunc

altero die quam: for the omission of post before quam cf. Liv. xxxi 14,
altero die quam a Brundusio soluit in Macedoniam traiecit: Suet. Claud.
17, 2, sexto quam profectus erat mense: Iul. 35, 2, intra quintum quam
affuerat diem: Tib. 60, in paucis diebus quam Capreas attigit. See KühnerStegmann, i 405.
..
duobus filiis: Aulus (the emperor) and Lucius (see on c. 15, 2).

Sextilia probatissima femina: praised by Tacitus also, H. ii 64,
Galéria imperatoris (i.e. Vitellius) uxor.. et pari probitate mater Vitelliorum
Sextilia, antiqui moris. She was spared and cared for by Otho at Rome,
even after her son had revolted against him (Plut. Oth. 5, 16). When he
entered Rome in triumph, Vitellius honoured her with the title of Augusta
(Тас. Н. ii 89). She died, old and feeble, a few days before the overthrow
of Vitellius, having gained nothing from his imperial dignity but sorrow
and a good repute (H. iii 67). For the rumour that she was poisoned by
the emperor see c. 14, 5. Ihm retains the form Sestilia, which is given
by M.
..

consules
eodem anno: in 48 A.D., a year in which the emperor
Claudius and their father L. Vitellius were censors (see c. 2, 4). Aulus
Vitellius, the subsequent emperor, was consul ordinarius at the beginning
of the year along with L. Vipstanus Poplicola, their names being used to
mark the year (Tac. A. xi 23, A. Vitellio L. Vipstano consulibus). The
younger brother Lucius was consul suffectus in the latter part of the year.
For the tenure of the consulship under the empire see on Dom. 2, 1. Lucius
also succeeded his brother Aulus as proconsul of Africa (c. 5 infr.).

senatus publico funere honoravit: a funus publicum or funeral at the
expense of the State was first given to Sulla, and always had to be
authorised by a decree of the senate; cf. Tac. A. vi 11, Piso
publico
funere ex decreto senatus celebratus est: A. iii 48, ut mors Sulpicii Quirini
publicis exsequiis frequentaretur, petivit a senatu. The senate might also
instruct a particular magistrate to deliver the panegyric on the dead
(laudatio funebris), e.g. Tacitus as consul was directed to pronounce the
panegyric on Verginius Rufus; cf. Quintil. iii 7, 2, funebres laudationes
pendent frequenter ex aliquo publico officio atque ex senatus consulto magistratibus saepe mandantur. See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 1187.

statua: the erection of a statue at Rome required the authorisation
of the senate: see on Galb. 23.

pro rostris: "on the front of the Rostra"; see on Vesp. 7, 2, pro
tribunali. For statues on the Rostra cf. Cic. Phil. ix 2; Vell. ii 61; Plin.
N.H. xxxiv 6; Dio xlii 18, xliii 49.

pietatis: allegiance, devotion to the emperor as a divine being and
father of his country (pater patriae); cf. Dom. 11, 3; Aug. 66, 2, laudavit
pietatem tanto opere pro se indignantium. In this sense pietas is frequent
in Tacitus; e.g. A. iii 51, Tiberius cum extolleret pietatem quamvis
modicas principis iniurias acriter ulciscentium. So impietas = maiestas
"treason," see on Dom. 10, 1.
•

§ 2. A. Vitellius natus est: for the difficulty in reconciling the
date given here for the birth of Vitellius with his age at death as
given in c. 18 see note there.
viii Kal. Oct.: Sept. 24.
vii Id. Sept.: Sept. 7.

Druso Caesare: son of the emperor Tiberius; consul with Norbanus
Flaccus in 15 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. i 55, Druso Caesare C. Norbano consulibus
decernitur Germanico triumphus. He was poisoned by Sejanus in 23 A.D.

Norbano Flacco: Gaius Norbanus Flaccus was praetor (urbanus) in
11 A.D. and consul (ordinarius) in 15 A.D. Either he or his brother Lucius
(cons. 19 A.D.) was slain by the German body-guard of Caligula when that
emperor was murdered in 41 A.D. See Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 416.
genituram.. mathematicis: see on c. 14, 4; Tit. 9, 2; Dom. 14, 1.

missum ad legiones: the legions in Lower Germany; see c. 7 infr. and
Oth. 8, 1.

pro afflicto lamentata sit: “mourned him as stricken"; cf. Dom. 2, 3,
pro mortuo deseri iussit: Claud. 37, 1, pro deprenso ("as if caught in the
act'") ad poenas raptus est: Tib. 52, 2, ut et praeclara facta eius pro
supervacuis elevarit: ib. 73, 1, pro contempto se habitum. Tacitus (H. ii 64)
mentions the reply that his mother Sextilia sent to the first letter of Vitellius
from Germany, in the superscription of which he had apparently described
himself as “Germanicus”: Dixisse quin etiam ad primas filii sui epistulas
ferebatur non Germanicum a se, sed Vitellium genitum. Nec ullis postea
fortunae inlecebris aut ambitu (‘‘interested homage") civitatis in gaudium
evicta ("won over to joy'") domus suae tantum adversa sensit.

Capreis: Capreae, mod. Capri, an island off Campania, was a favourite
haunt of Augustus, who acquired it from the people of Naples in exchange
for Aenaria (Aug. 92). In 27 A.D. the emperor Tiberius withdrew there
permanently and spent the last ten years of his life on the island, being
attracted by its solitude and inaccessibility (Tac. A. iv 67). He built
twelve villas, and is said to have given himself over to the most bestial
debauchery which is described in Suet. Tib. 40-43.

inter Tiberiana scorta: cf. Dio lxiv 4, ὅτι γε παιδικὰ τοῦ Τιβερίου ἐγεγόνει
(Οὐιτέλλιος) καὶ ὅτι ἀκολούθως τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ ταύτῃ ἔζη οὐκ ἐνενόησαν (οἱ στρατιῶται).
For scortum used "de viro" cf. Cic. Phil. ii 18 where Antonius is called
“vulgare scortum"; id. Sest. 17; Plaut. Curc. 472.
=

Spintriae:
qui muliebria patitur; cf. Tib. 43, 1: Calig. 16, 1.
Tacitus (A. vi 1) mentions spintria among the new terms of sensuality
introduced by Tiberius at Capreae: tunc primum ignota antea vocabula
reperta sunt sellariorum et spintriarum ex foeditate loci ac multiplici
patientia. Cratinus (ap. Hesych.) has σφίγκτης = κίναιδος. See L. and S.
Gr. Lex. s.v. σφιγκτήρ.

Gaio per aurigandi studium familiaris: cf. c. 17, 2, cum auriganti
Gaio ministratorem (se) exhiberet. Caligula gave many exhibitions of his
skill as a charioteer: Calig. 54, 1, aurigabat exstructo plurifariam circo.
He was so passionately devoted to the "Greens'' (prasina factio, c. 7, 1, n.)
in the Circus that he constantly supped and lodged in the stable where
their horses were kept. He made presents worth two million sesterces to
their charioteer Eutychus. On the day before the Circensian games he
used to send soldiers to enjoin silence in the neighbourhood, that the horse
Incitatus ("Speedy'") might not be disturbed. Not merely did he give this
horse a stall of marble, purple blankets, and a jewelled frontlet, but he also
provided him with a furnished house and a retinue of slaves for the
reception of those invited in the horse's name; it was said that he even
intended to make him consul (Calig. 55).

Claudio per aleae studium: Claudius was a confirmed gambler, playing
even while taking carriage-exercise; cf. Claud. 33, 2, aleam studiosissime
lusit, de cuius arte librum quoque emisit, solitus etiam in gestatione ludere,
ita essedo (“carriage") alveoque (“dice-board'') adaptatis ne lusus confunderetur. Seneca (Apoc. 14) describes Claudius being sentenced by
Aeacus in the underworld to gamble with a bottomless dice-box: Aeacus
iubet illum alea ludere pertuso fritillo. For the gaming propensities of
other emperors see on Dom. 21.

Neroni acceptior: Tacitus (H. ii 71) is very severe on the admiration
and imitation of the debauchee Nero by the debauchee Vitellius: Quantoque
magis propinquabat (Romam Vitellius), tanto corruptius iter inmixtis
histrionibus et spadonum gregibus et cetero Neronianae aulae ingenio
("characteristics'"); namque et Neronem ipsum Vitellius admiratione
celebrabat, sectari cantantem solitus non necessitate, qua honestissimus
quisque, sed luxu et saginae mancipatus emptusque.

propter eadem haec: Nero was an enthusiastic devotee of the Circus
and also drove a team himself; cf. Ner. 22, 1, equorum studio vel praecipue
ab ineunte aetate flagravit: ib. 24, 2, aurigavit quoque plurifariam,
Olympiis vero etiam decemiugem: ib. 53, quia Apollinem cantu, Solem
aurigando aequiperare existimaretur. He played at dice for 400,000
sesterces a point, i.e. for each pip of the winning throw (ib. 30, 3, quadringenis in punctum sestertiis aleam lusit). Dio (lxv 2) describes Vitellius
as a frequenter of pothouses and gaming dens and an associate of dancers
and charioteers.

peculiari merito: the only other example cited of peculiaris in the
sense of "praecipuus, insignis, singularis" is Just. xxxvi 4, 3, Omissa
deinde regni administratione, hortos fodiebat, gramina seminabat, et noxia
innoxiis permiscebat, eaque omnia veneni succo infecta, velut peculiare
munus, amicis mittebat. For another meaning of peculiaris see Galb. 12, 3.

praesidens certamini Neroneo: Vitellius was one of the ex-consuls
(consulares) whom Nero chose by lot to preside over the new quinquennial
contest called Neronia or Neroneus agon (Ner. 21, 1) which he established
in 60 A.D.; cf. Ner. 12, 3, Instituit et quinquennale certamen primus
omnium Romae more Graeco triplex, musicum gymnicum equestre, quod
appellavit Neronia .. Magistros toto certamini praeposuit consulares sorte,
sede praetorum: Tac. A. xiv 20, quinquennale ludicrum Romae institutum
est ad morem Graeci certaminis, varia fama, ut cuncta ferme nova. The
second lustrale certamen in 65 A.D. is mentioned in Tac. A. xvi 4. The
contest was discontinued after Nero's death (68 A.D.), but Domitian's agon
Capitolinus (see Dom. 4, 4) was a revival of it in another form. We find
mention of a celebration of Nero's lustrale certamen under Gordianus
Nepos; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 27, Eoque anno (242 A.D.) lustri certamine,
quod Nero Romam invexerat, aucto firmatoque, in Persas profectus est.
See Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 149 sqq.

citharoedos: see on Dom. 4, 4. Nero, who had previously performed
in the theatre at Neapolis (Naples), gave his first performance at Rome in
65 A.D. in the great theatre of Pompeius. The demand of the people to
hear his 'divine voice," a demand to which he gladly yielded, is described
in Ner. 21, 1: Cum magni aestimaret cantare etiam Romae, Neroneum
agona ante praestitutum diem revocavit flagitantibusque cunctis caelestem
vocem respondit quidem in hortis se copiam volentibus facturum, sed
adiuvante vulgi preces etiam statione militum, quae tunc excubabat, repraesentaturum ("would perform forthwith") se pollicitus est libens; ac sine
mora nomen suum in albo profitentium citharoedorum ("the list of competing lyre-players") iussit ascribi sorticulaque in urnam cum ceteris
demissa intravit ordine suo, simul praefecti praetorii citharam sustinentes,
post tribuni militum iuxtaque amicorum intimi. He then sang the part
of Niobe, and postponed the award of the prize and the rest of the contest
to the following year, that he might appear again. He made his professional tour of all the competitions in Greece in 66-67 (see Vesp. 4, 4). At
the outbreak of the revolt in Gaul against him nothing irritated him so
much as a proclamation of Vindex in which he was called a bad citharoedus.
Among his last utterances was the famous “Qualis artifex pereo!”
"What an artist I am to perish!"

quamvis flagitantibus cunctis: quamvis c. ptc. is not class. but is
frequent in post-Aug. writers; e.g. Tac. A. xv 38, quamvis patente effugio:
xv 71 quamvis absolutus. Suetonius has it in Iul. 26, 2; 48 (abl. abs.); 70:
Calig. 13; Claud. 20, 2 (abl. abs.); 27, 1: Vesp. 15. See KühnerStegmann, ii 445.
promittere: Becher would read prodire.

egressum theatro: Tacitus, in the account which he gives in A. xvi 4,
does not mention that Nero left the theatre and did not return till
Vitellius had prevailed upon him to appear. According to Tac. Nero
appeared first as a poet and then as a musician, his second performance
being given in response to the insistent demand of the people that he
would make public property of all his accomplishments: primo carmen
in scaena recitat; mox flagitante vulgo ut omnia studia publicaret
(haec enim verba dixere) ingreditur theatrum, cunctis citharae legibus
obtemperans, ne fessus resideret, ne sudorem nisi ea quam indutui gerebat
veste detergeret, ut nulla oris aut narium excrementa viserentur. Postremo
flexus genu et coetum illum manu veneratus sententias iudicum opperiebatur
ficto pavore.

quasi legatione suscepta: for quasi c. abl. abs. cf. Aug. 16, quasi
occasione ultionis oblata: ib. 19, quasi debita sibi fato dominatione: Cic.
Sen. 83, nec vero velim quasi decurso spatio ad carceres a calce revocari.
See Kühner-Stegmann, i 790 sq.

exorandumque praebuerat: = praestiterat ut exoraretur. Corrections
have been proposed (e.g. exoratumque Ernesti, exorabilemque Bentley),
but no change seems necessary.
trium principum: Caligula, Claudius, and Nero.

honoribus: including the consulship in 48 A.D., see c. 3, 1. Tacitus
(H. iii 86) says that Vitellius owed all his distinctions, including his
consulship and his priesthoods, to the renown of his father: consulatum,
sacerdotia, nomen locumque inter primores nulla sua industria, sed cuncta
patris claritudine adeptus.

sacerdotiis: Vitellius is mentioned as one of the Fratres Arvales
during Nero's reign in 57–60, 62 (?), 63, 66 (?) A.D. (C.I.L. vi 2039-2044,
2046: Henzen Acta Fr. Arv. p. lxiv sqq.). He appears on coins as quindecimvir sacris faciundis (Eckhel, vi p. 316: Cohen, i² p. 365), but it is
not certain that this was before he became emperor; see Prosop. Imp.
Rom. iii 449. Other examples of priesthoods conferred as honours were
those given to Galba (Galb. 8, 1) and Vespasian (Vesp. 4, 2).

proconsulatum Africae: Vitellius held this in 60 or 61 A.D. Cf. Tac.
H. i 70, pro consule Vitellium Siliani in Africa habuerant (‘Siliani" were
a famous cavalry corps called after C. Silius, legatus of Tiberius in Upper
Germany; this "ala Siliana" had served in Africa when Vitellius was
proconsul, and supported him afterwards against Otho). The proconsulship of Africa was also held by Galba (Galb. 7, 1), by Otho's father
(Oth. 1, 2), and by Vespasian (Vesp. 4, 3).
curam operum publicorum: this was one of the new offices established
at Rome by Augustus; cf. Aug. 37, Quo plures partem administrandae rei
publicae caperent, nova officia excogitavit: curam operum publicorum,
viarum, aquarum, alvei Tiberis, frumenti populo dividundi, praefecturam
urbis, etc. The first four of these departments had previously been under
the control of the censors. The curatores operum publicorum were two in
number. Their full official title seems to have been "curatores aedium
sacrarum, locorum et operum publicorum,” which in inscriptions is
abbreviated in various ways. The occupant of the position must be of
senatorial rank and have held the office of praetor; nearly all those who
are mentioned were ex-consuls. See Daremberg-Saglio, i 1022 sq.
Mommsen, Staatstr. ii³ 450, 1147 sqq.

innocentiam: see on 'innocens” c. 2, 4. Cf. Cic. Manil. 13, where
“innocentia imperatorum” is contrasted with "avaritia imperatorum.”
Tacitus (H. ii 97) records the integrity of Vitellius' administration of
Africa and contrasts it with that of Vespasian: Quippe integrum illic (i.e.
in Africa) ac favorabilem ("popular'") proconsulatum Vitellius, famosum
invisumque Vespasianus egerat: proinde socii de imperio utriusque
coniectabant, sed experimentum contra fuit. Suetonius gives quite a
different account of Vespasian's administration of Africa; see Vesp. 4, 3.
biennio continuato: abl. of duration of time; see on Galb. 6, 1.

succedenti fratri: his brother Lucius succeeded him as proconsul in
Africa; he had previously succeeded him as consul in the latter part of
48 A.D. (see с. 3, 1).

legatus: under the Empire, as under the Republic, a certain number
of legati were attached to the governors of provinces, to whom the governors
could delegate certain of their functions. Three were assigned to the
consular proconsuls in Asia and Africa and one to the praetorian proconsuls
in the inferior provinces like Sicily and Baetica. Nominally they were
chosen by the proconsul, but his choice had to be approved by the emperor.
They must be senators of a rank equal or inferior to the governor but not
superior (cf. Dio liii 14, where they are called πάρεδροι "assessors"). As
a rule the legati were of a lower rank. Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 248) says
that consular legati of a consular proconsul are exceptional and perhaps
only found in the case of relatives. Besides this example of the two
Vitellii in Africa, Mommsen cites C.I.L. viii 7059; Lucian, Demonax 30;
vit. Gordiani 7, 18. See also Greenidge, Rom. Public Life, p. 433.

substitisset: = remansisset in provincia (Baumg.-Cr., who points out
that fratri depends on legatus). The variant substitutus esset (X) yields
no satisfactory sense though read by some of the older editors, e.g.
Burman, who says: "Posset tamen ‘fratri substitutus esset' ita explicari
ut frater non venerit in provinciam sibi datam, sed absentis eius vices noster
Vitellius, ut legatus, gessisset." Graevius, reading substitutus esset, would
alter succedenti to decedenti (Heinsius secedenti).

in urbano officio: i.e. his position as curator aedium sacrarum, locorum
et operum publicorum.
surripuisse: used of sacrilegious pilfering also in Plaut. Men. 922, At
ego te sacram coronam surrupuisse Iovi scio: id. Trin. 83: Cic. Div. i 54,
cum ex aede Herculis patera aurea subrepta esset.

stagnum: cf. Plin. N.H. xxxiv 159, Plumbi nigri origo duplex est; aut
enim sua provenit vena nec quidquam aliud ex sese parit, aut cum argento
nascitur mixtisque venis conflatur. Huius qui primus fluit in fornacibus
liquor stannum appellatur; qui secundus, argentum. The forms in the
Romance languages, Ital. stagno, Fr. étain, Span. estaño, support stagnum
(so Ihm with the better MSS.) against stannum, which is the spelling
generally adopted. Walde (op. cit.) suggests a connexion with σταφύλη
"the plummet of a level," but prefers to regard stagnum as a word which
came from the Celtic, since Pliny mentions "tinning" as a Gallic discovery.

aurichalcum: this form of the word is due to a false assimilation to
(and derivation from) aurum, the more correct form being orichalcum from
ὀρείχαλκος, “mountain (ὄρος) copper” or “brass." Plato (Crit. 114 E)
describes ὀρείχαλκος, as a precious metal no longer existent; cf. Plin. N.H.
xxxiv 2, aurichalco, quod praecipuam bonitatem admirationemque diu
obtinuit, nec reperitur longo iam tempore effeta tellure. In Plautus it is
a precious metal and aurichalcum and aurum are used in similar phrases;
e.g. Epid. 407, non carust auro contra (‘he is worth his weight in gold''):
Pseud. 692, aurichalco contra non carum fuit. Cicero (Off. iii 23,92)
speaks of it as an existing metal of little worth: Si quis aurum vendens
orichalcum ("brass'") se putet vendere, indicetne ei vir bonus aurum illud
esse an emat denario, quod sit mille denarium? See Conington on Aen. xii
87, auro squalentem alboque orichalco | circumdat toricam umeris; Wilkins
on Hor. A.P. 202, tibia non ut nunc orichalco vincta tubaeque | aemula.

supposuisse: a similar fraud is alleged of Julius Caesar in Iul. 54:
in primo consulatu tria milia pondo auri furatus e Capitolio, tantumdem
inaurati aeris reposuit.

Petroniam: daughter of P. Petronius who was consul suffectus in 19 A.D.,
proconsul of Asia for six years (prob. 29-35), and legatus pro praetore of
Syria in 39-42; he is mentioned as an intimate of the emperor Claudius
in Sen. Apoc. 14, P. Petronius, vetus convictor Claudii, homo Claudiana
lingua disertus; he himself had married into the house of the Vitellii,
his mother-in-law's name being Vitellia (Tac. A. iii 49). Petronia was
divorced by Vitellius and she then married Cn. Cornelius Dolabella (see
Galb. 12, 2), a marriage which roused the animosity and suspicion of
Vitellius who ordered the death of Dolabella. This murder at the beginning
of his reign greatly damaged the reputation of Vitellius; cf. Tac. H. ii 64,
magna cum invidia novi principatus, cuius hoc primum specimen noscebatur.

captum altero oculo:
luscum “blind of one eye." The abl. of
respect or limitation was used with captus in the sense of "seized" by a
malady (Lucr. v 929, genus humanum multo fuit durius
nec facile
ex aestu nec frigore quod caperetur); cf. Liv. xxii '2, Hannibal altero
oculo capitur; id. xliii 7, princeps pedibus captus: Cic. Div. ii 3, 9, si
captus oculis sit, ut Tiresias fuit: Verg. G. i 183, oculis capti talpae
("moles"). See Kühner-Stegmann, i 392.
=

sub condicione,
si: cf. Iul. 68, 1, concessam sibi sub condicione
vitam si: Claud. 24, 1: Plin. Ep. viii 18, 4; so sub condicione, ut (or ne),
Suet. Tib. 13, 2:42, 2: Plin. Ep. iv 13, 10: Phaedr. iv 5, 8, matrem fecit
heredem senex Sub condicione, ut. Suetonius uses indifferently sub condicione (not in Cic.) and ea condicione (with ut in Galb. 15, 1: Vitell. 15, 1:
Dom. 9,2; with ne in Tib. 26, 1).
..

hunc manu emisit: two similar instances of children being emancipated from the patria potestas, in order that they might take inheritances,
are mentioned in Pliny's Letters: iv 2, filium Regulus emancipavit, ut
heres matris exsisteret (where see Merrill's note): viii 18, Curtilius Mancia,
perosus generum suum
sub ea condicione filiam eius, neptem suam,
instituerat heredem, si esset manu patris emissa. The right of a Roman
father to sell his children came to be used as a means whereby children
could be made independent of the patria potestas and so become capable
of inheriting property in their own right. The law of the Twelve Tables
laid down "Si pater filium ter venumduit ('sells'), liber esto.” The
father sold the son to a fictitious purchaser who at once manumitted him
(as he might manumit a slave he had purchased) and then the son reverted
into his father's power; this process was repeated a second time, but by
a third sale the son ceased to be in the power of the father, and was in
the “mancipium” of the fictitious purchaser, who could either manumit
him himself (thus acquiring the right of a patronus over a freedman to
succeed to half his estate at death), or, as was more usual, remancipated
or resold him to the father who himself manumitted him and became his
patronus. One sale was sufficient in the case of a daughter. Justinian
substituted for this cumbrous process a simple declaration before a magistrate (Inst. i 12, 6). See Roby, Rom. Private Law i 74, and Poste on
Gaius i 132 sqq.

insimulatum: insimulare is used here, as generally, of a false accusation
(Festus defines it as "crimen in aliquem confingere"); but the verb was
also used in the wider sense of accusare, whether the charge was false or
true. It does not occur elsewhere in Suet.

parricidii: "(attempted) parricide"; cf. Calig. 12, 3, etsi non de perfecto, at certe de cogitato quondam parricidio professus. Suetonius uses
parricidium for the murder (1) of a father: (2) of a mother, Ner. 34, 5:
(3) of other relatives, Tib. 66; Ner. 33, 1: (4) of one who was "pater
patriae,” Claud. 12, 3; so the Ides of March when Caesar was murdered
were called “Parricidium” (Iul. 88, 1): (5) of any freeman, Iul. 42, 3.
The wide sense in which parricidium was used from a very early period is
seen from Fest. p. 221 Müll: parricidii quaestores appellabantur, qui
solebant creari causa rerum capitalium quaerendarum. Nam parricida non
utique is, qui parentem cecidisset, dicebatur, sed qualemcumque hominem
indemnatum. Ita fuisse indicat lex Numae Pompilii regis, his composita
verbis: “Si qui hominem liberum dolo sciens morti duit, paricidas esto.”
Philologists usually reject the derivation from pater and caedo which is
accepted by Quintilian (viii 6, 34), who cites as an example of κατάχρησις
or abusio the extended use of parricida for matris aut fratris interfector.
See Walde, op. cit.

Galeriam Fundanam: highly praised by Tacitus (H. ii 64) for her
exemplary modesty and for keeping aloof from the horrors (tristia) with
which her husband was associated: Et Triariae (wife of Lucius Vitellius,
brother of the emperor) licentiam modestum e proximo exemplum onerabat
("made more invidious"), Galeria imperatoris uxor, non inmixta tristibus.
She is also mentioned (ib. 60) as protecting Galerius Trachalus, a relative
of her own and a leading Othonian, on the accession of her husband to the
throne. On the other hand, Dio (lxv 4) speaks of her extravagant requirements and says that she derided even the sumptuous appointments of
Nero's Aurea Domus as absurdly inadequate for her needs: ἡ γυνὴ δὲ
αὐτοῦ Γαλερία, ὡς ὀλίγου ἐν τῷ βασιλικῷ κόσμου εὑρεθέντος, κατεγέλα. In this
(according to Dio) she shared the sentiments of her husband Vitellius who,
though in general an ardent admirer of Nero (see c. 11, 2), blamed him
for having been badly housed and poorly provided with furniture. For
the splendours of the Aurea Domus see on Oth. 7, 1.

de hac.. liberos tulit: for this expression see on Vesp. 3. Vitellius,
when at Lugdunum on his way from Germany to Rome to assume the
empire, assembled his army to greet his infant son; he brought him out,
wrapped in a military cloak (paludamentum), and holding him in his arms
conferred on him the title of "Germanicus" with all the insignia of
imperial rank (Tac. H. ii 59; in Zon. xi 16 the boy is said to have been
six years old at the time). This “parvulus filius” was borne in a litter
in the sorrowful procession when Vitellius left the Palace to surrender the
empire (Tac. iii 67). He was put to death by order of Mucianus in the
following year (see c. 18 infr.). The daughter was of marriageable age
(nubilis, Tac. iii 78) on her father's accession in 69 A.D., and had been
betrothed by him to D. Valerius Asiaticus (Tac. i 59) who seems to have
died before the wedding, and, according to popular report, Vitellius tried
to detach Antonius Primus from the Flavians by offering him her hand
in marriage (Tac. iii 78). Suetonius (Vesp. 14) tells us that Vespasian
arranged a splendid match for her and gave her a handsome dowry, but
we are not told the name of the bridegroom. Both children appear on
coins of Vitellius with the superscription Liberi Imp. German. or Imp.
German. Aug. (Eckhel, vi 315; Cohen, i² 366; Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 454).

titubantia oris: "stammering” “stuttering"; cf. Claud. 30, linguae
titubantia. The form titubantia is not cited from any other author;
linguae titubatio occurs in Macrob. Sat. vii 6, 10. Cf. the use of titubare
in Ov. A.A. i 598, Fac titubet blaeso subdola lingua sono; Cic. dom. 54,
mente ac lingua titubante.

elinguem: tongueless” “tongue-tied"; cf. Liv. x 19, ex muto atque
elingui facundum etiam consulem haberent: Cic. post redit. 3, 7, mutum
forum, elinguem curiam, tacitam et fractam civitatem videbatis: Tac.
Dial. 36, mutum et elinguem videri deforme habebatur. The Gr. ἄγλωσσος
is used in the same way: e.g. Pind. Nem. viii 24, ἢ τιν᾿ ἄγλωσσον μέν, ἦτορ
δ᾽ ἄλκιμον, λάθα κατέχει | ἐν λυγρῷ νείκει.
..

a Galba missus est: the legions stationed in Lower Germany (i
Germanica, v Alaudae, xv Primigenia, xvi Gallica) were left without a
legatus of consular rank from the time that Fonteius Capito was put to
death by Galba in 68 A.D. (see Galb. 11) till Vitellius was sent there about
Dec. 1 in the same year. According to Tacitus (H. i 9) Galba thought
that by appointing a commander of noble birth, son of one who had been
three times consul and censor, the disaffected German legions would be
reconciled to the new régime, or would at least remain quiet: Inferioris
Germaniae legiones diutius sine consulari fuere, donec missu Galbae A.
Vitellius aderat, censoris Vitellii ac ter consulis filius: id satis videbatur.

inferiorem Germaniam: the two Germanies were not provinces in
the same sense as the other imperial provinces; they were merely two
frontier districts along the left (or Gallic) bank of the Rhine, each occupied
by four legions under a legatus of consular rank. Upper Germany
extended from Lake Constance to Brohl, midway between Bonn and Coblenz,
and Lower Germany from Brohl to the sea. The most important military
station in Upper Germany was Moguntiacum (Mainz). In Lower Germany
the civil capital was Colonia Agrippinensis (Cologne) and the military
capital was Vetera or Castra Vetera (Xanten). For the purposes of
civil administration the two Germanies formed part of Gallia Belgica and
their taxes were gathered by the procurator of that province. It was
probably after the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus (Dom. 6, 2) that
governors of the two Germanies were first appointed with full civil as
well as military authority. See Henderson, Five Roman Emperors p. 114.

T. Vini: see on Galb. 14, 2. Vinius, together with Laco and Icelus,
completely dominated Galba. The reading Vini was restored by Torrentius
for iuni or iunii of the MSS.; in Galb. 14, 2, iunius and lunius are variants
for uinius (Vinius).

factionis Venetae: the Blue was one of the four racing companies
(factiones) in the Circus; see on Dom. 7, 1. The devotion of Vitellius
(like Caracalla, Dio lxxvii 10) to the Blue is mentioned again in c. 14,
quosdam de plebe, quod Venetae factioni male dixerant, interemit. Dio
(lxv 5) says that Vitellius riding in state and wearing the imperial purple
seemed a ridiculous sight to those who remembered him wearing the dress
of the Blues and rubbing down the chariot-horses in the Circus (τοὺς
·ἀγωνιστὰς ἵππους ἐν τῇ οὐενετίῳ ἐσθῆτι ψήχοντα). The Green (prasina, viridis)
being the factio favoured by Domitian (as by Caligula and Nero), the
Blue is ridiculed by Martial, vi 46, Vapulat adsidue veneti quadriga
flagello, | nec currit : magnam rem, Catiane, facit. See also Mart. x 48, 23;
xiv 131. Walde (op. cit.) connects venetus “sea-blue” with unda.
..

nisi quod electum: i.e. the general opinion that Vitellius owed his
appointment to the influence of Vinius is shown to be false by Galba's
own statement of his reasons for his selection. Hand (Tursellinus, iv 235)
discusses various explanations given of the elliptical use of nisi quod ..
His own theory, which seems the simplest, is that nisi quod is a compressed
way of saying non est, si est quod, or non est, si in considerationem venit
quod. He explains nisi quia similarly. Suetonius uses nisi quod in three
other passages: Vesp. 4, 3; Dom. 4, 4; Iul. 45, 1, fuisse traditur
valitudine prospera, nisi quod tempore extremo repente animo linqui atque
etiam per somnum exterreri solebat. For instances in Plaut., Cic., Tac.,
etc., see Kühner-Stegmann ii 416.

qui de solo victu cogitarent: Dio (lxv 2) says that Vitellius cared
for nothing "divine or human" except self-indulgence: τῇ τε τρυφῇ καὶ
τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ προσκείμενος, οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων οὔτε τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων οὔτε τῶν θείων
ἐφρόντιζεν.

profundam gulam: cf. Curt. x 2, пес pudet profundo ventre devictarum
gentium spolia circumferentes, etc. In Plaut. Capt. 182 a greedy parasite's
stomach is described as a bottomless abyss (profundum).
For gula
("gullet'') in the sense of gluttony cf. c. 13, 3, homo non profundae modo
sed intempestivae gulae: Juv. 1, 140, quanta est gula, quae sibi totos |
ponit apros?
..

§ 2. exituro viaticum defuisse: cf. Curt. x 2 (Alexander upbraids his
troops): In Europam ire properatis, rege deserto, cum pluribus vestrum
defuturum viaticum fuerit, ni aes alienum luissem.

egestate rei familiaris: so Tacitus (H. ii 59) describes Vitellius on
his march to Rome "nullo principali paratu, sed vetere egestate con-
-spicuus"; cf. Plut. Galb. 22, (Οὐϊτέλλιος) τὴν λοιδορουμένην ὑπ᾽ ἐνίων πενίαν
δεῖγμα λαμπρὸν ἔχων χρηστότητος καὶ μεγαλοφροσύνης. The objective gen. "rei
familiaris'' is added as in Sall. Iug. 44, egestas pabuli; Tac. A. vi 23, eg.
cibi; Lucr. v 1211, eg. rationis; there is no example in Cic.

uxore et liberis: Galeria Fundana and her children, see c. 6. Tacitus-
(H. i 75) says that Vitellius sent letters from Germany to Titianus, brother
of Otho, threatening that he would make him answerable with his life for
the safety of his (Vitellius') mother and children at Rome.

quos Romae relinquebat: under the Republic provincial governors
could not bring their wives to the provinces, but under the early empire
this rule was frequently broken; in 21 A.D. the senate rejected a motion
“ne quem magistratum, cui provincia obvenisset, uxor comitaretur” (Tac.
A. iii 33); in 24 A.D. they decreed that a governor should be held accountable for any misconduct of his wife in the province, such as is described
in Juv. viii 128, where see Mayor's note.

meritorio: “hired"; cf. Iul. 57, meritoria raeda: Calig. 39, 1,
meritoria vehicula: Claud. 15, 4, meritoria scorta. The neut. pl. as a
subst. means "lodgings"; e.g. Juv. iii 234, quae meritoria somnum |
admittunt?

cenaculo: "attic” or “garret"; cf. Juv. x 18, rarus venit in cenacula
miles: Quintil. vi 3, 64, cum cenaculum eius perplueret: Apul. Met. ix 40.
Varro (L.L. v 162) explains how the word got this meaning: ubi cenabant
cenaculum vocitabant posteaquam in superiore parte cenitare coeperunt,
superioris domus universa cenacula dicta. Suetonius uses cenaculum in
two other passages: Aug. 45, 1, Ipse circenses ex amicorum libertorumque
cenaculis (“upper rooms”) spectabat; ib. 78, 2, in proximo cuiuscumque
domesticorum cenaculo manebat. Petronius, Satyr. 38, describes a nouveau
riche letting his garret, having purchased a house: C. Pompeius Diogenes
ex kalendis Iuliis cenaculum locat; ipse enim domum emit.

abditis: abdere with the abl. of place occurs also in Oth. 6, 3, abditus
sella muliebri: Iul. 20, 1: Tib. 12, 2, etc. Cicero (Arch. 12) has qui se
litteris abdiderunt (where Reid would insert in), but before the Silver
Age this constr. is almost entirely poetical, e.g. Verg. G. iii 96, abde domo.
Another constr. is used by Suetonius in Galb. 20, 2, in gremium abdidit.
Cicero elsewhere uses in c. abl., in c. acc., or acc. (Att. ix 6, 1, neque me
Arpinum hoc tempore abdam).

ablocaret: "let out,” alii habitandam locaret. This compound
(= ἀπομισθόω) is peculiar to Suetonius, who uses it also in Iul. 26, 2, ea
quae ad epulum pertinerent, quamvis macellariis ablocata (“though contracts had been given to the market-vendors''), etiam domesticatim .
apparabat.
matris: Sextilia (c. 3, 1).

unionem: uniones were the largest, most beautiful, and most highly
valued of all pearls. Pliny (N.H. xii 2) says that they were got from the
mare rubrum (Red Sea or Persian Gulf), and that they received their name
from each of them being unique, no two alike: N.H. ix 112, nulli duo
reperiuntur indiscreti, unde nomen unionum Romanae scilicet imposuere
deliciae. The two finest uniones ever seen were those worn as earrings by
Cleopatra (see on Galb. 18, 2). The number, weight, and value of the
uniones worn in the ears by Roman matrons are denounced by Seneca.
(Ben. vii 9, 4; Vit. Beat. 17, 2).

pigneraverit: "pawned," pignori dederit; cf. Juv. vii 73, alveolos et
laenam pignerat. The deponent pignerari means "to establish a lien on"
(pignoribus obstringere et devincire sibi), e.g. Suet. Claud. 10, 4 (of
Claudius' largess to the soldiers), primus Caesarum fidem militum etiam
praemio pigneratus: cf. Cic. Rep. i 8, Phil. xiv 32. For the perf. pigneraverit coupled with the imperf. ablocaret see on Galb. 3, 1; Bentley's conjecture ablocarit is needless.

creditorum turbam: Dio (lxv 3 and 5) says that Vitellius spent
incalculable sums (ἀμύθητα ἀνήλισκε) on gluttony, gambling, actors, and
charioteers; and he was in debt to so many that no one could see him in
the Forum on account of the multitude of his creditors (ὃν οὐδεὶς οὐδὲ ἐν τῇ
ἀγορᾷ πρότερον διὰ τὸ τῶν δανειστῶν πλῆθος ἰδεῖν ἐδύνατο). His creditors would
not let him start for Germany till he had given security (ἐξορμῶντος αὐτοῦ ..
ἐπελάβοντο, καὶ μόλις ποτὲ κατεγγυηθέντα ἀπέλυσαν).
Sinuessanos Formianosque: Sinuessa was a town on the Tyrrhenian
sea, on the borders of Latium and Campania, now ruins at the foot of
Monte Dragone. Formiae was 18 miles from Sinuessa, where the town of
