Mola di Gaeta now stands. Both Sinuessa and Formiae were on the Appia
Via.
"diverted to his own use” “embezzled"; cf. Cic.
Verr. ii 4, 68, interverso hoc regali dono: id. Phil. ii 79, promissum et
receptum intervertit, ad seque transtulit. Plautus, who first uses the verb,
has not merely intervortere aliquid, but also intervortere aliquem ("to
defraud'") and intervortere aliquem aliquo. We have no information as
to how Vitellius came to handle the revenues of these two towns. Even
if we assume that he could have been a redemptor vectigalium, the towns
would normally have been secured against loss by his sureties (praedes).
interverterat:

terrore calumniae: calumnia (from O. Lat. calvi "to deceive") was
used in two senses: (1) as here, a false action or prosecution brought by
one who "intelligit non recte se agere sed vexandi adversarii gratia
actionem instituit” (Gaius iv 178); cf. Suet. Dom. 9, 3; (2) an action or
conviction for dishonest litigation; cf. Cic. dom. 19, 49, accusare
propter calumniae metum non ausus est. See Poste on Gaius l.c.

iniuriarum: on the iniuriarum actio see Roby, Rom. Private Law ii 220.
The offence is defined generally in ad Herenn. iv 25, 35, Iniuriae sunt, quae
aut pulsatione corpus aut convicio aures aut aliqua turpitudine vitam
cuiuspiam violant. Proceedings might be either civil or criminal; cf. Just.
Inst. iv 4, 10, In summa sciendum est de omni iniuria eum qui passus est
posse vel criminaliter agere vel civiliter. Et si quidem civiliter agatur,
aestimatione facta, secundum quod dictum est, poena imponitur; sin
autem criminaliter, officio iudicis extraordinaria poena reo irrogatur.

formulam intendisset: a technical expression in the procedure per
formulas, i.e. by issues stated by the praetor. The word “formulae”
expressed the different forms in which the directions of the praetor were
given to the iudex or arbiter or reciperatores to whom he sent the case
for trial. The praetor could vary the formula to meet the requirements
of justice in each case. The phrase “formulam intendere’” (cf. actionem
intendere, Cic.) was used of the plaintiff; “formulam accipere” of the
defendant. In Suet. Claud. 14 “formula excidere” means "to fail in an
action"; cf. “formula cadere" (Sen.) and the common “causa cadere"
(= ''litem perdere"). Sandars (Institutes of Justinian p. 69) collects and
analyzes a specimen formula from Gaius: "Iudex esto: Quod Aulus
Agerius Numerio Negidio hominem vendidit; si paret Numerium Negidium
Aulo Agerio sestertium x. milia dare oportere, iudex Numerium Negidium
Aulo Agerio sestertium x. milia condemnato, si non paret, absolvito.''.
The words "Iudex esto” are the order for the appointment of the judge
(whose name would be inserted); from “quod” to “vendidit” is the
demonstratio or statement of the facts on which the plaintiff bases his
case viz. that he has sold the slave to N.N.; from “si paret” to “dare
oportere is the intentio or precise statement of the demand which the
plaintiff made against (tendebat in) his adversary.
The iudex has to
determine whether A.A. has sold the slave to N.N. at the price he alleges,
and whether the debt is still owing; if the judge is satisfied on these
points (si paret), he is instructed to pronounce judgment against N.N., if
not, he is to be acquitted; the words from "iudex Numerium” to the
end form what was known as the condemnatio.
quinquaginta sestertiis: about £425.

§3. male animatus
exercitus: Tacitus (H. i 8) mentions the
reasons for their disaffection, including the execution of their legatus
Fonteius Capito (see Galb. 11) by Galba's orders: Germanici exercitus,
quod periculosissimum in tantis viribus, solliciti et irati, superbia recentis
victoriae (over Vindex, see Galb. 9, 2) et metu tanquam alias partes fovissent. Tarde a Nerone desciverant; nec statim pro Galba Verginius: an
imperare noluisset dubium: delatum ei a milite imperium conveniebat.
Fonteium Capitonem occisum etiam qui queri non poterant, tamen indignabantur. Dux deerat, abducto Verginio per simulationem amicitiae; quem
non remitti atque etiam reum esse tanquam suum crimen accipiebant.

supinis manibus: with hands uplifted and upturned to heaven; cf.
Verg. A. iii 176, tendoque supinas | ad caelum cum voce manus (= ὑπτίας
χεῖρας ἀνατείνω). Hor. C. iii 23, 1, Caelo supinas si tuleris manus. If this
is the meaning here, the soldiers are represented as returning thanks to
the gods for the coming of Vitellius; but it is possible also to explain
“supinis manibus excepit" by the Gr. ὑπτίαις ταῖς χερσὶν ὑποδέχεσθαί τι
(Philostr. 771), the soldiers holding up their hands as if to catch a gift
dropping from the sky.

ter consulis filium: for the three consulships held by his father
Lucius Vitellius seé c. 2, 4. Cf. Tac. H. i 9, A. Vitellius censoris Vitellii
ac ter consulis filius: ib. 52, Vitellio tres patris consulatus, censuram,
collegium Caesaris et imponere iam pridem imperatoris dignationem et
auferre privati securitatem: Plut. Galb. 22 (quoted on c. 2, 4). For the
attributive use of ter see on “olim” c. 17, 2.

aetate integra: cf. Calig. 25, Caesoniam neque facie insigni neque
aetate integra amavit: Tib. 10, integra aetate ac valitudine. Suetonius
also uses integer aetate (Aug. 19, neque aetate neque corpore integer).
Vitellius was 53 years old at the time and hardly to be described as "aetate
integra''; Servius on Aen. ix 255 (integer aevi Ascanius) says "Integer
aevi, id est adolescens cui aetas integra superést.”
..
prodigo: cf. Auson. Carm. 259, 9, prodiga sceptra Vitelli.

persuasionem:
=
fidem, firmam opinionem; cf. Tib. 69, persuasionis
plenus cuncta fato agi: Plin. N.H. xxv 2, durat tamen tradita persuasio
in magna parte vulgi, veneficiis et herbis id cogi: Quintil. i 1, qui paulum
aliquid ultra primas litteras progressi, falsam sibi scientiae persuasionem
induerunt. In Cicero persuasio is used in an active sense for the act of
persuading: Inv. i 5, dicere apposite ad persuasionem.

caligatorum militum:
=
....
manipularium, gregariorum, "common.
soldiers'" "privates"; cf. Aug. 25, 3, vallares ac murales coronas
saepe etiam caligatis dabat: [Quintil.] decl. iii 15, cui parere caligatum
lex iubet: ib. 19, commendem tibi ordinem caligati militis. The caliga, or
boot of the rank and file, was of leather with soles thickly studded with
iron nails; see Mayor on Juv. xvi 24, offendere tot caligas, tot | milia
clavorum. The emperor Gaius got his nickname "Caligula" from being
brought up in the camp and wearing the private's uniform; Calig. 9,
Caligulae cognomen castrensi ioco traxit, quia manipulario habitu inter
milites educabatur.
quoque: "even"; see App. I. § 13.

stabula ac deversoria: cf. Plin. Ep. vi 19, urbem Italiamque non pro
patria sed pro hospitio (= deversorio, caupona) aut stabulo quasi peregrinantes habere. The stabulum provided accommodation primarily for
the horses or mules of the viatores, and there Vitellius would meet the
muliones; but the word is also found (e.g. in Mart. vi 94) in the general
sense of an inn. Ulpian, Dig. iv 9, 5, differentiates between cauponae,
for travellers only, and stabula, for beasts of burden: Caupo (mercedem
accipit), ut viatores manere in caupona patiatur; stabularius, ut permittat
iumenta apud eum stabulari. Lafaye (Daremberg-Saglio iv 1448) says:
"Il est probable que les clients du stabulum se contentaient souvent d'y
remiser leurs bêtes et leurs voitures les jours de marché, comme on le fait
encore dans toutes les petites villes; eux-mêmes n'y couchaient pas; le
soir venu, ayant terminé leurs affaires, ils reprenaient avec leurs bêtes le
chemin de la campagne. Il y avait à côté de l'écurie un cabaret et aussi
quelques chambres pouvant servir en cas de nécessité; en un mot, le
stabulum, c'est par excellence l'auberge des rouliers, l'osteria qu'on
rencontre au bord des grandes routes, à l'entrée des villes." Suetonius
elsewhere uses stabulum for "stable" (Calig. 55, 2) and "brothel"
(Iul. 49, 1).

comis: Tacitus (H. i 52) states that comitas was one of the virtues
falsely attributed to Vitellius by his supporters, while sterner judges
pronounced him a man of low tastes: Et ut Vitellius apud severos humilis,
ita comitatem bonitatemque faventes vocabant, quod sine modo, sine
iudicio donaret sua, largiretur aliena; simul aviditate imperi dandi ipsa
vitia pro virtutibus interpretabantur.

iantassent: "breakfasted"; cf. Mart. viii '67, 10, Ut iantes, sero,
Caeciliane, venis: Isidor. or. xx 2, 10, Iantaculum est primus cibus quo
ieiunium solvitur, unde et nuncupatum. Nigidius: Nos ipsi ieiunia
iantaculis levibus solvimus. On the forms iento, ianto, from *ieiunto,
*iaiunto see Lindsay, Lat. Lang. p. 17; in the MSS. of Plautus iaiunus is
the best attested form. The iantaculum was usually taken during the
third or, at the latest, the fourth hour, and consisted of bread dipped in
wine or eaten with honey, dates, olives, or salt: sometimes fried cakes.
and cheese were used. (Marquardt, Privatl.2 265.)

castra ingressus: the careful inspection of the winter-quarters of
the legions in Lower Germany by Vitellius, the newly arrived legatus, is
described in Tac. H. i 52: Sub ipsas superioris anni (i.e. 68 A.D.) kalendas
Decembres Aulus Vitellius inferiorem Germaniam ingressus hiberna
legionum cum cura adierat. The winter-quarters of the First legion were
at Bonna (Bonn), of the Sixteenth at Novaesium (Neuss), and of the
Fifth and Fifteenth at Castra Vetera (Xanten, below Wesel), which was
the chief military centre of the province (see on c. 7, 1).

ultro dempsit: cf. Tac. (l.c.): Redditi plerisque ordines, remissa
ignominia, adlevatae notae; plura ambitione, quaedam iudicio, in quibus
sordes et avaritiam Fontei Capitonis (the late commander, see Galb. 11)
adimendis adsignandisve militiae ordinibus integre mutaverat. The
centurions who had openly declared their adhesion to the cause of Nero
and Verginius Rufus, and thus compromised themselves in relation to
Galba, had been degraded and were now reinstated.

ignominiosis: = ignominia notatis. Some of the ignominiae or notae,
i.e. degrading punishments inflicted for military offences, are described in
Aug. 24, 2, Centuriones statione deserta, itidem ut manipulares, capitali
animadversione puniit, pro cetero delictorum genere variis ignominiis
adfecit, ut stare per totum diem iuberet ante praetorium (the general's
quarters), interdum tunicatos discinctosque, nonnumquam cum decempedis
(ten-foot poles) vel etiam caespitem portantes: Val. Max. ii 7, 9,
L. Calpurnius Piso consul, cum in Sicilia bellum adversus fugitivos gereret,
et C. Titius, equitum praefectus, fugitivorum multitudine circumventus
arma iis tradidisset, his praefectum ignominiae generibus adfecit. Iussit
eum toga laciniis abscissis amictum, discinctaque tunica indutum, nudis
pedibus, a mane in noctem usque ad principia per omne tempus militiae
adesse; interdixit etiam ei convictum hominum, usumque balnearum:
Frontin. Strateg. iv 1, 26, 27, 28. See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 572.

sordes: ''mourning garb." It was a regular artifice for an accused
person (reus) to appear in public unwashed and unkempt (squalidus), clad
in mean and soiled apparel (sordidatus); cf. Quintil. vi 1, 33, At sordes et
squalorem et propinquorum quoque similem habitum scio profuisse: Cic.
Cluent. 18, squalore huius et sordibus laetatur (where see Ramsay). So
sordes is used in describing those who have a trial hanging over their
heads; e.g. Cic. Att. i 16, satius esse illum (Clodium) in infamia relinqui
ac sordibus quam infirmo iudicio committi: Suet. Aug. 32, 2, diuturnorum
reorum et ex quorum sordibus nihil aliud quam voluptas inimicis quaereretur
nomina abolevit.

vixdum mense transacto: Vitellius had taken over command in Lower
Germany about Dec. 1, 68 A.D.; on the evening of Jan. 1, 69, while dining
at Cologne he received news that two legions (iv and xxii) in Upper
Germany had refused to renew the oath of allegiance to Galba. He made
known this news to his army, and on the following day Fabius Valens,
the legatus of the First legion, with the cavalry of that legion and of
the auxiliaries appeared at Cologne and greeted him as Imperator (Tac.
H. i 56, 57).

neque diei
ratione habita: the days following the Kalends, the
Nones, and the Ides were "black" (atri) or unlucky days for beginning
an enterprise; cf. Macrob. Sat. i 16, 21, dies autem postriduanos ad omnia
maiores nostri cavendos putarunt, quos etiam atros velut infausta appellatione damnarunt: ib. 15, 22, omnes autem postriduani dies seu post
Kalendas sive post Nonas Idusve ex aequo atri sunt: Gell. v 17: Varr.
L.L. vi 4, 29: Liv. vi 1, 12. In the Fasti Praenest. the 2nd of Jan. is:
marked as a “dies religiosus, ut sunt dies postridie omnes Kalendas, quod
iis sacrificium non fit."

temporis: 'the time of the day," explained by the following ac
iam vespere.

in veste domestica: cf. Claud. 17, 3, in veste palmata: Oth. 12, 1, in
lintea veste: Ner. 25, 1, in veste purpurea. Suetonius, like other post-Aug. authors, uses in c. abl. (cf. ἐν) or the simple abl. (e.g. Iul. 6, 2,
muliebri veste) in describing dress, where the best prose writers prefer
сит. For “vestis domestica,” common clothes worn in the house, cf.
Aug. 73, veste non temere alia quam domestica usus est, ab sorore et uxore
et filia neptibusque confecta: Sen. Tranq. i 5, placet non ex arcula
prolata vestis .. sed domestica et vilis, nec servata nec sumenda sollicite:
Cic. Fin. ii 24, 77, aut etiam, ut vestitum, sic sententiam habeas aliam
domesticam, aliam forensem, ut in fronte ostentatio sit, intus veritas
occultetur. The garments worn out of doors were called “forensia” or
““vestis forensis”; cf. Aug. 73, Et forensia autem et calceos numquam
non intra cubiculum habuit ad subitos repentinosque casus parata: Calig.
17, 2, posteriore epulo forensia viris distribuit. Among the equipment
provided by Alexander Severus for provincial governors (praesides provinciarum) were “vestes forenses binae, domesticae binae, balneares
singulares" (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 42).

imperator est consalutatus: cf. Galb. 10, 1: Tac. H. i 57, Proxima
legionis primae hiberna erant et promptissimus e legatis Fabius Valens.
Is die proximo (Jan. 2) coloniam Agrippinensem cum equitibus legionis
auxiliariorumque ingressus imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit. Secutae
ingenti certamine eiusdem provinciae (i.e. Lower Germany) legiones.

per celeberrimos vicos: the most crowded streets or quarters of
Colonia Agrippinensis itself. vicos is explained as "villages" or "towns"
by Rolfe, Thomson-Forester, Clarke, and Holland (who however gives
"streets" as an alternative rendering).

gladium tenens: the dagger (pugio) or sword was one of the insignia
assumed by a new emperor; see on Galb. 11.

detractum delubro Martis: cf. c. 10, 3, where Vitellius dedicates at
the same shrine of Mars in Cologne the sword with which Otho had
slain himself.
§ 2. praetorium: the general's quarters in the camp; see on "principia,” Oth. 1, 2.

flagrante triclinio ex conceptu camini: these words are difficult:
Stahr translates, "als das Speisezimmer durch Ansteckung eines Kamins
in Flammen stand"; Rolfe, "the dining-room caught fire from the stove
and was ablaze"; but it is doubtful if ex conceptu camini could mean
"owing to a catching fire, or an ignition, caused by the stove." The only
other passage where the subst. "conceptus" is used of fire seems to be
Plin. N.H. xvi 208, Teritur lignum ligno ignemque concipit attritu,
excipiente materia aridi fomitis ("tinder''), fungi vel foliorum facillimo
conceptu, i.e. the fungi and leaves most readily ignite; on the analogy
of this, "conceptus camini'' should mean that the fireplace, or rather
the chimney, itself caught fire (and so set fire to the room). The caminus
was a fireplace, often arched in shape, fitted with a chimney (‘chimney"
comes through “cheminée” from caminus), and was fed with logs. Its
use in the winter-quarters of troops is mentioned in Cic. Fam. vii 10, metuo
ne frigeas in hibernis; quamobrem camino luculento utendum censeo.
Sidonius (Ep. ii 2) mentions its use for heating dining-rooms in winter:
in hiemale triclinium venitur, quod arcuatili camino saepe ignis animatus
pulla fuligine infecit ("a roaring fire on an arched hearth often fills it with
smoke and smuts." Dalton). For ante
quam with the participle see
on Galb. 11, prius quam.. oppressis.
..

cum quidem inquit: for this use of cum quidem introducing a
memorable utterance on a certain occasion cf. Iul. 50, 2, cum quidem
plerisque vilitatem mirantibus facetissime Cicero: “Quo melius,” inquit,
“emptum sciatis, tertia deducta” (“It's a better bargain than you think,
for a third has been knocked off the price'"): Cic. Sen. 4, 11, cum quidem
Salinatori, qui amisso oppido fugerat in arcem, glorianti atque ita dicenti:
“Mea opera, Q. Fabi, Tarentum recepisti”; “Certe," inquit ridens,
“nam nisi tu amisisses, numquam recepissem.” See Draeger, Hist.
Synt. ii 568.

omine adverso: Frontinus, Strateg. i 12 (a chapter entitled “De dissolvendo metu quem milites ex adversis conceperint ominibus''), gives many
historical examples of commanders promptly construing unfavourable
omens as favourable; e.g., Epaminondas, cum fax de caelo nocte delapsa
eos qui adverterunt terruisset: ‘“Lumen,” inquit, “hoc numina ostendunt.'"
Chabrias Atheniensis classe dimicaturus, excusso ante navem
ipsius fulmine, exterritis per tale prodigium militibus: ‘“Nunc,” inquit,
““potissimum ineunda pugna est, cum deorum maximus Iuppiter adesse
numen suum classi nostrae ostendit."

adluxit: this impersonal use (cf. illucescit) is only found here. A. А.
Howard (Harvard Studies x 28) plausibly suggests that Bono animo estote!
nobis adluxit is a quotation from some tragedy, and he would complete
the line as an iambic senarius by the addition of deus.

consentiente superioris provinciae exercitu: cf. Tac. H. i 57, Et
superior (= superioris provinciae) exercitus speciosis senatus populique
Romani nominibus relictis tertium nonas Ianuarias (i.e. Jan. 3) Vitellio
accessit: scires illum priore biduo non penes rem publicam fuisse (i.e.
it had not been under the control of or subject to the Republic, though
on Jan. 1 the legions, iv and xxii, stationed at Moguntiacum, when required
to renew the oath of fealty to Galba, dashed down his images and swore
allegiance to the senate and the Roman people, i.e. the Republic; see on
Galb. 16, 2): Plut. Galb. 22, Εὐθὺς δὲ καὶ τὸ μετὰ Φλάκκου (i.e. Hordeonius
Flaccus, commander in Upper Germany) στράτευμα τοὺς καλοὺς ἐκείνους καὶ
δημοκρατικοὺς εἰς σύγκλητον (senatum) ὅρκους ἀφέντες ὤμοσαν Οὐϊτελλίῳ τῷ
αὐτοκράτορι (imperatori) ποιήσειν τὸ προστασσόμενον.

cognomen Germanici ..recepit: Tac. H. i 62, nomen Germanici Vitellio
statim additum. Plutarch (l.c.) says that for some days previously Vitellius
had seemed to dread the weight of sovereign power and to decline it, but
on the day when Fabius Valens and the cavalry saluted him as imperator
he had been entertaining his officers at a great banquet from midday, and
replete with food and drink he went out to them and accepted the title of
"Germanicus." For his mother's refusal to recognize her son Vitellius
under the name “Germanicus" see on c. 3, 2.

(cognomen) Augusti distulit: Tac. H. ii 62, praemisit in urbem
edictum, quo vocabulum Augusti differret, Caesaris non reciperet, cum de
potestate nihil detraheret (i.e. though he relinquished nothing of his actual
powers). The senate, on the receipt of the news of the defeat and death
of Otho and the acceptance of Vitellius by the city soldiery, had at once
decreed to him all the customary honours, the tribunician power, the title
of Augustus, etc. (H. ii 55). He was constrained by the people to accept
the title of "Augustus" on the day after he made his imposing entry
into Rome in Aug. 69 A.D.; H. ii 90, abnuentique nomen Augusti expressere,
ut adsumeret, tam frustra quam recusaverat. Vitellius reckoned the first
day of his reign (dies imperii) to be April 19, 69 A.D., when he was
recognised by the senate; Vespasian reckoned his dies imperii to be the
day on which he was first proclaimed by the legions in Egypt (see
Vesp. 6, 3).

(cognomen) Caesaris in perpetuum recusavit: cf. Plut. (l.c.) φασὶν (τὸν
Οὐϊτέλλιον) ..
προελθεῖν καὶ ὑπακοῦσαι Γερμανικὸν ὄνομα θεμένων αὐτῷ, τὸ δὲ
Καίσαρος οὐ προσδεξάμενον. Tacitus mentions that Vitellius at first declined
the title (see H. ii 62, quoted in preceding note, and i 62 Caesarem se
appellari etiam victor prohibuit); but he also states that Vitellius afterwards, when the Flavian forces were advancing on Rome, expressed a
wish to be saluted as "Caesar': iii 58, quin et Caesarem se dici voluit,
aspernatus antea; sed tunc superstitione nominis (“a superstitious feeling
about the name''), et quia in metu consilia prudentium et vulgi rumor iuxta
audiuntur. In the Acta Fratr. Arv. he appears as "Vitellius Germanicus
Imperator'' (C.I.L. vi 2051, Henzen Act. Fr. Arv. xcii sqq.). On his
earlier coins he is styled "A. Vitellius Imperator Germanicus"; on the
later the title "Augustus" is added. On some Alexandrian coins his name
appears as Ώλος (= Aulus) Οὐιτ. Καισ. Σεβ. (Σεβαστός = Augustus) Γερμ. αὐτ.
(αὐτοκράτωρ Imperator). It is probable that these coins were struck
before the news that Vitellius had rejected the title of "Caesar" reached
the provinces (Eckhel, vi 309).
=

caede Galbae: described in Galb. 19 and 20. Tacitus (H. i 64) says
that Valens (see next note) was already on his march when he received
the news of Galba's death: Nuntium de caede Galbae et imperio Othonis
Fabius Valens in civitate Leucorum (in N.E. Gaul, on the Moselle) accepit.
Nec militum animus in gaudium aut formidine permotus: bellum volvebat.

partitus est copias: Suetonius mentions only the division of the forces
of Vitellius into those sent in advance and those with which he followed
in person; the further division of the advance forces is described in Tac.
H. i 61. Vitellius decided that there were to be two generals and two
lines of march. Fabius Valens was ordered to advance through Gaul
(winning it over or, if necessary, ravaging it) and to invade Italy by way
of the Cottian Alps, the chain which divides Dauphiné from Piedmont,
with the pass over Mont Genèvre where Pompey and later Augustus had
made a military road. Aulus Caecina was to take the nearer route coming
down through Switzerland into Italy by the Pennine Alps, over the Great
St. Bernard pass from Martigny to Aosta. To Valens were entrusted the
picked troops of the army of Lower Germany, including the main part of
the Fifth legion, detachments from legions i, xv, and xvi, and the auxiliary
infantry and cavalry, the total force numbering about 40,000 men.
Caecina led 30,000 from the army of Upper Germany, the flower of his
force being the 21st legion, called Rapax. Vitellius followed later with
about 60,000 men, comprising the strength of the Germanic armies and
some 8000 who had been sent from Britain.

laetum evenit auspicium: mentioned also in Tac. H. i 62: Laetum
augurium, Fabio Valenti exercituique, quem in bellum agebat, ipso profectionis die aquila leni meatu, prout agmen incederet, velut dux viae
praevolavit; longumque per spatium is gaudentium militum clamor, ea
quies interritae alitis fuit, ut haud dubium magnae et prosperae rei omen
acciperetur. A similar favourable omen preluded a great victory of
Germanicus over Arminius; cf. Tac. A. ii 17 Interea pulcherrimum
augurium, octo (i.e. one for each of the 8 legions) aquilae petere silvas
et intrare visae imperatorem advertere. Exclamat irent, sequerentur
Romanas aves, propria legionum numina.
lustratis: = circu(m)itis. lustrare primarily meant "to purify," and
as the purification was often effected by processions round a place or by
the priest going round the persons to be purified and sprinkling them with
water, lustrare came to be used in the sense of circu(m)ire and also of
peragrare; e.g. Aen. x 224, adgnoscunt (Nymphae) longe regem, lustrantque (= circumnatant) choreis: ib. vii 391, te (Bacchum) lustrare choro
(= circum te saltare): Cic. Fin. v 87, Pythagoras Aegyptum lustravit.

antecessit: cf. Curt. iv 7, 15, corvi modico volatu prima signa antecedentes et modo humi residebant, cum lentius agmen incederet, modo se
pennis levabant ducentium iterque monstrantium ritu: Vell. Pat. i 4, 1,
classis cursum esse directum columbae antecedentis volatu ferunt.

ipso movente: for movere used absolutely, in the sense of moveri or
se movere, cf. Calig. 13, ut a Miseno movit: Iul. 60, cum minime quis
moturum putaret: Liv. xxxvii 28, 4, postquam movisse a Samo Romanos
audivit: Cic. Att. ix 1, 1, postquam ille Canusio moverat (where see Tyrrell
and Purser, who rightly deny that there is an ellipse of castra).

plurifariam: cf. Aug. 46 and 80; Tib. 43, 2; Calig. 54, 1; Claud. 21,
4; Ner. 24, 23; not found in any earlier writer. Suetonius also uses multifariam in many places" (e.g. Galb. 19, 1); bifariam "in two places"
(Aug. 100, 3); trifariam, quadrifariam ‘“in three (four) parts" (Vitell.
13, 1). Other similar adverbs collected by Neue, Formenlehre ii 677, are
alifariam, aliquotfariam, ambifariam, omnifariam, septifariam. All such
forms are Acc. Sg. Fem. of adjs. in -fārius; cf. Gr. -φάσιος from -φατιος,
e.g. τριφάσιος (Lindsay, Lat. Lang. p. 552).

corruerunt: so when Julius Caesar was setting out for the senate on
the fatal Ides of March, an image of him in the vestibule of his house
fell down of its own accord and was shattered (Dio xliv 18). Before
Nero's death exornati Lares in ipso sacrificii apparatu conciderunt
(Ner. 46, 2).
..

laurea excidit: see on Galb. 18, 3, sacrificanti coronam de capite
excidisse. Vitellius offered sacrifice when the expedition was setting out.
Suetonius uses either laurea corona (Iul. 45, 2; 79, 1; Tib. 69) or laurea
by itself (as in Dom. 6, 1; etc.).

in profluentem: sc. aquam. For this ellipse cf. Cic. Inv. ii 149, dum
culeus, in quem coniectus in profluentem deferretur, compararetur: Auct.
ad Herenn. i 23, Et lex: qui parentem necasse iudicatus erit, ut is obvolutus
et obligatus corio devehatur in profluentem: Flor. i 1, abiectus in profluentem: id. iv 12, arma in profluentes data. The full phrase aqua
profluens occurs in Cic. Q. Fratr. iii 1. The ellipse of aqua with frigida,
calida, etc., is common.

Viennae: Vienna, mod. Vienne, was on the Rhone, in the province of
Gallia Narbonensis. It had been the capital of the Allobroges, and seems
to have been made a Roman colony under Caligula. The fierce rivalry and
enmity which existed between it and Lugdunum (Lyons), on the opposite
bank of the Rhone, are described in Tac. H. i 65.
pro tribunali: see on Vesp. 7, 2.

gallinaceus: used absolutely (as in Plin. N.H., and Columella) for
gallus gallinaceus (Plaut., Cic., etc.) "a poultry-cock." It is fortunate
that Suetonius explains in c. 18 what was portended by the strange occurrence mentioned here, as otherwise we should have been at a loss to divine
it. Cf. the story of the hen (gallina) in Galb. 1.

supra umerum astitit: though the cock perching on his shoulder
and head was an omen of doom to Vitellius, an eagle lighting on the
shoulder or head was regarded as a sign of coming power; cf. Claud. 7,
evenit ut primitus ingredienti cum fascibus (i.e. as consul) Forum praetervolans aquila dexteriore umero consideret: Lact. Inst. i 11, 65, consedisse
(Iovi) aquilam in capite atque ei regnum portendisse. Valerius Maximus
(v 6, 4) tells a curious tale of a bird lighting on the head of Q. Aelius
Paetus when he was administering justice as praetor: Cui ius dicenti
cum in capite picus consedisset haruspexque affirmasset, conservato eo fore
domus ipsius statum felicissimum, reipublicae miserrimum; occiso, in contrarium utrumque cessurum: e vestigio picum morsu suo in conspectu
senatus necavit.

ostentis par respondit exitus: cf. Liv. ix 15, Papirio quoque brevi ad
spem eventus respondit: Cic. Div. ii 24, 52, quae (responsa haruspicum)
aut nullos habuerint exitus aut contrarios.

legatos suos: Aulus Caecina and Fabius Valens, who defeated the
forces of Otho at Betriacum. For the career of Caecina see on Tit. 6, 2.
Valens was appointed by Nero to command the 1st legion in Germany,
and after Galba's accession he put to death Fonteius Capito (see Galb. 11),
governor of Lower Germany, alleging that he was plotting revolution.
Thinking this service insufficiently rewarded by Galba, he persuaded
Vitellius to seize the empire. When Vitellius reached Rome, Valens and
Caecina were made consuls (Sept., 69 A.D.). They were sent from Rome
against the advancing forces of Vespasian. Valens was delayed in starting,
and when he heard of the rout of the rest of the Vitellian army by
Antonius Primus, he tried to cross over by sea to Gaul, to rouse that
province for Vitellius, but was captured and shortly afterwards executed.
Tacitus denounces in the strongest terms the profligacy, venality, and
cruelty of Valens (H. i 66, ii 56, iii 62).
Betriacensi victoria: see Oth. 9, 2 and notes.
Othonis exitu: see Oth. 11.

cum adhuc in Gallia esset: Dio lxv 1 (Zon. xi 16), ὄντι δ' ἐν τῇ Γαλατίᾳ
ὁ θάνατος ἠγγέλθη τοῦ Ὄθωνος. Vitellius was still on the road to Lugdunum
when he heard the tidings; cf. Tac. H. ii 57, Interim Vitellius victoriae
suae nescius ut ad integrum bellum reliquas Germanici exercitus vires
trahebat. Pauci veterum militum in hibernis relicti, festinatis per Gallias
dilectibus, ut remanentium legionum nomina supplerentur. Cura ripae (i.e.
the left bank of the Rhine) Hordeonio Flacco permissa: ipse e Britannico
exercitu delecta octo milia sibi adiunxit. Et paucorum dierum iter progressus prosperas apud Bedriacum res ac morte Othonis concidisse bellum
accepit.
quicquid: see on Galb. 1.

praetorianarum cohortium: for their history and organisation see on
Tit. 4, 2. Though disbanded by Vitellius they took service again to
support Vespasian; cf. Tac. H. ii 67, Proximus Vitellio e praetoriis
cohortibus metus erat. Separati primum, deinde addito honestae missionis
lenimento, arma ad tribunos suos deferebant, donec motum a Vespasiano
bellum crebresceret: tum resumpta militia robur Flavianarum partium
fuere.
Vitellius enrolled 16 new praetorian cohorts when Vespasian's
forces were advancing (Tас. Н. ii 93).

ut pessimi exempli: by reason of their desertion of Galba and their
appointment of Otho as emperor without the authority of the senate
and people. For pessimi exempli cf. Aug. 32, 1, pleraque pessimi
exempli
exstiterant: Plin. Ep. x 97, Sine auctore propositi
libelli (i.e. anonymous accusations) in nullo crimine locum habere
debent. Nam et pessimi exempli nec nostri saeculi est (i.e. "not in
accordance with the spirit of our times''). The abl. is also used by
Suetonius, Dom. 14, 4, utque domesticis persuaderet ne bono quidem
exemplo audendam esse patroni neceт.

exauctoravit: see on Vesp. 8, 2. This power belonged to the emperor
as head of the army (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 854). Suetonius says nothing
of the praetorians having been granted the honesta missio which is mentioned by Tacitus (ii 67, quoted above); this would carry with it the
bounty of 20,000 sesterces granted to time-expired praetorians (Dio lv 23).

iussas tribunis tradere arma: Tac. (l.c.), arma ad tribunos suos deferebant. Their standard-bearers (signiferi) also handed over their standards,
and so Antonius Primus, the general of Vespasian, when he was exhorting
his forces to a fresh attack on the Vitellians, said to the praetorians (who
had taken service again with Vespasian): “illic (i.e. in the hands of the
Vitellians) signa armaque vestra sunt'' (Tac. H. iii 24).

libellos: "petitions"; see on Dom. 14, 4, Epaphroditum a libellis.
Plutarch (Galb. 27) mentions the 120 petitions (βιβλία) presented to Otho
by those who claimed to have taken part in the murders of Galba, Piso,
Laco, and Vinius. With reference to the great number of these claimants
Plut. neatly quotes the words of the poet Archilochus “ ἑπτὰ γὰρ νεκρῶν
πεσόντων, οὓς ἐμάρψαμεν ποσίν, | χίλιοι φονῆες ἐσμέν.”

conquiri et supplicio adfici: very similar words are used by Tacitus,
H. i 44: Plures quam centum viginti libellos praemium exposcentium ob
aliquam notabilem illa die operam Vitellius postea invenit, omnesque
conquiri et interfici iussit. For supplicium in the sense of "capital
punishment'' see on c. 14, 1.

egregie: cf. Galb. 14, 1, quanquam multa documenta egregii principis
daret.

magis ex natura: sc. sua; cf. Tib. 59, 1, magis naturae obtemperans
("more in obedience to his natural instincts'').

§ 2. ritu triumphantium vectus est: Tacitus (ii 59) says that it was
Junius Blaesus, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, who first enabled Vitellius
to assume regal splendour: Ipse (Vitellius) Arare flumine devehitur nullo
principali paratu, sed vetere egestate conspicuus, donec Iunius Blaesus,
Lugdunensis Galliae rector, genere illustri, largus animo et par opibus,
circumdaret principi ministeria, comitaretur liberaliter.
flumina: the Arar (Saone) and the Rhodanus (Rhone).

delicatissimis navigiis: cf. Calig. 43, iter ingressus est confecitque
interdum adeo segniter delicateque (‘luxuriously") ut octophoro ("a litter
with eight bearers'') veheretur: Eumen. Paneg. Constantin. Aug. 13, delicata
fuit illa vectatio Principis otiosi: Cic. Att. ii 14, 1, delicatum convivium.
Casaubon compares the navis thalamegus (= cubiculata), the royal barge
fitted with staterooms, in which Cleopatra and Caesar sailed on the Nile
(Iul. 52).

variarum coronarum genere: Bentley's vario is approved by Ihm, but
the text is defended by Claud. 46, ex omnium magistratuum genere, and by
the many instances of similar transference (hypallage) of the epithet belonging to genus which are collected in Thes. Ling. Lat. vi 1906.

redimitis: cf. Curt. iv 4, 5, navigia conscendunt redimita coronis
floribusque: Ov. Am. iii 11, 29, puppis redimita corona: Sil. Ital. Pun.
xi 484, lauro redimita subibat | optatos puppis portus.
profusissimos: see on Tit. 7, 1.
obsoniorum: see on Dom. 4. 5.

apparatus: cf. Tac. H. ii 62, epularum foeda et inexplebilis libido:
ex urbe atque Italia inritamenta gulae gestabantur, strepentibus ab utroque
mari itineribus; exhausti conviviorum apparatibus principes civitatum;
vastabantur ipsae civitates; degenerabat a labore ac virtute miles adsuetudine voluptatum et contemptu ducis. See on Dom. 4, 1.

nulla disciplina: Tac. c. 68, apud Vitellium omnia indisposita,
temulenta, pervigiliis ac bacchanalibus quam disciplinae et castris propiora:
c. 69, et vires (militum) luxu corrumpebantur contra veterem disciplinam
et instituta maiorum. The outrages committed by the followers of Vitellius
are denounced by Tac. in c. 56: Ceterum Italia gravius atque atrocius
quam bello adflictabatur. Dispersi per municipia et colonias Vitelliani
spoliare, rapere, vi et stupris polluere: in omne fas nefasque avidi aut
venales non sacro, non profano abstinebant. Ipsique milites regionum
gnari refertos agros, dites dominos in praedam, aut, si repugnatum foret,
ad excidium destinabant, obnoxiis ducibus et prohibere non ausis. Cf. ib.
71, 87.

petulantiam: in Ner. 26, 1, Suet. describes the petulantia of Nero who
went about the streets like a footpad (grassator) at night: Petulantiam...
exercuit,.. redeuntes a cena verberare ac repugnantes vulnerare cloacisque demergere assuerat, tabernas etiam effringere et expilare. Juvenal
(iii 278 sqq.) gives a similar description of the wantonness of a drunken
bully (ebrius ac petulans).

in iocum vertens: cf. Aug. 67, 1, rem in iocum vertit: Liv. v 14, in
religionem vertentes: Tac. H. i 86, in prodigium et omen vertebatur:
Aristoph. Vesp. 1260, ἐς γέλων τὸ πρᾶγμ᾽ ἔτρεψας.
in libertatem asserebant: see on Vesp. 3.

repraesentantes: see on Oth. 5, 2. Holland renders: "they paid as
many as withstood them with whipping-cheer, blows, knocks, bloody wounds
oftentimes, yea and otherwhiles with present death.”

§ 3. campos adit: Tacitus (H. ii 70) gives a vivid account of the
visit of Vitellius to Bedriacum: Inde Vitellius Cremonam flexit et spectato
munere (gladiatorial show'') Caecinae insistere Bedriacensibus campis
ac vestigia recentis victoriae lustrare oculis concupivit. Foedum atque
atrox spectaculum intra quadragensimum pugnae diem: lacera corpora,
trunci artus, putres virorum equorumque formae, infecta tabo humus,
protritis arboribus ac frugibus dira vastitas, etc. Cf. Dio lxv 1, ὁ Οὐιτέλλιος δὲ εἶδεν ἐν Λουγδούνῳ μονομάχων (gladiatorum) ἀγῶνας καὶ ἐν Κρεμώνῃ· ὥσπερ
οὐκ ἀρκοῦντος τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἐν ταῖς μάχαις ἀπολωλότων, καὶ τότε καὶ ἔτι ἀτάφων
ἐρριμμένων, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐθεάσατο, διεξῆλθε γὰρ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ χωρίου ἐν ᾧ ἔκειντο
ἐμπιμπλάμενος τῆς θέας, ὥσπερ τότε νικῶν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκέλευσέ σφας οὐδ᾽ ὡς ταφῆναι.
For adit perf. cf. petit, Oth. 7, 1.

abhorrentes tabem: for abhorrere c. acc. see on Galb. 4, 2. Vitellius
displayed a callous insensibility to the awful spectacle; cf. Tac. (l.c.),
erant quos varia sors rerum lacrimaeque et misericordia subiret; at non
Vitellius flexit oculos nec tot milia (40,000, Dio lxiv 10) insepultorum
civium exhorruit, laetus ultro et tam propinquae sortis ignarus instaurabat
sacrum dis loci.

detestabili voce: Tacitus does not give this particular utterance of
Vitellius at Bedriacum, but in describing the death of Blaesus (see c. 14, 2
infr.) he cites one of similar brutality: H. iii 39, Quin et audita est
saevissima Vitellii vox, qua se (ipsa enim verba referam) pavisse oculos
spectata inimici morte iactavit.
..

optime olere et melius: this form of expression by which a comparative expresses a higher degree of a quality than a superlative is not
uncommon in Latin; e.g. Cic. Off. iii 121, Tibi persuade esse te quidem mihi
carissimum, sed multo fore cariorem, si talibus praeceptis laetabere: id.
Fam. xiv 3, 2, Ego hoc miserior sum quam tu, quae es miserrima: id.
Marcell. 33, Maximas tibi omnes gratias agimus, maiores etiam habemus:
Liv. iii 72, ne pessimum facinus peiore exemplo admitterent: Apul. Met.
x 12, servus nequissimus atque mulier nequior. Kühner-Stegmann (ii 481)
give the title "elative" to the use of the superlative to denote merely a
very high degree.
et: Ernesti suggested at, G. Becker set (sed).
nec eo setius: see on Tit. 5, 3.

lapidem memoriae Othonis inscriptum: the soldiers buried the remains
of Otho in a simple tomb, with no splendid monument, and no boastful
inscription; cf. Tac. H. ii 49, Othoni sepulchrum extructum est modicum
et mansurum. Plutarch visited the tomb and thus describes it (Oth. 18):
κρύψαντες δὲ τῇ γῇ τὰ λείψανα τοῦ ῎Οθωνος οὔτε μεγέθει σήματος οὔτ᾽ ἐπιγραφῆς ὄγκῳ
("pomp of epitaph ") τὸν τάφον ἐποίησαν ἐπίφθονον. Εἶδον δὲ ἐν Βριξίλλῳ γενόμενος
καὶ μνῆμα μέτριον καὶ τὴν ἐπιγραφὴν οὕτως ἔχουσαν, εἰ μεταφρασθείη· “ Δαίμοσι Μάρκου
Ὄθωνος.” (Δαίμοσι = Dis Manibus is a probable correction by Lobeck of
Δήλωσει “for the pointing out of Marcus Otho." Hardy ad loc. says
"It is difficult to see of what Latin formula Δηλώσει Μάρκου Όθωνος could
be the translation. It could hardly be “Memoriae M. Othonis,” as δηλώσει
would not be the natural rendering of this, and, besides, this form of dedication was not in use before the end of the 2nd century. See Wilm. 244.'")

Mausoleo: see on Vesp. 23, 4; the word, of course, is used derisively
by Vitellius.
pugionem

misit. dedicandum: swords and daggers were frequently dedicated to the gods in their temples: Caligula dedicated to
Mars Ultor three swords of his would-be assassins (Calig. 24, 3); Nero
dedicated to Jupiter Vindex the dagger of Scaevinus, who was involved in
the conspiracy of Piso against Nero (Tac. A. xv 74); Caracalla dedicated
the sword with which he slew his own brother (Dio lxxiii 4); the Arverni
dedicated a dagger which they claimed to have captured from Julius
Caesar in Gaul (Plut. Caes. 26).

Agrippinensem coloniam: Cologne (Köln), where Vitellius had been
first saluted as emperor (c. 8, 1). The original name of the town was
"Oppidum Ubiorum" (Tac. A. i 36). The Ubii, a German tribe on the
E. of the Rhine, were induced (c. 38 в.с.) by M. Vipsanius Agrippa to
cross and settle on the left bank to avoid the attacks of the Chatti.
Agrippina, grand-daughter of this Agrippa, daughter of Germanicus, and
wife of Claudius, was born in this town and she persuaded Claudius to
plant a colony of veterans there (51. A.D.); from that time the place was
called after her "Colonia. Agrippinensis" (Tac. A. xii 27; see also
Furneaux on Tac. Germ. 28).

Marti: from the same shrine of Mars at Cologne had been taken the
sword of Julius Caesar which was presented to Vitellius when he was
acclaimed emperor; see c. 8, 1.

in Appennini iugis: from Cremona Vitellius went to Bononia (Tac.
H. ii 71) which lies immediately at the foot of the Apennines; there was
a pass across the Apennines traversed by the modern highroad from Bologna
(Bononia) to Florence (Florentia), and Vitellius may have crossed by this
pass and then proceeded by the Via Cassia to Rome; see Hofstee ad loc.

pervigilium: see on Galb. 4, 3. This pervigilium of Vitellius was
nominally a religious thanksgiving for his victory over Otho, but presumably
it took the form of those all-night orgies (pervigilia ac bacchanalia) of
which Tacitus speaks so contemptuously in H. ii 69 (quoted above on ‘nulla
disciplina''). Caligula, according to Suet. Calig. 54, ordered a pervigilium for the sole purpose of taking advantage of the licence of the
occasion to make an auspicious first appearance on the stage: Nec alia
de causa videtur eo die, quo periit, pervigilium indixisse quam ut initium
in scaenam prodeundi licentia temporis auspicaretur. Dessau (Gesch.
röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1, 338) thinks it probable that the pervigilium of Vitellius
took place at the temple of Jupiter Appenninus, which was at the highest
point of the pass by which the Via Flaminia crossed the Apennines.

classicum: classicum primarily meant a signal given by the trumpet
(classicum appellatur quod buccinatores per cornu dicunt, Veget. ii 22),
and at times denoted the trumpet itself. As a signal the classicum seems
to have been given by all the trumpeters together (e.g. as a signal for
battle) and it was always given in the presence of the commander-in-chief
(imperator) and by his orders. See Daremberg-Saglio, i 753.

paludatus: Tacitus is probably right in stating that Vitellius laid
aside the paludamentum (see on Galb. 11) and assumed the toga praetexta
before entering the city, to avoid entering it as a conqueror: H. ii 89,
Ipse Vitellius a ponte Mulvio (2 miles N. of Rome) insigni equo, paludatus
accinctusque senatum ac populum ante se agens, quo minus ut captam
urbem ingrederetur, amicorum consilio deterritus, sumpta praetexta et
composito agmine incessit. Alexander Severus on his accession made a
similar concession to established usage by assuming the toga and entering
the city on foot (Dio lxxiv 1). The theory of Heraeus (on Tac. l.c.) is
that Vitellius wore military garb when entering by the Porta Flaminia
(which was extra pomerium and therefore ad urbem), but donned the toga
before passing through the Porta Carmentalis (?) into the city itself, and
that Suetonius, prone to exaggerate, describes him as paludatus when
entering the city. One of the coins in honour of his entry represents him
as togatus, another as paludatus.

signa atque vexilla: the signa were the standards of the maniples (see
on Galb. 12, 2); the vexilla here mentioned are probably the standards of
the cavalry, as in Tac. H. ii 18, 43, and other passages where we find the
two words joined.

sagulatis: the form sagulatus is only found here; sagatus (Cic., etc.)
occurs in Iul. 48. The sagum, or cloak, of the ordinary soldier was known
as the sagum (sagulum) gregale (e.g. Liv. vii 34), more rarely as paludamentum (e.g. Liv. i 26); the cleak of the officers was also called sagum
(Sall. Hist. ii frag. 21) but more frequently sagulum (e.g. Suet. Aug. 26, 1:
Val. Max. iii 2, 21); it differed from that of the private by its brighter
colour; the sagulum of the commander-in-chief, which was usually called
paludamentum, was, as a rule, scarlet or purple (sometimes white): cf.
Sil. Ital. Pun. iv 516, umeroque refulget | sanguinei patrium saguli decus:
ib. xvii 526, umeris imponit honorem | fulgentis saguli: Auct. Bell. Afr. 57,
cum Scipio sagulo purpureo uti solitus esset: Val. Max. i 6, 11, сит
in proelium exeuntibus album aut purpureum (paludamentum) dari soleret.
comitibus: “staff” “suite"; see on Vesp. 4, 4.

commilitonum: this is cited in the Thes. Ling. Lat. among the
passages where commilito (“evanida vi praepositionis'") is nearly
synonymous with miles gregarius; cf. Curt. vi 11, 2: Apul. Met. ix 39:
Macer Dig. xlix, 16, 12. Julius Caesar addressed his soldiers by the
blandius nomen of commilitones (Iul. 67). After the civil wars Augustus
never did so, and he forbade the use of the term by his sons and stepsons
who held military commands, regarding it as undignified and subversive
of discipline (Aug. 25). But when the Julio-Claudian line ended with
Nero, the emperors became much more dependent on the soldiers, and
freely addressed them as commilitones; cf. Galb. 20, 1 and Tac. H. i 35
(quoted on Galb. 19, 2). See Hardy on Plin. Ep. x 19 and 20, where Pliny
as governor of Bithynia asks Trajan whether he should use publici servi
or milites to guard prisoners, and Trajan replies: ‘“Nihil opus est ad
continendas custodias plures commilitones converti.”

§2. divino humanoque iure neglecto: cf. Tac. H. ii 91, adeo omnis
humani divinique iuris expers pari libertorum, amicorum socordia, velut
inter temulentos agebat: Dio lxv 2, αὐτὸς δὲ τῇ τε τρυφῇ καὶ τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ
προσκείμενος οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων οὔτε τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων οὔτε τῶν θείων ἐφρόντιζεν.

Alliensi die: July 18, the day on which in 390 B.C. the Romans
suffered a disastrous defeat from the Gauls under Brennus at the Allia, a
tributary of the Tiber, 11 miles N. of Rome. On the same day in 477 B.C.
the 300 Fabii were annihilated at the Cremera (another tributary of the
Tiber) by the Veientes. Cf. Tac. H. ii 91, Apud civitatem cuncta interpretantem funesti ominis loco acceptum est, quod maximum pontificatum
adeptus Vitellius de caerimoniis publicis xv kalendas Augustas edixisset
antiquitus infausto die Cremerensi Alliensique cladibus. The dies Alliensis
became for ever a dies religiosus at Rome; cf. Liv. vi 1, De diebus religiosis
agitari coeptum, diemque a.d. quintum decimum Kal. Sextiles, duplici clade
insignem a posteriore clade Alliensem appellarunt insignemque religione rei ullius publice privatimque agendae fecerunt: Cic. Att. ix 5.
...
pontificatum maximum: see on Tit. 9, 1.

comitia in decem annos ordinavit: Tac. H. iii 55, ipse
festinare
comitia, quibus consules in multos annos destinabat. For ordinavit see on
Vesp. 23, 2. The naming of magistrates for several years in advance had
been first done by the dictator Julius Caesar; Iul. 76, 3, Eadem licentia
spreto patrio more magistratus in plures annos ordinavit. Though the
senate nominally had the right of choice, the emperor under the Lex de
imperio had the right of commendatio of his own candidates (candidati
Caesaris) for a certain number of places (e.g. 2 out of 20 quaestors, 4 out
of 12 praetors; see Furneaux, Tac. Ann. Introd. c. vi); these candidates:
were elected as a matter of course. The emperor also claimed a wider
right of nominatio to all vacant posts, and as those "nominated" by him
were sure of the preference, the elections became a mere farce. Vitellius
however at the elections in July 69 went through the pretence of speaking
and canvassing for the candidates whom he had named as consules suffecti
for the rest of that year (Tac. H. ii 71, 91).

perpetuum consulem: so he is described in an inscription at Rome
(C.I.L. vi 929, Dessau 242): A. Vitellius L. f. imperator cos. perp.; on a
fragmentary milestone in Sardinia there is an inscription (C.I.L. x 8016,
Dessau 243) which Dessau restores as : [a] Turre xliii | [im]p. A. Vitellius
c[os. perp]. A life consulship was decreed to Caligula, but he declined it
(Dio lix 6); the senate also decreed continui consulatus to Nero (Tac. 4.
xiii 41); Domitian was made consul for a period of ten years (Dio lxvii 4),
and Tiberius for five years (Dio lviii 4).

inferias Neroni dedit: Tac. H. ii 95, Laetum foedissimo cuique apud
bonos invidiae fuit, quod extructis in campo Martio aris inferias Neroni
fecisset. Caesae publice victimae cremataeque; facem Augustales subdidere, quod sacerdotium
Caesar Tiberius Iuliae genti sacravit: Dio
1xv 7, ὅτι μέντοι τὸν Νέρωνα μιμεῖσθαι ἤθελε καὶ ἐνήγισε (= inferias dedit) τε αὐτῷ, καὶ
ὅτι τοσαῦτα ἐς τὰ δεῖπνα ἀνήλισκεν, οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι καὶ κατὰ ταῦτ᾽ ἔχαιρον, οἱ δὲ δὴ νοῦν·
ἔχοντες ἤχθοντο: Eutrop. vii 18, 4, Hic cum Neroni similis esse vellet atque
id adeo prae se ferret, ut etiam exequias Neronis, quae humiliter sepultae
fuerant, honoraret. From the Campus Martius one could look up to the
"Hill of Gardens" (Collis Hortulorum, Monte Pincio) and see the tomb
of the Domitii where the ashes of Nero were placed; cf. Suet. Ner. 50,
Reliquias gentili Domitiorum monimento condiderunt, quod prospicitur
e campo Martio impositum colli Hortulorum. For the slavish devotion of
Vitellius to Nero see on c. 4 supr.

citharoedum: see on Dom. 4, 4. On citharoedi at Roman banquets see
Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 175; Marquardt, Privatl.2 151. For Nero's performances as a citharoedus cf. c. 4, n.

dominico: dominicus (sc. liber) or dominicum was apparently the name
of a book containing Nero's compositions (or favourite pieces) which may
have been published by himself. Hofstee proposed to read dominicis (sc.
canticis). The adj. dominicus (from dominus "lord and master'') is used
at times in reference to the emperors, e.g. Cod. Iust. vii 38, res ("property'") dominica, coloni dominici. For the title dominus applied to the
emperor see on Dom. 13, 1. The variant Domitio (XN) is read in the early
editions. Nero's original name was L. Domitius Ahenobarbus, but after
his adoption by Claudius he was called Nero Claudius Caesar Drusus
Germanicus, and the use of his earlier name in addressing him was regarded by him as an insult (Ner. 7 and 41: Tac. A. xii 41); Oudendorp
rightly says that an admirer like Vitellius would not so speak of him.

diceret:
caneret, a poetical use found also in post-class. prose.

Neroniana cantica: for cantica see on Galb. 13. References to Nero's
=
performances are found in Suet. Ner. 21, Niobam se cantaturum .. pronuntiavit Tragoedias quoque cantavit personatus (“wearing a mask")
heroum deorumque, item heroidum ac dearum, personis ("masks") effectis
ad similitudinem oris sui et feminae, prout quamque diligeret. Inter cetera
cantavit Canacen parturientem, Oresten matricidam, Oedipodem excaecatum,
Herculem insanum: Dio lxi 20, ἐκιθαρῴδησέ τε῎Αττιν τινὰ ἢ Βάκχας: id. lxii 18,
τὴν σκευὴν τὴν κιθαρῳδικὴν λαβὼν ἦσεν ἅλωσιν ᾿Ἰλίου (cf. Suet. Ner. 38, 2, halosin
Ilii in illo suo scaenico habitu decantavit; these were probably lines from
his own poem Τρωϊκά): Philostrat. vit. Apoll. iv 39: Tac. A. xv 33, xvi 4:
Juv. viii 228 sq.

exultans: to jump up (exultare) or rise to one's feet (assurgere) was
a regular method of showing approval; e.g. Aug. 53, 1, сит universi
exultantes comprobassent: Ner. 24, 1, inter exultationes succlamationesque
populi: Plin. Ep. vii 24, exultabant, plaudebant, mirabantur: ix 23, omnes
repente consurgerent laudarentque: vi 17, non labra diduxerunt, non
moverunt manum, non denique adsurrexerunt, saltem lassitudine sedendi.

histrionum et aurigarum: these two classes are mentioned by Tacitus
as among the crowd which flocked from the city to welcome Vitellius on
his approach: H. ii 87, adgregabantur e plebe flagitiosa per obsequia
Vitellio cogniti scurrae histriones aurigae, quibus ille amicitiarum dehonestamentis mire gaudebat: ib. 71, quantoque magis propinquabat,
tanto corruptius iter inmixtis histrionibus et spadonum gregibus et cetero
Neronianae aulae ingenio. For the interest of Vitellius in aurigae see
c. 7, 1 and c. 4.

Asiatici: within three months after the accession of Vitellius this
infamous freedman had acquired a power at Rome which rivalled the sway
exercised in Nero's reign by the freedmen such as Polyclitus and Patrobius:
Тас. Н. ii 95, Nondum quartus a victoria mensis, et libertus Vitellii
Asiaticus Polyclitos Patrobios et vetera odiorum nomina (“the hated
names of earlier times") aequabat. Nemo in illa aula probitate aut industria certavit; unum ad potentiam iter, prodigis epulis et sumptu gula
ganeaque satiare inexplebiles Vitellii libidines. Asiaticus paid a heavy
penalty for this "mala potentia"; after the death of Vitellius, when
Mucianus and the victorious Flavians entered the city, he was crucified as
a slave, though Vitellius had made him an eques: H. iv 11, Asiaticus
enim (is libertus) malam potentiam servili supplicio expiavit. In Sidon.
Apollin. Εp. v 7 he is mentioned in a list of Rome's most notorious freedmen: Hi sunt, quorum comparationi digitum tollerent (i.e. "would acknowledge themselves inferior'") Narcissus, Asiaticus, Massa, Marcellus, Carus,
Parthenius, Licinus, et Pallas. Plutarch (Galb. 20) inaccurately says that
he was a freedman of Galba.

Puteolis: Puteoli, mod. Pozzuoli, on the coast of Campania near Baiae
and Naples.

poscam: a mixture of vinegar and water (ὀξύκρατον), which was
drunk by the lower classes, by slaves (e.g. Plaut. Mil. 836, alii [servorum]
ebrii sunt, alii poscam potitant), and by soldiers (e.g. Spart. Hadr. 10,
cibis etiam castrensibus libenter utens, hoc est larido, caseo, et posca).

statimque: -que is here used nearly as equivalent to autem or sed;
cf. Iul. 19, 1, is
quoniam inferior gratia esset, pecuniaque polleret.
This use is generally found after a negative, e.g. Cic. Tusc. i 29, 71,
Socrates nec patronum quaesivit nec iudicibus supplex fuit, adhibuitque
liberam contumaciam: Ov. Met. ii 811, quae neque dant flammas lenique
vapore cremantur; less often after an affirmative, e.g. Sall. Cat. 3, 3, studio
ad rempublicam latus sum ibique multa mihi advorsa fuere.

solvit: this reading is found in the ed. Basil., 1533; the MSS. give
coluit. Oudendorp proposed ex(s)olvit.
in deliciis habuit: = usus est ut delicato suo (see on Tit. 7, 2).

gravatus: this verb is always a deponent in Suetonius (as in Cic.)
and is used either with the acc. (Aug. 72, 3; Tib. 50, 2; Ner. 34, 1;
cf. Hor. C. iv 11, 27, Pegasus terrenum equitem gravatus) or with the
infin. (Aug. 34, 2; so Cic., Caes., Liv.); this is the only place where it is
used with ob.

circumforano: “journeying about to market-towns or fairs (fora)'';
cf. Cic. Cluent. 40, pharmacopola circumforan(e)us “an itinerant quack":
Apul. Met. ix 4, circumforaneum mendicabulum “a vagrant beggar." The
termination -anus (not -aneus) is strongly attested here; for the variations
in the MSS. of other authors see Thes. Ling. Lat.

lanistae: lanista (connected with lanius "butcher'") was the title of
the trainer in the school (ludus) where gladiators were kept; cf. Juv. xi 8,
scripturus leges et regia verba lanistae (see Mayor's note): Suet. Iul. 26, 3,
Tirones neque in ludo neque per lanistas sed in domibus per equites
Romanos erudiebat. The body of gladiators under a lanista was called
a familia; Augustus during a scarcity of food at Rome expelled the
lanistarum familiae (Aug. 42, 3). The lanistae not merely trained gladiators,
they also bought, sold, and let them out for hire. Itinerant lanistae engaged
in trafficking of this kind, and gave gladiatorial spectacles in country towns
or supplied gladiators; cf. Tac. A. iv 62, where there is a description
of a terrible disaster at Fidenae, in which 50,000 were killed or maimed,
owing to the collapse of a badly constructed amphitheatre where a speculative freedman was giving a display of gladiators.
muneris: sc. gladiatorii; cf. Tit. 8, 2.
provincia: Africa; see cс. 5.

primo imperii die: April 19, 69 A.D.; see on Oth. 11, 2 and Vesp. 6, 3,
principatus dies. Tacitus (H. ii 57) says that the honour was conferred
on Asiaticus when Vitellius, on his march from Germany, heard of his
victory at Bedriacum and the death of Otho.
aureis anulis: the sign of equestrian rank; see on Galb. 10, 3; 14, 2.
super cenam: for this use of super see on Tit. 8, 1.

rogantibus pro eo cunctis: Tac. H. ii 57, Postulante exercitu, ut
libertum suum Asiaticum equestri dignitate donaret, inhonestam adulationem
compescuit. Dein mobilitate ingenii, quod palam abnuerat, inter secreta
convivii largitur, honoravitque Asiaticum anulis, foedum mancipium
('slave'") et malis artibus ambitiosum.
vel praecipue: see on Dom. 19.

luxuriae...deditus: cf. Dio lxv 2, τῇ τε τρυφῇ καὶ τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ προσκείμενος :
ib. c. 3, καὶ ἐγένετο ὁ χρόνος ὁ τῆς ἀρχῆς αὐτοῦ σύμπας οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ μέθαι τε καὶ κῶμοι:
Eutrop. vii 18, Vitellius cum multo dedecore imperavit, et gravi saevitia
notabilis, praecipue ingluvie et voracitate, quippe cum de die quarto vel
quinto (i.e. 4 or 5 times a day) feratur epulatus: Oros. vii 8, 7, incredibili voracitatis appetitu: Sidon. Carm. iv 1.08, mihi (i.e. Rome) foeda
Vitelli | intulit ingluvies ventrem, qui tempore parvo|regnans sero perit:
Tac. H. ii 62, 95 (quoted on c. 10, 2 and c. 12): Lamprid. Heliogab. 24,
cenas et Vitellii et Apicii vicit (Heliogabalus).
saevitiae: Suetonius deals with this in the following chapter.

trifariam
quadrifariam: for the formation of these adverbs see
on plurifariam, c. 9. Dio (lxv 4) enumerates the feasts of Vitellius each
day: ἀκράτισμα (iantaculum), ἄριστον (prandium), δεῖπνον (cena), and
μεταδόρπια (comissationes).

iantacula: see on c. 7, 3. Though usually the iantaculum was a very
frugal meal, Vitellius made it a luxurious repast.
prandia: see on Dom. 21, prandebat ad satietatem.

cenas: after the prandium, or lunch, a siesta (meridiatio) was taken;
then came gymnastics or other exercises, followed by the bath, and dinner
(cena) was usually taken about the 9th hour (3.45 p.m. in summer, 2.15 in
winter). For a detailed account of the cena see Marquardt, Privatl.2
297 sqq.
comissationes: see on Dom. 21. To eat anything during a comissatio,
except as a relish to the wine, was most unusual.

facile omnibus sufficiens: though Vitellius was able to stand this
gluttony, his fellow-diners suffered badly from over-eating; cf. Dio lxv 2,
ἀφ' οὗπερ (sc. τὸ ἐξεμεῖν) καὶ ἀνταρκεῖν ἠδύνατο· ἐπεὶ οἵγε συνδειπνοῦντες αὐτῷ πάντες
κακῶς ἀπήλλασσον. Dio adds a good story about Vibius Crispus (Dom. 3, 1)
who was ill from the effects for some days and not able to attend the
banquets, and who wittily remarked "Had I not been ill, I would have
been killed entirely” (εἰ μὴ ἐνενοσήκειν, πάντως ἂν ἀπολώλειν).

vomitandi consuetudine: cf. Dio, l.c., τὸ πλεῖστον καὶ τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τῆς
νυκτὸς ἐδαπάνα, ἀπλήστως τε ἐμφορούμενος (‘"filling himself”) καὶ συνεχῶς πάντα
ἐξεμῶν, ὡς μόνῃ τῇ παρόδῳ τῶν σιτίων τρέφεσθαι. Vomiting, as a remedy for over-eating, was not confined to mere gluttons like Vitellius; it was commonly
resorted to by the wealthier classes at Rome, and the utility of it is recognised, and its use defined, by medical writers, e.g. Celsus (i 3). The
emperor Claudius was relieved in this way; Claud. 33, Nec temere umquam
triclinio abscessit nisi distentus ac madens, et ut statim supino ac per
somnum hianti pinna in os induceretur ad exonerandum stomachum.
Martial refers to the practice (iii 82, 9; vii 67, 10; etc.); Seneca (ad
Helv. 10, 3) denounces it: vomunt ut edant, edunt ut vomant, et epulas
quas toto orbe conquirunt, nec concoquere ("digest'") dignantur. See
Marquardt, op. cit. 330.

indicebat aliud alii: cf. Ner. 27, 3, indicebat familiaribus cenas (“he
invited himself to dinner at his friends' houses"). Dio (lxv 4) says
that the providing of feasts for Vitellius was a heavy burden on his
hosts, but that the wealthy vied in their eagerness to entertain him.
Elagabalus had each course of a banquet served at the house of a different
friend: Lamprid. Heliogab. 30, Celebravit item tale convivium, ut apud
amicos singulos singuli missus appararentur, et cum alter maneret in
Capitolio, alter in Palatio, alter super Aggerem, alter in Caelio, alter trans
Tiberim, et ut quisque mansisset, tamen per ordinem in eorum domibus
singula fercula ederentur, ireturque ad omnium domos: sic unum convivium vix acto die finitum est.

minus: Ursinus would read minoris, but cf. Ner. 30, 3, numquam minus
mille carrucis fecisse iter traditur. Such constructions are common in the
Latin of all periods (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 471).
apparatus: cf. c. 10, 2.

quadringenis milibus nummum: about £3,400. In Ner. 27, 3 Suetonius
tells us that one of Nero's friends, to whose house Nero had invited himself
for dinner, expended 4,000,000 sesterces on a cena mitellita, and another
expended considerably more on a cena rosaria. Dio says that Vitellius in
his brief reign spent 900 million sesterces on dinners, and that on one
dinner he expended 4 million sesterces; cf. Tac. H. ii 95, noviens milliens
sestertium paucissimis mensibus intervertisse ("squandered'') creditur:
iii 36. Gibbon (Decline and Fall of the Rom. Emp., c. 3) stigmatizes
"the beastly Vitellius, who consumed in mere eating at least six millions
of our money in about seven months, and whose vices it is not easy to
express with dignity or even decency.”

§ 2. famosissima: cf. Eutrop. vii 18, notissima certe cena memoriae
mandata est, quam ei Vitellius frater exhibuit, in qua super ceteros sumptus
duo milia piscium, septem avium adposita traduntur. Suetonius nearly
invariably uses famosus in a bad sense ("infamous" "notorious”), but
in Calig. 19, 2, we find curriculo biiugi famosorum (= celebrium) equorum.

super ceteras: for this pleonastic addition cf. Dom. 12, 2, praeter
ceteros acerbissime: Galb. 9, 1, multo praeter ceteras altiorem crucem.

cena adventicia: it was customary to give a dinner to a friend or
relative who had arrived safely from a journey (Gr. δεῖπνον ὑποδεκτικόν);
cf. Plaut. Bacch. 534, Salvos quom peregre advenis | cena detur: id. Stich.
512, Et magis par fuerat me vobis dare cenam advenientibus. The phrase
“adventicia (cena)" is used metaph. in Petron. Satyr. 91, quoties theatrum,
ut recitarem aliquid, intravi, hac me adventicia (sc. lapidibus) excipere
frequentia solet. Martial (xii praef.) uses “adventoria (cena)" of a book
of epigrams which he has provided to entertain a friend on his arrival.
The ante-penult. is long in adjectives in -icius formed from participles;
see Duff on Juv. iii 265.
fratre: Lucius Vitellius; see c. 3, 1; 5, 1.

lectissimorum piscium: cf. Plaut. Most. 730, Vino et victu, piscatu
probo electili | vitam colitis. The fish most highly esteemed at Rome were
the acipenser (sturgeon), aurata (gilt-bream), lupus (pike), scarus (wrasse ?),
mullus (mullet), murena (lamprey), and rhombus (turbot). See
Marquardt, op. cit. 432 sqq.

avium: these might include the lagopus (white grouse), scolopax (snipe),
attagen (hazel-hen), turdus (fieldfare), perdix (partridge), miliaria (ortolan),
ficedula (beccafico), coturnix (quail), pavo (peacock), Africa or Numidica
avis (guinea-fowl), phasianus or tetrao (pheasant), grus (crane), ciconia
(stork), phoenicopterus (flamingo).
patina: a deep earthenware dish (like the Gr. τρύβλιον) used for
cooking (especially fish, also ragoûts, etc., cf. Plaut. Asin. 180 where
patinarius "stewed" is opposed to assus "roast'"), and also for serving
food (cf. Plaut. Pseud. 840, Hor. Sat. ii 8, 43, Affertur squillas inter
murena natantes | in patina porrecta). Costly patinae for use at table
were sometimes made of silver. Aesopus, the tragic actor, had a patina
(of pottery) worth 100,000 sesterces (Plin. N.H. xxxv 163). Pliny (l.c.)
says that the patina of Vitellius cost 1,000,000 sesterces (£8,500) and that a
special oven had to be built for the making of it: At, Hercules, Vitellius
in principatu suo decies sestertium condidit patinam, cui faciendae fornax
in campis exaedificata erat, quoniam eo pervenit luxuriae ut etiam fictilia
pluris constent quam murrina (‘‘myrrhine vases''). Propter hanc Mucianus
(Vespasian's general, see Vesp. 6, 4) altero consulatu suo in conquestione
exprobravit patinarum paludes ("dishes as broad as the Pomptine marsh'')
Vitellii memoriae, non illa foediore, cuius veneno Asprenati reo Cassius
Severus (see Vitell. 2, 1) accusator obiciebat interisse convivas cxxx.
(lxv 3) differs in saying that the patina of Vitellius was made of silver,
being too large for pottery, and adds that it was afterwards melted down
by Hadrian: ἐπειδὴ ἀδύνατον ἦν κεραμεᾶν τηλικαύτην γενέσθαι, ἀργύρου τε ἐποιήθη,
καὶ ἔμεινε πολὺν χρόνον, ὥσπερ τι ἀνάθημα (res deis consecrata), μέχρις οὗ ῾Αδριανὸς
αὐτὴν ἰδὼν συνεχώνευσεν.
Dio
clipeum Minervae πολιούχου: the reference, most probably, is to the
colossal bronze statue of Athena Promachos by Pheidias on the Acropolis
at Athens. It was 50-60 ft. high, and represented the goddess holding up
her spear and shield in the attitude of battle; the shield is said to have
been engraved at a later period by Mys. Some think that the statue
referred to is the chryselephantine (gold and ivory) statue of Athena in
the Parthenon, the greatest of Pheidias' works at Athens. It was 40 ft.
high and represented the goddess with a spear in her left hand and an
image (4 cubits high) of Victory in her right. On the inner side of her
shield, which rested on the ground beside her, was embossed the battle
of gods and giants, and on the outer side the battle of the Amazons and
Athenians. πολιούχου was restored by Stephanus for τονδυχου of the MSS.
The title πολιοῦχος “protectress of the city" was often applied to Athena,
e.g. Aristoph. Eq. 581, Nub. 602, Αυ. 827; so Παλλάς πολιάοχος, Pind. 0. 5,
24, etc. Boissevain thinks that Vitellius was playing on the two words
πολιοῦχος and πολυοῦχος ("holding much'').

scarorum iocinera: it is uncertain what particular fish the scarus
was; it has been identified with the wrasse ("parrot-wrasse, Butler and
Owen on Apul. Apol. 39). Pliny (N.H. ix 62) describes it as the most
highly prized of fish, brought originally from the Carpathian sea (between
Rhodes and Crete) by Optatus, praefectus classis under Tiberius, and
planted in the sea between Ostia and Campania, where it was preserved
for the first five years. Ennius in his Hedyphagetica (cited in Apul. Apol.
39) calls it "cerebrum Iovis" (a proverbial expression with the Persians
for a rare delicacy): Quid scarŭ(m) praeterii cerebrum Iovi' paene supremi?
See also Athenaeus vii 113; Hor. Epod. 2, 50; id. Sat. ii 2, 22; Petron.
Satyr. 119; Mart. xiii 84.

phasianarum: the fem. form is used also in Plin. N.H. instead of the
more usual phasianus. According to tradition the pheasant was introduced
from the Phasis in Colchis by the Argonauts; cf. Mart. xiii 72, Argoa
primum sum transportata carina: | ante mihi notum nil nisi Phasis erat:
Petron. Satyr. 79, iam Phasidos unda | orbata est avibus. Seneca (ad
Helv. 10) denounces those who imported them to Rome: Dii istos deaeque
perdant, quorum luxuria tam invidiosi imperii fines transcendit.
Phasin capi volunt, quod ambitiosam popinam instruat.
Ultra

pavonum: the peacock was said to have been brought from Asia to
Samos and thence to Greece and Italy. The orator Hortensius, Cicero's
rival, first had it served at a banquet in Rome to celebrate his entry to
the college of augurs (Plin. N.H. x 45). It became a regular dish at all
sumptuous entertainments; cf. Varr. R.R. iii 6; Hor. Sat. ii 2, 23; Juv. i
143; etc.
among the contents of
ἐγκεφάλους (cerebella) καὶ
"redcerebella: mentioned also by Dio (lxv 3)
the mighty patina of Vitellius: γλώττας τε καὶ
ἥπατα (iocinera) καὶ ἰχθύων καὶ ὀρνίθων τινῶν ἐμβαλών. The dimin. cerebellum
was properly only used of the brains of animals other than man. The
brains of various birds were esteemed a dainty; cf. Lamprid. Heliogab. 20,
exhibuit magides (“dishes'') extis mullorum refertas et cerebellis
phoenicopterum ... et cerebellis turdorum: ib. 30, sescentorum struthionum
("ostriches") capita una cena multis mensis exhibuit ad edenda cerebella.

linguas phoenicopterum: the flamingo (Gr. φοινικόπτερος
winged'') was a native of the banks of the Nile (Heliod. Aethiop. vi 268);
the delicate flavour of its tongue was discovered by the notorious gourmet
Apicius (fl. 25 A.D.): Plin. N.H. x 133, Phoenicopteri linguam praecipui
saporis esse Apicius docuit nepotum omnium altissimus gurges; cf. Mart.
xiii 71: Sen. Ep. 110, non magnam rem facis, quod non desideras
linguas phoenicopterorum et alia portenta luxuriae iam tota animalia
fastidientis et certa membra ex singulis eligentis. In the temple which
Caligula erected to himself as a god flamingoes were among the victims
offered (Calig. 22).
Siculo

murenarum: lampreys were brought from the Straits of Messina
(fretum Siculum) to the fish ponds (piscinae) at Rome: Macrob. Sat. iii
15, 7, arcessebantur murenae ad piscinas nostrae urbis ab usque freto
illic enim optimae a prodigis esse creduntur; cf. Juv. v 99,
Virroni murena datur, quae maxima venit | gurgite de Siculo. A family
of the gens Licinia was given the name "Murena" from the fish:
Colum. viii 16, 5, Iam enim celebres erant deliciae popinales cum ad mare
deferrentur vivaria, quorum studiosissimi, velut ante devictarum gentium
Numantinus et Isauricus, ita Sergius Aurata (the fish "aurata" was the
gilt-bream) et Licinius Murena captorum piscium laetabantur vocabulis.

lactes: Gr. γαλακτίδες, the smaller entrails, "tender small guts"
(Holland). Priscian says that the sing. is haec lactis. Lampridius
(Heliogab. 23) mentions among the extravagant eccentricities of Elagabalus
““murenarum lactibus et luporum (“pikes'') in locis mediterraneis rusticos
pavit." The lactes of both men and beasts are often mentioned, especially
by the comic writers and satirists, e.g. Titin. (90, Ribb.): Pompon. (61,
•
Ribb.): Plaut. Curcul. 319, Pseud. 320: Persius 2, 30, Qua tu mercede
deorum | emeris auriculas? pulmone et lactibus unctis? ("a dishful of
lungs and greasy chitterlings," Conington).

a Parthia usque: the ransacking of sea and land to provide dainties
for Vitellius is described in Dio lxv 3: πάντα τε γὰρ τὰ τιμιώτατα καὶ ἀπ'
αὐτοῦ τοῦ ὠκεανοῦ, ἵνα μηδὲν εἴπω πλέον, καὶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς καὶ ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης
συνήγετο, καὶ πολυτελῶς οὕτως ἐσκευάζετο ὥστε Οὐιτελλιανὰ καὶ νῦν ἐξ ἐκείνου καὶ
πέμματα καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ βρώματα ὀνομάζεσθαι. Parthia and the fretum
Hispanicum are used here for the extreme E. and W., usually denoted by
India and Spain (e.g. Sen. N.Q. i pr. 13, ab ultimis litoribus Hispaniae
usque ad Indos). The genuineness of the reading Parthia has been
suspected, and various conjectures have been made, such as Carpathio (R
has pathia), Carteia, Carpetano.
freto Hispanico: the Straits of Gibraltar, also called fretum Gaditanum,
fretum Herculeum, fretum Tartessium, fretum Iberum, etc.

per navarchos ac triremes: in the Roman fleet the title navarchus
(ναύαρχος) seems to have been applied strictly to the captain of a larger
ship (quadrireme, quinquireme, etc.), trierarchus denoting the captain of
a smaller; but at times we find navarchus used for a commander of a
squadron. Cf. Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 513; Mommsen on C.I.L. x 3340;
Furneaux-Pelham on Tac. A. xv 51. For an example of the use of the
Roman fleet to import luxuries see on
“scarorum” above.

§ 3. non.. modo sed quoque: when quoque is thus used in the
second clause in place of the regular etiam, it marks a mere addition and
not an intensification or climax. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii 59, where
numerous instances from Cic. and Liv. are given.
profundae gulae: see on c. 7, 1.

viscus: the sing. is only found in poetry and post-Aug. prose. Both
viscus and viscera are used at times for “flesh"; cf. Serv. on Aen. vi 253
(et solida imponunt taurorum viscera flammis): Non exta dicit, sed carnes;
nam viscera sunt quidquid inter ossa et cutem est; unde etiam visceratio
dicitur convivium de carnibus factum. See Munro on Lucr. i 837.

farris frusta: "bits of the sacrificial cakes (liba)." Servius, commenting on adorea liba in Aen. vii 109, says: Ador proprie est genus
farris, Liba autem sunt placentae de farre, melle, et oleo, sacris aptae.
These cakes were either simply placed on the altar during the religious
ceremony or burnt in the fire. The reading is very uncertain; the principal
MSS. have merely farris, the others farra and farris frusta (-tra).
Preud 'homme reads farris frusta; Ihm, keeping farris, marks paene as
corrupt. Various corrections have been proposed: farris grana (Oudendorp);
farcimina (Bentley); farris panes (G. Becker, regarding the following
paene as a corruption of panes); liba farris (Roth). Of these conjectures
Becker's is the most attractive, though panem (cf. Catull. 59, quoted below)
seems preferable to panes and more likely to be corrupted into paепе.

paene rapta e foco: cf. Ter. Eunuch, 491, e flamma petere cibum (of
stealing food placed on the funeral pyre as an offering to the di inferi):
Catull. 59, uxor Meneni, saepe quam in sepulcretis | vidistis ipso rapere de
rogo cenam, | cum devolutum ex igne prosequens panem | ab semiraso tunderetur ustore. The Gr. βωμολόχος was derived from βωμός "altar" and
2 A
λοχάω “to lie in wait," and originally meant one who hung about the
altars to steal some of the meat offered. The emperor Claudius, who
rivalled Vitellius in gluttony (‘‘cibi vinique quocumque et tempore et loco
appetentissimus,” Claud. 33), on one occasion was sitting in court when
his nostrils caught the savour of a meal being made ready for the Salii in
the temple of Mars close by; he left the tribunal and went and joined the
priests at table.
fumantia: cf. Mart. i 41, 9, quod fumantia qui tomacla raucus | circumfert tepidis cocus popinis: Sid. Ep. viii 11.

pridiana atque semesa: cf. Tib. 34, 1, Et ut parsimoniam publicam
exemplo quoque iuvaret, sollemnibus ipse cenis pridiana saepe ac semesa
obsonia apposuit; Calig. 58, 1, marcente adhuc stomacho pridiani cibi onere.
The adj. pridianus (= ἕωλος, hesternus) is post-Aug.; cf. Apul. Apol. 6:
id. Met. vii 20, xi 7. For other compounds with semi- used by Suetonius
see on seminudus c. 17, 1.
cuiuscumque:
=
cuiusvis, cuiuslibet; see on Galb. 4, 3.

necem atque supplicium: Bremi rightly regards this as one of the
places where Suetonius couples two expressions which denote practically
the same thing; cf. Iul. 49, 2, ad cyathum et vinum stetisse: ib. 68, 1,
gratuitam et sine frumento stipendioque operam: Aug. 17, 4, venenum et
virus: Ner. 15, 2, dilationis ac morae: Galb. 9, 1, desidiam segnitiamque:
Calig. 11, animadversionibus poenisque. Suetonius (like Tacitus, see
Gerber and Greef Lex. Tac.) very often uses supplicium in the sense of
supplicium capitale or capitis, e.g. a few lines later we find quendam
supplicio traditum; cf. c. 10, 1. supplicium can, of course, be used of
other punishments especially torture; cf. Cic. Imp. Pomp. 5, 11, aliquem
vinculis ac verberibus atque omni supplicio excruciatum necare. A passage
which resembles ours is Tib. 62, 1, neque tormentis neque supplicio cuiusquam pepercit, but there supplicium denotes the execution which followed
the torture.
..

societatem imperii: cf. Tib. 25, 3, celerem successionem vel certe
societatem principatus opperiri; Oth. 8, 1, and Tit. 9, 3, consors imperii.

adlicefactos: this post-class. compound is found also in Sen. Ep. 118, 8,
quod invitat ad se et adlicefacit. It is a quite unnecessary addition to the
class. adlicere (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 135).

in aquae frigidae potione: in the same way as the poison of Locusta
was administered to Britannicus: Tac. A. xiii 16, frigida in aqua adfunditur venenum, quod ita cunctos eius artus pervasit, ut vox pariter et
spiritus raperentur; cf. Justin xii 14, 9 (the poisoning of Alexander the
Great), Philippus et Iollas praegustare ac temperare potum regis soliti,
in aqua frigida venenum habuerunt, quam praegustatae iam potioni
supermiserunt.

§2. faeneratorum: Vitellius must often have had to resort to these
usurers to try to meet his multitude of creditors (see c. 7, 2). For
Vespasian's restriction on faeneratores see Vesp. 11.

stipulatorum: these stipulatores were those who had given loans to
Vitellius by the process of stipulatio or legally enforceable verbal contract
(often registered for reference in writing), which took the form of the
question and answer Spondesne? Spondeo. The questioner was called
stipulator or reus stipulandi ("person concerned with stipulating'"), the
answerer usually promissor or reus promittendi. In cases of default the
money was recoverable by the summary procedure of a condictio certae
creditae pecuniae (the condictio being 30 days' notice). The repayment of
the capital, and the payment of interest required two distinct stipulationes
(Roby, Rom. Private Law ii 11 sqq., 71 sqq.).
publicanorum: like other vectigalia, the portoria here mentioned were
levied by the publicani, a title which strictly denoted those who farmed
the taxes from the State (qui publica vectigalia conducta habent), but was
also used (like portitores) of the actual tax-collectors, slaves or freedmen
(qui operas dabant publicanis).

portorium: a "toll" or transit charge levied on merchandise carried
through a country or over a bridge, also on vehicles and on persons; cf.
Sen. Const. Sap. 14, Quid ergo? Sapiens non accedet ad fores, quas durus
ianitor obsidet? Ille vero, si res necessaria vocabit, experietur, et illum,
quisquis erit, tanquam canem acrem, obiecto cibo leniet, nec indignabitur
aliquid impendere, ut limen transeat, cogitans et in pontibus quibusdam
pro transitu dari: Labeo Dig. xix 2, 60, cum (vehiculum) pontem transiret,
redemptor eius pontis portorium ab eo exigebat, etc.: Ulp. Dig. xxiv 1, 21,
si quis pro uxore sua vectigal, quod in itinere praestari solet, solvisset.
Suetonius also uses portoria in its other sense of duties paid on foreign
imports into a country: Iul. 43, 1, (Caesar) peregrinarum mercium portoria
instituit. See further on Vesp. 1, 2, publicum quadragesimae in Asia
egit.

flagitassent: Caes. B.G. i 16 and Cic. dom. 14 are the only exx. in
class. prose of flagitare with two accusatives, except where the acc. of the
thing is a neut. pron. (Kühner-Stegmann, i 300). See on “orabat,” Vesp.
16, 3.

quendam: it is generally assumed that this was Junius Blaesus, the
governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, who had been so lavishly generous to
Vitellius on his march to Rome (see on c. 10, 2). The poisoning of Blaesus
by Vitellius is described in Tac. H. iii 39, Trepidanti (Vitellio) inter scelus
metumque, ne dilata Blaesi mors maturam perniciem, palam iussa atrocem
invidiam ferret placuit veneno grassari. Addidit facinori fidem nobili (=
notabili) gaudio, Blaesum videndo. Quin et audita est saevissima Vitellii
vox, qua se (ipsa enim verba referam) pavisse oculos spectata inimici morte
iactavit. The only point, however, in common between the stories of
Tacitus and Suetonius is the remark of Vitellius, and more probably the
stories relate to two different acts of tyranny.
coram: see on Dom. 23, 1.

pascere oculos: cf. Cic. Verr. v 65, cum eius cruciatu atque supplicio
pascere oculos animumque exsaturare vellent: id. Phil. xi 3, 8, in eius
corpore lacerando atque vexando, cum animum satiare non posset, oculos
paverit suos.
Contrast "parcere oculis," Dom. 11, 3.
2A2

§3. heres meus es: for the custom of naming the emperor as heir
see on Dom. 9, 2.
Venetae factioni: see on c. 7, 1.

interemit: Domitian behaved in an equally tyrannical manner in the
amphitheatre (Dom. 10, 1).
=

nova spe: spe novarum rerum (mutationis imperii). The plur. novae
spes is used in the same way in Tac. A. xiv 58, xvi 23; cf. A. v 4, audiri
iam et legi novas ("revolutionary'') contiones, nova patrum consulta.

opinatus: this is the reading of X; obstinatus (M); obstinatosque (G).
•

§ 4. vernaculis: "scurrilous jesters"; cf. Mart. x 3, 1, vernaculorum
dicta, where they are coupled with circulatores “glib cheap-jacks," as
also in Sen. Ben. vi 11. The vernae, or home-born slaves, were allowed
