unusual licence by their masters and encouraged in pert insolence; cf.
Hor. Sat. ii 6, 66: Sen. Prov. 1, 6, cogita nos delectari vernularum
licentia,
horum ali audaciam: Tac. H. ii 88, vernacula utebantur
urbanitate. The vernaculi perhaps inspired the parody of Vitellius' proclamation which is mentioned here. A similar mock proclamation ridiculing
an enactment of Julius Caesar is quoted below (see note on "bonum
factum"), and in Iul. 20, 2, Suetonius describes how, when Julius Caesar
utterly ignored Bibulus his colleague in the consulship, the wits (urbani)
would sign and seal documents as "Done in the consulship of Julius and
Caesar'' (Iulio et Caesare consulibus actum), and also circulated the verses:
Non Bibulo quiddam nuper sed Caesare factum est; | nam Bibulo fieri
consule nil memini. The reading in our passage has been much disputed.
If a change were necessary, the simplest proposal is that of Sabellicus to
omit et and read vernaculis mathematicis "saucy astrologers." Scaliger
suggested veraculis or vericulis; Turnebus divinaculis; Madvig genethliacis,
i.e. those who calculated nativities. The text, however, is probably sound.
Suetonius was thinking of the contrast between Vitellius and Nero, who
bore with remarkable patience the gibes or lampoons (dicta aut carmina)
which were posted or circulated (proscripta aut vulgata) about him; see
Ner. 39, where Suetonius gives specimens of these and adds: sed neque
auctores requisiit et quosdam per indicem delatos ad senatum adfici graviore
poena prohibuit.

mathematicis: astrologi were called mathematici from the elaborate
mathematical calculations which they employed in casting a horoscope
(“genitura,” Tit. 9, 2). Tacitus (H. i 22) describes the mathematici as
“genus hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax, quod in civitate
nostra et vetabitur semper et retinebitur." As early as 139 B.C. astrologers
were expelled from Rome and Italy by a praetor's edict (Val. Max. i 3, 3).
In 33 B.c. Agrippa drove them from the city (Dio xlix 43). They were
banished from Italy, either by senatorial decree or imperial edict, under
Tiberius in 16 A.D. (Suet. Tib. 36, Tac. A. ii 32); under Claudius in 52 A.D.
(Tac. A. xii 52); and now again under Vitellius in 69 A.D. Within a few
months they were back, and Vespasian expelled them in 70 A.D., though he
himself made use of the masters of the craft, and even allowed the people
of Ephesus to celebrate a festival in honour of an astrologer (Dio lxvi 9).

deferretur: cf. Dom. 12, 2, ad fiscum deferebantur: ib. 15, 3, hunc
delatum. Post-Aug. writers use “deferre aliquem'' (= accusare); Cicero
has "deferre nomen alicuius,” e.g. Rosc. Am. 10, 28, ut nomen huius de
parricidio deferrent. Suetonius also uses "deferre nomen,” Iul. 30, 3,
delaturum se nomen eius. See note on "delatores,” Tit. 8. 5.

inauditum: see on Galb. 14, 3.
•

exacerbatus quod propositus est: where quod is used by Suetonius
with expressions of praising, blaming, accusing, grieving, etc., it is always
followed by the subjunctive except here and in Tit. 10, 1, Ner. 6, 2.

edictum: Tacitus mentions this expulsion of the astrologers (H. ii 62,
pulsi Italia mathematici), but it is not clear from his account whether the
edict ordering it was sent on in advance to Rome from Gaul by Vitellius,
like the edict concerning his titles (c. 8, 2). Dio, lxv 1, says that Vitellius
was already in the city when he published it: ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐν τῇ ῾Ρώμῃ ἐγένετο ..
πρόγραμμα ἔθετο (edictum proposuit), δι' οὗ τοὺς ἀστρολόγους ἐξήλασε, προειπών
σφισιν ἐντὸς τῆσδε τῆς ἡμέρας (ῥητήν τινα τάξας) ἐξ ἁπάσης τῆς Ἰταλίας χωρῆσαι.
..

iubebat excederent: for this constr. see on "iussit ponerent,"
Vesp. 23, 3.

Chaldaeos: another name for the mathematici or astrologers; cf. Gell. i
9, 6, vulgus autem, quos gentilicio vocabulo Chaldaeos dicere oportet, mathematicos dicit: Cic. Div. i 1, Principio Assyrii, propter planitiem magnitudinemque regionum quas incolebant, cum caelum ex omni parte patens
atque apertum intuerentur, traiectiones motusque stellarum observaverunt;
quibus notatis, quid cuique significaretur, memoriae prodiderunt. Qua in
ratione Chaldaei, non ex artis, sed ex gentis, vocabulo nominati, diuturna
observatione siderum, scientiam putantur effecisse, ut praedici posset, quid
cuique eventurum, et quo quisque fato natus esset. Berosus, a Babylonian
priest (c. 340-270 в.с.), was the first Chaldaean who practised astrology in
Greece (Vitruv. ix 7), whence it spread to Italy. The calculations of the
Chaldaean astrologers are referred to as “Babylonii numeri’” in Hor. C. i
11, 3. See also Mayor on Juv. x 94, xiv 248, Marquardt, Staatsv. iii²
91 sqq.

dicere: edicere, the reading of Ursinus, may be correct.
..

bonum factum: a formula prefixed “ominis causa" (cf. the Gr. τύχῃ
ἀγαθῇ) to the praetor's edict; commonly represented by the abbreviation
B.F., e.g. Edict. praet. de camp. Esquil. (C.I.L. vi 31614), B.F., nei quis
intra terminos ustrinam fecisse velit. Cf. Suet. Iul. 80 (describing a
placard posted up in derision of Caesar's admission of Gauls to the senate):
Peregrinis in senatum adlectis libellus propositus est: “Bonum factum:
ne quis senatori novo curiam (the senate-house) monstrare velit'': Tertull.
Pudic. 1, O edictum turpe, cui adscribi non poterit “Bonum factum":
Plaut. Poen. 16, bonum factum esse, edicta ut servetis mea: Aur. Vict.
Vir. ill. 49, 16. Similar formulae "bene precandi et auspicandi aliquid”
are "Quod felix, seu bonum, faustumque sit reipublicae,” and “Quod
bene vertat (vortat).”
Germanicus: for this title of Vitellius see c. 8, 2.

intra eundem Kalendarum diem: in the version of the story in
Dio lxv 1 the Kalends of Oct. are not mentioned, but we are told that
the astrologers in reply published a proclamation that Vitellius should
depart this life before the end of the very day on which he actually died
(Dec. 18): καὶ αὐτῷ ἐκεῖνοι νυκτὸς ἀντιπροθέντες γράμματα, ἀντιπαρήγγειλαν
ἀπαλλαγῆναι ἐκ τοῦ βίου ἐντὸς τῆς ἡμέρας, ἐν ᾗ ἐτελεύτησε. καὶ οἱ μὲν οὕτως
ἀκριβῶς τὸ γενησόμενον προέγνωσαν. This version reflects much greater
credit on the prophetic powers of the astrologers.

ne usquam esset: usquam here means "anywhere in the land of
the living"; “nusquam esse" was used (especially in poetry) for "to be
no more," e.g. Hor. S. ii 5, 102, Ergo nunc Dama sodalis | nusquam est? :
Prop. iii 13, 58, Nusquam est delapsis Amphiaraus equis.

§ 5. suspectus in: for this constr. cf. Suet. Gramm. 16, suspectus in
filia patroni (sc. stupri): Tac. H. i 13, suspectus in Popраса.

quasi prohibuisset: Tacitus uses tamquam with suspectus, e.g. H.
iii 35, suspecta Germania, tamquam in auxiliumi Vitellii accingeretur. See
also on Tit. 5, 3, suspicio, quasi temptasset.
4

matris: Sextilia (c. 3, 1). Tacitus does not mention any such scandal,
when he describes her death: H. iii 67, Erat illi (Vitellio) et fessa aetate
parens; quae tamen paucis ante diebus opportuna morte excidium domus
praevenit, nihil principatu filii adsecuta nisi luctum et bonam famam.

vaticinante Chatta muliere: for the Chatti, a German tribe, see on
Dom. 6, 1. The MSS. here have the usual variations in the spelling of the
name: Chattha (M has this with an erasure point under the first h),
Catha, Cata (cf. Pauly-Wissowa s.v.).
Preud 'homme reads Cattha. In
Prosop. Imp. Rom. (i 323) Klebs treats Cattha as the name of the prophetess, which is probably an oversight. The veneration paid to prophetesses
by the Germans is described in Tac. Germ. 8: Inesse (sc. feminis) quin
etiam sanctum aliquid et providum putant, nec aut consilia earum aspernantur aut responsa neglegunt. Vidimus sub divo Vespasiano Velaedam
diu apud plerosque numinis loco habitam; sed et olim \Albrunam et complures alias venerati sunt, non adulatione nec tamquam facerent deas.
Velaeda (of the tribe of the Bructeri) by her prophecies had fomented the
revolt of Civilis (Tac. H. iv 61, etc.); she was brought as a prisoner to
Rome, probably under Vespasian, and she was succeeded by another prophetess, Ganna, in the reign of Domitian (Dio lxvii 5). Strabo (vii 2, 293)
gives an account of the προμάντεις ἱέρειαι of the Cimbri in Northern
Germany.
adquiescebat: see on Tit. 7, 2.

ita demum: = tum demum (Germ. so nur = dann nur, so erst = dann
erst), used by post-Aug. writers, especially in a conditional proposition;
cf. Claud. 25, 3, Seleuco regi amicitiam et societatem ita demum pollicens,
immunes praestitisset: Plin. Ep. iii 9, 11, tam numerosum agmen
reorum ita demum videbamus posse superari, si per singulos carperetur
(Hand Tursell. ii 255). See also on "demum,” Oth. 6, 3.
si
Vitellius had been first

octavo imperii mense: i.e. August, 69 A.D.
saluted as emperor on Jan. 3; see c. 8, 1. The legions in Egypt took the
oath of fealty to Vespasian on July 1; those in Judaea, either on July 3
(Тас. Н. ii 79) or July 11 (Suet. Vesp. 6, 3); those in Syria, before
July 15 (Tac. ii 81); the armies in Moesia, Dalmatia, and Pannonia then
joined his side, perhaps in August, as Suetonius says here (Tacitus, ii 85
sq., does not fix the exact time). The narrative of Suetonius is at least
misleading, for his words give the impression that the armies in Moesia
and Pannonia were the first to revolt from Vitellius, and that the armies
in Judaea and Syria also revolted in the eighth month; whereas they
revolted, according to his own showing (Vesp. 6, 3), in the seventh (July).
Hofstee suggests that septimo should be read here for octavo (i.e.
VIIIMP ..for VIIIIMP ..). In Vesp. 6, 2 Suetonius describes how the
detachment of the Moesian army which arrived too late to aid Otho at
Betriacum, when they heard of his death, advanced as far as Aquileia and
after a turbulent outburst tried to elect Vespasian as emperor. The movement was checked for the time, and the troops returned to their allegiance
to Vitellius; but when their action became known, the prefect of Egypt
was the first to compel his legions to take the oath to Vespasian on July 1.

exercitus Moesiarum atque Pannoniae: for the legions constituting
the armies in Moesia (later Servia and Bulgaria) and Pannonia (extending along the Danube from Vienna to Belgrade) see on Vesp. 6, 2 and
Oth. 9, 3. The plur. "Moesiae" refers to the two provinces called Moesia
Superior (Western half) and Inferior (Eastern half) separated by the
Ciabrus, a trib. of the Danube. Marquardt (Staatsv. i² 303) shows that the
division took place under Domitian; and so Suetonius is guilty of an
anachronism. The defection of the Moesian and Pannonian armies from
Vitellius is described in Tac. H. ii 85 sq., Dio lxv 9.

exercitus Iudaicus et Syriaticus: see on Vesp. 6. The form
"Syriaticus" is attested by the MSS. here; Sabellicus, Beroaldus, and
many subsequent editors altered it to “Syriacus.” The adj. “Syriaticus”
(cf. Asiaticus, Hadriaticus, Cibyraticus, etc.) occurs also in Florus ii 9, 1;
11, 1; 12, 1. Elsewhere Suetonius uses ‘“Syriacus” (Vesp. 6, 4; Tib.
48, 2; Calig. 10, 1).
in verba iurarunt: for this expression see on Galb. 11, 1.

dilectum in urbe egit: Tac. H. iii 58, vocari tribus iussit, dantes
nomina sacramento adigit; superfluente multitudine curam dilectus in
consules partitur; servorum numerum et pondus argenti senatoribus indicit.
ea condicione, ut: see on c. 6.

missionem: under the normal conditions of service the honesta missio
could only be gained after a number of years. In the time of Augustus
the legionary had to serve 16 years (later, 20 years), the praetorians 16,
the urban cohorts 20, and the auxiliaries 25 (Marquardt, op. cit. ii² 542).

veteranorum commoda: the "bounties" granted to those who
obtained the honesta missio took the form either of land or of money, the
praetorians getting 5000 denarii (= 20,000 sesterces) and the legionaries
3000 denarii under Augustus (Dio lv 23); this latter sum was reduced to
1500 by Caligula (Suet. Calig. 44) and raised to 5000 by Caracalla (Dio
lxxvii 24). Cf. Galb. 12, 2.
iustae militiae: regular service in the army for a definite number of
years (legitima stipendia facere); cf. iusti milites (“regular soldiers''),
Galb. 12, 2.
..

§ 2. urgenti terra hosti: Mucianus (see Vesp. 6, 4) was advancing
from the East to Italy with the 6th legion and 13,000 vexillarii (Tас. Н.
ii 83). Before they arrived, Antonius Primus (see c. 18 infr.) with the
forces from Moesia and Pannonia had occupied the eastern districts of
Italy, won the battle of Betriacum against the Vitellians, and stormed
Cremona.
mari: Mucianus had ordered the Pontic fleet to muster at Byzantium,
contemplating the possibility of blockading the E. coast of Italy (Tac.
l.c.); the fleet at Ravenna (in N.E. Italy, on the Adriatic) under Bassus
went over to Vespasian's side (Tac. ii 100), and later the fleet at Misenum
(in Campania) revolted from Vitellius (Tac. iii 56, 57, 60).

fratrem: i.e. Lucius Vitellius, who was consul in the same year as his
brother Aulus, the future emperor (see c. 3, 1), and succeeded him as proconsul of Africa (c. 5). He was put in command of Rome when his brother
took the field against Vespasian's generals (Tac. iii 55). Following the
revolt of the fleet at Misenum, there was an outbreak in Campania, and
Lucius was sent with six cohorts and 500 cavalry to crush it. Suetonius
is incorrect in saying that the emperor gave to his brother the fleet and a
band of gladiators. We see from Tacitus (iii 57) that it was Claudius
Julianus whom the emperor sent to win back the allegiance of the fleet,
and that he sent with him a city cohort and a troop of gladiators. Julianus,
however, proved a traitor and joining forces with the mutineers he occupied
Tarracina in Campania. Lucius Vitellius effected through treachery the
capture of this city which was remissly guarded by seamen and gladiators
(Tac. iii 76, Dio lxv 16). Tacitus says that if Lucius had returned at
once with his victorious army to Rome, a conflict of great magnitude and
involving the destruction of the city must have ensued, for Tarracina was
captured at about the same time as the burning of the Capitol in the last
struggle between the Vitellian and Flavian forces (see below).

Betriacenses copias et duces: the same generals, Aulus Caecina and
Fabius Valens (see c. 9, 1), who had defeated Otho's army at Betriacum
(Oth. 9, 2), were again appointed to command for Vitellius. Caecina was
sent on in advance; Valens was delayed by illness and took no part in
the decisive second battle of Betriacum (Tac. ii 99; Joseph. Bell. Iud. iv
11, 2; Dio lxv 10). The force with Caecina was made up of the 5th and
22nd legions, with detachments of the 1st (Germanica), 14th, 15th, and 16th;
the rear was brought up by the 21st (Rapax) and the 1st (Italica) with
detachments of three British legions (2nd, 9th, 20th) and a chosen body of
auxiliaries. A body of cavalry was sent on in front to occupy Cremona
(Tac. ii 100).

superatus: decisively at the second battle of Betriacum in Oct. 69 when
his army was vanquished by that of Vespasian under Antonius Primus.
See the description of the fighting in Tac. iii 21 sqq. The victors then
burned the city of Cremona, a stronghold of the Vitellians.

proditus: the two most notorious traitors to the cause of Vitellius before
the battle of Betriacum were Lucilius Bassus, prefect of the fleet at
Ravenna (Tac. iii 12, ii 100), and Aulus Caecina, commander-in-chief of the
army of Vitellius, who tried to induce his soldiers to throw in their lot
with the mutinous fleet and to desert to Vespasian. Some of the officers
supported him, but the troops were wildly indignant; they put him in
fetters and chose as their leaders Fabius Fabullus, legatus of the 5th legion,
and Cassius Longus, prefect of the camp (Tac. iii 13, ii 99). The
treachery of Caecina was fatal to Vitellius, as Antonius Primus attacked
when the Vitellian forces were thus disordered and without a competent
leader. Among those who proved false to Vitellius after the battle were
Claudius Apollinaris, prefect of the fleet at Misenum, and Claudius Julianus
who was sent by Vitellius to Misenum to check the mutiny (Tac. iii 57);
also Alfenus Varus and Julius Priscus, prefects of the praetorians (Tac.
iii 61).

salutem sibi pepigit: according to Tacitus (iii 63), after the
Vitellian army had surrendered at Narnia in Umbria, the generals of
Vespasian (Antonius Primus and Arrius Varus) sent messengers to
Vitellius at Rome offering him a safe retirement for himself and his
children in Campania, together with a sum of money; Mucianus also sent
letters to the same effect: Non omisere per eos dies Primus ac Varus
crebris nuntiis salutem et pecuniam et secreta Campaniae offerre Vitellio,
si positis armis seque ac liberos suos Vespasiano permisisset. In eundem
modum et Mucianus composuit epistulas; quibus plerumque fidere Vitellius,
ac de numero servorum, electione litorum loqui. Tanta torpedo invaserat
animum ut, si principem eum fuisse ceteri non meminissent, ipse oblivisceretur: iii 66, nunc pecuniam et familiam (= servos) et beatos
Campaniae sinus promitti.

milies sestertium: sc. centena milia, i.e. 100,000,000 sesterces, about
£850,000. Cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 5, Vitellius ab Sabino urbi praefecto,
Vespasiani fratre, sestertium milies pepigerat arbitris militibus imperio
decedere. Tacitus nowhere specifies the amount.

Flavio Sabino: elder brother of Vespasian; for his career see on Vesp.
1, 3. He was praefectus urbi at this period, and after the surrender of the
Vitellian army the leading men at Rome invited him to seize the city.
Sabinus showed no eagerness to do so and held parleys with Vitellius
which are described in Tac. iii 65: Saepe domi congressi, postremo in aede
Apollinis, ut fama erat, pepigere.
Verba vocesque duos testes habebant,
Cluvium Rufum (the historian) et Silium Italicum (the poet).
procul visentibus notabantur, Vitellii proiectus et degener, Sabinus non
insultans et miseranti propior. When Sabinus was driven to take refuge
in the Capitol (see below), he sent a remonstrance to Vitellius for breaking
his agreement (Tac. c. 70).
Voltus

pro gradibus Palati: "standing forth on the steps of the Palace";
cf. Ner. 8, pro Palati gradibus imperator consalutatus: Tac. H. i 29, Piso
pro gradibus domus vocatos in hunc modum adlocutus est: iii 74, stantem
pro gradibus Palati Vitellium. For this meaning of pro cf. pro muris
(= stans in muris), Tac. A. ii 81; pro vallo (“from the rampart'"), id.
Agr. 35, H. i 36; pro ripa, A. xii 29; pro litore, A. xiv 30. See also on
pro tribunali, Vesp. 7, 2.

cedere se: Tac. H. iii 68, Vitellius, inter suos milites, prospectantibus
etiam feminis, pauca et praesenti maestitiae congruentia locutus, cedere se
pacis et rei publicae causa, etc.
cunctis reclamantibus: Tac. (l.c.), reclamantibus qui in contione adstiterant.

primo diluculo: the same phrase occurs in Cic. S. Rosc. 19, Apul. Met.
iii 25; also primulo diluculo (Plaut. Amph. 737), and diluculo (Afran. 70,
Cic. Att. xvi 13): “Diluculum” is defined in Censor. De die nat. 24, 2 as
"cum sole nondum orto iam lucet."

sordidatus: "in mourning"; see on "sordes” c. 8, 1. Tacitus (iii
67 sq.) describes how on Dec. 18 Vitellius clad in mourning robes (pullo
amictu) and surrounded by his sorrowing household went down from the
Palace to the Forum. His little son was carried on a litter as though in
a funeral procession. From the Rostra he told the people in a few words
that he was abdicating for the sake of peace and the State, and commended to their compassion his wife, children, and brother. Then, when
tears choked his utterance, he turned to the consul and tried to surrender
to him the dagger which he wore as Imperator. For the different sequence
of events in the narrative of Suetonius see below.

e libello: there is nothing in Tac. about Vitellius reading his speech
from a written document.

§3. interpellante milite ac populo: when Vitellius was going down
from the Palace to the Forum the people uttered greetings flattering but
inappropriate, while the soldiers preserved an ominous silence (Tac. iii 67,
voces populi blandae et intempestivae, miles minaci silentio). After his
speech, when Vitellius declared that he would go to the temple of Concord
and deposit his dagger there, and then go to his brother's house, there was
a fierce outcry: maior hinc clamor obsistentium penatibus privatis, in
Palatium vocantium. Interclusum aliud iter, idque solum, quo in Sacram
viam (the way back to the Palace) pergeret, patebat. Tum consilii inops
in Palatium rediit.

animum resumpsit: So Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, quasi renovato furore; it is
clear, however, from the account in Tac. that there was no display of
spirit by Vitellius at this juncture; he was “inops consilii,” and the events
which occurred next were due to the determination of his followers. His
vacillation is compared by Dio (lxv 16) to the tossing of a boat in a
storm: τῶν δὲ δὴ τοῦ Οὐεσπεσιανοῦ στρατηγῶν ἐπιόντων τῇ Ῥώμῃ, ἐξεπλάγη τε καὶ
ἐξέστη. ἓν μὲν γὰρ᾽ οὐδὲν οὔτε ἔπραττεν οὔτε ἐφρόνει, ἐμπλήκτως δὲ ἄνω καὶ κάτω
ἐφέρετο ὥσπερ ἐν κλύδωνι.

vi subita: an attack was made on the retinue of Sabinus, near the
Basin of Fundanius on the Quirinal, and the Vitellians had the better of
the encounter; Sabinus then sought safety by occupying the Capitol (Tac.
iii 69).

reliquos Flavianos: the Flaviani were the supporters of Vespasian
(Flavius Vespasianus); cf. partes Flavianae, Tac. ii 67, iii 1.
Mingled
with the soldiers who occupied the citadel were the consuls Quintius Atticus
and Caecilius Simplex, some senators and knights, and some women, of
whom Verulana Gratilla was the most prominent. During the first night,
owing to the carelessness of the investing force, Sabinus managed to bring
in his own children and his nephew Domitian, the future emperor.
succenso templo Iovis: for the storming of the Capitol by the Vitellians
and the burning of the temple of Capitoline Jove see Tac. iii 71 sqq.
According to Tacitus it is doubtful whether the attackers or defenders
were responsible for the conflagration; he denounces it as the most shameful
and regrettable event in the history of Rome: Id facinus post conditam
urbem luctuosissimum foedissimumque rei publicae populi Romani accidit,
nullo externo hoste, propitiis, si per mores nostros liceret, deis, sedem Iovis
Optimi Maximi auspicato a maioribus, pignus imperii conditam, quam non
Porsenna dedita urbe neque Galli capta temerare potuissent, furore principum exscindi. Tacitus sketches the history of the temple: the foundations were laid by Tarquinius Priscus, and the building progressed under
Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus; it was dedicated under the free
Republic in 507 B.C.; it was burned down, by persons unknown, in 83 B.C.
when Sulla marched on Rome; Sulla undertook the restoration but did not
live to dedicate the new building (hoc solum felicitati eius negatum), this
honour was reserved for Q. Lutatius Catulus (consul 69 B.C.), and the name
of Catulus remained inscribed on the temple down to the time of Vitellius.
The temple and its history are fully described by Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2,
8 sqq.

oppressit: when the Vitellians burst into the Capitol, any of the
Flavian officers who continued to resist were cut down. The young Domitian
succeeded in escaping (see Dom. 1, 2), as did also the sons of Sabinus and
the consul Simplex. Sabinus himself was captured along with the consul
Atticus and dragged in chains to the Palace of Vitellius. Though Vitellius
would have spared Sabinus, the rabble insisted on his being slain; Atticus
was saved by his confession, true or false, that he had fired the Capitol,
thus acquitting the Vitellians of the crime (Tac. iii 73–75).

Tiberiana domo: the Palace of Tiberius, at the back of that of
Augustus, was on the north-western part of the Palatine hill towards the
Capitoline, as is shown by this passage and by the statement that it
afforded to Otho an exit into the Velabrum (per Tiberianam domum in
Velabrum, Tac. H. i 27; see note on Oth. 6, 2, proripuit se a postica parte
Palatii). It was built by Tiberius on the site of the house of his father
(Ti. Claudius Nero) and the adjoining private mansions. At a later period
it was the favourite residence of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who
may have added the library mentioned by Gellius (xiii 19, 1). See also on
"Palatina domus,” Vesp. 25.

inter epulas: Pitiscus comments: Epulatus est Vitellius, ‘‘ne amitteret
moriturus prandium; et redundantioribus, ut in extremis solet, mensae sibi
ultimae dapibus refarciebatur, obruebatque se vini poculis, ut sensum
amitteret futuri, vel opprobrii, vel periculi." (Hegesipp. Exscid. Hierosol.
iv 32).
7, optimus est portus
paenitens consilii; with
The pers. and impers.

paenitens facti: the use of paenitens in a personal sense, either absolutely or c. gen., is found in Cic. Phil. xii 3,
paenitenti mutatio consilii: Sall. Hist. frag. i 49,
de in Suet. Claud. 43, paenitens de matrimonio.
uses of paenitere are discussed and illustrated by Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb.
ii 287 sqq.; Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre iii 657.

in alios culpam conferens: cf. Tac. H. iii 70, where Sabinus, forced to
take refuge in the Capitol, sends an envoy to Vitellius to remonstrate with
him for violating the compact whereby he was to have withdrawn peaceably
from Rome, and Vitellius puts the blame upon his uncontrollable soldiers:
Trepidus ad haec Vitellius pauca purgandi sui causa respondit, culpam in
militem conferens, cuius nimio ardori inparem esse modestiam suam.

vocata contione: Suetonius appears to be inaccurate in stating that the
assembly at which Vitellius offered his dagger to the consul was held after
the storming of the Capitol. Tacitus (who was probably an eye-witness of
these events; see Spooner, Tac. Hist. Introd. p. 14) describes the assembly
and the attempt of Vitellius to surrender his imperial dagger as taking
place before the attack on Sabinus; see above on "sordidatus.” Dio (lxv
16) agrees with Tacitus.
iuravit coegitque iurare: there is nothing corresponding to this in Tac.
antiquius: see on Vesp. 8, 1.

§ 4. pugionem: the symbol of imperial power; see on Galb. 11, 1. Cf.
Tac. iii 68, adsistenti consuli (Caecilius Simplex erat) exsolutum a latere
pugionem, velut ius necis vitaeque civium, reddebat. Aspernante consule,
reclamantibus qui in contione adstiterant, ut in aede Concordiae positurus
insignia imperii domumque fratris petiturus discessit. Dio (lxv 16) says
that Vitellius was jeered at by the bystanders for his action: καὶ τά
ἄλλα αὐτὸν ἐκερτόμουν, καὶ μάλιστα ὁπότε τὸ ξίφος ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τοῖς τε ὑπάτοις
καὶ τοις ἄλλοις βουλευταῖς ἄρεγέν, ὡς καὶ τὴν αὐτοκράτορα ἀρχὴν δι' αὐτοῦ ἀποτεθειμένος. οὔτε γὰρ ἐκείνων τις λαβεῖν αὐτὸ ἐτόλμα, καὶ οἱ προσεστηκότες ἐχλεύαζον.
TE

consuli: Tacitus says that this consul was Caecilius Simplex, who
was one of the Flavians afterwards besieged in the Capitol and who
managed to escape when it was stormed by the Vitellians. Hofstee acutely
points out that if we accept the sequence of events given by Suetonius we
must assume that the consul immediately after his escape ventured to
appear at a public assembly, which is almost incredible.

aede Concordiae: this temple (τὸ Ὁμονόειον, Dio lv 8) on the Clivus
Capitolinus overlooking the Forum was founded by Camillus in 367 B.c.,
and restored and rededicated in 12 A.D. by Tiberius (Suet. Tib. 20).
It
was used as a meeting-place for the senate (e.g. Cic. Cat. iii 9, 21, Phil. ii
8, 19), and in the 3rd cent. A.D. is called curia ("senate-house''), cf.
Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 6, cum senatus frequens in curiam, hoc est in aedem
Concordiae templum inauguratum, convenisset. See Jordan, Topogr.
Rom i 2, 336 sqq.; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ '928.

Concordiae cognomen: there is no other reference to this as a
cognomen of Vitellius. “Concordia" is found as a woman's name in
several inscriptions; e.g. C.I.L. vi 2145, Coeliae Concordiae virgini Vestali
maximae. The goddess Concordia appears on coins of the emperors from
Nero onwards (Cohen, Méd. imp.2 Néron 66, 67, Vitellius 13-16, etc.).
Torrentius compares the assumption of the cognomen "Pietas" by
L. Antonius who pretended that he was only opposing Caesar in the
interests of his brother M. Antonius, the triumvir (Dio xlviii 5; Sturz ad
loc. cites as a modern parallel the assumption of the title "Citoyen
Égalité" by the Duke of Orleans at the time of the French Revolution).

suasit senatui, ut . . mitterent: for the constructio ad sensum cf. 10, 1;
15, 1; Galb. 10, 2.

legatos: Tac. iii 80, Mox vocato senatu deliguntur legati ad exercitus,
ut praetexto rei publicae concordiam pacemque suaderent. The envoys
were sent to Antonius Primus, who was advancing by the Via Flaminia,
and to Petilius Cerealis, who was advancing by the Via Salaria. The
envoys who met Cerealis were rudely rejected; one of them, the praetor
Arulenus Rusticus (the Stoic, afterwards executed by Domitian, Dom. 10),
was wounded and his lictor killed. Those who met Antonius were more
favourably received, as his troops were under better control. Tacitus
mentions that the famous Stoic philosopher, Musonius Rufus, a man of
equestrian rank, went with the envoys and expatiated to the troops on
the perils of war and the blessings of peace; fortunately for himself, he
was persuaded to desist from displaying his ill-timed wisdom (intempestiva
sapientia).

virginibus Vestalibus: the Vestals were sent to Antonius with a
letter from Vitellius asking for a delay of one day that a settlement
might be arranged. The sacred virgins were sent back with honour, but
the answer returned to Vitellius was that his slaying of Sabinus and
burning of the Capitol had broken off all the usual courtesies of war
(dirempta belli commercia, Tac. c. 81). Dio, lxv 18, says that it was to
Cerealis that the Vestals (ἀειπαρθένοι) were sent. The veneration accorded
to the Vestals lent great weight to their intercessions. Julius Caesar in
his early youth owed his pardon by Sulla to their pleadings (Suet. Iul. 1, 2,
per virgines Vestales
veniam impetravit). Cf. also Tac. A. xi 32,
Messalina .Vibidiam virginum Vestalium vetustissimam oravit pontificis:
maximi (i.e. the emperor Claudius) aures adire, clementiam expetere: id.
A. iii 69: Val. Max. v 4, 6: Cic. Font. 17, 48.
hostem appropinquare: Tacitus (iii 82) describes the advance of the
forces of Vespasian in three divisions, the centre along the Via Flaminia,
the right wing along the banks of the Tiber, the left along the Via
Salaria to the Colline Gate. The rabble and slaves had been armed by
the Vitellians, and they tried to prevent the enemy entering, but were
driven back into the city. Fierce fighting took place in the streets, recalling
the days of Sulla and Cinna. With the storming of the praetorian camp
(held by Germanic soldiers, whom Vitellius substituted for the praetorian
cohorts which he disbanded) the Flavian army broke down the opposition
and the city passed into their hands. According to some accounts 50,000
perished in this capture of Rome.

continuo: Tacitus (c. 84) says that it was after the capture of the city
that Vitellius sought concealment in the house of his wife (not his father)
on the Aventine: Vitellius capta urbe per aversam Palatii partem Aventinum
in domum uxoris sellula defertur.

abstrusus gestatoria sella: see on Oth. 6, 3, abditus propere muliebri
sella. For petit = petiit cf. Oth. 7, 1 n.

in Campaniam: where his brother Lucius had captured Tarracina;
see on c. 15, 2. The design of Vitellius to escape to Campania is mentioned also by Tac. (c. 84), ut si diem latebra vitavisset, Tarracinam ad
cohortes fratremque perfugeret: Dio lxv 20, γνώμην ἔχων τῆς νυκτὸς ἐς τὴν
Ταρρακῖναν πρὸς τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀποδρᾶναι.
rumore
..,

tamquam pax impetrata esset: a clause with tamquam
(as with quasi, see on Tit. 5, 3) often takes the place of the acc. c. inf. in
post-class. Latin; cf. Aug. 6, tenet vicinitatem opinio, tamquam natus ibi
sit: Aug. 94, 8, quem (puerum) cum detrahi iussisset, prohibitus monitu
dei, tamquam is ad tutelam rei p. educaretur.

referri se in Palatium: Tacitus (c. 84) attributes this return, not
to any rumours of peace, but to the characteristic vacillation of Vitellius:
dein mobilitate ingenii et, quae natura pavoris est, cum omnia metuenti
praesentia maxime displicerent, in Palatium regreditur.

deserta omnia: Tac. (l.c.): Palatium vastum desertumque, dilapsis
etiam infimis servitiorum aut occursum eius declinantibus. Terret solitudo
et tacentes loci; tentat clausa, inhorrescit vacuis.
simul erant: Bentley conjectured simul ierant (G has simulaverant).

zona: money was often carried in a belt and zona was used in the
sense of "purse"; cf. Hor. Ep. ii 2, 40, ibit eo quo vis qui zonam perdidit:
Gracchus ap. Gell. xv 12, cum Romam profectus sum, zonas, quas plenas
argenti extuli, eas ex provincia inanes rettuli: Liv. xxxiii 29, negotiandi
ferme causa argentum in zonis habentes. Plautus (Trin. 862) uses sector
zonarius for a "cut-purse” (βαλαντιοτόμος).
aureorum: see on Galb. 20, 2.

cellulam ianitoris: cf. Oros. vii 8, cum se in quandam proximam
Palatio cellulam contrusisset. There was a small hut or lodge for the
porter or doorkeeper beside the entrance to the Palace: Aur. Vict., Caes. 8,
calls it "tugurium ianitoris." The small rooms of servants were called
cellae (servorum, familiares, etc.); and they were sometimes designated
as occupied by a particular functionary; e.g. cella atriensis (cf. Calig. 57).
The cella ianitoris was also called cella ostiarii (Petron. Satyr. 29). Dio, lxv
20, says that Vitellius hid in a dark room where the dogs were kept:
ὁ Οὐιτέλλιος φοβηθεὶς χιτωνίσκον τε ῥακώδη καὶ ῥυπαρὸν ἐνέδυ, καὶ ἐς οἴκημα σκοτεινόν,
ἐν ᾧ ἐτρέφοντο κύνες, ἐκρύφθη. Tacitus (c. 84) uses a vague phrase: pudenda
latebra semet occultans.

religato pro foribus cane: the custom of having watch-dogs chained
near the porter's cella is illustrated in the description of Trimalchio's house
where there was a figure of an enormous dog in mosaic or colours
on the wall, and also a live watch-dog, Scylax ("Barker'") chained
at the door: Petron. Satyr. 29, ad sinistram intrantibus non longe ab
ostiarii cella canis ingens, catena vinctus, in pariete erat pictus superque
quadrata littera ("in capital letters'') scriptum “CAVE CANEM”: ib.
64, Trimalchio Scylacem iussit adduci nec mora ingentis formae adductus est canis catena vinctus, admonitusque ostiarii calce, ut cubaret, ante
mensam se posuit: ib. 72, ad ianuam venimus, ubi canis catenarius tanto
nos tumultu excepit, ut Ascyltos etiam in piscinam ceciderit.

culcita: "mattress"; cf. Ner. 48, 4, receptus in proximam cellam decubuit super lectum modica culcita: Tib. 54, 2, Druso autem adeo alimenta
subducta, ut tomentum (“stuffing'") e culcita temptaverit mandere: Sen.
Ep. 87, culcita in terra iacet, ego in culcita: Petron. Satyr. 97, institis
quibus sponda culcitam ferebat (i.e. the webbing which held up the mattress
on the frame of the bed). "culcita” is used at times to denote a pillow
(cervical); the emperor Claudius was so apprehensive of assassination that
he would never visit a sick person “nisi explorato prius cubiculo culcitisque
et stragulis praetemptatis et excussis'' (Claud. 35, 1).

agminis antecessores: the advanced guard (of the Flavians), cf. Auct.
Bell. Afr. 12, per speculatores et antecessores equites nuntiatur. Another
military term for advanced parties was antecursores (πρόδρομοι), e.g. Caes.
B.G. v 47; Livy uses praecursores.

nemine: this ablative (for nullo or nulla) does not occur in class. Lat.;
the only apparent instance, Cic. orat. tog. cand. frag. 19, neque alio nemine
is corrected by Müller into ne quem alium nominem; it is found in Plautus
and in post-Aug. writers (3 times in Justin, twice in Tac., and 9 times in
Suet.). See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 128.
On the other hand, Suetonius
uses nullo = nemine 7 times, e.g. Vitell. 15, 4: Vesp. 11.
..

rimabantur: cf. Tac. H. ii 29, spolia occultari clamitantes (milites
seditiosi) tabernacula ducis ipsamque humum pilis et lanceis rimabantur.
Suetonius does not use the verb elsewhere.

ab his extractus: Tacitus is more definite: H. iii 84, ab Iulio Placido,
tribuno cohortis, protrahitur.

sciscitantes
ubi esse Vitellium sciret: Madvig would read ubi
esset Vitellius num sciret; Bentley ecubi esset Vitellius. Bremi explains
the text as meaning "asking him where he knew that Vitellius was"; the
form of expression implying that the captors assumed that he did know.
Baumg.-Cr. (iii 837) regards the passage as an instance of a “duplex
sententia in unam contracta,” the meaning being the same as if Suetonius
had actually written num sciret ubi esset Vitellius, and he thinks that the
acc. c. inf. (instead of the subjunct. esset) is similar to the ordinary use in
orat. obl. of this constr. in questions with the first or third person. This
is also the view of Freund (De Suet. genere dicendi p. 6), but neither he
nor Baumg.-Cr. cites any parallel for the omission of num. The text seems
scarcely defensible, and perhaps Madvig's correction should be adopted,
though I would prefer si sciret to his num sciret; the loss of si between
Vitellius and sciret would account for the rest of the corruption. For si
(= num) in indirect questions see Kühner-Stegmann, ii 426.

ignorabatur: for this use of ignorari cf. Tac. H. iii 74, Domitianus
prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus,
lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum inmixtus ignoratusque:
ib. iv 36, servili habitu per tenebras
ignoratus evasit: Ter. Phorm. 930, fugitive, etiam nunc credis te
ignorarier?

vel in carcere: i.e. in the old state prison; he did not claim the
privilege of being kept merely in the libera custodia of some distinguished
citizen (see on c. 2, 3, in custodiam fratri datus). The carcer (called
Mamertinus in mediaeval Latin) was situated between the temple of Concord
and the Curia at the foot of the Capitol.
religatis
manibus, etc.: Tac. iii 84, Vinctae pone tergum manus;
lacerata veste, foedum spectaculum ducebatur (sc. laqueo): Dio lxv 20,
τὴν ἐσθῆτα αὐτοῦ περιρρήξαντες, καὶ τὰ χεῖρε εἰς τοὐπίσω δήσαντες, τῷ τε αὐχένι
σχοινίον περιθέντες, κατήγαγον ἐκ τοῦ παλατίου τὸν Καίσαρα τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ ἐντρυφήσαντα.

seminudus: this rare compound is first found in Livy, e.g. ix 6, consules
prope seminudi sub iugum missi. Other compounds with semi- in Suet. are
semiambustus, semianimis, semibarbarus, semicrudus, semesus, semigraecus,
semiperfectus, semiustus, semiustulandus.

Forum: where he had often addressed the people; Dio (l.c.), ἔς τε τὴν
ἀγορὰν ἐσεκόμισαν τὸν Αὔγουστον, ἐν ᾗ πολλάκις ἐδημηγόρησε.

inter ludibria: Dio (l.c.), οἱ μὲν ἐρράπιζον αὐτόν, οἱ δὲ τοῦ γενείου ἔτιλλον,
πάντες δὲ ἔσκωπτον καὶ πάντες ὕβριζον. Josephus also mentions the despiteful
treatment of Vitellius, Bell. Iud. iv 11, 4, συρεὶς δὲ διὰ τοῦ πλήθους καὶ παντοδαπαῖς αἰκίαις ἐξυβρισθεὶς ἐπὶ μέσης τῆς ῾Ρώμης ἀποσφάττεται. Tacitus (l.c.) says:
multis increpantibus, nullo inlacrimante, deformitas exitus misericordiam
abstulerat.

viae Sacrae: down from the Palace to the Forum, the road along which
he had so often proudly ridden in state; Dio (l.c.), διὰ τῆς ἱερᾶς ὁδοῦ ἔσυραν
τὸν αὐτοκράτορα τὸν ἐν τῷ βασιλικῷ δίφρῳ πολλάκις σοβήσαντα.

reducto coma capite: the head was drawn back to make the criminal
expose his face to the gaze of all; cf. Plin. Pan. 34, describing the informers being led through the arena with their faces forcibly upturned
to the spectators in the amphitheatre: nihil saeculo dignius quam quod
contigit desuper intueri delatorum supina ora retortasque cervices.

ceu noxii solent: sc. trahi; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, iniecto laqueo, parricidarum more, ad scalas Gemonias pertractus. Casaubon prefers ceu
noxiis solet. The adv. ceu (= velut) is used in poetry (Catull., Lucr., Verg.,
Hor.) and in later prose (Colum., Sen., and especially Plin. N.H.); cf. Suet.
Tib. 52, 2, victorias ceu damnosas rei publicae increparet.

mento mucrone gladii subrecto: Tac. (l.c.), Vitellium infestis
mucronibus coactum erigere os et offerre contumeliis
propulere: Dio
1xv 21, αἰσχυνομένου τε ἐπὶ τούτοις αὐτοῦ καὶ κάτω βλέποντος, οἱ στρατιῶται ξιφιδίοις
αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τὸ γένειον ὑπεκέντουν, ἵνα καὶ ἄκων (vel invitus) ἄνω βλέπῃ : [Aur. Vict.]
Epit. 8, ne homo impudens in extremis saltem malorum, quae gesserat,
rubore faciem demitteret, subiecto in mentum gladio: Eutrop. vii 18, 5,
erecto coma capite et subiecto ad mentum gladio. The reading subiecto in
these last two passages is found also in most of the later MSS. of Suet.,
and appears in the ed. Veneta (1471). The act. use of subrigo (surgo)
occurs in Verg. Aen. iv 183, tot surrigit aures; in Livy, e.g. vii 10 mucrone
subrecto, viii 8 hastas subrecta cuspide in terra fixas; later in Sen., Plin.
N.H., Stat., Sil. Ital., etc.

§ 2. stercore et caeno incessentibus: Eutrop. (l.c.), stercore in vultum
et pectus ab omnibus obviis appetitus: Aur. Vict. (l.c.), multis caeno
fimoque et ceteris turpioribus dictu purgamentis vultum eius incessentibus:
Oros. vii 8, 8, passim fimum in os eius coniectantibus.

incendiarium: referring to his burning of the Capitol (c. 15, 3). Nero
also was reviled as an "incendiarius” for having caused the great fire
which devastated Rome in his reign (Tac. A. xv 67).

patinarium: “trencherman'” “gormandizer," with special reference to
his famous patina described in c. 13, 2.
corpore

enormis proceritas: cf. Calig. 50, statura fuit eminenti
enormi. The adj. enormis is post-Aug. and means (1) huge, enormous,
(2) shapeless, constructed on no plan or rule (norma), e.g. enormes vici,
Tac. A. xv 38.

rubida: a Plautine adj.; cf. Gell. ii 26, 14, ‘rubidus” autem est rufus
atrior et nigrore multo inustus.

venter obesus: Dio lxv 20, τά τε ἄλλα καὶ τὴν ἀσωτίαν αὐτοῦ ἐπιλέγοντες
(exprobrantes), ἐπειδὴ καὶ γαστροπίων (ventre obeso) ἦν. Cf. Dom. 18, deformis obesitate ventris: Ner. 51, ventre proiecto: Tit. 3, 1, ventre paulo
proiectiore.

subdebile: this word apparently does not occur elsewhere. Suetonius
also uses subflavus (Aug. 79, 2; Ner. 51), and subrutilus (Dom. 20).

quadrigae: the sing. quadriga is poetical and occurs at times in post-class. prose. Gellius (xix 8, 17) notices its use by Varro: “quod unum
ergo rarissimum videbatur, invenimus quadrigam numero singulari dictum
in libro saturarum M. Varronis qui inscriptus est Ecdemeticus." Suetonius
also uses the post-Aug. sing. biga (Tib. 26, 1).
auriganti Gaio: see on c. 4, Gaio per aurigandi studium familiaris.

cum ministratorem exhiberet: for the ellipse of se cf. Quintil. xii 2, 7,
qui vere civilem virum exhibeat: Justin xxvii 2, pro fratre hostem exhibuit: Ov. Met. vi 43, formamque removit anilem | Palladaque exhibuit.
Several of the MSS. (GPOST) give ministratorem se. Vitellius may have
been acting as one of the sparsores, whose duty seems to have been either
to refresh the horses or to pour water on the wheels of the chariot to
prevent their taking fire (Daremberg-Saglio, i 1199). For Dio's mention
of Vitellius rubbing down or currying the horses of the Blue faction in the
Circus see note on "factionis Venetae,” c. 7, 1.

apud Gemonias: Tac. iii 85, Vitellium ... postremo ad Gemonias,
ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere. Una vox non degeneris animi
excepta, cum tribuno insultanti se tamen imperatorem eius fuisse respondit.
Ac deinde ingestis volneribus concidit. The full phrase Gemoniae scalae
occurs in Val. Max. vi 3, ix 13, Oros. vii 8; but the subst. is regularly
omitted in Tac. and Suet. Pliny (N.H. viii 145) uses gradus gemitorii.
These "Stairs of Groanings" were a flight of steps from the Capitol to
the Forum, near the Mamertine prison; on them the bodies of executed
criminals were exposed (e.g. that of Sejanus for 3 days, Dio lviii 11). We
find no mention of the Gemoniae (scalae) before the time of Tiberius. See
Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 324. Dio (lxv 21) says that when the soldiers
dragged Vitellius to the Gemoniae (πρὸς τοὺς ἀναβαθμούς), they slew him and
cut off his head which they carried round the city, and that the body was
buried by his wife Galeria Fundana; but according to Eutrop. vii 18, 5
(followed by Oros. vii 8, 8) ‘“in Tiberim deiectus etiam communi caruit
sepultura."

minutissimis ictibus: cf. the fiendish cruelty of Caligula described in
Calig. 30, 1, Non temere in quemquam nisi crebris et minutis ictibus animadverti passus est, perpetuo notoque iam praecepto: ‘“Ita feri ut se mori
sentiat." Josephus (Ant. Iud. xix 1, 107) mentions that Chaerea arranged
that Caligula himself should be slain by the conspirators with a multitude
of wounds: προνοίᾳ τοῦ Χαιρέου . · τὸ μὴ μιᾷ πληγῇ διεργάσασθαι τὸν Γάϊον, ἀλλὰ
τιμωρεῖσθαι μειζόνως πλήθει τραυμάτων.

excarnificatus: this compound is found earlier in Cicero, N.D. iii 33,
82, Anaxarchum Democriteum a Cyprio tyranno excarnificatum accepimus.
Seneca has it once of bodily tortures (Ep. 24 mille alia instrumenta excarnificandi particulatim hominis) and twice of mental anguish (Ira iii 4, 3:
Clem. i 16, 33 so too in Ter. Heaut. 813). Livy (xxiv 15) uses the simple
verb carnificare. Suetonius does not mention here what is related by Dio
(lxv 21) that the first wound dealt to Vitellius was by a Gallic (?) soldier
out of pity for his humiliating sufferings: ἰδὼν δὲ τοῦτο Κελτός τις, οὐκ
ἤνεγκεν, ἀλλ' ἐλεήσας αὐτόν “ ἐγώ σοι,” ἔφη “ βοηθήσω, ὡς μόνως δύναμαι.” καὶ ὁ
μὲν ἐκεῖνόν τε ἔτρωσε καὶ ἑαυτὸν ἔσφαξεν. οὐ μέντοι καὶ ὁ Οὐιτέλλιος ἀπέθανεν ἐκ τοῦ
τραύματος. Tacitus (iii 84) suggests various explanations for this soldier's
action: Obvius e Germanicis militibus Vitellium infesto ictu per iram vel
quo maturius ludibrio eximeret an tribunum adpetierit, in incerto fuit:
aurem tribuni amputavit ac statim confossus est (the tribune referred to
is Julius Placidus who had dragged Vitellius from his hiding-place).

unco tractus in Tiberim: when criminals were strangled in the
Mamertine prison, their bodies were dragged by a hook to the Gemoniae
scalae and after being exposed there for some time were dragged to the
Tiber; cf. Suet. Tib. 54, 2, cum ei carnifex laqueos et uncos ostentaret:
ib. 61, 4, nemo punitorum non in Gemonias abiectus uncoque tractus: ib.
75, 1, alii uncum et Gemonias cadaveri minarentur: Juv. x 66, Seianus
ducitur unco (where see Mayor): Ov. Ibis 163, carnificisque manu populo
plaudente traheris | infixusque tuis ossibus uncus erit. Tacitus (A. vi 19)
gives a gruesome picture of those executed by Tiberius for complicity with
Sejanus; their bodies were cast down the Gemoniae and lay guarded by
soldiers till corruption began; they were then dragged by the flesh-hook
to the Tiber. Dio (lx 35) relates a jest of Gallio, Seneca's brother, on
the "deification of the emperor Claudius: ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τοὺς ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ
(carcere) θανατουμένους ἀγκίστροις (uncis) τισὶ μεγάλοις οἱ δήμιοι (carnifices) es te
τὴν ἀγορὰν (forum) ἀνεῖλκον, κἀντεῦθεν ἐς τὸν ποταμὸν (Tiberim) ἔσυρον, ἔφη τὸν
Κλαύδιον ἀγκίστρῳ ἐς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνενεχθῆναι.

periit cum fratre: Lucius Vitellius had set out from Tarracina in
Campania (see on c. 15, 2) to bring help to his brother Aulus, the emperor,
but learned on his march of his death; he was met by forces sent by
Antonius Primus, and surrendered to them. Dio (lxv 22) says that they
agreed to spare his life; but he and his followers were brought captive to
Rome and thrown into prison, and shortly afterwards Lucius was executed.
Tacitus mentions his death, and describes his character in very unfavourable
terms: H. iv 2, dein Lucius Vitellius interficitur, par vitiis fratris, in
principatu eius vigilantior, nec perinde prosperis socius quam adversis
abstractus ("dragged down by his brother's fall''): iii 77, quippe L.
Vitellio quamvis infami inerat industria; nec virtutibus, ut boni, sed
quomodo pessimus quisque, vitiis valebat.

filio: named Germanicus; see on c. 6, de hac (i.e. Galeria Fundana)
liberos tulit. Dio (l.c.) says that he was put to death at the same time
as his uncle Lucius Vitellius. According to the account in Tacitus (iv 80)
the execution of Germanicus did not take place for nearly a year after the
death of his father, the execution being ordered by Mucianus, Vespasian's
general, who had made himself all-powerful at Rome: Isdem diebus
Mucianus Vitellii filium interfici iubet, mansuram discordiam obtendens
(''alleging'"), ni semina belli restinxisset.
anno vitae septimo quinquagesimo: so Tac. iii 86, septimum et quinquagesimum aetatis annum explebat: Eutrop. vii 18, periit aetatis

anno septimo et quinquagesimo: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 8, vixit annos quinquaginta septem. This, however, is irreconcilable with the date of his
birth as given by Suetonius in c. 3, 2, viz. Sept. 24, 15 A.D. If he was
born then and slain on Dec. 22 (?), 69 A.D., he was only aged 54 years and
89 days at his death, which is what is stated in Dio lxv 22 (Zonar. xi 16).
Such chronological discrepancies with regard to the age, etc., of the
emperors are frequent in Suetonius (see on Galb. 23; Oth. 11, 2; Tit. 11).
No satisfactory explanation of them has been suggested: Reimar (on
Dio l.c.) assumes that Suetonius took the dates of birth and the ages of
the emperors at death from different authorities and did not trouble to
consider whether they were consistent. Suetonius does not state the length
of Vitellius' reign, which is variously given by other authors; e.g. by Dio
(Zonar.) as 1 year all but 10 days (Vitellius was first saluted as Imperator
by the army in Germany on Jan. 3); by Aur. Vict. as 8 months (the day
of his accession being Apr. 19, see on Oth. 11, 2); by Josephus (Bell. Iud.
iv 11, 4) as 8 months and 5 days; by Eutropius as 8 months and 1 day;
by Tertullian (adv. Iud. 8) as 8 months and 27 days. See Dessau, Prosop.
Imp. Rom. iii 450.
augurio Viennae: see c. 9.

Gallicani hominis: the adj. Gallicanus was specially used with reference
to the provinces of Gallia Cisalpina and Gallia Narbonensis. In Suet. Ner.
43, 1 “Gallicani homines” are the inhabitants of Cisalpine Gaul, and in
Cic. Cat. ii 3, 5 "Gallicanae legiones" are the troops stationed in that
province. In Cic. Quinct. 25, 80 ‘‘fundus Gallicanus" is used of an estate
held by a Roman in Narbonese Gaul, and it is to this province that Suet.
is referring here. See also R. Ellis on Catull. 42, 9, catuli Gallicani.

Antonio Primo: born in Gaul, he became a senator at Rome, but was
banished under Nero for forgery: he was restored by Galba and given
command of the 7th legion (Galbiana) in Pannonia: he offered his services
to Otho but was rejected: he induced the legions in Pannonia and Moesia
to declare for Vespasian: he defeated the Vitellian forces at Betriacum,
stormed Cremona, and entered Rome at the head of his victorious army:
for a brief time he exercised an almost autocratic power at Rome, but on
the arrival of Mucianus he was reduced to a subordinate position (Tас. Н.
iv 11): incensed at this he went to Alexandria to complain to Vespasian,
but was coldly received by him; later we hear of him as a friend and patron
of Martial who (Epigr. x 23) mentions him as living peacefully at the age
2B2
of 75 in 98 A.D. Tacitus (H. ii 86) thus describes Antonius: Labantibus
Vitellii rebus Vespasianum secutus grande momentum addidit, strenuus
manu, sermone promptus, serendae in alios invidiae artifex, discordiis et
seditionibus potens, raptor largitor, pace pessimus, bello non spernendus.

Tolosae: mod. Toulouse, in Gallia Narbonensis, on the Garumna
(Garonne); it was the capital of the Tolosani or Tolosates; captured by
the Romans in 106 B.c., it afterwards became a colonia Latina. It is
mentioned as the birthplace of Marcus Antonius Primus in Mart. ix 99, 3,
Marcus Palladiae non infitianda Tolosae. | gloria, quem genuit Pacis alumna
Quies (the epithet Palladia, applied to Tolosa also by Auson. and Sidon.
Apollin., marks it as a centre of the literary culture of Gaul).

cui cognomen Becco fuerat: Becco is probably dat. by attraction
to cui; cf. Iul. 59, cui Salvitoni cognomen erat: Aug. 7, 1, infanti
cognomen Thurino inditum est. This attraction is very frequent in Plaut.;
in Cic. both nom. and dat. are used; in Caes. only nom.; in Liv. the dat. is
the more usual; Tac. only uses the dat. with adjs., e.g. A. i 31, cui nomen
Superiori. The name in the gen. is first found in post-Aug. writers; e.g.
Suet. Calig. 60, quibus Gai praenomen fuit: Tac. A. xii 55, nationes quibus
Clitarum cognomentum: Val. Max. i 8, cui nomen erat Equi. See KühnerStegmann i 420. beccus (Ital. becco, Fr. bec, Eng. beak) seems to be a
Gallic word. As a proper name it occurs in C.I.L. xii 2514, deo Apollini
Beccus ex voto. A derivative is Becciacus vicus (Bessay, Vendée),
Greg. Tur. glor. Mart. 89. Becco is another form of the name: C.I.L. xii
5381, (Tolosae) deo Silvan(o) dom(estico) Becco v.s.l.m. (i.e. votum solvit
libenter merito); also found in Greg. Tur. Iul. 16. Becca as the name of a
cinaedus occurs in Anth. 321, 3.

valet: = significat; cf. Varr. R.R. i 31, ὠκέως valet cito: Cic. Fin.
ii 4, 13, quaerimus verbum Latinum par Graeco et quod idem valeat:
Quintil. x 1, 13, et “intellego” et “sentio” et “video” saepe idem valent
quod “scio.” So δύνασθαι, e.g. Thucyd. vii 58, τὸ νεοδαμῶδες δύναται (valet)
ἐλεύθερον εἶναι.

gallinacei: see on c. 9. Suetonius does not mention the coincidence
between gallus (a cock) and Gallus (a Gaul).

rebellione: rebellare in Suet. (Iul. 75, 3: Aug. 21, 2: Vesp. 4, 5) has
its ordinary meaning of bellum renovare; and rebellio is so used in Calig.
51, 3, audita rebellione Germaniae. Here, however, rebellio seems to be
used in the more general sense of an armed revolt against the government
to which one owes allegiance, a tyrannical usurpation of authority. Galba,
Otho, and Vitellius are described as "tyranni" in Oros. vii 9, anno ab
urbe condita octingentesimo vigesimo quinto, brevi illa quidem sed turbida.
tyrannorum tempestate discussa, tranquilla sub Vespasiano duce serenitas
rediit. Marcilius cites the Gloss. Cyrill. rebellio ἀπόστασις: rebellis ἀποστάτης, τύραννος.

vagum: shifting (fluxum), unsettled, insecurely based or established,
opp. to stabile; cf. Cic. N.D. ii 1, de dis immortalibus habere non errantem
et vagam, ut Academici, sed ut nostri, stabilem certamque sententiam.

suscepit firmavitque: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, Vespasianus
diu fessumque terrarum orbem brevi refecit.
exsanguem

gens Flavia: Flavius, as a plebeian gentile name, in the last three
centuries of the Republic was fairly widespread throughout Italy, not merely
in the Sabine territory, but in Lucania, Etruria, etc. Under the Empire
it is found with greater frequency after the rise to power of the Flavian
dynasty.

illa quidem sed tamen: this use of ille with quidem (in a concessive sense) followed by a qualification introduced by sed or tamen or
sed tamen is common in Cic.; e.g. Tusc. iii 35, tarda illa quidem medicina,
sed tamen magna. Outside Cic. it is very rarely found (Nep. 18, 1, 1:
Plin. Ep. ii 5, 11: Sall. Iug. 24, 9: Ov. Met. v 506: isolated instances in
Apul. and Stat.). See Kühner-Stegmann, i 623 sq.
This is the only instance in Suet.

sine ullis maiorum imaginibus: cf. Aug. 4, 1, multis in familia
senatoriis imaginibus (so Sall. Iug. 85, homo veteris prosapiae et multarum
imaginum): Galb. 3, 1, imagines et elogia (= titulos) universi generis exsequi longum est: Calig. 23, 1, Agrippae se nepotem neque credi neque
dici ob ignobilitatem eius volebat succendebatque, si qui vel oratione vel
carmine imaginibus (= maioribus) eum Caesarum insererent. The ius
imaginum distinguished the nobiles at Rome, being the privilege of those
who held curule magistracies. See on Galb. 2, stemma in atrio.

rei p. nequaquam paenitenda: the gerundive paenitendus is found first
in Livy, e.g. i 35, 5, sub haud paenitendo magistro: xl 56, 3, neque
pudendum aut paenitendum eum regem fore. For the personal use of
paenitere, which justifies a gerundive, see on Vitell. 15, 3.

cupiditatis: cf. Dom. 9, 1, where cupiditas is coupled with avaritia
and they are opposed respectively to abstinentia and liberalitas. In Vesp.
16, 1 we find the full phrase cupiditas pecuniae, but elsewhere simply
cupiditas (e.g. Galb. 14, 2, cupiditatis immensae: Vesp. 19, 1: Dom. 10, 1).

saevitiae: the cruelty of Domitian is illustrated in Dom. 10.

poenas luisse: cf. Suet. Rhet. 6 paene poenas luit (but Calig. 37, 3,
сит morae culpa capite lueretur). Servius (on Aen. x 32 peccata luant)
censures the loose expression luere poenam for luere peccatum:‘“Dicimus
et 'luo poenam, sed melius est ‘luo peccatum': nam peccatum solvitur
poena. Qui enim crimine tenetur obnoxius, poena eum a pristina liberat
obligatione. Contra, ‘luo poenam' si dixeris, non procedit, quasi poena
solvatur. Auctoritas tamen ista confundit licenter more, quo solet poni,
vel a sequenti, quod praecedit: vel a praecedenti, quod sequitur."
phrase luere poenas is, however, used by Cicero, etc.
