§ 2. municeps Reatinus: Reāte (mod. Rieti) was a very ancient Sabine
city in a fertile valley (Cic. Att. iv 15, 5; Verg. Aen. vii 712) on the banks
of the river and lake Velinus. In Cicero's time it was merely a praefectura
(see Mayor on Cic. N.D. ii 2). We learn from inscriptions that in 27 B.C.
under the early Empire it had municipal privileges and its own magistrates
(C.I.L. ix 4686), and that under Vespasian a number of veterans were
settled there, though it did not obtain the rank of a colonia (C.I.L. ix 4682-
4685). Suetonius seems to be using municeps anachronistically here when
referring to the period of the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey,
while Reate was still a praefectura.
..

centurio an evocatus: the form of disjunctive questions became so
abbreviated that an came to be used almost as identical with aut or vel
(Kühner-Stegmann, ii 527); this use is found in Cic., e.g. Fin. ii 104, сит
ei Simonides an quis alius polliceretur (a fuller form in Cic. Acad. ii 63,
iocansne an ita sentiens); it is common in poetry and late Lat., e.g. Tac.
A. ii 42, finem vitae sponte an fato implevit: Suet. Claud. 13, 2, casu
quodam an divinitus. See also on Oth. 1, 1, matre incertum an ingenua.

evocatus: cf. Galb. 10, 3.
The evocati (ἀνάκλητοι) were time-expired
veterans who were invited to renew their service under very favourable
conditions. They were exempt from ordinary duties and ranked above the
privates (gregarii), apparently as the equals of centurions (we find evocati
and centuriones coupled, e.g. in Caes. В.С. і 17, 4 iii 53, 1; the same man
is called evocatus in Vell. Pat. ii 70, 3 and centurio or ἑκατόνταρχος in
Val. Max. ix 9, 2, Dio xlvii 46). See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 387 sqq.

Pharsalica acie: the decisive battle at Pharsalus in Thessaly where
Pompey was defeated by Julius Caesar in 48 B.C.

venia: in Iul. 75 Suetonius describes and illustrates the wonderful selfrestraint and mercy of Caesar in his hour of victory: moderationem
clementiamque cum in administratione tum in victoria belli civilis admirabilem exhibuit.
missione: for the honesta missio see on Vitell. 15, 1.

coactiones argentarias: the argentarii or bankers at Rome conducted
private sales or public auctions. At auctions they registered the articles
sold, their prices and purchasers, and received the payments; cf. Ner. 5, 2,
argentarios pretiis rerum coemptarum fraudaverit: Cic. Caecin. 6, 16:
Sen. Controv. i praef. 19, Hortensius a Sisenna provocatus in auctione
persedit per diem totum et omnes res et pretia et emptores ordine suo
argentariis recognoscentibus ita ut in nulla re falleretur recensuit. At
times they used their clerks or servants as collectors (coactores) of the
payments. Horace's father was a coactor (Hor. S. i 6, 86; cf. Suet. vit.
Horat. 1, patre libertino et exactionum coactore).

primipilarem: primipilaris (on the analogy of consularis, etc.) is used
by post-Aug. writers for one who had held the highest position as centurion.
The legion consisted of 10 cohorts, each cohort containing 2 centuries (or
1 maniple) of each of the three divisions hastati, principes, and pilani
(the pilani were earlier known as triarii; each ordo of pilani was called
a pilus). The cohorts ranked according to their numbers (the tenth being
the lowest), and the 60 centurions in the legion rose in an ascending scale,
the lowest being the subordinate centurion of the hastati of the tenth
cohort (decumus hastatus posterioris centuriae); the highest was usually
called primus pilus (also primipilus, primi pili centurio, primi ordinis
centurio), and was regarded as the best soldier in the legion, being called
in to the military councils along with the tribunes. See Marquardt, op.
cit. ii² 360 sqq.

ordines duceret: the phrase ordinem ducere meant to be a centurion'';
cf. Tac. H. ii 22, (Cerealis) primipilaris et Caecinae haud alienus, quod
ordines in Germania duxerat (i.e. had been a centurion under him in G.):
Caes. B.C. i 13, L. Pupius primi pili centurio, qui hunc eundem ordinem
in exercitu Cn. Pompei antea duxerat. Caesar uses ordo ten times in the
sense of centuria.

sacramento solutum : the oath (sacramentum) taken by a soldier
joining the Roman army was binding on him till he got his discharge
(missio). A discharge was of 3 kinds: (a) honesta missio after the legal
term of service had expired (see on Vitell. 15, 1); (b) causaria missio
through physical disablement or ill-health; (c) ignominiosa missio, summary
dismissal for serious offences. For (b) cf. Ulp. Dig. iii 2, 2, missio est
causaria quae propter valetudinem laboribus militiae solvit (militem);
those so incapacitated were called causarii (cf. Liv. vi 6, 14: Spartian.
Hadr. 10, etc.). Marquardt, op. cit. 384.

per causam: here of a genuine reason, but more frequently of a
pretence or pretext (= sub praetextu, ἐπὶ προφάσει), e.g. Oth. 3, 2, per
causam legationis: Iul. 2, per causam exigendae pecuniae: Caes. B.G. vii 9,
per causam supplementi equitatusque cogendi.

publicum quadragesimae in Asia egit: the regular expression for
one who did this was "conductor publici quadragesimae portuum Asiae.”
The amount of the portoria or import duties varied in different places:
5 p.c. (vicesima) in Sicily, 2 p.c. (quinquagesima) in Spain, 2 p.c. (quadragesima) in Gaul and Asia. The portoria were farmed out to the publicani
(generally equites); see on Vitell. 14, 2. The farming of those in Asia
is mentioned in Cic. Att. i 17, 9, Ecce aliae deliciae equitum vix ferendae!
...
Asiam qui de censoribus conduxerunt questi sunt in senatu se cupiditate
prolapsos nimium magno conduxisse: ut induceretur. (“cancelled") locatio
postulaverunt. The word “publicum” was used like τὸ δημόσιον, τὸ κοινόν,
for the public revenue (vectigal), e.g. Hor. Ep. i 1, 77, conducere publica:
Plaut. Truc. 140, habere publicum "to be a farmer of the public revenue."
For the use of “agere" cf. C.I.L. vi 8591, Iucundus Aug. lib. actor xxxx
Gal. (i.e. quadragesimae Galliarum): Sen. Ep. 119, 5, circumspiciebam in
quod me mare negotiaturus immitterem, quod publicum agitarem, quas
arcesserem merces.

manebantque: a reading which is almost certainly corrupt. The
imperfect is explained by Ernesti as referring to the time when Vespasian
was emperor, which seems quite impossible. Baumg.-Cr. takes the meaning
to be that the statues were in existence for some time, and that Suet.
had found them mentioned in his authorities, but was unaware whether
they were still in existence in his own time; but, even if the text could
convey this meaning, there is the difficulty that Suet. could easily have
got definite information on the point. The future manebunt would be
much more intelligible; the provincials would be careful to preserve for
example's sake statues to that rarest of all officials, an honest publicanus.
Lipsius conjectured mantantque or monebantque; Casaubon manent hodieque, which is approved by Oudendorp.
Καλῶς τελωνήσαντι : the Greek words for the "tax-farmers" who
"bought" the taxes were τελῶναι, ὠνηταί, δημοσιῶναι, the terms for
the "selling" of taxes being πρᾶσις, πωλεῖν, ἐκδιδόναι (locare), and for the
“buying” ὠνή, ὠνεῖσθαι, πρίασθαι (conducere). In late Lat. we find telonium
(-eum) = τελώνιον “custom-house'' (Tertull. Idol. 12, Bapt. 12); telonarius
"collector of customs" occurs in Cod. Theodos. xi 28, 3, and another
form telonearius in Nonius (p. 35, Lindsay): Portitores dicuntur telonearii, qui portum obsidentes omnia sciscitantur, ut ex eo vectigal accipiant.
A fragmentary inscription at Rome, consisting of the same two words
with the addition of AN, inscribed upon the base of a statue believed to
be that of Sabinus, is mentioned by Casaubon and by Baumg.-Cr. who
explains AN as ἀνέστησαν οι ἀνέθηκαν, the name of those who erected the
statue having been lost. Dennison (Amer. Journ. Archaeol., 1898, p. 53)
notices this inscription as 'reported first by Boissard, Ant. Rom. i Tab. 51,
then by Montfaucon, Ant. Expl. iii 1, 10, Tab. 1, afterwards by Franz,
C.I.G. 5897, and recently by Kaibel, Inscr. Graec. Sicil. et Ital. 123*, who
regards it as spurious."

§ 3. faenus exercuit: the phrase "faenus exercere” is common in
post-Aug. writers for practising money-lending; e.g. Tac. A. vi 16, primo
xii tabulis sanctum ne quis unciario faenore amplius exerceret (sc. faenus):
Apul. Met. i 21, faenus copiosum sub arrabone auri et argenti crebriter
exercens: Dig. xxxiii 8, 26, si id faenus nomine filii exercuisset. Stein
(Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2610) takes our passage as meaning that Flavius
Sabinus discharged the same function in Gaul as in Asia and so was one
of the conductores (or mancipes) quadragesimae Galliarum.

Helvetios: a people of Gallia Lugdunensis dwelling in the mod.
Switzerland. Caesar (B.G. i 1 sq.) fixes their habitation between the Jura
mts. on the W., the Rhone and lake Lemannus (Geneva) on the S., and
the Rhine on the E. and N. Tacitus (Germ. 28) thinks it probable that
the Helvetii were once in Germany, and occupied the district between the
Hercynian Forest, the Rhine, and the Moenus (Main).

diem obiit: = mortuus est; cf. Tib. 4, 3, Gramm. 5: Plaut. Aul. 20,
etc.: Nep. Dion 10, 3: Plin. N.H. ii 248. Suet. also uses supremum diem
obire in Claud. 1, 3, and mortem obire in Aug. 4, 1: Tib. 39: Claud. 46.

Sabinus: Flavius Sabinus served with his brother Vespasian in Britain
under Aulus Plautius (43 A.D.) and was legatus of Moesia for 7 years.
Nero made him praefectus urbi, probably in 56, since he held the office for
12 years (Tac. H. iii 75, septem annis quibus Moesiam, duodecim quibus
praefecturam urbis obtinuit) though not without intermission, for in 61
Pedanius Secundus was praefectus urbi when murdered (Tac. A. xiv 42);
Borghesi thinks that Sabinus succeeded Pedanius and was praefectus for
only 7 years, and he would alter duodecim in Tac. H. iii 75 into totidem
or vii (see Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2611). Sabinus was removed from this office
by Galba, but was reinstated by Otho. When Vespasian's troops were
advancing on Rome, Vitellius offered to surrender the supreme power to
Sabinus pending the arrival of Vespasian; but Vitellius' soldiers besieged
Sabinus in the Capitol which was set on fire and Sabinus was captured
and killed (Vitell. 15: Tac. H. iii 64-75). Tacitus (c. 75) praises him
highly, mentioning as universally admitted that before the accession of
Vespasian the dignity of the family was centred in Sabinus: quod inter
omnes constiterit, ante principatum Vespasiani decus domus penes Sabinum
erat.

praefecturam urbis: Tacitus (A. vi 11) sketches the history of this
office. The praefectus urbi was appointed to control the city during the
temporary absence from Rome of the kings and, later, the consuls (ne urbs
sine imperio foret, in tempus deligebatur qui ius redderet ac subitis
mederetur). The creation of the praetor urbanus in 367 B.c. rendered the
praefectura urbis unnecessary, but a shadow (simulacrum) of it survived
in the annual appointment of a praefectus during the absence of the consuls
at the feriae Latinae. Augustus (Suet. Aug. 37) made the praefectura
urbis part of his new scheme of government; Maecenas discharged the
duties though without the title, and there were three other praefecti urbi
under Augustus. During the long absence of Tiberius for the last 11 years
of his reign the praefectus urbi became a permanent official of great and
ever increasing power. In later days the holder of the office not merely
possessed imperium, but exercised a jurisdiction from which there was no
appeal save to the Princeps himself. See Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 661 sqq.,
ii³ 1059 sqq.
-, COS.

Polla: Bormann (Arch. Epig. Mitth. aus Öster. xv 1892, pp. 34-37)
refers to this Vespasia Polla an inscription (date 37-41 A.D.) at Spoletium
in Umbria, which, as supplemented by him, reads: C. Caesari Augusto
Germanico, | Germanici Caesaris f., Ti. Caesaris Aug. n., | divi Augusti
pron., pont. max., trib. pot.
| Vespasia f. Polla.
Newton (The Epigraph. Evidence for the Reigns of Vespasian and Titus,
p. 99) agrees that it most probably refers to our Vespasia Polla on the
grounds that Suet. says below that there were many memorials of the family
between Nursia and Spoletium; that the name Polla (from Paulla) is not a
common one; and that the mother of Vespasian would feel especial gratitude
to the emperor Gaius (Caligula) for his favours to her son (cf. Vesp. 2).
praefectum castrorum: the location of the troops in fixed quarters led to
the appointment of a new class of officers, the praefecti castrorum, who are
mentioned from the reign of Augustus to that of Septimius Severus (193-211
A.D.). They were chosen chiefly from centurions of long service, especially
primipili. Though a camp frequently contained several legions in the 1st
cent. A.D., there was generally only one praefectus castrorum; but when
Domitian ordained that each legion should have a separate camp (see
Dom. 7, 3), the “praefectus castrorum legionis (primae, etc.)” came in
time to be designated more briefly as “praefectus legionis," and finally,
under Gallienus (253-268 A.D.), supplanted the old senatorial "legatus
legionis." In peace time the praefectus castrorum was mainly concerned
with garrison duties, the distribution of military watches, etc. (cf. Tac.
Anm. i 20); in time of war he had to supervise the construction of camps,
the transport, the siege engines, the water supply, etc. (Veget. ii 10). See
Marquardt, op. cit. ii² 458.

Nursia: mod. Norcia, a Sabine town in the valley of the Nar at the
foot of the Apennines. It was the birthplace of Sertorius and in later
times of St. Benedict. Latin poets refer to the coldness of its climate;
e.g. Verg. Aen. vii 716, frigida Nursia: Sil. Ital. viii 416, habitata pruinis
Nursia. Suetonius (Aug. 12) describes how its inhabitants were punished
by Augustus for their republican sympathies and the aid which they gave
to L. Antonius in the Perusine war (41 в.с.).

Spoletium: mod. Spoleto, a town in Umbria between Interamna and
Trebia. A Roman colony was settled there in 240 в.с.
It became a
municipium by the Lex Iulia municipalis (45 в.с.).
The Via Flaminia
from Rome to Ariminum did not, up to Vespasian's time, pass through
Spoletium which lay to the right of it, but in later times the Itineraries
mention the road through Spoletium and Interamna as that usually taken.
There was always a branch road from the Via Flaminia to Spoletium, and
another branch road from Spoletium to Nursia. See Bunbury in Smith's
Dict. Geogr. ii 1032.

euntibus: this so-called “dativus absolutus," or dat. of reference,
denoting when (under what circumstances) a thing shows itself, is a
Graecism; cf. Galb. 4, 1, sinistrorsus Fundos petentibus: Varr. L.L. v 47,
sacrae viae pars quae est a Foro eunti primore clivo: Caes. B.C. iii 80,
oppidum primum Thessaliae venientibus ab Epiro: Liv. xxvi 26, sita
Anticyra est
laeva parte sinum Corinthiacum intranti. KühnerStegmann, i 321.
Vespasiae: this place does not seem to be mentioned elsewhere.
§ 4. non negaverim: for the subjunctive see on Oth. 12, 2 (“putem'').

mancipem operarum: Petro arranged for the supply of farm labourers
from Umbria and hired them out again at a profit to the Sabine farmers.
Heitland, who cites this passage in his Agricola (pp. 222, 327), does not
mention any other reference to migratory farm labour in Italy, nor does
Dorigny (Daremberg-Saglio, iv. 918) who inaccurately reproduces
Suetonius by saying: "On avait encore la ressource d'employer des
étrangers qui venaient, chaque année, faire la moisson dans les pays
fertiles. Le plus souvent, ces mercénaires étaient embauchés au delà du
Pô par un entrepreneur qui les conduisait dans l'Ombrie et le Latium et
y louait leurs services dans les grandes exploitations rurales."
=
subsedisse: cf. Vitell. 1, 3, quosdam ex Vitellis subsedisse Nuceriae.

curiose:
diligenter, accurate, attente; cf. Aug. 40, 4, cum curiose
cavisset: Calig. 16, 2, equites Romanos severe curioseque
recognovit:
Cic. Brut. 133, conquiram ista posthac curiosius. Lewis and Short (Lat.
Dict.) wrongly give this adv. the meaning of 'inquisitively, curiously” in
our passage, though it bears that meaning at times in other authors (e.g.
Cic. Brut. 231, ne vos curiosius eliceretis ex me quid de quoque iudicarem).
Suetonius uses the subst. curiosus in the sense of "eavesdropper, spy"
(Aug. 27, 3).

Falacrinae: this is most probably dat. sing. and not nom. pl.; see
note on "Becco,” Vitell. 18. The MSS. have Phalacrinae (or -ne).
Hülsen (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 1968) gives the name of the village as Falacrinae
(Falacrinis as abl. occurring in the Tab. Peut.). In the Itin. Ant. 366
Falacrino is the abl. from another form Falacrinum, and Cluver would
read Falacrino here. It was on the Via Salaria (see on Vesp. 12) in the
district of Reate near the mod. Civita Reale. Hülsen places it at the
village of Collicelli where there is still a church of S. Silvestro in Falacrino.
XV Kal. Decb.: Nov. 17.

Q. Sulpicio Camerino: Q. Sulpicius Q.f. Q.n. Camerinus was consul
ordinarius in 9 A.D. (Fast. Cap.: Plin. N.H. vii 158: Dio lvi arg. and c. 1).
He may possibly be identified with the epic poet mentioned in Ov. Pont. iv
16, 19, quique canit domitam Camerinus ab Hercule Troiam.

C. Poppaeo Sabino: C. Poppaeus Q. f. Q.n. Sabinus, who also was
consul ordinarius in 9 A.D., was the grandfather of Poppaea the wife of
Nero (Oth. 3, 1). He received triumphal honours in 26 A.D. for his victories
in Thrace. For 24 years he governed such important provinces as Moesia,
Achaia, and Macedonia "nullam ob eximiam artem, sed quod par negotiis
neque supra erat" (Tac. A. vi 39). He died in 35 A.D.

ante quam Augustus excederet: Augustus died on the 19th of Aug.,
14 A.D. (Suet. Aug. 100). For excederet see on c. 3.
Tertulla: wife of T. Flavius Petro Reatinus (c. 1, 2).

praediis Cosanis: Cosa (or Cosae, Aen. x 167) was a coast town of
Etruria with an important harbour, the Portus Cosanus. A Roman colony
was planted there in 273 в.с. Rutilius (Itin. i 285 sqq.) describes its
desolation in his time (c. 400 A.D.). Its interesting ruins bear the name
of Ansedonia. See Dennis, Cities and Cemeteries of Etruria ii³ 245-262.
Other Cosana (praedia) are mentioned in Cic. Att. ix 6, xv 27. It has
been doubted whether the Cosa in our passage is Cosa in Etruria. Repetti
thinks that it is rather Cossa or Compsa a town of the Hirpini (see Dennis,
p. 262), and Hülsen (Pauly-Wissowa, iv 1667) says "Das (praedium)
Cosanum bei Cic. ad Att. xv 27, 1 kann mit Cosa zusammenhängen, schwerlich dagegen die praedia Cosana wo Vespasian erzogen wurde"; on the
other hand, Stein (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2627) says it is the Cosa in Etruria.

locum incunabulorum: cf. Cic. Att. ii 15, 3, Ego vero “in montes
patrios et ad incunabula nostra” pergam: Ov. M. viii 99, Iovis incunabula,
Creten: Justin xxxi 8, Romanos avitos lares et incunabula maiorum
inexplebile desiderium videndi tenebat.

ne quid oculorum consuetudini deperiret: there is a very similar
expression in Plin. Ep. iv 13, Interim ne quid festinationi meae pereat
("that my impatience may lose nothing," i.e. "to satisfy my impatience''),
quod sum praesens petiturus hac quasi praecursoria epistula rogo. For
"oculorum consuetudo” cf. Cic. N.D. ii 96, assiduitate cotidiana et consuetudine oculorum assuescunt animi: Vel. Long. Orthogr. vii 69, 14, quicquid per consuetudinem aurium ita licuerit enuntiare.

sollemnibus ac festis diebus: Bremi explains these as family festivals,
birthdays, wedding days, etc., not public festivals.

pocillo: this dimin. of poculum occurs in Cato (R. R. 156 pocillum
fictile), Liv., Plin. N.H., etc. Suetonius uses a large number of diminutives;
see Appendix i. § 1. d. For the abl. with potare cf. Prop. i 14, 2, Lesbia
Mentoreo vina bibas opere (= ex opere "from cups chased by Mentor's
hand'').

perseveraverit: a favourite verb with Suet. who uses it 26 times,
either c. inf., or in aliqua re, or absolutely.

§ 2. sumpta virili toga: boys laid aside the toga praetexta and assumed
the toga virilis at the festival of the Liberalia on March 17. The normal
age for assuming it was between the completion of the 14th and the
completion of the 16th year (Marquardt, Privatl.2 123 sqq.); e.g. Augustus,
born on the 23rd of Sept. 63 B.c., assumed it in Oct. 48.

latum clavum: a broad purple stripe (or two stripes, see Marquardt,
op. cit. 547) woven into or stitched on to the tunica was distinctive of the
senatorial order, the equites being only entitled to wear the angustus clavus.
Augustus allowed the sons of senators to wear the tunica lati clavi on
assuming the toga virilis, and to attend meetings of the senate (Aug. 38, 2).
He also granted the right of wearing the latus clavus as a special favour
to some who were merely sons of equites, as a preliminary qualification
for entering the senate. An instance of this honour being bestowed on
the sons of equites is afforded by Ovid and his brother; cf. Trist. iv 10, 28,
liberior fratri sumpta mihique toga (i.e. the toga virilis) est: | induiturque
umeris cum lato purpura clavo. Those on whom the latus clavus was thus
conferred became eligible for the vigintivirate and the quaestorship.
quanquam: see on Tit. 7, 2.
fratre: Sabinus (c. 1, 3).

extudit: for this metaph. use of extundere (“to hammer out'') in the
sense of extorquere ab invito cf. Plaut. Most. 221, eundem animum oportet
nunc mihi esse gratum, ut impetravi, | atque olim, priusquam id extudi:
Val. Max. v 2, 13, perseveranti postulatione extuderunt ut, etc.: id. i 4, 4,
corvi duo in os eius adversum veluti iter impedientes advolaverunt: vixque
extuderunt ut domum rediret.

dum appellat: dum can be used not merely in a temporal but also
in a causal sense. Cicero has the perf. ind. with dum when so used; later
writers, especially Tacitus, prefer the present (Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii²
p. 607).

anteambulonem: the name for a slave who went before his master
in the streets to clear a way for him (cf. Plin. Ep. iii 14, 7); it was also
used contemptuously for the clients who went before the sella or lectica
of their patronus when he appeared in public; e.g. Mart. ii 18, 5, Sum
comes ipse tuus tumidique anteambulo regis (= patroni): id. iii 7, 3,
anteambulonis congiarium lassi: id. x 74, 3, anteambulones et togatulos
inter (cf. Juv. vii 143, x 44). See Marquardt, op. cit. 148.

§ 3. tribunus militum
meruit: all the better MSS. have tribunatum
for tribunus, and this is accepted by Roth, Ihm, and Preud'homme. The
reading tribunus (Torrentius) is rightly defended by Alexander (Textual
Criticisms on Suet. p. 8). No parallel is cited for tribunatum meruit in
the sense of "served as a tribune," and the usage of Suetonius seems
decisive; cf. Tit. 4, 1, tribunus militum et in Germania et in Britannia

meruit: vit. Horat. 1, bello Philippensi.. tribunus militum meruit: Tib. 9,
1, stipendia prima expeditione Cantabrica tribunus militum fecit. The
alternative explanation of tribunatum meruit, viz. that Vespasian earned
the post of tribunus militum by valour in Thrace, is contrary to what we
are told in Suet. Aug. 38, that those who received the latus clavus began
their career as military tribunes. Lipsius conjectured tribunatu meruit,
adopted by Casaubon and Ernesti.

Thracia: Vespasian served as military tribune in Thrace during the
reign of Tiberius when that country was in a very unsettled state, at
first through disputes between rival native kings who had been appointed
by Augustus (Tac. A. ii 64-67), and later through discontent at the rulers
established by Tiberius (A. iii 38). In 26 A.D. there was a revolt of the
highland tribes against the conscription which the Romans had introduced
into Thrace, but the rebels were forced to surrender by Poppaeus Sabinus
(see above), who was awarded triumphal distinctions (A. iv 46-51).

Cretam et Cyrenas: Cyrene (or Cyrenae) was the capital of the
district of Cyrenaica in N. Africa which was brought under Egyptian rule
by Ptolemy, son of Lagos, in 321 B.c. Apion, the bastard son of Ptolemy
Physcon, received Cyrenaica from his father as a special kingdom and
at his death bequeathed it by will to the Romans in 95 B.C. Rome at
first left the cities in Cyrenaica free, but was driven by their internal
quarrels to reduce Cyrenaica to a province (c. 75 в.с.), and it was united
with Crete on the subjugation of that island by Q. Metellus Creticus in
67 B.C. Augustus assigned the combined province (known as Creta-Cyrene,
Creta et Cyrene, or Creta simply) to the senate and it was put under a
propraetor who bore the title of proconsul.

provinciam sorte cepit: under the Empire no quaestors were sent to
imperial provinces (Gaius i 6), but the proconsular governor of each
senatorial province had one of the quaestors of the year allotted to him
with the title quaestor pro praetore; cf. Tac. Agr. 6, 2, sors quaesturae
provinciam Asiam dedit (Agricolae).

aedilitatis: for his unpleasant experience as aedile (in 38 A.D.) see
с. 5, 3.

illam: this correction of the meaningless etiam of the MSS. was made
by Torrentius, and the following hanc was restored by Bentley and Duker
for ac.

repulsa: the tech. term for defeat at an election. ferre repulsam
meant to be defeated"; renuntiari ‘‘to be returned."
sexto loco: i.e. he got in last. Julius Caesar added to the existing
four aediles two new ones called "Cereales" (qui frumento praeessent),
so that there were six in all; cf. Digest i 2, 32: Dio xliii 51. Marius
was returned last when he stood for the praetorship: Val. Max. vi 9, 14,
praeturae candidatus (Marius) supremo loco inhaesit.

in primis: to be distinguished from “primus,” as is shown by Cic.
Pis. 1, me cum quaestorem in primis, aedilem priorem (there were two
curule aediles), praetorem primum cunctis suffragiis populus Romanus
faciebat. Cf. Mur. 8, 18, where Cic. says: Neque enim vestrum quemquam
fugit, cum multi pares dignitate fiant, unus autem primum locum solus
possit obtinere, non eundem esse ordinem dignitatis et renuntiationis,
propterea quod renuntiatio gradus habet, dignitas autem est persaepe eadem
omnium.
praetor: in 39 A.D.

infensum senatui Gaium: the wrath of Caligula against the senate
is described in Suet. Calig. 48 sq.; he accused them of robbing him of
his well-earned triumph for his victory in Germany, and when they sent
envoys asking him to hasten his return to Rome, he roared out "I will
come and this (smiting his sword) will be with me"; he made proclamation.
that he was returning only to those who wished his presence, i.e. the equites
and the commons, for to the senate he would never more be fellow-citizen
or prince, and he forbade any senator to meet him. infensum (Lipsius)
is a necessary correction, as infensus of the MSS. can only be interpreted
unsatisfactorily of Vespasian's indignation against the senate for their
treatment of him when he stood for the aedileship, the election of magistrates having been transferred by Tiberius from the comitia to the senate.

ne quo non genere demereretur: see on Vitell. 2, 5, Claudium
ne qua non arte demereretur.
..

ludos extraordinarios: i.e. in addition to the ordinary games celebrated every year; see Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 482 sqq. In 22 B.C. Augustus
assigned to the praetors the charge of the games at Rome (Galb. 6, 1, n.),
though the quaestors occasionally gave gladiatorial shows (Dom. 4, 1).

pro victoria Germanica: in Sept. 39 A.D. Caligula undertook an
expedition, nominally against the Germans, of which little is known.
Ancient writers agree in deriding it, e.g. Tacitus, H. iv 15, Gaianarum
expeditionum ludibrium: Germ. 37, ingentes Gai Caesaris minae in
ludibrium versae; cf. Suet. Calig. 44–47, Dio lix 21 and 25. Merivale
(Rom. Hist. vi 80) suggests that Caligula's main object was to assert his
authority over Gaetulicus, the turbulent legatus of Upper Germany, who
was conspiring against him (see next note), and to cow the Rhine legions.
Furneaux (Tac. Ann., vol ii, Introd. p. 17) takes a similar view. Caligula
announced to the senate a great victory over the Germans (Pers. vi 43,
missa est a Caesare laurus | insignem ob cladem Germanae pubis, etc.).
He may have actually repulsed some band of Germans attempting to invade
Gaul (see Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. c. xiv). He wintered at Lugdunum,
extorting money from the Gauls, and in the spring of 40 he assembled a
large force at Bononia (Boulogne) for the conquest of Britain; but having
reviewed the troops on the shore, he ordered them to pile arms and pick
shells which were sent to Rome as a sign of his great victory over the
ocean and its island.

coniuratorum: Aemilius Lepidus and Lentulus Gaetulicus. The latter
commanded the legions on the Upper Rhine for 10 years (see Galb. 6, 2),
and had already defied the emperor Tiberius to remove him when he was
charged with sapping the loyalty of the legions. He was implicated in the
plot of Aemilius Lepidus (an imperial favourite married to Drusilla sister
of Caligula) to slay Caligula and seize the throne. Agrippina and Julia,
sisters of Caligula, took part in this plot, which was discovered in 39 A.D.
Lepidus and Gaetulicus were executed, while Agrippina and Julia were
banished (Calig. 24: Claud. 9: Dio lix 22).

insepulti: loss of burial was part of the penalty paid by those condemned for treason (perduellio, maiestas), e.g. Tiberius Gracchus, Val.
Max. iv 7, hostis iudicatus, ultimo supplicio affectus, sepulturae honore
spoliatus. Cf. Ulpian (Digest lxviii 24): corpora eorum qui capite
damnantur cognatis ipsorum neganda non sunt, et id se observasse etiam
divus Augustus libro decimo de vita sua scribit; hodie autem eorum, in
quos animadvertitur, corpora non aliter sepeliuntur, quam si fuerit petitum
et permissum, et nonnunquam non permittitur, maxime maiestatis causa
damnatorum. Besides loss of burial their memory was for ever condemned
(damnata memoria) and their relatives were forbidden to wear mourning
(Digest iii 2, 11; xi 7, 35; xxxi 76, 9; Suet. Tib. 61, 2).

egit gratias: this returning of thanks to the emperor in the senate
is often mentioned; it was done either by an individual member for an
imperial favour bestowed (Oth. 2, 2), or by the senate collectively (e.g.
Iul. 16, 2: Tib. 53, 2: Ner. 7, 2; 10, 2: Tit. 11). Such an actio
gratiarum to the emperor was customary on the part of a consul entering
on office (e.g. Pliny's Panegyricus on Trajan).

amplissimum ordinem: amplissimus = senatorius, as in Calig. 49, 1:
Oth. 8, 1. So amplissimus magistratus = consulatus (Aug. 26, 2); amplissimi honores = magistratus curules (Iul. 72, Vitell. 5). Cicero has amplissimus ordo with reference to the senate twelve times in his speeches. In
Vesp. 9, 2 Suet. uses amplissimi ordines for senators and equites.

honore cenae: a coveted honour, according to the amusing story in
Calig. 39. The emperor Caligula found out that a wealthy provincial had
bribed those who issued the invitations (vocatores) with a sum of 200,000
sesterces, to be smuggled in as a guest at the imperial table. Caligula
was not in the least annoyed that the honour was rated so highly (nec
tulerat moleste tam magno aestimari honorem cenae suae), but next day
when he saw this man present at an auction of furniture which Caligula
was holding, he sent a messenger to hand him some trifle or other at the
price of 200,000 sesterces, and to say that he should dine that day with
Caesar on Caesar's own invitation (vocatu ipsius). Statius (Silv. iv 2)
writes in ecstatic terms of the honour of dining with Domitian; so too
Martial describes the divine" Domitian's banquets as ambrosiae dapes
(e.g. iv 8,8: viii 39, 2). Pliny (Ep. vi 31) highly appreciates the honour
of acting as Trajan's legal assessor and of dining with him when the
cases had been heard.

Flaviam Domitillam duxit uxorem: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 1,
Titus matre liberta Domitilla nomine genitus: ib. 11, 1, Domitianus
Vespasiani et Domitillae libertae filius, germanus Titi. Mommsen (Staatsr.
ii³ 822, n. 1) shows that this Flavia Domitilla cannot have been deified,
since Statius (Silv. i 1, 97 sqq.), though mentioning Domitian's son,
brother, father, and sister as among the gods, makes no mention of his
mother. Thus inscriptions and coins on which diva Domitilla occurs are
to be referred to the daughter (see below) and not the mother. Stein
(Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2732) thinks that as the mother was not deified she
did not receive the title of Augusta, and so he refers C.I.L. vi 31287
(= Newton 229), in which Domitilla Augusta occurs, to the daughter. If
he is correct, the only inscription to Vespasian's wife is C.I.L. x 1419
(= Newton 228): Flaviae Domitillae [Imp.] Vespasian[i C]aesar[is] Aug.
Coins issued under Titus with the legend memoriae Domitillae may be in
honour of the mother (Stein, l.c.) or the daughter (Eckhel, vi 346).

equitis R.: there were numerous instances of provincials attaining
the rank of eques at Rome, e.g. Seneca's father who came from Corduba
in Spain; cf. Tac. A. xiv 53, where the younger Seneca says “Egone,
equestri et provinciali loco ortus, proceribus civitatis adnumerer?" So
too Columella was probably an eques from Cadiz. For the cosmopolitan
character of the Roman knighthood see Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 146.
Caligula included in it the eminent men of every province; cf. Vesp. 9, 2.

Sabratensis: Sabrata (Σάβρατα or Σάβραθα Ptol., Σαβαραθά Procop.)
is mentioned as a Phoenician foundation in Africa; Sil. Ital. iii 256,
Sabratha tum Tyrium vulgus Sarranaque Leptis, | Oeaque Trinacrios Afris
permixta colonos, | et Tingin rapido mittebat ab aequore Lixus. It lay
to the W. of Oea (mod. Tripoli), and these two towns together with Leptis
Magna made up the Tripolis Africana or Regio Tripolitana. Afterwards
Sabrata became a Roman colony (Itin. Anton. p. 61), and is the mod.
Sabart or Tripoli Vecchio.

delicatam: = delicias, concubinam, amicam; cf. “delicatus,” Tit. 7, 2.
Latinae condicionis: the status of half-emancipated libertini. Those
manumitted by any of the three statutory methods, vindicta, censu, testamento, became cives Romani. There were also informal modes of manumission, e.g. per epistolam (the master writing to the slave that he was
free); inter amicos (a statement of the master in the presence of his
friends that the slave was free); adhibitione cenae (the master inviting
the slave to dine). These informally manumitted slaves, though their
freedom was secured to them, were still slàves in the eyes of the law,
any property they acquired belonging legally to their masters. The Lex
Iunia Norbana (19 A.D. ?) gave them legal status: they were made freemen with the rights of Latin colonists (Latini coloniarii) i.e. commercium
without conubium, with the important restriction that they could not make
a will or take under a will. Such freedmen were called Latini Iuniani as
distinct from the older Latins. Gaius (i 28, where see Poste) mentions
many ways by which Latini Iuniani might become cives, e.g. re-manumission (iteratio) in one of the statutory modes, serving six years in the
Roman guards, imperial grant (beneficium imperiale), begetting three
children (ius trium liberorum). Justinian (Cod. vii 7) abolished the status
of Latinitas altogether. Cf. Roby, Roman Private Law i 28 sqq.
mox: see on Oth. 10, 1.

reciperatorio iudicio: reciperatores (recup-) “recoverers” were first
appointed to adjudicate on the recovery of property between Rome and
foreign states, and in private suits between cives Romani and peregrini.
They were generally 3 or 5 in number, chosen by the praetor, and some
might be peregrini, whereas only a civis could be a iudex proper. We find
reciperatores acting in cases of many kinds, e.g. cases of debt (Plaut.
Bacch. 270), cases of extortion (Tac. A. i 74), fiscal cases (Suet. Ner. 17),
and cases of disputed legal status as ingenuus, libertus, servus (Plaut.
Rud. 1282: Suet. Dom. 8, 1: Cic. Flacc. 17, 40, Atque huic eidem nuper
tres equites Romani (acting as reciperatores) honesti et graves, cum in
causa liberali eum, qui adserebatur, cognatum suum esse diceret, non
crediderunt). Roby, ii 316 sqq.

patre asserente: in cases affecting freedom (causae liberales) the
persons whose status was involved could not conduct the claim themselves,
as their status was undetermined, but must act through a representative
called an assertor (in libertatem). The claim for freedom could be maintained, even though the person affected was unwilling, by father, son, or
kinsmen, or, failing them, by mother, daughter, or kinswomen (Digest xl
12); cf. Suet. Gramm. 21, quamquam asserente matre permansit tamen in
statu servitutis. The phrase "asserere manu aliquem in libertatem (or
liberali causa)" meant to lay one's hand on the person whose claim to
freedom was maintained"; the opposite phrase occurs in Tib. 2, 2, virginem
ingenuam in servitutem asserere.
Cf. Dom. 8, 1: Vitell. 10, 2.
Ferenti: see on Oth. 1, 1.

nec quicquam amplius quam:
modo; see on “nihil aliud quam,” Dom. 21.
=
= et nihil amplius quam et tantumquaestorio scriba: the scribae quaestorii formed an important collegium,
divided into 3 decuriae, and controlled by the sex primi and a princeps
(Cic. N.D. iii 30, 74: C.I.L. vi 1805: Plut. Cat. min. 16); they were
probably 27 in number before Sulla's time and 36 later. They dealt with
the business of the aerarium and public accounts, and also with the
various state records kept in the aerarium. Two were attached to each
provincial governor (cf. Dom. 9, 3). Some were liberti, but the majority
ingenui. They claimed to belong to the ordo equester, and are included
in it by Cicero (de domo 28, 73), though at other times, when it suits his
purpose, Cicero speaks of this rank of theirs with contempt (Verr. iii 60,
137; 79, 184). In the suite of provincial governors they came after the
staff officers of equestrian rank. We read of scribae who afterwards became quaestors, curule aediles, and praetors. The slighting manner in which
Suet. speaks of them here is due to the fact that they were mercenarii,
and so were looked down upon in comparison with officials and magistrates
who were not paid; cf. Nep. Eum. 1, quod (i.e. the position of scriba,
γραμματεύς) multo apud Graios honorificentius est quam apud Romanos:
namque apud nos re vera, sic ut sunt, mercenarii scribae existimantur.
See Mommsen, Staatsr. i 346 sqq. The poet Horace, after serving as
tribune in the Republican army, bought a position as scriba quaestorius
(Suet. vit. Horat.).

ex hac liberos tulit: Suetonius is very fond of the phrase "ferre liberos
ex (once de, Vitell. 6) uxore," which is used of the father in the same
sense as "tollere liberos" (see on Tit. 4, 2) or “suscipere liberos"; cf.
Aug. 4, 1, quos ex Atia tulerat Augustus: Aug. 63, 1: Calig. 7: Claud. 1,
6; 27, 1: Ner. 35, 3: Oth. 1, 3 (bis): Dom. 3, 1. He uses ferre without
ex uxore in Tib. 47, qui quattuor liberos tulerat; this occurs earlier in
Sen. Herc. O. 1604, quem (Philocteten) tulit Poeas, and Statius has a
similar expression, Silv. i 2, 72, quem
Nobilitas gavisa tulit
("Nobilitas” being personified as a father; see Vollmer). Titus was
born on Dec. 30, 39 A.D., Domitian on Oct. 24, 51 A.D.

Domitillam: this Flavia Domitilla is referred to (without being
named) as sister of the emperor Domitian in Quintil. Inst. Orat. iv
prooem. 2, and in Stat. Silv. i 1, 98; in the latter passage she is mentioned
as one of the deified members of Domitian's family. See the note above
on her mother Flavia Domitilla. The name of the husband of this daughter
of Vespasian is unknown; she had a daughter, also called Flavia Domitilla,
who became the wife of Flavius Clemens (see Dom. 15, 1; 17, 1).

adhuc privatus: i.e. before July 1, 69 A.D.
=

excessum: mortem; cf. Tib. 22; 70, 3: Calig. 1, 1; 9; 48, 1:
Ner. 5, 2. The mysterious passing of Romulus is called excessus by
Cicero: Legg. i 1, 3 Romulus post excessum suum; Rep. ii 30, post obitum,
vel potius excessum, Romuli. Elsewhere in Cic. either excessus e vita
(opp. to in vita mansio, Fin. iii 18, 60) or excessus vitae (Tusc. i 12, 27).
The use of excedere by itself in the sense of mori is unclassical (Cic. has
2 c
excedere vita or e vita); it is first found in Tac. and occurs with especial
frequency in Suet. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 487.

Caenidem: described in a titulus sepulcralis or sepulchral inscription
(C.I.L. vi 12037, Newton 237) as Antonia Aug(ustae) l(iberta) Caenis;
there is another inscription (C.I.L. vi 18358, Newton 238) to Flavia Helpis
Caenidiana, a slave of Vespasian and attendant on Caenis, who on manumission took the gentile name of Vespasian and a cognomen formed from
the cognomen of Antonia Caenis. Dio (lxvi 14) praises Caenis for her
fidelity and the excellence of her memory, and tells how once her mistress
Antonia gave her a letter about Sejanus to bear to Tiberius and charged
her to see that it was at once destroyed so as to leave no trace: whereupon Caenis replied that such a charge was useless as her retentive memory
would preserve the contents of the letter for ever. As concubine of
Vespasian she had great influence and acquired vast wealth, for all who
wished to get posts from the emperor would load her with presents; this
being done, as rumour said, with the connivance of the penurious Vespasian
(see on Vesp. 16). Domitian, however, treated her with contempt (see
Dom. 12, 3). She died before 75 A.D., and Vespasian kept many concubines
in her place (Vesp. 21).

Antoniae: this younger daughter of Marcus Antonius, the triumvir,
was born in 36 B.c. and married Drusus, brother of the emperor Tiberius,
to whom she bore (1) Germanicus, the father of the emperor Caligula:
(2) the emperor Claudius: (3) a daughter named Livilla.
a manu: = amanuensis, which is used in Tit. 3, 2, where see note.

contubernium: here = concubinatus. It was primarily used of soldiers
sharing the same tent (tabernaculum), and was then extended to intimacies
of any kind, often illicit ones. We see the transition in Cic. Verr. vi 104,
ubi illud contubernium muliebris militiae in illo delicatissimo litore?

iustae uxoris: cf. Calig. 24, 1, Drusillam
in modum iustae uxoris
propalam habuit; so iustum matrimonium, e.g. Ner. 28, 1, Acten libertam
paulum afuit quin iusto matrimonio sibi coniungeret. Latin jurists use
the phrases iustum matrimonium and iustae nuptiae for legal wedlock which
required conubium, pubertas, consensus (Roby, op. cit. i 128 sqq.).
•

Claudio principe missus est: cf. Eutrop. vii 19, 1, ut qui a Claudio
in Germaniam et deinde in Britanniam missus tricies et bis cum hoste
conflixerit, duas validissimas gentes, viginti oppida, insulam Vectam
Britanniae proximam imperio Romano adiecerit. Hübner (Hermes xvi,
p. 528, n. 5) notices the inscriptional style of the words of Suetonius in
the opening sentences of this chapter, “Worte denen wohl der Text einer
Triumphalinschrift zu Grunde liegt."

Narcissi gratia: Narcissus was a notorious freedman and secretary
(ab epistulis) of Claudius. He and another freedman Pallas, the treasurer
(a rationibus), made themselves all-powerful in the emperor's palace
(Claud. 28, Tit. 2; Dio lx 17), and both accumulated enormous fortunes
(cf. Juv. xiv 329). Narcissus insisted on the execution of Messalina, wife
of Claudius (see on Vitell. 2, 5). He opposed Agrippina, the new empress,
and supported the claim of Britannicus (son of Messalina) against that
of Nero (son of Agrippina) to be designated as successor to Claudius.
Shortly after Nero's accession (54 A.D.) he was driven to suicide. Dio (lx 19)
says that when the soldiers of Plautius were unwilling to embark in Gaul
for Britain, Narcissus was sent from Rome and mounting the tribunal of
Plautius tried to address the mutineers, who howled the ex-slave down with
cries of Io Saturnalia!, but nevertheless they suddenly became submissive
to the orders of their commander. Furneaux (Tac. Ann. Vol. ii Introd.
c. 5) suggests that the prominence of Narcissus in the story of the despatch
of the expedition points to the cupidity of freedmen and other courtiers
as a great prompting motive of the undertaking.

legatus legionis: Augustus perpetuated the custom introduced by the
dictator Caesar of placing the whole legion under the command of a
legatus. These legati legionum (or legati Augusti legionum) were
always senators either of praetorian rank or qualified to attain such
rank (Tac. A. ii 36). Vespasian was given command of the 2nd legion at
Argentoratum (Strassburg) after his praetorship; cf. Tac. H. iii 44,
Britanniae inclinatus erga Vespasianum favor, quod illic secundae legioni
a Claudio praepositus et bello clarus egerat: id. Agr. 13, divus Claudius
auctor iterati operis (i.e. the conquest of Britain) transvectis legionibus et
adsumpto in partem rerum Vespasiano, quod initium venturae mox fortunae
fuit: domitae gentes, capti reges et monstratus fatis Vespasianus. The
four legions sent under Plautius against Britain were the 2nd (Augusta)
and 14th (Gemina Martia) from Upper Germany: the 20th (Valeria Victrix)
from Lower Germany: the 9th (Hispana) from Pannonia.

tricies conflixit: Eutropius (vii 19, 1) says tricies et bis.
Nothing
definite is known with regard to these engagements. Dio (lx 20) mentions
Vespasian and his brother Sabinus as effecting the crossing of an unspecified river (most probably the Medway) and slaughtering many of
the foe. Thence the Britons retired across the Thames. This was before
the arrival of Claudius (see below). In the last three years of Plautius'
command (44-47) Vespasian and the 2nd legion seem to have subjugated
Hampshire and as far as Exeter and South Wales. See Furneaux (l.c.)
and Haverfield in Furneaux-Anderson, Tac. Agr. Introd. xliii sqq. Josephus
(Bell. Iud. iii 1) eulogizes Vespasian for having pacified the West by
subduing the Germans, and for having won Britain by force of arms,
thus affording Claudius a triumph without any sweat of his own (χωρὶς
ἱδρῶτος ἰδίου).

duas validissimas gentes: these have been identified with the Belgae
and Atrebates. The chief towns of the Belgae were Ischalis (Ilchester),
Aquae Sulis (Bath), and Venta Belgarum (Winchester); the capital of
the Atrebates was Calleva (Silchester).

Vectem: Vectis or Vecta (Οὐηκτίς) is the Isle of Wight, opposite to
Portus Magnus (Portsmouth).

Auli Plauti: Aulus Plautius Silvanus was an experienced officer
brought from Pannonia to act as commander-in-chief in Britain (43-47 A.D.).
He had been one of the consules suffecti in 29 A.D. Dio (lx 19) describes
him as βουλευτὴς (senator) λογιμώτατος. He was rewarded for his achievements in Britain with an ovatio, an honour which, like the triumphus, was
reserved for members of the imperial family, and the emperor Claudius
2c2
walked by his left side to and from the Capitol (Suet. Claud. 24, Dio lx 30,
Tac. A. xiii 32)..

legati consularis: Plautius was the first governor of the province of
Britain; cf. Tac. Agr. 14, consularium primus Aulus Plautius praepositus
ac subinde Ostorius Scapula (47-52 A.D.), uterque bello egregius: redactaque paulatim in formam provinciae proxima pars Britanniae. In the
imperial provinces (provinciae Caesaris) the emperor was himself proconsul
but governed through legati Augusti pro praetore, who as a rule were
chosen by him from those who had been consuls or praetors; hence they
are spoken of as legati consulares or praetorii.

Claudi ipsius ductu: Plautius landed in Kent with 40,000 men, and
made his way in spite of the vigorous resistance of the Britons to the
south bank of the Thames at a point where it could be crossed, near
London. He then sent for the emperor himself to assume the supreme
command. Dio (lx 21) says that Claudius was only 16 days in Britain.
He left Rome in July, 43 A.D., joined the waiting army on the Thames,
at once crossed with it, conquered in a pitched battle, took Camulodunum
(Colchester) the capital of the native prince Cunobelinus (Cymbeline) and
subdued or received the surrender of many of the enemy. Having
repeatedly accepted the salutation of imperator from the troops, he gave
over command to Plautius and returned to Rome where he celebrated a
magnificent triumph. Suetonius (Claud. 17) says that it was the desire
to win the full honours of a triumph (iusti triumphi decus) that led him
in the first instance to plan the conquest of Britain.

§ 2. triumphalia ornamenta: these included the right to be styled
“triumphalis," to wear the toga picta, tunica palmata, and aurea corona,
and to carry an ivory sceptre (scipio eburnus); the honour of a statua
triumphalis or laureata was usually added (cf. Tac. Agr. 40). From 14 в.с.
triumphs were reserved for the imperial family, and successful legati
received merely the ornamenta (or insignia). In Aug. 38 Suetonius says
that Augustus granted these ornamenta more than 30 times, and in Tib. 9
he says that according to some they were first given by him to Tiberius
(in 12 B.с.). Tiberius as emperor degraded the distinction by giving it to
unworthy people (Dio lviii 14); so too Claudius, who conferred the
ornamenta e.g. on senators who accompanied him on his expedition to
Britain (Dio lx 23). Suetonius (Claud. 24) mentions a joint petition from
the legions to Claudius asking that these ornamenta should be bestowed
ex officio on all legati consulares, to prevent them seeking pretexts for
war. Nero gave them even to quaestors and equites and for other than
military services (Ner. 15). From Trajan's time all consuls had the right
to use them on official occasions and the distinction lost all value. See
Mommsen, Staatsr. is 465; Daremberg-Saglio, v 491.

duplex sacerdotium: from the evidence of coins Eckhel (vi 331)
concludes that these priesthoods were the augurship and chief pontificate.
Cf. Galb. 8, 1, Vitell. 5 for similar honours.
..

consulatum menses: he was consul suffectus in Nov.-Dec. 51 A.D.;
see Dom. 1, 1.
proconsulatum: he became proconsul of Africa; see below (§ 3).

in otio secessuque egit: cf. Galb. 8, 1, ex eo tempore prope ad medium
Neronis principatum in secessu plurimum vixit. Another secessus of
Vespasian is mentioned below (§ 4).

Agrippinam: a daughter of Germanicus (see on Vitell. 2, 3). In spite
of the intrigues of Narcissus on behalf of Aelia Paetina, she was made
the wife of her uncle the emperor Claudius in 49, after the death of
Messalina. Nero was her son by an earlier husband Domitius Ahenobarbus.
With the aid of Locusta she poisoned Claudius in 54. On the accession
of Nero she was responsible for the death of her enemy Narcissus among
others. The young Nero tried to shake off the ascendancy of his arrogant
mother, and when she threatened to replace him as emperor by Britannicus
(son of Messalina), he had Britannicus poisoned. Her opposition to Nero's
amours with a freedwoman Acte and later with Poppaea (wife of Otho)
led to her death. After an unsuccessful attempt to drown her, she was
stabbed to death by Nero's agents in 59 (cf. Oth. 3, 1: Tac. 4. xiv 8).

potentem: this potentia of Agrippina is mentioned by Tacitus; e.g.
A. xiii 12, infracta paulatim potentia matris delapso Nerone in amorem
libertae: xiv 1, cupientibus omnibus infringi potentiam matris.

defuncti Narcissi: the forced suicide of Narcissus in 54 A.D. is
mentioned in Tac. A. xiii 1, nec minus properato Narcissus Claudii libertus,
de cuius iurgiis adversus Agrippinam rettuli, aspera custodia et necessitate
extrema ad mortem adigitur, invito principe (i.e. Nero), cuius abditis adhuc
vitiis per avaritiam ac prodigentiam mire congruebat.
quoque: = etiam; see on Vitell. 7, 3.

amicos perosam: the better MSS. have amici (retained by Roth,
Preud 'homme, and Ihm); amicos is read by all the earlier editors and is
supported by Madvig (Adv. ii 570). Modderman proposed amicitiam periculosam. The difficulty in amici (= any friend of Narcissus) is the use of
the gen. with perosam, for until a very late period this verb always takes
the acc. (used, e.g., by Augustus ap. Suet. Tib. 21, 7), the gen. occurring
only in Prudent. Peristeph. iii 41, perosa quietis (Boethius, Cons. Phil. ii 4,
has vitae huius exosa), where the participle is used adjectivally. It would
be easy to read amicum (amicū being corrupted to amici through assimilation
to defuncti and Narcissi). Alexander, who defends amici, explains the
passage as meaning "fearing Agrippina, who still held dominant influence
over her son and hated as well the dead Narcissus, his (Vespasian's)
friend'; for the adjectival use of perosam (“full of hatred against'")
he compares exosa (“contemptuous of'") in Boeth. and veritus ("regardful of'") in Cic. Att. viii 4, 1, ne tui quidem testimonii veritus.
..

§ 3. sortitus Africam: the date of his proconsulship is uncertain, but
it was after the death of Agrippina in 59. Borghesi says it was before
62 (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2629); Bury assigns it to 63. For sortitus see on
Galb. 7, 1, Africam optinuit extra sortem.

integerrime administravit: this conflicts with what Tacitus says,
H. ii 97: integrum illic (i.e. in Africa) ac favorabilem ("popular'') proconsulatum Vitellius, famosum invisumque Vespasianus egerat. Suetonius
agrees with Tac. about Vitellius (Vitell. 5, in provincia singularem innocentiam praestitit). Which is the true account of Vespasian's governorship is uncertain, but at the time of his accession he was very unpopular
in Africa; cf. Tac. H. iv 49, nec ambigitur provinciam (i.e. Africa) et
militem alienato erga Vespasianum animo fuisse. Silius Italicus (iii 599)
eulogizes Vespasian: compescet ripis Rhenum, reget impiger Afros, |
palmiferamque senex bello domitabit Idumen.
nisi quod: see on Vitell. 7, 1.

Hadrumeti: on the E. coast of Tunis. Sallust (Iug. 19) mentions it
as a Phoenician colony older than Carthage.
It sided with Rome in the
third Punic war, and on the destruction of Carthage it was guaranteed
its independence as a populus liber. It also figures in the civil war on
the side of Pompey against Caesar (Bell. Afr. 3, 62, 97). Trajan made
it a Roman colony, its official title in inscriptions being "col. Concordia
Ulpia Traiana Augusta Frugifera Hadrumetina.”” Destroyed by the
Vandals it was restored by Justinian as Justinianopolis. Its ruins are at
the mod. Susa.

rapa in eum iacta sunt: even the emperors were exposed to such
manifestations of popular indignation; e.g. Claudius was pelted with
bits of bread in the Forum on account of a scarcity of grain (Claud. 18, 2),
and for the same reason Antoninus Pius was pelted with stones (Aur. Vict.
Epit. 15).

rediit nihilo opulentior: he must have refrained from the plundering
which so often led to accusations for extortion (res repetundae) against
provincial governors; cf. Oth. 2, 2.

labefactata fide: in other authors labefactare fidem means "to sap or
undermine the loyalty of"; e.g. Tac. A. xiii 21, provinciarum fidem labefactatam: Cic. Cluent. 68, 194: Liv. xxiv 20, 15.
Suetonius uses labefacto
only here; in Ner. 38, 1 and Calig. 57, 1 he has labefño of structures
collapsing or being demolished.

fratri: i.e. Flavius Sabinus (see c. 1, 3). The mortgage led to illwill between the brothers according to Tac. H. iii 65: namque Flavius
Sabinus aetate prior privatis utriusque rebus auctoritate pecuniaque
Vespasianum anteibat et credebatur adfectam eius fidem praeiuvisse (parce
iuvisse, Heraeus) domo agrisque pignori acceptis; unde, quamquam manente
in speciem concordia, offensarum operta metuebantur.

obligaret: cf. Claud. 9, 2, cum obligatam aerario fidem liberare non
posset: Plaut. Truc. 214, fundi et aedes obligatae sunt: Cic. Agr. iii 2, 9,
obligata praedia; so with pignori (as in opponere pignori “to mortgage''),
Digest xxxix 2, 44, aedes pignori obligare.

mangonicos quaestus: mango (from which comes Eng. "monger'')
was used for a dealer who employed every artifice and attraction to get
rid of his wares; cf. Gr. μάγγανον "a charm,” μαγγανεύω. It was
specially used of slave-dealers (e.g. Suet. Aug. 69, 1: Dom. 7, 1), but
Pliny (N.H.) has it of dealers in wine, precious stones, perfumes, and
drugs. Apparently Vespasian traded in mules, and Marcilius cites glosses
of Philoxenus (ἱπποβοσκός· mango and κυνοτρόφος· mango) to show that mango
could be used of a vendor of animals. Weynand (in Pauly-Wissowa, vi
2629) and Heitland (Agricola 327) prefer to regard Vespasian as a slavedealer.

descenderit: for the perf. subjunct. coupled with the imperf.
(obligaret) see on Galb. 3, 1. When he became emperor, Vesp. still
stooped to trading (c. 16, 1), though even senators were legally debarred
from it (Friedl. Sitteng. i10 130). Pertinax, when consularis, carried on a
business in Liguria through the agency of his slaves (Capit. Pert. c. 3).

mulio vocabatur: “propter mangonicos quaestus e mulis Reatinis, qui
tum maxime in usu et pretio. Vespasiani autem praedia in agro Reatino"
(Casaubon). Reate (c. 1, 2), like Arcadia, was famous for its asses, some
of which fetched 60,000 or 100,000 sesterces; they were used especially
for the breeding of mules (Varr. R.R. ii 1, 14; Plin. N.H. viii 167).
Ernesti and Bremi think that Vespasian hired out mules for transport
purposes. Lipsius explains mulio as meaning, not that Vesp. was a vendor
of mules, but that he was an itinerant merchant always on the road like
a muleteer; in support of this he quotes Seneca (Apoc. 6) who describes
Hercules as having tramped more lands “quam ullus mulio perpetuarius.”
The nickname of ‘‘mulio” was earlier given to Ventidius Bassus by Plancus
(Cic. Fam. x 18) and by Cicero (Plin. N.H. vii 135). Bassus, who celebrated a triumph in 38 B.C. for his victory over the Parthians, made a
livelihood in his youth by supplying mules; cf. Gell. N.A. xv 4, сит
adolevisset, victum sibi aegre quaesisse, eumque sordide invenisse comparandis mulis et vehiculis quae magistratibus, qui sortiti provincias forent,
praebenda publice conduxisset; in isto quaestu notum esse coepisse C.
Caesari, etc.

latum clavum: see on c. 2, 2. Vespasian had used his influence with
Nero to obtain the honour for this youth. Such unprincipled conduct
brought him into disrepute in his earlier years; cf. Auson. Caes. x, olim
qui dubiam privato in tempore famam, | rarum aliis, princeps transtulit
in melius.

impetrarat: see Kühner-Stegmann ii 544 sqq., where many examples
are given, from early Latin and from Sall., Liv., and later writers, of the
indic. in subordinate clauses in Oratio Obliqua. It is common in Suetonius;
e.g.. Tib. 44, 2, fertur utrique mox, quod mutuo flagitium exprobrarant,
crura fregisse: Iul. 9, 2, referens Caesarem in consulatu confirmasse
regnum, de quo aedilis cogitarat: Iul. 30, 2, Pompeius dictitabat, quod
neque consummare, quae instituerat, neque populi expectationem, quam
fecerat, explere posset, turbare omnia voluisse (Caesarem).
eo nomine: = eâ causâ; cf. Galb. 16, 1, eo nomine omnes exacerbavit :
Ner. 30, 1, laudabat Gaium nullo magis nomine, quam quod, etc.
“nomen”
properly meant the heading under which an item was entered in an account;
cf. Vesp. 8, 3, calciarii nomine: Iul. 25, 1, stipendii nomine. The extended
use of the word is frequent in Cicero; e.g. Lael. 25, multis nominibus
("under many heads," "on many accounts'') est hoc vitium notandum.

§ 4. peregrinatione Achaica: Suetonius (Ner. 22 sq.) says that all the
Greek cities which held musici agones had adopted the rule of sending to
Nero the citharoedorum coronae, and Nero welcomed their messengers and
told them that the Greeks were the only people with an ear for music
and that they alone were worthy of hearing his musical efforts. In Sept.
66 A.D. he visited Greece, singing publicly at all the contests. No matter
at what date the historic festivals were due, they were all crowded into
the space of one year, and a musical competition was introduced even at
the Olympic games. Early in 68 he returned to Rome in triumph with the
roll of his victories carried before him, wearing his Olympic crown and
bearing in his hand the crown won at the Pythian festival. His crowns,
which numbered 1808, were hung by him on an obelisk in the Circus
Maximus. Cf. Tac. A. xv 33; Philostrat. vit. Apoll. iv 24, 36; Dio lxiii 8,
21; Juv. viii 224, haec opera atque hae sunt generosi principis artes |
gaudentis foedo peregrina ad pulpita cantu | prostitui Graiaeque apium
meruisse coronae.

comites: cf. Galb. 15, 2: Vitell. 11, 1. The comites Augusti or companions of the emperor on a journey or campaign were selected from his
amici (see on “cohors amicorum,'' Galb. 7, 1) and were either senators or
less frequently knights. They were paid for their services.
Suetonius
(Tib. 46) mentions as a proof that Tiberius was “pecuniae parcus ac
tenax" the fact that he never allowed a salarium but only cibaria (i.e. their
keep) to his comites. They discharged various duties, administrative,
judicial, or military, assigned to them by the emperor. See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii 835, Hermes iv 120.

cum cantante eo discederet: a heinous offence in Nero's eyes; cf.
Ner. 23 (when Nero was in Greece), cantante eo ne necessaria quidem causa
excedere theatro licitum est. Itaque et enixae quaedam in spectaculis
dicuntur et multi taedio audiendi laudandique clausis oppidorum (i.e.
entrances to the theatre) portis aut furtim desiluisse de muro aut morte
simulata funere elati. In Tac. A. xvi 5 there is a vivid account of the
discomforts endured by the audience compelled to remain in their places
as long as Nero figured on the stage during the quinquennial games at
Rome in 65 A.D.

aut praesens obdormisceret: Suetonius is here describing Vespasian's
behaviour when he was with Nero in Greece in the latter part of 66;
Tacitus (l.c.) mentions a similar indiscretion on Vespasian's part when he
was one of Nero's audience at Rome in 65: ferebantque Vespasianum,
tamquam somno coniveret, a Phoebo liberto increpitum aegreque meliorum
precibus obtectum, mox imminentem perniciem maiore fato effugisse.
Weynand (in Pauly-Wissowa vi 2629) thinks that Suetonius and Tacitus,
though differing as to the time and place, must be referring to one and
the same occurrence, on the ground that Vesp. would hardly have imperilled
his life a second time by repeating his offence. Furneaux (on Tac. l.c.)
argues that the interval which Suet. mentions between the banishment of
Vesp. from court and his appointment to Judaea supports the date given
by Tac. for the offence rather than that given by Suet. himself. But if
we assume that the account in Tac. is the correct one, then the influence
of Vespasian's friends must not merely have saved his life but also led
to his being included among the comites of Nero on his tour in Greece.
Dio (lxvi 11, quoted on c. 14) agrees with Suet. that it was in Greece that
Vesp. was banished from Nero's presence; so too Josephus (Bell. Iud. iii 1)
says that it was while Vesp. was with Nero in Greece that he was given
command in Judaea, and adds that Nero mollified Vesp. with flattering
words, which implies a previous estrangement.
prohibitus: for the summary method in which he was excluded from
court see c. 14. Such a sign of disfavour might be regarded as a deathwarrant; cf. Tac. A. xv 23, when the senate rush out to Antium to congratulate Nero on a daughter borne by Poppaea, and Thrasea is forbidden
to present himself with them: Thraseam prohibitum inmoto animo praenuntiam inminentis caedis contumeliam excepisse.

contubernio:
=
comitatu. The word contubernium (see on c. 3) is
often used of the intimacy which the emperor allowed to those who were
admitted to his immediate circle; e.g. Tib. 14, 4, quem ut sapientiae professorem contubernio admoverat: ib. 56, Seleucum grammaticum
primum a contubernio removit.

publica salutatione: at Rome the early morning salutationes or
receptions by the emperor were attended daily by his amici (see on c. 14
and Galb. 7, 1); a public reception (publica or promiscua salutatio),
crowded by those of every standing, was usually held on festival days
such as the anniversary of the emperor's accession and the Kalends of
January. A full account of imperial salutationes is given by Friedlaender,
Sitteng. i10 90 sqq.

extrema:
extremum supplicium, mortem; cf. Calig. 54, 2, extrema
metuentes: Tac. A. v 5, non quidem extrema decernerent: Plat. Pol. 297 E,
πᾶσι τοῖς ἐσχάτοις ζημιοῦσθαι.

provincia
oblata est: Vesp. was appointed to Judaea at the end
of 66 or very early in 67.

§ 5. percrebruerat Oriente
opinio: so Tacitus, H. v 13, describing
prodigies and prophecies preceding the siege of Jerusalem: apertae repente
delubri fores et audita maior humana vox excedere divos; simul ingens
motus excedentium. Quae pauci in metum trahebant: pluribus persuasio
inerat antiquis sacerdotum litteris contineri, eo ipso tempore fore ut valesceret Oriens profectique Iudaea rerum potirentur. Quae ambages
Vespasianum ac Titum praedixerat; sed vulgus more humanae cupidinis
sibi tantam fatorum magnitudinem interpretati ne adversis quidem ad vera
mutabantur. Orosius (vii 9, 2) says the Jews were misled by oracles from
Mt. Carmel: Iudaei quibusdam in Carmelo monte seducti sortibus, quae
portenderent exortos a Iudaea duces rerum potituros fore, praedictumque
ad se trahentes in rebellionem exarserunt. Josephus (Bell. Iud. vi 5, 4)
holds that the ambiguous oracle, which encouraged the Jews to revolt,
really foretold the rise of Vespasian to power: τὸ ἐπάραν αὐτοὺς μάλιστα
πρὸς τὸν πόλεμον ἦν χρησμὸς ἀμφίβολος ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς εὑρημένος γράμμασιν, ὡς κατὰ
τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον ἀπὸ τῆς χώρας τις αὐτῶν ἄρξει τῆς οἰκουμένης. τοῦτο οἱ μὲν ὡς
οἰκεῖον ἐξέλαβον, καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν σοφῶν ἐπλανήθησαν περὶ τὴν κρίσιν· ἐδήλου δ᾽ ἄρα
περὶ τοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ τὸ λόγιον ἡγεμονίαν, ἀποδειχθέντος ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίας αὐτοκράτορος.
Hegesippus (Exscid. Hierosolym. v 44) and Eusebius (Hist. Eccl. iii 8)
reject the interpretation of Josephus, as Vespasian became ruler of the
Roman empire only and not of the whole world, and they explain the
prophecies as Messianic prophecies of Christ's dominion over the world
(cf. Daniel ii 35, 44: Micah v 2).

esse in fatis: cf. Claud. 43, sibi quoque in fatis esse matrimonium:
Sen. N.Q. ii 37, ita non est hoc contra fatum, sed ipsum quoque in fato
est. The phrase “in fatis esse" seems to be used first by Ovid; e.g. Met. i
256, esse quoque in fatis reminiscitur, adfore tempus, quo, etc.

paruit: here, as in Aug. 95 (immolanti .. victimarum iocinera replicata
paruerunt) and Calig. 8, 5 (abunde parere arbitror), the MSS. are
decisively in favour of parere against apparere, though Bentley and
Madvig would restore the compound, Madvig saying “pareo pro appareo
(extra iuris usum) antiquissimis et Apuleio similibusque relinquendum.”
The simple verb parere in the sense of apparere is not found in Caesar,
nor in Cic. except in the legal use of paret (= ‘it is proven"); it occurs
in Virg., Stat., Mart., Quintil., etc.

caesoque praeposito: Gessius Florus, a Greek of Clazomenae, was
appointed Roman procurator of Judaea in 64 A.D. Josephus paints in lurid
colours his plundering and oppression of the Jews, and says that it was
he who provoked the Jewish rebellion in order to escape impeachment.
Three million Jews at the Feast of the Passover in 65 appealed in vain
for protection to the proconsul of Syria, and finally, goaded by wrongs,
they rejected the pacifying influences of their king Agrippa II and the
rebellion broke out in the spring of 66; cf. Joseph. Antiq. xiv 9, xviii 1,
xx 9-11; Bell. Iud. ii 15 sq.; Tac. H. v 10, duravit tamen patientia
Iudaeis usque ad Gessium Florum procuratorem; sub eo bellum ortum.
Suetonius may be incorrect in saying that Gessius Florus was slain, for
Josephus, who describes (Bell. Iud. ii 15, 6) how Florus retired to Caesarea
after some street fighting in Jerusalem, nowhere mentions his having been
slain during the revolt. Ernesti takes caeso as fugato cum magna militum
caede, which is very improbable. Orosius (vii 9), though copying Suetonius
almost verbally, has extinctisque Romanis praesidiis for caesoque praeposito,
and some would read caesoque praesidio here.

legatum Syriae consularem: this was Cestius Gallus; Tac. H. v 10,
comprimere (bellum) coeptantem Cestium Gallum Suriae legatum varia
proelia ac saepius adversa excepere. Qui ubi fato aut taedio occidit, missu
Neronis Vespasianus fortuna famaque et egregiis ministris intra duas
aestates (67 and 68 A.D.) cuncta camporum omnesque praeter Hierosolyma
urbes victore exercitu tenebat. C. Cestius Gallus was consul (suffectus) in
42; as legatus of Syria he marched against the Jews in 66 with an army
of over 33,000 including the 12th legion (Fulminata) and detachments of
2000 each from the other Syrian legions (Joseph. Bell. Iud. ii 18, 9). Не
took Joppa and entered Jerusalem, but was unable to take the Palace or
the Temple there. For some unknown reason he abandoned the siege, and
made a disastrous retreat through the pass of Beth Horon, losing 5680 men
as well as his engines and baggage. See Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp.
(Eng. Trans.) ii 209 sq.

suppetias ferentem:
opem ferentem, subvenientem. The subst.
suppetiae (only in nom. and acc.) does not seem to occur between Plautus
(who uses it freely) and Suet. except in the Bell. Afric. where we find the
phrases suppetias ire, venire, proficisci, occurrere, mittere. The verb
suppetiari is read in Cic. Att. xiv 18 (see Tyrrell and Purser) and is found
in Apuleius.

rapta aquila: apparently the "eagle" of the 12th legion, as there
were only detachments (‘‘vexillationes,” Galb. 20, 1, n.) of the other
legions with Cestius. The loss of this eagle is not mentioned elsewhere,
and the accuracy of Suet. has been doubted. Vespasian did not use the
12th legion against the Jews, but Titus, when he took over the command,
made it part of his army and Josephus (Bell. Iud. v 1) says that it was
eager to avenge the humiliation it had suffered under Cestius. When
Titus dispersed his forces after the capture of Jerusalem, he remembered
that this legion under Cestius had yielded to the Jews, and so he withdrew
it from Syria and sent it to Melitene on the Euphrates (Bell. Iud. vii 1).

industriae expertae: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 4, Vespasianus nova senator
familia industria rebusque pacis ac militiae longe nobilis habebatur.
The passive use of expertus occurs from Livy on; other deponent participles used passively by Suetonius are adeptus, interpretatus, meditatus,
modulatus, mentitus.

nec metuendus nominis: in appointing to military commands the
emperors were on their guard against possible aspirants to the throne;
cf. Vitell. 7, 1, where Suet. says that the principal consideration which
influenced Galba in appointing Vitellius to the command in Lower Germany
was that he regarded him as non metuendus, on account of his gluttony.
Vespasian's political unimportance was a strong recommendation in Nero's
eyes.

§ 6. additis ad copias duabus legionibus, etc.: this statement is
obscure, for copias is naturally taken to mean the forces in Judaea and
there were no legions in Judaea after Cestius Gallus had been compelled
to return defeated to Syria. It is possible that by copias Suet. means
the legions available in Syria (where Mucianus was appointed as governor
to succeed Cestius); Josephus (Bell. Iud. iii 1) loosely says that
Vespasian was sent by Nero “ ληψόμενος τὴν ἡγεμονίαν τῶν ἐπὶ Συρίας
στρατευμάτων." The numbers given by Suet. of alae and cohortes do not
tally with those given by Josephus in his detailed account in B.I. iii 4.
Mommsen (Prov. Rom. Emp. ii 210 sq.), following Josephus, describes the
army of Vespasian as consisting of one Syrian legion (the 10th Fretensis,
which Mommsen suggests may have suffered least in the campaign of
Cestius) and two legions of the West (the 5th Macedonica from Moesia
and the 15th Apollinaris from Pannonia, which happened to be still in
Asia after the Partho-Armenian war conducted by Corbulo).
three legions there belonged 5 alae and 18 cohortes of auxilia.
also the previous garrison in Palestine of 1 ala and 5 cohortes. The four
client-kings of the Commagenians, the Hemesenes, the Jews (see below on
provinciam), and the Nabataeans supplied in all 11,000 infantry (mainly
archers) and 4000 cavalry. The 3 legions contained 18,000 men; the 23
cohortes (10 of 1000 men, 13 of 720) contained 19,360; the 6 alae contained 3000; add to these the client-kings' contingent of 15,000, and the
total of Vespasian's command was 55,360 (Josephus gives the round
number of 60,000). Mommsen, on the ground that the above figures are
based on each division being at its utmost normal strength, would reduce
the effective aggregate number to 50,000 at most.

lemma: additis ad copias duabus legionibus, etc.

text:
inter legatos maiore filio assumpto: Oros. vii 9,3 Titum filium suum
maiorem inter legatos habuit; nam multas et validas legiones secum in
Syriam traiecit. Titus was appointed legatus of the 15th legion (Apollinaris); see on Tit. 4, 3, legioni praepositus. M. Ulpius Traianus, father
of the emperor Trajan, was legatus of the 10th (Fretensis), and Sex.
Vettulenus Cerealis of the 5th (Macedonica).

provinciam: Becker proposed provinciam <suam>. Judaea was part
of the province of Syria from 63 to 40 B.C., and from 40 to 4 B.C. a
dependent principality under Herod the Great. In 4 B.C. it was divided
into three parts: (1) Judaea, with Samaria and Idumaea, under king
Archelaus; in 6 A.D. this became a Roman province under an imperial
procurator; (2) Batanaea and the adjoining regions, under Philip as
tetrarch; (3) Galilee and the land beyond the Jordan (Peraea), under
Herod Antipas as tetrarch. In 37-41 A.D. the three were united as a
kingdom under Herod Agrippa, but on his death in 44 Judaea became
again a procuratorial province until 70. In 53-55 Herod Agrippa II
received the districts of Batanaea, Auranitis, Trachonitis, Gaulonitis, and
Abilene, with the title of king, and also Tiberias and Tarichea in Galilee,
and Julias in Peraea. He remained faithful to the Romans during the
Jewish war. In 70 A.D., on the fall of Jerusalem, Judaea was made a
first-class imperial province under a legate with the 10th legion under his
orders.
proximas: sc. provincias, Syria and Egypt.

convertit in se: cf. Tit. 5, 1, quaqua iret, convertit homines. The full
phrase was convertere ora, oculos, etc.; e.g. Liv. xxvi 50, 1, quacumque
incedebat, converteret omnium oculos.

βάλλει τὸν Οὐεσπασιανὸν βέλει κατὰ τὸν ταρσὸν τοῦ ποδός, καὶ τιτρώσκει μὲν

districts see Mommsen, op. cit. 212 sqq.; Schiller, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i
