in spem imperii venit conceptam: cf. Tib. 14, 1, magna nec incerta
spe futurorum, quam et ostentis et praedictionibus ab initio aetatis conceperat. The combination of the two phrases in spem venire and speт
concipere is remarkable. Suetonius means that Vespasian's earlier vague
hopes now began to take a more definite form. His alternating hopes and
misgivings are mentioned in Tac. H. ii 74: Vespasianus modo in spem
erectus, aliquando adversa reputabat.

ostenta: Tacitus (H. i 10) drily observes that it was only after
Vespasian's rise to power that the Romans came to believe that such was
the secret will of fate and that he had been marked out for sovereignty
by omens and oracles: Occulta fati et ostentis ac responsis destinatum
Vespasiano liberisque eius imperium post fortunam credidimus.

§ 2. suburbano: sc. praedio; cf. Dom. 17, 3, in suburbano suo. This
ellipse of praedium is frequent in Cic. and post-Aug. writers.

quercus Marti sacra: the oak was usually sacred to Jove; cf.
Ov. M. vii 623, sacra Iovi quercus: Plin. N.H. xvi 11, aesculus Iovi sacra.
In class. prose sacer takes the gen., e.g. Cic. Verr. ii 1, 48, (Delos) illorum
deorum sacra putatur; the dat. is used in poetry and post-Aug. prose.

tres Vespasiae partus: Vespasia, wife of Flavius Sabinus, bore a
daughter (mentioned here) and then two sons, the elder being Flavius
Sabinus and the younger the emperor Vespasian (see c. 1, 3).

a frutice: this is noted in the Thes. Ling. Lat. as the only place
where frutex is used of the stirps or stem of a tree. Oudendorp explains
a frutice as meaning "ab ea parte, qua frutex, qui e radice annosae quercus
circum trunci infima pullularat, ex ipsa arbore enatus erat, dedit arbor
singulos ramos" (i.e. frutex, which properly means a bushy growth and
so the bushy growth of shoots at the base of the trunk of an oak tree, is
used here for the base of the tree itself). The reading has been suspected,
and Lipsius ingeniously suggested an frutices; Bentley, less plausibly, a
radice.
arefactum: cf. Galb. 1, silva omnis exaruit radicitus. The form arefacio is ante-class. and post-Aug.

non perannavit: “perannare” is used here like the Gr. διετίζειν “to
live through the year"; cf. Macrob. Sat. i 12, eodem quoque mense Martio
ad Annam Perennam sacrificatum itur ut annare perennareque (al.
perannareque) commode liceat. Warde Fowler (Rom. Fest. p. 51), citing
these words of Macrobius, comments: "Annare perennare is to complete the
circle of the year: cp. Suet. Vesp. 5. Anna Perenna herself is probably
a deity manufactured out of these words and the idea they conveyed...;
not exactly a deity of the year, but one whom it would be desirable to
propitiate at the beginning of the year." The expression non perannavit
is used erroneously in the spurious inscription, C.I.L. vi 412* and add.
p. 49*, of the daughter (and not the sister) of Vespasian (see Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2730). In the form “perennare” the verb is used in poetry
and post-Aug. prose, generally intrans. to last for many years,” e.g.
Ov. 4.4. iii 42, arte perennat amor; in Colum. xii 19, 2: 20, 8, it is trans.
"to make to last for years."

instar arboris: cf. Aug. 6, locus cellae penuariae instar: Ner. 31, 1,
stagnum maris instar. Suet. also uses instar for a statue or likeness
(effigies, simulacrum), Iul. 61, cuius (equi) instar pro aede Veneris .. postea
dedicavit; cf. Galb. 10, 2, e primoribus vel instar senatus (i.e. a miniature
senate) instituit: Calig. 5, quod apud Parthos iustitii instar est (i.e. represents the Roman iustitium, is a sign of public mourning).
Sabinum: see c. 1, 3.
haruspicio: see on Galb. 19, 1.

confirmatum: cf. Galb. 9, 2, confirmabatur cum secundissimis auspiciis
et ominibus, tum virginis honestae vaticinatione: Tit. 5, 1, de imperii spe
confirmatus est.
nec quicquam aliud quam: see on Dom. 21.

§ 3. aedilem: Vesp. was aedile in 38 A.D., in the reign of Gaius
(Caligula); see c. 2, 3.

verrendis viis: part of the cura urbis which was one of the functions
of the aediles (Cic. Legg. iii 3, 7, suntoque aediles curatores urbis, annonae,
ludorumque sollemnium); they were responsible for the cleansing (vias
verrere, purgare) repairing (reficere) and paving (sternere) of the streets;
cf. Plaut. Stich. 347 sqq., where Pinacium, giving orders about cleansing
the house with brooms (scopae) and watering-pots (nassiternae), is compared to an aedile.

luto
oppleri: Dio (lix 12) mentions this occurrence and the
significance which later was attached to it: πηλὸν πολὺν ἐν στενωπῷ τινι
ἰδὼν (ὁ Γάιος) ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ἐς τὸ τοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ τοῦ Φλαβίου ἱμάτιον,
ἀγορανομοῦντός (aedilis) τε τότε καὶ τῆς τῶν στενωπῶν καθαριότητος ἐπιμελουμένου,
ἐμβληθῆναι. καὶ τοῦτο οὕτω πραχθὲν παραχρῆμα μὲν ἐν οὐδενὶ λόγῳ ὤφθη, ὕστερον
δὲ τοῦ Οὐεπασιανοῦ τὰ πράγματα τεταραγμένα καὶ πεφυρμένα παραλαβόντος τε καὶ
καταστησαμένου ἔδοξεν οὐκ ἀθεεὶ γεγονέναι, ἀλλ᾽ ἄντικρυς αὐτῷ τὴν πόλιν ὁ Γάιος
πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν ἐγκεχειρικέναι.

praetextae: the robe of office of the curule aedile (as of other curule
magistrates) was the toga praetexta, the white toga bordered with purple.
Plebeian aediles could not wear the praetexta; nor had they a sella
curulis, but only a subsellium.

non defuerunt qui interpretarentur: the same phrase occurs in
Galb. 8, 2: Tit. 5, 3: Dom. 23, 2. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii 306 sq.

gremium: a place of shelter and protection; cf. Aen. ix 261, quaecumque mihi fortuna fidesque est, | in vestris pono gremiis: ib. viii 713
(of the river-god Nilus represented with a dark blue robe), pandentemque
sinus et tota veste vocantem | caeruleum in gremium latebrosaque flumina
victos.

§ 4. prandente eo
subiecit: Dio (lxvi 1) κύων, σῖτον αὐτοῦ
αἱρουμένου, χεῖρα ἀνθρωπίνην ὑπὸ τὴν τράπεζαν ὑπέβαλε. See on "prandia,”
Vitell. 13, 1.

canis extrarius: the appearance of a strange dog was regarded as an
omen; cf. Ter. Phorm. 705, quot res postilla monstra evenerunt mihi! |
intro iit in aedes ater alienus canis, etc. The adj. and subst. extrarius was
used especially as the opp. of domesticus or ex eadem familia; e.g. Ter.
Phorm. 579, hanc condicionem (“marriage proposal'") si quoi tulero
extrario: Apul. Met. viii 22, servus habens ex eodem famulitio conservam coniugem, liberae cuiusdam extrariaeque mulieris flagrabat cupidine.

e trivio: refuse (purgamenta) of all kinds and, at times, dead bodies
were thrown out at the cross-roads; cf. Petron. Satyr. 134, quae striges
comederunt nervos tuos, aut quod purgamentum nocte calcasti in trivio aut
cadaver?: Auson. Epigr. 72, abiecta in triviis inhumati glabra iacebat |
testa hominis nudum iam cute calvitium. Dogs naturally frequented the
trivia; cf. Phaedr. i 27, 11, canis trivio conceptus, et educatus stercore.
..

manum humanam: ‘“manu humana denuntiabatur fore ut Vespasiani
manu omnia regerentur. Manus nempe dextra imperii signum, cuius et
instrumentum est'” (Marcilius).

cenante irrupit: Dio (l.c.), βοῦς ἐν τῷ ἄγρῳ, ἐν ᾧ τὴν δίαιταν ὡς πλήθει
ἐποιεῖτο, δειπνοῦντι προσελθὼν ὤκλασε, καὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑπέθηκε.

bos arator: cf. βοῦς ἀροτήρ (Hesiod): Ov. F. i 698, cedebat taurus
arator equo. Other instances of a subst. in appos. like an adj. are intercessores tribunos (Iul. 29, 1), serpens draco (Tib. 72, 2), excubitori tribuno
(Claud. 42, 1), anus matronas (Ner. 11, 1), tironem militem (Galb. 6, 3).
cervicem summisit: as the Roman empire was to bow to Vespasian.

arbor resurrexit: Tac. H. ii 78, recursabant animo vetera omina:
cupressus arbor in agris eius conspicua altitudine repente prociderat ac
postera die eodem vestigio resurgens procera et latior virebat; grande id
prosperumque consensu haruspicum et summa claritudo iuveni admodum
Vespasiano promissa. Dio (l.c.), κυπάρισσός τε περιφανής πρόρριζος ὑπὸ σφοδροῦ
πνεύματος ἀνατραπεῖσα, ἔπειτα τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ὑφ᾽ ἑαυτῆς ἀνέστη, καὶ ἀκμάζουσα
διετέλεσε. Dio's statement about the strong gale contradicts Suetonius'
words "sine ulla vi tempestatis," and Boissée proposed ὑπ᾽ οὐ σφοδροῦ. The
second downfall of this cypress, signifying the overthrow of Domitian, is
mentioned in Dom. 15, 2, arbor, quae privato adhuc Vespasiano eversa surrexerat, tunc rursus repente corruit.

cupressus: this is prob. the genitive; cf. arbor palmae, Aug. 94, 11.
The specifying gen. with arbor is found first in Liv. xxiv 3, proceris
abietis arboribus. Pliny (N.H.) uses both the nom. in appos. with arbor
and also the gen.; Varro and Quintilian have the nom., Columella always
the gen. In the Thes. Ling. Lat. “cupressus" here is taken as a nom.,
as in Tac. H. ii 78 (see preceding note).
in agro avito: = in praediis Cosanis, c. 2, 1.

sine ulla vi tempestatis evulsa: Pliny (N.H. xvi 132) gives other
examples of this: Est in exemplis et sine tempestate ullave causa alia
quam prodigi cecidisse multas (arbores) ac sua sponte resurrexisse. Factum
hoc populi Romani Quiritibus ostentum Cimbricis bellis Nuceriae in luco
Iunonis ulmo, postquam etiam cacumen amputatum erat, quoniam in aram
ipsam procumbebat, restituta sponte, ita ut protinus floreret, a quo deinde
tempore maiestas populi Romani resurrexit, quae ante vastata cladibus
fuerat. Memoratur hoc idem factum et in Philippis salice procidua atque
detruncata, et Stagiris in museo populo ("poplar'") alba, omnia fausti
ominis.

§ 5. at: at (like δε) is often used, especially in poetry, with a weakened
force as a particle of transition in passing to a fresh narration, or in an
enumeration of instances, etc. (see Hand Tursell. i 422, Kühner-Stegmann ii
84); cf. Galb. 7, 2: Dom. 4, 1: 16, 1.

in Achaia: when accompanying Nero on his musical tour (c. 4, 4).
Dio (l.c.), καὶ παρ' ὀνείρατος ἔμαθεν ὅτι, ὅταν ὁ Καῖσαρ Νέρων ὀδόντα ἀποβάλῃ,
αὐταρχήσει· καὶ τοῦτό τε τὸ κατὰ τὸν ὀδόντα τῇ ἐπιούσῃ ἡμέρᾳ συνηνέχθη.

dens exemptus esset: cf. Mart. x 56, 3, eximit aut reficit dentem
Cascellius (a dentist) aegrum.

atrium: the hall or entrance-room of the house where Nero was
staying. On a journey the comites of the emperor, of whom Vespasian
was one, lived with the emperor, or provision was made for their housing
(Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 79).
tantum quod: "only just,” vixdum (a gloss recenter has ousted the
genuine reading in many of the MSS.); cf. Aug. 63, 1, tantum quod
pueritiam egressus: ib. 98, 2, de navi quae tantum quod appulerat:
Ner. 6, 1, tantum quod exoriente sole. The expression is found only in
Cicero's Letters and in post-class. writers; cf. Cic. Fam. vii 23, 1, tantum
quod ex Arpinati veneram, cum mihi litterae a te redditae sunt. Suetonius
is peculiar in using it with the participle. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 272, say
that tantum quod in this sense arose from tantum (= tantillum) temporis
exactum est, quod. (Distinguish tantum quod = nisi quod, e.g. Cic. Verr. i
116, tantum quôd hominem non nominat, causam quidem totam perscribit).

§ 6. apud Iudaeam: in the vulgar speech apud c. acc. was used instead
of in c. abl. Hand (op. cit. i 414) says that in good writers it is so used
only in certain formulae such as apud forum, apud villam, but in the
comic writers and in late authors, especially Tac. and Suet., it is used of
islands, cities, etc. Cf. Nonius 522 М. (p. 840, Lindsay): Error consuetudinis ‘‘aput’” pro ‘‘in’” utitur; itaque vitiose dicimus, cum nos in
foro fuisse dicamus, aput aut ad forum fuisse, cum aput iuxta significet.

Carmeli dei: Carmēlus was the name both of the mountain and also
of the god to whom it was sacred. The mountain is a continuation of
the Antilibanus range on the borders of Phoenicia and Palestine; now
Jebel Mar Elyas (i.e. Elijah) or Kurmul. From remote antiquity it has
been a sacred place. Scylax (Periplus 42) describes it as ἱερὸν Διός.
Iamblichus (vit. Pythag. 4) says that Pythagoras dwelt for some time in
solitude in a temple on Carmel. It is familiar in Scripture history from
the story of Elijah's triumph over the priests of Baal. Tacitus (H. ii 78)
describes Vespasian's visit to Carmel: Est Iudaeam inter Suriamque
Carmelus: ita vocant montem deumque. Nec simulacrum deo aut templum
(sic tradidere maiores): ara tantum et reverentia. Illic sacrificanti
Vespasiano, cum spes occultas versaret animo, Basilides sacerdos inspectis
identidem extis: “quidquid est,” inquit, ‘“Vespasiane, quod paras, seu
domum extruere seu prolatare agros sive ampliare servitia, datur tibi
magna sedes, ingentes termini, multum hominum.” Has ambages et statim
exceperat fama et tunc aperiebat, nec quidquam magis in ore volgi;
crebriores apud ipsum sermones, quanto sperantibus plura dicuntur.

sortes: here used in its extended sense of any kind of oracular
deliverance (cf. Cic. Div. ii 56, 115: Verg. Aen. iv 346, etc.). Sortes
were properly little tablets or lots on which was written some verse or
proverb; these were mixed together, and one drawn at random was taken
as an omen. Divination by sortes of this kind was practised at Praeneste
(Suet. Tib. 63), at the Fons Aponus near Patavium (Tib. 14), and probably
at the oracle of Fortuna at Antium (Calig. 57).

quidquid cogitaret: cf. Sall. Iug. 63, where a soothsayer at Utica,
after examining the victims offered to the gods, encourages Marius:
proinde, quae animo agitabat fretus dis ageret, fortunam quam saepissume
experiretur, cuncta prospere eventura.

proventurum: = successurum.
This use of provenire (cf. προχωρεῖν) is
common in Tac. (e.g. H. iv 18, si destinata provenissent), but occurs only
here in Suet.

Iosephus: the Jewish historian, who, as he tells us himself (Vita 1),
was descended on his mother's side from Asmonaean princes and inherited
from his father the priesthood which ranked highest. He commanded the
Jewish forces in Galilee against Vespasian, and was captured at the fall
of Jotapata (67 A.D., see on Vesp. 4 ad fin.). His life was spared on the
intercession of Titus. He describes (Bell. Iud. iii 8) his interview with
the victorious Vespasian, where he said among other things to the future
emperor: “Νέρωνί με πέμπεις ; τί γάρ; οἱ μετὰ Νέρωνα μέχρι σου διάδοχοι μένουσι;
σὺ Καῖσαρ, Οὐεσπασιανέ, καὶ αὐτοκράτωρ σὺ καὶ παῖς ὁ σὸς οὗτος. Δέσμει δέ με νῦν
ἀσφαλέστερον, καὶ τήρει σαυτῷ. Δεσπότης μὲν γὰρ οὐ μόνον ἐμοῦ σύ, Καῖσαρ, ἀλλὰ
καὶ γῆς καὶ θαλάσσης καὶ παντὸς ἀνθρώπων γένους.” Dio (lxvi 1) makes Josephus
predict that his liberation by Vespasian as emperor would be in a year's
time: 'Ιώσηπος δὲ ἀνὴρ Ἰουδαῖος, ἀχθείς τε ὑπ' αὐτοῦ πρότερον καὶ δεθείς, ἐγέλασε
καὶ ἔφη “Νῦν μέν με δήσεις, μετ᾽ ἐνιαυτὸν δὲ λύσεις αὐτοκράτωρ γενόμενος.” He was
eleased when Vespasian was proclaimed emperor by the armies in Syria
and Judaea, and he was with Titus at the siege of Jerusalem. He accompanied Titus to Rome in 71 and was granted Roman citizenship by
Vespasian, adopting the nomen gentilicium of Flavius; he also received
an annual allowance and land in Judaea which Domitian made tax-free.

constantissime asseveravit: cf. Oros. vii 9, 3, maxime Iosephi
Iudaeorum ducis sententia, qui captus, cum in vincula coiceretur, constantissime dixerat, sicut Suetonius refert, continuo se ab eodem sed imperatore
solvendum.

§ 7. Neronem monitum per quietem: cf. Dio lxvi 1, καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ
Νέρων ἔδοξέ ποτε ἐν τοῖς ὕπνοις τὸν τοῦ Διὸς ὄχον ἐς τὴν Οὐεσπασιανοῦ οἰκίαν
εἰσαγαγεῖν. For per quietem see on c. 25.

tensam: tensae were the sacred cars richly adorned with ivory and
silver, which conveyed the statues of the gods with their decorations
(exuviae) in the solemn procession (pompa) from the Capitoline to the
Circus at the opening of the Ludi Circenses (Tit. 2). The statues were
placed on couches (pulvinaria) during the games and afterwards borne
back in the tensae to their shrines. See the illustrations in Daremberg-Saglio v 115.

sacrario: when not in use, the tensae were kept under the care of the
aediles in a special building on the Capitol known as "aedes t(h)ensarum”;
see Mommsen Staatsr. ii³ 500, Annali dell' Inst. 1858 p. 203: Jordan,
Topogr. Rom i 2, 52.

deduceret: the tensae were escorted (deducere) by the chief senators,
who, along with pueri patrimi et matrimi (i.e. children who were ingenui
and whose fathers and mothers were still alive), laid hold of the bridles
and traces, or assisted in dragging the tensae by thongs (lora) attached
for the purpose (Livy, v 41 ix 40, having ducere tensas). The most prob.
deriv. of tensa is that of Asconius on Cic. Verr. i 59 "tensae, sacra
vehicula sic dictae, quod ante eas lora tenduntur.”” In Suet. Aug. 43
we are told that even when ill Augustus accompanied the tensae in a litter
(accidit votivis Circensibus, ut correptus valitudine, lectica cubans tensas
deduceret). This deductio apparently became one of the duties of the
emperor, and Nero's dream foretold that not he but Vespasian would in
future discharge it.
...

comitia secundi consulatus ineunte Galba: these words present considerable difficulty and some (e.g. Wolf) have regarded them as a gloss
on non multo post. Galba, consul under Tiberius in 33 A.D., became consul
for the second time on Jan. 1, 69 A.D., a few days after his arrival in
Rome as emperor (Tac. H. i 1 and 11). According to Tacitus and Plutarch
(see following note) the portent occurred after the death of Galba. Moreover the meaning of comitia ineunte is by no means clear. Baumg.-Cr.
thinks that inire comitia in the sense of auspicari comitia may be defended
by the indiscriminate use of these two verbs with bellum, proelium, militiam,
etc. But if the text is sound, Ernesti and Bremi seem right in their
explanation that the miraculous event took place when Galba was going
into the electoral assembly of the people in the Campus Martius; the
actual elections were held in the senate, but the people still assembled in
the Campus Martius to hear the results announced (Dom. 10, 4, n.), and
the statue of Julius Caesar on the island in the Tiber would be visible
from the Campus. For the construction comitia consulatus cf. Auson. 419,
2 D
42, comitia consulatus mei (which suggests that sui may have fallen out
here after consulatus). Various corrections have been proposed. Marcilius
warmly approved of a reading in comitio secundum consulatum ineunte
Galba, introduced by Ursinus from his alleged "codex"; Burman
hazarded several conjectures, e.g. non multo post comitia secundi consulatus,
ineunte Capitolium Galba, and post comitia secundum consulatum ineunte
Galba; Oudendorp would read non multo post initia secundi consulatus,
intereunte Galba. But in the 15 other passages where non (nec, neque,
haud) multo post is used by Suetonius post is always an adv., not a prep.

statuam conversam: presaging the transfer of the empire from
the West to the East (i.e. to Vespasian commanding in the East). Tacitus
(H. i 86) mentions it among the alarming prodigia reported when Vitellius
was advancing against Otho: statuam divi Iulii in insula Tiberini amnis
sereno et immoto die ab Occidente in Orientem conversam. Plutarch (Oth.
4) says it happened at the time when the partizans of Vespasian were
becoming openly active: τὸν ἐν μεσοποταμίᾳ νήσῳ Γαΐου Καίσαρος ἀνδριάντα μήτε
σεισμοῦ γεγονότος μήτε πνεύματος ἀφ᾽ ἑσπέρας μεταστραφέντα πρὸς τὰς ἀνατολάς· ὅ
φασι συμβῆναι περὶ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας ἐν αἷς οἱ περὶ Οὐεσπασιανὸν ἐμφανῶς
ἤδη τῶν πραγμάτων ἀντελαμβάνοντο.
acie Betriacensi: see on Oth. 9, 2.

duas aquilas: typifying Otho and Vitellius; cf. Aesch. Agam. 115,
where two eagles typifying Agamemnon and Menelaus appear to the Greek
host. The story in Tac. H. ii 50 is quite different: Die, quo Bedriaci
certabatur, avem invisitata specie apud Regium Lepidum (between Parma
and Modena) celebri luco consedisse incolae memorant, nec deinde coetu
hominum aut circumvolitantium alitum territam pulsamve donec Otho se
ipse interficeret; tum ablatam ab oculis; et tempora reputantibus initium
finemque miraculi cum Othonis exitu competisse. Dio (lxiv 10) agrees
with Tac.: ὅπου τέ φασι πρὸ τῆς μάχης ἄλλα τε φανῆναι σημεῖα, καί τινα ὄρνιν
ἐξαίσιον, ὁποῖον οὐ πώποτε ἑωράκεσαν, ἐπὶ πολλὰς ἡμέρας ὀφθῆναι.

tertiam: typifying Vespasian, who conquered Vitellius the conqueror
of Otho. Cf. the ἔφεδρος or suppositicius in boxing or wrestling contests
who met the victor of a preceding round. Valerius Maximus (i 4, 6)
records an earlier instance of contending eagles foreshadowing the issue
of a battle: -M. Brutus cum reliquias exercitus sui adversus Caesarem et
Antonium eduxisset, duae aquilae ex diversis castris advolaverunt, et edita
inter se pugna, ea, quae a parte Bruti fuerat, male mulcata fugit. See
Plut. Brut. 48.

§ 2. Moesiaci exercitus bina
milia: the province of Moesia
(Vitell. 15, 1, n.) was occupied by three legions, the 3rd (Gallica), 7th
(Claudia), and 8th (Augusta). Suetonius says here that it was not till
after Otho's death that detachments of these legions reached Aquileia.
Tacitus (H. ii 46) says that an advance guard from Moesia (praemissi e
Moesia) were with Otho just after his defeat at Bedriacum and encouraged
him by reporting that the Moesian legions had entered Aquileia; also in
H. ii 85 Tacitus speaks of the Moesian legions as being at Aquileia, where
they maltreated the messengers who brought news of Otho's death, tore
the standards which displayed the name of Vitellius, and finally plundered
the military chest. Spooner (on H. ii 46), following Lipsius, gratuitously
accuses Suetonius of mixing up the detachments from the Moesian with
those from the Pannonian legions mentioned in H. ii 11, Laeta interim
Othoni principia belli, motis ad imperium eius e Dalmatia Pannoniaque
exercitibus. Fuere quattuor legiones, e quibus bina milia praemissa; ipsae
modicis intervallis sequebantur. Hardy (in an article "Tacitus as a military
historian," J. Ph. xxxi 136) rightly defends the accuracy of Suetonius,
arguing that he had probably derived his information from his father who
was a tribune in the 13th legion from Pannonia which fought for Otho
(see Oth. 10, 1), and that various incidents mentioned by Tacitus (H. ii 85,
96 iii 5) clearly imply that the Moesian legions could not have been at
Aquileia, though detachments may have been. Furthermore the legions
were certainly in Moesia in July or August, when they declared for
Vespasian (H. ii 85), and Tacitus says nothing of their having been sent
back there, though he gives a precise account of the Othonian legions sent
back to their provinces by the victorious Vitellius (H. ii 66, 67). Suetonius
is alone in his statement that it was the Moesian detachments at Aquileia
who first selected Vespasian as emperor and, though checked for the time,
inspired the later action of the legions in Egypt and the East. Tacitus
(H. ii 85), after describing the acclamation of Vespasian by the armies in
Egypt, Judaea, and Syria, mentions how the army of Illyricum (i.e.
Moesia, Pannonia, Dalmatia) came over to Vespasian's side and hastened
his movements by its ardour. Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 10) narrates the
events in the same order. This too is a matter on which Suetonius may
have had special information, though Dessau (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1.
346 n.) characterizes his account as one of his many blunders ("ein Irrtum
Suetons, wie sich manche bei ihm finden'"). Dessau holds that the three
legions in Moesia felt themselves compromised by the gross insubordination
of their detachments sent to Italy. When these detachments had been
quieted and had rejoined the main body in Moesia, the reunited legions
were uneasy lest they should have to pay the penalty to the new emperor
Vitellius; so they looked about for some suitable person to support
against Vitellius, and decided to throw in their lot with Vespasian who
had been chosen by the armies in the East.
vim vitae suae attulisse: see Oth. 11.
setius: for the forms setius and sequius see on Tit. 5, 3.

Aquileiam: the capital of Venetia in the N.E. corner of Italy at
the head of the Adriatic, mod. Aquileja or Aglar.
quasi: in a causal sense, see on Tit. 5, 1.

grassati: grassari "to go," "to proceed" was used especially of
proceeding, or acting, with violence (e.g. grassari ferro, veneno). Cf.
Aug. 67, 2, superbe avareque in provincia grassatos: Calig. 56, 1, ita
bacchantem atque grassantem: Galb. 14, 2, his diverso vitiorum genere
grassantibus. Sometimes with in (cf. saevire in), e.g. Ner. 36, 1, пес
minore superbia in exteros grassatus est; and with adversus, e.g. Calig.

hominum genus grassatus est: Suetonius also uses grassator for "a footpad" (e.g. Aug. 43, 1) and grassatura for brigandage" (e.g. Tib. 37, 1).

timerent: cf. Tac. (l.c.), unde metus et ex metu consilium: posse
imputari Vespasiano, quae apud Vitellium excusanda erant, i.e. that acts
might be made a merit of with Vespasian, which would have to be excused
to Vitellius.

consilium inierunt eligendi
imperatoris: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 3,
milites praedicti (i.e. of Moesia and Pannonia), postquam Othonem praetoriis, Vitellium Germanicianis legionibus factum comperere, aemuli, ut
inter se solent, ne dissimiles viderentur, Vespasianum perpulere: Oros. vii
8, 3, de Hispania siquidem ilico Galba surrexerat; quo mox oppresso, Otho
Romae, Vitellius in Germania, Vespasianus in Syria imperia simul atque
arma rapuerunt.

Hispaniensi exercitu: Galba was acclaimed as emperor by the 6th
legion in Spain; and thus, as Tacitus (H. i 4) says, a constitutional secret
was disclosed that an emperor could be appointed elsewhere than at Rome
(evolgato imperii arcano, posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri). See
Galb. 10.

praetoriano: the praetorians, disgusted with the parsimony of Galba,
offered to support Otho (Tac. H. i 23 sq.); he was saluted as Imperator
by a handful of them who carried him off to the praetorian camp, the
gates of which were at once thrown open and the revolution was complete
(ib. 27, 36: Suet. Oth. 6).
The affection and loyalty (animus fidesque)
of the praetorians towards Otho are described by Suetonius (Oth. 8); and
Tacitus (H. ii 46) calls them ‘“proprius Othonis miles.”

Germaniciano: Suetonius is the first to use this adj., applying it to
the army in Germany; cf. Tib. 25, 2: Galb. 20, 1: Oth. 8, 1. It is
found also in Eutrop. vii 17, x 15; Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 3. A similar formation
is ‘‘urbaniciani" for the soldiers garrisoned in the city (of Rome), Spart.
Carac. 4, Get. 6: Paul. Dig. iv 6, 35; “Illyricianus” occurs in Treb. Poll.
Claud. 14. For the proclamation of Vitellius as emperor by the legions
in Germany see Oth. 8, 1: Vitell. 8, 1.

§ 3. legione tertia: the transference (in 67-68) of the 3rd (Gallica)
legion from Syria to Moesia is mentioned in Tac. H. ii 74: tertiam
legionem, quod e Syria in Moesiam transisset, suam ("devoted to himself'") numerabat (Vespasianus). It repulsed with great slaughter an
invasion of Moesia by the Sarmatae (H. i 79). It was the first legion in
Moesia to declare for Vespasian; H. ii 85, Adcelerata interim Vespasiani
coepta Illyrici exercitus studio transgressi in partes. Tertia legio exemplum
ceteris Moesiae legionibus praebuit.
nomen eius vexillis inscripserunt: Tacitus (H. ii 85) mentions that
the Moesian legions at Aquileia tore the ensigns which bore the name of
Vitellius: laceratis vexillis nomen Vitellii praeferentibus. For this sign
of revolt cf. H. iii 13, miles praescriptum Vespasiani nomen, proiectas
Vitellii effigies aspexit: iii 31, primores castrorum nomen atque imagines
Vitellii amoliuntur. Under the Empire the name of the emperor and of
the corps was embroidered, probably in gold, on the vexilla which were
made of cloth generally red, sometimes purple (or white). A similar practice
prevailed under the Republic; cf. Dio xl 18 (speaking of the army of
Crassus in Parthia in 53 Β.C.), σημεῖον δέ τι τῶν μεγάλων, τῶν τοῖς ἱστίοις
ἐοικότων καὶ φοινικᾶ γράμματα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς πρὸς δήλωσιν τοῦ τε στρατοῦ καὶ τοῦ
στρατηγοῦ σφων τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος ἐχόντων, ἐς τὸν ποταμὸν . . ἐνέπεσε.

numeris: "detachments," also called vexillationes (Galb. 20, 1) or
vexilla as serving under a vexillum instead of their proper signa; cf. Tac.
H. i 6, multi numeri e Germania ac Britannia et Illyrico: id. Agr. 18,
sparsi per provinciam numeri.

Tiberius Alexander: a Jew, son of the alabarch in Alexandria and
nephew of the writer Philo. He renounced the Jewish faith and was
made procurator of Judaea by Claudius (c. 46 A.D.). He accompanied
Corbulo in his Armenian campaign in 64 (Tac. A. xv 28). Under Nero
he was made prefect of Egypt (67-70 A.D.). An edict issued by him as
prefect is still preserved (Rhein. Mus. ii 133 sqq.), in which his name
appears as Τιβέριος Ἰούλιος ᾿Αλέξανδρος. During his administration there
was a riot between the Jews and Greeks in Alexandria, and 50,000 Jews
were slain by the Roman legionaries. He was rewarded for his devotion
to Vespasian's cause by being made lieutenant-general of the army under
Titus, and he was present at the capture of Jerusalem. See Joseph.
Antiq. xx 4 sq.: Bell. Iud. ii 11, 15, 18, etc.

praefectus Aegypti: Alexander had been raised to the rank of eques
by Claudius. The prefect of Egypt by the arrangement of Augustus
must be an eques; cf. Tac. H. i 11, Aegyptum copiasque, quibus coercetur,
iam inde a divo Augusto equites Romani obtinent loco regum: ita visum
expedire, provinciam aditu difficilem, annonae fecundam, superstitione ac
lascivia discordem et mobilem, insciam legum, ignaram magistratuum, domi
retinere. Regebat tum Tiberius Alexander, eiusdem nationis. Alexander's
espousal of the cause of Vespasian is referred to in Tac. H. ii 74, praefectus
Aegypti Ti. Alexander consilia sociaverat.

primus
legiones adegit: Tac. H. ii 79, Initium ferendi ad
Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro,
qui Kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit. See on Galb. 11, in
verba sua iurasse cognovit.

principatus dies: primus principatus dies (Tac. l.c.), usually called
dies imperii; in later authors natalis imperii (e.g. Spart. vit. Hadr. 4).
The dies imperii, marking the beginning of a reign, was the day on which
the proconsular imperium was conferred on the new Princeps. It is a
disputed point whether this imperium could legitimately be conferred by
either the senate or the army, or whether the senate exclusively had the
right to confer it, so that in cases where the title Imperator was conferred
by the soldiers it required the formal confirmation of the senate.
former view is defended by Hardy on Plin. ad Trai. 52, following Mommsen
Staatsr. ii³ 842 sq.; the latter by Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. ch. ii n. E,
following Herzog Röm. Staatsverfassung ii 610 sq.
The

Iudaicus exercitus: consisting of three legions, the 5th (Macedonica),
10th (Fretensis), and 15th (Apollinaris). Cf. Vitell. 15, 1. Josephus
(Bell. Iud. iv 10), from a desire to claim the honour for his country, says
that the proclamation of Vespasian as emperor took place in Judaea
earlier than in Egypt, and that Vespasian wrote to Tiberius Alexander to
ask for his support.

Idus Iul.: i.e. the 11th of July; Tacitus, however, says that it
was on the 3rd (quinto Nonas Iulias), and his statement has been generally
accepted as correct. Ernesti goes so far as to substitute Nonas for Idus
in our text. Tacitus also says that before the Ides (15th) of July the
whole of Syria had taken the oath of allegiance to Vespasian: c. 81, ante
Idus Iulias Syria omnis in eodem sacramento fuit. Fabia (Les Sources de
Tacite p. 155) infers that Suetonius confused the two armies in Syria and
Judaea.

§ 4. iactatum:
in manibus hominum versatum. More usually Suet.
has iactari in the sense of in ore hominum esse; e.g. Galb. 6, 2: 12,3:
Oth. 12, 2: Vesp. 1, 4.

extrema obtestatione: the letter probably purported to convey a
last charge written by the vanquished Otho in the hours before his suicide
(see Oth. 10, 2); cf. Suet. vit. Horat. 1, extremis iudiciis (of a last will
and testament). But extrema might also mean "most urgent."
obtestatio (adjuration, solemn entreaty) cf. Tib. 40, revocante (Tiberium)
assidua obtestatione populo: Vitell. 2, 3, suorum obtestatione.
For

rumor: this report was spread by Mucianus; cf. Tac. c. 80, Nihil
aeque provinciam exercitumque accendit quam quod asseverabat Mucianus
statuisse Vitellium, ut Germanicas legiones in Syriam ad militiam
opulentam quietamque transferret; contra Syriacis legionibus Germanica
hiberna caelo ac laboribus dura mutarentur.

praesidibus provinciarum : praeses (ἡγεμών) was a general title
denoting a governor; cf. Macer Digest i 18, 1, praesidis nomen generale
est, eoque et proconsules et legati Caesaris et omnes provincias regentes,
licet senatores sint, praesides appellantur. Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 240 n. 3)
points out that praeses provinciae is not found till after the first century,
when it is used by Tacitus (A. vi 41, xii 45), by the younger Pliny (Pan. 70),
by Trajan (ep. ad Plin. 44) and by Suetonius (Iul. 35, 1; Aug. 23, 1;
Tib. 32, 2; 41; Claud. 17, 3; Oth. 7, 1; Dom. 6, 2; 8, 2). At a later
period it came to be applied particularly to the governors of the lowest
class, those of equestrian rank, who had no distinguishing title; cf.
Mattingly, Imp. Civ. Serv. p. 147.

Licinius Mucianus: consul in 52 under Claudius, but afterwards he
roused that emperor's suspicions and was forced to withdraw into a retired
part of Asia "as like an exile as he was later like an emperor" (Tac.
H. i 10, tam prope ab exule fuit quam postea a principe). Restored to
favour by Nero he was made governor of Syria in '67 with command of
four legions, while Vespasian was in Judaea in command of three. He
called on Vespasian to seize the throne (H. ii 76) and proclaimed him
emperor in the theatre at Antioch (ib. 80). He was appointed to act as
general against Vitellius, while Vespasian and Titus remained behind in
the East (ib. 82). According to Dio (lxv 8) he hoped to share the imperial
power, though Vespasian bore the name of emperor: ὁ Μουκιανὸς ἰσχυρῶς
προσέκειτο (instabat) ἐλπίσας τὸ μὲν ὄνομα τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐκεῖνον ἕξειν, αὐτὸς δὲ διὰ
τὴν ἐπιείκειαν αὐτοῦ ἰσομοιρήσειν. For the character of Mucianus see c. 13
and notes there.

Vologaesus: the correct form of this name is uncertain: “Vologeses" Vologaeses” “Vologesus'” ،“Vologaesus" are all found in the
MSS. of Tacitus, and "Vologesus" is a variant here. See Prosop. Imp.
Rom. iii 475; Furneaux on Tac. A. xii 14. Vologaesus I was king of
Parthia, 51-78 A.D. He made repeated efforts to establish his brother
Tiridates as king of Armenia. This brought him into conflict with the
Roman forces under Corbulo, peace being ultimately made in 63 by
Tiridates consenting to receive the crown of Armenia as a gift from
the hands of Nero at Rome. Vespasian sent envoys to the Parthians
when he was preparing for war (Tac. H. ii 82) and he was already
aware of the defeat and death of Vitellius when envoys from
Vologaesus arrived at Alexandria with the offer of 40,000 men (H. iv 51).
Vespasian thanked the king and directed him to send ambassadors to the
senate and to learn for himself that peace had been restored; this he did
and secured a renewal of his alliance with Rome (Suet. Ner. 57). He
sent a golden crown to Titus on the fall of Jerusalem (Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii
5). His request for Roman auxiliaries, with one of Vespasian's sons as
their leader, to aid him against the Alani was refused; see Dom. 2, 2.

deposita simultate: the initial distrust and jealousy between Mucianus
and Vespasian as commanders of strong forces in neighbouring provinces
was removed largely through the conciliatory agency of Vespasian's son
Titus; cf. Tac. H. ii 5, Ceterum hic (Mucianus) Syriae, ille (Vespasianus)
Iudaeae praepositus, vicinis provinciarum administrationibus invidia discordes, exitu demum Neronis positis odiis in medium consuluere, primum
per amicos, dein praecipua concordiae fides Titus prava certamina communi
utilitate aboleverat, natura atque arte compositus alliciendis etiam Muciani
moribus.

Syriacum promisit exercitum: there were four legions (3rd Gallica,
4th Scythica, 6th Ferrata, 12th Fulminata) in Syria when Mucianus was
appointed governor (Tac. H. і 10). The 3rd was transferred to Moesia
(see on § 3). Mucianus, in urging Vespasian to strike for empire, says to
him (H. ii 76): Tibi e Iudaea et Syria et Aegypto novem legiones (4 in
Syria, 3 in Judaea, 2 in Egypt viz. 3rd Cyrenaica and 22nd Deiotariana)
integrae, nulla acie exhaustae, non discordia corruptae, sed firmatus usu
miles et belli domitor externi; classium alarum cohortium robora et fidissimi reges et tua ante omnes experientia.

sagittariorum: Tacitus (H. iv 51) calls them equites, the famous
Parthian bowmen being cavalry.

ducibus copiisque praemissis: Mucianus was the commander of
the forces which Vespasian sent ahead from the East; but Antonius
Primus, without waiting for the arrival of Mucianus, advanced into Italy
with the legions of Moesia, Dalmatia, and Pannonia, and defeated the
Vitellians; see on Vitell. 18. Tacitus (H. ii 83) describes the troops of
Mucianus and the manner of his march: Mucianus cum expedita manu,
socium magis imperii quam ministrum agens, non lento itinere, ne cunctari
videretur, neque tamen properans, gliscere famam ipso spatio sinebat, gnarus
modicas vires sibi et maiora credi de absentibus; sed legio sexta et tredecim
vexillariorum milia ingenti agmine sequebantur. The 6th legion had been
stationed in Syria since the reign of Tiberius; the 13,000 vexillarii were
most probably detachments of 2,600 from each of the five legions left
behind, two in Syria and three in Judaea (Heraeus ad loc.).

Alexandriam transiit: Dio lxv 9, τὸν μὲν Μουκιανὸν ἐς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ἐπὶ τὸν
Οὐιτέλλιον ἔπεμψεν, αὐτὸς δὲ ἐς τὴν Αἴγυπτον ἐκομίσθη: Oros. vii 9, 3, per
Alexandriam profectus est Romam; sed cognita interfectione Vitelli paulisper Alexandriae substitit. Titus was left to carry on the war against the
Jews; Tac. H. ii 82, Titum instare Iudaeae, Vespasianum obtinere claustra
Aegypti placuit: sufficere videbantur adversus Vitellium pars copiarum et
dux Mucianus et Vespasiani nomen ac nihil arduum fatis ("the destiny
before which all difficulties vanish," Church and Brodribb).

claustra Aegypti: usually explained as Alexandria and Pelusium (cf.
Hirtius, B. Alex. 26, tota Aegyptos maritimo accessu Pharo, pedestri
Pelusio, velut claustris munita existimatur); but Alexandria alone may be
meant, as in Liv. xlv 11 Pelusium is called claustra Aegypti, so too Philae
in Luc. x 313. Braithwaite explains claustra Aegypti as "the stronghold
of Egypt," Aegypti being a genitive of definition, but this interpretation
finds no support in any of the uses of claustrum cited in the Thes. Ling.
Lat. Vespasian argued that by controlling Egypt, the key of the corn-supply (claustra annonae), and by cutting off the revenues of the richest
provinces (Syria, Asia, and Egypt), the army of Vitellius could be forced
to surrender by lack of corn and pay (Tac. H. iii 8). For the vital
importance of the occupation of Egypt cf. Tac. A. ii 59, Augustus ..
seposuit ("kept for himself'") Aegyptum, ne fame urgueret Italiam, quisquis eam provinciam claustraque terrae ac maris quamvis levi praesidio
adversum ingentes exercitus insedisset: id. H. i 11 (quoted on c. 6, 3
praefectus Aegypti).

capturus auspicium: Tac. H. iv 82, altior inde Vespasiano cupido
adeundi sacram sedem (Serapidis dei), ut super rebus imperii consuleret.
The phrase capere auspicium occurs also in Apul. Met. ix 8; cf. c. augurium
(Aug. 95): с. omen (Cic. Div. i 104): c. praesagia belli (Luc. vii 331).

aedem Serapidis: the splendour of this temple is described in Amm.
Marc. xxii 16, 12: His accedunt altis sufflata fastigiis templa, inter quae
eminet Serapeum, quod licet minuatur exilitate verborum, atriis tamen
columnariis amplissimis et spirantibus signorum figmentis et reliqua operum
multitudine ita est exornatum, ut post Capitolium, quo se venerabilis Roma
in aeternum attollit, nihil orbis terrarum ambitiosius cernat. The worship
of Serapis (or Sarapis) prevailed at Alexandria from c. 300 B.C. to c.
400 A.D. Many divergent accounts of its introduction are collected in
Plut. De Is. et Osir. 28, 29 and Tac. H. iv 83, 84. Some said that
Ptolemy I (323-285 в.с.) in obedience to a vision brought the colossal
statue from Sinope in Pontus; others that Ptolemy III (247-222) introduced the god from Seleucia in Syria, or from Memphis in Egypt where
a large Serapeum was excavated in 1850 by Mariette Bey. The Serapeum
was a temple erected in connexion with the sepulchres of the dead Apis
bulls, whose mummies were placed there in subterranean corridors described
by Bevan, Ptolemaic Egypt p. 41. The name of the god is a blend of
Osiris and Apis, the Egyptian Osir-Hapi; see Tit. 5, 3, n. Macrobius
(Sat. i 7) says that the Egyptian priests of the older faith only accepted
the worship of Serapis when forced to do so by the Ptolemies; but he
was the principal god in the Greek and Roman towns of Egypt.
identification of Serapis with various other divinities is mentioned in Tac.
The
(l.c.): deum ipsum multi Aesculapium, quod medeatur aegris corporibus,
quidam Osirin, antiquissimum illis gentibus numen, plerique Iovem ut
rerum omnium potentem, plurimi Ditem patrem (i.e. Pluto), insignibus
quae in ipso manifesta, aut per ambages coniectant. The statue of Serapis
at Alexandria perished when the temple was destroyed by Theodosius in
389 A.D. The worship of Serapis was introduced into Italy through Sicily
and the Greek towns of Campania in the 2nd cent. B.C. For the triumph
of the cults of Isis and Serapis in the Western world see Dill, Rom.
Society from Nero to M. Aurelius 560 sqq.

summotis omnibus: cf. the story as told in Tac. H. iv 82: Arceri
templo cunctos iubet. Atque ingressus intentusque numini, respexit pone
tergum e primoribus Aegyptiorum nomine Basiliden, quem procul
Alexandria plurium dierum itinere et aegro corpore detineri haud ignorabat.
Percontatur sacerdotes num illo die Basilides templum inisset; percontatur obvios num in urbe visus sit: denique missis equitibus explorat
illo temporis momento octoginta milibus passuum afuisse. Tunc divinam
speciem et vim responsi ex nomine Basilidis interpretatus est. This last
sentence is explained by Doederlein: “Tunc agnovit illum, quem pone
tergum conspexit, ipsum deum fuisse responsi loco apparentem, qui consulenti sub persona Basilidis fortunam principalem (βασιλείαν) portenderet."

verbenas: verbenae was used in the general sense of greenery of any
kind (leaves, twigs, branches) employed for sacred purposes; cf. Donatus
on Ter. Andr. 726: verbenae sunt omnes herbae frondesque festae. At
times the term denotes more specifically rosemary, myrtle, bay, olive, and
vervain itself (verbenaca, ἱερὰ βοτάνη); so Serv. on Aen. xii 120: Verbena
proprie est herba sacra, ros marinus, ut multi volunt,
abusive tamen
verbenas iam vocamus omnes frondes sacratas, ut est laurus, oliva, et
myrtus. For the various purposes (offerings, wreaths, etc.) for which
verbenae were utilised see Daremberg-Saglio, v 736.
..

panificia: panificium is used by Varro (L.L. v 105) of the process
of breadmaking, by Celsus (ii 18) of the bread that is made. Here it
seems to mean a sacrificial cake such as those offered to Osiris which are
called popana in Juv. vi 541, tenui popano corruptus Osiris (πόπανα =
πλακούντια πλατέα καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ περιφερῆ, Schol. ad Plat. Rep. v 227). So
at Roman sacrifices placentae or liba were used.

Basilides: the priest consulted by Vespasian on Mount Carmel (see
c. 5, 6) bore, according to Tac. H. ii 78, the same name, a name (from
βασιλεύς “king") which augured well for Vespasian's hopes of empire.

libertus: Tacitus (H. iv 82) describes Basilides as an Egyptian noble
(e primoribus Aegyptiorum), and Suet. may be incorrect in his description,
though his version of the story differs in other respects from that of Tac.
(e.g. Tac. makes Vespasian's visit to the Serapeum a consequence of the
miraculous cures which he had effected). Torrentius, Marcilius, and others
regard libertus as a mere interpolation of some ‘“malus grammaticus.’”
Casaubon's theory is that it may have got into the text through a dittography of the last two syllables of Basilides. Oudendorp proposed liberius;
Bentley uberius. I would suggest Libye ortus. Ernesti defends libertus
on the ground that Vespasian would have been familiar with the appearance of one of his own freedmen, whereas it is improbable that on his
first visit to Alexandria he would have known this Egyptian noble, and
that the very fact that he had given Basilides his freedom was a happy
omen for his deliverance of Rome from oppression. We know of another
Basilides, probably a procurator, who is mentioned as an imperial freedman
(Καίσαρος ἀπελεύθερος) in a decree of the prefect of Egypt in 49 A.D. (C.I.G.
4956; Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. i 229).

advenere litterae: Suetonius speaks as if the news of the defeat of
Vitellius (near the end of October) and of his death (near the end of
December) reached Vespasian at Alexandria simultaneously. Tacitus is
more precise. In H. iii 48 he says that Vespasian had not yet reached
Alexandria when he got news of his victory: Vespasianum Cremonensis
proelii nuntius in Aegypto adsequitur. Eo properantius Alexandriam
pergit, etc.; in iv 51 he says that many Romans of every rank risked the
perils of the wintry sea to bring tidings to Vespasian at Alexandria of
the fall of Vitellius: ut Vespasiano post Cremonensem pugnam et prosperos
undique nuntios, cecidisse Vitellium multi cuiusque ordinis, pari audacia
fortunaque hibernum mare adgressi, nuntiavere.

Cremonam: the two battles known as the battles of Betriacum (or
Bedriacum) were fought much nearer to Cremona; see on Oth. 9, 2.
Cremona was very loyal to Vitellius, and after the second battle (Oct., 69),
in which the Vitellians were routed, Antonius Primus captured, sacked,
and burned the city.
in urbe interemptum: as described in Vitell. 17.

§ 2. auctoritas.. maiestas: similarly Dio (lxvi 8) says that Vespasian
was invested with σεμνότης by the miracles which he performed at
Alexandria: τὸ θεῖον τούτοις αὐτὸν ἐσέμνυνεν (his rebus numen eum venerabilem effecit); cf. Tac. iv 81, multa miracula evenere, queis caelestis favor
et quaedam in Vespasianum inclinatio numinum ostenderetur.

ut scilicet inopinato principi: scilicet is quite pleonastic after ut
(= utpote), and its genuineness has been suspected. Torrentius approved
the reading ut solet given in one of the MSS. which he used; but ut solet
is probably due to ut illic assolet a few lines above.
There is another
remarkable pleonasm in Tit. 7, 3, abstinuit alieno, ut si quis umquam,
where see note.

e plebe quidam: cf. Tac. (l.c.): E plebe Alexandrina quidam oculorum
tabe notus genua eius advolvitur remedium caecitatis exposcens gemitu,
monitu Serapidis dei, quem dedita superstitionibus gens ante alios colit;
precabaturque principem ut genas et oculorum orbes dignaretur respergere
oris excremento. Alius manum aeger, eodem deo auctore, ut pede ac
vestigio Caesaris calcaretur orabat.

debili crure: Tac. says manum aeger, and so Dio (lxvi 8) Οὐεσπασιανὸς
τυφλόν τέ τινα, καὶ ἕτερον οὐκ ἀρτίχειρα, . . . τοῦ μὲν τὴν χεῖρα πατήσας, τοῦ δὲ
τοῖν ὀφθαλμοῖν προσπτύσας, ὑγιεῖς ἀπέφηνε.

pro tribunali: "at the front of the tribunal," having, as it were,
the tribunal behind him; cf. pro suggestu (Caes., etc.) of a speaker standing
forward on the platform, and pro rostris, which is used by post-Aug.
writers of speakers (e.g. Calig. 10, 1, defunctam pro rostris laudavit)
and of statues, etc., on the Rostra (e.g. Vitell. 3, 1). Tenney Frank
(Rivista di Filologia lii 1, 1925), discussing phrases like pro tribunali
where the original meaning of pro was "before," says that tribunal
originally signified the seat of the tribunes, on whom the orator turned his
back; afterwards it was used to denote the fixed platform on which this
seat came to be placed (Class. Quart. xx 1, 1926).

per quietem: cf. Dio (l.c.), ἐξ ὕψεως τῶν ὀνειράτων. We constantly
read of dreams in connexion with Serapis: the bringing of the statue of
the god from Sinope to Alexandria was due to a vision which appeared
to Ptolemy per quietem (Tac. H. iv 83); cf. Cic. Div. ii 59, qui (= quo) igitur
convenit aegros a coniectore ('interpreter’”) somniorum potius quam a
medico petere medicinam? an Aesculapius, an Serapis potest nobis praescribere per somnium curationem valetudinis, Neptunus gubernantibus non
potest?: Artemid. Oneirocr. v 92, νοσῶν τις εὔξατο τῷ Σεράπιδι, εἰ μέλλει
σωθήσεσθαι, τὴν δεξιὰν αὐτῷ χεῖρα ὄναρ ἐπισείεσθαι, εἰ δὲ μή, ἀριστεράν. Sleeping
in the temples of Serapis and Aesculapius (ἐγκοίμησις, incubatio) in order
to get such visions was a common practice; Strabo (xvii 801) says that
the most distinguished men used to sleep in the temple of Serapis at
Canobus, to have cures revealed to them.

inspuisset: cf. Plaut. Capt. 550, qui insputatur morbus (epilepsy,
comitialis morbus). For the supposed curative effects of saliva see Plin.
N.H. xxviii 7, where ophthalmia, among other diseases, is said to yield to
it. Spitting was also supposed to avert the "evil eye" and to aid the
effects of medicine: Plin. (l.c.), terna despuere deprecatione in omri
medicina mos est atque ita effectus adiuvare. In the N.T. the healing of
a deaf man and of a blind man by spittle are mentioned among the
miracles, and Casaubon, in his note on our passage, says: "Agnoscis,
pie lector, falsam imitationem miraculorum Christi. Sic solitus illudere
hominibus & δαίμων.” David Hume in his famous sceptical Essay on
Miracles adduces this miracle of Vespasian. Spartianus, vit. Hadr. 25,
mentions two cases of blindness being cured by contact with the emperor
Hadrian. Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, was said to have been able to cure
splenetic persons by touching them with his toe (Plin. N.H. vii 20).

§ 3. cum vix fides esset
successuram: for the constr. see on
Oth. 5, 2, haud dubia fiducia plures adfuturos.

ne experiri quidem auderet: Tacitus (iv 81) describes how Vespasian
was gradually induced to make the attempt: Vespasianus primo inridere,
aspernari; atque illis instantibus modo famam vanitatis metuere, modo
obsecratione ipsorum et vocibus adulantium in spem induci. Postremo
aestimari a medicis iubet an talis caecitas ac debilitas ope humana superabiles forent. Medici varie disserere: huic non exesam vim luminis, et
redituram si pellerentur obstantia; illi elapsos in pravum artus, si salubris
vis adhibeatur, posse integrari. Id fortasse cordi deis, et divino ministerio
principem electum, denique patrati remedii gloriam penes Caesarem, inriti
ludibrium penes miseros fore. Igitur Vespasianus cuncta fortunae suae
patere ratus nec quicquam ultra incredibile, laeto ipse voltu, erecta quae
adstabat multitudine, iussa exsequitur. Statim conversa ad usum manus,
ac caeco reluxit dies. Utrumque, qui interfuere, nunc quoque memorant,
postquam nullum mendacio pretium.

pro contione: in front of the assembled populace, facing them; a
very favourite phrase with Suet. who uses it twenty times (e.g. Galb. 17,
Oth. 6, 3). For examples in Sall., Liv., and other authors see KühnerStegmann, i 514. "in contione" is constantly used in pre-class. and
class. writers.

nec eventus defuit: eventus is used at times in the Latin of this
period for "a successful result"; cf. Iul. 20, 5, desperans tam praecipitis
consilii eventum: Tac. A. ii 26, satis iam eventuum, satis casuum: Plin.
Εp. v 20, egi ego pro Vareno non sine eventu.

Tegeae: Tegea (mod. Paleo-Episkopi) in Arcadia was one of the
oldest towns in the Peloponnesus. It possessed a famous temple of Athena
Alea, described by Pausanias (viii 45). Strabo (fl. 25 B.C.) says that
while the other well-known towns of Arcadia had perished, leaving scarcely
a trace behind, Tegea was still in a tolerable state of preservation: viii 388,
Τεγέα δ᾽ ἔτι μετρίως συμμένει, καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τῆς ᾿Αλέας ᾿Αθηνᾶς.

reversus: on his voyage from Alexandria Vespasian visited Rhodes
and several cities in Asia Minor. He crossed from Ionia to Greece
and then from Corcyra to the Iapygian promontory on the Tarentine Gulf,
and was warmly welcomed by the Italian cities and by the capital. Cf.
Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 2, 4. He did not arrive at Rome before September,
70 A.D.

acto de Iudaeis triumpho: it was not till June, 71 A.D., that this
triumph was celebrated. The senate had decreed separate triumphs to
Vespasian and Titus; Vespasian decided that one should suffice, and for
the first time in its history Rome saw a father and son triumphing together (cf. Tit. 6, 1: Dom. 2, 1). The triumph as described by Josephus
(vii 5, 4) was of unparalleled splendour (magnificus triumphus, Oros. vii
9, 8). Vespasian was weary of the pompous ceremony before its close,
and chided himself for his folly in wanting a triumph at his age; see c. 12.

addidit: Vespasian's first consulship was in
51 A.D. under Claudius, when he was consul suffectus for the last two
months of the year. He held the office for the second time in 70 along
with Titus, the senate bestowing it by decree (Tac. H. iv 3, 38); again
in 71 with Nerva, and in 72, 74, 75, 76, 77, 79 with Titus (cf. Tit. 6, 1).

consulatus octo
censuram: Vespasian and Titus assumed the censorship in 73, probably in April. For the epigraphic evidence of this see Newton (op. cit.
p. 28 sqq.) and Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2'655). According to
Censorinus (de die natali 18, 14) the lustrum which closed the censorship
took place in 74; but in spite of the lustrum conditum, the title of
"Censor" is frequently given as an honorary title to Vespasian and
Titus in inscriptions in the following years. Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 350,
n. 3) shows that in Plin. N.H. vii 162, census quem intra quadriennium
imperatores Caesares Vespasiani pater filiusque censores egerunt, the words
intra quadriennium have been usually misinterpreted as meaning "during
four years (71-74)," whereas the real meaning is "four years ago," i.e.
four years before the date at which Pliny was writing.

nihil habuit antiquius: cf. Vitell. 15, 3, iuravit.. nihil sibi antiquius
quiete publica fore: Claud. 11, 1, nihil antiquius duxit quam id biduum
..
memoriae eximere. The phrase aliquid (or nihil) antiquius habere, used
at all periods of Lat., is exactly the Gr. πρεσβύτερόν τι (οr οὐδὲν) ἔχειν.

§ 2. ignominiae: the “humiliating defeat" of the Vitellians at
Betriacum (or Cremona, see c. 7, 1). For this sense of “ignominia’” cf.
Oth. 9, 3, ne victis quidem adeo afflictis ut non in ultionem ignominiae
quidvis discriminis
subirent: Ner. 39, 1, ignominia ad Orientem legionibus in Armenia sub iugum missis: Aug. 23, graves ignominias cladesque
duas accepit.
civitates liberae: these free states or cities "although geographically,
were not juristically within a province at all" (Greenidge, Roman Public
Life p. 317). Under the Republic they were free from Roman taxation
and enjoyed complete autonomy. They were outside the jurisdiction of
the governor, who could only enter a civitas libera as its guest. Under
the Empire, however, their libertas no longer conferred immunity from
Roman taxation (Greenidge, p. 428; cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 654 sqq.,
Marquardt, Staatsv. i² 71 sqq.).
nec non et see on Tit. 5, 2.

regna: client kingdoms on the frontiers of the Empire (such as
Commagene, mentioned below in § 4), ruled by kings in alliance with Rome
(reges socii), each bound by terms of his special treaty (valid only during
his lifetime), but all under an obligation to furnish troops if required.

Vitellianorum . . exauctoravit plurimos: exauctorare (= ab auctoramento, id est obligatione militari, et iuramento solvere) was at times used
of an honorable discharge (see on "missio,” Vitell. 15, 1), but more often
of a summary and dishonorable dismissal (cf. Vitell. 10, 1). Tacitus
(H. iv 46) describes the steps taken by Mucianus, before Vespasian's
arrival at Rome, to reinstate the praetorians who had been dismissed by
Vitellius and had then sided with Vespasian, and to get rid of the 16
praetorian cohorts formed by Vitellius from the Germanic legions. These
cohorts could not safely be disbanded all at once, and Mucianus was
forced to proceed very gradually: quibus aetas et iusta stipendia, dimissi
cum honore, alii ob culpam, sed carptim ac singuli. Vespasian restored the
old number of 9 praetorian cohorts. The legions with which Vespasian
dealt drastically were those of which merely detachments had fought for
Vitellius at the second battle of Betriacum (Vitell. 15, 2, n.), but of
which the main body had remained in Germany and taken part in the
revolt of Civilis (69-70 A.D., see Tac. H. iv 12 sqq.; not mentioned by
Suet.). Three of them (i Germanica, iv Macedonica, xvi Gallica) were disbanded; apparently also xv Primigenia which surrendered to Civilis at
Castra Vetera (H. iv 23, 60) and is not mentioned after 70 A.D. (see Dessau
Inscr. 2275 n.). It is a disputed point whether v Alaudae was disbanded
by Vespasian or was annihilated either in 86 by the Dacians or in 92 by
the Sarmatians (Dom. '6, 1). See the articles "Legio" by Cagnat in
Daremberg-Saglio and by Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa; also Parker, The
Roman Legions, 107 sqq.

adeo nihil.. indulsit: the only special payment which we know was
made to Vespasian's victorious soldiers was one by Mucianus of 100
sesterces each (Dio lxv 22). Vespasian had resolutely refused to promise
the usual lavish donativa (see on Dom. 2, 3); cf. Tac. H. ii 82, donativum
militi neque Mucianus
nisi modice ostenderat, ne Vespasianus quidem
plus civili bello obtulit quam alii in pace, egregie firmus adversus militarem
largitionem eoque exercitu meliore. For adeo nihil
ut (= tantum
abest ut .., ut) cf. c. 12 adeo nihil appetivit, ut; it occurs from Livy
on (Hand Tursell. i 141).

legitima praemia: praemia is frequently used by Suetonius for the
bounties (commoda, see on Vitell. 15, 1) to which time-expired soldiers
were entitled on their discharge; cf. Iul. 70, missionem et praemia flagitantes: Aug. 15, promissa veteranis praemia: ib. 49, 2, quicquid ubique
militum esset, ad certam stipendiorum (i.e. service-time) praemiorumque
formulam astrinxit. So‘commoda praemiorum” in Aug. 24, 1: (legiones)
immodeste missionem postulantes citra ("without") commoda emeritorum
praemiorum exauctoravit.

§ 3. fragrantem unguento: fragrare is a poetic word, not found earlier
in prose (see Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb.); it is used either with the abl.
as here (cf. Catull. 6, 8) or with the acc. (e.g. Apul. Met. vi 11, Venus
balsama fragrans).

praefectura: the command of an ala or squadron of auxiliary cavalry
(see on Galb. 10, 2), one of the posts held by a young Roman qualifying
in the army with a view to obtaining office at Rome and admission to
the senate; cf. Aug. 38, 2, liberis senatorum
militiam auspicantibus
non tribunatum modo legionum, sed et praefecturas alarum dedit; ac ne
qui expers castrorum esset, binos plerumque laticlavios praeposuit singulis
alis.

nutu aspernatus: “aspernari est averti, non solum corpore, sed etiam
animo” (Donat. on Ter. Phorm. 371). nutus is used here of drawing
back or tossing back the head in disgust; cf. nutare in Plaut. Mil. 208,
capite nutat: non placet quod repperit, where Ussing comments “non
adnuens, sed renuens, nutu aspernatus, ut ait Sueton.”

alium oboluisses: so in Plaut. Most. 39, oboluisti alium. The acc.
was freely used with olere and its compounds; e.g. Varr. Men. 63, alium
ac caepe olere: Cic. Phil. ii 63, redolere vinum (Kühner-Stegmann, i 277).
alium “garlic survives in the Romance languages: Ital. aglio, Fr. ail,
Span. ajo. On the forms alium and allium (given here by QR) Vollmer
(Thes. Ling. Lat.) says: “proba scriptura est ‘alium' firmata titulo
Pompeiano Corp. iv 2070 et codicibus melioribus (ut Ambr. Plaut.
Poen. 1314 ali[i] ); tamen iam primo post Chr. saeculo scribebant
“allium” (Inscr. Pompei. p. 1620, 15) quae scriptio fere regnat apud librarios
recentiores."
=
litteras: "letters patent,” “commission," dati officii codicillos
(Claud. 29, 1, suppositos aut etiam palam immutatos datorum officiorum
codicillos). For "litterae" used of official ordinances cf. Cic. Verr. v 56,
cedo mihi eiusdem praetoris litteras et rerum decretarum et frumenti
imperati.

revocavit: revocare in the sense of rescindere is not used in class.
prose; it occurs in Sen., Tac., etc.

classiarios ab Ostia et Puteolis: Ostia (at the mouth of the Tiber,
16 miles from Rome) and Puteoli (on the coast of Campania) were two
of the squadron-stations of the main Roman fleet at Misenum. In Claud.
25, 2 Suetonius mentions that Claudius stationed cohorts at Ostia and
Puteoli to guard against the danger of fires (Puteolis et Ostiae singulas
cohortes ad arcendos incendiorum casus collocavit). It is not definitely known
whether those cohorts consisted of classiarii “marines” (so Daremberg-Saglio, i 1222), or were two of the cohortes urbanae (so Smilda ad loc.,
following Mommsen, Hermes xvi 645). See also on Oth. 8, 2.

calciarii: sc. argenti "shoe-money"; cf. Digest ii 15, 8, 14, de
calciario quoque arbitrio praetoris transigendum est: xxxiv 1, 21, neque
vestiarium neque calciarium deberi palam est. Similarly clavarium “shoenail-money," Тас. Н. iii 50, seditiosae militum voces .. clavarium (donativi
nomen est) flagitantium. See Parker, Rom. Legions 223.
nomine: see on c. 4, 3.

quasi parum esset: cf. Calig. 29, 1, Monenti Antoniae aviae tamquam
parum esset non oboedire: “Memento,” ait, “omnia mihi et in omnes
licere.'"

excalciatos: here, as in other writers, excalciare has a personal object;
contrast Vitell. 2, 5, petit ut sibi pedes praeberet excalciandos. Varro (ap.
Non. 478 M.) has excalciari as a deponent: ad Herculis, ut introeat, nemo
se excalciatur. Suetonius also uses discalciatus "unshod" "barefooted"
(Ner. 51).

cursitare: these classiarii seem to have been used as couriers (cursores);
see Hirschfeld, Kaiserl. Verwaltungsb.2 228, 3.

§ 4. Achaiam: Augustus assigned the province of Achaia to the
senate and it was governed by a proconsul (Dio liii 12). In 16 A.D. Tiberius
made it an imperial province (Tac. A. i 76), but Claudius gave it back
to the senate (Claud. 25). Nero abolished the province and proclaimed
the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games in 67 (Ner. 24: Plut.
Flamin. 12: Dio lxiii 11). Vespasian declared the Greeks incapable of
freedom and restored the senatorial province with a yearly tribute (Paus.
vii 17).

Lyciam: the cities-league of Lycia (Λυκίων τὸ κοινόν) was a civitas libera
et foederata from the Sullan period on. It suffered much under Cassius
in 43 B.C., but its freedom was recognised a second time by M. Antonius
and it continued to enjoy it till 43 A.D. when Claudius took it away
(Claud. 25, Lyciis ob exitiabiles inter se discordias libertatem ademit).
Dio (lx 17) says that Claudius added Lycia to the praefectura of
Pamphylia, but from the evidence available it seems to have been first
formed into a province along with Pamphylia under Vespasian in 74. They
formed an imperial province under the governorship of a praetorius legatus
Augusti pro praetore. See Marquardt, Staatsv. i² 374 sqq.

Rhodum: Rhodes had been made a civitas foederata for its staunch
support of Rome in the Macedonian and Mithridatic wars (Appian Bell.
Civ. iv 66 sqq.). It lost its freedom in 44 A.D. for crucifying some Roman
citizens (Dio lx 24), but recovered it in 53, Nero pleading its cause before
Claudius (Suet. Claud. 25 libertatem Rhodiis ob paenitentiam veterum
delictorum reddidit: Tac. A. xii 58, reddita Rhodiis libertas, adempta
saepe aut firmata, prout bellis externis meruerant aut domi seditione
deliquerant). Presumably Rhodes and Samos (see below) were brought
into the province of Asia by Vespasian. Marquardt (op. cit. 348) points
out that this was the origin of the mistaken statement in Sextus Rufus
Brev. 10, sub Vespasiano principe Insularum provincia facta est. The
Insularum provincia, ἐπαρχία νήσων (κυκλάδων), is first mentioned in the
reign of Diocletian, 284-305 A.D. (C.I.L. iii 450).

Byzantium: Byzantium became a civitas foederata as a reward for
its services to Rome in the war with the pseudo-Philip of Macedon (c.
150 в.с.). Later it became a civitas libera with freedom revocable by
Rome at pleasure, whereas the freedom of a civitas foederata was guaranteed
by a definite foedus. In Cic. Prov. Cons, 4, 6 it is mentioned as a civitas
libera which had been outrageously plundered by the proconsul L. Piso.
In the time of Claudius it was no longer immunis, for envoys appeared
before the senate in 53 A.D. asking for relief, and Claudius helped them
to secure a remission of tribute for 5 years on account of their losses in
recent Thracian wars (Tac. A. xii 62). Pliny, N.H. iv 11, speaks of it as
an oppidum liberae condicionis, but Vespasian took away its freedom.
For its relation to the province of Macedonia, and later to that of Bithynia,
where the younger Pliny was governor, see Hardy on Plin. Ep. x 43.

Samum: the island of Samos was united to the province of Asia in
84 B.C. Augustus wintered at Samos in 20-19 в.с. and bestowed freedom
on the islanders as a reward for their hospitality (Dio liv 7, 9). It is
mentioned as a free state in Plin. N.H. v 37 (Pliny's work was dedicated
to Titus in 77 A.D.).

Trachiam Ciliciam: the reading of all the better MSS. is thraciam,
which was corrected by Turnebus to Tracheam and by Bentley to Trachiam
(found in Ⅱ), both these forms representing the Gr. Τραχεῖαν, and the
adoption of either correction is necessary. Thraciam (retained by Roth
and Preud'homme) is meaningless, for Thrace had been already made a
province under a procurator in 46 A.D., and only Cilicia Trachia, not
Cilicia generally, could be described in the words of Suet. “dicionis regiae
usque ad id tempus.” The mountainous western part of Cilicia was known
as τραχεῖα aspera, the eastern plainland as πεδιάς campestris, the boundary
being the city of Soli. When the province of Cilicia (first constituted in
102 B.C.) was re-organised in 64 B.c., the mountainous parts were left to
tributary native princes. M. Antonius gave Cilicia Trachia to Cleopatra
in 36 B.C. Later it was held by Amyntas, king of Galatia. On his death
in 25 B.c. it was given by Augustus to Archelaus of Cappadocia and after
his death in 17 A.D., when Cappadocia became a province, his family seem
to have remained in possession of Cilicia Trachia until Caligula gave it
along with Commagene to Antiochus IV (Dio lix 8). Caligula later deposed
Antiochus, but Claudius restored him (Dio lx 8) and he ruled Cilicia
Trachia until Vespasian finally attached it to the province of Cilicia in 74.
See Marquardt, op. cit. i² 313, who points out that the same confusion of
Trachia and Thracia occurs in the repetition of the words of Suet. by
Eutrop. (vii 19), Aur. Vict. (Epit. 9), and Hieron. (Eusebii Chron. p. 159
Schoene).

Commagenen: this district lay between Cappadocia on the N. and
Syria on the S.; it was bounded on the E. by the Euphrates, and on the
W. by Cilicia. For over a hundred years it had its own kings connected
with the family of the Seleucidae in Syria. In 17 A.D., on the death of
Antiochus III, it was made a Roman province by Tiberius, but was given
back by Caligula in 38 to Antiochus IV, a son of the late king. In 72
the governor of Syria deposed him, by command of Vespasian, for
intriguing with Parthia, and Commagene was made part of the province
of Syria; its capital Samosata received the additional name of Flavia.

in provinciarum formam redegit: cf. Eutrop. vii 19; Aur. Vict.
Caes. 9, Epit. 9; Oros. vii 9. Similar punishments by deprivation of
freedom were inflicted by Augustus (Aug. 47, urbium quasdam foederatas
sed ad exitium licentia praecipites libertate privavit, these cities being
Cyzicus, which was shortly after reinstated, Tyre, and Sidon); by Tiberius
on Cyzicus (Tib. 37); by Claudius on Rhodes and Lycia (Claud. 25); by
Septimius Severus in 196 on Byzantium, which must have recovered the
freedom taken from it by Vespasian (Dio lxxiv 14). For the technical
expression in formam provinciae redigere” to denote the subjection of
a community to Rome by placing it under a Roman governor see Mommsen,
Staatsr. iii 1166.

Cappadociae: in 15 A.D. Tiberius, out of pique for a want of respect
shown to him when staying at Rhodes, treacherously invited Archelaus,
king of Cappadocia, to Rome and kept him there till his death in 17, when
his kingdom was made a Roman province (Tac. A. ii 42, 56; Dio lvii 17;
Strab. xii 534). From that time on it was governed by procurators (Tac.
A. xii 49) until Vespasian gave it a consular governor with a legionary
force. The evidence of inscriptions shows that Vespasian joined Cappadocia
(with Lesser Armenia, etc.) to Galatia in one vast administrative sphere,
and that this arrangement continued till the later years of Trajan, who
made Galatia and Cappadocia separate provinces with separate governors.
See Brandis in Pauly-Wissowa vii 552; Henderson, Five Rom. Emperors
p. 60.

legiones addidit: cf. Tac. H. ii 81, inermes legati regebant (the
Asiatic provinces in 69) nondum additis Cappadociae legionibus. One of
the legions was the 12th Fulminata, and the other (as von Domaszewski
suggests) was probably the 16th Flavia, a new legion organised by Vesp.
in place of the disbanded 16th Gallica. Josephus (Bell. Iud. vii 1, 3) says
the 12th legion was sent to Melitene in Cappadocia late in 70, so the
consular legatus must have been appointed by that time (Marquardt, p. 367).

pro eq. R.: Dio (lvii 17) mentions that Tiberius gave the administration of Cappadocia to an eques: κακ τούτου (i.e. from 17 A.D.) ἡ Καππαδοκία τῶν τε ῾Ρωμαίων ἐγένετο καὶ ἱππεῖ ἐπετράπη. Such personal agents of
Caesar (procuratores Caesaris pro legato) governed the less important
outlying districts which were reckoned under the imperial provinces.

§ 5. deformis urbs: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, Romam deformem incendiis
veteribus ac ruinis, permissa, si domini deessent, volentibus aedificandi
copia, Capitolium, aedem Pacis, Claudii monumenta reparavit multaque nova
instituit. In addition to his restorations and constructions of buildings
in Rome, Vespasian repaired at his own expense the streets which were in
a sorry condition; cf. the senate's decree of thanks in the latter part of
71 (C.I.L. vi 931, Newton 113): Imp. Caesari Vespasiano Aug., pont.
max., tr. pot. iii, imp. iix, p.p., cos. iii, des. iiii, s.c., quod vias urbis neglegentia superior. tempor. corruptas inpensa sua restituit.

incendiis: the great fire at Rome in '64 A.D., which Suetonius (Ner. 38)
attributes to Nero himself, and the burning of the Capitol by the Vitellians
(see Vitell. 15, 3).
2E
..
sine

vacuas areas aedificare: area meant a vacant space (cf. Paul. Fest.
11, area proprie dicitur locus vacuus: Digest 1 16, 211, locus
aedificio in urbe area, rure ager appellatur), and so a building-site; e.g.
Iul. 26, 2, Forum . . incohavit, cuius area super sestertium milies constitit :
Hor. Ep. i 10, 13, ponendaeque domo quaerenda est area primum. For
aedificare with acc. of the site cf. Varro L.L. v 147, aedificatus locus:
Liv. i 35, 10, privatis aedificanda divisa sunt loca. In Digest xli 4, 13,
aream emit et aedificare coepit, most probably aedificare is to be taken
absolutely, as it may be in our passage.

cuicumque: see on Galb. 4, 3.
..

ipse restitutionem adgressus: the same account is given in Dio
lxvi 10, τόν τε νεὼν τὸν ἐν τῷ Καπιτωλίῳ εὐθὺς οἰκοδομεῖν ἤρξατο, αὐτός τε τοῦ χοῦ
πρῶτος ἐκφορήσας, καὶ δηλονότι καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῖς ἐπιφανεστάτοις τὸ αὐτὸ τοῦτο
κελεύσας, ἵνα καὶ τῷ λοιπῷ πλήθει ἀπαραίτητον τὸ διακόνημα γένηται. The difficulty
is that Vesp. did not arrive in Italy and Rome till the late summer of 70,
and Tacitus (who was probably an eyewitness) in describing the ceremonies
at the dedication of the site and the laying of the foundation-stone of
the new temple on June 21 does not mention the emperor as taking part,
but says that he commissioned Vestinus to supervise the work: H. iv 53,
curam restituendi Capitolii in Lucium Vestinum confert, equestris ordinis
virum, sed auctoritate famaque inter proceres. Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa,
vi 2648) tries to get over the difficulty by assuming that Vesp., when he
arrived later at Rome, helped to clear away the débris.

ruderibus: rubbish from the buildings which had been destroyed by
fire; cf. Aug. 30, 1, alveum Tiberis laxavit ac repurgavit, completum olim
ruderibus et aedificiorum prolationibus (‘extensions") coartatum: Ner. 38,
3 (of Nero after the great fire at Rome), pollicitus cadaverum et ruderum
gratuitam egestionem: Tac. A. xv 43 (referring to the same), ruderi
accipiendo Ostienses paludes destinabat, utique naves, quae frumentum
Tiberi subvectavissent, onustae rudere decurrerent. The more usual
meaning of rudus is a kind of concrete made from broken stones mixed
with lime and used for building purposes.

manus primus admovit: similarly Nero, to stimulate the praetorians
at the attempt to dig through the Isthmus of Corinth, ‘primus rastello
('mattock') humum effodit et corbulae ('basket') congestam umeris
extulit” (Ner. 19, 2). Germanicus, at the construction of a mound over
the bones of the legions of Varus, "primum extruendo tumulo caespitem
posuit'' (Tac. A. i 62).

suo collo: cf. Apul. Met. ix 7, calamitosus faber collo suo gerens
dolium: Luc. i 603, Salius laeto portans ancilia collo: Catull. 10, 23,
fractum qui veteris pedem grabati | in collo sibi collocare posset.
aerearum tabularum: all engagements entered into by Rome with
foreigners, whether international treaties or privileges conferred on individuals, were engraved on bronze tablets and affixed to the walls of
public buildings and temples, more especially in the immediate neighbourhood of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. Polybius (iii 26) saw the old
trade treaties between Rome and Carthage ἐν χαλκώμασι παρὰ τὸν Δία τὸν
Καπετώλιον ἐν τῷ τῶν ἀγορανόμων ταμιείῳ (‘"the archives of the aediles'').
Cf. also Appian Syr. 39 (on the treaty with Antiochus in 189 в.с.), ταῦτα
συγγραψάμενοί τε καὶ ἐς τὸ Καπιτώλιον ἐς δέλτους χαλκᾶς ἀναθέντες, οὗ καὶ τὰς
ἄλλας συνθήκας ἀνατιθέασιν : Cic. Phil. ii 36, toto Capitolio tabulae figebantur,
neque solum singulis venibant immunitates, sed etiam populis universis;
civitas non iam singillatim, sed provinciis totis dabatur unum egregium
de rege Deiotaro, populi R. amicissimo, decretum in Capitolio fixum. See
Mommsen, Staatsr. i3 257; Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 52. Tacitus (H. iv
40) says that the senate before the arrival of Vesp. had appointed a
commission “qui aera legum vetustate delapsa noscerent figerentque." It
is uncertain whether this was another version of what Suet. says, or
whether Vesp. supplemented the labours of this commission (see Spooner
ad loc.).

undique investigatis exemplaribus: cf. Dom. 20, exemplaribus undique
petitis (when Domitian was restoring the libraries consumed by fire at
Rome). The copies (exemplaria) used by Vespasian were such as are
mentioned in Liv. xxvi 24, 14, haec convenerunt conscriptaque biennio
post Olympiae ab Aetolis, in Capitolio ab Romanis, ut testata sacris monumentis essent, sunt posita: C.I.G. 2485 (an alliance between Rome and
Astypalaea in 105 B.c., a copy of which was to be preserved on bronze at
the temple of Athena in Astypalaea).

instrumentum: in apposition with aerearum
milia. The word is
used here of an official record; cf. Calig. 8, 5, sequenda est publici instrumenti (i.e. the acta publica or acta diurna) auctoritas: Quintil. xii 8, 12,
opus est intueri omne litis instrumentum (i.e. every document connected
with the case): Digest xxiv 1, 58, emptionum instrumenta suo nomine
confecit. Lawyers use "instrument" for a writing acknowledging or
certifying to a claim, or recording the terms of a contract, deed, or grant.

senatus consulta: e.g. the decree (78 B.c.) granting friendship and
privileges to Asclepiades of Clazomenae, Polystratus of Carystus, and
Meniscus of Miletus, three naval captains who had rendered services to
Rome in 90-89 during the Italian revolt (C.I.L. i 203; Bruns, Fontes Iuris
Rom. p. 176; Wordsworth, Frag. and Spec. p. 205). A similar grant of
privileges was decreed by the senate to Onesimus a Macedonian for services
rendered by his father to Rome in the war against Perseus (Liv. xliv 16).
As M has the reading consultam, Bentley would insert ac (or et) after
consulta.

plebi scita: e.g. the Lex Antonia de Termessibus (71 B.c.) confirming
the autonomy granted to Termessus, a town in Pisidia (C.I.L. i 204; Bruns,
p. 92; Wordsworth, p. 209). This measure was introduced by the tribune
C. Antonius “de s(enatus) s(ententia)," i.e. with the sanction of the
senate, in accordance with Sulla's ordinance (88 B.c.) requiring such sanction
for any measure brought before the plebeian assembly; but in 70 B.C. the
Lex Pompeia restored the unrestricted legislative validity secured for plebi
scita by the Lex Hortensia in 287.
=

privilegio: in class. Lat. privilegium meant a special ordinance, an
exceptional measure in favour of or directed against an individual (privus
singulus), which in Republican times was illegal. It was under the Caesars
that the word first acquired the sense of a prerogative or "privilege”
granted by a special ordinance; class. writers express this by beneficium,
ius praecipuum, etc. (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb.).

cuicumque: see on Galb. 4, 3.
2E2

nova opera: the inscriptions bearing on the building activity of the
reigns of Vespasian and Titus, not merely in Rome but also in Italy and
the provinces, are collected by Newton, op. cit. 46 sqq. Among these inscriptions are C.I.L. iii 6702, 11194-11196; vi 301, 369, 814, 934 (where
Vesp. is described as restitutor aedium sacrarum), 935, 936, 939, 940 (where
there is mention of a collegium subrutorum whose work, according to
Mommsen, ad loc., was to dig out the ruins of buildings destroyed by fire,
etc.); x 1406, 1481; xi 598; xiv 3485.

templum Pacis: cf. Dio lxvi 15, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἕκτον καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ
Τίτου τέταρτον ἀρχόντων (75 A.D.) τὸ τῆς Εἰρήνης τέμενος καθιερώθη : Aur.
Vict. Caes. 9, Romae Capitolium, quod conflagravisse supra memoravimus,
aedes Pacis, Claudii monumenta, amphitheatri tanta vis multaque alia ac
forum coepta seu patrata. Josephus (Bell. Iud. vii 5) says of the building
of this temple: “ταχὺ δὲ δὴ μάλα, καὶ πάσης ἀνθρωπίνης κρεῖττον ἐπινοίας
ἐτετελείωτο,” and describes its ornaments which included vessels of gold
and silver from the Temple in Jerusalem. Pliny (N.H. xxxvi 102) ranks it
among the "pulcherrima operum quae umquam vidit orbis," and mentions
several famous statues and pictures in it (xxxiv 84, xxxv 74, 109, 122).
Domitian may have added some finishing touches to it, and he seems, in
characteristic fashion (see Dom. 5), to have claimed the credit for the
whole, which is given to him by the court poet Statius (Silv. iv 3, 17, qui
Pacem propria domo reponit). The temple was burned down shortly
before the death of Commodus (192 A.D.), but was soon restored. It seems
to have been reduced to ruins by an earthquake in 408 A.D. Newton
(p. 46, n. 7) points out that no inscription of this temple has been found,
but no divinity was so frequently inserted by Vespasian on his coins as
Pax (see Eckhel, vi p. 334) and there are several dedications to the "Pax
Vespasiani'' in inscriptions, e.g. C.I.L. vi 200, Paci aeternae domus Imp.
Vespasiani Caesaris Aug. liberorumq. eius sacrum.

Foro: the Forum Romanum, to the N. of which the temple stood.
The temple was built in an enclosed space, like the temple of Venus
Genetrix in Caesar's forum and that of Mars Ultor in the forum of
Augustus, and in the period after Constantine we find this space called
forum Pacis (φόρον Εἰρήνης), e.g. in Amm. Marc. xvi 10, Procop. Bell. Goth. iv
21. Domitian connected the forum Augusti with the templum Pacis or
forum Pacis by the forum Transitorium (see Dom. 5).
(templum) Divi Claudi: cf. Claud. 45, funeratus est sollemni principum
pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum
("neglected") abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum. A portico surrounding it is probably that mentioned in Mart. Spect. 2, 9: Claudia
