diffusas ubi porticus explicat umbras | ultima pars aulae deficientis erat
(i.e. the end of the Golden House of Nero was on this part of the Caelian
mount). The temple is mentioned by Frontinus, de Aquaed. 20, 76, in
connexion with the Aqua Claudia; also in C.I.L. vi 10251 a, T. Flavio Aug.
lib. Trophimo constitutori collegi numinis dominorum quod est sup templo
divi Claudi. There are still remains, not of the temple, but of the massive
substructions; see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 232: Burn, Rome
and the Campagna p. 221.

Caelio monte: between the Aventine and Esquiline, now the Lateran
Mount; originally called Mons Querquetulanus from the oak-trees on it,
it received the name Caelius from the Etruscan chief Caeles Vibenna
(Etrusc. Kaile Fipne); under Tiberius the name was changed for a short
time to Mons Augustus to commemorate the munificence of Tiberius in
restoring it when devastated by fire (Suet. Tib. 48, Tac. A. iv 64).
the Caelian were chapels of Dea Carna (Macrob. Sat. i 12), Minerva Capta
(Ov. F. iii 837), and Diana (Cic. Har. Resp. 15); also a temple of Isis
(Trebell. Poll. trig. tyrann. 24).

Agrippina: see on c. 4, 2.
On

a Nerone prope funditus destructum: Platner-Ashby (Topogr. Dict.
Rome p. 120) would account for this destruction partly by the construction
of the distributing station of the Aqua Claudia, which Nero extended to
the Caelian, and partly by the construction of the Domus Aurea.

amphitheatrum: the vast Flavian amphitheatre, known as the
Colosseum since about 1000 A.D. (Platner-Ashby, p. 6), was built in the
valley between the Esquiline and Caelian on the site of the stagnum
Neronis, i.e. the great pleasure lake of Nero's Golden House; cf. Mart.
Spect. 2, 5, Hic ubi conspicui venerabilis amphitheatri | erigitur moles,
stagna Neronis erant. It was begun by Vespasian in 72, continued and
dedicated by Titus in 80, and completed by Domitian in 823; further
additions were made by Alexander Severus (ob. 235) and Gordianus (ob.
238). The building was about a third of a mile in circumference, and
could accommodate over 50,000 spectators. The magnificent remains attest
the truth of Martial's lines (Spect. 1, 7): Omnis Caesareo cedit labor
amphitheatro, | unum pro cunctis fama loquetur opus. See Jordan-Huelsen,
op. cit. i 3, 282 sqq. Coins of Vesp. and Titus which depict the Flavian
amphitheatre under different aspects are described by Eckhel, vi pp. 357-
359, 375, vii 271, 315; Cohen, i² p. 461, etc.

ut destinasse compererat Augustum: we do not read elsewhere of this
design of Augustus to build an amphitheatre in the heart of the city.
The first stone amphitheatre was constructed by Statilius Taurus in the
reign of Augustus (29 B.C.; cf. Suet. Aug. 29, Tac. A. iii 72, Dio li 23).
It was in the Campus Martius. In the record of his reign contained in
the Monumentum Ancyranum Augustus says (c. 22): Venationes bestiarum
Africanarum meo nomine aut filiorum meorum et nepotum in circo aut in
foro aut in amphitheatris populo dedi sexiens et viciens. Mommsen, Mon.
Anc.² 94, commenting on the pl. amphitheatris, says that the word, first
found here, was originally a plural “cum essent amphitheatra tanquam
theatra duo," and that Aug. is referring only to the new amphitheatre
of Taurus and not to other temporary wooden structures. But more
probably amphitheatrum meant a building in which the θέατρον (i.e. the
space for spectators, Zuschauerraum) ran round in a ring; see Meier in
Pauly-Wissowa, i 1959.

§ 2. amplissimos ordines: the ordo senatorius and ordo equester. The
title amplissimus ordo was applied especially to the senate (see on c. 2, 3),
but Cicero had already used amplissimi ordines to include senatores, equites,
and tribuni aerarii, from all of whom the iudices were drawn at the time
(e.g. Sull. 5, 15: Mil. 2, 4, where see Clark's note). Lipsius needlessly
proposed to alter amplissimos to amplissimum, attaching it to the preceding sentence as an epithet of amphitheatrum, and Casaubon would
either accept this change or read ambos ordines.

purgavit: a precedent for this "purgation" was that effected by
Augustus; cf. Aug. 35, 1, Senatorum affluentem numerum deformi et incondita turba - erant enim super mille, et quidem indignissimi et post
necem Caesaris per gratiam et praemium adlecti, quos orcinos (i.e. slaves
set free by their master's will) vulgus vocabat - ad modum pristinum et
splendorem redegit duabus lectionibus (these two lectiones or “revisions"
were in 29 and 18 в.с.).
supplevit: Aur. Vict. (Caes. 9) says that there were barely 200 gentes
when Vesp. came to the throne, and that he raised the number to 1000:
censu more veterum exercito, senatu motus probrosior quisque, ac lectis
undique optimis viris, mille gentes compositae, cum ducentas aegerrime
repperisset, exstinctis saevitia tyrannorum plerisque.

recenso equite: Augustus established an annual probatio equitum
(ἐξέτασις τῶν ἱππέων, Dio lv 31) combining the old annual travectio, or
parade of those equites who had the equus publicus, and the recognitio
equitum which had been held periodically by the censors. Before the
parade, the emperor aided by ten senators held a strict investigation into
the life of each of the equites and those who were proved unworthy were
either degraded or reprimanded with varying degrees of severity; see
Aug. 38 and 39 with Shuckburgh's notes. Suetonius also mentions the
recognitio equitum by Caligula and Claudius: Calig. 16, 2, Equites R.
severe curioseque nec sine moderatione recognovit, palam adempto equo
quibus aut probri aliquid aut ignominiae inesset, eorum qui minore culpa
tenerentur nominibus modo in recitatione praeteritis: Claud. 16, 1,
Recognitione equitum iuvenem probri plenum, sed quem pater probatissimum sibi affirmabat, sine ignominia dimisit, habere dicens censorem
suum, etc.

summotis: in the case of senators movere senatu (or senatorio loco)
was the usual expression for expulsion; cf. Dom. 8, 3.
Tacitus

indignissimis: cf. Aug. 35, 1 (quoted above on purgavit).
tells of Tiberius expelling senators “prodigos et ob flagitia egentes” (A. ii
48, cf. Suet. Vitell. 2, 2) and another "quod in acta d. Augusti non
iuraverat” (A. iv 42). Claudius enforced the resignation of those who
were "famosi probris” (A. xi 25). Domitian expelled an ex-quaestor
“quod gesticulandi saltandique studio teneretur” (Suet. Dom. 8, 3).
Among those expelled by Vespasian was Palfurius Sura; see on Dom. 13, 1.
sed

Italicorum ac provincialium: cf. Tac. A. iii 55, novi homines e типіcipiis et coloniis (terms denoting the towns of Italy) atque etiam provinciis
in senatum crebro adsumpti domesticam parsimoniam intulerunt
praecipuus adstricti moris auctor Vespasianus fuit, antiquo ipse cultu
victuque. Vespasian himself was a novus homo from Reate. Claudius, in
his speech (partly preserved on a bronze tablet at Lugdunum, cf. Tac. A. xi
24) successfully advocating the admission of Gallic senators, says that
Tiberius had freely enrolled senators from Italian towns. The first
Paelignian senator was admitted under Augustus (C.I.L. ix 3306). Julius
c, 9, 2.]
Caesar had introduced some Gallic senators, who were received with bitter
hostility at Rome (Iul. 76, 80). Otho, in 69 A.D., describes the senate as
"caput imperii et decora omnium provinciarum” (Tac. H. i 84). A full
account of the gradual admission of provincials to the senate is given by
Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 107 sqq. In recruiting the equestrian order from
the whole Roman empire Vespasian was following the example of Caligula
of whom Dio (lix 9) says: τοῦ τε τέλους (ordinis) τοῦ τῶν ἱππέων ὀλιγαν -
δροῦντος, τοὺς πρώτους ἐξ ἁπάσης καὶ τῆς ἔξω ἀρχῆς τοῖς τε γένεσι καὶ ταῖς περιουσίαις
μεταπεμψάμενος κατελέξατο. See also on c. 3 supr.

adlecto: legere in senatum was the phrase used under the Republic
of the censors retaining the names of old senators or admitting those newly
qualified; adlectio is the tech. term under the Empire for the admission to
the senate by imperial favour of those not regularly qualified.
These
adlecti were given varying rank among those senators who had been
quaestors, praetors, etc. (adlecti inter quaestorios, aedilicios, tribunicios,
praetorios, and, from the 3rd cent. A.D., consulares). See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii 939 sqq.; Willems, Le Sénat Romain i 626 sqq. Examples of
those who were adlecti inter tribunicios or praetorios by Vespasian and
Titus as censors are to be found in C.I.L. ii 4130, iii 335, vi 1359, viii 7057,
ix 5533 (see Vesp. 13, note on Salvium Liberalem), xi 1834, xiv 2925;
Plin. Ep. i 14. New patricians also were created in their censorship; see
note on Oth. 1, 3, adlectum inter patricios. Among them were Annius
Verus, grandfather of the emperor Marcus Aurelius (Capitol. Marc.
Antonin. Philos. 1), and Agricola (Tac. Agr. 9). Two of the equites
created by Vespasian were Hormus, one of his freedmen (Tac. H. iv 39),
and Claudius (father of Claudius Etruscus, Stat. S. iii 3, 145), a freedman
of Tiberius, who was a rationibus under Nero and still held that post
under Domitian.

remaledici: the compound remaledicere (= ἀντιλοιδορεῖν) is first found
here, and occurs later in Tertull. Idol. 21, Hieron. Ep. 69, 9.
..

civile: conduct befitting a true citizen living on terms of mutual
respect with his fellow-citizens, neither submitting to insults nor insulting
others. civilis (κοινός, δημοκρατικός) is repeatedly used by Suetonius of
rulers who behave unassumingly, avoiding tyrannical arrogance (ὕβρις)
and respecting the rights of those under their authority; e.g. Vesp. 12,
ceteris in rebus civilis ac clemens: Claud. 12, 1, in semet augendo parcus
atque civilis: Tib. 11, 1, genus vitae civile admodum instituit: Tib. 26, 1,
civilem admodum ac paulo minus quam privatum egit: Calig. 3, 2, domi
forisque civilis: Claud. 1, 4, fuisse creditur civilis animi: Dom. 12, 3,
minime civilis animi: Tit. 6, 1, praefecturam praetorii egit aliquanto
incivilius et violentius. So civilitas for moderation, constitutional conduct;
Claud. 35, 1, primis imperii diebus iactator civilitatis :
Aug. 51, 1,
clementiae civilitatisque eius multa et magna documenta sunt. This use
of civilis is not found before the Aug. period (Ov., Liv.). It is frequent
in Tacitus; e.g. in H. iv 3, describing Vespasian's letter to the senate, he
says: ut princeps loquebatur, civilia de se et rei publicae egregia.

litium series: the very rare pl. series occurs earlier in the same phrase
in Vell. Pat. ii 118, simulantes fictas litium series.

excreverant: excrescere is not found in class. Lat.; Suetonius uses it
in Galb. 21 of a morbid excrescence on the body.

intercapedine: Fest. p. 111 M., intercapedo, tempus interceptum, сит
scilicet mora est ad capiendum. Cf. Aug. 38, 3, post longam intercapedinem
reducto more travectionis: Plin. Εp. iv 9, 11, dicentis calor.. continuatione
servatur, intercapedine et quasi remissione languescit: Cic. Fin. i 18, 61,
in eorum vita nulla est miseriae intercapedo: Cic. Fam. xvi 21, non paenitebat intercapedinem scribendi ("a break in our correspondence") fecisse.
The law courts had been suspended at Rome during the turmoil of civil
strife in 69-70, and the rights of property must have been ruthlessly
ignored in the armed violence which prevailed.

sorte elegit: Tac. H. iv 40, tum sorte ducti per quos redderentur bello
rapta (Tacitus mentions this among the measures passed by the senate
before the return of Vespasian). These special commissioners would be
reciperatores (see on c. 3), and reciperatores were usually chosen by lot by
the praetor urbanus when the case was between cives, by the praetor
peregrinus when the case was between a civis and a peregrinus.

iudicia centumviralia: it is doubtful whether the centumviral court
is to be traced back to Servius Tullius or was established after the time
(?241 B.C.) when the number of tribes was raised to 35. Festus says that
the centumviri were nominated by the praetor, three from each of the
35 tribes. At some time under the early Empire the number was raised
to 180, four panels of 45, each of which might hear separate cases, or two
might sit together, or the whole four in important trials. The decemviri
stlitibus iudicandis seem to have controlled the court; later, ex-quaestors;
and finally Augustus reinstated the decemviri, acting under the superintendence of the praetor, who was styled hastarius or ad hastas, because the
hasta as the symbol of dominium or ownership was planted in the ground
before the place where the court was sitting. The centumviri dealt with
questions of status, inheritance, dominium ex iure Quiritium, iura in re
aliena such as rights of way, usufruct, etc.
They originally sat in the
Forum, but under the Empire in the Basilica Iulia. Most of the speeches
of the younger Pliny were delivered in this court.

vix suffectura aetas: cf. Cod. Iust. iii 1, 13, properandum nobis
visum est, ne lites fiant paene immortales et vitae hominum modum
excedant. Justinian introduced various changes in legal procedure, to
ensure that justice be administered in a reasonable time. Complaints of
the law's delays are frequent in Latin writers. Martial (vii 65) refers to
a case dragging on for 20 years: Lis te bis decimae numerantem frigora
brumae | conterit una tribus, Gargiliane, foris; cf. Juv. xvi 42, Expectandus
erit qui lites incohet annus | totius populi. Sed tum quoque mille ferenda |
taedia, mille morae. Suetonius tells of ordinances of Augustus (Aug. 32),
Claudius (Claud. 23), and Galba (Galb. 14, 3) to increase the number of
days available for legal business. For a discussion of the number of these
dies iudiciarii (opp. to dies feriati) see the article "Actus rerum” in Pauly-Wissowa, i 331 sqq.
ut

extra ordinem diiudicarent: these commissioners were empowered to
take the most pressing cases first, so that each case had not to wait its
turn for a prolonged hearing before the centumviri. For “extra ordinem”
cf. Tac. A. xiii 51, edixit
Romae praetor, per provincias qui pro
praetore aut consule essent iura adversus publicanos extra ordinem redderent: Sen. Ep. 106, 2, dubitavi utrum differrem te an ius tibi extra
ordinem dicerem. A defendant whose case could claim precedence was
called extraordinarius reus (Cic. Fam. viii 8). Under the Roman legal
system of formulae (Vitell. 7, 2, n.) there were certain cases which the
praetor himself decided without sending them to a iudex. In such cases
the praetor was said extra ordinem cognoscere, and the proceedings were
termed extra ordinem cognitiones, iudicia, or actiones. See also on
Dom. 8, 1.

auctor senatui fuit decernendi: Vespasian frequently attended the
meetings of the senate and consulted them on his proposals; Dio lxvi 10,
ἔς τε τὸ συνέδριον διὰ παντὸς ἐφοίτα καὶ περὶ πάντων αὐτοῖς ἐπεκοίνου. A special
ius referendi (ad senatum) was granted to Augustus in 23 B.C., giving him
the right of making the first relatio at each meeting of the senate (Dio liii
32), and subsequent emperors had the same privilege; cf. the Sc. de imperio
Vespasiani (Bruns, Fontes p. 202), utique ei senatum habere, relationem
facere, remittere, senatus consulta per relationem discessionemque facere
liceat. Later we read of the emperors making 4 or 5 relationes before
the ordinary business of the senate (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 898). At first
they made them in person, but more usually they sent them in the form of
letters (litterae, epistulae) or speeches (orationes) to be read by the consuls
or quaestors. Sometimes Titus read Vespasian's speeches in the senate;
see Tit. 6, 1.
ut.

ancilla haberetur: Vespasian re-enacted with modifications the
senatus consultum Claudianum which is often mentioned by Roman jurists.
The emperor Claudius got this passed by the senate in 52 A.D.; cf. Tac.
A. xii 53, Inter quae refert ad patres de poena feminarum quae servis
coniungerentur; statuiturque, ut ignaro domino ad id prolapsae in servitute,
sin consensisset pro libertis haberentur. See also Gaius Inst. i 84-91 on
which Poste says: "The Sc. Claudianum introduced some special enactments respecting the intercourse of freewomen with slaves, which, however,
were subsequently abolished. (a) If a freewoman had intercourse with a
slave with the consent of his proprietor she retained her freedom, though
degraded to the class of a freedwoman, but her issue was the slave of the
proprietor. The slavery of this issue was abolished by Hadrian. (b) If
a freewoman persisted in intercourse with the slave of another person
against the will and in spite of the prohibition of the proprietor, after
three denunciations on his part she was awarded to him by the magistrate
as a slave, and her issue, whether born before or after the adjudication,
became slaves of the same person, who also acquired her estate by a species
of universal succession. This terroristic law, which, from the minuteness
with which the details are developed (Paulus 2, 21), appears to have been
often applied, was not abrogated till the time of Justinian, Inst. 3, 12, 1.
(c) If a freeman had intercourse with a slave whom he supposed to be
free, her male children were born into freedom. This relief of error was
abolished by Vespasian as anomalous (inelegans, Gaius § 85)." Vespasian
in this last case declared that the offspring, male or female, should be
slaves and the property of the mother's owner.

filiorum familiarum: a filius- or filia-familias was a male or female
descendant in the power (potestas) of a pater-familias. On the legal
position of filii familiarum see Roby, Rom. Priv. Law i '64 sqq. Their
position was in some respects similar to that of slaves. In law they had
no property; their father might allow them a peculium, but this was like
a slave's peculium which legally was the master's property; cf. Suet.
Tib. 15 (when Tiberius aged 44 was adopted as a son by Augustus in
2 A.D.), Nec quicquam postea pro patre familias egit aut ius, quod amiserat,
ex ulla parte retinuit. Nam neque donavit neque manumisit, ne hereditatem
quidem aut legata percepit ulla aliter quam ut peculio referret accepta
(i.e. to place them to the credit of the peculium which he held with the
permission of Augustus).

exigendi crediti ius: Vespasian was only re-enacting, after the
confusion of the civil wars, a measure of Claudius to stop money-lenders
advancing money to youths on the post-obit system by which either the
capital plus the interest, or the capital, was to be paid up after the
father's death; cf. Tac. A. xi 13, lege lata saevitiam creditorum coercuit
ne in mortem parentum pecunias filiis familiarum faenori darent. The
Roman jurists mention a decree of the senate dealing with a usurer of
this kind named Macedo; cf. Ulp. Dig. xiv 6, 1, Verba senatus consulti
Macedoniani haec sunt: “Cum inter ceteras sceleris causas Macedo, quas
illi natura administrabat, etiam aes alienum adhibuisset, et saepe materiam
peccandi malis moribus praestaret, qui pecuniam, ne quid amplius diceretur,
incertis nominibus (i.e. doubtful payers) crederet: placere, ne cui, qui filio
familias mutuam pecuniam dedisset, etiam post mortem parentis eius, cuius
in potestate fuisset, actio petitioque daretur: ut scirent qui pessimo
exemplo faenerarent, nullius posse filii familias bonum nomen exspectata
patris morte fieri.” (Cf. also Cod. Iust. iv 28). This Sc. Macedonianum
is probably to be identified with that of Vespasian, though some regard
it as that of Claudius; see Bruns, Fontes p. 203. Horace (Sat. i 2, 14)
refers to the lending of money to tirones who had just donned the toga of
manhood: Quinas hic capiti mercedes exsecat atque, | quanto perditior
quisque est, tanto acrius urget; | nomina sectatur modo sumpta veste virili |
sub patribus duris tironum. The Lex Plaetoria (c. 186 B.c.) enacted that
contracts with minores (under 25 years of age) were only legally binding
when entered into in the presence of a curator appointed by the praetor
(Plaut. Rud. 1381, Pseud. 303; Cic. N.D. iii 30, 74: Off. iii 15, 61).

hoc est mortem: Burman, Oudendorp, and others suspect that
these words have got into the text through a gloss on umquam. Lipsius
would omit at least hoc est. See on Dom. 17, 1, quando et quomodo, id est,
lavantemne an cenantem, aggrederentur.

ceteris in rebus
civilis: cf. Dio lxvi 11, τό τε σύμπαν, τῇ προνοίᾳ
τῶν κοινῶν, αὐτοκράτωρ ἐνομίζετο· ἐς δὲ δὴ τἄλλα πάντα κοινὸς καὶ ἰσοδίαιτός
σφισιν ἦν: Eutrop. vii 19, Romae se in imperio moderatissime gessit. For
civilis see on c. 9, 2.

mediocritatem:
=
conditionem mediocrem vel tenuem (Baumg.-Cr.).
Cf. Tac. A. xiv '60, (vulgus) cui minor sapientia et ex mediocritate fortunae
pauciora pericula sunt, where med. fort. means their humble or insignificant
position. Suetonius uses mediocris frequently, but mediocritas in only one
other passage, Aug. 101, 3, excusata rei familiaris mediocritate, i.e. the
small amount of his property was urged as an excuse.

neque ac: this sequence is very exceptional and only post-classical;
cf. Tac. Agr. 10, Apul. Met. iii 3, x 14. neque (nec)
. que (Tib. 11, 5:
51, 2) is Ciceronian (e.g. Fin. i 48, Lael. 104) but rare. neque (nec)
et is common at all periods. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 48.
..

conantes
originem referre: similarly the flatterers of Pallas,
the notorious freedman of Claudius, said that he was "regibus Arcadiae
ortus," i.e. descended from Pallas the mythical ancestor of Evander (Tac.
A. xii 53). The Julian family traced their line back to Venus (Suet.
Iul. 6); Galba claimed descent from Jupiter and Pasiphaë (Galb. 2); the
Vitellii were said to be sprung from Faunus king of the Aborigines and
a goddess Vitellia (Vitell. 1, 2). The fondness of the Romans for such
mythical pedigrees is fully illustrated by Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 120.

conditores Reatinos: there is no definite tradition of the foundation
of Reate (c. 1, 2, n.), but various legends refer it to a remote antiquity
and connect it with the Aborigines and Pelasgi (Dion. Hal. i 14, 15, ii 49;
Varr. L.L. v 53). See Pauly-Wissowa, I.A. 346.
comitem Herculis: presumably at the time when Hercules passed
through Italy on his return from Spain with the captured oxen of Geryon
(Aen. vii '662, viii 201 sqq.). We do not read elsewhere of any companions
of Hercules on that occasion, nor is there any other mention of the
monument on the Via Salaria. Pitiscus follows Lipsius in assuming that
the flatterers of Vespasian gave to this companion of Hercules the name
of Flavus (Xanthus ?) and included him among the founders of Reate
where Vespasian was born. Two of the great Roman families, the Fabii
and Antonii, claimed to be descended from Hercules. On his return
journey from Spain Hercules himself was said to have founded the cities
of Alesia and Nemausus in Gaul. A cult of Hercules at Reate is mentioned in C.I.L. ix 4672, 4673.

Salaria via: this road ran north-east from Rome to Reate in the
Sabine territory and Asculum in Picenum. It was said to have derived its
name from being the route by which salt was conveyed into the interior
of Italy from the salt-pits near Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber. The
Colline gate of Rome from which it started was earlier known as the
Porta Salaria.
adeo nihil,
..
ut: see on c. 8, 2.

triumphi: his joint triumph with Titus for their victories over the
Jews; see c. 8, 1.

merito se plecti: cf. Phaedr. i 31, 13, merito plectimur: Cic. Off. ii 8,
28, iure igitur plectimur: Nep. Att. 11, qui cavit ne qua in re iure
plecteretur.

senex: Vespasian was born in 9 A.D. (c. 2, 1) and the triumph was
celebrated in June, 71. The fact that he was 60 years of age was taken
into account by him in considering his prospects in a conflict with
Vitellius in 69; cf. Tac. H. ii 74, Vespasianus modo in spem erectus,
aliquando adversa reputabat: quis ille dies foret, quo sexaginta aetatis
annos et duos filios iuvenes bello permitteret?

tribuniciam potestatem: on Dec. 22, 69 A.D. the senate decreed to
Vespasian “cuncta principibus solita" (Tac. H. iv 3) which included the
tribunicia potestas (cf. H. i 47, decernitur Othoni tribunicia potestas et
nomen Augusti et omnes principum honores). The position of the Princeps
seems to have rested on (a) the proconsulare imperium, (b) the tribunicia
potestas, (c) a special law investing him with miscellaneous prerogatives
not given to him by (a) and (b); a large part of the lex de imperio conferring these prerogatives on Vespasian is still extant (C.I.L. vi 930,
Newton 2, Bruns Fontes p. 202, Bury Stud. Rom. Emp. c. ii n. D.). The
tribunicia potestas, granted for life, was formally assumed afresh every
year, and the Princeps reckoned the years of his reign as the years of his
tribunician power. It was conferred by a rogatio (following a decree of
the senate) which was brought before the people in the Comitia. An
interval (trinum nundinum) elapsed between the senate's decree and the
Comitia and so the assumption of the tribunicia potestas came some time
after the dies imperii (see on c. 6, 3). This interval in the case of Nero
was 53 days, of Otho 45, of Domitian 17, of Vitellius 12. Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii³ 875, explains our corrupt passage as referring to an unusually
long interval in the case of Vespasian (cf. Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2635). This
explanation is not satisfactory, for though the reading here is uncertain,
the general sense seems clearly to be that Vespasian did not accept the
tribunicia potestas for some time after it was formally conferred upon
him (cf. Vitell. 8, 2, cognomen Germanici delatum ab omnibus cupide
recepit, Augusti distulit, Caesaris in perpetuum recusavit). Bury (op. cit.
p. 377), following Herzog (Röm. Staatsverfassung ii 288 sq.), says:
"Vespasian made no alteration in the constitution of the Principate; but
he attempted to introduce some innovations in practice. He seems to
have laid less stress than his predecessors on the tribunicia potestas, and
to have even intended to discontinue the official counting of the years of
his reign as tribunician years. He seems to have contemplated a return
to the first system of Augustus (27-23 B.C.) which based the position of
the Princeps mainly on the consulate. He was ordinary consul himself
in every year of his reign except two (73 and 78 A.D.), and his son and
consort Titus was generally his colleague." Tacitus does not mention any
delay in Vespasian's receiving the tribunicia potestas, and in a military
diploma of March 6, 70 A.D. (C.I.L. iii 849, Newton 30) we find “Imp.
Vespasianus Caesar August., tribunic. potest., cos. II"; so on a milestone
in Sardinia (C.I.L. x 8005, Newton 125), dating between January and
July, 70 A.D., he is described as “pont. max., tr[ib. po]t., cos. II, i[mp]
desig. III, p.p. (i.e. pater patriae)." Vespasian's tribunicia potestas was
...
reckoned from July 1, 69 A.D. (his dies imperii, c. 6, 3) and not from
Jan. 70, as is shown by a diploma of Dec. 2, 76 (C.I.L. iii p. 853, Newton
35) with tr. p. VIII (not VII).

aut: there is a hiatus between potestatem and patris patriae in all
the principal MSS. except & which has nec patris patriae; some of the
later have et patris or patrisque. Roth suggested aut, which is ably
defended by Alexander (op. cit. p. 10 sq.) who tabulates the connectives,
adversatives, and disjunctives which follow ne
quidem in Suetonius,
and shows that aut is used almost exclusively in cases where nouns in
their various relations are to be brought together (e.g. Vitell. 13, 3, ne in
sacrificio quidem umquam aut itinere ullo temperavit). Hirschfeld and
others would insert statim after potestatem, assuming that it was lost
through haplography; Bücheler statim пес.

patris patriae appellationem: Vespasian does not bear this title in
the diploma of March 6, 70 A.D., though he does on the Sardinian milestone of the same period (see above on tribuniciam potestatem); it is
found in inscriptions of 71 and subsequent years (e.g. diploma of Apr. 5,
71, C.I.L. x 897, Newton 31). The title of pater (or parens) patriae is
applied by Livy to Romulus and Camillus; by Cicero to Marius; Cicero
himself was so saluted in the senate by Catulus (cf. Juv. viii 244, Roma
patrem patriae Ciceronem libera dixit, with Mayor's note). The dictator
Caesar received it by decree shortly before his death. In 2 B.C. the
"senate, knights, and people" named Augustus pater patriae (Mon.
Ancyr. 6, 24: Suet. Aug. 58), and his successors (except Galba, Otho, and
Vitellius) received this title some time after their accession. The first offer
of it was often refused, e.g. by Nero (Ner. 8), Vespasian, and Hadrian
(Spart. Hadr. 6); Tiberius definitely declined it (Tib. 26, 67: Tac. A. i
72, ii 87). Pertinax (192 A.D.) was the first who received the title on his
accession (Capitol. Pert. 5, primus sane omnium ea die qua Augustus est
appellatus etiam patris patriae nomen accepit). Dio (liii 18) says that
though the title might seem to invest the emperors with the patria postestas
over their subjects, yet it was originally only given as an honour and an
admonition (ἔς τε τιμὴν καὶ ἐς παραίνεσιν) that they should love their subjects
as they would their children, and that their subjects should revere them
as they would their fathers (cf. Sen. Clem. i 14, 2). See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii³ 779 sqq.

nam: Kraffert's conjecture iam is needless. nam is used here (as in
c. 14, Tit. 1, Dom. 4, 1, etc.) elliptically, the connecting thought having
to be supplied (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 116). It was not surprising that
Vespasian did not hedge himself about with state and cared little for
triumphs or imperial titles, for he was careless even about taking the
customary precautions to secure an emperor's safety.

consuetudinem scrutandi salutantes: the danger of assassination led
to the introduction of this scrutatio by Augustus when he was "purging”
the senate; cf. Aug. 35, 2, ne admissum quidem tunc quemquam senatorum
nisi solum et praetemptato sinu (i.e. the fold of the toga where weapons
might be concealed). Under Claudius the examination of callers
(salutatores) was very thorough (Claud. 35, 1, salutatoribus scrutatores
semper apposuit, et quidem omnibus et acerbissimos); men, women, and
children were rigorously searched, and the cases for pens and styles
(calamariae et graphiariae thecae) were taken from every man's attendant
or scribe. Senatorial envoys to Septimius Severus on his march to Rome
(193 A.D.) were searched: Spart. Sev. 6, legati senatus excussi ne quid
ferri haberent. We read of scrutatores employed by the Eastern kings:
Justin xxxviii 1, scrutator ab Ariarathe regio more missus. Plutarch
(Dion 19) says that Plato was the only person allowed into the presence
of Dionysius without being searched (ἀδιερεύνητος), and he also tells
(Timol. 15) how when this younger Dionysius was living at Corinth, having
lost the tyranny at Syracuse, some one visited him and jestingly shook out
his robe when he entered his apartment as is customary when persons
approach a tyrant, whereupon Dionysius bade him "do the same when he
went out, that he might not carry off some of the moveables."
omiserat: Dio lx 3, ἡ ἔρευνα ἡ διὰ πάντων ἐπὶ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἐπαύσατο.

amicorum libertatem: cf. (Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, ferebat patienter
amicorum motus, contumeliis eorum, ut erat facetissimus, iocularibus respondens. Tacitus (Dial. 8) describes Vesp. as patientissimus veri. For libertas
in the sense of παρρησία ‘"freedom of speech" cf. Aug. 54, nec ideo libertas
aut contumacia fraudi cuiquam fuit: Ov. Her. 15, 68, hoc mihi libertas, hoc
pia lingua dedit; it is mainly post-Aug., especially frequent in Quintilian
(see Bonnell, Lex. Quintil.), e.g. iii 8, 48, quae in aliis libertas est, in aliis
licentia vocatur: ix 2, 27, quid minus figuratum quam vera libertas?

causidicorum: Eutrop. vii 20, convicia a causidicis et philosophis in se
dicta leniter tulit (Vespasianus). The term causidicus (= causarum actor)
was most frequently used in a contemptuous sense; see Wilkins on Cic.
de or. i 202, non enim causidicum nescio quem neque clamatorem aut
rabulam..conquirimus. The causidicus, like our barristers, was instructed
by a solicitor (pragmaticus), who provided the pleader with "weapons"
(Quintil. xii 3, 4, qui tela agentibus subministrant).
The abusive tactics
and malpractices of Roman pleaders at this period are often referred to;
see Quintil. xii 9, 8 and 10: Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 186.
=

figuras: obliqua dicta, indirect attacks, veiled sarcasms, innuendoes
(ὑπόνοιαι); cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, Sed quid mirum in amicis, cum etiam
causidicorum obliqua dicta, et philosophorum contumaciam contemneret?
Quintilian (ix 1, 14) says that figura (σχήμα) was limited by recent
rhetoricians to cases where aliud simulatur dici quam dicitur; and again
(ix 2, 65): genus... in quo per quandam suspicionem quod non dicimus
accipi volumus, non utique contrarium, ut in εἰρωνείᾳ, sed aliud latens et
auditori quasi inveniendum. Quod iam fere solum schema a nostris
vocatur
...
Eius triplex usus est: unus si dicere palam parum tutum est,
alter si non decet, tertius qui venustatis modo gratia adhibetur, etc. Cf.
Macrob. Sat. vii 3, loedoriam (λοιδορίαν) exprobrationem esse ac directam
contumeliam: scomma (σκῶμμα) enim paene dixerim morsum figuratum,
quia saepe fraude vel urbanitate tegitur, ut aliud sonet, aliud intellegas:
Plut. 631 E, ὀνειδισμὸς γάρ ἐστι τῆς ἁμαρτίας παρεσχηματισμένος τὸ σκῶμμα:
Spart. Sev. 14, damnabantur plerique, cur iocati essent, alii, cur tacuissent, alii, cur pleraque figurata (i.e. with double meanings) dixissent, ut
“ecce imperator vere nominis sui, vere Pertinax, vere Severus.” For
other examples of dicta figurata see Suet. Dom. 10.

philosophorum contumaciam: Vespasian was forced to banish these
Stoic and Cynic philosophers when they fomented sedition: Dio lxvi 13,
ὡς δ' οὖν καὶ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ ἐκ τῶν στωικῶν καλουμένων λόγων προαχθέντες (excitati),
μεθ᾽ ὧν καὶ Δημήτριος ὁ κυνικός, συχνὰ καὶ οὐκ ἐπιτήδεια τοῖς παροῦσι δημοσίᾳ, τῷ
τῆς φιλοσοφίας προσχήματι καταχρώμενοι, διελέγοντο, κἀκ τούτου καὶ ὑποδιέφθειρόν
τινας, ἔπεισεν ὁ Μουκιανὸς τὸν Οὐεσπασιανὸν πάντας τοὺς τοιούτους ἐκ τῆς πόλεως
ἐκβαλεῖν . . καὶ πάντας αὐτίκα τοὺς φιλοσόφους ὁ Οὐεσπασιανός, πλὴν τοῦ Μουσωνίου
(i.e. Musonius Rufus, the Stoic), ἐκ τῆς ῾Ρώμης ἐξέβαλε, τὸν δὲ δὴ Δημήτριον καὶ
τὸν Ὁστιλιανὸν καὶ ἐς νήσους κατέκλεισε. The leader of the Stoic opposition
to Vespasian was Helvidius Priscus (see below c. 15). Philosophers were
again expelled from Rome by Domitian in 93 A.D. (Dom. 10, 3).

Licinium Mucianum: see on c. 6, 4. Tacitus describes his character,
H. i 10: Luxuria industria, comitate adrogantia, malis bonisque artibus
mixtus. Nimiae voluptates, cum vacaret: quotiens expedierat (i.e. when
on service), magnae virtutes. Palam laudares: secreta male audiebant (i.e.
his private life was in bad repute). Sed apud subiectos, apud proximos,
apud collegas variis illecebris potens, et cui expeditius fuerit tradere
imperium quam obtinere. In H. ii 5 Tac. says that if his faults and those
of Vespasian were removed and their virtues were united in one man, such
a man would have made an excellent emperor: egregium principatus
temperamentum, si demptis utriusque vitiis solae virtutes miscerentur. In
an arrogant letter to the senate (H. iv 4) Mucianus boasted that he had
the imperial power in his hands, and made a present of it to Vespasian:
Id vero erga rem publicam superbum, erga principem contumeliosum, quod
in manu sua fuisse imperium donatumque Vespasiano iactabat.

impudicitiae: ‘‘impudicitia de flagitiis contra naturam commissis sive
stupro marium, atque ita opponitur libidinibus et adulteriis” (Baumg.-
Cr.); cf. Iul. 52, 3, et impudicitiae eum et adulteriorum flagrasse infamia:
Aug. 71, 1, infamiam impudicitiae facillime refutavit (though not free
from libidines).
,

hactenus
ut: the use of hactenus.
ut to express a limited
amount or degree occurs also in Ner. 31, 2, domum hactenus comprobavit, ut se diceret quasi hominem tandem habitare coepisse: ib. 34, 1:
40, 4: Gramm. 2; cf. Cic. de or. ii 27, 119, artem quidem et praecepta
dumtaxat hactenus requirunt, ut certis dicendi luminibus ornentur. For
other uses of hactenus in Suet. see on Dom. 16, 2.

retaxare: a compound not found elsewhere. The post-Aug. taxare
(connected with tangere) means (1) to touch sharply (2) to twit or censure
(3) to appraise or value a thing by feeling it, and so, generally, to assess.
For (2) cf. Aug. 4, 2, non tantum ut pistoris, sed etiam ut nummulari
nepotem taxat Augustum: Dom. 10, 43; for (3) cf. Calig. 38, 3, taxato
prius modo summae: Aug. 41, 1, senatorum censum ampliavit ac pro
octingentorum milium summa duodecies sestertium (i.e. 1,200,000 sesterces)
taxavit.
..

clausulam: a correction by Duker of clausulae, the reading of all MSS.
clausula was used for the concluding words of a speech, letter, story,
poem, or play; cf. Aug. 99, 1, (Augustus) percontatus, ecquid eis videretur
mimum vitae commode transegisse, adiecit et clausulam : εἰ δέ τι | ἔχοι καλῶς
τὸ παίγνιον, κρότον δότε, κ.τ.λ.: Ner. 39, 3, Atellanarum histrio . in novissima clausula "Orcus vobis ducit pedes” senatum gestu notarat: Cic.
de or. ii 240, a te ipso ficta narratio; addidisti clausulam: Val. Max. v
10, 2, hanc adiciendo clausulam (orationi).

vir sum: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, namque Licinium Mucianum, quo
adiutore ad imperium provenerat, fiducia meritorum insolentem flectebat,
adhibito aliquo utrique familiari, id unum dicens: “nosti me virum esse.''
Vespasian used vir as the opposite of impudicus or muliebria passus; cf.
Verg. E. iii 7, parcius ista viris tamen obicienda memento (Damoetas
warns the debauched Menalcas not to bring charges of theft against him).

Salvium Liberalem: C. Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus, four times
quinquennalis of Urbs Salvia in Picenum and patronus of the same colonia,
was admitted to the senate by Vespasian and Titus when censors (see on
c. 9, 2) at first inter tribunicios and later inter praetorios. His distinctions
are given in C.I.L. ix 5533 (Dessau 1011): [C. Salv]io C. f. Vel. Liberali
[Nonio] Basso cos., procos. provin[ciae Macedoniae, legato Augustorum
[iuridi]c. Britann., legato leg. V Maced., [fratri A]rvali, allecto ab divo
Vespasiano [et divo Ti]to inter tribunicios, ab isdem [allecto] inter praetorios, quinq. IIII, p.c. Hic sorte [procos. fac]tus provinciae Asiae se
excusavit. He was famous as an eloquent pleader at Rome. Under
Domitian he was brought to trial (Plin. Ep. iii 9, 23) and probably
banished (relegatus), but in the reign of Trajan we find him defending
Marius Priscus, governor of Africa, who was accused by Pliny and Tacitus
(Plin. Ep. ii 11, 17, dixit pro Mario Salvius Liberalis, vir subtilis, dispositus, acer, disertus) and in the same year (100 A.D.) he also appeared
for Caecilius Classicus who was indicted by the provincials of Baetica in
Spain, their case being conducted by Pliny (Ep. iii 9, 36).

quid ad Caesarem, si
habet?: an example of the causidicorum
figurae mentioned above, the implication being that the avaricious Vespasian
might wish to have Hipparchus unjustly condemned in order to seize his
vast wealth. For the formula “quid (sc. attinet) ad?'' cf. Plaut. Men. 722,
quid id ad me?: Cic. Verr. ii 45, 116, quid id ad praetorem uter possessor
sit?

Hipparchus: this may have been (Ti. Claudius) Hipparchus (falsely
called Plutarchus by Suidas s.v. Ηρώδης). He was condemned for treason
and his property was confiscated (Philostrat. vit. soph. ii 1 p. 56 Kayser;
cf. C.I.A. iii 38, τὰ Ἱππάρχου χωρία τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ φίσκου πραθέντα).
His son
was Ti. Cl. Atticus Herodes, consul under Trajan and again under Hadrian.

Demetrium Cynicum: this antimonarchical champion of Cynic independence was banished to an island by Vespasian in 71 (Dio lxvi 13).
He had been equally defiant of Nero; Epictetus (Dissert. i 25, 22) cites
him as saying to Nero: ἀπειλεῖς μοι θάνατον, σοὶ δ᾽ ἡ φύσις (Tu mihi mortem
minitaris, natura tibi). Caligula had tried to win him over by an offer
of 200,000 sesterces, which was rejected with scorn (Sen. Ben. vii 11).
Tacitus mentions him in A. xvi 34 as being present during the last hours
of the doomed Thrasea Paetus (66 A.D.) and discussing with him the
immortality of the soul; again in H. iv 40 as incurring ill-repute for
defending Egnatius Celer who was accused by the Stoic Musonius Rufus
in 70 A.D. Seneca bestows enthusiastic praise on his friend Demetrius
('Demetrius noster," Dial. i 3, 3; Ep. 20,9; 62, 3; 67, 14; 91, 19);
in Ben. vii 8 he says "Huic non dubito quin providentia et talem vitam
et talem dicendi facultatem dederit, ne aut exemplum saeculo nostro aut
convicium deesset.” Philostratus in his fantastic Life of Apollonius of
Tyana says that Demetrius (whom he describes as ἀνὴρ συνειληφὼς πᾶν τὸ
ἐν Κυνικῇ κράτος) was a friend and would-be disciple of Apollonius, whom.
he met at Corinth (iv 25) and later at Athens (v 19). He also mentions
that Tigellinus had Demetrius banished from Rome under Nero (iv 42);
that Apollonius recommended Demetrius to Titus at Antioch to teach
him how to rule (vi 31); and that Demetrius was living at Puteoli in the
reign of Domitian (vii 10).

ἀνέσταν.

oblatrantem: this compound is used (with dat., acc., or absol.) in
post-Aug. writers to describe snarling abuse; e.g. Sil. Ital. viii 249,
infima dum vulgi fovet, oblatratque senatum: Sen. Ira iii 43, quid illum

story about Demetrius differently. He says that when Demetrius, even
after being sentenced to exile, kept on provoking the emperor by insults,
Vespasian sent a message to him to say that even though Demetrius courted
death he would not put to death a mere barking dog: Σὺ μὲν πάντα ποιεῖς
ἵνα σε ἀποκτείνω, ἐγὼ δὲ κύνα ὑλακτοῦντα οὐ φονεύω.

ex ministris, quibus officium admittendi

servi ab admissione, or ab officiis et admissione, and in later times

Helvidio Prisco: Tacitus (H. iv 5) sketches the character of this
remarkable man. In his youth he had devoted himself to the study of
the Stoic philosophy, “non ut plerique, ut nomine magnifico segne otium
velaret, sed quo firmior adversus fortuita rem publicam capesseret civis,
senator, maritus, gener, amicus, cunctis vitae officiis aequabilis, opum contemptor, recti pervicax, constans adversus metus. Erant quibus adpetentior
famae videretur, quando etiam sapientibus cupido gloriae novissima
exuitur.'" He married Fannia, daughter of Thrasea Paetus (cf. Plin.
2F2
Ep. vii 19), and like his father-in-law cherished vain republican ideals and
celebrated the birthdays of Brutus and Cassius (Juv. v 36). Thrasea was
put to death by Nero, and Priscus was banished (66 A.D.) but returned
under Galba and carried on a bitter warfare with Eprius Marcellus the
accuser of Thrasea (Tac. H. iv 6-9). By his meaningless and persistent
defiance of Vespasian, who in his eyes was as bad as Nero, he drove the
emperor into ordering first his banishment and shortly afterwards (in 73)
his execution. Dio (lxvi 12) attributes Vespasian's hatred of him to his
revolutionary denunciations of imperial power: ὅτι ταραχώδης τε ἦν, καὶ τῷ
ὄχλῳ προσέκειτο, βασιλείας τε ἀεὶ κατηγόρει, καὶ δημοκρατίαν ἐπῄνει, καὶ ἔπραττεν
ἀκόλουθα τούτοις, καὶ συνίστη τινάς, ὥσπερ που φιλοσοφίας ἔργον ὂν τό τε τοὺς
κρατοῦντας προπηλακίζειν, καὶ τὸ τὰ πλήθη ταράττειν, τό τε τὰ καθεστηκότα συγχεῖν,
καὶ τὸ νεώτερα αὐτοῖς πράγματα ἐπεισάγειν.

relegatum: we are not told what form his banishment took; he may
have been sent to an island. When first banished by Nero in 66, he went
to Apollonia in Macedonia. relegatio was a milder penalty than exilium
and did not necessarily involve a loss of civil or personal rights.
were two forms of it: (1) the condemned person was forbidden to live at
Rome, or at any other specified place; (2) he was compelled to live on an
island or within some other limited area. Either form might be temporary
or permanent. The relegatus retained his civitas, and forfeiture of his
property, either total or partial, could only be directed by the judge in
cases of perpetua relegatio (Ulp. Dig. xlviii 22, 7, etc.). See also on
Tit. 8, 5, in asperrimas insularum avehi. In Plin. Ep. vii 19 and Tac. H. i 3
(contrast Ann. xvi 35) exilium is loosely used of Priscus' banishment.

Dio (lxvi 2) says that it was Mucianus who set the example and encouraged Vespasian in exacting money for the treasury, his maxim being that
money forms the sinews of empire (νεῦρα τῆς ἡγεμονίας τὰ χρήματα).
Modern historians take the view that Vespasian incurred undeserved
odium for avaritia through his statesmanlike measures to put the
shattered finances of the empire on a sound footing: see Duruy, Histoire
des Romains iv² 653 sqq.: Schiller, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i 514 sqq.:
Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. 378 sqq.

non contentus
revocasse: Dio (lxvi 8) says that Vespasian at
Alexandria renewed taxes which had been dropped, increased existing taxes,
and introduced fresh ones: πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τέλη (vectigalia), τὰ μέν τινα
ἐκλελειμμένα ἀνενεώσατο, τὰ δὲ καὶ νομιζόμενα προσεπηύξησε, καινά τε ἕτερα
προσκατεστήσατο. Dio adds that he adopted the same course later in the
rest of the subject territory, in Italy, and in Rome itself. Cf. von
Domaszewski, Gesch. röm. Kaiser ii³ 149.

omissa sub Galba vectigalia: the only tax which we know was abolished
by Galba was one of 24 per cent., quadrage(n)suma, of an unspecified
nature (Schiller, op. cit. i 368); cf. the coins of Galba with the words
quadragensuma remissa; quadragens, remissae; xxxx remissae (Eckhel, vi
p. 296). Hofstee (on Galb. 15) thinks that this tax was the quadragesima
Galliarum (see on Vesp. 1, 2), which Galba abolished as a reward to the
Gauls who had supported Vindex. Tacitus (H. i 51) mentions that Galba
remitted of the tribute paid by the Gauls. Under the head of vectigalia
were included decumae, tithes for the occupation of state-domains in Italy
or the provinces; scriptura for grazing cattle on public pastures; customsduties (portoria); 5 per cent. on manumissions and inheritances (vicesima
manumissionum et hereditatum); 4 per cent. on the sale of slaves (quinta
et vicesima mancipiorum venalium); 1 per cent. on sales of other kinds
(centesima rerum venalium); etc.

nova addidisse: e.g. the vectigal urinae (c. 23, 3) and the fiscus
Iudaicus (Dom. 12, 2).

tributa provinciis: tribute paid by the provinces was of different
kinds: (a) decumae, tithes of the produce of the land; (b) stipendium, a
tax of fixed amount, either a land tax (tributum soli) or a poll tax
(tributum capitis); (c) annona, the supply of corn, etc., either for the
officials and army of occupation (annona militaris) or for Rome (annona
civica), this latter coming from Africa and Egypt. The fiscus Alexandrinus,
assigned to Vespasian's reign, was probably connected with this corn-supply; see Hirschfeld, Verwaltungsb. 370.

negotiationes vel privato pudendas: the locus classicus for Roman
views on trades, etc., unbecoming a gentleman is Cic. Off. i 42, where
quaestus liberales are distinguished from quaestus inliberales et sordidi,
the latter including the occupations of faeneratores, portitores, mercenarii,
opifices, and all retail traders, “sordidi etiam putandi qui mercantur a
mercatoribus quod statim vendant; nihil enim proficiant, nisi admodum
mentiantur, nec vero est quicquam turpius vanitate (misrepresentation).'"
The only honourable occupation for senators was husbandry (agri cultura).
Vespasian had trading experience before he became emperor; see c. 4, 3.

exercuit: "carried on”; cf. Aug. 4, 2, modo unguentariam tabernam
modo pistrinum exercuisse: Vitell. 2, 1, Antiochi
furnariam exercentis
filia: Gramm. 23, 2, cum et officinas promercalium vestium exerceret. See
also on Vesp. 1, 3, faenus exercuit.
=

distraheret:
divenderet. This special use of distrahere (rem in
venditione) “to sell piecemeal" is found first in Tac. A. vi 17, copiam
vendendi secuta vilitate aegrius distrahebant (agros); cf. Suet. Calig.
...
39, 2, cui instrumento ("furniture'') distrahendo nihil non fraudis ac
lenocinii (“cajolery") adhibuit. In later writers distrahere was used
simply in the sense of vendere, e.g. Apul. Met. xi 28, veste mea quamvis
parvulo distracta, sufficientem conrasi summulam.

§ 2. honores
absolutiones venditare: Dio (lxvi 14) says this
trafficking was carried on through Caenis (see c. 3) Vespasian's concubine:
Πλεῖστόν τε ... ἴσχυσε (ἡ Καινίς), καὶ πλοῦτον ἀμύθητον ἤθροισεν, ὥστε καὶ νομισθῆναι ὅτι δι' αὐτῆς ἐκείνης ἐχρηματίζετο. πάμπολλα γὰρ παρὰ πολλῶν ἐλάμβανε, τοῖς
μὲν ἀρχάς, τοῖς δὲ ἐπιτροπείας, στρατείας, ἱερωσύνας, ἤδη δέ τισι καὶ ἀποφάσεις αὐτοῦ
(responsa principis) πιπράσκουσα. ἀπέκτεινε μὲν γὰρ ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς χρημάτων
ἕνεκεν οὐδένα, ἔσωσε δὲ πολλοὺς τῶν διδόντων. καὶ ἡ μὲν λαμβάνουσα ἐκείνη ἦν,
ὑπωπτεύετο δὲ ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἑκὼν αὐτῇ ἐπιτρέπειν τοῦτο ποιεῖν, ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων ὧν
ἔπραττεν.

procuratorum: these would be more especially the procuratores Caesaris
who managed the finances in the imperial provinces, and also those in
charge of the imperial fiscus at Rome; the title procurator was, however,
applied to a vast multitude of officials under the Empire (see Daremberg-Saglio, iv 662 sqq.; Hirschfeld, 410 sqq.).

pro spongiis uti: with this has been compared a saying of the Cynic
Diogenes; when he was asked how Dionysius (the younger, tyrant of
Syracuse) used his friends, he said, "Like bags; those which are full he
hangs up, and those which are empty he throws away" (Diog. Laert. vi 2, 6,
᾿Ερωτηθεὶς πῶς χρῆται Διονύσιος τοῖς φίλοις; ἔφη, ὡς θυλάκοις, τοὺς μὲν πλήρεις
κρημνῶν, τοὺς δὲ κενοὺς ῥίπτων). The process of making peculators of public
money disgorge (in the literal sense) their plunder is described by Demos
in Aristoph. Eq. 1145 sqq., τηρῶ γὰρ ἑκάστοτ᾽ αὐ- | τοὺς οὐδὲ δοκῶν ὁρᾶν |
κλέπτοντας· ἔπειτ᾿ ἀναγ- | κάζω πάλιν ἐξεμεῖν | ἅττ᾽ ἂν κεκλόφωσί μου | κημῷ
καταμηλῶν.

exprimeret umentes: for the squeezing of moisture out of sponges
cf. Plaut. Rud. 1008, Iam ego te hic, itidem quasi peniculus (= spongia)
novos exurgeri solet, | ni hunc amittis, exurgebo quidquid umoris est tibi.
Martial (xiii 47) compares the swelling of bread in milk to a sponge
absorbing water: Picentina Ceres (i.e. bread of Picenum) niveo sic nectare
crescit, | ut levis accepta spongia turget aqua.

§ 3. negata gratuita libertate: this herdsman had no savings (peculium)
wherewith to buy his freedom (cf. Sen. Ep. 80, peculium suum, quod
comparaverunt ventre fraudato, pro capite numerant); so he had to fear
the fate which, according to Plutarch (Cato 4), befell the age-worn herdsmen and other slaves of the elder Cato, viz. of being sold for a trifle as
useless encumbrances, a practice which Plut. strongly condemns.
buying of freedom by farmslaves is referred to in Verg. E. i 32; cf. also
Tac. A. xiv 42, Pedanium Secundum servus ipsius interfecit, seu negata
libertate cui pretium pepigerat, etc.
The

quam imperium adeptum orabat: orare with two accusatives is not
class., unless the acc. of the thing is a neut. pron. (Kühner-Stegmann, i
299). See on “flagitassent,” Vitell. 14, 2.

vulpem pilum mutare non mores: cf. Paul. Diac. (Migne 20 col. 715)
Sed vulpecula fuit semper fraudibus studens: ingenium suum mutare
nescit. The Greeks had the same proverb of the wolf: ὁ λύκος τὴν τρίχα,
οὐ τὴν γνώμην ἀλλάττει. Otto (Sprichwörter der Röm.) gives as the German
proverb "Der Fuchs wechselt den Balg und bleibt ein Schalk." Cf. also
Pindar, Ol. x 20 : τὸ γὰρ ἐμφυὲς οὔτ᾽ αἴθων ἀλώπηξ | οὔτ᾽ ἐρίβρομοι λέοντες διαλλάξαιντο ἦθος. A. A. Howard (Harv. Stud. x 28) suggests that there may
have been some fable in the style and metre (iambic senarii) of Phaedrus in
which were the words [Fabula haec] Vulpem pilum mutare non mores
[docet], or in a direct form Vulpes pilum mutare non mores [potest].

manubias: in ordinary speech, especially under the Empire, manubiae
was often a mere synonym of praeda either in the sense of booty taken
in war, or in the figurative sense of spoil or plunder of any kind. In the
latter sense Suet. uses it also in Calig. 41, 1, ne quod non manubiarum
genus experiretur, lupanar in Palatio constituit: Ner. 38, 3, ne non hinc
(i.e. from the burning of Rome) quoque quantum posset praedae et manubiarum invaderet. When used of booty taken in war, manubiae and praeda
were originally distinct. Gellius (xiii 25, 26) says that manubiae meant
money obtained from the sale of booty (praeda): nam praeda dicitur
corpora ipsa rerum quae capta sunt, manubiae vero appellatae sunt pecunia
a quaestore ex venditione praedae redacta. More probably, however,
Asconius (on Cic. Verr. ii 1, 154) is right in saying that manubiae meant
the general's share of the praeda: Manubiae sunt praeda imperatoris pro
portione de hostibus capta. The booty was divided between the Roman
treasury, the soldiers, and the general. The general usually devoted his
share to public buildings; e.g. Suet. Iul. 26, 2, Forum de manubiis incohavit: Tib. 20, Dedicavit et Concordiae aedem, item Pollucis et Castoris
... de manubiis: Aug. 30, 1, vias triumphalibus viris ex manubiali pecunia
sternendas distribuit. See Daremberg-Saglio, iii 1582.

inopia: for the combination of two or more
necessitate compulsum
ablatives in Suet. see App. i. § 3. D. f.

aerarii fiscique: fiscus originally denoted a basket in which money was
stored in the public treasury, as opposed to cista a private money-chest.
Under the principate the title fiscus or fiscus Caesaris (see on Vitell. 2, 2)
was given to the emperor's own treasury or privy purse, supplied mainly
by the revenues from the imperial provinces, certain dues from the
senatorial provinces, the confiscated goods of condemned criminals (bona
damnatorum) and lapsed inheritances (bona vacantia); out of it were met
the costs of provincial administration, the army and navy, the corn-supply,
etc. Distinct from the fiscus was the aerarium (or aerarium Saturni from
its old office in the temple of Saturn in the Forum); this was the public
treasury, which in theory was controlled by the senate but in practice by
the emperor (Dio liii 16, λόγῳ μὲν γὰρ τὰ δημόσια ἀπὸ τῶν ἐκείνου ἀπεκέκριτο,
ἔργῳ δὲ καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὴν γνώμην αὐτοῦ ἀνηλίσκετο). The aerarium paid for
public worship, public festivals, public buildings, roads, etc. There was a
third treasury, the aerarium militare which supplied army pensions; it was
instituted by Augustus and received the imposts on inheritances (vicesima
hereditatum) and on sales (centesima rerum venalium). See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii3 998 sqq.
=

quadringenties milies: sc. centena milia sestertium, 40,000,000,000
sesterces, about £340,000,000. Budaeus would reduce this colossal sum by
reading quadragies, which is approved by Oudendorp and others. Mommsen
(op. cit. ii³ 1010) also suspects some corruption in the figures. Humbert
(Les Finances chez les Romains i 211, 287) holds that this vast amount was
not a capital debt but an annual deficit in the revenue required to meet
the necessary expenses of the State. On the other hand, Marquardt
(Staatsv. ii² 297) regards it not as an annual revenue but as a sum required
once for all to stabilize the finances: "Eine jährliche Einnahme scheint
auch hier nicht gemeint zu sein, da der ganze Schatz, den Tiberius nach
einer habsüchtigen Regierung zurückliess, nur 2700 Mill. HS betrug (Suet.
Calig. 37), sondern eine Summe, die ein für allemal nöthig war, um die
Finanzen zu reguliren." Schiller (l.c.) summarizes the calculations on
which Vesp. based his estimate: "Natürlich war hierunter nicht nur der
laufende Bedarf und die Ansammlung eines Staatsschatzes mit gerechnet,
sondern namentlich die kostspieligen Bauherstellungen von Tempeln und
öffentlichen Bauten, die Ergänzung der öffentlichen Dienerschaft, die
enormen Ausgaben für Magazin- und Fuhrwesen, welches für die Getreideversorgung Italiens nötig war, aber auch die grossen Summen, welche für
militärische Zwecke, Strassen-, Festungs- und Flottenbauten, Verabscheidung und Neuerrichtung von Legionen aufzuwenden waren." See
also Herzog, Röm. Staatsverfassung ii 296.

ut res p. stare posset: for this use of stare (opp. to cadere, concidere,
ruere, corruere) cf. Oth. 5, 1, neque enim dissimulabat, nisi principem se
stare non posse, nihilque referre ab hoste in acie an in Foro sub creditoribus
caderet: Cic. Cat. ii 10, 21, qui in vetere aere alieno vacillant
si
stare non possunt, corruant: Cic. Phil. ii 10, quae si valuissent, res publica
staret, tu tuis flagitiis concidisses: Liv. xxiii 48, nisi fide staret res
publica, opibus non staturam (i.e. if the State were not supported by
credit, it would not be able to support itself by its present resources).

quando: apart from the indef. si quando (4 instances) Suetonius uses
quando in a temporal sense only twice: Galb. 15, 1 (as a conjunction),
Dom. 17, 1 (as an interrog. adv.). He uses it 15 times (excluding
quotations) in a causal sense; 10 times with the subjunctive, 5 times with
the indicative. This causal sense is frequent in Livy; otherwise mostly
poet. and post-Aug.

male partis optime usus est: cf. the old proverb, Naev. Trag. 54
(Ribb.), male parta male dilabuntur, “ill got, ill spent": Plaut. Poen. 844,
male partum male disperit: Liv. ix, 9, male partam victoriam male perdiderunt. Ausonius (Caes. x) says of Vespasian: Quaerendi adtentus,
moderato commodus usu, | auget nec reprimit Vespasianus opes "Set upor
gathering, in reasonable spending generous, Vespasian increased his wealth,
not straitened it" (H. E. White).

in omne genus liberalissimus: so, too, Augustus ‘liberalitatem
omnibus ordinibus per occasiones frequenter exhibuit'' (Aug. 41, 1). Cf.
the use of liberalitas in Tac. and Suet. (Galb. 15, 1) in the concrete sense
of a gift bestowed by imperial favour.

explevit censum senatorium: under the Republic no property qualification was legally necessary for a senator, but wealth was taken into
consideration in elections to the senate (cf. Willems, Le Sénat i 189 sqq.;
Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 876; Tyrrell and Purser on Cic. Fam. xiii 5).
Augustus made a definite census or property qualification legally necessary.
According to Suet. (Aug. 41), he fixed it first at 800,000 sesterces (double
the qualification of an eques), and later at 1,200,000; he also made up the
amount for those who did not possess it (supplevitque non habentibus).
Dio (liv 17) says he raised it from 400,000 to 1,000,000. Mommsen (i3
498) thinks Dio's statement the more accurate with regard to the higher
figure (1,000,000 not 1,200,000), but considers it improbable that Augustus
had ever fixed the sum so low as 400,000, which would have equalised the
qualifications of senators and equites. Tacitus (A. ii 37) mentions that
Augustus presented Hortensius Hortalus, a grandson of the orator, with
1,000,000 sesterces to enable him to keep up senatorial rank, and Tiberius
gave the same amount to Propertius Celer for the same purpose (A. i 75).
Hadrian's generosity enabled certain bankrupt (decoctores) senators to
resume their position: Spart. Hadr. 7, senatoribus qui non vitio suo
decoxerant, patrimonium pro liberorum modo senatoriae professionis
explevit. For similar aid given by Antoninus Pius see Capitol. Anton.
Pius 9; Fronto ad L. Verum, 6. Other instances in Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10
134 sqq.

quingenis annuis sustentavit: Vespasian was following the example
of Nero in making these annual allowances; cf. Ner. 10, 1, senatorum
nobilissimo cuique, sed a re familiari destituto, annua salaria et quibusdam
quingena constituit: Tac. A. xiii 34, sed nobili familiae honor auctus est
oblatis in singulos annos quingenis sestertiis, quibus Messala paupertatem
innoxiam sustentaret. Aurelio quoque Cottae et Haterio Antonino annuam
pecuniam statuit princeps (Nero), quamvis per luxum avitas opes dissipassent.

per totum orbem
restituit: Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, per omnes terras,
qua ius Romanum est, renovatae urbes cultu egregio. The names of the
cities restored by Vespasian are not recorded. There are only a few inscriptions which mention buildings of his in the provinces, e.g. one at
Seleucia in Syria (C.I.L. iii 6702, Newton, 103) and one at Patara in Lycia
(Le Bas 1265, Newton 14). A considerable number of inscriptions, principally on milestones, show that he constructed roads and bridges throughout the provinces; see Newton p. 57 sqq., Pauly-Wissowa vi 2690.

civitates terrae motu afflictas: we only know that Vespasian restored
the temple of Rhea, Mother of the Gods, at Herculaneum after that town,
together with Pompeii, had been partly destroyed by an earthquake either
in 62 (Tac. 4. xv 22) or '63 (Sen. N.Q. vi 1, 2); cf. C.I.L. x 1406, Newton
100: Imp. Caesar Vespasianus Aug., pontif. max., trib. pot. vii, imp. xvii,
p.p., cos. vii, design. viii, templum Matris Deum, terrae motu conlapsum,
restituit (this was found at Herculaneum in Campania; its date is MarchJune, 76). In 79 an earthquake destroyed three cities in Cyprus; cf.
Euseb.-Hieron. Chron., p. 159 Schoene, Tres civitates Cypri terrae motu
conruerunt. Earthquakes, especially in Asia Minor, occurred with great
frequency in the first two centuries of the Empire; see Friedlaender,
Sitteng. iii¹º 29. Augustus (Mon. Ancyr. vi 4) mentions that he had given
countless gifts (dona innumerabilia) to cities in Italy and the provinces
destroyed by fire and earthquake. In 17 A.D. a great earthquake wrecked
twelve famous cities in Asia Minor and Tiberius gave generous grants to
restore them; cf. A. ii 47: Suet. Tib. 48, 2, Ne provincias quidem liberalitate ulla sublevavit, excepta Asia, disiectis terrae motu civitatibus.
Examples of grants made to cities destroyed by fire are that of 10 million
sesterces to Bononia (Bologna) in 53 A.D. under Claudius (Tac. A. xii 58),
and that of 4 million sesterces to Lugdunum (Lyons) in 65 under Nero
(4. xvi 13).

ingenia
fovit: Augustus had set the example; cf. Aug. 89, 3, ingenia saeculi sui omnibus modis fovit. For ingenia (= homines ingeniosi)
cf. Tac. Agr. 2, monumenta clarissimorum ingeniorum in comitio
urerentur: Sen. Suas. vi 22, candidissimus omnium magnorum ingeniorum aestimator T. Livius: Verg. G. ii 382, praemiaque ingeniis pagos
et compita circum | Thesidae posuere. Among the successors of Vespasian
who fostered the liberal arts were Hadrian (Spart. Hadr. 16), Antoninus
Pius (Capitol. Anton. 11), and Alexander Severus (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 44);
see Dill, Rom. Society from Nero to M. Aurelius p. 148.
fisco: see on c. 16, 3.

Latinis Graecisque rhetoribus: Quintilian was the first to fill the
Chair of Latin Rhetoric endowed by Vespasian at Rome; he may have
held it from 72-92 A.D., the period of his greatest fame being 85-89
(Petersen, Quintil. x, Introd. p. viii). By the middle of the 2nd cent.
not only the large cities but also many of the smaller towns in Italy and
the provinces had such professors appointed by the communities (Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii10 192; Marquardt, Privatl.2 111, Staatsv. ii² 106).
Rhetoric at Rome was originally taught by Greeks and in Greek. There
was a strong conservative prejudice against Latin rhetores teaching in
Latin, and they were sternly discountenanced by an edict of the censors
in 92 B.c. (Gell. xv 11, 2; Suet. Rhet. 1). Gradually, however, from the
time of Cicero's youth they succeeded in establishing themselves, and both
Latin and Greek teachers of rhetoric were numerous at Rome in the
1st cent. of the Empire.

annua: annuum as a subst. (= quod praestatur quotannis or salarium)
is found first in Sen. Ben. i 9, 4, alienae uxori annuum praestat; cf. Suet.
Gramm. 23, quanquam ex schola quadringena annua caperet: Juv. vi 480,
sunt quae tortoribus annua praestent: Plin. Ep. x 40, publici servi annua
accipiunt.
centena: sc. sestertia, 100,000 sesterces, about £850.

poetas: e.g. the poet Saleius Bassus; cf. Tac. Dial. 9, laudavimus
nuper, ut miram et eximiam, Vespasiani libéralitatem, quod quingenta
sestertia Basso donasset. For eulogies and invocations of Vespasian by
poets see Sil. Ital. Pun. iii 594 sqq., Val. Flacc. Arg. i 8 sqq. The
unprofitable nature of poetical pursuits at Rome and the liberality of the
emperors to poets are discussed by Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 234 sqq.

Coae Veneris: this brilliant emendation of the corruptions coevenerit,
coemerit, coemit, is due to Graevius. It is uncertain whether Suetonius is
referring to a picture or a statue. The "Aphrodite Anadyomene" of
Apelles (ft. 336-323 в.с.), the most celebrated of Grecian painters, was
originally in the temple of Aesculapius at Cos, and was brought to Rome
to adorn the temple of Julius Caesar by Augustus, who in return remitted
100 talents of Coan tribute (Strab. xiv p. 657). Pliny (N.H. xxxv 91) says
that when the lower part was injured no one could be found to restore
(reficere) it, and when in course of time the panel of the picture fell into
decay, Nero substituted for it a copy made by Dorotheos (aliam pro ea
substituit Nero Dorothei manu); E. Sellers (The Elder Pliny's Chapters
on the History of Art, p. 128) comments on this: "substituit may be an
exaggeration, as the picture of Apelles seems still to have been in existence
under Vespasian, when Suetonius speaks of its being again restored."
Pliny goes on to mention that Apelles had begun another Aphrodite at
Cos, intending to surpass even the fame of his earlier work, but at his
death no one was found to finish the outlines already traced. Graevius
thought that Suetonius is referring to this incomplete picture. Oudendorp
and Baumg.-Cr. are more probably right in holding that the restoration
mentioned here was of the statue of Venus, by an unknown sculptor,
which was placed by Vesp. in his temple of Peace. Pliny (xxxvi 5) says:
Ignoratur artifex eius quoque Veneris, quam Vespasianus Imperator in
operibus Pacis suae dicavit, antiquorum dignam fama. If this view is
correct, we must assume that the statue came from Cos. Other readings
which have been suggested are scenae (to be taken with artifices), Lipsius;
coronavit, Böttiger.

Colossi: this colossal statue of Nero by Zenodorus was 120 feet in
height, and stood originally in the vestibule of Nero's Aurea Domus (see
on Oth. 7, 1); it was removed by Vespasian to the Via Sacra; later
Hadrian placed it to the N.W. of the Colosseum, where the base is still
preserved. It was converted into a statue of the Sun (Plin. N.H. xxxiv 45),
apparently by Vespasian (see Friedlaender on Mart. Spect. 2, 1, Hic ubi
sidereus propius videt astra colossus). Spartianus (Hadr. 19) says that it
was Hadrian who consecrated it to the Sun after removing the features
of Nero, while Lampridius (Commod. 17) states that Commodus replaced.
the head of Nero by his own. See also Dio lxvi 15, lxxii 22.

congiario: a congiarium (from congius a measure of about 6 pints)
was originally a distribution of free oil or wine among the plebs. Under
the Empire we find it used of a largess of money to the people, while
donativum meant a similar gift to the soldiers; e.g. Ner. 7, 2, populo
congiarium, militi donativum proposuit.
The word was also used in a
general sense for a gift, especially of money, as here and in Iul. 27, 1,
vel invitatos vel sponte ad se commeantes uberrimo congiario prosequebatur; cf. Cic. Att. x 7, 3: Sen. Ep. 29, 5: Quintil. vi 3, 52: Mart. iii
7,2, Centum miselli iam valete quadrantes | anteambulonis congiarium
(= sportula) lassi.

mechanico: mechanicus and machinator are both found answering to
the Gr. μηχανοποιός. According to Daremberg-Saglio (iii 1663) machinatores were Roman citizens, generally military engineers, while the term
mechanici was originally applied to foreigners, slaves or freedmen, mainly
Greeks who brought in with them the designation mechanicus (μηχανικός),
which occurs in ante-class. and post-Aug. writers (first in Lucilius of an
equilibrist, petaurista, who performed by the aid of mechanical appliances;
later of architects and engineers of various kinds).

grandes columnas perducturum: mechanical contrivances for the
conveyance of columns are described in Vitruvius x 2 and illustrated in
Daremberg-Saglio iii 1467.
in Capitolium: for the restitutio Capitolii see c. 8, 5.

plebeculam: Ihm reads plebiculam, which has better support but seems
a doubtful form, perhaps due to a confusion with plebicola. The
diminutive was probably used by Vespasian in a merely pitying way;
but elsewhere it is contemptuous, e.g. Cic. Att. i 16, illa contionalis hirudo
aerarii, misera ac ieiuna plebecula: ib. xvi 8: Hor. Ep. ii 1, 186,
his nam plebecula gaudet: Pers. iv 6. Wilkins, on Hor. l.c., suggests
that Suetonius puts the word in the mouth of Vespasian as "a specimen
of the rough language of the low-born emperor."

pascere: by allowing only manual labour to be used, and so giving
more employment.

ludis: at the games to celebrate the original dedication of this theatre
Augustus met with a slight mishap: Aug. 43, 5, commissione (i.e. at the
opening) ludorum, quibus theatrum Marcelli dedicabat, evenit ut laxatis
sellae curulis compagibus caderet supinus.

Marcelliani theatri: Marcellus, son of Octavia sister of Augustus,
and adopted son of Augustus, died in 23 B.C., at the age of 20; cf. Verg.
Aen. vi 883 sqq., Prop. iii 18. In 44 в.с. Julius Caesar had projected and
laid the foundations of a huge theatre (it afterwards held 10,000) which
Augustus completed and called after Marcellus; cf. Iul. 44, 1, destinabat
..
extruere theatrum summae magnitudinis Tarpeio monti accubans:
Dio xliii 49, θέατρόν τέ τι κατὰ τὸν Πομπήιον (i.e. as Pompey had done)
οἰκοδομῆσαι ἐθελήσας προκατεβάλετο μέν, οὐκ ἐξετέλεσε δέ. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν ὁ
Αὔγουστος μετὰ ταῦτα ἐκποιήσας ἀπὸ Μάρκου Μαρκέλλου τοῦ ἀδελφιδοῦ ἐπωνόμασε:
Mon. Ancyr. 21, Theatrum ad aedem Apollinis in solo magna ex parte a
privatis empto feci, quod sub nomine M. Marcelli generi mei esset: Suet.
Aug. 29, 4, quaedam etiam opera sub nomine alieno . . fecit, ut .. theatrum
Marcelli. The building was so far advanced in 17 B.C. that there was a
performance given in it at the Ludi Saeculares, and it was finished and
dedicated in 13 B.с. (Dio liv 26) or 11 в.с. (Plin. N.H. viii 65). It suffered
damage in 69 A.D. at the storming and burning of the Capitol by the
Vitellians. Martial (x 51, 11) mentions it among the most conspicuous
buildings of Rome. For its subsequent history and the extant remains in
the Via del Teatro di Marcello (between the S.W. end of the Capitoline
and the Tiber) see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 516 sqq.

acroamata: acroāma (ἀκρόαμα) means a thing heard, especially music,
also plays, recitations, entertainments of any kind. The performer or
"artiste” was also called acroama (e.g. Cic. Sest. 116, of an actor: Nep.
Att. 14, of an anagnostes or reader); cf. the description of the dinners of
Augustus, Aug. 74, ad communionem sermonis tacentes vel summissim
fabulantes provocabat, et aut acromata et histriones aut etiam triviales ex
circo ludios (i.e. strolling players from the circus) interponebat ac
frequentius aretalogos (i.e. story-tellers). Pliny, Ep. vi 31, 13, mentions
acroamata at Trajan's dinner-parties. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 337;
Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 176.

Apellae: the MSS. have appellari, apellari, apelli. The reading in
the text is a correction by Bücheler. Apollinari is read in Ed. Rom. ii
and most subsequent editions; Roth and Preud'homme adopt Politian's
Apellari; but nothing is known of any actor named Apollinaris or Apellaris.
Apelles may possibly be the Apelles of Ascalon, a famous tragic actor,
who was at first an intimate friend and favourite of the emperor Caligula
(Dio lix 5), but later, as Suetonius tells us, he had a painful experience
of Caligula's eccentricity: Calig. 33, Inter varios iocos, cum assistens
simulacro Iovis Apellen tragoedum consuluisset uter illi maior videretur,
cunctantem flagellis discidit conlaudans subinde vocem deprecantis quasi
etiam in gemitu praedulcem. Apelles is referred to in Petron. Satyr. 64
as a peerless actor: Quando parem habui nisi unum ("the one and only'")
Apelletem? The difficulty lies in assuming that this Apelles was still
acting in the reign of Vespasian, 30 years after his maltreatment by
Caligula.
quadringenta sestertia: about £3,400.

Terpno: Terpnus was a famous citharoedus who taught Nero to play
upon the cithara and to sing to it (Ner. 20, 1). He was one of those in
the train of Nero on his musical tour to the Greek contests (see Vesp. 4, 4)
and competed unsuccessfully against the emperor (Dio lxiii 8). Apollonius
of Tyana, according to Philostratus (v 7), spoke scornfully of Nero's
doffing the robes of Augustus and Julius in order to don those of a
Terpnus at the festivals in Greece.
Diodoro: Diodorus also was defeated by Nero at the Greek musical
contests. He had the honour of riding with Nero in the triumphal car
when the emperor entered Rome after his "victories" in Greece (Dio lxiii
20).
=
super: praeter; see on c. 24.

coronas aureas: in Ner. 53 we read of the scaenicae coronae which
Nero won by his victories on the stage. The custom of rewarding actors
with golden crowns must have been common in the later days of the
Republic, as Plutarch (Cat. min. 46) says that Cato cut down the expenses
of official theatrical entertainments by giving the players crowns not of
gold but of wild olive like the prizes at Olympia. Varro (L.L. v 178)
mentions "corollae in scaena dari solitae cum placuerant actores," but
does not specify the material. Pliny (N.H. xxxiv 94) states that actors'
crowns of bronze, if dyed with ox-gall, present the appearance of gold.
Sometimes a successful actor was awarded a corollarium, which was a
wreath of bronze leaves silvered or gilded (cf. Plin. N.H. xxi 5: Merrill
on Plin. Ep. vii 24). A golden olive-crown was the prize at the musical
contest (agon) held by Domitian at his Alban villa (cf. Stat. Silv. iii 5,
28, etc.). See Dom. 4, 4.

convivabatur: "gave dinner parties"; cf. Aug. 74, convivabatur
assidue nec umquam nisi recta: Iul. 48, convivatum assidue per provincias:
Dom. 21, convivabatur frequenter ac large, sed paene raptim: Claud. 32,
convivia agitavit et ampla et assidua: Tit. 7, 2, convivia instituit iucunda
magis quam profusa.

recta: sc. cenâ, a regular formal dinner of successive courses (fercula,
lit. 'trays'"). The smallest number of courses was three, viz. the gustatio
(hors d'oeuvres), cena, and secunda mensa (dessert). At times Augustus
had six (Aug. 74) and Juvenal (i 94) mentions fercula septem, these
numbers being made up by subdividing the second of the three old courses
(the cena) into prima cena, altera cena, tertia cena, etc. A cena recta
was opposed to a mere sportula or distribution of portions of food to
clients; cf. Mart. viii 50, 10, promissa est nobis sportula, recta data est.
See on Dom. 7, 1, sportulas publicas sustulit revocata rectarum cenarum
consuetudine.

dapsile: this form of the adv. occurs in Pompon. Atell. 161, verrem
sume dapsile; Naevius (com. 39 R.) has dapsiliter suos amicos alit; Lucilius
(xxx 55 M.) uses the comparative, qui invitavit dapsilius se. The adj.
dapsilis (δαψιλής) is found in Plautus, e.g. Aulul. 167, dotes dapsiles
(dapsilas, Nonius), and in post-Aug. authors. See Neue - Wagener,
Formenlehre ii 150, 687.

macellarios: "market-vendors"; cf. Iul. 26, 2, quae ad epulum pertinerent, quamvis macellariis ablocata ("let out on contract"), etiam
domesticatim apparabat. The subst. is found earlier in Varr. R.R. iii 2, 11;
4, 2. Macellum (μάκελλον) is connected with the Hebr. mikhela, makhela
""enclosure.'" The first macellum at Rome was built in 179 в.с., and was
replaced under Augustus by the macellum Liviae. In order to enforce his
sumptuary laws, Julius Caesar had guards placed to prevent the sale of
forbidden dainties in the macellum (Iul. 43), and Tiberius proposed that
the prices in the macellum should be revised annually by the senate, to
check profiteering, e.g. the sale of mullets (mulli) at 10,000 sesterces apiece
(Tib. 34).

dabat Saturnalibus apophoreta: apophoreta (ἀποφορητά) was the word
used for the presents which guests received at table to take home with
them, especially during the festival of the Saturnalia (Dec. 17-23). The
name is familiar as the title of the 14th book of Martial's Epigrams,
which consists of distichs, like mottoes, to accompany such presents, which
were either cheap (e.g. nuts) or costly (e.g. works of art); in the introductory epigram Martial associates them with the Saturnalia. Augustus
gave these presents; cf. Aug. 75, Saturnalibus, et si quando alias libuisset,
modo munera dividebat, vestem et aurum et argentum, etc. Tiberius sent
Claudius "quadraginta aureos in Saturnalia et Sigillaria” (Claud. 5).
Caligula gave 2,000,000 sesterces "in apophoretis" to the charioteer
Eutychus (Calig. 55). The Schol. on Juv. vi 202 says that apophoreta
were given at weddings: solebant enim antea per nuptias recedentibus
dulcia (sweetmeats or cakes) erogare pro apophoretis.

per Kal. Mart.: = singulis Kalendis Martiis. For the change of constr.
from Saturnalibus to per Kal. Mart. cf. Iul. 16, 1, vi ac per arma: Sall.
Iug. 7, per vim atque insidiis: Tac. H. ii 77, per fastidium ac contumacia.
See also App. i. § 15. d. On the 1st of March, "the New Year's day of
the Roman religious calendar," the matrons celebrated the festival of the
Matronalia in honour of Juno Lucina whose temple on the Esquiline was
dedicated on that day, probably in 379 B.C. (see Warde Fowler, Rom. Fest.
p. 38). Ovid (Fast. iii 229 sqq.) describes the origin and nature of the
festival; cf. Hor. C. iii 8, Martiis caelebs quid agam Kalendis? For the
custom of making presents to women at the Matronalia cf. Juv. ix 53,
munera femineis tractat secreta Kalendis: Plaut. Mil. 690, da mihi, vir,
Kalendis: Tibullus (Lygdamus) iii 1: Mart. v 84 (where Martial describes
the Martiae Kalendae as the women's Saturnalia). See Marquardt,
Staatsv. iii² 571 sq.
cupiditatis infamia: see on c. 16, 1.

§ 2. Alexandrini: Dio (lxvi 8) says that the Alexandrians taunted
Vespasian with being avaricious enough to exact even so petty a sum as
six obols (about 9d.), a taunt to which Vesp. replied by promptly levying
six obols from each of the inhabitants of the city. Dio also says that
they regarded Vesp. as ignorant of how to act like a Caesar (Καισαρεύειν)
i.e. to be prodigally lavish like Nero. The Alexandrians were notorious
for their pungent criticisms of their rulers; cf. Herodian iv 9, 2, πεφύκασι
δέ πως εἶναι φιλοσκώμμονες, καὶ λέγειν εὐστόχως ὑπογραφὰς ἢ παιδιάς, ἀπορριπτοῦντες
ἐς τοὺς ὑπερέχοντας πολλὰ χαρίεντα μὲν αὐτοῖς δοκοῦντα, λυπηρὰ δὲ τοῖς σκωφθεῖσι:
Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 19, itaque loquax et ingeniosa in contumelias praefectorum provincia, in qua etiam qui vitaverunt culpam, non effugerunt
infamiam. For Vespasian's new taxation at Alexandria see on c. 16, 1.
Dio

Cybiosacten: this reading was restored by Torrentius for cybiotanten
of the MSS. Strabo (xvii 796) says that after the expulsion of Ptolemy
Auletes in 58 B.C. the Alexandrians made his daughter Berenice queen,
and as husband for her they brought in from Syria a certain Cybiosactes
(Κυβιοσάκτης τις) who claimed descent from the royal house of Syria;
Berenice, however, murdered him in a few days, οὐ φέρουσα τὸ βάναυσον καὶ
τὸ ἀνελεύθερον (cum eius sordes illiberalitatemque ferre non posset).
(xxxix 57) gives the name of Berenice's husband as Seleucus; it is doubtful whether he was a son or a bastard son of Antiochus X (see Pauly-Wissowa, s.v. Seleukos). Sturz, Dial. Mac. et Alex. 77, explains κυβιοσάκτης
as "salsamentarius, qui salsamenta componit et vendit.”
κύβιον (cybium)
was the flesh of the pelamys, or tunny-fish, cut up into dice-shaped pieces
and salted (Plin. N.H. xxxii 146, 151; Athen. iii 116, 118); σάττειν
properly meant “onus iumento imponere," as is done by itinerant vendors,
and so κυβιοσάκτης is the same as ταριχέμπορος or ταριχοπώλης (Casaubon on
Strab. l.c.). salsamentarii, salt-fish vendors, were held in contempt at
Rome; cf. Auct. ad Herenn. iv 54, Suet. vit. Horat. 1.

Favor: as an actor's name this is found frequently in inscriptions
(Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2078).

archimimus: the director and principal actor in the company (grex)
