which performed a mimus or loosely constructed character-sketch of
common life. These mimi were notorious for their vulgarity and
immorality; see Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 113 sqq. The number of the
company varied with the piece, and female parts were played by women.
The one word mimus is used both for the actor and for the piece. The
term archimimus occurs also in Sen. frag. 36, doctus archimimus, senex iam
decrepitus, cotidie in Capitolio mimum agebat: Porphyr. (on Hor. S. ii 6,
7'2), archimimus iucunde et molliter et saltaret et eloqueretur: Dig. xxxviii
1, 25: C.I.L. iii 7343, etc. The fem. archimima is also found, C.I.L. vi
10107.

personam eius ferens: this seems to be the only passage where we
are told that it was customary for a mask of the deceased to be worn
at his funeral by an actor, though we often hear of the imagines or wax-
2G
masks of distinguished ancestors (see on c. 1, 1) being worn in the funeral
procession (e.g. Polyb. vi 53, Plin. N.H. xxxv 6). In the illustrations
which we have of Etruscan funeral processions the deceased is depicted as
playing an active part, and according to Martha, Art étrusque pp. 417 sqq.,
the deceased was represented in the procession by a mannequin or an actor
(Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1383). In a triumphal procession an actor attired
in all the splendour of the triumphator provided amusement to the populace
by his imitations of the victorious general trampling or dancing(ἐπορχούμενος,
insultans) on his foes (App. Рип. 66).

pompa: the pompa funebris or funeral procession was organised by
the funeral-marshals (dissignatores) after the fashion of the pоmра
circensis or pompa triumphalis. It was headed by musicians (tibicines,
tubicines, siticines, cornicines), followed in the old days by praeficae or
women chanting dirges (naeniae), who were later replaced by choirs of
men. After them came dancers and actors; then the wearers of the
imagines, each attired in the robe of the office held by the ancestor whom
he represented, and driving in a car of state preceded by the appropriate
number of lictors. After them came bearers of crowns, spoils, and other
records of victories and triumphs won by the deceased. The procession
was closed by torch-bearers and lictors with fasces reversed; these pre-.
ceded the bier which in the case of emperors was borne by magistrates
and senators (Suet. Iul. 84, Aug. 100). See Marquardt, Privatl.2 353 sqq.

sestertium centiens: = centiens centena milia sestertium, 10,000,000
sesterces, about £85,000. Nero was buried at a cost of 200,000 sesterces
(Ner. 50).

exclamavit
proicerent: apparently the Romans did not regard as
unseemly at an emperor's funeral such an exhibition of the licence which
had become familiar on the stage. In the later days of the Republic
mimi were allowed great freedom in the way of political allusion (cf. Cic.
Att. xiv 3, populi ἐπισημασίαν et mimorum dicta perscribito). Laberius
revenged himself on the dictator Caesar, for compelling him to act in his
own mimes, by the two famous lines “Porro Quirites! libertatem perdimus''
and "Necesse est multos timeat quem multi timent" (Macrob. Sat. ii 7).
The audience were quick to detect allusions to the alleged effeminacy of
Augustus and the debauchery of Tiberius at Capri (Suet. Aug. 68, Tib. 45).
Caligula buried alive a composer of Atellanae for a double entendre
reflecting on him (Calig. 27). Nero's poisoning of Claudius, his attempt
to drown Agrippina, and likewise the harshness and avarice of Galba
were hinted at upon the stage (Ner. 39, Galb. 13). Helvidius Priscus was
executed by Domitian for making his farce (exodium) entitled “Paris
and Oenone" a satire on the emperor's divorce (Dom. 10, 4). Further
examples are given by Friedlaender (l.c.).

in Tiberim: cf. Tib. 75, 1, morte eius ita laetatus est populus, ut ad
primum nuntium discurrentes “Tiberium in Tiberium!”” clamitarent.
The body of the emperor Elagabalus was thrown into the Tiber (Lamprid.
Heliog. c. 17). See also Vitell. 17, 2.

statura fuit quadrata: quadratus as applied to the build of men or
other animals meant well-proportioned, not too long or too short, and not
too plump or too spare; this is shown by Celsus ii 1, corpus habilissimum
quadratum est, neque gracile neque obesum; nam longa statura, ut in
iuventute decora est, sic matura senectute conficitur, gracile corpus infirmum,
obesum hebes est. Columella (vii 12) says that a dog for guarding a
farmhouse (villaticus canis) should be “quadratus potius quam longus aut
brevis"; while a dog for guarding cattle (pecuarius canis) should possess
a "status longior productiorque
quam brevis aut etiam quadratus.”
The Greek τετράγωνος is used metaph. of those who stand four-square,
well-balanced in body and mind.
•

compactis membris: "with well-knit limbs"; cf. Plin. Ep. vii 24,
compacto corpore et robusto: Pallad. iv 11, 2, (sint boves) cervice torosa
atque compacta.

urbanorum: "wits"; cf. Domitius Marsus (ap. Quintil. vi 3, 105):
Urbanus homo erit, cuius multa bene dicta responsaque erunt; et qui in
sermonibus, circulis, conviviis, item in contionibus, omni denique loco
ridicule commodeque dicet. The opposite of urbanitas is rusticitas:
Quintil. vi 3, 17, urbanitas
. qua quidem significari video sermonem praeferentem in verbis et sono et usu proprium quendam gustum urbis et
sumptam ex conversatione doctorum tacitam eruditionem, denique cui contraria sit rusticitas. Gr. ἀστεῖος opp. to ἄγροικος.
siquidem: see on Dom. 6, 2.

ut in se aliquid diceret: cf. Cic. Phil. ii 17, 42, At vero adhibes ioci
causa magistrum, suffragio tuo et compotorum tuorum rhetorem, cui concessisti ut in te quae vellet diceret, salsum omnino hominem, sed materia
facilis est in te et in tuos dicta dicere. Cicero uses dicta dicere "to utter
witticisms (mots)" also in Planc. 85, de or. ii 244; so dicax (from dico)
"witty." in does not mean "against," but “on” “concerning"; see
Holden on Cic. Off. i 28.

cum ventrem exonerare desieris: the same jest on a person who had
a strained look occurs in Mart. iii 89: Utere lactucis, et mollibus utere
malvis: | nam faciem durum, Phoebe, cacantis habes (cf. id. x 48, 7,
Exoneraturas ventrem mihi villica malvas | attulit).

valitudine prosperrima usus est: but he was gouty, for Dio (lxvi 17)
says that his last illness was not his "accustomed gout" but a fever
(νοσήσας οὐ τῇ ποδάγρᾳ τῇ συνήθει ἀλλὰ πυρετοῖς).
•

fauces defricaret: fricare, fricatio, frictio, and their compounds
are very often used of massage, friction, either dry or with unguents
which are rubbed in; see Thes. Ling. Lat., where abundant instances are
cited from Pliny N.H. and medical writers like Celsus, Serenus Sammonicus,
and Scribonius Largus.
=

ad numerum: certo finitoque numero (Baumg.-Cr.); cf. Cels. ii 14,
neque audiendi sunt qui numero finiunt, quoties aliquis perfricandus sit:
id enim ex viribus hominis colligendum est; et si is perinfirmus est, potest
2G2
satis esse quinquagies, si robustior, potest ducenties esse faciendum; inter
utrumque deinde, prout vires sunt.

sphaeristerio: in the last century of the Republic the Romans played
their games of ball in the open space of the Campus Martius (Hor. Sat. i 6,
126, Sen. Ep. 104), but under the Empire they preferred a closed-in court
for the purpose. These ball-courts formed part of every gymnasium and
were adjuncts of the various public baths at Rome. Private mansions
possessed them, and the younger Pliny had a sphaeristerium (σφαιριστήριον)
close to the baths in both his elaborate country-houses (Plin. Ep. ii 17, 12:
▼6, 27). The players stripped for the game; Pliny mentions an apodyterium or dressing-room in connexion with the sphaeristerium.
inediam unius diei: cf. Cels. vii 7, 4, abstinentia ("fasting'") unius
diei. The curative value of abstinence from food (λιμός, νηστεία, abstinentia,
inedia) is mentioned in the medical writers from Hippocrates on; e.g. Cels.
ii 16, neque ulla res magis adiuvat laborantem quam tempestiva abstinentia.
Hippocrates declared that privation (ἔνδεια) is the mother of health (ὑγιείας
μητήρ). Protracted inedia was a common means of suicide under the
Empire, e.g. in the case of Silius Italicus (Plin. Ep. iii 7); cf. Suet. Aug.
53, 3, inedia mori destinantem . ad vitam revocavit: Tib. 53, 2, mori
inedia destinanti, per vim ore diducto, infulciri cibum iussit.

interponeret: interponere is used in Celsus of introducing at intervals
certain changes of treatment, diet, etc.; e.g. iii 6, poteritque a balneo
etiam pinguius aut dulcius dari vinum; poterit semel aut bis interponi
Graecum salsum.

ordinem vitae: ordo denotes the systematic portioning out of each
day between the successive officia which have to be discharged; cf. Juv. 1
127, ipse dies pulchro distinguitur ordine rerum: Plin. Ep. iii 1 (of the
life of Spurinna), nihil est illo vitae genere distinctius (i.e. better distributed)
parva haec, parva, si non cotidie fiant, ordine quodam ac
velut orbe circumagit. “Ordinare diem” and “disponere diem” were
used for the methodical arrangement of one's day.

tenuit: so [Aur. Vict.] Εpit. 9, Institutum vero uniforme omni imperio
tenuit. Vigilare de nocte publicisque actibus absolutis caros admittere,
dum salutatur calceamenta sumens et regium vestitum. Post autem
negotiis, quaecumque advenissent, auditis exerceri vectatione, deinde
requiescere, postremo ubi lavisset, remissiore animo convivium curabat.

de nocte: "while it was still night." On this temporal use of de
see Kühner-Stegmann, i 498, where de die and de nocte are explained
"vom Tage her, von der Nacht her = noch bei Tage, am hellen Tage,
noch in der Nacht, in der Nacht"; cf. Ter. Ad. 840, Hor. Ep. i 2, 32, ut
iugulent homines, surgunt de nocte latrones.
officiorum: officia here is practically equivalent to "officials," a
meaning which we find more definitely in later Latin; e.g. [Treb. Poll.]
Gall. 17, cum iret ad hortos
omnia Palatina officia sequebantur. The
concrete use of officium appears in the younger Pliny; e.g. Ep. iii 12, erunt
officia antelucana (i.e. callers, salutatores, abroad before dawn), in quae
incidere impune ne Catoni quidem licuit: Pan. 76, ipsius officium (‘suite'')
tam modicum; cf. Juv. x 44, praecedentia longi | agminis officia ('attentive
clients''): Apul. Met. iv 31, marinum obsequium = dii marini obsequentes.
Abstracts like servitium, remigium, ministerium, are often used in a concrete sense; see Draeger, Hist. Synt. i² 22-24.

breviariis: ''summaries," "condensed reports." Seneca (Ep. 39) condemns breviarium as a barbarism: vide, ne plus profutura sit ratio ordinaria
quam haec, quae nunc vulgo breviarium dicitur, olim cum Latine loqueremur,
summarium vocabatur. Suetonius uses it also in Aug. 101, breviarium totius
imperii (called rationarium imperii in Aug. 28, 1): Galb. 12, 3 dispensatori
breviarium rationum offerenti: Gramm. 10, Ateius Sallustium breviario
rerum omnium Romanarum instruxit; cf. Plin. N.H. vii 97, xviii 230, and
the “Breviarium Historiae Romanae" by Eutropius. Cicero (Att. xiii 8,
etc.) uses epitome (ἐπιτομή) for an abridgement.

amicos admittebat: Dio (lxvi 10) describes the accessibility of
Vespasian. The door of his palace in the Sallustine Gardens stood open
all day long; no one was denied admission, senator or plebeian. His
intimate friends were admitted even while he was still in bed. The elder
Pliny used to visit him before dawn: Plin. Ep. iii 5, ante lucem ibat ad
Vespasianum imperatorem, nam ille quoque noctibus utebatur. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. v 31) describes Vespasian, while still at Alexandria,
as engaged on his correspondence long before dawn. Einhard in his Life
of Charlemagne (c. 24) imitates Suetonius very closely: cum calciaretur
et amiciretur, non tantum amicos admittebat, verum etiam, si comes palatii
litem aliquam esse diceret, quae sine eius iussu definiri non posset,
lite cognita sententiam dixit. See Introd. ii ad fin.

calciabat ipse se: persons of rank were usually assisted in their toilet
by numerous attendant slaves (see Marquardt, Privatl. 145); cubicularii
would put on their robes, and calciatores their shoes. Pliny (Ep. iii 16)
mentions the argument used by Arria when imploring the soldiers to allow
her to go on board the ship which was to bear her husband Thrasea Paetus
as a prisoner to Rome: “nempe enim,” inquit, “daturi estis consulari
viro servolos aliquos, quorum e manu cibum capiat, a quibus vestiatur, a
quibus calcietur: omnia sola praestabo.”

amiciebat: the only part of amicio used by the best writers is amictus
(sum).
post decisa
..
..

negotia: cf. Hor. Ep. i 7, 56 sqq., praeconem ...
et ludis et post decisa negotia Campo, a passage which
gaudentem
shows that decidere negotia could be used in the general sense of transacting
or completing any business, and not merely in the limited legal sense of
deciding or settling a case (e.g. Capitol. M. Antonin. Phil. 10, multis praetoriis et consularibus privatis decidenda negotia delegavit): it is in the
latter sense that the words of Suet. are understood in [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9,
quoted above.

gestationi: gestatio, which is a post-Aug. word, was used especially of
taking exercise either by being carried in a litter (lectica) or driving in
a carriage (cf. Galb. 8, 1). The word denoted not merely the exercise
itself but also the part of the grounds of Roman villas where the gestatio
took place (cf. Plin. Ep. ii 17, 13; v 6, 17). Seneca refers to the advantages
of gestatio as a form of exercise; Ep. 15, gestatio et corpus concutit et
In
studio non officit: possis legere, possis dictare, possis loqui, possis audire.
(Claudius even played at dice; Suet. Claud. 33, 2, solitus etiam in gestatione
aleam ludere, ita essedo alveoque adaptatis ne lusus confunderetur.)
Ep. 55 Seneca also mentions the tired feeling produced by the motion:
a gestatione
venio non minus fatigatus quam si tantum ambulassemi
quantum sedi.
Medical writers recommend gestatio; e.g. Cels. ii 15,
gestatio longis morbis aptissima est
genera autem gestationis plura
sunt: lenissima est navi vel in portu vel in flumine, vehementior vel in
alto, vel lectica, etiamnum acrior vehiculo.
quieti: i.e. the siesta (meridiatio).

pallacarum: the form pallaca (= Gr. παλλακή) is very rare, the only
other example cited being Plin. N.H. xxxv 86, dilectam sibi (i.e. Alexander
the Great) e pallacis suis praecipue, nomine Pancasten. The usual Lat.
word for a mistress or concubine is paelex (pellex), the derivation of
which is uncertain; see Walde, Lat. Etym. Wörterb.
Caenidis: see on c. 3.

a secreto: i.e. from the private apartment where he had been resting.
For secreto see on Oth. 3, 1.
balneum tricliniumque: bathing was a regular preliminary to dining,
e.g. Plin. Ep. vi 20, mox balneum, cena, somnus inquietus et brevis. The
usual time for the bath was the eighth hour or a little later; see on
Dom. 21.
ea momenta.. ad aliquid petendum

captabant: cf. Ov. Pont. iii 1,
129, eligito tempus, captatum saepe, rogandi: Liv. xxxiii 35, temporum
opportunitates captasse ad rebellandum.

et super cenam autem: for super cenam see on Tit. 8, 1; for the
position of autem see on Dom. 13, 33; for et autem followed by et cf.
Aug. 73, Et forensia autem et calceos habuit ad subitos casus parata.

et semper alias: this reading has been reasonably suspected, and the
variant super aleas (so Ts; super alias, PO) was approved by Casaubon
and read by Burman; Graevius, on the ground that the pl. aleas is indefensible, suggested aleam. The only example of the pl. of alea given
in the Thes. Ling. Lat. is Amm. xiv 6, 25, pugnaciter aleis certant.
Preud 'homme marks off the words et semper alias comissimus as a
parenthesis.

comissimus: com(m)unissimus (Ts) is read by the editors before
Roth; cf. Claud. 21, 5, nec ullo spectaculi genere communior ("more
familiar'") aut remissior erat. Torrentius preferred the reading cum
amicis given by one of his MSS.

multa ioco transigebat: i.e. he settled many matters by dismissing
them with a bon mot; cf. Hor. Sat. i 10, 14, ridiculum acri | fortius et
melius magnas plerumque secat res: Cic. de or. ii 236, odiosas res saepe,
quas argumentis dilui non facile est, ioco risuque dissolvit. Vespasian
could take a joke as well as make one: ἔσκωπτε δημοτικῶς, καὶ ἀντεσκώπτετο
ἡδέως (Dio lxvi 11).

praetextatis
verbis: this phrase for "obscene expressions" is very
obscure. It occurs also in Gell. N.A. ix 10, non praetextatis, sed puris
honestisque verbis, and in Macrob. Sat. ii 1, 9, impudica et praetextata
verba. The first of the two explanations given by Festus (p. 245 M.) is
rather on the "lucus a non lucendo" principle: praetextum (al. praetextatum) sermonem quidam putant dici, quod praetextatis (i.e. boys who
have not yet assumed the toga virilis) nefas sit obsceno verbo uti; alii,
quod nubentibus, depositis praetextis, a multitudine puerorum obscena (i.e.
Fescennina) clamentur. Freund explains praetextata verba as velata verba
"verblümte (i.e. disguised in flowery language) Worte": Forcellini says
"praetextata verba esse ea, quibus aliquid praefari vel praetexi debet
honoris causa, quemadmodum obscenis dictis 'honos sit auribus' praetexere solemne fuit." Juvenal (ii 170), describing Armenian envoys who
had been initiated in evil practices at Rome, has the line "Sic praetextatos
referunt Artaxata mores," which the Schol. explains "mores quos filii
senatorum intra urbem habent, obsides in suis patriis redeuntes reportant,
quos ceteri apud se ephebi discant'"; and praetextata verba is prob. to be
understood either of the foul language used by such young libertines, or
(as Gronovius on Gell. l.c. suggests) of the language which the seducers
of youth employed (verba quibus ad nequitiam sollicitarentur).

facetissima: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, ferebat patienter amicorum motus,
contumeliis eorum, ut erat facetissimus, iocularibus respondens.

Mestrium Florum: Lucius Mestrius Florus took part in the first
battle of Betriacum in 69 A.D. as an unwilling follower of Otho. It is
uncertain in what year he was consul. He was proconsul of Asia under
Domitian (prob. in 83/4), as is shown by coins of Smyrna and an inscription at Ephesus (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii p. 370). Plutarch made
his acquaintance in literary circles at Rome, and Florus accompanied him
through Cisalpine Gaul, showing him over the plain of Betriacum; cf.
Plut. Oth. 14. Florus is introduced by Plutarch in his Quaestiones Conviviales (1,9; 3, 3-5; 5, 7. 10; 7, 1. 2. 4. 6; 8, 1. 2. 10) as giving banquets
and taking part in discussions at table, the author describing him as an
antiquarian (φιλάρχαιος).

"plaustra" potius quam "plostra'': the emperor's speech displayed
rusticitas in this pronunciation of the word for wagons.
Lindsay (Lat.
Lang. p. 40) says: “o for au is a feature of the Umbrian language (e.g.
ote, Lat. aut) and other dialects, and was preserved in 'rustic' Latin
and even in the Latin of the streets of Rome
Cicero's rival Clodius
was the first of the gens to change the name Claudius to the plebeian
form Clodius, no doubt with the view of conciliating the mob. Cicero
himself in his letters often uses the more homely forms with o, e.g.
loreolam, pollulum, oricula, while plodo is quoted from his 'De Gloria'
by Diomede." Cf. Priscian i 52, au transit in o productam more antiquo,
ut “lotus” pro lautus, “plostrum” pro plaustrum, “cotes” pro cautes;
sicut etiam pro o, au, ut “austrum” pro ostrum, “ausculum” pro osculum,
frequentissime hoc faciebant antiqui. “Plostrum” and “plostellum,” as
the vulgar forms, are read in Hor. Sat. i 6, 42: ii 3, 247, but in the Odes
and Epistles of Hor. “plaustrum” is the form favoured by the MSS. (cf.
Wilkins on Εp. ii 2, 74).

"Flaurum": Vespasian scored by substituting for "Florus" (from
flos) the form "Flaurus" which at once suggests φλαῦρος (vilis, inutilis,
nequam).

expugnatus: cf. Tib. 21, 2, expugnatum precibus uxoris: Iul. 1, 3,
Sullam, cum deprecantibus .. aliquamdiu denegasset, atque illi pertinaciter
contenderent, expugnatum tandem proclamasse, etc.: Liv. xxxvii 56, 9,
senatum omni modo expugnaturum pertinaciam legatorum.
quasi: in a causal sense; see on Tit. 5, 1.

amore deperiret: cf. Dom. 3, 1, Paridis histrionis amore deperditam: Plaut. Cist. 132, is amore misere hanc deperit mulierculam:
Catull. 35, 12, quae illum deperit impotente amore. So too deperire
(without amore) = perdite amare “to love to distraction" "to be dying
with love for'"; e.g. Plaut. Bacch. 470, meretricem indigne deperit; cf.
Prop. ii 30, 29, (Iuppiter) ut Semela est combustus, ut est deperditus Io,
where Io is the accus.

suo: the MSS. vary, as usual, between suo and sui; in some the word
is omitted altogether, and Modderman (Lectiones Suetonianae р. 67)
suggests that this is due to the fact that the reading in the archetype was
amore se deperiret, a construction which the copyist failed to understand.

perductae: this verb is frequently used de feminis ad stuprum ductis
(e.g. Tib. 45, Calig. 25, 2, Cic. Verr. v 31, Hor. S. ii 5, 77, Ov. Am. iii 12,
11); so perductor for a pander or pimp (Plaut., Cic., etc.). Casaubon
proposed perducta and Burman perducta ei, making Vespasian the payee
and not the payer, on the ground that the penurious emperor would never
have paid 400,000 sesterces for the favours of a lady who was only too
anxious to grant them; but, as Ernesti pointed out, perducta requires
the further change of expugnatus to expugnato, and Vespasian's conduct
would have been so unutterably sordid that Suetonius would have mentioned it in c. 16 and not here. Vespasian was extravagant in matters of
love (cf. c. 21 where plurimae pallacae of his are mentioned), and it is
unnecessary to accuse him of behaving like the gallant captain Pyrgopolinices whose minimum fee was a talentum Philippum (Plaut. Mil. 1061).

sestertia quadringenta: about £3,400. Vesp. bestowed the same
amount on an actor, c. 19, 1. The variant quadraginta (GTQ) is read
by Burman and Ernesti.

admonente quem ad modum, etc.: the steward raised the question
"quem ad modum summam rationibus vis inferri?” Cf. Tit. 8, 1. For
the use of the pres. ptc. in the sense of a perf. or of a Greek aorist ptc.
cf. Iul. 65, ac subinde observandum se admonens repente interdiu vel
nocte se subtrahebat: ib. 73, Catullum.. satisfacientem eadem die adhibuit
cenae: Galb. 5, 2, revocante: ib. 10, cohortantibus: ib. 11, supervenientibus. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 757.

dispensatore: the dispensator ("payer out, lit. "weigher out'") was
the steward who had charge of the accounts (hence he was called at times
a rationibus) and made the payments; cf. Galb. 12, 3: Ner. 44, 1: Aug.
67, 1. He was nearly invariably a slave or freedman, and the value of
the position (dispensatio, c. 23, 2) is shown by the story in Oth. 5, 2 that
Otho extorted a million sesterces from a slave whom he had recommended
as dispensator to Galba.

Vespasiano adamato: dat. case; cf. the phrase ferre alicui expensum
"to debit" (referre alicui acceptum “to credit"). Baumg.-Cr. explains
it as the abl. (= Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἐρασθέντος). Marcilius suggested that in
adamato there is a play on adhamato (“hooked"). The compound
adamare, which is first found in Cicero, is nearly always used in the
perfect forms (for rare exceptions see Thes. Ling. Lat.). It is a stronger
word than amare; cf. Sen. Ep. 71, 5, si
virtutem adamaveris, amare
enim parum est. The meaning of illicit love which it has in our passage
is found also in Ov. A.A. ii 109, Sit licet antiquo Nireus adamatus
Homero: Plin. N.H. viii 157, xxxvi 22: Petron. Satyr. 110, etc.

ut et de: the MSS. vary between et de (Ihm), et ut de, and ut de.
The correction ut et de, suggested by Preud'homme and defended by
Alexander, seems absolutely required by the use of the imperfect utebatur;
Suetonius gives two instances of what was a general habit of Vespasian.
a
a

improbiusque nato: if the text is not corrupt, natus here is to be
interpreted in the light of the meaning that natura sometimes has, viz.
the natural parts (e.g. Cic. N.D. iii 22, 55: Div. ii 70, 145), improbe
being used in the sense of enormiter; cf. Charis. i 102, 1, Chilones improbius labrati ('blubber-lipped''): Marc. Emp. 31, ad eos, quibus intestinum
improbe prominet. Casaubon, however, maintained that improbe natus
means ὁ κακῶς πεφυκώς, "homo deformi et turpi proceritate corporis," and
that ἔγχοs "hic dicitur de corpore producto ad instar perticae longuriive
(i.e. like a long staff or pole)"; so too Salmasius. Marcilius took improbe
natus as 'natura improbus, i.e. impudens," and explained the comparison
with
spear in
curious way: “Impudentiam huiusce Longini
Vespasianus argute cum hastae vibratione comparavit, quia impudenter
petens, et instans atque urgens, quasi hastam vibrare videtur atque intentare.'" Among the corrections suggested for nato are mutoniato and
vasato (both = magna mentula instructo); these give the sense required,
but neither explains the corruption. Suetonius may have written improbiusque venato (ve- being lost by haplography). vena is often used for
membrum virile (e.g. Mart. iv 66, 12: vi 49, 2), and though venatus does
not occur elsewhere, Suet. has several participial adjs. in -atus not found
earlier, e.g. cycladatus, discalciatus, fistulatus, infulatus, sagulatus, sericatus, tessellatus; cf. also pedatus (Oth. 12, 1) which means lit. "furnished
with feet."
μακρὰ . . . ἔγχος: Hom. Il. vii 213, νέρθε δὲ ποσσὶν | ἤϊε μακρὰ βιβάς, κ.τ.λ.,
describing Ajax about to give battle to Hector. The equivocal sense in
which Vespasian was using ἔyxos has its parallel in the play on the word
δόρυ by Diogenes the Cynic quoted by Diog. Laert. (vi 2, 53), and in
hasta = mentula.

Cerylo liberto: this freedman of Vespasian is not mentioned elsewhere, but Friedlaender plausibly suggests that it is with reference to
him that Martial chooses the name Cerylus in i 67, Liber homo es nimium,
dicis mihi, Ceryle, semper. | In te quis dicit, Ceryle, liber homo es?

ob subterfugiendum ius fisci: Vespasian occupied the position of a
patronus in relation to his freedman Cerylus. The rights of the patronus
in the estate of his freedman are described fully by Roby, Rom. Priv. Law i
270 sqq. When the freedman had no natural children born since his
manumission, the patron was entitled to one moiety of the estate. If he
left no own heirs (sui heredes) or natural children at all, the patron
succeeded to the whole estate. Under the Lex Papia (in the reign of
Augustus), if the freedman left fewer than three children, the patron
was to have one equal share (pars virilis), i.e. one-third if there were two
children, a moiety if he left only one, provided the estate exceeded 100,000
sesterces. The amount due to Vespasian on the death of Cerylus would
be collected by the officials of the fiscus (see on c. 16, 3).
The use of ob with the gerund or gerundive is found in early Latin
(Cato R.R., etc.); in Cic. frequently with pecuniam accipere or dare (ob
rem iudicandam, ob ius dicendum, ob innocentem condemnandum, etc.);
in Sall. (Iug. 89, 102), and Tac. (A. i 79, iv 31, xi 5). See KühnerStegmann, i 750.

ingenuum se
ferre: for se ferre in the sense of "to give oneself
out as" "pass oneself off as," cf. Vell. Pat. i 11, 1, qui se Philippum
regiaeque stirpis ferebat, cum esset ultimae: Tac. H. ii 72, extiterat
quidam Scribonianum se Camerinum ferens: iv 10, proditor corruptorque
amicitiae, cuius se magistrum ferebat.

Lachetem: it is not easy to see why Cerylus chose the name
"Laches," as it was one of the stock names for slaves in Greek comedy;
cf. Amm. Marc. xxviii 4, 27, Cum mutuum illi quid petunt, soccos et
Miconas videbis et Lachetas (i.e. they employ the wheedling style of slaves
in comedy): Dio Chrys. Orat. 74, οὐ κατὰ Λάχητα, οὐδὲ κατὰ Σίμωνα.
ὦ Λάχης ... Κηρύλος: the opening words, ὦ Λάχης, Λάχης, are from an
unknown play of Menander (frag. 921, Kock); the second line, ἐπὰν . . ἔσει,
is from the Θεοφορουμένη of Menander (frag. 223, 2, Kock), and Vespasian
added the words σὺ Κηρύλος, his meaning being that in dealing with the
estate of Cerylus the fiscus would treat him as a freedman in spite of his
claim to be freeborn and his change of name.

dicacitatem adfectabat: adfectare, like ζηλοῦν, was a tech. rhetorical
term for aiming at a certain effect in speech or writing. It is very
frequent in Quintilian, e.g. xi 1, 30, adfectata scurrilitas. Cf. the use of
captare in Hor. Sat. i 4, 82, qui captat risus hominum, famamque dicacis.

ut invidiam cavillatione dilueret: diluere as a rhet. term means "to
weaken the force of an opponent's argument or a charge brought," and
it was widely used in the general sense of extenuare or minuere in such
phrases as diluere infamiam, dedecus, nefas, peccata, etc. For cavillatione
see on Tit. 8, 2.

transferretque ad sales: the object of transferret is invidiam (not
lucra) and the verb here means 'to make use of for a new purpose"; cf.
Quintil. vi 2, 30, hoc animi vitium ad utilitatem non transferemus?
In
Tac. A. ii 65 "transferre invidiam" is used quite differently of transferring odium from oneself to another.

§2. dispensationem: see on dispensatore, c. 22.
exacta pecunia: cf. Oth. 5, 2, servo Caesaris pro impetrata dispensatione decies sestertium expresserat.

ordinavit: "appointed,” lit. "assigned him the rank or position
(ordo)"; cf. Iul. 76, 3, magistratus in plures annos ordinavit (for which
in Vitell. 11, 2, comitia in decem annos ordinavit, seque perpetuum consulem); so of appointing to commands, Aug. 46, equestrem militiam
petentes etiam ex commendatione publica cuiusque oppidi ordinabat. This
use of the verb does not seem to occur earlier, and Suetonius is also the
first to use ordinatio for "appointment to office." He frequently uses
ordinare in its more usual sense of arranging or putting in order; e.g.
Iul. 56, 7, ordinare bibliothecas (= digerere bibliothecas, Iul. 44):
Galb. 7, 1, electus ad ordinandam provinciam inquietam: Aug. 31,
annum (i.e. the calendar) a Divo Iulio ordinatum, sed postea neglegentia
conturbatum atque confusum, rursus ad pristinam rationem redegit.

ad calciandas mulas: in ancient times shoes were not put on mules
or horses except when a bad stretch of road had to be traversed or
when their hoofs were weak, and the shoes were never fastened by nails
but by strings or straps (lemnisci, fasciolae, Veget. i 26), no farrier being
needed to fix them. The shoe (solea, ὑπόδημα) was generally of iron, e.g.
Catull. xvii 26, ferream ut soleam (derelinquit) tenaci in voragine mula;
Nero's mules had shoes of silver (Ner. 30) and Poppaea's had shoes of
gold (Plin. N.H. xxxiii 140). calciare (calceare) is the word used by
Palladius, Pliny, Vegetius, etc., for putting on the shoes. See Reinach's
article "Mulomedicus" in Daremberg-Saglio.
non

§3. urinae vectigal: Dio lxvi 14, πρὸς τὸν Τίτον ἀγανακτοῦντα τῷ τοῦ
οὔρου τέλει, ὁ καὶ αὐτὸ μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων κατεδείχθη, εἶπε, λαβὼν ἐξ αὐτοῦ χρυσοῦς
πεπορισμένους καὶ δείξας αὐτῷ, “ Ἰδού, τέκνον, εἴ τι ὄζουσιν." At Rome, at least
as early as the 2nd cent. B.c., public urinals were placed in alleys (angiportus); Macrobius, Sat. iii 16, 15, quotes from C. Titius, a contemporary
of Lucilius, "dum eunt, nulla est in angiporto amphora quam
impleant.” The receptacles were amphorae or dolia (cf. Lucr. iv 1026,
Mart. xii 48, 8). Fullers (fullones) and tanners (coriarii), who used large
quantities of urine in their trades, were probably taxed by Vespasian for
the right of placing these receptacles and emptying them. This is the
explanation given by Beroaldus, and is much more probable than the
alternative assumption that the public were charged for the use of the
amphorae in the same way as, according to one interpretation of Juv. iii
38, they were charged for the use of the foricae or public jakes. It is
by no means certain that foricae in Juv. bears this meaning; the Schol.
also explains it as shops near the Forum, and this is accepted as correct by
Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 280.

admovit ad nares: Casaubon suggests that this was done because
the sense of smell was used by moneychangers and others as a means of
testing the genuineness of metals; cf. Aristot. de mirabil. 1088, Arrian
Epict. Dissert. i 20.

odore: Juvenal is referring to this story in his famous words lucri
bonus est odor ex re | qualibet (xiv 204).

non mediocris summae: Dio (lxvi 14) states the sum as 250,000 denarii
(= 1,000,000 sesterces), about £8,500.

statuam colosseam: like the Colossus of Nero, see on c. 18; the same
expression occurs in Plin. N.H. xxxiv 39 and 78 (cf. xxxv 51, Nero
iusserat colosseum se pingi).

iussit
ponerent: the MSS. vary between poneret (MGS) and
ponerent. Suetonius has iubere ut in Tib. 22 (lectis codicillis quibus ut
id faceret iubebatur), and the subjunctive with ut omitted in Vitell. 14, 4
(edictum quo iubebat urbe mathematici excederent); 'generally he
uses iubere with the acc. and inf. Ernesti and Burman read ponere,
arguing that the constr. legatos iussit ponerent is not found till a
much later period. Bentley made the same correction, and it is adopted
by Ihm. Bentley however is inconsistent, as in Ter. Andr. 412 he would
read: Erus me relictis rebus iussit Pamphilum | hodie observarem.
Alexander (op. cit. p. 18) also points out that the passive constr. in Suet.
Tib. 22 (quoted above) implies an active ‘‘lectis codicillis qui eum iusserunt
ut id faceret,” i.e. with an accusative preceding and a subjunctive
following. Roth conjectured ponere et (adopted in Preud'homme's text),
the best correction, if any were needed.

cavam manum: like the hand of a beggar; cf. Aug. 91, 2, stipem
quotannis die certo emendicabat a populo, cavam manum asses porrigentibus
praebens: Aristoph. Eq. 1083, ἔμβαλε κυλλῇ (sc. χειρί).

paratam basim: the pile of money was to be the statue resting on
his hand as base. For basis cf. Dom. 15, 2, a basi statuae triumphalis:
Aug. 31, 1, sub Palatini Apollinis basi. On the basis were inscribed the
name and honours; cf. Plin. Ep. iii 6, 5, iube basim fieri, ex quo voles
marmore, quae nomen meum honoresque capiat. The Greek origin of the
word basis (βάσις) is preserved in the case-forms like baseos (gen.) and
basin (acc.) which are found occasionally (see Thes. Ling. Lat.).

§ 4. ne in metu quidem
mortis abstinuit iocis: [Aur. Vict.]
Epit. 9, seriis ioca, quibus delectabatur, admiscens interiit. Cf. the spirit
of playfulness (τὸ παιγνιώδες) shown by Theramenes when drinking the hemlock (Xen. Hell. ii 3, 56).
lemma:
ne in metu quidem
mortis abstinuit iocis

text:
prodigia: the same portents of his death are mentioned in Dio lxvi 17,
ἐγεγόνει δὲ σημεῖα αὐτῷ φέροντα εἰς τοῦτο, ὅ τε ἀστὴρ κομήτης ἐπὶ πολὺ φαντασθείς,
καὶ τὸ μνημεῖον τὸ τοῦ Αὐγούστου αὐτόματον ἀνοιχθέν.

Mausoleum: in 28 B.C. Augustus built in the northern part of the
Campus Martius a tomb for members of the house of the Caesars. It
was called the Mausoleum Augusti after the tomb built for the Carian
prince Mausolus (ob. 353 в.с.) by his wife Artemisia (cf. Aug. 100, Strab. v
236, Dio lviii 22). In shape it was circular with a base of white marble
about 300 ft. in circumference and 60 ft. in height, on which rose a mound
of earth covered with evergreens, the interior being divided into sepulchral
chambers to contain the ashes. A bronze statue of Augustus crowned
the whole. Tacitus calls it the tumulus Augusti or tumulus Iuliorum
(Ann. iii 4, xvi 6). The first whose ashes were laid there was the young
Marcellus (23 B.C.); then Agrippa (12 B.c.); Drusus, brother of Tiberius
(9 B.C.); Lucius and Gaius, adopted sons of Augustus (2 and 4 A.D.);
Augustus (14 A.D.); Germanicus (20 A.D., died in 19); Livia (29 A.D.);
Tiberius (37 A.D.). Caligula transferred to it the ashes of his mother and
his brother (Calig. 15), but was not himself buried there. Claudius,
Britannicus, and Vespasian were probably entombed in it, as were Nero's
wife Poppaea and the emperor Nerva. The other members of the Julio-Claudian and the Flavian houses were, with few exceptions, laid elsewhere
(see Jordan-Huelsen Topogr. Rom i 3, 614 sqq.). Dio (lxix 23) says that
by Hadrian's time the Mausoleum of Augustus was filled, and Hadrian
built another on the other side of the Tiber, the Mausoleum Hadriani
(mod. Castello di S. Angelo).
patuisset: so before Nero's death: de Mausoleo, sponte foribus patefactis, exaudita vox est nomine eum cientis (Ner. 46, 2).

stella crinita: the appearance of a comet betokened a ruler's death;
cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 41, taetrum sidus regnis quod crinitum vocatur: Suet.
Ner. 36, 1, stella crinita, quae summis potestatibus exitium portendere
vulgo putatur, per continuas noctes oriri coeperat: Claud. 46, praesagia
mortis eius praecipua fuerunt exortus crinitae stellae, etc.: Verg. G. i 489
(describing portents at the death of Julius Caesar), non alias
totiens arsere cometae: Shakespeare Jul. Caes. ii 2, When beggars die
there are no comets seen; The heavens themselves blaze forth the death
of princes. Seneca (N.Q. vi 3, 3) first uses crinitum sidus as a translation of κομήτης (ἀστήρ); the luminous tail of the comet was compared to
floating hair (κόμη, crinis).
diri

Iuniam Calvinam: daughter of M. Iunius Silanus (cons. 19 A.D.) and
of Aemilia Lepida. Her name Calvina was derived from her paternal
grandmother Domitia Calvina (Mommsen, Ephem. Epigr. i 64).
She is
mentioned in Tac. A. xii 4 as the "decora et procax soror" of L. Iunius
Silanus and daughter-in-law of L. Vitellius (censor 48 A.D.), being wedded
to L. Vitellius brother of the emperor Aulus (see Vitell. 3, 1). A charge
was trumped up against her of having incestuous relations with her
brother Silanus, and he was driven to suicide in 49 A.D., while she was
banished from Italy (Tac. A. xii 8). Ten years later she was restored
from exile by Nero (A. xiv 12).

e gente Augusti: she was a great-great-granddaughter of Augustus,
and, as such, might be buried in the Mausoleum Augusti. Her mother
Aemilia Lepida was a daughter of Aemilius Paulus and of Julia, who was
a granddaughter of Augustus.

pertinere: this verb is very frequently used of the application of
portents; e.g. Phaedr. iii 3, 6, ad consulendos currit maerens hariolos; | hic
pertinere ad domini respondet caput: Val. Max. i 6, haruspices ad salutem
imperatoris pertinere dixerunt.

Parthorum regem qui capillatus esset: in contrast to Vespasian who
was bald; cf. Dio lxvi 17, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς περὶ τοῦ κομήτου τι διαλαλοῦντας,
“ Οὐκ ἔμοιγε,” εἶπεν, “ἀλλὰ τῷ τῶν Πάρθων βασιλεῖ προσημαίνει· ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ
κομᾷ (comatus est), ἐγὼ δὲ φαλακρός (calvus) εἰμι.” The Parthians, the successors of the Persians, wore the same flowing locks (τὸ ἄφετον καὶ ἀνειμένον
τῆς κόμης, Suid. s.v. Λεόννατος: Hdt. vi 19, τῶν Περσέων ἐόντων κομητέων).
In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, 18 it is the Persian king whom Vespasian is said
to have mentioned: cum crinitum sidus apparuisset, “Istud,” inquit, "ad
regem Persarum pertinet, cui capillus effusior." The king of Parthia at
Vespasian's death was Vologaesus, successor to the Vologaesus mentioned
in c. 6 who must have died before June 78 as from that time a new image
appears on the coinage (Prosop. Imp. Rom. i 476; Gardner, Parthian
Coinage p. 76).

prima morbi accessione: Dio (l.c.) says that it was when Vespasian
believed that he was going to die (ἐπειδὴ ἐπίστευσεν ὅτι τελευτήσει) that he
said “ Θεὸς ἤδη γίγνομαι.”" Accessio (more rarely accessus) is regularly
used by post-Aug. writers for a "coming on" or "attack" of any
malady, especially an intermittent fever; the abatement of the attack is
decessio (decessus) or remissio. Cicero uses accedere in the same way:
Att. vii 2, alteram quartanam (sc. febrim)
dixit decessisse et alteram
leviorem accedere. Greek medical writers have εἰσβολή, προσβολή, ἐπίληψις,
ἐπισημασία, and παροξυσμός in the sense of accessio.

vae: some of the later MSS. have ut (so edd. princ., vulg.) or ne.
Many corrections have been proposed: vah (Graevius), nae (Gronovius), at
(Burman), eu (Modderman); but vae is rightly defended by Ernesti, who
says: Non modo iocus est in eo quod pro ‘morior” dixit “Deus fio," sed
etiam acumen in eo quod dolentis voce utitur in re, quae, si proprie diceretur,
felicitas esset.

deus fio: referring to the deification of the Roman emperors after
death, expressed by such phrases as inter divos referre (Aug. 97,2):
in numerum deorum referre (Claud. 45): caelum decernere (Tac. A. i 73):
caelestes honores decernere (A. xii 69). The honour was decreed by the
senate on the motion of the reigning emperor. Vespasian's deification is
mentioned by Pliny (Pan. 11), when congratulating Trajan on his reasons
for deifying Nerva: Quem tu .. templis honestasti, non imitatus illos qui
hoc idem, sed alia mente, fecerunt. Dicavit caelo Tiberius Augustum, sed
ut maiestatis crimen induceret, Claudium Nero, sed ut inrideret, Vespasianum
Titus, Domitianus Titum, sed ille, ut dei filius, hic, ut frater videretur. Tu
sideribus patrem intulisti, non ad metum civium, non in contumeliam.
numinum, non in honorem tuum, sed quia deum credis. Vespasian's
worship was in the care of the collegium Flavialium (Dom. 4, 4).
Tiberius, Caligula, Nero, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius were not deified,
and the senate was not cowed into granting the honour to Domitian
(see Dom. 23). Imperial deification, or apotheosis, is delightfully satirised
in Seneca's Apocolocyntosis (“Pumpkinification") of Claudius. Nero,
with grim humour, used to call mushrooms (boleti) the food of the gods
(deorum cibus) after they had been used to poison Claudius (Dom. 14, 1, n.).
consulatu suo nono: in 79 A.D.; see on c. 8, 1.

Campania: where Pompey also was stricken with fever; cf. Juv. x
283, provida Pompeio dederat Campania febres.

motiunculis: slight attacks, touches of fever or ague accompanied
by shivering; cf. Sen. Ep. 53, 6, levis aliquem motiuncula decipit, sed
cum crevit et vera febris exarsit, etc. Celsus (iii 5) uses motio for an
ague-fit. Cicero has commotiuncula in Att. xii 11, commotiunculis
συμπάσχω; cf. xiv 5, leviter commotus ("slightly indisposed'').

Cutilias: a Sabine village about 7 miles from Vespasian's native
place Reate. There was a small lake there (mod. Lago di Contigliano)
which Varro called the umbilicus Italiae as being in the centre of the
peninsula (Plin. N.H. iii 17). Close to it were springs, sulphureous and
others, and the Romans went there for "cures" either by drinking the
waters or by bathing in them. There is an epigram (Anth. Pal. ix 349)
addressed by Leonidas to Vespasian at Aquae Cutiliae on his birthday:
Ὑδατά σοι Κοτίλεια γενέθλιον ἦμαρ ὁρῶντι, | Καῖσαρ, ἐπιβλύζοι σωρὸν ἀκεσφορίης, |
ὄφρα σε κόσμος ἅπας πάππον τρισὶν αὐγάζηται, | ὡς πατέρα τρισσῆς εἴσιδεν εὐτοκίης.
Titus, like his father, died at Cutiliae; see Tit. 11.

Reatina rura: see c. 1, 2.
This

aestivare: cf. Galb. 4, 3, Tusculum, ubi aestivare consuerat.
verb is almost entirely post-Aug.; the only earlier writer who uses it is
Varro, e.g. R.R. ii 2, 9, mihi greges in Apulia hibernabant, qui in Reatinis
aestivabant. For petit = petiit cf. Oth. 7, 1.

frigidae aquae: the extreme coldness of the springs at Cutiliae and
their curative powers are mentioned in Plin. N.H. xxxi 10, Iuxta Romam
Albulae aquae volneribus medentur egelidae; sed Cutiliae in Sabinis gelidissimae suctu quodam corpora invadunt ut prope morsus videri possit, aptissimae stomacho, nervis, universo corpori: Vitruv. viii 3, Est autem aquae
frigidae genus nitrosum, uti Pinnae Vestinae, Cutiliis aliisque locis
similibus, quae potionibus depurgat per alvumque transeundo etiam
strumarum minuit tumores: Celsus iv 5 (on stomachic disorders), consistere
in frigidis medicatisque fontibus, quales Cutiliarum
sunt, salutare est.

super urgentem valitudinem etiam: cf. Liv. xxviii 46, Punicum
exercitum super morbum etiam fames affecit. The use of super in the
sense of praeter begins in prose with Livy and is common in later writers.
Suetonius has it repeatedly, and often follows it with etiam, quoque, or ct.

alvo
soluta: a regular phrase in medical writers; so too venter
solutus. In describing the last illness of Augustus, Suetonius (Aug. 97,
3) says: causam valitudinis contraxit ex profluvio alvi. Dio (lxvi 17),
while stating as an ascertained fact that Vesp. died of fever at the
Sabine springs, adds that there were some, including the future emperor
Hadrian, who falsely asserted that he was poisoned at a banquet by Titus.
Tacitus (A. xii 67, xiii 15) mentions "soluta alvus” as an effect of the
poison administered to the emperor Claudius and to Britannicus.

imperatorem stantem mori oportere: (Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, deinde
ventris eluvie fessus, et assurgens, ‘“Stantem,” ait, “imperatorem excedere
terris decet'': Dio lxvi 17, τῶν δὲ ἰατρῶν ἐπιτιμώντων ὅτι τῇ τε ἄλλῃ διαίτῃ
ὁμοίᾳ νοσῶν ἐχρῆτο, καὶ πάντα τὰ προσήκοντα τῇ ἀρχῇ ἔπραττε, “ Τὸν αὐτοκράτορα”
ἔφη “ ἑστῶτα δεῖ ἀποθνήσκειν.” Dio (lxix 18) attributes a like utterance to
Turbo, prefect of the praetorian guard in Hadrian's reign, who, when
advised by the emperor to take a rest when ill, replied: “Tὸν ἔπαρχον
(praefectum) ἑστῶτα ἀποθνήσκειν δεῖ.” Cf. Sen. Ep. 82, 21, quis post hanc
(contionem) dubitet se infestis ingerere mucronibus et stans mori (where
stans is opp. to fugiens): id. Ep. 37, 2, recto tibi invictoque moriendum
est. Seneca is always inculcating the Stoic doctrine that the "wise” man
should die in harness (in actu mori).

consurgit ac nititur: niti could be used by itself = "to make an effort
Holland
to rise"; cf. Sall. Iug. 101, niti modo ac statim concidere.
strangely takes nititur in the same sense as nitens in c. 20, and translates:
"As he was rising therefore and straining still to ease his body."
viiii Kal. Iul.: June 23.

annum agens sexagensimum ac nonum: a very careless expression,
though the meaning is clear; he was aged (natus) 69 yrs. 7 mths. and 7 days,
but in (agens) his 70th year. The variant gerens is preferred by Graevius,
Gronovius, Marcilius, Oudendorp, and Bremi. See on Dom. 1, 1, adulescentiae tempus
gessisse fertur.

mensem ac diem septimum: septimum is to be taken with mensem as
well as with diem; see App. i § 16. (d). Dio (lxvi 17) says that Vespasian
lived 69 yrs. 8 mths. (Zonaras adds "and 8 days"), and reigned 10 yrs.
all but 6 days. He was born on Nov. 17, 9 A.D. (see c. 2, 1), and died
on June 23, 79 A.D.; so that the calculation of his age by Suetonius as
69 yrs. 7 mths. 7 days is accurate. He reigned from July 1, 69 A.D., when
he was first proclaimed imperator at Alexandria (c. 6, 3), to June 23,
79 A.D., i.e. 10 yrs. all but 8 days.
See also on c. 25.

genitura: ''horoscope"; see on Tit. 9, 2. Cf. Eutrop. vii 20, Genituram
filiorum ita cognitam habuit, ut, cum multae contra eum coniurationes
fierent, quas patefactas ingenti dissimulatione contempsit, in senatu dixerit,

aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem: Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, divinis
deditus, quorum vera plerisque negotiis compererat, successores fidebat
liberos Titum ac Domitianum fore.
lemma: aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem

text:
coniurationes: Dio (lxvi 16) describes how Julius Sabinus, a Gaul
who had taken part in the unsuccessful effort of Classicus to establish an
Imperium Galliarum in 70 A.D., and who styled himself a Caesar as being
descended from a bastard son of Julius Caesar, was brought to Rome in
79 after being nine years in hiding and was put to death by Vespasian's
orders along with his wife Epponina. He mentions at the same time the
conspiracy of Caecina Alienus and Eprius Marcellus, on both of whom the
emperor had lavished favours. For Caecina Alienus and his fate see on
Tit. 6, 2. Eprius Marcellus exercised great power both as an orator (cf.
Tac. Dial. 5. 8. 13) and informer (delator) in the reign of Nero. It was
he who secured the condemnation of Paetus Thrasea. At the beginning
of Vespasian's reign he was impeached by Helvidius Priscus, son-in-law of
Thrasea, but escaped through his influence with Mucianus and Domitian.
He enjoyed the friendship of Vespasian and was proconsul of Asia (70-
73 A.D.). When he was condemned by the senate for conspiring with
Caecina against the emperor in the later years of his reign, he committed
suicide (Tac. A. xii 4, xiii 33, xvi 23, etc.; H. ii 53, iv 6-8).

aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem: Dio lxvi 12, “Ἐμὲ μὲν υἱὸς
διαδέξεται ἢ οὐδεὶς ἄλλος.” Dio says that the words followed a display of
defiant insolence by Helvidius Priscus in the senate; see on c. 15. The
remark of Vespasian is much more appropriate if, as Suet. says, it was
made "post assiduas in se coniurationes" and so, presumably, towards the
end of his reign. There is no evidence that Priscus (executed in 73)
organised any conspiracy, though his denunciations of the empire were
revolutionary. Rostovtzeff (Social and Economic Hist. Rom. Emp. c. iv
n. 4) thinks that Priscus had been advocating in the senate the selection
as emperor of the best man of the senatorial class, taking the Stoic and
Cynic point of view, and that Vesp. would not listen to the suggestion
and uttered these words which mean that the reestablishment of the
Republic would be better than the method suggested by Priscus.
lemma: aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem

text:
per quietem: "in a dream," cf. Iul. 7, 2:81, 3: Tib. 74: Claud.
37, 1: Ner. 7, 1:46, 1: Oth. 7, 2: Vesp. 5, 7:7, 2; so in Val. Max.,
Tac., etc. Cic. has in quiete and secundum quietem ("after going to
sleep''); Val. Max. also uses inter quietem.

stateram: stătēra was used either in the general sense of a scales or
balance (libra, trutina) or in the special sense of a steelyard. The mention
of the two scales (lances) shows that the former is the meaning here, as
in many other passages, e.g. Petron. Satyr. 35, stateram in cuius altera
parte scriblita erat, in altera placenta; see Wilkins on Cic. de or. ii 159,
aurificis statera. Vitruvius (x 3, 4) describes statera as a steelyard with
a beam or yard (scapus) marked by points (puncta), the hanging weight
(aequipondium) moving along the scapus, and the object weighed being
placed in a scale (lancula).

Palatinae domus: Augustus at first dwelt in the modest town house
of Hortensius, the orator, on the Palatine (Aug. 72, 1). When this was
struck by lightning, he gave the site for the stately temple to Apollo (Aug.
29, 3), and close to it he built a palace for himself. Tiberius built a
second palace near that of Augustus (see on Vitell. 15, 3, Tiberiana domus),
and in official documents the designation of the imperial buildings on the
Palatine continued to be Domus Augustana et Tiberiana or Domus
Palatina; cf. Dom. 15, 2. In popular speech and gradually in literature
Palatium, the name of the Palatine hill, came to be used for the palace
of the Caesars (e.g. Galb. 18, 1: Vitell. 15, 2); see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr.
Rom i 3, 64, where the double use of Quirinale in Italian is cited as a
parallel.

examine aequo: the examen was the tongue or needle which worked
in an eye (agina) or opening in the upper part of the balance and showed
whether the two scales were in equipoise; cf. Verg. A. xii 725, Iuppiter
ipse duas aequato examine lances | sustinet: Pers. i 6, examenque improbum in illa | castiges trutina.
filii: Titus and Domitian.
quando: see on c. 16, 3.

totidem annis: approximately 27 years.
(41-54 A.D.); Nero 14 (54-68); Vespasian 10
Domitian 15 (81-96).
Claudius reigned 13 years
(69-79); Titus 2 (79-81);

parique temporis spatio: by adding these words Suetonius presumably means that the two periods, when calculated accurately in years,
months, and days would exactly correspond. He does not himself furnish
us with the precise length of each reign, and the figures which we derive
from other sources vary considerably. Claudius reigned 13 yrs. 2 m. 20 d.
(Dio, Zonar., Joseph.). Nero reigned 13 yrs. 8 m. (Dio; Zonaras adding
"all but two days''); 13 yrs. 8 d. (Joseph.). Vespasian (see on c. 24)
reigned 10 yrs. all but 6 days (Dio); 11 yrs. 11 m. 22 d. (Clem. Alex.,
who mentions that some say 11 yrs. precisely); 10 yrs. 8 d. (Cedrenus);
9 yrs. 7 m. 12 d. (Epiphanius). Titus reigned 2 yrs. 2 m. 20 d. (Suet.,
Dio, Zonar.; for other figures see on Tit. 11). Domitian reigned 15 yrs.
5 d. (Dio, Zonar., Eutrop.).
2 H

cognomine paterno: Titus bore the cognomen of his father Vespasian;
his brother took the cognomen “Domitianus" from their mother
Domitilla (Vesp. 3). Titus' full name was Titus Flavius Vespasianus, the
nomen gentilicium “Flavius" being found only in C.I.L. xiv 3902. In
early inscriptions under Vespasian he appears as Vespasianus Caesar
(C.I.L. iii p. 849, x 8110, vi 346, etc.; Newton 30, 299, 324, 325); in
authors he is called simply Titus (Tacitus once calls him Titus Vespasianus,
H. ii 1); so in C.I.L. x 5405, Newton 168, and frequently on coins
(Eckhel, vi 350-364; Cohen, i² 428-464).
vir

amor ac deliciae generis humani: cf. Eutrop. vii 21, Titus
omnium virtutum genere mirabilis, adeo ut amor et deliciae humani
generis diceretur: Suidas, Τίτος, βασιλεὺς ῾Ῥωμαίων, Οὐεσπασιανοῦ υἱός, ἀνὴρ πᾶν
ἀρετῆς συνειληφὼς γένος, ὡς πρὸς ἁπάντων ἔρως τε καὶ τρυφή (deliciae) τοῦ θνητοῦ
προσαγορευθῆναι γένους: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 6, Huius sane mors adeo provinciis luctui fuit, uti, generis humani delicias appellantes, orbatum orbem
deflerent. Pliny (N.H. praef. 1) addresses Titus, to whom his work is
dedicated, as iucundissime; Augustine (Civ. Dei v 21) calls him suavissimus. Pacatus (Panegyr. in Theod. 11), referring to Titus, repeats the
phrase amor generis humani. Ausonius (Caes. xi) characterizes him as
“Felix imperio, felix brevitate regendi, | expers civilis sanguinis, orbis
amor."
•

ad promerendam omnium voluntatem: cf. Calig. 3, 1, promerendi
amoris
studium: Cic. Mur. 70, homines tenues unum habent in nostrum
ordinem aut promerendi aut proferendi beneficii locum. Suetonius also
uses promereri c. acc. pers., Aug. 3, 2, in promerendis sociis; Cic. uses
de of persons, Off. ii 53, paratiores erunt ad bene de multis promerendum.

artis: the artfulness of Titus in courting popularity is illustrated
by Suetonius in c. 8, 2.

fortunae: Dio (lxvi 18) says that men contrasted Augustus, who
would not have been so loved had he not lived so long, with Titus, who
would not have been so loved had he lived longer. Dio adds that if Titus
had lived long, it might have been shown that he owed his fame more to
good fortune than to merit: ὁ Τίτος
ἐπιεικῶς ἄρξας, ἐν ἀκμῇ τῆς δόξης
ἀπέθανε, τάχα ἂν ἐλεγχθείς, εἴγε ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἐβεβιώκει, ὅτι εὐτυχίᾳ πλείονι ἢ ἀρετῇ
ἐχρήσατο.

superfuit: = abunde fuit, redundavit (not adfuit, as Sabellicus and
others explain it). Gellius (i 22) condemns the use of superesse for adesse
reo, defendere causam (a use which occurs in Suet. Aug. 56, 3), and says:
Qui integre locuti sunt, magnam partem ‘‘superesse” ita dixerunt ut eo
verbo significarent superfluere et supervacare atque esse supra necessarium
modum.

et: = et quidem; cf. Tib. 34, 2, consuerat quadriplam strenam et de
manu reddere; Ner. 12, 1, etc.

quod difficillimum est, in imperio: Pitiscus aptly quotes Capitol.
Anton. Philos. 15, nemo fit principum quem non gravis fama perstringat,
usque adeo ut etiam Marcus in sermonem venerit, etc. Titus differed from
other Roman emperors, to many of whom might be applied the words of
Tacitus on the kings of the Suevi, A. xii 30, subiectis, dum adipiscerentur
dominationes, multa caritate, et maiore odio, postquam adepti sunt.

quando: for the causal sense of quando see on Vesp. 16, 3. Trachmann
(op. cit. p. 37) comments on its use here: “Quando” hic non causam
affert enuntiati principalis, cur Tito tantum vel ingenii vel artis vel fortunae
superfuerit, sed tanquam additamentum explicativum continet, cur scriptor
adiunxerit “et quod difficillimum est, in imperio"; hic enim, nisi fallor,
sententiarum nexus est: tantum illi.. superfuit, et, quod difficillimum
est, in imperio, id quod eo magis commemorandum vel mirandum est, quando
privatus non caruit.

privatus: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 3, ubi patriae curam suscepit,
incredibile est, quantum, quem imitabatur, anteierit, praecipue clementia,
liberalitate, honorificentia, ac pecuniae contemptu, quae eo amplius grata
fuere, quod ex nonnullis a privato adhuc patratis, asperior luxuriaeque et
avaritiae amans credebatur fore. What Suetonius says here of Titus is
said of Vespasian by Ausonius (Caes. x): olim qui dubiam privato in
tempore famam, | rarum aliis, princeps transtulit in melius.

odio: he incurred this odium through his high-handed conduct as
prefect of the praetorian guard; see с. 6.
vituperatione publica: on account of his alleged vices people predicted that he would be a second Nero; see c. 7.
III. Kal. Ian.: Dec. 30.

insigni anno Gaiana nece: the emperor Gaius Caligula was assassinated
on Jan. 24, 41 A.D.; see on Oth. 6. 1. Suetonius is wrong in his dates.
Titus was born in 39, not in 41, as Suet. himself admits when he says
that Titus died (81 A.D.) in his 42nd year; see on c. 11. Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2697) suggests a possible confusion with Britannicus (see c. 2)
who was born in 41. Dio (lxvi 18) says correctly that Titus was 39 years,
5 months, and 25 days old when he succeeded Vespasian on June 24, 79 A.D.

Septizonium: from this passage it is clear that there was an older
Septizonium before the "Septizonium Severi" built in 203 A.D. by the
emperor Septimius Severus at the S.E. of the Palatine to provide a stately
front to his palace where it faced the Via Appia; cf. Spart. Sept. Sev. 19,
24 (where there is a variant Septizodium): Amm. Marc. xv 7, 3 (355 A.D.),
cum plebs ad Septemzonium (al. -zodium) convenisset, celebrem locum,
ubi operis ambitiosi nymphaeum Marcus (Aurelius) condidit. This building
of Severus apparently consisted of three stories of balconies or terraces
supported by columns and was destroyed in the 16th cent. by Sixtus V
who used the stone for building the Vatican (Burn, Rome and the
Campagna, p. 180). A "septizonium" at Lambaesus in Numidia is mentioned in C.I.L. viii 2657 (c. 225 A.D.) and a "septizodium" at some town
in the Roman province of Africa, C.I.L. viii (suppl.) 14372. Various views
have been held on the original meaning of “septizonium." Some suggest
2H2
that it was a structure consisting of 7 colonnades rising in tiers, each
narrower than the one supporting it, and semicircular in form: others
think that it rose in steps, or that it had 7 circular walls of different
heights and colours like Ecbatana in Media as described in Hdt. i 98.
According to Dombart (Pauly-Wissowa, ii A. 1578 sqq.), "septizonium”
corresponded to ἡ ἑπτάζωνοs, which was used primarily in a spatial sense
of the 7 zones into which the heavens and also the earth were divided, and
then in a temporal sense of the order of rotation of the 7 planets which
marked the 7 days of the week; “Septizonium,” as the name of a building,
denoted an ornamental structure serving in the main as a great public
calendar, displaying on its front (1) figures of the 7 planets (Saturnus,
Sol, Luna, Mars, Mercurius, Juppiter, Venus), (2) the 12 signs of the
zodiac marking the months, (3) the numbers of the days in the month.
There were holes to receive a peg (moved daily) opposite the various
planets, signs of the zodiac, and numbers of the days, so that the day of
the week, the day of the month, and the month of the year were visible
at a glance; see the illustrations given by Dombart in the article cited.
He regards "septizodium" as a corruption of "septizonium," while
Jordan-Huelsen (Topogr. Rom i 3, 100) favour the view of Maass (Die
Tagesgötter 106 sqq.) that “Septizodium" meaning "The House of the
Seven Planets (ἑπτὰ ζῴδια)" is the correct form, and that "Septizonium"
was a vulgar distortion of this.
perparvo: see on “perinfamis,” Vitell. 2, 4.
nam: see on Vesp. 12.

educatus in aula: at the court of Claudius. The emperors granted
this honour to children of illustrious families and of foreign rulers; see
Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 85. His father Vespasian had risen to the
highest offices at Rome under Claudius through his military achievements
and the favour of Narcissus (Vesp. 4, 1). Otho's grandfather was reared
in the house of Livia Augusta (Oth. 1, 1); Marcus Aurelius grew up at
Hadrian's court (Capitol. Anton. Philos. 4); Agrippa, great-grandson of
Herod the Great, was among those educated at the court of Claudius
(Joseph. Ant. xix 360).

Britannico: born in 41 A.D., son of the emperor Claudius and Valeria
Messalina. He was called at first Tiberius Claudius Germanicus, but after
his father's victories in Britain (43 A.D.) the senate decreed to the son
the title "Britannicus," to be his distinctive name (Claud. 27, Dio lx 22).
At the instigation of his second wife Agrippina (Galb. 5, 1) Claudius
adopted Domitius, her son by a former husband, into the Claudian house
with the name of Nero, and gave him precedence over Britannicus. Every
humiliation was inflicted on Britannicus, and when he was charged by
Agrippina with disrespect towards the adopted Nero, Claudius put to death
or exiled all his best instructors (Tac. 4. xii 41, optimum quemque
educatorem filii exilio aut morte adficit), and he was placed under the
control of persons appointed by his stepmother. Nero succeeded Claudius,
and in the second year of his reign (55 A.D.) poisoned Britannicus (Suet.
Ner. 33, Tac. A. xiii 16).
disciplinis: see on Galb. 5, 1.

magistros: including Sosibius, who is mentioned in Tac. A. xi 1 as
“Britannici educator." Sosibius, who, as Furneaux says, was probably a
freedman like Anicetus the tutor of Nero, was used as a tool by Messalina
and rewarded with 1,000,000 sesterces, nominally “quod Britannicum praeceptis, Claudium consiliis iuvaret” (4. xi 4); as an instructor of
Britannicus he was put to death by Claudius at the instance of Agrippina
(Dio lx 32).

metoposcopum: the custom of forecasting a person's future from an
examination of his brow by a μετωποσκόπος is referred to by Pliny (N.H.
xxxv 88) when describing the marvellous fidelity of the portraits painted
by Apelles: Imagines adeo similitudinis indiscretae pinxit ut—incredibile
dictu Apio grammaticus scriptum reliquerit quendam ex facie hominum
divinantem, quos metoposcopos vocant, ex iis dixisse aut futurae mortis
annos aut praeteritae. Juvenal also mentions it, vi 583, frontemque manumque | praebebit vati crebrum poppysma roganti. Metoposcopy and
Chiromancy were reckoned by Artemidorus (Oneirocr. ii 69) among the
more vulgar forms of soothsaying (Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 213).
physiognomon, or physiognomist, differed from the metoposcopus by telling
characters, not fortunes; cf. Cic. Fat. 5, Quid? Socratem nonne legimus,
quemadmodum notarit Zopyrus physiognomon, qui se profitebatur hominum
mores naturasque ex corpore, oculis, vultu, fronte pernoscere? Stupidum
esse Socratem dixit et bardum,
addidit etiam, mulierosum: Cic.
Tusc. iv 37.

Narcisso: see on Vesp. 4, 1.
The

utique: here utique means "certainly," as in Ner. 22, 1; in Tib. 47,
Calig. 53, 1, and Ner. 28, 2 it means "especially"; it is used with a neg.
in Ner. 15, 2, triumphalia ornamenta
tribuit, nec utique (“necessarily'")
de causa militari. In Cicero this adv. occurs almost exclusively in the
Letters; Livy and Seneca use it very frequently.

potione: Suetonius (Ner. 33) describes how the first weak poison compounded by the archpoisoner (venenariorum index) Locusta proved ineffective when administered to Britannicus. Nero compelled her to make
a stronger potion which was tried first on a kid, and the animal lingered
for five hours. A still stronger brew was tried on a pig, which died at
once, and Nero ordered this mixture to be taken to the triclinium and
given to Britannicus, who dropped dead at the first taste (ad primum
gustum concidit). That account hardly tallies with what Suetonius says
here about Britannicus draining the draught (potione hausta), and about
Titus, who tasted it, escaping death. Tacitus (A. xiii 16), describing the
second attempt to poison Britannicus, says that a harmless draught of
very hot wine and water was offered to him after it had been tasted in
his presence, and when he rejected it as too hot, some cold water containing the virulent poison was poured in, and this proved fatal instantaneously.

cubans: used inaccurately instead of sedens. Children sat at table
and did not recline. The grandsons of Augustus sat beside him on the
lowest couch; Aug. 64, 3, neque cenavit una, nisi ut in imo lecto assiderent.
Claudius always had his children present at dinner along with the sons
and daughters of distinguished men, and they sat at the ends (arms) of
the couches as they ate: Claud. 32, adhibebat omni cenae et liberos suos
cum pueris puellisque nobilibus, qui more veteri ad fulcra sedentes vescerentur. Nero kept up this custom, but the children (including Britannicus)
sat at a table of their own more frugally furnished: Tac. A. xiii 16, mos
habebatur principum liberos cum ceteris idem aetatis sedentes vesci in
aspectu propinquorum propria et parciore mensa. See Marquardt, Privatl.2
p. 300.
iactantur
gravique morbo adfiictatus diu: cf. Cic. Cat. i 13, homines aegri febri
deinde multo gravius adflictantur. Oudendorp's suggestion
that sit has fallen out has nothing to recommend it. Suetonius expresses
himself with his usual brevity, but the meaning seems clearly to be that
Titus was believed to have tasted the poison and in consequence to have
been prostrated by a long illness. The illness was not a matter of opinion
or belief, the cause of the illness was. Fuisse is to be supplied with
adflictatus; cf. Calig. 50, creditur potionatus a Caesonia: Vesp. 16, 2,
creditur solitus promovere.
Alexander (op. cit. p. 18) argues that -que
should be regarded as an interpolation. Similarly -que is rejected by Polak
in Claud. 1, 4, Fuisse autem creditur non minus gloriosi quam civilis animi;
nam ex hoste super victorias opima quoque spolia captasse summoque
saepius discrimine duces Germanorum tota acie insectatus. In his note
on that passage Smilda defends -que as having an explicative force.

mox: =
postea; see on Oth. 10, 1.
statuam in Palatio posuit: cf. Oth. 1, 3.

quae circensi pompa praefertur: so among the honours decreed to
Germanicus after death was "ut ludos circenses eburna effigies praeiret'
(Tac. A. ii 83). In the procession at the opening of these games images
of the gods were carried in litters (fercula) on the shoulders of men or
in sacred cars (tensae, Vesp. 5, 7; cf. Dion. Hal. vii 72). An ivory image
of Julius Caesar was borne in a tensa while he was still alive (Iul. 76,
Aug. 43), and the honour was frequently decreed to the emperors after
death. The pompa circensis was marshalled on the Capitoline hill, and
then passed down the Sacra Via to the Forum, turned to the right through
the Vicus Tuscus, the Velabrum, the Forum Boarium, and through the
main entrance of the Circus (the Porta Pompae), and then passed once
round the metae. For a detailed account of this brilliant spectacle see
Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 44 and Mayor on Juv. x 36-46.

hodieque: = hodie quoque; see on Galb. 1.
prosecutus est: in the pompa circensis.
Suet. uses prosequi very
frequently both in the sense of accompanying as a mark of respect
(προπέμπειν), and in the general sense of honouring; e.g. Oth. 1, 3, Senatus
honore rarissimo, statua in Palatio posita, prosecutus est eum: Dom. 9, 2,
omnes circa se largissime prosecutus.

corporis animique dotes: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 2, a puero praeclaris
studiis, probitatis, militiae, litterarum, instantissime deditus, quo contenderit, animi et corporis muneribus ostendit. dos, in the sense of a
bodily or mental gift or endowment, is a favourite word with Ovid, who
has dos corporis, formae, oris, ingenii, etc. So in prose writers of the
Silver age, e.g. Sen. Vit. Beat. 8, 2, corporis dotes. Suet. uses virtutes in
the same way, e.g. Calig. 3, 1, corporis animique virtutes.

explenduerunt: explendescere is found earlier in Nepos, Att. 1, in
pueritia nobilis inter aequales ferebatur, clariusque explendescebat. Cicero
uses the simple verb; e.g. Sen. 9, 28, canorum illud in voce splendescit
etiam in senectute. Cf. the metaph. uses of effulgere, emicare, enitere.

non minus auctoritatis quam gratiae: cf. Tac. H. ii 1, Titi ingenium
quantaecumque fortunae capax, decor oris cum quadam maiestate.
quanquam: see on c. 7, 2.

ventre paulo proiectiore: so Nero is described as “ventre proiecto”
(Ner. 51). Persius uses protensus, i 57, pinguis aqualiculus (“paunch'')
protenso sesquipede extet.

memoria singularis: this is the reading of nQ; the other MSS.
have memoriae, but the nom. is required. Oudendorp suggested memoria
et singularis docilitas. The whole passage very closely resembles the
description of Germanicus in Calig. 3, 1, Omnes Germanico corporis animique
virtutes, et quantas nemini cuiquam, contigisse satis constat: formam et
fortitudinem egregiam, ingenium in utroque eloquentiae doctrinaeque genere
praecellens, benivolentiam singularem conciliandaeque hominum gratiae ac
promerendi amoris mirum et efficax studium.

docilitas ad: Suet. extends to the subst. the constr. often found
with the adj., e.g. Calig. 54, 2, docilis ad cetera. In class. Lat. docilis is
used either abs. or c. ad; in poetry at times c. gen.; in post-Aug. writers
at times c. abl.

tum belli tum pacis: it was exceptional to excel in both; cf. Hom.
Il. xiii 730, ἄλλῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα, κ.τ.λ. : Prop. iii 9, 19,
hic satus ad pacem, hic castrensibus utilis armis: Plin. Pan. 4, Enituit
aliquis in bello, sed obsolevit in paсе. Alium toga, sed non et arma
honestarunt: Claud. Laud. Stil. i 27, bellis insignior ille, Sed pacem foedat
vitiis
Partitum; singula quemque Nobilitant. Titus was like Scipio
Aemilianus, whom Velleius (i 12) describes as “omnibus belli ac togae
dotibus ingenique ac studiorum eminentissimus saeculi sui.”
..

§ 2. armorum et equitandi peritissimus: Suetonius uses the same
words of Julius Caesar (Iul. 57).

Latine Graeceque: Eutrop. vii 21, facundissimus, bellicosissimus,
moderatissimus; causas Latine egit, poemata et tragoedias Graece composuit: Suidas, τῇ μὲν Λατίνων ἐπιχωρίῳ γλώττῃ πρὸς τὰς τῶν κοινῶν ἐχρῆτο
διοικήσεις, ποιήματα δὲ καὶ τραγῳδίας Ἑλλάδι φωνῇ διεπονεῖτο. Suidas also styles
Titus εὐγλωττότατος (facundissimus).

orando: Quintilian (prooem. 4) uses ars orandi for the oratorical art.
In Calig. 3, 2, Suetonius has orare causam (so Livy); cf. orare litem (Cic.).

fingendis poematibus: fingere (like πλάττειν) was used by the poets
in the sense of composing; e.g. Hor. C. iv 2, 31, operosa parvus Carmina
fingo. Pliny (N.H., praef. 5) eulogizes the eloquence and poetic skill of
Titus: Fulgurat in ullo umquam verius dicta vis eloquentiae, tribuniciae
potestatis facundia? Quanto tu ore patris laudes tonas! quanto fratris
amas! quantus in poetica es! O magna fecunditas animi!

ad usque: the position of usque varies; cf. Vesp. 24, usque ad
defectionem: Tib. 51, 1, ad simultatem usque processit: Galb. 19, 2, in
Forum usque: Tib. 2, 4, usque in Capitolium.

extemporalitatem: Suetonius seems to have coined this subst. to
express what he elsewhere calls "ad subita extemporalis facultas'' (Aug.
84, 1). The adj. extemporalis is common in post-Aug. writers (Quintil.,
Plin. Ep., Mart., Tac., etc.); Cicero uses subito dicere and subita et fortuita
oratio (de or. i 33, 150); also ex tempore, e.g. Arch. 8, 18, magnum
numerum optimorum versuum dicere ex tempore: de or. iii 50, 194, versus
fundere ex tempore.

musicae: Friedlaender (Sitteng. ii10 183 sqq.) traces the modifying
influence of Greek manners and customs on the old Roman prejudice not
merely against professional but also against amateur musicians. Nepos
(Epam. 1) states bluntly the old point of view that music was unseemly
for a man of prominent position: musicen nostris moribus abesse a principis persona. Under the Empire musical dilettantism was very widespread even in the highest circles. Nero, Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius,
Commodus, Alexander Severus, Elagabalus, Caracalla were among the
emperors who cultivated the art.

cantaret et psalleret: psallere was specially used of playing on the
cithara (κυρίως ψάλλειν τὸ τῷ ἄκρῳ τῶν δακτύλων τῶν χορδῶν ἅπτεσθαι, Suidas),
e.g. Hor. C. iv 13, 7, docta psallere Chia. We frequently find psallere
joined with cantare or canere (e.g. Cic. Cat. ii 10, qui non solum
cantare et psallere, sed etiam sicas vibrare didicerunt), and psallere
itself was used of singing to the harp (cf. "psalm'').
scienter: an adverb often used of a skilful musical performance;
cf. Cic. Brut. 54, ex nervorum sono in fidibus quam scienter ei pulsi sint,
intellegi solet: Nepos (praef. 1), saltasse eum (Epaminondam) commode,
scienterque tibiis cantasse. Terence (Eun. 133) has the phrase scire
fidibus "to be skilled on the lyre"; so too scitus is used with the gen.
of the instrument played on, e.g. Ov. F. v 54, scita Thalia lyrae.

notis: notae (σημεῖα) = “shorthand'; notarius (σημειογράφος, ταχυγράφος)
= 'shorthand writer." The signs used in shorthand at Rome were known
as Notae Tironis, from Tiro the freedman and secretary of Cicero. For
such contractions in MSS. see Lindsay, Introd. to Lat. Text. Emend. p. 91.
Cato's speech against Caesar on the subject of the Catilinarian conspiracy was the first speech in the senate reported in shorthand.
system was developed and augmented by Maecenas and Seneca.
Tiro's

excipere velocissime: in the epigram (146) of Ausonius entitled "Ad
Notarium Velocissime Excipientem'' the speed of the notarius is described
in an exaggerated fashion: Tu sensa nostri pectoris | ut dicta iam ceris
tenes |... Tu me loquentem praevenis. | Quis, quaeso, quis me prodidit? |
Quis ista iam dixit tibi, | quae cogitabam dicere? Cf. Mart. xiv 208,
Currant verba licet, manus est velocior illis; | nondum lingua suum, dextra
peregit opus: Manil. iv 197, Ille scriptor erit felix, cui littera verbum
est, | quique notis linguam superet cursumque loquentis, | excipiens longas
nova per compendia voces: Sen. Ep. 90, 25, Quid (loquar) verborum notas,
quibus quamvis citata excipitur oratio et celeritatem linguae manus
sequitur?

amanuensibus: the subst. amanuensis is first found in Suetonius, who
uses it also in Ner. 44, 1. It denotes a secretary, a confidential slave or
freedman, servus a manu; cf. Aug. 67, 2, Thallo a manu, quod pro epistula
prodita denarios quingentos accepisset, crura ei fregit: Iul. 74, 1, Philemon
a manu: Vesp. 3, Caenis, Antoniae liberta et a manu. Another phrase is
ab epistulis; e.g. Claud. 28, Narcissus ab epistulis, Pallas a rationibus.

chirographa: chirographum (χειρόγραφον), first used by Cicero, has three
meanings in Suetonius: (1) handwriting (as here; Aug. 64, 3, ut imitarentur
chirographum suum; Ner. 52, versibus ipsius chirographo scriptis): (2) a
letter or document in a person's handwriting (as Tit. 6, 2, chirographum
eius praeparatae apud milites contionis, Aug. 87, 3,; Dom. 1, 1; Iul. 17, 1;
Calig. 24, 3): (3) a bond (cautio) under one's own hand, guaranteeing the
fulfilment of an obligation (Calig. 12, 2, deque ea re et iure iurando et
chirographo cavit).

falsarium: falsarius is found once earlier in Cato (or. inc. frag. 28,
Meyer) of one who is guilty of “suppressio veri”: Tu, inquam, si verum
supprimis, falsarius agnosceris; si falsa confingis, mendax esse videris..
In Suetonius and later writers it means a forger of written documents,
especially wills. Precautions devised against falsarii in the reign of Nero
are mentioned in Ner. 17: adversus falsarios tunc primum repertum, ne
tabulae, nisi pertusae, ac ter lino per foramina traiecto, obsignarentur, etc.
When a falsarius was convicted before Claudius, some one in court cried
out that his hands should be cut off, whereupon the emperor at once ordered
the executioner to be summoned with knife and butcher's block (Claud.
15, 2). Banishment and confiscation of goods were the penalties for
forgery under the Lex Cornelia de falsis (81 B.c.) also known as the Lex
testamentaria. Cicero uses testamentarius for a forger (Off. iii 73,
Sest. 39). For Domitian's allegation that Titus falsified Vespasian's will
see Dom. 2, 3.

tribunus militum
meruit: see on Vesp. 2, 3. Titus would be at
least 20 when he was appointed tribune (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 366),
probably nearer 25 (Mommsen, Hermes iii 43). Military service, generally
for a year, was a necessary preliminary to a senatorial career (Galb. 6, 1,
n.); e.g. the younger Pliny served as military tribune in Syria (Plin.
Ep. iii 11). See also on “praefectura,” Vesp. 8, 3.

in Germania: cf. the speech of Mucianus to Vespasian, Tac. H. ii 77:
Tuae domui triumphale nomen, duo iuvenes, capax iam imperii alter (i.e.
Titus) et primis militiae annis apud Germanicos quoque exercitus clarus.
The statement made by Heraeus (on Tac. H. ii 1) and by Spooner (on
H. ii 77) that Titus served as military tribune under his father Vespasian
when he was in command of a legion in Germany (Vesp. 4, 1) is absurd.
Vespasian got his command in Germany in 41/42 A.D., and Titus was born
in 39 A.D. (41 A.D., according to Suet. Tit. 1). Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa,
vi 2697) erroneously says that Titus is given the title of “Germanicus"
in Tac. H. iii 66, for the Germanicus mentioned there is a son of Vitellius.
The elder Pliny, in the Preface to his N.H. (dedicated to Titus), refers to
his having served in the army with Titus: et nobis quidem qualis (tu) in
castrensi contubernio! Nothing definite is known as to when and where
Pliny (born 23/24 A.D.) and Titus served together; for the theory that it
was during the war in Judaea see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 51, Weynand l.c.

in Britannia: Dio (1x 30) makes the statement, which is chronologically impossible, that Titus accompanied Vespasian to Britain in 43 A.D.,
and saved his father's life when he was sore pressed by the Britons in 47.
See Furneaux, Tac. Ann. Vol. ii² p. 132 n. Vespasian's military achievements in Britain are mentioned in Vesp. 4, 1.
industriae: his father was characterised by the same energetic discharge of military duties; cf. Vesp. 4, 5 delectus est ut industriae expertae.

modestiae: “disinterestedness,” “integrity'"; cf. the use of modestus
(= ἐγκρατής) in Dom. 8, 2 of magistrates and provincial governors who
refrain from extortion, etc.

statuarum multitudine: these presumably were set up after the
establishment of the Flavian dynasty at Rome.

titulis: inscriptions on the base ('basis,” Vesp. 23, 3) of statues and
busts, giving the distinctions of the person represented; cf. Dom. 15, 2,
Galb. 2.

§2. Foro operam dedit: at Rome under the Empire the forum
Romanum, the forum (Iulii) Caesaris, and the forum Augusti were
used for the trial of lawsuits; hence triplex forum in Mart. iii 38, 4,
"Causas,” inquis, “agam Cicerone disertior ipso, | atque erit in triplici
par mihi nemo foro.”

honestam magis quam assiduam: Titus did not appear regularly in
court, but only in cases where glory was to be won. Pliny (Ep. vi 29),
after enumerating various kinds of cases which a pleader ought to undertake, says: "Ad haec ego genera causarum, ambitiose fortasse, addam
tamen claras et inlustres. Aequum est enim agere ("to plead") поп
numquam gloriae et famae, id est suam causam.”

Arrecinam: the correct form of this name was restored by Roth;
the MSS. have adrecidiam (arr-, ПR). Arrecina Tertulla was the daughter
of M. Arrecinus Clemens, who was praetorian prefect under Caligula in
41 A.D. (Tac. H. iv 68, Joseph. Ant. Iud. xix 37 sqq.). Her brother,
M. Arrecinus Clemens, also was praetorian prefect and twice consul; see
Dom. 11, 1. Arrecina Tertulla is twice mentioned in inscriptions: C.I.L. vi
12355 (Newton 234), Dis manibus M. Arrecini Melioris, Arrecina Tertulla
delicio suo fecit. v(ixit) a(nnis) viii d(iebus) x: C.I.L. vi 12357 (Newton
235), D. m. Arrecinae Gnomes, Arrecina Tertulla delicio suo fecit.

praefecto praetorianarum cohortium: the highest office open to the
equestrian order (summa equestris gradus, Galb. 14, 2; cf. Tit. 6, 1). In
Republican days the praetoria cohors was the bodyguard attached to the
