general; cf. Paul. ex Fest. p. 223 Müll.: praetoria cohors est dicta quod
a praetore non discedebat. Scipio enim Africanus primus fortissimum
quemque delegit, qui ab eo in bello non discederent et cetero munere militiae
vacarent et sesquiplex stipendium acciperent. Under Augustus there were
9 cohorts in different parts of Rome and in the places in Italy where he
usually stayed. Each cohort consisted of 1000 men (10 centuries) and
10 turmae of cavalry. Sejanus, under Tiberius, concentrated the cohorts
Their
in a camp outside the Viminal gate of Rome (Galb. 19, 1, n.). They were
increased to 11 or 12 under Caligula or Claudius. Vitellius disbanded
them (Vitell. 10, 1), but later enrolled 16 new cohorts. The number was
reduced to 9 by Vespasian, and was subsequently fixed at 10.
supreme commander was the emperor, but he delegated his command,
usually to 2 praefecti praetorio (-ii), sometimes to 1, after the time of
Commodus to 3. Suetonius uses praefectus praetorii in Galb. 11:14, 2:
Claud. 12, 1: Ner. 21, 1: Calig. 56, 1; praefectus (sc. praetorii) in Calig.
23, 2: Claud. 21, 3: Ner. 35, 5. The designation praefectus cohortium
praetorianarum used here and in Dom. 6, 1 is irregular. Though writers
at times use cohortes praetorianae, the regular phrase in inscriptions,
especially military diplomata, is cohortes praetoriae. See Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii³ 866 sqq.

Marciam Furnillam: daughter of the Antonia Furnilla, wife of
Q. Marcius Barea Sura, who is mentioned in an inscription at Rome
(Dessau, 953): Antonia A. f. Furnilla Q. Marcii Q. f. C. n., C. et Gemini
Artori pronepotis, Bareae Surae.
splendidi: see on Oth. 1, 3.

sublata: tollere was used of the father taking up and acknowledging
as his the new-born child which was laid at his feet, and so tollere liberos =
procreare, gignere; cf. Ner. 5, 2, sublato filio Nerone ex Agrippina:
Tib. 7, 2, sublato ex ea filio Druso: Cic. Phil. xiii 10, qui ex Fadia sustulerit
liberos.

filia: named Julia. She was born before 67, and Jerusalem was taken
by Titus on her birthday in 70 (see c. 5, 2). She received the title
"Augusta" in her father's reign, and is so styled on coins of Titus with
the legend Iulia Augusta T(iti) Aug(usti) f(ilia) or Iulia Imp. T. Aug. f.
Augusta (Eckhel, vi p. 367; Cohen, i² p. 465 sq.). After being offered in
marriage to Domitian, who refused her (Dom. 22), she wedded her cousin
Flavius Sabinus. When he was put to death by Domitian's orders (Dom.
10, 4), Domitian, who was separated at the time from his wife Domitia,
lived with Julia as with a wife, and even after he took back Domitia
(Dom. 3, 1) he continued his illicit relations with his niece, and was the
cause of her death through abortion (Dom. 22). She died before 90 A.D.,
as she is called diva on a coin of that year (see Friedlaender, Mart. Introd.
p. 57). Martial (vi 3 and 13) writes of her as already deified, that book
of his epigrams being published in 90. Her name appears in the vow of
the Fratres Arvales for the safety of the imperial family, January 3, 87
(C.I.L. vi 2065), but is omitted in the vow of January 3, 90 (C.I.L. vi
2067), so that presumably she died before the latter date (see Newton,
op. cit. p. 101).
§ 3. quaesturae: the minimum age for the quaestorship was 25; presumably Titus was quaestor in 64 or 65.

legioni praepositus: when Vespasian was appointed by Nero in the
winter 66/67 to conduct the war in Judaea (see Vesp. 4, 5), he sent Titus
to Alexandria to lead as legatus the 15th legion (Apollinaris) from there
to Judaea. Vespasian went from Achaea overland via the Hellespont, and
was joined by Titus at Ptolemais (Acre) on the coast of Phoenicia (Joseph.
Bell. Iud. iii 8, 64).

Taricheas: read by Ursinus, Roth, Preud'homme: Tarichias, Bentley;
Tarichaeas, Ihm; Taricheam, Herm. Barbarus; the MSS. have thracias
(thacias, G; trachias, Πк). The city of Taricheae (Ταριχέαι, Strab.;
Ταριχαῖαι, Joseph.; Tarichea, Plin. N.H.) was in Galilee on the western
side of the sea or lake of Tiberias (Gennesaret). Strabo (xvi 764) says
it got its name from the fish-curing industry (ἡ λίμνη ταριχείας ἰχθύων ἀστείας
παρέχει). It was fortified by Josephus who made it his headquarters in the
rebellion of the Jews against Rome. It was taken by Titus with great
slaughter (Joseph. Bell. Iud. iii 485 sqq.).

Gamalam: opposite Taricheae, on the eastern side of the lake. Built
on a precipitous hill resembling a camel's hump (hence the name), it too
was strongly fortified by Josephus and fiercely defended by the Zealots
against Vespasian. Titus, who had been sent on a mission to Mucianus,
the legatus of Syria, found on his return that Vesp. had been beaten back
from Gamala. At the head of a small body of picked troops Titus forced
his way into the city and Vesp. sent back his whole army to support him.
The city was captured during a violent storm and 9000 of the inhabitants
perished (Joseph. iv 1 sqq.). Titus also effected the capture of Gischala,
and with its downfall the conquest of Galilee was complete.
sunt

equo sub feminibus amisso: cf. Coel. or. frag. 3 (Paul. ex Fest.
p. 182 M.), equusque mihi sub feminibus occisus erat. Isidorus (Orig. 11, 1,
106) mentions the phrase in his attempt to differentiate between femora
and femina: "femora”
ab inguinibus usque ad genua,
“femina” autem per derivationem femorum partes sunt, quibus in equitando tergis equorum adhaeremus; unde et proeliatores olim sub feminibus
equos amisisse dicebantur. Formations from femin- are much more frequent
than those from femor- in the plur. of femur (femen); see statistics in
Thes. Ling. Lat. Suetonius uses femur, femore, femina, feminibus.

inscenso: Suet. also has the more usual conscendere equum, ascendere
equum (in equum, Cic.).
less.

rector: "rider," as in Tac. and Sil. Ital.; vector (Heinsius) is needcirca se: "by his side." For se instead of eum see on Vesp. 15, 1,
qui
se salutaverat. The use of circa is the same as in Claud. 36,
quodam cum ferro circa sacrificantem se deprehenso. Suetonius uses
circa very freely in the spatial sense of prope (in c. 9, 2 = utrubique "on
both sides of'"); he also has it of those who are about a person, his
suite, associates, etc. (cf. οἱ περί τινα); e.g. Dom. 9, 2, omnes circa se
largissime prosecutus. See also on Oth. 11, circa lucem: Dom. 3, 2, circa
administrationem imperii. The late variant contra se is adopted by most
of the early editors (not by Oudendorp, Wolf, or Bremi), with the view
of enhancing the valour of Titus.

missus: he was sent by Vespasian; cf. Tac. H. i 10, nec Vespasiano
adversus Galbam votum aut animus: quippe Titum filium ad venerationem
cultumque eius miserat: H. ii 1, Titus Vespasianus e Iudaea, incolumi
adhuc Galba, missus a patre. Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 498) says that king
Agrippa went from Judaea along with Titus to pay homage to Galba;
he also says that Vespasian wished to receive directions from Galba with
regard to the war in Judaea. In Gall. 23 Suetonius mentions Vespasian's
belief that Galba had sent emissaries from Spain to Judaea to assassinate
him.

quaqua iret: quaqua (= quacumque or quocumque) is ante- and post-class.; e.g. Plaut. Mil. 92, quaqua incedit: Apul. Met. xi 4, quaqua perfluebat. Cf. Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii 635. For the use of the subjunctive see App. i § 8. b. (2).

convertit: see on Vesp. 4, 6.

quasi arcesseretur: quasi is widely used in Silver Lat. in a causal
sense. The cause or reason introduced by quasi is often purely subjective,
but there is no necessary implication of falsehood. Suetonius has it (a) with
the subjunctive as here and in Dom. 10, 4, occidit Helvidium, quasi
taxasset: Vesp. 6, 2, perseveraverunt, quasi rumori minus crederent:
Aug. 11, medicus custoditus, quasi venenum volneri indidisset; (b) with
nouns, adjs., ptcples.; e.g. Oth. 1, 2, praepositos suos, quasi defectionis
auctores, occiderant : Galb. 3, 4, ne quasi ignaram fallere videretur:
Aug. 86, 2, increpat Antonium, quasi scribentem ea. For examples in other
authors see Kühner-Stegmann, ii 456.

adoptionis gratia: Tac. H. ii 1, Titus causam profectionis officium
erga principem (i.e. Galba) et maturam petendis honoribus iuventam ferebat
("alleged"), sed vulgus fingendi avidum disperserat accitum in adoptionem.
Materia sermonibus senium et orbitas principis et intemperantia
('impatience'") civitatis, donec unus eligatur, multos destinandi.
Galba's choice of an adopted son and successor see Galb. 17.

sed ubi
sensit: the considerations which influenced Titus in
deciding whether he should return, or continue his journey to Rome, are
described by Tac. (l.c.): Ubi Corinthi certos nuntios accepit de interitu
Galbae et aderant qui arma Vitellii bellumque affirmarent, anxius animo
paucis amicorum adhibitis cuncta utrimque perlustrat. Si pergeret in
urbem nullam officii gratiam in alterius honorem suscepti ac se Vitellio
sive Othoni obsidem fore: sin rediret, offensam haud dubiam victoris, sed
incerta adhuc victoria et concedente in partes patre filium excusatum. Sin
Vespasianus rem publicam susciperet, obliviscendum offensarum de bello
agitantibus. His ac talibus inter spem metumque iactatum spes vicit.
This is the only passage in which Suetonius uses ubi in a temporal sense.

redit: perf. Tacitus (H. ii 2) describes his return journey from
Corinth. He coasted along Achaea (Attica and Euboea) and then sailed
across the Aegaean to Asia Minor, and descending that coast and leaving
it on the left, he arrived at Rhodes and Cyprus. From Cyprus he sailed
by a bolder course (audentioribus spatiis) across the open sea to Syria.
adito Paphiae Veneris oraculo: Tac. (l.c.), Atque illum cupido incessit
adeundi visendique templum Paphiae Veneris inclitum per indigenas
advenasque. The foundation of this famous temple and oracle at Paphos
in Cyprus, where Aphrodite was said to have landed when she rose from
the sea, is discussed by Tacitus (H. ii 3, cf. A. iii 62). The image of the
goddess was merely a cone-shaped stone, and the altar, though in the open
air, was never wet by rain. Pausanias (i 14) says that her worship was
introduced at Paphos from Assyria, but more probably it was Phoenician
colonists who spread the cult of Venus Urania (= Astarte); cf. Hdt. i 105.
A grove and altar of Aphrodite at Paphos are mentioned in Hom. Od. viii
362. One of the functions of the sea-born goddess was to grant to mariners
a favourable voyage; hence such titles of hers as Εὔπλοια (Roscher, Lex.
Myth. i 402).

dum de navigatione consulit: Tac. H. ii 5, Titus de navigatione
primum consuluit. Postquam pandi viam et mare prosperum accepit, de se
per ambages interrogat caesis compluribus hostiis. Sostratus (sacerdotis
id nomen erat) ubi laeta et congruentia exta magnisque consultis adnuere
deam videt, pauca in praesens et solita respondens petito secreto futura
aperit. Titus aucto animo ad patrem pervectus suspensis provinciarum
et exercituum mentibus ingens rerum fiducia accessit.

confirmatus est: like Vespasian, when he consulted the oracle of the
god of Carmel, Vesp. 5, 6; cf. also Galb. 9, 2.

§2. cuius brevi compos: cuius refers to spe; cf. Liv. xxix 22, spei
conceptae compos: Suet. Aug. 28, 2, fecit ipse se compotem voti: Aug. 58,
2, compos factus votorum meorum:
Romanum voti compotem fecit.
Calig. 13, imperium adeptus populum
The hopes of Titus were as good as
realised when his father Vespasian was chosen as emperor.

ad perdomandam Iudaeam relictus: cf. Tac. H. v 1, eiusdem anni
(70 A.D.) principio Caesar Titus perdomandae Iudaeae delectus a patre:
Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, Iudaeique (in pacem coacti) annitente filio Tito, quem
transgrediens in Italiam reliquerat externae militiae: Oros. vii 9, relictoque
in castris ad procurationem obsidionis Hierosolymorum filio Tito: Joseph.
Bell. Iud. iv 658, κατὰ τάχος τὰ κατὰ τὴν ᾿Αλεξάνδρειαν διώκει (Οὐεσπασιανός)
τὸν δ' υἱὸν Τίτον μετὰ τῆς ἐκκρίτου δυνάμεως ἀπέστειλεν ἐξαιρήσοντα Ἱεροσόλυμα.
Vespasian was proclaimed emperor by the legions in Egypt, Judaea, and
Syria in July, 69 (Vesp. 6, 3). Towards the close of that year he went to
Alexandria along with Titus.
Before setting out for Italy he made
arrangements for the occupation of Egypt, so that he could cut off the
corn-supply of Rome and compel Vitellius to surrender by famine (Tac.
H. iii 48). Titus was sent back to Palestine to conduct the siege of
Jerusalem.

Hierosolymorum: the name Ἱεροσόλυμα (Hierosolyma) for Jerusalem
seems to occur first in Hecataeus of Abdera, a contemporary of Alexander
the Great. It is used in the Apocrypha, while the form generally found
in the Septuagint is Ἱερουσαλήμ. The name Ἱεροσόλυμα was explained as
ἱερὸν Σολύμων, and this gave rise to the belief that the Jews were identical
with the Solymi (ancient dwellers in Lycia, mentioned by Homer and
Herodotus); cf. Tac. H. v 2, clara alii Iudaeorum initia, Solymos, carminibus Homeri celebratam gentem, conditae urbi Hierosolyma nomen e suo
fecisse.
..

duodecim confecit: Joseph. v 288, δώδεκα αὐτὸς τῶν προμάχων ἀναιρεῖ:
Eutrop. vii 21, 2, in oppugnatione Hierosolymorum sub patre militans
duodecim propugnatores duodecim sagittarum confixit ictibus.
cepit: the siege of Jerusalem by Titus began in the spring of 70 A.D.
and lasted over five months. The Temple with its treasures was destroyed
by fire, probably on Aug. 6, and on Sept. 2 the upper city, where the last
resistance was offered, was stormed by the Romans (Joseph. vi 260 sqq.,
393 sqq.).

ea: this is the reading of M; the other MSS. have eam (sc. urbem, to
be supplied κατὰ σύνεσιν from Hierosolymorum).
filiae: Julia; see on c. 4, 2.

imperatorem eum consalutaverint: Oros. vii 9, 6, Titus imperator ab
exercitu pronuntiatus: Joseph. vi 316, τὸν Τίτον μετὰ μεγίστων εὐφημιῶν
ἀπέφηναν αὐτοκράτορα (Joseph. says that this salutation by the soldiers took
place after the burning of the Temple). The title imperator (αὐτοκράτωρ)
was given by acclamation on the field of battle; e.g. Caes. B.C. ii 26,
Curio.. universi exercitus conclamatione imperator appellatur. The earliest
example is that of Scipio Africanus (209 B.c., Liv. xxvii 19). The last
occasion on which the honour of being acclaimed imperator was granted
to a private person was in 22 A.D., when Tiberius allowed it to Junius
Blaesus, proconsul of Africa; Tac. A. iii 74, Tiberius Blaeso tribuit ut
imperator a legionibus salutaretur prisco erga duces honore, qui bene gesta
re publica gaudio et impetu victoris exercitus conclamabantur... Concessit
quibusdam et Augustus id vocabulum, ac tunc Tiberius Blaeso postremum.
The Emperors were saluted in this way for victories gained either by
themselves or by their lieutenants (legati), and the number of these
salutations appeared in the list of their titles.

nec non et:
atque etiam, "and even"; cf. Calig. 40. In other
passages Suetonius uses nec non et merely as a copula ("and also") connecting individual terms or concepts (Vesp. 8, 2:18: Dom. 14, 1).
poetry and late prose nec non et is frequently used to connect sentences
(not individual words); e.g. Verg. G. ii 53, Aen. i 748, viii 461: Colum. viii
15, 6: Plin. N.H. vii 183, etc.: Quintil. ix 4, 25, etc. See KühnerStegmann, i 826 sq., on this and other combinations such as nec non etiam,
nec non .. quoque, nec non et quoque.

efflagitantes: Titus did not yield to the solicitations of the troops.
He broke up his army when his task in Judaea was accomplished. The
12th legion was sent back to Melitene on the Euphrates; the 10th was
left in Jerusalem; the 5th and 15th accompanied him to the various cities
which he visited in the eight months which elapsed before he returned to
Rome. Before setting out on his homeward voyage from Alexandria he
sent back these two legions to their earlier quarters, the 5th to Moesia
and the 15th to Pannonia (Joseph. B.I. vii 18–20, 117).

§ 3. suspicio quasi
temptasset: in post-Aug. writers quasi c. subj.
is used for the acc. c. inf. with verbs of saying, believing, accusing, etc.,
as well as with nouns such as fama, rumor, opinio, suspicio, the clause with
quasi having a strong subjective colouring (cf. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 456).
Suetonius uses this constr. freely; e.g. Tit. 8, 1, admonentibus domesticis,
quasi plura polliceretur quam praestare posset: Tib. 21, 2, scio vulgo
persuasum, quasi vox Augusti per cubicularios excepta sit: Aug. 94, 8,
somnium aliter exponunt, quasi Iuppiter demonstrasset: Aug. 28, 1,
obiectum sibi ab eo saepius, quasi per ipsum staret ne redderetur (res
publica): Dom. 22, erat fama, quasi develleret: Aug. 14, rumore dilato,
quasi necasset: Aug. 6, concepta opinione veteri, quasi temere adeuntibus
horror quidam et metus obiciatur. For similar uses of tamquam see on
Vitell. 16.
..

Alexandriam petens: when Jerusalem had been captured, Titus went
down to Caesarea on the sea. He was hindered from undertaking the
voyage to Rome immediately, as it was the winter season (70/71 A.D.).
He held celebrations of various kinds at Caesarea on the sea, Caesarea
Philippi, Berytus, and the cities of Syria. He then went by Antiochia to
Zeugma on the Euphrates, where he received an embassy from the Parthian
king Vologaesus (Vesp. 6, 4) who presented him with a golden crown for
his victory in Judaea. Finally, he set out for Egypt, visiting the ruins
of Jerusalem on his journey, and arrived at Alexandria at the beginning
of May, 71. There he embarked for Italy.

Memphim: the oldest capital of Egypt, about 15 miles south of
Cairo, on the western bank of the Nile.

Apide: Apis ("Απις, Egyptian Hapi "the hidden") was a sacred bull
worshipped with the greatest reverence by the Egyptians at Memphis
(Hdt. iii 27-29; Plut. Is. et Osir. 20, 29, 43, etc.; Lucian de sacrif. 15;
Pomp. Mel. i 9). He was regarded as the incarnation of the god Ptah,
or of Osiris, or of the Sun, and was connected with the river-god Nilus.
Fire was said to come down from heaven upon the cow, which thereupon
conceives Apis. The calf which is so called is black with a square spot
of white upon his forehead, and on his back the figure of an eagle; the
hairs in his tail are double, and there is a scarab or beetle upon his tongue
(Hdt. iii 28). The ceremony of consecrating the new-born bull is described
in Ael. Hist. An. xi 10, Diod. Sic. i 85, Plin. N.H. viii 71, Amm. Marc. xxii
14. He was not allowed to live for more than 25 years. If he died
before that age, he was splendidly entombed in a chamber under the
temple of Serapis at Memphis which was called the Serapeum. After
death he became Osiris-Apis (Osir-Hapi), the most probable origin of the
name Serapis (Sarapis); see on Vesp. 7, 1.

diadema gestavit: the wearing of a diadem suggested regal aspirations.
In its most general sense diadema was a synonym of taenia, vitta, fascia,
stemma, strophium, mitra, and the other Gr. and Lat. words denoting a
band encircling the head (Daremberg-Saglio, ii 119). It was used for the
band round the brow of priests and celebrants of religious rites. As a
symbol of sovereignty it was worn by Assyrian and Persian kings, by
Alexander (after his conquest of Darius), by the Diadochi, etc. The
diadema as a regni insigne (Cic. Ph. iii 5) was hated by the Romans and
refused by Caesar (Suet. Iul. 79, where it is described as a white band,
fascia candida). Caligula thought of assuming it and establishing a
regnum or absolute monarchy (Calig. 22, 1). In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 35 we
are told that Aurelianus (270-275) was the first Roman emperor to wear a
diadem; but the first represented with it on coins is Constantine (306-337).

sequius: a comparative of the adv. secus (Tit. 11, Galb. 14, 1) from
sequor, lit. "following" "not attaining to" and so "inferior” “worse'';
cf. Tib. 2, 1, multa egregia merita, multa etiam sequius admissa in
rem p. extant. The form sequius is found first in Afran. 293 R., sin, id
quod non spero, ratio talis sequius ceciderit; it does not occur in class.
Lat. though secus does (e.g. Cic. Att. vi 2, 2, ne quid fiat secus quam
volumus), but is fairly common from Livy on. Distinguish sētius, which
is joined with non, nec, neque, nihilo, eo, and quo, and is equivalent to
minus (e.g. Vesp. 6, 2: Dom. 2, 2: Vitell. 10, 3). It is very doubtful
whether setius is connected with secus and sequius, though the Roman
grammarians regarded it as a byform of sequius; see Lindsay, Lat. Lang.
566: Zimmermann, Archiv Lexik. iv 604.

Regium: a town in the extreme S.W. of Italy on the Sicilian strait,
mod. Reggio di Calabria.

Puteolos: see on Vitell. 12.
inopinanti patri: Josephus (B.I. vii 119) says that his father was
expecting Titus and went forth to welcome him: τοῦ πλοῦ δ᾽ αὐτῷ κατὰ
νοῦν ἀνυσθέντος, ὁμοίως μὲν ἡ ῾Ρώμη περὶ τὴν ὑποδοχὴν εἶχε καὶ τὰς ὑπαντήσεις
ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ πατρός, λαμπρότερον δ᾽ ἦν Τίτῳ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ πατὴρ ὑπαντῶν καὶ
δεχόμενος.

arguens: redarguens, refellens, refutans; cf. Tac. A. iv 11, mihi
tradendi arguendique rumoris causa fuit, ut claro sub exemplo falsas
auditiones depellerem. This use of arguere is not found before Livy.

rumorum: the canards that he would not return to Italy, but would
found a new kingdom in the East.

temeritatem: = vanitatem "groundlessness” “idleness"; cf. Dom. 15,
3, ad coarguendam temeritatem artis (mathematicae). The relations
between Titus and Vespasian are examined exhaustively by Weynand
(Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2706 sqq.), and he shows that there is not the smallest
reason to assume any want of loyalty on the part of Titus towards his
father, or the existence of any friction between them. In the interview
which, according to Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vi 30), took place at Tarsus
between Titus and Apollonius of Tyana, the philosopher Apollonius congratulates Titus on his readiness to subordinate himself in all things to
his father and to render him homage.

participem imperii agere: so Tacitus (H. ii 83) describes Mucianus
as “socium magis imperii quam ministrum agens." For agere in the
sense of agere partes cf. Claud. 29, 1, non principem sed ministrum egit:
Tib. 12, 2, obnoxium et trepidum agit: 26, 2, privatum egit. Distinguish
agere se gerere se "to pass oneself off as"; Claud. 25, 1, libertini, qui
se pro equitibus R. agerent. For the position of the particeps (consors)
imperii in relation to the Princeps see on Tit. 9, 3, consortem successoremque.
Titus returned to Rome ἰσομοιρήσων τῆς ἀρχῆς τῷ πατρί (Philostr. l.c.). Bury
(Stud. Rom. Emp. p. 377) says: “Vespasian followed the example of
Augustus and the more recent example of Galba, in taking to himself a
consort in the Empire. Both the proconsular imperium and the tribunician
power were conferred on his son Titus at the same time, and thus Titus
held a position like that which Tiberius held in the last years of Augustus.
The object of Vespasian was not to lighten his own labours, but to secure
the succession for his son. Titus was allowed to assume more of the
imperial privileges than had been conceded to any consort before. He
wore the laurel wreath and vota were offered in his name. He also
styled himself Imperator; but while Vespasian used this title as a
praenomen, Titus bore it as a cognomen (Titus Caesar Imperator
Vespasianus)." The difficulties connected with the varying application of
the title Imperator to Titus on coins and in inscriptions during his father's
reign are discussed by Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2708 sqq.); Schiller,
Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i 508; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1154.

triumphavit censuramque gessit una: see Vesp. 8, 1 (notes).

collega in tribunicia potestate: marking him as Vespasian's successor.
The tribunicia potestas had previously been shared by Augustus, first with
Agrippa and then with Tiberius, and by Tiberius with Drusus; cf. Tac.
A. iii 56, Tiberius
mittit litteras ad senatum, queis potestatem
tribuniciam Druso petebat. Id summi fastigii vocabulum Augustus
repperit, ne regis aut dictatoris nomen adsumeret ac tamen appellatione
aliqua cetera imperia praemineret. Marcum deinde Agrippam socium eius
potestatis, quo defuncto Tiberium Neronem delegit, ne successor in incerto
foret. See also on Vesp. 12.

septem consulatibus: in 70, 72, 74-77, 79 A.D.; cf. Vesp. 8, 1. Pliny
(N.H. praef. 3), addressing Titus, says: Triumphalis et censorius tu,
sexiesque consul, ac tribuniciae potestatis particeps: et quod his nobilius
fecisti dum illud patri pariter et equestri ordini praestas, praefectus praetorio
eius. Pliny's work was published in 77 A.D.
orationes in senatu recitaret: Vespasian used both his sons (Titus
and Domitian) for this purpose according to Dio lxvi 10, ὅσα μὴ ἐδύνατο
αὐτὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ γήρως ἀναλέγεσθαι, ἢ καὶ ὅσα ἀπὼν ἐπέστελλε τῇ βουλῇ, διὰ τῶν υἱέων
αὐτοῦ ὡς τὸ πολὺ ἐκέλευεν ἀναγιγνώσκεσθαι, τιμῶν κὰν τούτῳ αὐτήν. For orationes
see on Dom. 2, 3.

quaestoris vice: the principal duty of those quaestors who were
nominated by the emperor (quaestores Caesaris, see on Vitell. 1, 2) was to
read to the senate communications from him; cf. Aug. 65, 2, libello per
quaestorem recitato notum senatui fecit: Dio liv 25, τὸ βιβλίον τῷ ταμίᾳ
(quaestori) ἀναγνῶναι δούς : Tac. A. xvi 27, oratio principis per quaestorem
eius audita est. Nero departed from the usual custom; Suet. Ner. 15, 2,
orationes ad senatum missas, praeterito quaestorum officio, per consulem
plerumque recitabat. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 569.

praefecturam praetorii: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, 10, (Titum) victorem
praefectura praetorio extulerat (Vespasianus). Unde etiam is honos, ingens
a principio, tumidior atque alter ab Augusto imperio fuit. For an account
of this office see on c. 4, 2. Suetonius is inaccurate in saying that Titus
was the first prefect who was not an eques, for Arrecinus Clemens (see
Dom. 11, 1), who was appointed by Mucianus before the arrival of Vespasian
in Rome in the autumn of 70, was a senator; Tac. H. iv 68 Arrecinum
Clementem praetorianis praeposuit, dictitans
ipsum, quamquam
senatorii ordinis, ad utraque munia (i.e. the duties of senator and prefect)
sufficere. Augustus had followed the advice of Maecenas in ordaining that
these prefects should be equites. M. Aurelius lamented that he could not
make Pertinax praefectus praetorii because he was a senator (Capitol.
Pert. 2). Alexander Severus made it his practice to promote his prefects
of the guard to the rank of senator, in order that they might belong to
the class of Viri Clarissimi and be so addressed (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 21).

egit: sc. praefecturam; cf. Tib. 24, 1, principatum agere.

incivilius: cf. Flor. i 26, altius se et incivilius efferens. See note on

summissis: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 4, praefecturam praetorianam patre
imperante adeptus, suspectum quemque et oppositum sibi, immissis, qui per
theatra et castris invidiosa iactantes ad poenam poscerent, quasi criminis
convictos oppressit. Suetonius uses summittere in the sense of sending
secretly, e.g. Galb. 23; also in the sense of suborning (subornare, ὑφιέναι),
e.g. Ner. 28, 1, Acten libertam paulum afuit quin iusto sibi matrimonio
coniungeret, summissis consularibus viris qui regio genere ortam peierarent.

theatra: in the theatres and circus the people, accustomed to call
for their favourite actors and gladiators, often indulged in outbursts of
political feeling and clamorously demanded reforms, executions, etc.
Cicero mentions such demonstrations in his day (e.g. Att. i 16, Sest. 54,
115); and under the Empire, when public assemblies were abolished, the
gatherings of the people in the theatres and at other shows became the
regular occasions of giving expression to public demands. Cf. Dom. 13, 1;
Тас. Н. i 32, 72; A. vi 13. Tiberius avoided the shows on account of this
licence: Tib. 47, Neque spectacula omnino edidit; et iis quae ab aliquo
ederentur rarissime interfuit, ne quid exposceretur. See Hardy on Plut.
Galb. 17, & ῾Ῥωμαίων δῆμος . ἐν πᾶσι θεάτροις καὶ σταδίοις αἰτούμενος ἐκεῖνον (i.e.
demanding the execution of Tigellinus; cf. Suet. Galb. 15, 2).

§2. Aulum Caecinam: Aulus Caecina Alienus was quaestor in
Hispania Baetica in 68 A.D., the year of Nero's death. He was one of the
first to side with Galba, who gave him the command of a legion in Upper
Germany; but shortly afterwards Galba ordered his prosecution for
peculation, and Caecina, to be revenged, induced his troops to declare for
Vitellius (Tac. H. i 53). He was chosen general by Vitellius and led an
army into Italy, taking part in the battle of Betriacum. When Vitellius
took possession of Rome, Caecina was made consul (Sept. 1, 69). Later
he was sent by Vitellius to meet Antonius Primus and the Flavian forces,
but he proved a traitor (see note on “proditus,” Vitell. 15, 2).
(lxvi 16) agrees with Suetonius that Titus had Caecina assassinated on
account of his revolutionary designs against Vespasian: 'Αλιηνὸς μὲν αὐτοῦ
ἐν τῷ βασιλείῳ, ἐξαναστὰς ἐκ τοῦ συσσιτίου, εὐθὺς ἀπεσφάγη, τοῦ Τίτου κελεύσαντος,
μὴ καὶ φθάσῃ τι τῆς νυκτός νεοχμῶσαι· τῶν γὰρ στρατιωτῶν συχνοὺς προπαρεσκεύαστο.
In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 4 a different reason is assigned: Caecinam consularem adhibitum cenae, vixdum triclinio egressum, ob suspicionem
stupratae Berenices uxoris suae iugulari iussit.

καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἐς τὴν ῾Ρώμην μετὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τοῦ ᾿Αγρίππα ἦλθε. καὶ ὁ μὲν
στρατηγικῶν τιμῶν ἠξιώθη, ἡ δὲ ἐν τῷ Παλατίῳ ᾤκησε, καὶ τῷ Τίτῳ συνεγίγνετο,

ἐρωτικὸν μοναρχήσας ἔπραξεν, ἀλλὰ σώφρων,
καίτοι καὶ τῆς Βερενίκης ἐς ῾Ρώμην αὖθις ἐλθούσης, ἐγένετο. Julia Berenice was
a daughter of Agrippa I, king of the Jews, and was born in 28 A.D. After
a brief early marriage to Marcus, son of the alabarch Alexander, she
wedded her uncle Herod, and on his death in 48 she lived (incestuously?)
with her brother Agrippa II. The apostle Paul appeared before them in
60 (Acts 25, 26). She and her brother tried to dissuade the Jews from
rebellion, and after the war broke out they seem to have lived in the
Roman camp. She was a warm supporter of Vespasian; cf. Tac. H. ii 81,
nec minore animo regina Berenice partes iuvabat, florens aetate formaque
et seni quoque Vespasiano magnificentia munerum grata. In 75 she came
to Rome along with her brother, and lived with Titus as though she were
his wife. Juvenal (vi 157) mentions a diamond ring of hers on sale at
Rome: adamans notissimus et Berenices | in digito factus pretiosior: hunc
dedit olim | barbarus incestae, dedit hunc Agrippa sorori.

mutavit

cognitionibus: restored by Torrentius for contionibus.
proposed negotiationibus; Boden cocionibus; Cornelissen auctionibus.
Cognitio in the special sense was a legal term for a iudicium extra
ordinem, a hearing of a case not in the ordinary courts but by the emperor,
the senate, or magistrates commissioned by them, such as provincial
governors; cf. Claud. 15, 1, negantem cognitionis rem sed ordinarii iuris
esse. In Plin. Ep. vi 31 we have examples of the variety of cognitiones
conducted by Trajan aided by assessors (of whom Pliny was one), and in
Ep. x 96 Pliny mentions cognitiones de Christianis by provincial governors.
Cognitio was also used at times in the wider sense of iudicium, any
ordinary trial (ius ordinarium).

nundinari: Titus trafficked in the influence which he could use with
his father to have a case decided in a certain way. For the metaph. use
of nundinari in the sense of illicit trafficking by selling or buying cf.
Apul. Met. x 33, iudices sententias suas pretio nundinantur: Cic. Verr. i
119, qui ab isto ius ad utilitatem suam nundinarentur: Cic. Phil. iii 4,
una in domo omnes, quorum intererat, totum imperium populi Romani
nundinabantur.

praemia pacisci (Baumg.-Cr.), "to stipulate for a
reward." The word is not cited from any other author, but praemiati has
been suggested as a correction of praeminate in a corrupt line of Novius
(Ribb. Com. Rom. Frag. p. 257).

alterum, “a second"; cf. Tac. H. iv 73, ne quis alius
Ariovistus regno Galliarum potiretur: Curt. ix 8, alium Liberum patrem

pater. This use of alius is post-class.; see Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 132:

pro bono cessit: "turned out to his advantage"; cf. Sall. Iug. 22,
populum Romanum neque recte neque pro bono ("to their advantage'')
facturum, si etc. "Cedere pro aliqua re” meant to go for (to be counted
as),'' e.g. Tac. Germ. 14, epulae . pro stipendio cedunt (see Thes. Ling.
Lat. iii 732). Suetonius might have used in bonum cessit; cf. Plin. N.H.
xviii 110, montium culpa in bonum cedit: Sen. Ep. 71, mala in bonum
abibunt: Cic. Brut. 141, hoc vitium huic uni in bonum convertebat.

conversa in maximas laudes: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 6, sed haec in

§ 2. convivia iucunda magis quam profusa: like the dinners of
Augustus, Aug. 74, cenam ternis ferculis ("courses”) aut cum abundissime
senis praebebat, ut non nimio sumptu, ita summa comitate.

amicos elegit, quibus usi: the term amici is not used here in the
general sense of those admitted to receptions at court (salutationes, see
Vesp. 4, 4); it denotes the trusted confidants and advisers (consiliarii) of
Titus; cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 835, n. 3. Similarly Pliny (Pan. 88)
says of the imperial freedmen of Trajan: neminem in usu habes nisi aut
tibi aut patri tuo aut optimo cuique principum (especially Titus) dilectum.

adquieverunt: adquiescere is used by Suetonius (1) of finding peace
or comfort in, Calig. 51, 3, uno solacio adquiescens; (2) of taking delight
in, Tib. 56, convictores Graeculos quibus (dat.) vel maxime adquiescebat;
(3) of being satisfied with, content to rely upon, as here and in Vitell. 14,
5, vaticinante Chatta muliere, cui velut oraculo adquiescebat; (4) of being
content to devote one's whole attention to something, Tib. 31, negante eo
destinatos magistratus abesse oportere, ut praesentes honori (i.e. their
office) adquiescerent (Bentley and Mommsen would read adsuescerent).

Berenicen dimisit: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 7, Denique, ut subiit
pondus regium, Berenicen nuptias suas sperantem regredi domum, et
enervatorum greges abire praecepit. Quo facto, quasi signum protulit
mutatae intemperantiae. According to Dio (quoted above on "Berenices
amorem''), Titus sent away Berenice during his father's reign, when he
saw that the Roman people were displeased at the way in which she
behaved as if she were already his wife; she returned to Rome when he
became emperor, but he would not yield to her blandishments.
The dismissal of Berenice by the emperor Titus is the theme of Racine's Bérénice,
which is thus summarised by Victor Hugo: Acti Titus Act ii reginam
Berenicen Act iii invitus Act iv invitam Act v dimisit. By his action Titus
"freed Rome from the danger of a second Cleopatra" (von Domaszewski,
Gesch. der röm. Kaiser, ii 155).

delicatorum: both delicatus and delicata (Vesp. 3) were used in the
sense of deliciae; cf. Petron. Satyr. 63, ipsimi nostri delicatus decessit
("my master's favourite died'').

quanquam: Suet. uses quanquam (a) c. subjunct. (never c. indic.),
see on Galb. 14, 1, quanquam
daret; (b) c. ptc., e.g. Galb. 19, 1, qu.
haud dissimulans; (c) c. abl. abs., e.g. Vesp. 2, 2, qu. fratre adepto latum
clavum; (d) c. abl. qual., e.g. Tit. 3, 1, qu. neque procera statura et ventre
paulo proiectiore; (e) c. gen. qual., e.g. Ner. 20, 1, qu. exiguae vocis et
fuscae; (f) c. adject., e.g. Aug. 8, 1, qu. expers belli; (g) c. subst., e.g.
Claud. 35, 1, qu. iactator; (h) c. prep., Aug. 27, 5, qu. sine censurae honore.
There is only one instance in Cic. of quanquam without a finite verb;
Fin. v 68, si omnia illa, quae sunt extra, quanquam expetenda, summo bono
continerentur (to avoid the repetition of sunt). For instances in other
authors see Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii² 815; Kühner-Stegmann, ii 445.

cf. Cic. Orat. 161, quod si indocta consuetudo tam est artifex suavitatis:

ut scaenam tenuerint: cf. Euseb.-Hieron. Chron., ad a. 1974 (43 в.с.),.

in publico coetu: Torrentius deleted coetu, and Burman regarded it
as having originated from the last syllable of publico and the first of
supersedit. Suetonius uses in publico for "in public" in Claud. 13, 1;

§ 3. nulli civium quicquam ademit: cf. Plin. Pan. 27, nihil largiatur
Princeps, dum nihil auferat.

abstinuit alieno: cf. Plin. Ep. vi 8, Atilius Crescens alieni abstinentissimus, sui diligens (contrast Sall. Cat. 5, L. Catilina alieni appetens, sui
profusus): Tac. H. i 49, Galba pecuniae alienae non appetens, suae parcus,
publicae avarus. So abstinentia (ἐγκράτεια χρημάτων) is opposed to avaritia
and rapacitas; e.g. Dom. 9, 1:10, 1:23, 2.

ut si quis umquam: Ernesti would omit ut, but there is as unusual a
pleonasm in Claud. 21, 5, immixtis interdum frigidis et arcessitis iocis:
qualis est ut cum Palumbum (“The Dove," name of a gladiator) postulantibus daturum se promisit, si captus esset (Ernesti rejects qualis est as
a gloss on ut). Cf. also Vesp. 7, 2, ut scilicet. In Xen. Anab. ii 6, 8
some MSS. have ἱκανός, ὡς εἴ τις καὶ ἄλλος, φροντίζειν ἦν. Plutarch and later
writers use ὡς οἷον, ὡς οἷα, etc.

ne concessas quidem conlationes recepit: in the case of some of
the earlier emperors Suetonius mentions conlationes, either freely given or
as involuntary as English “benevolences.” For a free-will offering cf.
Aug. 57, 2, In restitutionem Palatinae domus, incendio absumptae, veterani,
decuriae, tribus, atque etiam singillatim e cetero genere hominum, libenter
ac pro facultate quisque contulerunt. The compulsory conlatio is illustrated by Ner. 38, 3 (after the burning of Rome), conlationibus non receptis
modo verum et efflagitatis provincias privatorumque census prope exhausit:
Ner. 44, 2, In praeparanda expeditione (against Vindex) partem census
omnes ordines conferre iussit, et insuper inquilinos privatarum aedium;
atque insularum (‘lodging-houses'") pensionem annuam repraesentare (i.e.
to pay a year's rent at once) fisco. Caligula, when his daughter was born,
pleaded poverty and received conlationes for the girl's maintenance and
dowry (Calig. 42). On New Year's day all the citizens brought a strena
or "luck-penny" to the emperor (Aug. 57, Tib. 34, Calig. 42). Pliny
(Pan. 41) mentions “conlationes remisisse" among Trajan's benefactions;
this presumably refers to the aurum coronarium which was paid by the
provincials and others on the occasion of an emperor's accession, any
great victory, or any important event in the imperial house; the payment
of it was remitted by Hadrian, Alexander Severus, and Julian, as it had
been by Augustus (in 29 B.C.) in the case of the Italian municipia and
coloniae.
nemine: for this form see on Vitell. 17, 1.

amphitheatro: the Colosseum, see Vesp. 9, 1. It was dedicated in
80 A.D. by Titus with a festival lasting 100 days.
thermis: these baths of Titus were probably built, not on the ruins,
but in a garden or park, of the Aurea Domus of Nero which extended
from the Palatine to the Esquiline (see Oth. 7, 1). They were connected
with the Flavian amphitheatre by a portico, traces of which can still be
seen. It was near the site of these thermae that the famous group of
Laocoon and his sons was found. The earliest thermae under the Empire
were those bequeathed to Rome by M. Agrippa in the reign of Augustus.
These were followed by those of Nero, Titus, Trajan, Caracalla, Diocletian,
and Constantine. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 275 sqq.; Jordan-Huelsen,
Topogr. Rom i 3, 307 sqq. thermae, as distinct from balneae (ordinary
bathing-rooms or houses), were luxurious establishments on the model of
the Greek γυμνάσιον, containing, besides hot and vapour baths, all the
equipment for gymnastic exercises, colonnaded halls (exedrae) where
philosophers and poets congregated, etc.

celeriter: this correction by Calderinus of celebriter is based on Mart.
Spect. 2, 7, Hic ubi miramur velocia munera thermas, | abstulerat miseris
tecta superbus ager (i.e. Nero's proud domain had robbed the poor of
their dwellings).

munus edidit: munus edere (more rarely dare) was the regular phrase
for giving a gladiatorial show, the giver being called editor by the
writers of the Historia Augusta. So edere (dare) gladiatores (spectaculum gladiatorium). See also on munerarius in Dom. 10, 1.

apparatissimum largissimumque: cf. Cic. Sest. 54, ludi apparatissimi
et magnificentissimi.

in veteri naumachia: naumachia was used in two senses: (1) a Roman
representation of a sea-fight (navale proelium); (2) as here, the place
where the representation was given (= navale stagnum, Stat. S. iv 4, 5:
Tac. A. xiv 15). The first public naumachia was exhibited by Julius
Caesar (46 B.c.) in a district called Codeta Minor, prob. in the Campus
Martius near the Tiber (Suet. Iul. 39, Dio xliii 23). The second was a
representation by Augustus (2 B.C.) of the battle of Salamis in a new
basin (1800 × 1200 ft., Mon. Ancyr. 23) dug in the Transtiberine region
and surrounded by a grove called the nemus Caesarum after the young
Lucius and Gaius (Aug. 43). The third was a splendid spectacle by
Claudius (52 A.D.) on Lake Fucinus (Claud. 21: Tac. A. xii 56). Nero's
naumachiae are mentioned in Dio lxi 9, lxii 15; they were held either in
the amphitheatre or in the stagna Neronis, a huge basin in the grounds
of Nero's Golden House. Titus exhibited two sea-fights, the one mentioned
here in the vetus naumachia of Augustus, which continued in use after
others had been made, and the other (between the Corcyraeans and
Corinthians) in the flooded arena of the new amphitheatre (Dio lxvi 25:
Mart. Spect. 24). Domitian had a new and larger lake dug below the
Vatican, and also gave a naumachia in the Flavian amphitheatre (Dom. 4:
Dio lxvii 8).

ibidem et gladiatores: in his account of the spectacles exhibited by
Titus in the vetus naumachia Dio (lxvi 25) says that on the first day the
basin was partly covered with planks supported on piles, and it furnished
an arena for gladiatorial contests and a venatio (wild-beast hunt); on the
second day, the basin being drained, there was a chariot-race; on the
third, the basin being refilled, there was a naval battle of 3000 Athenians
and Syracusans, in the course of which the Athenians landed on an island
in the basin and took a fort there. These diverse spectacles are lauded
by Martial, Spect. 28: Quidquid et in Circo spectatur et Amphitheatro,
id dives, Caesar, praestitit unda tibi. | Fucinus et diri taceantur stagna
Neronis: | hanc norint unam saecula naumachiam.

quinque milia
ferarum: Eutrop. vii 21, Romae amphitheatrum
aedificavit, et quinque milia ferarum in dedicatione eius occidit. The
total of wild and tame animals killed was 9000 according to Dio (l.c.). In
the 26 venationes given by Augustus 3,500 African wild beasts were slain:
Mon. Ancyr. 22, Venationes bestiarum Africanarum meo nomine aut
filiorum meorum et nepotum in circo aut in foro aut in amphitheatris
populo dedi sexiens et viciens, quibus confecta sunt bestiarum circiter tria
milia et quingentae. At the celebration of Trajan's second Dacian triumph
(107 A.D.) 11,000 animals were slain. For other examples see Friedlaender,
Sitteng. ii10 81.

omne genus: cf. Dom. 4, 5, omne genus rerum missilia sparsit: Claud. 34,
2, de fabrorum ac ministrorum atque id genus numero. Originally id genus,
omne genus, etc., stood in apposition to the nom. or acc., but from Varro's
time are joined with other cases in a purely adverbial fashion; e.g. Varr.
R.R. iii 9, 17, aliis id genus rebus: Lucr. vi 917, hoc genus in rebus. So
quod genus = cuius generis; e.g. Cic. Inv. ii 157, quod genus pecunia est.
Suetonius uses another adverbial acc. in Gramm. 4, 2, alia hoc genus; and
in Aug. 44, 3, muliebre secus omne, Gronovius' conjecture omnes seems
right. Cf. also illud aetatis in Galb. 14, 2.

dehinc: sometimes so used in post-Aug. writers referring to a point
in past time "from that time on” “thenceforward,” inde ab hoc, Germ.
von da an, von dem an; cf. Calig. 58, 2, duplex dehinc fama est (= de
rebus quae inde ab eo tempore factae sunt, duplex est fama). See Hand
'Tursell. ii 231.

beneficia: Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1126, shows by numerous examples
that beneficia (τιμαί) was the technical term for the advantageous rights
bestowed by the emperor on communities, classes, and individuals, such as
the free occupation of State lands, and exemptions of various kinds. These
beneficia were revocable by the emperor who granted them, and became
invalid at his death. At first they were only renewed after a separate
examination of each case by his successor.

aliter rata non haberent: rata, which was supplied by Egnatius, gives
excellent sense and would easily have been lost after aliter.
Alexander
proposed to omit principibus and to read beneficia a superioribus concessa
<aseconcessa> aliter non haberent.

uno confirmavit edicto: Dio lxvi 19, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλα πρός τε τὸ ἀσφαλές
καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἄλυπον τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατεστήσατο. καὶ γὰρ γράμματα ἐξέθηκε,
βεβαιῶν πάντα τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν προτέρων αὐτοκρατόρων δοθέντα τισίν, ὥστε μὴ καθ'
ἑκάστους σφῶν αἰτοῦντας αὐτὸν πράγματα ἔχειν: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 2, denique
cum concessa per priores principes firmari ab insequentibus mos esset, simul
imperium cepit, talia possidentibus edicto sponte cavit. The edicts of the
emperors were a continuation of the magisterial edicts of Republican
times. Sometimes they contained a definite command, sometimes a mere
communication or exhortation or remonstrance (cf. Mommsen, ii 905;
Hardy on Plin. Ep. x 58). Augustus used them even to answer lampoons:
iocis quorundam invidiosis aut petulantibus lacessitus, contradixit edicto
(Aug. 56, 1, where see Shuckburgh). Claudius issued as many as 20 in a
day, one being "ut uberi vinearum proventu bene dolia picarentur,
(Claud. 16, 4). The innovation of Titus in confirming previous beneficia
by one general edict was followed by subsequent emperors. Pliny (Ep. x
58) has recorded in full the edict of Nerva; Domitian's is mentioned by
Dio (lxvii 2), and that of Marcus Aurelius by his son Commodus (quoted
in Dig. xxvii 1, 8).

hominum: Bentley ingeniously suggested that this is a corruption
of hunc morem; cf. Ner. 15, 1, cognoscendi morem eum tenuit, ut
Galb. 4, 4, morem obstinatissime retinuit, ut On the other hand, homines
is often used by Suetonius for the people" "the emperor's subjects";
e.g. Ner. 39, 1, mirum fuerit nihil eum patientius quam maledicta et
convicia hominum tulisse. Bentley would further alter tenuit ne to tenuit
ut ne, which is quite needless.

tenuit, ne : "held firmly to his rule of not..." Livy and later
writers use tenere with ut or ne in the sense of carrying one's point; e.g.
Liv. ii 42, 2, tenuere patres, ut Fabius consul crearetur: iv 30, 16, plebs
tenuit, ne consules in proximum annum crearentur: Plin. Ep. vi 5, scripseram tenuisse Varenum ut sibi evocare testes liceret.
admonentibus domesticis: cf. Vesp. 22, admonente dispensatore.
quasi plura polliceretur: for quasi see on c. 5, 3.

tristem discedere: Eutrop. vii 21, facilitatis et liberalitatis tantum
fuit, ut, cum nulli quicquam negaret et ab amicis reprehenderetur, responderit nullum tristem debere ab imperatore discedere: Cedrenus (p. 178),
ἀπὸ βασιλέως δεῖ σκυθρωπὸν μὴ ἀποπέμπεσθαι. For tristis used of a disappointed
applicant cf. Lucr. iii 997, Qui petere a populo fasces saevasque secures |
imbibit et semper victus tristisque recedit.

super cenam: "over" i.e. "during" dinner. Cf. Germ. über Tische,
über Tafel; Gr. ἐπὶ δείπνῳ, ἐπὶ κύλικι (Baumg.-Cr.). super in a temporal
sense (= inter) is post-Aug. and found only in a few phrases: super cenam
(11 times in Suet., e.g. Vesp. 22: Vitell. 12: Dom. 14, 1:21; Curt. viii 43:
Plin. Ep. iii 5, etc.: Juv. xv 14); super mensam (Curt. vii 4); super
mensas et pocula (Flor. iv 2, 69); super vinum et epulas (Curt. viii 4);
super hos divum .. honores (Stat. Th. i 676).

acc. and inf. is fully discussed by Madvig (Opusc. Acad. ii 232 sqq.) and
Kühner-Stegmann (ii 274 sqq.). There are a few apparent instances in
old Lat.: Plaut. Asin. 52, scio iam filius quod amet meus istanc meretricem
(where Brix takes quod amet as amicam): Cato in Plin. N.H. 29, 14,
quod bonum sit illorum litteras inspicere, non perdiscere, vincam (where
some explain quod bonum sit as quid boni sit). In class. Lat. there is
no sure instance. The first certain example is in Auct. Bell. Hisp. 36,
renuntiarunt quod Pompeium in potestate haberent. In post-class. times
it occurs in Petron. 71, scis, quod epulum dedi: Plin. Ep. ii 11, 6,
adnotatum experimentis, quod ... habent: Justin i 7, 9, cognito quod
inlatum Croeso bellum esset: Tac. A. xiv 6, reputans ideo se fallacibus
litteris accitam et praecipuo honore habitam, quodque litus iuxta non ventis
acta navis concidisset (where quodque may be taken as et id, quod).
From the middle of the 2nd cent. it occurs with increasing frequency in
Apuleius, Gellius, the Scriptores Hist. Aug., Eutropius, Ammianus, and the

Christian writers. The use in Gr. of οἵνεκα, ὁθούνεκα, διότι instead of ὅτι
with verba sentiendi and declarandi is similar.

memorabilem vocem: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 9, Quadam etiam die,
recordans vesperi nihil se cuiquam praestitisse, venerando caelestique dicto
"Amici,” ait, “perdidimus diem”: quia erat magnificae liberalitatis:
Themistius Orat. vi, Τίτου τοῦ γενναίου τὸ λαμπρὸν καὶ μέγα ἐκεῖνο ῥῆμα, ὅτι
Τήμερον οὐκ ἐβασίλευσα· οὐδὲν γὰρ εὖ ἐποίησα: Zonaras xi 18, Τούτου ἐστὶ καὶ
ἡ ἀοίδιμος ἐκείνη φωνή, εἰπόντος: σήμερον οὐκ ἐβασίλευσα, ἐπεὶ οὐδένα εὐηργέτησα.
Ausonius, Grat. Act. xvi, says that the fame of the utterance was due to
the contrast of such generosity with the meanness of Vespasian: Celebre
fuit Titi Caesaris dictum, perdidisse se diem, quo nihil boni fecerat; sed
celebre fuit, quia Vespasiani successor dixerat, cuius nimia parsimonia et
austeritas vix ferenda miram fecerat filii lenitatem.

diem perdidi: since Eutropius (vii 21, 3) gives the utterance as
“amici, hodie diem perdidi" (so too Euseb.-Hieron. Chron.) and Themistius
and Zonaras have τήμερον and σήμερον, Casaubon would read hodie diem
here. Hase quotes from the speech of Titus in Racine's Bérénice (iv 4):
“Où sont ces heureux jours que je faisais attendre? | Quels pleurs ai-je
séchés? Dans quels yeux satisfaits | Ai-je déjà goûté le fruit de mes
bienfaits? | L'univers a-t-il vu changer ses destinées? | Sais-je combien le
ciel m'a compté de journées? | Et de ce peu de jours, si longtemps
attendus, | Ah! malheureux! combien j'en ai déjà perdus!”
Pliny
(Pan. 56) in his flattery of Trajan says that he did not let even a moment
pass without some benefaction: Quod momentum, quod immo temporis
punctum, aut beneficio sterile, aut vacuum laude? So too Ausonius (l.c.)
says to Gratianus: "Neque vero unum aliquod bonum uno die praestas,
sed indulgentias saeculares per singula horarum momenta multiplicas.”

§ 2. proposito: sc. per edictum; cf. Aug. 42, 2, proposito congiario:
Ner. 7, 2, populo congiarium, militi donativum proposuit: Claud. 18, 2,
negotiatoribus certa lucra proposuit.
editurum: see on c. 7, 3.

ut peterent, ultro adhortatus est: Pliny (Pan. 33) says the same
of Trajan's readiness to give spectacles: Impetratum est quod postulabatur;
oblatum quod non postulabatur; institit ultro, et, ut concupisceremus,
admonuit. The adv. ultro meant (1) ‘to the further side" (opp. to citro);
(2) "furthermore”; (3) ‘beyond what could be expected of one,” “of
one's own accord." Gladiators who were kept in reserve and only produced
at the special request of the spectators were called postulaticii (Sen.
Ερ. 7, 4).

armaturae Thraecum: the class of gladiators known as Thraeces were
so called from their small round shields like those of the Thracians (a
similitudine parmularum Thraciarum, Paul. ex Fest. p. 366 M.); cf. parmae
Threcidicae, Plin. N.H. xxxiii 129. They carried a short curved sword
(sica, Suet. Calig. 32; falx supina, Juv. viii 201) and wore greaves (ocreae).
They were usually pitted against murmillones (so called from the image
of a fish mormyr, μορμύρος, on their helmets), who were heavily armed and
carried a big oblong shield (scutum). Caligula fought as a Thraex, and
reduced the amount of armour of the murmillones (Suet. Calig. 54, 55).
On one occasion a murmillo fought him in a sham contest with wooden
swords (rudes) and fell on purpose, whereupon Caligula stabbed him with
a real sica, and ran about with a palm-branch as victors do (ib. 32). The
form Thraex, to denote a gladiator, is attested by the best MSS. and by
inscriptions (see Orelli-Mewes on Hor. S. ii 6, 44, Thraex est Gallina Syro
par?); Thrax meant a Thracian.

cum populo cavillatus est: this is rightly explained by Baumg.-Cr.
as cum populo, diversae factioni favente, iocose altercatus est ut fautor
Thraecum. Suetonius always uses cavillatio in the sense of a jest or
witticism; cf. Vesp. 23, 1, ut invidiam aliqua cavillatione dilueret: Tib.
57, 2, acerba cavillatio “a brutal witticism": Gramm. 3, cavillatio nominis
"a pun on a name." For cavillari cum cf. Cic. Att. ii 1, 5, familiariter
cum ipso cavillor ac iocor.

ut fautor: partizanship in the amphitheatre, though not so intense
as in the circus, was very strong among all classes, and some of the
emperors were notorious for it. This partizanship was exhibited not only
towards individual gladiators, but also towards the various kinds of
combatants (Friedl. Sitteng. ii10 75). Caligula and Titus favoured the
Thraeces; Domitian the murmillones (see Dom. 10, 1, and notes there).
Tacitus (H. ii 91) says of Vitellius: omnem infimae plebis rumorem
("applause") in theatro ut spectator, in circo ut fautor adfectavit.

maiestate salva: cf. Tac. A. i 47, maiestate salva, cui maior e longinquo
reverentia. Contrast the undignified conduct of Claudius at the gladiatoria
munera, as described in Claud. 21, 5: Nec ullo spectaculi genere communior aut remissior erat, adeo ut oblatos victoribus aureos ("gold coins")
prolata sinistra pariter cum vulgo voce digitisque numeraret ac saepe
hortando rogandoque ad hilaritatem homines provocaret, "dominos"
identidem appellans, immixtis interdum frigidis et arcessitis (“farfetched'') iocis. Vespasian too was lacking in dignity in his lighter
moments; see Vesp. 22.

aequitate: the same impartiality in observing the leges harenae and
bestowing on the victors the promised rewards, regardless of the class
to which they belonged, is attributed to Trajan by Pliny, Pan. 33, Quam
deinde in edendo (munere gladiatorio) liberalitatem, quam iustitiam exhibuit
omni affectione aut intactus aut maior!
ne quid praetermitteret: cf. Vesp. 8, 3, ne quam occasionem corrigendi disciplinam praetermitteret.
thermis suis: see c. 7, 3.

admissa plebe lavit: an example followed by Alexander Severus; cf.
Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 42, Thermis et suis et veterum frequenter cum populo
usus est, et aestate maxime, balneari veste ad Palatium revertens, hoc
solum imperatorium habens quod lacernam cocceam accipiebat. Einhard
(c. 22) relates the same of Charlemagne: Non solum filios ad balneum,
verum optimates et amicos, aliquando etiam satellitum et custodum corporis
turbam invitavit; ita ut nonnunquam centum vel eo amplius homines
lavarentur.

§ 3. sub eo: "in his reign"; cf. Calig. 21, opera sub Tiberio semiperfecta: Tac. Agr. 6, gnarus sub Nerone temporum: ib. 45, praecipua
sub Domitiano miseriarum pars erat. Such designations of time are post-class. (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 557).

fortuita: the subst. fortuita (= fortuito accidentia) is used of accidents
of fortune, disasters; cf. Ner. 39, 1, Accesserunt tantis ex principe malis
probrisque quaedam et fortuita: pestilentia unius autumni, etc.; Tac. A. xiv
3, nihil tam capax fortuitorum quam mare.

ac: intensive, ac quidem. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 16.

conflagratio Vesuvii: the famous eruption on the 24th of August,
79 A.D., which overwhelmed Herculaneum and Pompeii. It is vividly
described by Pliny in two letters to Tacitus (vi 16 and 20); his uncle,
the elder Pliny, perished in it. See also Dio lxvi 21-23. The earthquake
which accompanied it caused widespread havoc in Campania. The corruptions in the MSS. make it impossible to determine which of the various
forms of the name of the volcano (Vesuvius, Vesevus, Vesaevus, Vesvius,
Vesbius) was used by Suetonius. Here ue*bii is the reading of M, uesubii
of G, ueseui of N; a few lines later M has uesuuio, G uesubio, L uesieuio,
the rest ueseuio or ueseuo. Roth and Preud'homme adopt the form Vesvius,
Ihm Vesuvius.

incendium Romae: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 12, Huius tempore mons
Vesuvius in Campania ardere coepit, incendiumque Romae sine nocturna
requie per triduum fuit. Dio (lxvi 24) mentions that the fire occurred in
80 A.D., while Titus was absent from Rome relieving the distress in
Campania; he also gives a list of the principal buildings which were
destroyed by the fire: πῦρ δὲ δὴ ἕτερον ἐπίγειον τῷ ἑξῆς ἔτει πολλὰ πάνυ τῆς

τό τε βαλανεῖον τὸ τοῦ ᾿Αγρίππου, καὶ τὸ Πάνθειον, τό τε Διριβιτώριον, καὶ τὸ τοῦ

κατέκαυσεν. Of these buildings the Serapeum, Isaeum, Saepta, Templum

all situated in the southern part of the Campus Martius, on the north side
of the Capitoline.

pestilentia: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 13, lues quoque, quanta vix unquam
antea fuit. This must be the plague at Rome in which on many days
about 10,000 perished, assigned to the reign of Vespasian in Euseb.-Hieron.
Chron. (ad a. 2093, i.e. 77 A.D.): Lues ingens Romae facta, ita ut per
multos dies in ephemeridem decem milia ferme mortuorum referrentur.
Dio (lxvi 23) says that the ashes from Vesuvius were carried to Rome
(also to Africa, Egypt, and Syria) and overhung the city, obscuring the
sun, and that this was the cause of the pestilence which came later: ἡ μὲν
οὖν τέφρα αὕτη οὐδὲν μέγα τότε κακὸν αὐτοὺς εἰργάσατο, ὕστερον δὲ νόσον σφίσι
λοιμώδη δεινὴν ἐνέβαλε. Plagues raged at Rome and throughout Italy in
23 and 22 B.C. (Dio liii 33, liv 1), and in 65 A.D. during Nero's reign Rome
was devastated by a pestilence, the horrors of which are depicted in Tac.
A. xvi 13; the 30,000 burials recorded in the Temple of Libitina during
that autumn were only a fractional part of the total mortality (Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 31).
non temere: see on c. 6, 2.
talibus: Cornelissen suggested fatalibus.

conlapsa restituit. For Vespasian's restoration of a temple at Herculaneum

bona quorum heredes non extabant: these, as bona vacantia, would
escheat to the fiscus.

nihil publice nisi perisse testatus: there is considerable variation
in the MSS. here: nichil nisi sibi perisse testatus publice (r); nichil nisi
sibi publice perisse testatus (OT vulg.); nichil nisi sibi perisse publice
testatus (N); nihil publice perisse testatus (Torrentius, from what he
describes as an "optimus codex," now unknown; Roth and Preud 'homme
adopt this reading). The confusion seems due to a mistaken effort to
connect the words nihil publice with perisse and not with testatus; but
the latter is the right construction, as is shown by Oth. 6, 3: nihil magis
pro contione testatus est, quam id demum se habiturum, quod sibi illi
reliquissent. Possibly se should be inserted after nisi. The only public
pronouncement of Titus was that he was a ruined man, i.e. that he would
be ruined by the cost of the rebuilding which he had at once resolved to
undertake at his own expense. Alexander (op. cit. p. 20) thinks the
original reading was nihil publice nisi sibi perisse testatus which he translates "nothing had perished in a public way save only so far as he was
concerned," the meaning being that Titus would shoulder the whole burden
and that there would be no extra tax-levies on the unfortunate citizens to
restore the ruined edifices. But though either nihil publice perisse or nihil
nisi sibi perisse would be intelligible, nihil publice nisi sibi perisse seems
very improbable.

praetoriorum: praetorium was used in the sense of a country mansion;
see Mayor on Juv. i 75 (criminibus debent hortos praetoria mensas) where
he cites Colum. i 6 to show that the villa in the wider sense, country seat,
was divided into (1) urbana, hall or residence; (2) rustica, farm; (3) fructuaria, stores, barns, etc.; and the urbana as "the headquarters of the
peaceful camp" was named praetorium (Pallad. i 8, 2 etc.). Augustus
disliked palatial country mansions (Aug. 72, 2, ampla et operosa praetoria
gravabatur). Caligula in building praetoria delighted in overcoming
natural obstacles by filling up seas and valleys and cutting away rocks and
mountains (Calig. 37, 2). praetorium has the same sense in Tib. 39;
Stat. S. i 3, 25: Mart. x 79, etc. Suetonius also uses it for the headquarters in a camp (e.g. Vitell. 8, 2) and for the praetorian guard (e.g.
Tit. 6, 1).

medendae valitudini: for the dative of purpose see on Oth. 3, 1. The
acc. with mederi (instead of the usual dat.) is very rare; it occurs once in
Terence (Phorm. 822) and then not till Livy (see the instances collected by
Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre iii 5).

nullam .. opem non adhibuit: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 14, quibus tamen
malis, nullo vexato, pecunia propria subvenit, cunctis remediorum generibus,
nunc aegrotantes per semetipsum reficiens, nunc consolans suorum mortibus
afflictos.

sacrificiorum: the plague was interpreted as a manifestation of divine
wrath for some offence which required to be expiated by the sacrifice of
hostiae piaculares.

§5. adversa: subst. = mala, calamitates; so a few lines earlier, in iis
tot adversis ac talibus.

delatores: this term for “informers” was derived from the giving
in the name (delatio nominis) of an accused person to the presidents of
the quaestiones perpetuae. The rewards to be obtained in some cases,
even under the Republic, from the goods of the condemned led to the
quadruplatores (later delatores) becoming a professional class. Under
the early Empire Tacitus describes delatores as “genus hominum publico
exitio repertum et ne poenis quidem satis coercitum’” (Ann. iv 30). Among
their many activities they denounced to the agents of the imperial Treasury
any possession of property which the Treasury could claim (res fisci).
They profited by the praemia given by Augustus for convictions of
violations of his marriage laws, and especially by the Lex Iulia de
maiestate (lèse-majesté) which gave the accuser + of the estate of the
condemned. Tiberius at first discouraged, but afterwards encouraged them
(Tib. 61: Tac. A. i 73, iv 30). Caligula on his accession “negavit se
delatoribus aures habere" (Calig. 15, 4), and Nero in his early days
reduced their rewards (Ner. 10, 1). Domitian began by repressing them
(Dom. 9, 3), but later used them as tools for his extortions (Dom. 12, 1).
Trajan followed the example of Titus by punishing them severely and
banishing them (Plin. Pan. 34, 44).
mandatores: those who suborn, or furnish materials to, informers
(delatores). The jurist Callistratus (Dig. xlix 14, 2) says that under the
Antonines mandatores were to be punished equally with delatores: Divus
Pius Caecilio Maximo rescripsit constitutionem patris sui, qua compelleretur
delator edere mandatorem ac, nisi edidisset, ut in vincula deduceretur, eo
pertinere, non ut delator poenae subduceretur, si mandatorem haberet, sed
ut mandator quoque perinde atque si ipse detulisset puniretur: cf. xlix 14,
24, non tantum delator punitur, si non probaverit, sed et mandator: quem
exhibere debet delator. There can be no doubt that mandatores is the
right reading in our passage, but Ihm keeps amendatores, the reading of M.

assidue caesos: cf. Mart. vi 46, vapulat assidue veneti quadriga
flagello: Pelagon. 365, assidue aut flagello aut voce excitari debet: Salvian.
de gub. dei i 57, assidue flagellamur: Suet. Calig. 30, 2, equestrem ordinem
assidue proscidit ('tongue-lashed," Rolfe).
..

flagellis ac fustibus: cf. Lamprid. Comm. 18, where the outcries of the
senate against the delatores at the death of Commodus are quoted: “Nunc
securi sumus; delatoribus metum. Ut securi simus, delatoribus metum. Ut
salvi simus, delatores de senatu, delatoribus fustem. Te salvo delatores ad
leonem. Te imperante delatoribus fustem.” "Now at last we are secure;
let informers tremble. That we may be secure, let informers tremble. That
we may be safe, cast informers out of the senate, the club for informers!
While you are safe, to the lions with informers! While you are ruler,
the club for informers!" (Magie). Marcilius points out that slaves were
beaten with flagella, free men with fustes; cf. Macer (Dig. xlviii 19, 10):
Ex quibus causis liber fustibus caeditur, ex his servus flagellis caedi, et
domino reddi iubetur; et ex quibus liber fustibus caesus in opus publicum
damnatur, ex his servus sub poena vinculorum, ad eius temporis spatium,
flagellis caesus domino reddi iubetur. The delatores, as free men about to
be sold as slaves, receive both punishments.

traductos per harenam: Martial (Spect. 4) refers to this: Turba
gravis paci placidaeque inimica quieti, | quae semper miseras sollicitabat
opes, | traducta est, ingens nec cepit harena nocentes: | et delator habet
quod dabat exilium. | Exulat Ausonia profugus delator ab urbe: | haec
licet impensis principis adnumeres. Friedlaender (on Mart. l.c.) suggests
that this exhibition of the delatores took place in the early morning, like
the executions in the amphitheatre before the regular spectacles. traducere
means 'to lead in procession as in a triumph"; e.g. Liv. xxxvi 40, cum
captivis nobilibus equorum quoque captorum gregem traduxit.

subici: sc. hastae or praeconi (sub praeconem and voci praeconis
subicere are also used by Cic.); cf. Aug. 24, 1, ipsum bonaque subiecit
hastae. For subicere used absolutely cf. Calig. 38, 4, reliquias omnium
spectaculorum subiecit et venditavit.

imperavit: Pliny (Pan. 35) mentions the edictum Titi against the
delatores, and says that Nerva made some additions to it, while Trajan
improved it so much that he might be regarded as the originator of it.
Suetonius uses imperare 16 times with the acc. and inf. pass. (in Tib. 57, 2
with the inf. act. and pass., adtractum ad se recipere debitum ducique ad
supplicium imperavit); once with ut (Calig. 46), and once with the
subjunct. without ut (Ner. 1, 1).

in asperrimas insularum: cf. Sen. ad Helv. 6, 4, deserta loca et asperrimas insulas Sciathum et Seriphum, Gyarum et Corsicam percense: nullum
invenies exilium, in quo non aliquis animi causa moretur. For insularum
instead of insulas cf. Liv. x 2, gravissimas navium; xxviii 39, terrarum
ultimas. Banishment to islands was common under the Empire; e.g.
Augustus banished his daughter Julia to Pandataria, off Latium, and later
her son Agrippa to Planasia, off Etruria (Aug. 19:65); Tiberius banished
his daughter-in-law to Pandataria (Tib. 53), and the son of Germanicus
to Pontia, off Latium. The different grades of banishment distinguished
by Callistratus (Dig. xlviii 19, 28) are (1) in insulam deportatio, (2) deportatio, (3) in insulam relegatio, (4) in perpetuum relegatio, (5) in tempus
relegatio. (deportatio involved loss of all civil and personal rights, relegatio
loss of none; Vesp. 15, n.) The miseries of an exile on a barren isle are
illustrated by Seneca's epigrams on his exile in Corsica. An exhaustive
account of such banishment will be found in Mayor's note on Juv. i 73,
aude aliquid brevibus Gyaris (islet in Aegaean) et carcere dignum, | si vis
esse aliquid.

avehi: cf. Iul. 66, vetustissima nave impositos quocumque vento in
quascumque terras iubebo avehi: Ter. Phorm. 977, non hoc publicitus
scelus hinc asportarier | in solas terras! Dio (lxvi 19) merely says that
Titus banished the delatores from Rome: τοὺς μηνυτὰς ἐξήλασεν ἐκ τῆς
πόλεως.

vetuit de eadem re pluribus legibus agi: to prevent the delatores, in
the event of their having unsuccessfully brought a charge under a certain
law, from renewing the charge under some other law. This enactment of
Titus was in accordance with the general principle of Roman civil law
that a matter once tried should not be tried again (except by way of
appeal), even though the form of suit was different. Fresh proceedings
were (with certain exceptions) barred by the Exceptio rei iudicatae; cf.
Ulp. Dig. xliv 2, 7, 4, Exceptio obstat quotiens inter easdem personas eadem
quaestio revocatur vel alio genere iudicii; xliv 2, 5, De eadem re agere
videtur et qui non eadem actione agat, qua ab initio agebat, sed etiam si
alia experiatur, de eadem tamen re. (Roby, Rom. Priv. Law ii 388 sqq.)
lemma: vetuit de eadem re pluribus legibus agi

text:
statu: the legal position of a person according as he was freeborn
(ingenuus), freedman (libertus), or slave (servus). The delatores would
try to prove that a deceased person had had no right to the status of free-born, and that so his testamentary dispositions were invalid.

ultra certos annos: the number of years is unknown; it may have
been five, the number fixed later by Nerva and Marcus Aurelius; cf.
Callistr. Dig. xl 15, 4, primus omnium divus Nerva edicto vetuit, post quinquennium mortis cuiusque de statu quaeri (the words primus omnium contradict what Suet. says about Titus); Capitol., Marc. Anton. 10, de statu
etiam defunctorum intra quinquennium quaeri iussit. Marcus Aurelius
also ordained that if any one had been formally declared freeborn (ingenuus), no revision of this declaration could be made except during his
lifetime, and that any suit commenced for contesting such a declaration
was at once extinguished by his death. Hadrian decided that the status
of a living person could not be questioned if it would affect that of a
person dead more than five years; cf. Dig. xl 15, 1, where Marcianus
states that at times the five years' limitation was not observed if the
investigation was in favour of, and not prejudicial to, the deceased, e.g.
to show that the mother of a living slave was a freewoman and not an
ancilla. See Roby, op. cit. i 50.
2 к

pontificatum maximum: the chief pontificate, the highest religious
power, was conferred apart from the other imperial powers on all the
emperors from Augustus to Gratianus, who (c. 382) formally renounced
it, and none of his successors appears as pontiff. It usually comes first in
the order of imperial titles recorded in inscriptions; e.g. C.I.L. ii 4838,
Imp. Tito Caesare Vespasiano Aug., pont. max., trib. pot. IX, imp. XV,
p. p., cos. VIII. It had been conferred on Julius Caesar, and on his
assassination it was usurped by Lepidus, on whose death (13 в.с.), and
not before, Augustus accepted it (Aug. 31, 1). As pontifex maximus the
emperor could deal with all offences against religion. It was in this
capacity that Domitian punished the Vestal virgins charged with incest
(Dom. 8, 3). The office also carried great powers of patronage, and the
emperor by his nomination or commendation could secure admission for
his favourites to the religious colleges. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 72,
780, 783, 1106 sqq.; Greenidge, Rom. Public Life p. 351.

puras manus: as the context shows, puras here means free from
bloodguiltiness, a limited meaning which occurs e.g. in Hor. S. i 4, 68, at
bene si quis | et vivat puris manibus (where see Palmer); so καθαραὶ (opp.
to φονίαι) χεῖρες, Aesch. Eum. 313, etc. Bremi refers to the belief that it
was a pollution for a priest even to look upon a corpse.

nec auctor.. necis nec conscius: Dio lxvi 19, οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Τίτος οὐδένα
τῶν βουλευτῶν (senatorum) ἐν τῇ αὑτοῦ ἡγεμονίᾳ ἀπέκτεινεν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ ἄλλος τις
αὐτῷ ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀρχῆς ἐτελεύτησεν: C. 18, ὁ δὲ δὴ Τίτος οὐδὲν φονικὸν . .
μοναρχήσας ἔπραξεν, ἀλλὰ χρηστός, καίπερ ἐπιβουλευθείς, ἐγένετο. Ausonius
(Caes. xi) praises Titus as "expers civilis sanguinis, orbis amor." Cf.
also Oros. vii 9, 13, cuius tanta tranquillitas in imperio fuit, ut nullius
omnino sanguinem in re publica administranda fudisse referatur: Eutrop.
vii 21, 2, Romae tantae civilitatis in imperio fuit, ut nullum omnino puniret,
convictos adversum se coniurationis dimiserit, et in eadem qua antea
familiaritate habuerit. Nerva took an oath in the senate that he would
not slay any senator, and he kept his pledge in spite of plots against him
(Dio lxviii 2).
duos patricii generis, etc.: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 3, Neque minus sancte
facilis in tuendis, qui forte in se coniuravissent, adeo ut, cum amplissimi
ordinis duo abnuere cogitatum scelus nequirent patresque censuissent de
confessis supplicium sumendum, deductos in spectaculum se utrimque
adsidere iusserit petitoque ex industria gladiatoris (mirmillonum, Epit. 10,
3), quorum pugnae visebantur, gladio quasi ad explorandam aciem uni
atque alteri committeret. Queis perculsis et constantiam mirantibus:
"videtisne,” inquit, “potestates fato dari frustraque temptari facinus
potiundi spe vel amittendi metu?” Dio (lxviii 3) tells precisely the same
story about Nerva, except that the emperor's daring is made the more
remarkable by the statement that the conspirators, when invited to the
gladiatorial show, had no knowledge that their plot had been detected.
Aelian (Var. Hist. vi 14) describes how Dareius, son of Hystaspes, dealt
in the same bold fashion with Aribazus, when he conspired with others to
slay the Persian king during a hunt.

convictos in: for this constr. cf. Claud. 14, in maiore fraude convictos:
Cic. Sull. 83, in hoc scelere convictus. Suetonius also uses (a) the gen.,
Tib. 1, 2, alter latrocinii, caedis alter convictus est; (b) the abl., Ner. 31, 3,
scelere convictos; (c) the inf., Vesp. 4, 3, convictus ducenta sestertia
expressisse iuveni.

adfectatione imperii: though adfectare in the sense of niti ad, cum
studio expetere occurs from Sallust on, the subst. adfectatio is not found
before Val. Max. In other passages of Suet. it is used for literary
affectation; Tib. 70, 1, adfectatione et morositate nimia obscurabat stilum;
Gramm. 10, 1, nimia priscorum verborum adfectatione.

nihil amplius quam monuit: Julius Caesar had acted in the same
lenient way towards conspirators; cf. Iul. 75, 4, Si qua posthac aut
cogitarentur gravius adversus se aut dicerentur, inhibere maluit quam
vindicare. Itaque et detectas coniurationes conventusque nocturnos non
ultra arguit, quam ut edicto ostenderet esse sibi notas, et acerbe loquentibus
satis habuit pro contione denuntiare ne perseverarent.
For the elliptical
nihil amplius quam see on Dom. 21, nihil aliud quam deambulabat.
•

§ 2. cursores suos: Domitian's couriers are mentioned in Tac. Agr. 43,
supremo quidem die momenta ipsa deficientis (Agricolae) per dispositos
cursores nuntiata constabat.`

non solum sed et: see on c. 8, 3.
..

familiari cenae adhibuit: a special mark of imperial favour; cf.
Ner. 22, 3, Instituerant civitates, apud quas musici agones edi solent,
omnes citharoedorum coronas ad ipsum (Neronem) mittere. Eas adeo grate
recipiebat, ut legatos, qui pertulissent, non modo primos admitteret, sed
etiam familiaribus epulis interponeret.

circa se: see on c. 4, 3; cf. Liv. xlii 52, 5, constitit in tribunali circa
se habens filios duos.

ex industria: "deliberately," Gr. ἐπιτηδές; cf. Vesp. 16, 2: Dom. 16,
2:19. Suetonius also uses the Ciceronian de industria, e.g. Galb. 19, 2.
Livy seems to be the first to use ex.

ferramenta pugnantium inspicienda: ferramenta, which usually means
iron tools, is very rarely used as here in the sense of arma; cf. Cic.
Sull. 19, in munere servili obtulit se ad ferramenta prospicienda; id. Cat. iii
5. At the gladiatorial spectacles, after the opening parade of the gladiators
through the arena, there was often some sham fighting with harmless
weapons (arma lusoria) in which gladiators gave a display of their exercises
and noble amateurs often took part; Dio (lxvi 15) says that Titus defeated
Alienus (prob. the consul in 69) in such sham fighting at games in his
native place Reate. When this terminated, the giver of the spectacle
(editor) was asked to examine the real weapons (arma pugnatoria,
decretoria) about to be used, to see that they conformed with the regulations.
Drusus, son of Tiberius, apparently conducted this probatio armorum with
rigour, and the variety of gladiator's sword with the sharpest edge was
called after him (Δρουσιανὰ ξίφη, Dio lvii 13). Domitian at his spectacles
seems to have deprived the gladiators of defensive armour (see Friedl. on
Mart. viii 80). Marcus Aurelius, when he presided at the shows given in
his name, would only allow the combatants to use blunted swords (gladii
2 к 2
hebetes) or weapons with the point protected by a ball or button (arma
praepilata). See Friedl., Sitteng. ii¹º 73; Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1594.

cognita utriusque genitura: genitura meant (a) the day and hour of
birth, (b) the calculations based upon this by the soothsayers or astrologers
(genethliaci, mathematici, astrologi, Chaldaei, Babylonii) who cast the
horoscopes or nativities predicting the future fate or fortune of the child
from the position of the stars at its birth; cf. Vitell. 3, 2, Vesp. 25. The
Greek word γένεσις was also used in Lat. for a horoscope; e.g. Vesp. 14:
Dom. 10, 3: Juv. xiv 248, nota mathematicis genesis tua. Suetonius
(Aug. 94, 12) tells how Augustus and Agrippa visited a mathematicus,
Theogenes, in Apollonia, who predicted great good fortune for Agrippa.
Augustus at first, fearing a less favourable forecast, would not divulge the
time of his birth (reticere genituram suam perseverabat). At last the
mathematicus prevailed on him to do so, and when he heard it, Theogenes
sprang up and paid homage. Augustus afterwards had such confidence in
his destiny that he published the thema or horoscope, and struck a silver
coin with Capricorn, his natal star, upon it. Later emperors were experts
in astrology; e.g. Tiberius (who foretold the rise of Galba, Galb. 4, 1, n.),
Hadrian, and Septimius Severus (Spartian. Sever. 2, in quadam civitate
Africana, cum sollicitus mathematicum consuluisset positaque hora ingentia
vidisset astrologus, dixit ei “tuam, non alienam, pone genituram’';
cumque Severus iurasset suam esse, omnia ei dixit quae postea facta sunt:
c. 3, cum amissa uxore aliam vellet ducere, genituras sponsarum requirebat,
ipse quoque matheseos peritissimus, et cum audisset esse in Syria quandam
quae id geniturae haberet ut regi iungeretur, eandem uxorem petit).

quandoque: "at some future time," the prevalent meaning of the
word in Suetonius; but he also has it in its other sense of "whenever"
(= quandocumque), e.g. Claud. 1, 4, se rei p. statum, quandoque posset,
restituturum.

§ 3. fratrem insidiari sibi non desinentem: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 11,
fratrem quoque Domitianum parantem insidias, militumque animos sollicitantem flens saepius obtestatus est, ne parricidio assequi cuperet, quod et
se volente esset obventurum ei et iam haberet, cum sit particeps potestatis.
The plotting of Domitian against Titus from the time of Vespasian's
death is described in Dom. 2, 3, neque cessavit ex eo insidias struere fratri
clam palamque. Titus had displayed a spirit of brotherly affection (pietas)
towards Domitian at the beginning of their father's reign by interceding
for him when unfavourable rumours had reached Vespasian about him
(Tac. H. iv 52). A remark which Pliny (Ep. iv 9, 2) makes about Julius
Bassus, "Titum timuit ut Domitiani amicus," suggests that the forbearance of Titus towards his brother was not extended to his brother's
friends.

ex professo : = palam, aperte, "openly and avowedly"; cf. Sen. Ερ. 14,
Macrob. S. ii 9. Apuleius (Apol. 2) uses de professo. The passive sense
of the deponent ptc. professus is first found in Ov. Am. iii 14, 6, solaque
famosam culpa professa facit. See Neue-Wagener, Formenl. iii 43.
Similar adverbial phrases used by Suet. are ex compacto, ex improviso, ex
inopinato, ex composito, ex destinato.

fugam: presumably to join some army in the provinces and lead it
against Titus.
501.

seponere: such "sequestration" was a thinly disguised form of
relegatio (Vesp. 15, n.), as it really banished a person by sending him away
from Rome under some specious pretext; cf. Oth. 3, 2, sepositus est per
causam legationis in Lusitaniam: Aug. 65, 1, Agrippam
Surrentum. Tacitus mentions several instances; e.g. A. iv 44, hunc
seposuit Augustus in civitatem Massiliensem, ubi specie studiorum nomen
exilii tegeretur.
seposuit

consortem successoremque: the titles consors imperii (Oth. 8, 1) and
particeps imperii (Tit. 6, 1, Dom. 2, 3) are used indifferently of the
emperor's co-regent by Suet., Tac., and other authors. Under the constitution of the Principate the Princeps was given no right of appointing
