a successor, and Augustus had recourse to a consortium imperii, the co-regent being invested with extraordinary tribunician and pro-consular
powers and placed in a position above all other magistrates, second only
to the Princeps. Mommsen compares the relation of the co-regent to the
Princeps with that of the praetor to the consul (Staatsr. ii³ 1146).
the death of the Princeps, the co-regent, though having no legal claim, in
practice succeeded to the vacant throne, unless prevented by revolution.
See also Dom. 15, 1. In spite of the protestations of Titus mentioned
here by Suetonius, he did not in reality associate Domitian in the government of the Empire. Neither the proconsulare imperium nor the tribunicia
potestas was conferred upon him. He did not allow him to have the title
of Imperator (allowed by Vespasian to Titus, see on c. 6, 1); this is
shown by inscriptions in the reign of Titus, e.g. C.I.L. iii 318 (80 A.D.)
where Domitian appears merely as "Caesar, Divi filius, Domitianus, consul
VII, princeps iuventutis."
..

ut mutuo erga se animo vellet esse: for the constr. cf. Tac. H. iv
49, nec ambigitur militem alienato erga Vespasianum animo fuisse; for
the use of mutuus cf. Cic. Fam. v 2, 1, Quod autem ita scribis, “pro
mutuo inter nos animo,” quid tu existimes esse in amicitia “mutuum”
nescio; equidem hoc arbitror, cum par voluntas accipitur et redditur:
Catull. 45, 20, mutuis animis amant amantur: Hor. C. iv 1, 30, Iam nec
spes animi credula mutui, "the fond hope of finding a heart to answer
mine'' (Wickham): Cic. Att. xvi 16 a, tua voluntas erga me meaque erga
te par atque mutua. Modderman, who asserts that mutuus animus erga
aliquem is meaningless, would read mutato.
lemma: ut mutuo erga se animo vellet esse

text:
morte praeventus est: "he was cut short (taken off) by death";
cf. Iul. 44, 4, talia agentem atque meditantem mors praevenit: Tib. 62, 3,
nisi eum mors praevenisset: Justin 32, 3, peregissetque ultionem, nisi
morte praeventus fuisset. Sallust once (Iug. 71) uses praevenio; it is
not found in Cic. or Caes.

maiore hominum damno quam suo: Titus, like Agricola, was
“felix opportunitate mortis” (Tac. Agr. 45). Ausonius, Caes. xi, addresses
him as "Felix imperio, felix brevitate regendi”; cf. Dio lxvi 18, quoted
on c. 1. For the modal abl. cf. Tib. 41, magno dedecore imperii nec minore
discrimine: Claud. 16, 2, sed suo maiore dedecore. Bagge (De elocutione
Suet., p. 82) says that in these passages the omission of cum is contrary to
the usage of the best prose writers. But in class. Lat., when the modal
abl. has an attribute with it, cum is more frequently omitted, and in Cic.
we find cum sometimes used and sometimes omitted in the same expressions;
e.g. Cat. ii 21, minore dolore perire: Cluent. 30, maximo cum dolore emori:
Rep. 6, 15, celeritate mirabili: N.D. ii 97, cum admirabili celeritate. See
Kühner-Stegmann, i 410.

spectaculis absolutis: the spectacles which Titus gave at the opening
of the new amphitheatre and baths in '80 A.D. (see c. 7, 3) lasted 100 days
(Dio lxvi 25). It was not till the summer of 81 that he went to the Sabine
territory and died there, so that Suetonius is inaccurate in his statement
here. Titus was present at the meeting of the Collegium of the Fratres
Arvales on May 19, 81 A.D. (C.I.L. vi 2060, Newton 1'60).
populo coram: see on Dom. 23, 1.

fleverat: Dio lxvi 26, διατελέσας δὲ ταῦτα, καὶ τῇ γε τελευταίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ καταδακρύσας, ὥστε πάντα τὸν δῆμον ἰδεῖν, οὐδὲν ἔτι μέγα ἔπραξεν, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπιγιγνομένῳ
ἔτει . . καθιερώσας ὅσα εἴρηται, μετήλλαξεν (excessit, obiit) ἐν τοῖς ὕδασιν ἐν οἷς καὶ
ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ. The ὕδατα mentioned by Dio as the scene of the deaths
of Vespasian and Titus are the medicinal springs of Cutiliae near Reate;
see Vesp. 24.

Sabinos: his Sabine property at Reate (Vesp. 1, 2). For Sabini in
the sense of a Sabine estate cf. Hor. C. ii 18, 14, satis beatus unicis Sabinis,
the property in a district being described by the name of the people in
the district (see Page on Hor. l.c.; Mayor on Plin. Ep. iii 4).
petit: = petiit, cf. Oth. 7, 1.

tristior, quod hostia aufugerat: for the indicative see on Vitell. 14,
4, exacerbatus, quod propositus est.
The escape of a victim about to be
sacrificed was always a dirum omen.
The victim which broke away was
called effugia, and the auspices at which the mischance occurred were
called piacularia auspicia as requiring expiatory offerings; cf. Festus
p. 245, Piacularia appellantur auspicia cum aut hostia ab ara fugit, aut
percussa mugitum dedit, aut in aliam quam oportuit partem corporis cecidit.
Escapes of victims from the altar are mentioned in Iul. 59; Galb. 18, 1;
Тас. Н. iii 56; Liv. xxi 63; Verg. A. ii 223; Luc. vii 165; Sil. Ital. v 63,
xvi 264.
..

tempestate serena tonuerat: cf. Verg. G. i 487 (describing the portents
of Caesar's death), non alias caelo ceciderunt plura sereno | fulgura. Often
we find this regarded as a favourable sign; e.g. Ennius Ann. 155, сит
tonuit laevum bene tempestate serena: Xen. Hell. vii 1, 31, ἐξ αἰθρίας
ἀστραπάς τε καὶ βροντὰς λέγουσιν αἰσίους αὐτῷ φανῆναι : Hom. Od. xx 112 sqq.;
Ov. F. iii 370. Horace (C. i 34) professes that he was converted from
atheism by this phenomenon.

primam statim: cf. Claud. 39, 1, postero statim die "on the very next
day'": Ner. 6, 2, primo statim conatu. Similarly statim is joined with
the participle and not with the principal verb, in order to fix more closely
the time-relation; e.g. Liv. xxviii 7, 9, quod viso statim hoste in deditionem
concessissent: Suet. Aug. 28, 1, de reddenda re p. bis cogitavit: primum
post oppressum statim Antonium, etc. Kühner-Stegmann, i 789.

mansionem: manere is often used in the sense of pernoctare, and in
post-class. authors mansio (μονή) means "night-quarters" (statio nocturna,
σταθμός); distance was measured by mansiones, stations, day's journeys,
e.g. Plin. N.H. xii 52, a quo (monte) octo mansionibus distat regio.

febrim nanctus: for this very rare use of nancisci cf. Nep. Att. 21,
nactus est morbum: [Suet.] vit. Verg. 35, languorem nactus est.

pallulis: pallula, which in Plautus is used for a small cloak, here
means a curtain, a sense which is attested for palla (Sen. Ira 3, 22, 2, сит
inter dicentes et audientem palla interesset: Gloss. Philox. παραπέτασμα,
velum, palla). Of the many variants in the MSS. (paludamentis, pellibus,
palliolis, plagulis, etc.) plagulis is read in most of the old editions, plagula
being used for the hanging or coverlet of a lectus (Liv. xxxix 6, 7; Non.
86, 7;378; 537, 20). The lectica was roofed with an arch (arcus) of
leather (pellis) and there were horizontal curtain-rods from which the
curtains (vela, pallulae, plagulae) fell; cf. Mart. xi 98, 11, lectica nec te
tuta pella veloque | nec vindicavit sella saepius clausa. A newer variety
of lectica had windows made of lapis specularis (talc?) which opened or
shut (Juv. iv 21, cf. iii 242). See Daremberg-Saglio, iii 1005; Marquardt,
Privatl.2 738.
..

excepto uno: Dio lxvi 26, ὁ δ' οὖν Τίτος ἀποψύχων εἶπε μὲν ὅτι “Εν μόνον
ἐπλημμέλησα. τί δὲ δὴ τοῦτο εἴη οὐ διεσάφησεν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἄλλος οὐδεὶς ἀκριβῶς
ἀνέγνω· οἱ μὲν γὰρ τό, οἱ δὲ τὸ κατείκασαν. Dio says that the prevalent opinion
was that Titus' one regret was having had intercourse with Domitian's
wife, but he himself inclines to the view that the regret was for not
having put Domitian to death for plotting against him, his forbearance
exposing the Empire to such a successor. Ausonius (Caes. xi) refuses to
believe Titus guilty of any offence: Unum dixisti moriens te crimen
habere: | sed nulli de te, non tibi credidimus ("but we believe none
speaking thus of thee not even thee thyself'"). Duruy (Hist. des Romains
iv 674) suggests that the unum factum paenitendum was the putting to
death of Caecina without trial (Tit. 6, 2); and other equally improbable
conjectures have been hazarded. See Henderson, Five Roman Emperors
p. 10.
§ 2. consuetudinem: see on Oth. 2, 2.

habuerit: an example of the fondness of Suetonius for the perf.
subj. instead of the normal pluperf. or imperf. See App. i. § 9. с.

persancte iurabat: cf. Ner. 35, 5, persancte iurasset: Ter. Нес. 771,
deierat persancte. Suetonius also uses perindigne, perraro, persaepe.
Domitia: see Dom. 3, 1.

haud negatura, si qua
fuisset: cf. Iul. 30, 1, bello vindicaturus, si
quid gravius a senatu constitutum esset. This use of the fut. participle
as apodosis to express the inference from a hypothetical proposition is first
found in Livy (e.g. iii 60, egreditur castris Romanus, vallum invasurus, ni
copia pugnae fieret) and occurs frequently in later writers (e.g. Tac. A. i
36, si omitteretur ripa, invasurus hostis). See Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii² 754.

excessit: there are many conflicting accounts of the cause of Titus'
death. Dio (lxvi 26) says that rumour (ἡ φήμη) attributed it to Domitian,
who plunged him into a vessel full of snow while he was still breathing
(cf. Cedren. p. 179), but that some writers stated that he died of disease.
Suetonius (Dom. 2, 3) says that Domitian ordered the attendants of Titus
to abandon him before he was dead. Aur. Vict. (Caes. 10, 11) declares
that Domitian poisoned him, but in Epit. 10, 15 we are told that he died
of fever. Plutarch (de Sanitate 3) cites Titus as an example of the fatal
use of the bath in sickness, and mentions that this was the view of those
who had tended him. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vi 32) says that Domitian
poisoned him with a poisonous fish called λαγῶς θαλάσσιος (lepus marinus);
so too Tzetzes (Chil. vi 278): Τίτος δὲ θνῄσκει βεβρωκὼς λαγῶν τῶν θαλασσίων.
Suidas (s.v. Δομετιανός) repeats the poisoning charge; cf. Herodian iv 5, 6.
The Jews believed that Titus' early death was a vengeance from Heaven
for the sacking of Jerusalem; cf. the fantastic account in the Jewish
Talmud which is thus given by Duruy: “Les Juifs en savaient bien plus
long sur cette mort prématurée, et le Talmud raconte encore que Titus,
retournant en Italie avec les vases sacrés ravis par lui dans le temple de
Jéhovah, fut assailli par une furieuse tempête: 'Le Dieu des Juifs, s'écriat-il, n'a donc de force que sur la mer où il a déjà englouti Pharaon. S'il
est vraiment Dieu, qu'il me combatte sur terre.'
A ces mots une voix
répondit: 'Méchant, fils de méchant, J'ai donné la vie à une créature
infiniment petite, c'est elle qui combattra pour moi. '
Dès que Titus eut
touché le rivage d'Italie, un moucheron entra dans ses narines et monta
dans son cerveau qu'il rongea durant sept années. Un jour que le prince
passait devant la boutique d'un forgeron, le bruit du marteau sur l'enclume
arrêta l'insecte et l'atroce souffrance. Titus alors donna quatre pièces
d'argent par jour à un homme qui se tint près de lui en frappant incessamment sur une enclume. Pendant un mois, le moyen réussit; mais au bout
de ce temps l'insecte, accoutumé au bruit, se rémit à ronger. Quand Titus
mourut, on ouvrit son crâne et on y trouva un moucheron gros comme une
hirondelle, armé d'ongles de fer et d'un bec d'airain” (Hist. des Romains,
iv 676 sq.).

in eadem qua pater villa: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 10, 15, in eodem, quo
pater, apud Sabinos agro febri interiit: Oros. vii 9, 14, in eadem villa,
qua pater eius, morbo absumptus est: Euseb.-Hieron. ad a. 2096 (81 A.D.),
Titus morbo periit in ea villa, qua pater eius, anno aetatis xlii: Eutrop. vii
22, morbo periit in ea, qua pater, villa. This villa was at Aquae Cutiliae,
a pagus in the ager Reatinus (see Vesp. 24). The omission of the prep.
with the rel. is regular where the same verb is either repeated or understood in the rel. clause; e.g. Cic. Tusc. i 94, in eadem brevitate, qua illae
bestiolae, reperiemur: id. Legg. iii 33, in ista sum scientia, qua te fuisse
semper scio.
...
..

post biennium patri: Titus died on Sept. 13, 81 A.D.; his reign
began on June 24, 79 A.D., the day after Vespasian's death (Vesp. 24).
Dio (lxvi 26) agrees with Suetonius that Titus reigned for 2 yrs. 2 m. 20 d.
Eutropius (vii 22) inaccurately says 2 yrs. 8 m. 20 d.; Joh. Antioch.
(Müller, Fr. Hist. Gr. iv 579) 2 yrs. 8 m.; Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 5, biennio
post, ac menses fere novėm interiit, but [Aur. Vict.] Epit. xi, imperavit
annos duos, et menses duos, diesque viginti. Ausonius (258, 11) is writing
with poetic freedom when he says "Ter, dominante Tito, cingit nova laurea
Ianum” (referring to the custom of the new consul putting a fresh wreath
on the statue of Janus on January 1).

altero et quadragesimo aetatis anno: Dio (l.c.), Euseb.-Hieron., and
Eutrop, agree with Suetonius that Titus died in his 42nd year; but the
statement does not tally with the date of the birth of Titus given by
Suetonius (c. 1), viz. Dec. 30, 41 A.D., for if that date were correct, he
would only have been in his 40th year as Aur. Vict. says, Caes. 10, 5, anno
aevi quadragesimo interiit (but Epit. 10, 1, vixit annos quadraginta
unum). That he was born in 39, and not in 41, is shown by Dio (lxvi 18)
who gives his age at his accession as 39 yrs. 5 m. 25 d. (see on c. 1).
Similar inconsistencies on the part of Suetonius occur with regard to Galba
(see on Galb. 23), Otho (Oth. 11), and Vitellius (Vitell. 18). Other examples
of his chronological carelessness are: (a) in Ner. 7 he says that Nero was
in his eleventh year when he was adopted by Claudius, whereas we know
from Tac. A. xii 25 that the adoption took place in 50 A.D., while Nero
was born on Dec. 15, 37 A.D. (Ner. 6); (b) in Claud. 27 he says that
Britannicus was born on the 20th day of the reign of Claudius and in
his second consulship, whereas Claudius began to reign on Jan. 25, 41 A.D.
(Claud. 10), and his second consulship did not begin till 42 (Nipperdey
and Smilda would delete inque secundo consulatu).

non secus atque in domestico luctu maerentibus: Eutrop. vii 22,
tantus luctus eo mortuo publicus fuit, ut omnes tamquam in propria
doluerint orbitate: Aur. Vict. Caes. 10, 6, huius sane mors adeo provinciis
luctui fuit, uti orbatum orbem deflerent: Epit. 10, 16, huius mors vix
credi potest quantum luctus urbi provinciisque intulerit, adeo ut eum
delicias publicas, sicut diximus, appellantes, quasi perpetuo custode orbatum
terrarum orbem deflerent: Oros. vii 9, 14, cum ingenti omnium luctu
morbo absumptus est. The sorrow of the people for the death of Titus
has an earlier parallel in that for the death of Germanicus; cf. Tac. A. ii
82, where, after describing the indignation of the people at Tiberius'
treatment of Germanicus, Tacitus says: Hos vulgi sermones audita mors
(Germanici) adeo incendit ut ante edictum magistratuum, ante senatus consultum, sumpto iustitio desererentur fora, clauderentur domus. Passim
silentia et gemitus, nihil compositum in ostentationem; et quamquam neque
insignibus lugentium abstinerent, altius animis maerebant.
lemma: non secus atque in domestico luctu maerentibus

text:
senatus prius quam edicto convocaretur: the usual method of convening (vocare, convocare, cogere) the senate was by edict; cf. Iul. 80, 4,
senatus Id. Mart. in Pompei curiam edictus est: Gell. N.A. iii 18, 7, (edicti)
quo nunc quoque consules, cum senatores in curiam vocant, servandae consuetudinis causa tralaticio utuntur, verba
haec sunt: "Senatores
quibusque in senatu sententiam dicere licet”: Liv. xxiii 32, 3;
xxviii 9, 5; Cic. Fam. xi 6, 2, cum tribuni pl. edixissent, senatus adesset
a. d. xiii Kal. Ian. In cases of emergency the senators were summoned by
criers (per praecones) sent round to their houses. See Mommsen, Staatsr.
iii³ 918.

ad curiam concurrit: the same account is given in Eutrop. vii 22,
senatus, obitu ipsius circa vesperam nuntiato, nocte inrupit in curiam et
tantas ei mortuo laudes gratiasque congessit, quantas nec vivo umquam
egerat nec praesenti. Contrast the wild joy of the senate at the death of
Domitian (Dom. 23, 1). Some MSS. (QSN) have the reading cucurrit,
which appears in various early editions.

obseratisque adhuc foribus: because, as Eutropius (l.c.) tells us, it
was nighttime. I adopt the punctuation advocated by Casaubon and
Baumgarten-Crusius, connecting obseratis foribus with what precedes.

tantas gratias egit laudesque congessit, quantas: in the Editio
Veneta of 1471 and other early editions we find gratias egit laudesque,
quantas congessit, which is supported by Gronovius (on Liv. xxvi 48, dis
immortalibus laudes gratesque egit) who cites Liv. vii 36, dis laudes
gratesque agunt: xxvii 13, dis immortalibus, ut in tali re, laudes gratesque
ago; Plaut. Trin. 821, Neptuno laetus lubens laudes ago et grates, gratiasque habeo. The MSS. of Suetonius are decisively against this reading.
lemma: tantas gratias egit laudesque congessit, quantas

text:
Domitianus: a cognomen derived from his mother Flavia Domitilla,
who died before his father Vespasian became emperor; cf. Vesp. 3.
Similarly Vespasian derived his cognomen from his mother Vespasia Polla.

natus est: on Oct. 24, 51 A.D., his father being consul for the last
two months of that year (Vesp. 4, 2). His birthday is mentioned C.I.L. x
444, ίχ. Κ. Novembr. natal. Domitiani Aug. n(ostri).

regione urbis sexta: Servius Tullius divided the city within his walls
into 4 regiones: the Suburan, the Esquiline, the Viminal or Colline, and
the Palatine (Varro L.L. v 41 sqq.; Dion. Hal. iv 14). Augustus was
born regione Palati (Aug. 5). The city, within and without the Servian
walls, was divided by Augustus in 7 B.C. into 14 regiones and 265 vici or
parishes (Aug. 30; Plin. N.H. iii 66). The names of these regiones are
unknown; they may have been distinguished merely by numbers. At the
beginning of the 4th cent. the names of the 14 regiones were: I Porta
Capena, II Coelimontium, III Isis et Serapis, Iv Templum Pacis, v Esquiliae,
VI Alta Semita, VII Via Lata, VIII Forum Romanum, Ix Circus Flaminius,
x Palatium, XI Circus Maximus, XII Piscina Publica, XIII Aventinus,
XIV Transtiberim. The "Alta Semita," from which the sexta regio took
its name, ran all along the back of the Quirinal, on the line of the mod.
Strada di Porta Pia.

ad Malum Punicum: this "Pomegranate street" was on the line of
the mod. Via delle Quatro Fontane; see Jordan-Huelsen Topogr. Rom i 3,
426, with the plan (no. vii) of the Quirinal. It probably got its name from
a tree that grew there; cf. Mart. i 117, 6, where the poet mentions his
lodgings on the Quirinal in the street of the Pear-tree (ad Pirum).
Augustus was born in the street of the Ox-Heads (ad Capita Bubula),
which led from the valley of the Colosseum up the slope of the Palatine
(Aug. 5). A house could be designated in the same way; e.g. the villa of
Livia was known as ad Gallinas (Galb. 1); so too a vicus; e.g. that at the
Porta Collina was called ad tres Fortunas from three temples of Fortune
there. The pomegranate (malum Punicum) was introduced into Italy from
the north of Africa; cf. Plin. N.H. xiii 112, Africa circa Carthaginem
Punicum malum cognomine sibi vindicat; aliqui granatum appellant:
Colum. xii 42, mala granata (i.e. with many seeds, grana), quae Punica
vocantur: Mart. xiii 42, 43.
..

domo convertit: cf. Mart. ix 20, 1, Haec, quae tota patet tegiturque
et marmore et auro, | infantis domini (i.e. Domitian) conscia terra fuit.

templum gentis Flaviae: see c. 5. Besides this temple on the Quirinal,
Domitian also built temples to Divus Titus and Divus Vespasianus between
the Clivus Capitolinus and the Capitol. These temples are much praised
by Martial; e.g. ix 1, 8, Manebit altum Flaviae decus gentis | cum sole et
astris cumque luce Romana. | Invicta quidquid condidit manus, caeli est:
ix 34, Iuppiter Idaei risit mendacia busti | dum videt Augusti Flavia templa
poli; cf. Stat. S. v 1, 240, aeternae modo qui sacraria genti | condidit
inque alio posuit sua sidera caelo. In the dedication to Vespasian of his
Argonautica Valerius Flaccus (i 15) says of Domitian: Ille tibi cultusque
deum delubraque genti | instituet, cum iam genitor lucebis ab omni |
parte poli. Domitian intended the templum gentis Flaviae to be a tomb
for members of his house. The ashes of Vespasian were brought thither
from the Mausoleum Augusti (see on Vesp. 23, 4), and there too were
placed the ashes of Titus and his daughter Julia (see Dom. 17, 3), and
finally those of Domitian himself. This temple was in existence in the
4th cent., but no traces of it remain (Jordan-Huelsen, p. 426).

pubertatis: Macrob. Sat. vii 7, 4, secundum iura publica duodecimus
annus in femina et quartus decimus in puero definit pubertatis aetatem.

adulescentiae: defined by Varro (ap. Censor. 14) as from 15 to 30 yrs.
of age; by Isidorus (Orig. xi 2, 4) as from 14 to 28.
infamia: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, Domitianus maculosae adulescentiae.

tempus gessisse: this use of gerere for agere is very rare; cf. Sulpic.
ap. Cic. Fam. iv. 5, ut cum aliquo adulescente primario coniuncta aetatem
gereret: Petron. Satyr. 63, vitam Chiam gessi: Val. Flacc. vi 693, semivir
impubemque gerens sterilemque iuventam: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 44, annos
gerens proxime quadraginta. Casaubon would read egisse. In Vesp. 24,
annum agens aetatis sexagesimum, there is a variant gerens.

ut nullum argenteum vas
haberet: during Domitian's riper boyhood and early youth his father Vespasian, after his proconsulship in Africa,
was in very straitened circumstances and was compelled to mortgage all
his property (see Vesp. 4, 3). Even in the families of the poorer classes
it was usual to have the salinum and patera of silver, as these were used
in sacrifices to the household gods. From the middle of the 3rd cent. B.C.
the use of silver in wealthy houses became more and more widespread, not
merely for ordinary table service (argentum escarium, potorium) but also
for display on the abacus. The argentea vasa in a big house are referred
to in Plaut. Aul. 341, hic autem apud nos magna turba ac familia est, |
supellex, aurum, vestis, vasa argentea. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 318 sq.

constat: Burman, Oudendorp, and others prefer constet, the conjecture
of Lipsius, connecting it with ut in the preceding sentence, on the ground
that an example of Domitian's infamia is required as well as of his inopia.
With constat, the example of infamia is given in the form of a separate
statement, independent of the ut clause. Wolf's reasonable objection to
constet is that it attributes to Suet. such a clumsy expression as “Fertur
aetatem gessisse tanta infamia, ut satis constet,” when he could easily
have written “Clodiusque conservarit, etc."
Clodium Pollionem: not mentioned elsewhere.

poema Neronis "Luscio'": Nero's poetical productions included
lyrics, tragic monodies, an epic entitled "Troica," poems (probably elegiac)
on amatory subjects (cf. Mart. ix 26, 9, Nero lascivum iuvenis cum
a
tibi lusit opus: Plin. Ep. v 3), and lampoons, of which the “Luscio”
would be one, others being referred to in Suet. Ner. 24, quamvis id ipsum
in rege Mithridate carmine quodam suo reprehendisset: Tac. A. xv 49,
Quintianus mollitia corporis infamis et
Nerone probroso carmine
diffamatus. "Luscio," which does not occur elsewhere, is presumably
connected with luscus (“one-eyed''), and Casaubon suggested that there
may be a reference to the "Luscio” in Pers. i 128, lusco qui possit dicere
"lusce," as that Satire of Persius is (in his opinion) full of attacks on
Nero and his poems. Juvenal is probably hitting at Nero's pretensions
as a satirist in iv 106, improbior saturam scribente cinaedo. The originality
of Nero's poetry is denied by Tacitus (A. xiv 16), and defended by
Suetonius (Ner. 52) on the ground that he had seen the rough drafts and
corrections in Nero's own handwriting. See Friedl., Sitteng. ii¹º 218 sq.;
Ribbeck, Gesch. röm. Dichtung iii 44 sqq.
chirographum: see on Tit. 3, 2.

Nerva: Marcus Cocceius Nerva, emperor from 96 to 98 A.D. He was
consul with Vespasian in 71, and with Domitian in 90. There does not
seem to be any evidence in support of the charge against him mentioned
here.

§ 2. confugit in Capitolium: he was not with Flavius Sabinus (elder
brother of Vespasian, Vesp. 1, 3) when he occupied the Capitol against
the Vitellians (Vitell. 15, 3), but under cover of darkness Sabinus succeeded
in bringing in Domitian along with his own children; cf. Tac. H. iii 69,
Sabinus arcem Capitolii insedit Vitellianus miles socordi custodia
clausos circumdedit; eoque concubia nocte suos liberos Sabinus et
Domitianum fratris filium in Capitolium accivit. Martial (ix 101, 13)
speaks flatteringly of Domitian as having played a leading part in the
conflict: Adseruit possessa malis Palatia regnis, | prima suo gessit pro
Iove bella puer; cf. Stat. Th. i 21, Defensa prius vix pubescentibus annis |
bella Iovis: id. Silv. i 1, 79: Sil. Ital. Pun. iii 609, Nec te terruerint
Tarpeii culminis ignes, etc.

parte praesentium copiarum: i.e. part of the miles urbanus (the 4 city
cohorts) and the vigiles who had flocked to the house of Sabinus (who was
praefectus urbis); Tac. iii 69, primores senatus plerique equestris ordinis
omnisque miles urbanus et vigiles domum Flavii Sabini complevere. It
was thus a medley of senators, knights, and soldiers who occupied the
Capitol along with Sabinus.

ardente templo: for the burning of the temple of Jupiter Opt. Max.
on the Capitol see Vitell. 15, 3.

apud aedituum clam pernoctavit: Tac. iii 74, Domitianus prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus. When his father Vespasian was established as emperor, Domitian pulled down the chamber of the aedituus and
built a small shrine to Jupiter Conservator, with an altar on which his own
adventures were represented in marble. At a later period he built a
temple on the Capitol to Jupiter Custos (Dom. 5). Piso, the adopted son
of Galba (Galb. 17), had previously found temporary shelter from the
soldiers of Otho in the chamber of an aedituus of the temple of Vesta
(Tac. i 43). The aedituus or temple-guardian" (also called aeditumus,
Varr. R.R. i 2; aedituens Lucr. vi 1273; Gr. ἱεροφύλαξ) dwelt either in
the temple or close to it. Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 214 sqq., divides aeditui
into aeditui magistri who had charge of the buildings, treasures, records,
etc., and aeditui ministri who kept the temple clean, showed visitors round,
etc.

Isiaci celatus habitu: at the ingenious suggestion of a freedman,
according to Tac. iii 74: sollertia liberti lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum
inmixtus ignoratusque. A similar disguise was used by the proscribed
aedile Volusius in 43 B.C.; cf. App. Bell. Civ. iv 47, Οὐολούσιος δὲ ἀγορανομῶν
προεγράφη, καὶ φίλον ὀργιαστὴν τῆς Ἴσιδος ἔχων ᾔτησε τὴν στολήν, καὶ τὰς ὀθόνας
ἐνέδυ τὰς ποδήρεις καὶ τὴν τοῦ κυνὸς κεφαλὴν ἐπέθετο καὶ διῆλθεν οὕτως ὀργιάζων
αὐτῷ σχήματι ἐς Πομπήιον: Val. Max. vii 3, 8. The Isiaci, priests and
worshippers of Isis, wore linen garments (ὀθόναι); cf. Oth. 12, 1, traditur
(Otho) sacra Isidis saepe in lintea religiosaque veste propalam celebrasse.
The epithet liniger is often applied to the goddess and her devotees (Ov.
Am. ii 2, 25; Met. i 747, etc.: Juv. vi 533: Mart. xii 29, 19). The Isiac
worship was introduced at Rome about the time of Sulla, and survived
repeated attempts of the government to suppress it. Augustus would only
tolerate it outside the city walls. In 19 A.D. Tiberius, in consequence of a
flagrant scandal, ordered the priests of Isis to be crucified and her image
to be thrown into the Tiber. Now, in 69 A.D., we find an Iseum or temple
of Isis on the Capitol, though in 58 B.C. and three times shortly afterwards
her temple there was wrecked by the consuls. The first state temple to
Isis was built in the Campus Martius; the date is uncertain, but it is first
mentioned in connexion with the triumph of Vespasian and Titus in 71 A.D.
See Wissowa, Religion der Römer2 351 sqq.

sacrificulos: Tacitus calls them sacricolae. The word sacrificulus:
"sacrificer'" (only here in Suet.) may be used in the same contemptuous
sense as it bears at times in Livy where it is joined with vates in describing
the false priests and soothsayers who brought in foreign superstitious rites
at Rome (especially in periods of national danger), in opposition to the
regular priests and augurs of the Roman state religion; see Weissenborn.
on Liv. xxv 1, 8, sacrificuli ac vates ceperant hominum mentes: xxxix 16, 8,
quotiens hoc patrum avorumque aetate negotium est magistratibus datum,
uti sacra externa fieri vetarent, sacrificulos vatesque foro circo urbe prohiberent.

variae superstitionis: vanae, the reading of some of the later MSS.,
is generally adopted in the old editions; also by Roth and Preud'homme,
but not by Ihm. variae may mean "shifting" "fickle," or "complex”
"many-sided" as Turnebus explained it: "varia esse potuit illa religio,
variusque cultus et caerimonia, variique cultores, unde et facilior Domitiano
latebra." See also Alexander (op. cit., 21 sqq.). Iac. Gronovius ingeniously
suggested Phariae (i.e. Egyptian), but all the examples quoted of the use
of that epithet are from poetry.

trans Tiberim: Tacitus differs in saying (iii 74) that it was close to
the Velabrum (on the near side of the river) that he found refuge in the
house of Cornelius Primus, a client of his father.

comite uno: his cousin Sabinus, son of Flavius Sabinus (Dio lxiv 17).
For the sociative abl. without the normal cum (Kühner-Stegmann, i 407)
cf. Aug. 8, paucissimis comitibus subsecutus.

§ 3. Caesar consalutatus: Tac. iii 86, Domitianum, postquam nihil
hostile metuebatur, ad duces partium progressum et Caesarem consalutatum
miles frequens, utque erat in armis, in paternos penates deduxit: Dio lxvi 1,
Καίσαρες ὅ τε Τίτος καὶ ὁ Δομιτιανὸς ἐπεδείχθησαν. Claudius was the first to
assume the cognomen “Caesar" as an imperial title (see on Galb. 1), and
this was continued by each successive dynasty, Vitellius alone refusing to
be thus styled (Vitell. 8, 2). The title “Caesar'" was borne not merely
by the founders of these dynasties, but also by their agnate descendants,
and was distinctively used of the sons and grandsons of the reigning
emperor. When Hadrian made his adoptive son Verus assume the name
of Caesar, he gave to "Caesar" the limited meaning of the prospective
"Augustus" or emperor, and “Caesar" continued to be used as the title
of the designated successor to the throne. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³
770 sq.

praeturae urbanae consulari potestate: Tac. iv 3, ipsi (Vespasiano)
consulatus cum Tito filio, praetura Domitiano et consulare imperium decernuntur. Domitian succeeded Frontinus as praetor: iv 39, et mox eiurante
("resigning") Frontino Domitianus praeturam cepit. He was given the
consulare imperium (Suetonius loosely says cons. potestas) in the absence
from Rome of the two consuls, his father in Egypt and his brother in
Palestine. It was quite unprecedented for a praetor urbanus to receive
the consulare imperium; see Mommsen, ii³ 650, on the combination of the
consulare imperium with the praetorship and propraetorship.

titulo tenus: “in name only," discharging none of the judicial duties
appertaining to the office; cf. Dom. 13, 3, consulatus .. paene titulo tenus
gessit: Iul. 76, 2, tertium et quartum consulatum titulo tenus gessit contentus dictaturae potestate: Claud. 25, 1, instituit imaginariae militiae
genus quo absentes et titulo tenus fungerentur. Similar phrases are
verbo tenus (Cic. Liv. Tac.), nomine tenus (Tac.), ore tenus (e.g. Tac. A. xv
45, Graeca doctrina ore tenus exercitus).

collegam proximum: presumably the praetor peregrinus, who ranked
next to the praetor urbanus in the exercise of urbana iurisdictio. The
name of the praetor peregrinus in 70 A.D. is unknown. Baumg.-Crusius
and Bremi say that it was Mucianus, but he was consul suffectus (for the
second time) in that year.

vim dominationis licenter exercuit: cf. Tac. H. iv 2, nomen sedemque
(i.e. the palace) Caesaris Domitianus acceperat, nondum ad curas intentus,
sed stupris et adulteriis filium principis agebat (i.e. played the part of
emperor's son): Tac. Agr. 7, iuvene admodum (18 yrs. old) Domitiano et
ex paterna fortuna tantum licentiam usurpante.

ne exequar singula: cf. Calig. 37, 3, ne singula enumerem: Claud. 29,
1, ne singillatim minora quoque enumerem: Galb. 3, 1, elogia universi
generis exequi longum est: Liv. xxvii 27, multos circa unam rem ambitus
fecerim, si . omnia exequi velim.

contrectatis uxoribus: contrectare, to stroke or caress, was used in
the further sense of violare (Plaut., Tac., etc.; contrectatio, Cic.); so
adtrectare, e.g. Ner. 26, 2, a quodam laticlavio, cuius uxorem adtrectaverat,
prope ad necem caesus. Here M has contract- (so Ihm and Preud 'homme),
but contrect- in Calig. 42; Claud. 35, 2; Ner. 34, 4.

Domitiam Longinam: daughter of Domitius Corbulo, the famous
general of Claudius and Nero. On the arrival of Vespasian from Egypt,
Domitian kept her among his mistresses on his estate near the Alban Mount
and afterwards married her; cf. Dio lxvi 3, ὁ δὲ Δομιτιανὸς ... τῷ ἔρωτι τῆς
Δομιτίας τῆς Κορβούλωνος θυγατρὸς προσέχων ἐτύγχανε· ταύτην γὰρ Λουκίου
Λαμίου Αἰλιανοῦ (Αἰμιλιανοῦ codd.) τοῦ ταύτης ἀνδρὸς ἀποσπάσας τότε μὲν ἐν ταῖς
ἐρωμέναις ἐποιήσατο, ὕστερον δὲ καὶ ἔγημεν. Her subsequent history is narrated
in Dom. 3, 1. See also Tit. 10, 2.

Aelio Lamiae: his full name was L. Aelius Plautius Lamia Aelianus
(C.I.L. vi 2059; iii p. 854). In 80 A.D., under Titus, he was consul
suffectus. He was put to death by Domitian for a jesting reference to
the emperor's abduction of his wife; see c. 10, 2. The Lamiae were the
oldest and most illustrious family of the gens Aelia; cf. Hor. C. iii 17,
Aeli vetusto nobilis ab Lamo, etc.; Juv. iv 154, Sed periit (Domitianus)
postquam cerdonibus esse timendus | coeperat .. Hoc nocuit Lamiarum
caede madenti; vi 385, quaedam de numero Lamiarum ac nominis Appi.

officia distribuit: Dio lxvi 2, πολλοῖς ἀρχάς (governorships) τε καὶ
ἐπιτροπείας (procuratorships) αὐτὸς (i.e. Mucianus) καὶ ὁ Δομιτιανὸς ἔδοσαν, καὶ
ἐπάρχους (prefects) ἄλλους ἐπ᾿ ἄλλοις καὶ ὑπάτους (consuls) ἀπέδειξαν. Tacitus
(H. iv 39) describes the reckless conduct of Domitian at Rome before the
arrival of Vespasian: vis penes Mucianum erat; nisi quod pleraque
Domitianus, instigantibus amicis aut propria libidine (“caprice'”), audebat.

Vespasiano dictitante: Dio (l.c.) says that Vespasian wrote to thank
Domitian for not having dismissed him: πάντα αὐτοὶ (i.e. Mucianus and
Dom.) ὡς αὐταρχοῦντες ἐποίουν, ὥστε τὸν Οὐεσπασιανὸν ἐπιστεῖλαί ποτε τῷ
Δομιτιανῷ ὅτι “ χάριν ἔχω σοι, τέκνον, ὅτι με ἐᾷς ἄρχειν καὶ οὐδέπω με καταλέλυκας.”
Reports had reached Vespasian in Egypt of Domitian's presumptuous
behaviour: Tac. iv 51, Vespasianus in Italiam resque urbis intentus
adversam de Domitiano famam accipit, tamquam terminos aetatis et concessa filio egrederetur.
•

expeditionem incohavit: in 69 A.D. the Batavian auxiliaries of the
Rhine legions under Civilis had revolted, and on the death of Vitellius,
Classicus, prefect of an ala of the Treveri, in concert with Civilis, proclaimed an independent "Imperium Galliarum," to which the Roman
legions in Germany swore allegiance. The government of Vespasian sent
7 legions under Cerealis against Classicus and Civilis, and shortly after,
when exaggerated reports of the rebels' successes reached Rome, Mucianus
and Domitian set out for the war: simul Domitianus Mucianusque accingebantur, dispari animo, ille spe ac iuventa properus, hic moras nectens queis
flagrantem (Domitianum) retineret, ne ferocia aetatis et pravis inpulsoribus,
si exercitum invasisset, paci belloque male consuleret (Tac. Η. iv 68).
When near the Alps, they heard of the defeat of the Treveri by Cerealis,
and Mucianus seized the opportunity to advise Domitian that the subjugation of an already defeated foe was a task unworthy of him, and
that he should merely display from Lugdunum (Lyons) the might and
prestige of imperial power (ib. 85). Domitian saw through the artifice
(ib. 86), but apparently went no farther than Lugdunum. Josephus, the
panegyrist of the Flavian emperors, attributes the surrender of the Treveri
and Batavi to the news of Domitian's approach (Bell. Iud. vii 85 sqq.);
cf. Mart. ii 2, 4: vii 7, 3: Sil. Ital. iii '607, At tu transcendes, Germanice,
facta tuorum, | iam puer auricomo praeformidate Batavo.
Germanias: Germania Superior and Germania Inferior; see on
Vitell. 7, 1.
..

ut fratri se adaequaret: Tacitus (H. iv 86) says that Domitian,
when at Lugdunum, secretly sent envoys to Cerealis asking him if he
would hand over the army and the command to him if he came to the
Rhine. Cerealis eluded the "boyish" request by judicious temporizing,
and it was left uncertain whether Domitian's idea was to wage war
against his father or to provide himself with resources against his brother:
qua cogitatione bellum adversus patrem agitaverit an opes viresque adversus
fratrem, in incerto fuit; nam Cerealis salubri temperamento elusit ut vana
pueriliter cupientem. The ambitious nature of the youthful Domitian is
mentioned in Dio lxvi 3, οὐδὲν γὰρ μικρὸν ἐπενόει.
aetatis: born in 51, he was 18 years old at this time.

habitabat cum patre: that he might be under his father's supervision
Dio
and be made to realize that he was subject to the patria potestas.
(lxvi 9, quoted on c. 3, 1) says that for some time before Vespasian 's
return Domitian had been living at his Alban villa, and that a guilty
conscience made him so apprehensive of his father's arrival that he even
simulated madness, to create an impression that he was not responsible
for his conduct. Vespasian, when emperor, dwelt mainly in the Horti
Sallustiani (between the Quirinal and Pincian hills) and seldom lived in
the Palace (Dio lxvi 10).
sellam: i.e. a sella gestatoria or sedan-chair, the occupants of which
sat upright, as opposed to the lectica or litter in which they were borne
reclining or half-reclining. Dio, lx 2, says that Claudius was the first
emperor to use the sella gestatoria, and that after him emperors and ex-consuls continued to use it down to Dio's day (flor. 180 A.D.); whereas
Augustus and Tiberius had been carried in lecticae, such as were used by
women (and children). See also on Oth. 6, 3, muliebri sella.
quotiens: see on Galb. 10, 2.

triumphum utriusque Iudaicum: for this joint triumph of Vespasian
and Titus see Vesp. 8, 1; Tit. 6, 1.

equo albo comitatus est: cf. Zonar. xi 17, τῶν δ' Ἱεροσολύμων ἁλόντων ὁ
Τίτος εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ἐπανελθὼν τὰ ἐπινίκια αὐτός τε καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐφ᾽ ἅρματος
ἔπεμψαν, συνέπεμψε δέ σφισιν αὐτὰ καὶ ὁ Δομετιανὸς ὑπατεύων (consul) ἐπὶ κέλητος :
Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 152, μεθ' & Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἤλαυνε πρῶτος, καὶ Τίτος εἵπετο,
Δομετιανὸς δὲ παρίππευεν, αὐτός τε διαπρεπῶς κεκοσμημένος καὶ τὸν ἵππον παρέχων
θέας ἄξιον. At the triumph of Augustus in 29 B.c. for his victory at Actium,
Tiberius (aged 13) rode on the left trace-horse of the emperor's chariot,
while Octavia's son Marcellus (aged 14) rode the one on the right (Suet.
Tib. 6). The white horse of Domitian was in keeping with the white
horses which drew Vespasian and Titus. White chariot-horses, recalling
the white steeds of Jupiter and the Sun (Liv. v 23), were used by Camillus
in his triumph in 396 B.C.; later by Julius Caesar (Dio xliii 14) and by
the emperors (Suet. Ner. 25, Plin. Pan. 22, etc.).

quin et e sex consulatibus: this is Ihm's certain correction for quis
ex or qui sex or in sex of the MSS. Burman had already conjectured quin
ex sex, and Bentley suggested quin ex consulatibus or eque sex or quinis
ex; but quin et is the regular combination in Suet., e.g. Tit. 8, 1; 8,2;
Vesp. 12; Oth. 12, 1. That ex and not in is the prep. required is shown
by Dom. 13, 3, ex quibus (consulatibus) septem medios continuavit;
Claud. 14, ex quibus (consulatibus) duos primos iunctim gessit; Calig. 17, 1,
ex omnibus (consulatibus) duos novissimos coniunxit. The six consulships
referred to are those which Domitian held before Vespasian's death; he
was altogether 17 times consul, see c. 13, 3.

unum ordinarium: he was consul ordinarius in 73 A.D., his colleague
being M. Valerius Messalinus; he was consul suffectus in 71, 75, 76, 77,
79. The consuls elected at the beginning of the year gave their names to
the year and were known as ordinarii; those appointed later in the year
were called suffecti, but their names too were recorded in the Fasti.
From the time of Augustus the consuls elected on Jan. 1 did not usually
hold office throughout the year, but resigned after some months and were
succeeded by suffecti (Dio xlviii 35). In the second half of Augustus'
reign 6 months was the usual tenure; so too under Nero (Suet. Ner. 15,
consulatum in senos plerumque menses dedit); but the tenure mainly
depended on the caprice of the emperor, as in the case of Tiberius.
In
the year of confusion 69 A.D. there were 15 consuls. From the time of
Vespasian 4 months or 2 months became the normal tenure. When the
emperors themselves assumed the consulship, they generally held it for an
even shorter period than private persons, sometimes for a few months,
sometimes only for a few days (Dom. 13, 3). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³
82 sqq.

cedente
fratre: Titus was colleague of the emperor Vespasian in
seven consulships 70, 72, 74-77, 79 A.D. Before the consular election in 73
he withdrew in favour of Domitian, and presumably it was in consequence
of his action that Vespasian also decided not to hold the office in that year
(for a list of Vespasian's consulships see on Vesp. 8, 1). By his withdrawal Titus gave another example of the brotherly affection (pietas)
which he always showed towards Domitian in spite of his hostile attitude
(see on Tit. 9, 3). Domitian held his first consulship in 71, when he was
consul suffectus from March 1 to June 30, the ordinarii for the year being
Vespasian and M. Cocceius Nerva. In the same year he appears on coins
as consul designatus iterum, i.e. designated again as consul suffectus for
72, Vespasian and Titus being designated as ordinarii. Apparently at the
spring comitia in 72 Titus allowed Domitian to be designated in his place
as consul ordinarius for 73, and Domitian, waiving his claim to be consul
suffectus in 72, continued to be consul designatus throughout that year,
and then became consul ordinarius on Jan. 1, 73. See Gsell, Essai sur le
régne de l'empereur Domitien p. 19; Weynand, in Pauly-Wissowa vi 2548.

§ 2. simulavit et ipse modestiam: not only did his father humble
him (Dio lxvi 10, ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἐκείνου ἐταπείνου τὸ φρόνημα), but he himself affected a retiring modesty; cf. Tac. H. iv 86, Domitianus sperni a
senioribus iuventam suam cernens, modica quoque et usurpata antea munia
imperii omittebat, simplicitatis ac modestiae imagine in altitudinem conditus ("wrapping himself in a profound reserve," C. and B.) studiumque
litterarum et amorem carminum simulans, quo velaret animum et fratris
aemulationi subduceretur, cuius disparem mitioremque naturam contra interpretabatur.

poeticae studium: Domitian seems to have essayed epic poetry, his
themes being (a) the fight for the Capitol between the Flavians and
Vitellians in Dec. 69; cf. Mart. v 5, 7, ad Capitolini caelestia carmina
2L
belli | grande cothurnati pone Maronis opus: (b) the Jewish War; cf.
Val. Flacc. i 7 (addressing Vespasian), versam proles tua pandet Idumen |
(namque potest), Solymo nigrantem pulvere fratrem. The astronomical
Aratea sometimes attributed to him is by Germanicus, son of Drusus.
Quintilian (x 1, 91) speaks in extravagantly fulsome terms of Domitian 's
poetic gifts: Hos nominavimus (as epic poets) quia Germanicum Aug. (i.e.
Domitian) ab institutis studiis deflexit cura terrarum, parumque diis visum
est esse eum maximum poetarum. Quid tamen his ipsis eius operibus in
quae donato imperio iuvenis secesserat sublimius, doctius, omnibus denique
numeris praestantius? Quis enim caneret bella melius quam qui sic gerit?
Quem praesidentes studiis deae propius audirent? etc. So too Pliny (N.H.
praef. 5) praises Titus as a poet who could emulate his brother: Quantus
in poetica es! O magna fecunditas animi! quemadmodum fratrem quoque
imiteris excogitasti. Silius Italicus (iii 619) says of Domitian: Quin et
Romuleos superabit voce nepotes | quis erit eloquio partum decus: huic sua
Musae | sacra ferent, etc.

postea spretum et abiectum: see c. 20.
recitavit publice: a practice indulged in even by emperors. Claudius
gave constant recitals of his prose works through a professional reader
(Claud. 41, assidue recitavit per lectorem). Nero recited his poems himself, not only at home but in the theatre; this caused such delight that a
festival of thanksgiving was voted and the poems, inscribed in letters of
gold, were dedicated to Jupiter Capitolinus (Ner. 10). On the subject of
recitationes, which were such a feature (and such an infliction) of social
life under the Empire, see Friedl. Sitteng. ii¹º 225 sqq.
setius: see on Tit. 5, 3.
Vologaesus: see on Vesp. 6, 4.

Alanos: a great nomad race, divided into various branches, dwelling
in the steppes north of the Caspian and from the Tanais (Don) to the
Caucasus. Pompey in the war against Mithridates came in contact with
the "duros aeterni Martis Alanos” (Luc. viii 223; cf. Amm. Marc. xxiii 5).
Nero shortly before his death was preparing an expedition against them
(Тас. Н. і 6). Their devastating incursion into Media and Armenia in
the time of Vespasian is described in Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 244 sqq.
Vespasian took measures to guard the Caucasus passes against them, and
a Roman garrison was stationed beyond the Armenian frontier in the
Iberian fortress Harmozika near Tiflis (see Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp.
ii 64). Later, under Hadrian, the Alani renewed their inroads (Dio lxix 15),
and it was then that the historian Arrian, prefect of Cappadocia, wrote
his "Εκταξις κατ' 'Αλανῶν on the tactics to be used against them.

quia discussa res est: discutere (lit. 'to pull to pieces'") was used in
the sense of irritum facere "to bring to nought," "to render null and
void"; cf. Cic. Q. Fr. ii 10 (12), de Commageno, quod rem totam discusseram, mirifice mihi blanditur Appius: Liv. xxxiv 56, eam rem litterae
Ti. Sempronii discusserunt: xxxix 10, obsecrare ut eam rem quocumque
modo discuteret. Dio, lxvi 15, says that Vespasian declined to meddle in
a conflict between the Parthians and Alans which did not concern him:
τοῖς δὲ Πάρθοις πολεμωθεῖσι πρός τινας, καὶ τῆς παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ συμμαχίας δεηθεῖσιν οὐκ
ἐβοήθησεν, εἰπὼν ὅτι οὐ προσήκει αὐτῷ τὰ ἀλλότρια πολυπράγμονεῖν. Imhof (T.
Flav. Domitianus, p. 33) thinks that a more genuine reason for Vespasian 's
refusal was his unwillingness to send Domitian at the head of an army
to the East. Vologaesus had cause to feel hurt by Vespasian's refusal,
for he had laid Vesp. under an obligation by his offer to provide him
with 40,000 Parthian bowmen to aid him against Vitellius (Vesp. 6, 4).

alios Orientis reges: Tiridates, king of Armenia, and Pacorus, king
of Media, whose kingdoms had been overrun and ravaged by the Alani,
were both brothers of Vologaesus. The solicitations of Domitian would
be addressed principally to the king of Armenia, as his was a vassal
kingdom in alliance with Rome.
§ 3. patre defuncto: Vespasian died on June 23, 79 A.D. (Vesp. 24).

cunctatus an: for the indirect question with cunctari cf. c. 17, 1,
cunctantibus conspiratis, quando et quomodo aggrederentur: Claud. 21,
6, diu cunctatus an omnes igni ferroque absumeret: Plin. Ep. vi 16, 11,
cunctatus paulum an retro flecteret: Stat. Th. xi 595, cunctatur nescia
virgo, | quid paret. First in Sall. Cat. 52, de parricidis quid statuatis,
cunctamini?

duplum donativum: i.e. double the largess which his brother Titus
offered them to ensure their support. The elevation to power of a new
emperor was preceded or followed by a donativum to the soldiers. Augustus
left by will a donativum of 1000 sesterces for each praetorian, 500 for
each soldier of the urban cohorts, and 300 for each legionary; the total
amount thus distributed by his heir and successor Tiberius being nearly
72,000,000 sesterces. Tiberius, in turn, bequeathed a donativum of the
same amount, which Caligula on his accession doubled. Claudius on
receiving the imperium bought the loyalty of the praetorians by a largess
of 15,000 sesterces to each, and gave the same sum each year on the
anniversary of his accession. Nero paid the same price. Galba estranged
the army by refusing a “donativum grandius solito" which had been
promised (see Galb. 16, 1). Vitellius, lacking money, gave the soldiers
every licence in lieu thereof (Tac. H. ii 94). Vespasian paid each man
merely 100 sesterces, and was none the less well served (Dio lxv 22, Tac.
H. ii 82). The amounts paid by Titus and Domitian are not specified.
Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus, and M. Aurelius paid 20,000 sesterces. See
Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 140; Daremberg-Saglio, ii 385.

participem imperii: Domitian's expectation that he would be left
particeps imperii with Titus was not fulfilled, but Titus from the very
beginning of his reign was ready to proclaim him as his consors and
successor (Tit. 9, 3, where see note). Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vi 32)
says that Domitian poisoned Titus, not because he objected to sharing
the throne with his brother, but to sharing it with one who was both
gentle and good: οὐ τὸ ξὺν ἀδελφῷ ἄρχειν δεινὸν ἡγούμενος, ἀλλὰ τὸ ξὺν πράῳ τε
καὶ χρηστῷ.

fraudem testamento adhibitam: the allegation being that this was
done by Titus, who possessed the qualifications of a master forger, if he
chose to use them; see Tit. 3, 2.

insidias struere fratri: cf. Tit. 9, 3, fratrem insidiari sibi non
desinentem, sed paene ex professo sollicitantem exercitus, etc.: Dio lxvi 26,
(ὁ Τίτος) μετήλλαξεν (obiit) .. ὡς μὲν ἡ φήμη λέγει πρὸς τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ ἀναλωθείς,
ὅτι καὶ πρότερον ἐπεβεβούλευτο ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ.
2L2

pro mortuo deseri iussit: for the conflicting accounts of the death
of Titus and the charges made against Domitian, either of poisoning him
or of accelerating his death when he was ill, see on Tit. 11. Dio (l.c.)
says that while Titus was still breathing, Domitian rode post-haste to
Rome, entered the praetorian camp, received the title and authority of
emperor, and gave the soldiers the same donativum as Titus had done.
For pro see on Vitell. 3, 2, pro afflicto lamentata est.

consecrationis: cf. Dio lxvii 2, αὐτός τε γὰρ καὶ φιλεῖν τὸν ἀδελφὸν καὶ
πενθεῖν προσεποιεῖτο, καὶ τούς τε ἐπαίνους τοὺς ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ μετὰ δακρύων ἔλεξε, καὶ ἐς
τοὺς ἥρωας αὐτὸν σπουδῇ ἐσέγραψε, πάντα τὰ ἐναντιώτατα ὧν ἠβούλετο σκηπτόμενος:
Eutrop. vii 22, (Titus) inter divos relatus est. Pliny, Paneg. 11 (quoted on
Vesp. 23 ad fin.), asserts that Titus deified Vespasian, and Domitian deified
Titus, merely in order that they might be thought, the one a son, the other
a brother of a god. Domitian built in the Campus Martius an elaborate
Porticus Divorum containing two aedes for the worship of the deified
Vespasian and Titus, hoping doubtless that there would be a third aedes
in his own honour when he was consecrated (Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr.
Rom i 3, 565). Domitian, however, was not deified.

obliquis orationibus: these orationes were those known as orationes
principis ad senatum. The proposals (relationes) which the emperor
brought before the senate, though in form they kept up the fiction that
the emperor himself was speaking, were usually read to the senate by one
of the quaestores Caesaris (see on Tit. 6, 1). For the use of obliquus
"indirect" cf. Tac. A. xiv 11, temporum Claudianorum obliqua insectatione:
[Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, causidicorum obliqua dicta (= 'figurae,” Vesp. 13):
Amm. Marc. xv 5, 4, Silvano rogante obliquis verbis; so too the adv., e.g.
Tac. A. v 2, consulem oblique perstringens.

edictis: addressed to the people; see on Tit. 8, 1. An example of an
edict of Domitian which reflected on Titus was that in which he forbade
the making of eunuchs; see on Dom. 7, 1.

inter initia principatus: cf. Ner. 22, 1, inter initia imperii; so inter
initia without gen., e.g. Dom. 9, 1, inter initia ab omni caede abhorrebat. This use of inter initia for initio is post-Aug. (Kühner-Stegmann, i
551).

secretum sibi horarum sumere solebat: it is very doubtful whether
horarum for aliquot horarum is defensible. horarium is the reading in
the Ed. Rom. ii (1470) and the Ed. Venet. (1471). The adj. horarius
(= unius horae), with which Wolf compares momentarius and temporarius,
does not occur in any other author, and is not given in any of the MSS.;
a subst. horarium (= horologium, an instrument for measuring time) is
found in Censorinus. Most probably some numeral has fallen out before
horarum (or after it, according to Casaubon, who proposed horarum iii).
Voss conjectured lararium, which is very improbable. The same difficulty
arises in Ner. 37, 2, mori iussis non amplius quam horarum spatium dabat,
where G has iii horarum, and some of the late MSS. duarum horarum;
Beroaldus read horarium.
For secretum see on Oth. 3, 1; cf. Tac. Agr. 39, (Domitianus) secreto
suo satiatus, "after taking his fill of his usual seclusion" (Furneaux-Anderson). The inaccessible solitude in which Domitian spent so much
time brooding during the years of his despotic cruelty at Rome is mentioned in Plin. Pan. 48, non adire quisquam, non alloqui, audebat, tenebras
semper secretumque captantem; nec unquam ex solitudine sua prodeuntem,
nisi ut solitudinem faceret.
nec quicquam amplius quam: see on c. 21, nihil aliud quam deambulabat.

muscas configere: Dio (lxvi 9) says that Domitian did this in
his Alban villa at the time when he was pretending to be half-witted,
through fear of Vespasian's wrath on his return to Italy, and that he
kept up the practice when he became emperor: ὑπὸ γὰρ τοῦ συνειδότος ὧν
TE
ἐφρόνει καὶ ὧν ἐπεποιήκει οὔτε ἐθάρσει, καὶ προσέτι καὶ μωρίαν ἔστιν ὅτε
προσεποιεῖτο. ἐν γοῦν τῷ ᾿Αλβανῷ χωρίῳ τὰ πλεῖστα διάγων ἄλλα τε πολλὰ καὶ
γελοῖα ἔπραττε, καὶ τὰς μυίας γραφείοις κατεκέντει. τοῦτο γὰρ εἰ καὶ ἀνάξιον τοῦ
τῆς ἱστορίας ὄγκου ἐστίν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι γε ἱκανῶς τὸν τρόπον αὐτοῦ ἐνδείκνυται, ἀναγκαίως
ἔγραψα· καὶ μάλισθ' ὅτι καὶ μοναρχήσας ὁμοίως αὐτὸ ἐποίει, Aurelius Victor
(Caes. 11, 5) assigns it to the period of Domitian's reign when he was
enervated by his excesses: dehinc atrox caedibus bonorum segnisque,
ridicule, remotis procul omnibus, muscarum agmina persequebatur, postquam ad libidinem minus virium erat.

stilo praeacuto: the stilus (γραφίς, γραφεῖον, graphium), which was used
for writing on wax-covered tablets, was made of bone, ivory, or metal
and was sharpened to a very fine point, the upper end being generally
circular and flat for the purpose of smoothing the wax and deleting what
had been written. It could be used as a weapon; e.g. Julius Caesar, when
he was attacked by the conspirators, stabbed Casca through the arm
with a graphium or stilus (Suet. Iul. 82).
Vibio Crispo Q. Vibius Crispus was consul (suffectus) under Nero,
and a second and third time under Vespasian or Domitian; proconsul of
Africa under Vespasian. As a pleader he accumulated a vast fortune
(300,000,000 sesterces, according to Tac. Dial. 8; cf. Mart. iv 54, 7, divitior
Crispo). Tacitus (H. ii 10) describes him as “pecunia potentia ingenio.
inter claros magis quam inter bonos.” His eloquence is praised by
Quintilian, x 1, 119, Vibius Crispus compositus (“finished'') et iucundus
et delectationi natus. He was one of Vespasian's chief friends; cf. Tac.
Dial. 8, (Marcellus Eprius et Crispus Vibius) per multos iam annos potentissimi sunt civitatis ac, donec libuit, principes fori, nunc principes in Caesaris
(i.e. Vespasian) amicitia agunt feruntque cuncta. Juvenal (iv 81 sqq.)
mentions him as a councillor of Domitian and says that he owed his long
life of 80 years to his unfailing astuteness in swimming with the stream
(numquam direxit bracchia contra | torrentem). One of his best known
mots was on the banquets of Vitellius (see note on Vitell. 13, 1). Quintilian
(v 13, 48: viii 5, 15) gives other examples of his wit.

ne muscam quidem: Dio lxvi 9, ὅθεν οὐκ ἀχαρίτως τις εἶπε πρὸς τὸν
ἐρωτῶντα “ τί πράττει Δομιτιανός;” ὅτι “ ἰδιάζει τε, καὶ οὐδὲ μυῖα αὐτῷ
παρακάθηται.” So in [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 8, Hinc percontanti cuidam,
quisquamne in palatio esset, responsum “Ne musca quidem"; in Aur.
Vict. Caes. 11, 5 the reply is given as "Ne musca quidem, nisi forte apud
palaestram.” A proverbial method of describing a deserted place was to
say that not even a fly was there; cf. Plaut. Truc. 281, Quas tu mulieres |
mihi narras? ubi musca nulla femina est in aedibus (i.e. not even a
female fly). Otto, Sprichw. p. 235.

Domitiam: see c. 1, 3.
=
in secundo suo consulatu: in 73 A.D.; see on c. 2, 1.

filium tulerat :
filium sustulerat, susceperat; see on Vesp. 3. The
name of the boy is unknown; for the view that it was "Vespasianus" see
on "Vespasianum," Dom. 15, 1. He probably died in the first few years
of his father's reign. From the fact that on the coins where the boy
appears as "Divus Caesar” Domitian does not bear the title "Germanicus,"
which he assumed in 83 after his victory over the Chatti (c. 6, 1), it has
been inferred that the son died before that year (Gsell, op. cit. 53, n. 4;
Stein, in Pauly-Wissowa v 1514). His deification is referred to in Stat.
S. i 1, 97: Sil. Ital. iii 629. Martial (iv 3), describing Domitian sitting
through a fall of snow at the games in 88, represents the snow-shower as
a prank of the deified boy: Quis siccis (“frozen”) lascivit aquis et ab
aethere ludit? Suspicor has pueri Caesaris esse nives. For the coins of
his mother Domitia on which the youthful “Divus Caesar" figures see
Eckhel, vi 401: Cohen, i² 535.

alteroque anno filiam, consalutavit Augustam: a reading suggested
by Madvig (Adv. Crit. ii 581), which I have adopted faute de mieux, though
there is no evidence that Domitian had any children except the one son.
Roth had already conjectured consalutavit, concluding that this is given
in a dismembered form in M, where the reading is alteroque anno consulatu
filium *** vit Augustam (some letters being erased before vit, while a
later hand has written on the margin deest aliquid). The other MSS. have
either consulatus (-tu in R) filium et Augustam (Gr) or consalutaverat ut
Augustam (X). The latter is the vulgate before Roth's ed.; but Domitian
cannot have saluted Domitia as "Augusta" in 74, seven years before he
was emperor. This chronological difficulty may be removed by reading
ex qua in septimo (for secundo, i.e. IN VII for IN II) suo consulatu
filium tulerat, alteroque anno consalutaverat Augustam. Suetonius would
thus put the son's birth in 80; and say correctly that Domitian saluted
Domitia as "Augusta" in 81 when he became emperor. For the omission
of the relative pronoun (quam) in the second clause see the examples in
Kühner-Stegmann, ii p. 324. In the texts of Roth and Preud'homme a
lacuna is marked between tulerat and alteroque anno consalutavit Augustam;
in that of Ihm between anno and consalutavit Augustam. Numerous
corrections have been proposed; e.g. alteroque anno a consulatu filiam,
Augustam eandem ... repudiavit (Lipsius): in octavo suo consulatu...
alteroque anno ab hoc consulatu filiam, Augustam eandem
repudiavit
(Graevius): alteroque anno suo consalutaverat Augustam, etc. (Ernesti,
who deletes suo after secundo and explains anno suo as "year of his
reign''): filiam tulerat alteroque anno filium, ac consalutaverat Augustam
(Oudendorp): alterumque imperii altero anno, consalutavit Augustam
(Mommsen): alteroque anno principatus [or quam imperium adeptus est]
amisit (Ihm): filiam tulerat alteroque anno principatus filium, eodem illo
anno consalutavit Augustam (Alexander).
..

consalutavit: this compound, which generally denotes the mutual
greetings of a number of friends or the acclamations of a multitude (e.g.
Dom. 1, 3: Tit, 5, 2), is rarely used of individuals; cf. Tac. H. i 57, is
..
imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit: Petron. Satyr. 7, 131: Apul. Met.
viii 31.

Augustam: Domitia must have received this title about the time of
Domitian's accession (Sept. 13, 81), for she is so styled in the Acta Arvalia
of Oct. 1, 81 (C.I.L. vi 2060, Henzen p. cxi); cf. Euseb.-Hieron. Chron.
p. 160 Schoene, under the year 2097 (Oct. 1, 80-Sept. 30, 81): Domitiani
uxor Augusta appellata. The title of "Augusta" was first conferred by
Augustus in his will on his wife Livia (Tac. A. i 8). Caligula offered it
to his grandmother Antonia, wife of Drusus, mother of Germanicus and
Claudius (Calig. 15); she refused it during her lifetime, and Claudius
conferred it on her after her death (Claud. 11). Agrippina, wife of
Claudius and mother of Nero, was styled "Augusta" (Tac. A. xii 26),
as were Poppaea, wife of Nero, and her daughter Claudia (A. xv 23).
Vitellius honoured his mother with the title (id. H. ii 89). Julia, daughter
of Titus, appears as "Augusta" on the coins of her father (see on Tit. 4,
2). For the various inscriptions and coins where Domitia bears this title
see Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 26. From Domitian's time the wife of
the emperor is regularly called "Augusta." Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³
821.

Paridis: a famous pantomimus, born in Egypt, who was the darling
of the licentious Roman matrons, and was so influential at the court of
Domitian that appointment to posts of state depended on his patronage.
The alleged banishment of Juvenal to Egypt is said (Schol. Juv. i 1, vii 92)
to have been due to his attack on Paris in Sat. vii 86 sqq. (cf. vi 82 sqq.).
Dio (lxvii 3) states that Domitian caused Paris to be murdered in the
public street for intriguing with Domitia, and also put to death some of
his admirers who scattered flowers and perfumes on the spot where he
fell. Suetonius (c. 10 infr.) says that Dom. put to death a pupil of
Paris, who resembled his master in form and skill. Martial (xi 13) has a
well-known epitaph on Paris: Urbis deliciae salesque Nili, | ars et gratia,
lusus et voluptas, | Romani decus et dolor theatri | atque omnes Veneres
Cupidinesque | hoc sunt condita, quo Paris, sepulcro.
amore deperditam: see on Vesp. 22, quasi amore suo deperiret.

repudiavit: according to Dio (lxvii 3), Domitian had thoughts of
putting Domitia to death, but he spared her on the intercession of Ursus
(i.e. Flavius Ursus, to whom Statius addresses Silv. ii 6). She was
banished from court probably between the end of 82 and 84 A.D.; see Stein
in Pauly-Wissowa, v 1515.

quasi efflagitante populo: Dio (l.c.) mentions this demand of the people
as a fact: εἶτα δεηθέντος τοῦ δήμου κατηλλάγη τῇ Δομιτίᾳ. Quasi (like ut,
velut, sicut, tanquam, nec aliter quam, haud secus quam, perinde atque).
was used, especially in post-class. writers, with participial clauses in a
subjective sense to express an ostensible reason, a pretended motive, an
imaginary condition, etc. (Kühner-Stegmann, i 790 sq.).

reduxit: Domitia, though taken back by Domitian, lived in constant
dread of his vengeance, and she was privy to the plot which brought about
his death; see c. 14, 1. It is uncertain whether she bore any more
children to him; but Martial (vi 3, in 90 A.D.) refers to the expected birth
of an imperial offspring. Domitia outlived Domitian by many years, and
probably died not long before 140 A.D. (Stein, l.c.).

§ 2. circa administrationem:
cf. Iul. 45, 2, circa corporis curam
morosior: Tib. 69, circa deos ac religiones neglegentior: Ner. 51, circa
cultum habitumque adeo pudendus. This use of circa in the sense of de or
quod attinet ad is not found in class. Lat. (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 253).
For other meanings of circa in Suet. see on Oth. 11, 2.

mixtura quoque .. vitiorum atque virtutum: cf. Tac. H. i 10, Mucianus
malis bonisque artibus mixtus: id. A. vi 51, (Tiberius) inter bona
malaque mixtus incolumi matre. It is probable that quoque is a corruption
due to the following quoque, and that the correct reading is mixturaque
(Lipsius). Bentley suggested mixtura prope aequabili; Ernesti reads
mixtura aequabili.
=

super ingenii naturam: super is difficult: the context clearly requires
Rolfe's rendering “contrary to" (so Stahr wider seine angeborene
Natur''), but there does not seem to be any parallel to this; if, as most
do, we take super praeter (cf. Oth. 5, 1), then the statement that
Domitian's natural tendencies to rapacity and cruelty were increased by
need and fear contradicts what Suetonius says in c. 9 about his natural
mildness and freedom from avarice, his later rapacity and cruelty being
described in c. 10 and c. 12. It is possible that natura should be read,
and super taken in the sense of de (cf. Iul. 5: 20, 1: Tib. 13, 2), the
meaning being "as far as one can guess about his natural disposition, it
was need that made him rapacious and fear that made him cruel.”

amphitheatro: the Flavian amphitheatre (Colosseum); see Vesp. 9, 1:
Tit. 7, 3.

Circo: the Circus Maximus in the valley between the Aventine and
Palatine hills. It was improved by Julius Caesar to hold 150,000
spectators. As the upper tiers of seats and the galleries were of wood,
it suffered repeatedly from fires. Augustus restored it with added
splendour after a destructive fire in 31 B.c. It was partly burned down
in 36 A.D. and Claudius restored and enlarged it to accommodate 250,000.
Nero had it rebuilt within four years after the great fire at Rome in 64 A.D.
which broke out in the Circus (Tac. 4. xv 38). In Domitian's reign the
Circus was once more damaged by fire (see Dom. 5).

bigarum quadrigarumque cursus: racing-chariots were usually bigae
and quadrigae, sometimes trigae, and exceptional instances of six-horsed
chariots (seiuges, seiugae) are mentioned. Connected with the chariotraces were the races between the riders of two horses, who leaped from one
to the other during the race (desultores); cf. Iul. 39, 2, circensibus
quadrigas bigasque et equos desultorios agitaverunt nobilissimi iuvenes:
Dion. Hal. vii 73, πρῶτος ὁ τῶν τεθρίππων τε καὶ συνωρίδων καὶ τῶν ἀζεύκτων
ἵππων ἐγίγνετο δρόμος. See Friedlaender in Marquardt Staatsv. iii² 524.
...

proelium
equestre ac pedestre: these conflicts between divisions
of troops, foot or cavalry, were a development of the armaturae or military
evolutions, either on horseback (arm. equestris) or on foot (arm. pedestris),
and the mock-fights carried out by the young citizens in the Circus from
the days of the Republic (cf. Liv. xliv 9). Distinct from the armatura
equestris was the Ludus Troiae or manoeuvres executed on horseback by
the young nobles (Iul. 39, Aug. 43, Calig. 18, Claud. 21; cf. Verg. Aen. v
596 sqq.). Julius Caesar in his triumphal games included a battle between
two opposing armies, with 500 foot-soldiers, 20 elephants, and 30 horsemen
on each side (Iul. 39).
commisit: see on Galb. 6, 1, commissione ludorum Floralium.
at: see on Vesp. 5, 5.

in amphitheatro navale proelium: no details of this naval spectacle
are given by any writer. Nero, in 57 or 58 A.D., flooded the arena of the
amphitheatre which he built in the Campus Martius, and exhibited a naval
battle between the Athenians and Persians, the water containing fish and
sea-monsters of all kinds (Ner. 12); he gave a similar spectacle in 64
(Dio lxii 15). In 80 A.D. Titus used the flooded arena of the new Flavian
amphitheatre for a battle between the Corcyraeans and Corinthians (Dio
lxvi 25; see on Tit. 7, 3).

nam: see on Vesp. 12. A sea-fight in the amphitheatre was not the
only unusual spectacle he gave, for he also gave venationes, etc., by
artificial light, and held contests between women as well as men.

venationes: spectacles in which wild animals were killed by other
animals or by men. They were introduced at Rome by M. Fulvius Nobilior
at his triumphal games in 186 B.C. They became more and more elaborate,
and under the Empire a wonderful variety of animals was provided: lions,
tigers, bears, panthers, leopards, elephants, hippopotami, rhinoceroses,
crocodiles, etc. At first they formed part of the Ludi Circenses. Julius
Caesar built a wooden amphitheatre for the venationes (θέατρον κυνηγετικόν,
Dio xliii 22; Dio uses the same phrase for the amphitheatre of Statilius
Taurus, and for that of Titus). They continued, however, to be given in
the Circus as well as in the amphitheatre. The men who fought against
the beasts (bestiarii) were condemned criminals or prisoners of war or
hirelings who were trained in a special school for the purpose (ludus
bestiariorum). See Friedl., Sitteng. ii10 77 sqq.

ad lychnuchos: cf. Cic. Quint. Fr. iii 7, 2, ad lychnuchum ligneolum
scribere; so ad lumina "by torch light" (Calig. 45, 1, etc.), ad lunam
(Aen. iv 513), ad lucernam (Flor. iv 2, 71). The lychnuchus (λυχνοῦχος)
was a lampholder or candelabrum; for the varieties see Marquardt,
Privatl.2 711. Julius Caesar at his triumph "ascendit Capitolium ad
lumina, quadraginta elephantis dextra sinistraque lychnuchos gestantibus”
(Iul. 37, 2). Statius (Silv. i 6, 85 sqq.) describes the illumination of the
amphitheatre at one of Domitian's entertainments: Vixdum caerula nox
subibat orbem, | descendit media nitens harena | densas flammeus orbis
inter umbras | vincens Gnosiacae facem coronae (i.e. Ariadne's crown). |
Conlucet polus ignibus nihilque | obscurae patitur licere nocti. Vollmer
(ad loc.) points out that as the amphitheatre was open to the sky the
lights must have been hung from a huge post in the centre of the arena.
nec modo, sed et see on Tit. 8, 3.

pugnas feminarum: in Nero's reign women of high family took part
in the gladiatorial combats and the venationes; cf. Tac. A. xv 32, feminarum
illustrium senatorumque plures per harenam foedati: Juv. i 22, cum
Mevia Tuscum | figat aprum et nuda teneat venabula mamma (where see
Mayor). Titus, at the dedication of the new amphitheatre, had some of the
9000 beasts in the venatio (Tit. 7, 3) slain by women of low rank (γυναῖκες,
οὐ μέντοι ἐπιφανεῖς, Dio lxvi 25). The participation by women in the contests of the arena under Domitian is also mentioned by Dio, lxvii 8, ἔστιν
ὅτε καὶ νάνους (“dwarfs'") καὶ γυναῖκας συνέβαλλε (committebat); cf. Stat.
S. i 6, 53, stat sexus rudis insciusque ferri | et pugnas capit improbus
viriles; Mart. Spect. 6, etc. In 200 A.D. Septimius Severus forbade women
to enter the arena (Dio lxxv 16).

quaestoriis muneribus: Claudius in 47 A.D. had imposed on the quaestors
the duty of furnishing gladiatorial shows at their own expense. Suetonius
(Claud. 24) says he put this burden on the "college of quaestors" in lieu
of paving the streets: Collegio quaestorum pro stratura viarum gladiatorium munus iniunxit (for street-paving as a charge borne by quaestors
see Hirschfeld, Kais. Verwaltungsb. p. 261). Claudius was acting on a
resolution moved by a servile senator Dolabella: Tac. A. xi 22, P. Dolabella
censuit spectaculum gladiatorum per omnes annos celebrandum pecunia
eorum qui quaesturam adipiscerentur. The burden fell on quaestores designati as we see from Tac. A. xiii 5, where its abolition under Nero in 54 A.D.
is mentioned: ne designatis quaestoribus edendi gladiatores necessitas
esset. It was reimposed by Domitian, and continued to the end of the
Empire.
=

olim:
iamdudum, iamdiu, πάλαι. This use of olim is peculiar to
writers of the Silver age.

paria postulandi: Seneca (Ep. 7, 4) distinguishes ordinaria paria
(par = pair of gladiators) from postulaticia paria, the latter being kept in
reserve by the munerarius and only produced in response to the insistent calls
of the spectators (Summers ad loc.). Such demands of the spectators are
often mentioned; e.g. Claud. 21, 5, cum Palumbum (a gladiator) postulantibus
daturum se promisit, etc.: Mart. Spect. 20, Cum peteret pars haec Myrinum,
pars illa Triumphum, | promisit pariter Caesar utraque manu. | Non potuit
melius litem finire iocosam. | O dulce invicti principis ingenium! (Friedlaender says that Myrinus and Triumphus were bestiarii, as in the case of
gladiators the spectators would clamour for a special pair.)

e suo ludo: a ludus gladiatorius, or training-school for gladiators,
belonging to the emperor Caligula is mentioned in Plin. N.H. xi 245.
Later there were four imperial schools at Rome: (1) the ludus matutinus
for the training of bestiarii (this probably existed in the time of Claudius);
(2) the ludus magnus; (3) the ludus Gallicus; (4) the ludus Dacicus.
It is generally held that the last three were established by Domitian as
dependencies of the Colosseum; the Gallicus and Dacicus deriving their
names from the nationality of the gladiators trained there. See Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1580. When ludus is used without specification, as here and in
c. 17, it probably means the ludus magnus (Hirschfeld, op. cit. 290).
Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 1071) thinks that after the building of the Colosseum
private individuals were forbidden to maintain troupes of gladiators at
Rome as they had been in the habit of doing. Imperial gladiatorial schools
were also to be found in other parts of Italy (e.g. Capua and Praeneste)
and in the provinces.

aulico apparatu: more splendidly accoutred than the ordinary
gladiators supplied by the lanista to the munerarius (see on Vitell. 12).
Pertinax sold as part of the belongings of Commodus “arma gladiatoria
gemmis auroque composita" and also "torques (necklets) gladiatorias”
(Capitol. Pert. 8). On the rich and artistic equipment of gladiators see
Friedl. Sitteng. ii10 60. The adj. aulicus (αὐλικός, = ad aulam, i.e. domum
regiam, pertinens) is also used by Suet. in Ner. 45, 1, aulicis luctatoribus;
Oth. 2, 2, aulicam libertinam. The word occurs only once earlier as a
subst., "courtier," in Nepos Dat. 5, 2, invidiam aulicorum excepit; so in
Suet. Calig. 19, 3, causam ab interioribus aulicis (“"most confidential
courtiers'') proditam. For apparatus (sumptuousness, magnificence) cf.
Vitell. 10, 1: Claud. 17, 2, triumphavit maximo apparatu: Cic. Tusc. v 9,
maximo ludorum apparatu; Cic. Off. ii 55, ludorum venationumque apparatu
pecunias profundunt.

§ 2. coccinatus: this rare form (= coccino indutus) occurs in Mart. i
96, 6; ν 35, 2. Suetonius also uses the subst. coccum for scarlet (threads
or strands); Ner. 30, 3, purpura coccoque funibus nexis. The dye was got
from a worm, the cochineal kermes (coccus ilicis); Pliny (N.H. ix 141)
wrongly describes it as a vegetable product (granum). See Marquardt,
Privatl.2 506.

parvo portentosoque capite: "with a small and monstrously misshapen head"; or "with a prodigiously small head" (Thomson-Forester).
portentosus is often used of monstrous growths, freaks of nature; e.g.
Cic. Div. ii 28, 60, si quando aliqua portentosa aut ex pecude aut ex
homine nata dicuntur; so too prodigiosus, e.g. Quintil. ii. 5, 11, distortis et quocunque modo prodigiosis corporibus. Dwarfs and physical
monstrosities of every kind enjoyed extraordinary favour both at Court
and among the wealthy classes at Rome under the Empire. Augustus was
exceptional in his loathing for them; cf. Aug. 83, pumilos (‘dwarfs'')
atque distortos et omnes generis eiusdem, ut ludibria naturae malique
ominis abhorrebat. Mayor on Juv. viii 32 has collected a number of
passages on this subject; cf. Friedl. Sitteng. ii¹º 372. Ernesti needlessly
proposed to alter parvo to pravo.

cum quo: here (as in Iul. 6, 2; 52, 1: Aug. 35, 3: Tib. 4, 3) Suetonius
puts cum before the relative, an order of words found at times in Cic.
and constantly in Nepos and Livy (Kühner-Stegmann, i 585).

auditus est dum ex eo quaerit: a remarkable constr. instead of
the normal cum ex eo quaereret. At a dinner given by Tiberius, a dwarf
who was standing by among the jesters suddenly asked Tiberius why
Paconius, who was charged with treason, remained so long alive; the
emperor rebuked him for his pertness, but a few days later wrote to the
senate to expedite the execution of Paconius (Tib. 61).
lemma: auditus est dum ex eo quaerit

text:
ordinatione: = constitutione praesidum provinciarum (Baumg.-Cr.). See
on ‘‘ordinavit,” Vesp. 23, 2.
Aegypto praeficere: see on “praefectus Aegypti,” Vesp. 6, 3.

Mettium Rufum: Marcus Iunius Mettius Rufus is frequently mentioned in papyri as prefect of Egypt. These references (including Pap.
Hamb. i 2 p. 125 sq., Pap. Oxyrh. i 72, 10, ii 237 col. viii 43, ii 247, Рар.
Strassb. 22, 25, Pap. Amherst. 68 col. ii p. 81) are tabulated in chronological order by Janssen (ad loc.), who shows that Rufus was already
prefect (ἡγεμών) in Aug. 89, and that he was still in office in 94; his
successor Petronius Secundus is mentioned as prefect in March 95 (Dessau,
Inscr. Lat. 8759 d.). See also Mommsen, Eph. Epigr. vii p. 427; Dessau,
Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii p. 374.

edidit navales pugnas.. lacu: Dio lxvii 8, ἐν καινῷ τινι χωρίῳ ναυμαχίαν
ἐπετέλεσε. The "new place" of which Dio speaks is distinguished from
the vetus naumachia of Augustus used also by Titus (see on Tit. 7, 3).
The new basin which Domitian constructed was probably in the Vatican
valley.
The title regio Naumachiae for the quarter extending from
St. Peter's to the Castle of St. Angelo (Mausoleum Hadriani) survived all
through the Middle Ages; see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 661.
Domitian's basin was destroyed in a short time and the stone was used
for other purposes (Dom. 5).

iustarum: "regular," "full-sized.” Suetonius is fond of the use
of iustus in the sense of “qualis quis ex iure esse debet vel ex recepta
consuetudine esse solet” (Baumg.-Cr.); e.g. Vesp. 3, habuit paene iustae
uxoris loco: Galb. 12, 2, iustos milites fecerat: Vitell. 15, 1, iustae militiae
commoda: Galb. 21, statura fuit iusta: Claud. 17, 1, iusti triumphi decus.

inter
imbres perspectavit: Dio (l.c.) says that not only did nearly
all of the combatants in the naval fight die, but also many of the spectators.
When a violent storm with torrential rain came on, Domitian allowed no
one to leave, and though he changed his own robe, nobody else was allowed
to do so; in consequence, numbers fell sick and died. To console the
populace, Domitian gave a public banquet lasting all night long.

§ 3. fecit ludos Saeculares: in 88 A.D. Tacitus, who was one of the
Quindecimviri sacris faciundis who had charge of the Ludi Saeculares,
when mentioning (A. xi 11) the previous celebration under Claudius in 47,
refrains from describing them, as he says he had already given a description
of those of Domitian (in one of the books of the Historiae now lost).
Other references to Domitian's celebration are in Mart. iv 1, 7, Hic (i.e.
Domitian) colat ingenti redeuntia saecula lustro, | et quae Romuleus sacra
Tarentos habet; x 63,3; Stat. Silv. i 4, 17; iv 1, 37 (Janus addresses
Domitian), mecum altera saecula condes | et tibi longaevi revocabitur ara
Tarenti. In these passages Tarentos (-um) is the name of a volcanic fissure
in the Campus Martius where there was an ara Ditis patris et Proserpinae
and the Ludi Saeculares were performed; hence, under the Republic, they
were called the Ludi Tarentini. The festival lasted three days and three
nights. The ceremonies are described in Zosimus ii 5 (quoted in full by
Wickham in his Introd. to the Carmen Saeculare of Horace, an ode sung
to Apollo in the celebration by Augustus in 17 в.с.). In 1887 the subterranean ara Tarenti was discovered, and in 1890 fragmentary tables of
marble with inscriptions commemorating the Ludi Saeculares of Augustus
and Septimius Severus were found in the bed of the Tiber (Mommsen,
Eph. Epigr. viii 225 sqq.; Daremberg-Saglio, iv 990 sqq.).

computata ratione temporum: the chronology of the Ludi Saeculares
(Tarentini) is very obscure and depends mainly on statements in the De
die natali of Censorinus (238 A.D.). Dio (liv 18) says that the celebration
by Augustus was the fifth, and Censorinus (17, 8) mentions four earlier
in 449, 348, 249, 149 (146) в.с. The saeculum was reckoned as 100 or
110 years, the latter estimate being connected with the Greek belief that
a new cycle, a παλιγγενεσία, began after four periods of 110 years. The
Quindecimviri adopted the period of 110 years, and when Augustus (who
was chief Quindecimvir) wished to celebrate the games in 17 B.C., the
Quindecimviri invented records of previous celebrations in 456, 346, 236,
126 в.с. Claudius held the Ludi in 47 A.D., the 800th year from the
