foundation of Rome, and said that Augustus had been premature: Claud. 21,
Fecit et saeculares, quasi anticipatos ab Augusto nec legitimo tempori
reservatos, quamvis ipse (Claudius) in historiis suis prodat, intermissos eos
Augustum multo post diligentissime annorum ratione subducta in ordinem
redegisse. At this celebration the summons of the herald to behold games:
"quos nec spectasset quisquam nec spectaturus esset'" caused much amusement, as many were still alive who had seen them under Augustus.
Domitian, though professing to follow the calculation of Augustus and
the period of 110 years, was six years in advance in holding them in
88 A.D. Subsequent celebrations were (1) by Antoninus Pius in 147, the
900th year from the foundation of Rome; (2) by Septimius Severus in 204,
after two intervals of 110 years from the Ludi of Augustus in 17 в.с.;
(3) by the emperor Philippus in 247, the 1000th year of Rome.
Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 385 sqq.
See

centum missus: the chariot race (missus, ἆθλον, ἅμιλλα) was usually
seven laps (curricula, spatia) round the metae at either end of the arena,
the finishing-point being a chalk line (creta, calx).
The total distance
traversed was about 9 kilometres, and Friedlaender (in Marquardt, Staatsv..
iii² 515) calculates that the number of races per hour would average 3.
Dio (lix 7) says that in races held by Caligula in 37 A.D. there were 20 on
the first day and 24 on the second, whereas 12 was the biggest number
previously. From the time of Claudius and Nero the usual number seems
to have been 24, though there are instances of 30, 36, 40, and 48. It is
almost incredible that Domitian could have got through 100 missus in
one day, even by reducing the number of laps. Dio (lxxii 16) mentions
that Commodus got through 30 in 2 hours; but, as Friedl. says, the missus
must have been much shortened or held in a smaller circus. In our passage
Friedl. would read diebus for die, but in the Ludi Saeculares of Augustus
the Circenses only occupied one day. In fixing the number of races at
100 Domitian was probably influenced by the number of years in the
saeculum.

§ 4. quinquennale certamen: Nero, eager for glory as a poet, singer,
and player on the cithara, introduced Greek agones (ἀγῶνες, certamina) or
artistic competitions at Rome in 60 A.D.; cf. Ner. 12, 3, instituit et quinquennale certamen primus omnium Romae more Graeco triplex, musicum
(singing, instrumental music, poetry, oratory) gymnicum equestre, quod
appellavit Neronia. Apparently this was discontinued at Nero's death,
and in 86 A.D. Domitian, to celebrate his restoration of the temple of
Jupiter Capitolinus, founded a similar agon Capitolinus. The prizes were
oaken wreaths; cf. Mart. iv 54, 1, O cui Tarpeias licuit contingere quercus,
etc.: Juv. vi 387, an Capitolinam deberet Pollio quercum | sperare? The
contest in Gr. and Lat. declamation was soon abandoned; that in Gr. and
Lat. poetry became widely famed, and a poet's chief ambition was to be
crowned by the emperor's hand. Statius often (e.g. S. v 3, 225 sqq.)
laments his want of success with his Thebais.

coronarum: this reading of Stephanus for coronatorum is supported
by Ner. 22, 2, palmarum numerum ampliare, and is accepted by nearly all
subsequent editors. Ihm retains coronatorum, but it seems very doubtful
Latin.

et prosa oratione: et means "as well as in poetry." Both prosa
(= proversa "straightforward") oratio and prosa by itself are used by
Quintil. and other post-class. writers; Cic. has oratio soluta, opp. to vincula
numerorum. The praise of Jupiter Capitolinus was a stock theme in the
contests in eloquence at the agon Capitolinus (Quintil. iii 7, 4, laudes
Capitolini Iovis, perpetua sacri certaminis materia). Suetonius mentions
that Palfurius Sura had once received the prize (Dom. 13, 1).

citharoedos chorocitharistae psilocitharistae: the citharoedus sang to
the accompaniment of his cithara; the psilocitharista (-es) played without
singing; the chorocitharista played an accompaniment to a chorus (cf.
choraules). The form χοροκιθαριστής is not found in Greek, but χοροκιθαρεύς
occurs in inscriptions (C.I.G. 2758 F, 2759); ψιλοκιθαριστής is not found
outside inscriptions, but we have such expressions as ψιλὴ κιθάρισις καὶ
αὔλησις (Plat. Legg. 669 E), and ψιλή μουσική, instrumental music, opposed
to ἡ μετὰ μελῳδίας, accompanied by song (Aristot. Pol. viii 5, 11). Suetonius
is the only Lat. author cited as using chorocitharista and psilocitharista,
but citharoedus (κιθαρῳδός) is found frequently.
stadio: see c. 5.

cursu etiam virgines: cf. Dio lxvii 8, ἐποίησε δὲ καὶ θέαν (spectaculum)
πολυτελῆ, ἐν ᾗ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδὲν ἐς ἱστορίαν ἐπίσημον παρελάβομεν, πλὴν ὅτι καὶ
παρθένοι τῷ δρομικῷ ἠγωνίσαντο. This innovation of Domitian's was soon discontinued. He may have been copying the Spartans (cf. Xen. de rep.
Lac. 1, 4; Eur. Androm. 595 sqq.; Propert. iii 14) or the famous races
between girls at the festival in honour of Hera at Olympia which are
described in Pausan. v 16, 2.

crepidatus: the pallium and crepidae were the distinctive Greek dress,
as opp. to the Roman toga and calcei; cf. Tib. 13, 1, redegit se, deposito
patrio habitu, ad pallium et crepidas. Caligula, besides the military boot
(caliga) from which he got his name, also wore cothurni and crepidae
(Calig. 52). Latin comedies with Greek themes and dresses were called
fabulae palliatae, while fábulae crepidatae denoted Latin tragedies of a
like kind.
purpurea toga Graecanica: Mommsen (Staatsr. i3 417 n.) explains
this as the vestis Graecula (C.I.L. vi 8552), the Greek festal attire which
the Roman emperors wore during their stay in Greek cities (e.g. Claudius
in Naples, Dio 1x 6, ἐν μὲν ταῖς τῆς μουσικῆς θεωρίαις ἱμάτιον καὶ κρηπίδας, ἐν δὲ
τῷ γυμνικῷ ἀγῶνι πορφυρίδα καὶ στέφανον χρυσοῦν ἐλάμβαve: Hadrian in Athens,
Dio lxix 16); also on festal occasions at Rome (e.g. Nero on his triumphal
entry into Rome after his victory at the Olympic games, Ner. 25, in veste
purpurea distinctaque stellis aureis chlamyde: Commodus in the Roman
theatre, Dio lxxii 17). The ἀγωνοθέται, or presidents at the Greek games,
wore a purple robe (πορφυρίς) and a golden crown, and so Domitian as
ἀγωνοθέτης at his agon Capitolinus conformed to the Greek usage. Suetonius
uses Graecanicus = "in the Greek fashion" (Varr. L.L., Plin. N.H., etc.)
only here; elsewhere always Graecus.

coronam cum effigie: an illustration of a similar crown with three
medallions inset is given in Daremberg-Saglio, i 1525, fig. 1986.
temples of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva were all on the Capitol.
The

assidentibus: they not only sat beside him but also acted as assessors
or judges of the contests along with him; cf. C.I.L. ix 2860, coronatus
est inter poetas Latinos omnibus sententiis iudicum. In Herodian i 9, 2
the emperor Commodus at the Capitoline contests is described as θεατὴς καὶ
ἀθλοθέτης σὺν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἱερεῦσιν.

Diali sacerdote: the flamen Dialis attached to Jupiter (Diespiter) was
one of the three flamines maiores (the other two were the Martialis and
Quirinalis). The office, which lasted for life, was of great dignity but
involved many disabilities. The Dialis had a seat in the senate, was
preceded by a lictor, etc., but he was forbidden e.g. to mount on horseback, to be absent from Rome, or to swear an oath (sometimes, to enable
him to hold a magistracy, his colleague took the oath for him; Liv. xxxi
50). Candidates for the office were few, and it was in abeyance from 87
to 11 B.C. when Augustus restored it (Aug. 31, 4). See Marquardt,
Staatsv. iii² 328 sqq. The flamen Dialis sat beside Domitian at these contests, as the emperor was the earthly representative of Jove.

collegio Flavialium: the Flaviales were the priests who had charge of
the worship of the deified Flavian emperors, Vespasian and Titus. Such
worship began with the appointment of the Augustales (sodales, sacerdotes,
25 in number) by Tiberius in honour of Augustus and the Julian gens (see
on Galb. 8, 1). Besides the title Flaviales we also find in inscriptions
Flaviales Titiales, Titiales Flaviales, or simply Titiales; Titus, as the most
popular of the Flavian emperors, giving his name to the priesthood of
the gens. Other similar collegia were the Claudiales, Hadrianales,
Antoniniani (Ant. Pius), Aureliani (M. Aurelius), and lastly Alexandriani
(Alexander Severus).
nisi quod: see on Vitell. 7, 1.

Albano: the estate and villa, which may have originally belonged
to Pompey, at the foot of the Mons Albanus in Latium was a favourite
resort of the earlier emperors and was developed by Domitian into a
walled area including a palatial residence, baths, theatre, amphitheatre,
camp for the praetorians, etc. It became the notorious arx Albana of
which Tacitus (Agr. 45) and Juvenal (iv 145) speak with such bitterness.
Dio mentions the "Albanum" of Domitian and says (lxvii 1): τοῦτο τὸ
χωρίον ὑπὸ τὸ ὄρος τὸ ᾿Αλβανόν, ἀφ᾽ οὗπερ οὕτως ὠνομάσθη, ὂν ὥσπερ τινα ἀκρόπολιν
ἐξείλετο.

Quinquatria: the more usual form is Quinquatrus (pl.), originally a
festival of Mars on the 19th of March (five days after the Ides, whence
the name according to Varr. L.L. vi 14), but when the temple of Minerva
on the Aventine was dedicated on that day, the festival ceased to be
purely military and was celebrated by various arts and trades in honour
of their patroness Minerva. From 168 B.C. it lasted from the 19th to the
23rd of March and the name came to be misunderstood as the "five-day"
festival (cf. Ov. Fast. iii 809-834). It was a holiday time in schools
(Juv. x 115, with Mayor's note). Augustus on one occasion spent every
day of the Quinquatrus at the gaming-table (Aug. 71, 3); Nero, when
trying to compass the death of his mother Agrippina, invited her to Baiae
to celebrate the Quinquatrus with him (Ner. 34, 2; Oth. 3, 1, n.).

Minervae: cf. Dio lxvii 1, θεῶν μὲν γὰρ τὴν ᾿Αθηνῶν ἐς τὰ μάλιστα ἤγαλλε,
καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ Παναθήναια (= Quinquatria) μεγάλως ἑώρταζε, καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς
ἀγῶνας καὶ ποιητῶν καὶ λογογράφων, μονομάχων (gladiatorum) τε κατ' ἔτος, ὡς
εἰπεῖν, ἐν τῷ ᾿Αλβανῷ ἐποίει. Domitian worshipped Minerva with superstitious
veneration (superstitiose colebat, c. 15, 3); he regarded himself as her
especial favourite, and is said to have even claimed to be her son (Philostr.
vit. Apollon. vii 24). Quintilian (x 1, 91) speaks of her as the familiare
numen of Domitian; cf. Mart. viii 1, 4, Pallas Caesariana; ix 3, 10:
Stat. S. i 1, 5; iv 1, 22. He erected temples to her at Rome including
that in the Forum Transitorium (begun by Dom. and completed by Nerva,
see Dom. 5), and that to Minerva Chalcidica in the Campus Martius. Her
image appears on many of his coins. He gave the title of Prima Minervia
to a new legion enrolled by him.

magisterio: used of the directorship of a cult, the presidency of a
religious body, as in Calig. 22, 3 (of Caligula's own worship), magisteria
sacerdotii ditissimus quisque, et ambitione et licitatione maxima, vicibus
comparabant; cf. Capitolin. M. Anton. Philos. 4, fuit in eo sacerdotio (i.e.
the Salii) et praesul et vates et magister et multos inauguravit atque
exauguravit nemine praeeunte quod ipse carmina cuncta didicisset.

venationes: Juvenal (iv 99) mentions these as held at the arx Albana
of Domitian: profuit ergo nihil misero quod comminus ursos | figebat
Numidas, Albana nudus harena | venator. Suetonius refers to them again
in c. 19.

poetarum certamina: it was at this Alban festival that Statius three
times won the golden olive-crown, though he was unsuccessful at the agon
Capitolinus; cf. Silv. iv 2, 63 (describing a banquet with Domitian), qua
mihi felices epulas mensaeque dedisti | sacra tuae, talis longo post tempore
venit | lux mihi, Troianae qualis sub collibus Albae, | cum modo Germanas
ācies, modo Daca sonantem | proelia Palladio tua me manus induit auro.
Martial mentions the golden olive-crown: iv 1, 5, hic (i.e. Domitian) colat
Albano Tritonida (= Minervam) multus in auro: ix 23, 1, O cui virgineo
(= Palladio) flavescere contigit auro, etc.: ix 24, 5, non solam tribuit
Pallas tibi, Care, coronam. See on Vesp. 19, 1, coronas aureas.
§5. congiarium: see on Vesp. 18.

nummorum trecenorum: this was the normal amount given in the
1st cent. A.D. by various emperors: Tiberius, Caligula (twice), Claudius,
Vespasian, Nerva. Augustus gave five congiaria, one being 300 sesterces;
cf. Aug. 41, 2, congiaria populo frequenter dedit, sed diversae fere summae:
modo quadringenos, modo trecenos, nonnunquam ducenos quinquagenosque
The total amount
nummos. Nero gave 400 sesterces (Ner. 10, 1).
distributed at each of the three congiaria of Domitian was 60,000,000
sesterces (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 138).

ter dedit: the first two congiaria may have been given at the triumphs
over the Chatti and Dacians in 83 and 89; see c. 6, 1. The third was
given in 93 to celebrate the victory over the Sarmatians; cf. Mart. viii 15,
Dum nova Pannonici numeratur gloria belli, | omnis et ad reducem dum
litat ara Iovem, | dat populus, dat gratus eques, dat tura senatus, | et
ditant Latias tertia dona tribus.

epulum: this presumably is the same banquet as that mentioned in
c. 13, 1, in amphitheatro epuli die. Janssen would identify it with that
given by Domitian in the amphitheatre on the Kalends of December, which
is so vividly described in Stat. Silv. i 6, and also with those mentioned in
Dio lxvii 4, τοῖς τε θεωμένοις συχνὰ διὰ τῶν σφαιρίων (= tesserarum) ἐδίδου, καί
ποτε καὶ ἐδείπνισεν αὐτοὺς κατὰ χώραν καθημένους: Mart. v 49, 8, Hic error
tibi profuit Decembri, | tum, cum prandia misit Imperator, | cum panariolis
tribus redisti: viii 50, 7, Vescitur omnis eques tecum populusque patresque, |
et capit ambrosias cum duce Roma dapes. Friedlaender explains Mart. v
49 as referring to the banquet (prob. in 88) described by Statius, but
thinks that in viii 50 Martial refers to another banquet (prob. in Jan. 93)
given by Dom. after his victory over the Sarmatians. Vollmer (on Stat.
l.c.) reasonably regards it as purely arbitrary to identify the banquet
described by Statius with any of those mentioned elsewhere. Janssen
seems to overlook the chronological difficulty of identifying the banquet
described by Statius as given on Dec. 1 with that mentioned by Suetonius
as given at the Septimontium on Dec. 11 (or the following days); another
difficulty in this identification is noticed on c. 13, 1.

Septimontiali sacro, cum quidem: this is a correction by Iac.
Gronovius of sacrorum quidem. Some of the "codices deteriores" have
sacro quidem (read by Roth and Preud'homme) and sacrorum quidem die
(read by Sabellicus and most of the early editors). Among the emendations
which have been proposed are:-Sept. sacro quondam (Torrentius and
Bentley): Sept. sacro senatui quidem (Politian, followed by Baumg.-Cr.) :
Sept. sacro primoque die (Oudendorp): Sept. sacro, primo quidem die
(Ernesti). All readings except that of Gronovius involve putting a fuil
stop after epulum and treating the following sentence as an independent
statement. Ihm regards the correction of Gronovius as probable, and it
is defended by Alexander (op. cit. 27 sqq.) and read by Janssen and Rolfe.
The Septimontium or Septimontiale sacrum was celebrated on Dec. 11.
The seven montes were the three divisions of the Palatine, viz. Palatium,
Cermalus, Velia; the three of the Esquiline, viz. Mons Oppius, Mons
Cispius, and the Fagutal; and the Subura (on this and the correction
"Sucusa" see Platner-Ashby, Topogr. Dict. Rome). Originally the festival
ranked among sacra popularia or publica, but with the extension of Rome
it was considered as one of the feriae privatae celebrated by the montani,
and not by the pagani who inhabited what was at first the farm-land
round Rome. On the day of the Septimontium there was a sacrifice
(palatuar) on the Palatine by the flamen Palatualis, and no vehicles drawn
by beasts of burden were allowed in the old city (Plut. Quaest. Rom. 69).
See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 190; Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 113. In Domitian's
time apparently the Septimontium must have lasted for more than one
day, part of the celebration consisting of gladiatorial displays as in the
case of the Quinquatria, etc.

panariis: cf. Calig. 18, 2, panaria cum obsonio viritim divisit: Stat.
S. i 6, 27 (describing the imperial servants distributing the food in the
amphitheatre), Ecce autem caveas subit per omnes | insignis specie, decora
cultu | plebes altera non minor sedente. | Hi panaria candidasque mappas |
subvectant epulasque lautiores, | illi marcida vina largiuntur, etc. panarium
(panis), lit. "bread-basket," is used in Plin. Ep. i 6, 3 for a "luncheonbasket"; Martial (v 49, 10) has the diminutive panariola for the small
baskets (sportellae) of food provided for the people by Domitian.

sportellis: like sportula (see on c. 7, 1), sportella was a dim. from
sporta (σπυρίς, σπείρω) a plaited basket; it occurs also in Cic. Fam. ix 20,
Petron. Satyr. 40.

obsonio: obsonium (ὀψώνιον) denoted any cooked food eaten in addition
to bread, but more especially fish (Marquardt, Privatl.2 432); it often
2 м
implies "dainties," e.g. Vitell. 10, 12, inter profusissimos obsoniorum
apparatus: Iul. 43, 2, legem praecipue sumptuariam exercuit dispositis circa
macellum custodibus, qui obsonia contra vetitum proposita retinerent.

initium vescendi primus fecit: cf. Stat. S. i 6, 42, Una vescitur omnis
ordo mensa, | parvi, femina, plebs, eques, senatus: | libertas reverentiam
remisit. Et tu quin etiam (quis hoc vacare, | quis promittere possit hoc
deorum?) | nobiscum socias dapes inisti. | Iam se, quisquis is est, inops
beatus | convivam ducis esse gloriatur. For the pleonasm cf. Liv. vi 12, 10,
primum initium certaminis: iii 54, 9, prima initia inchoastis libertatis.
omne genus: adverbial acc., see on Tit. 7, 3.
rerum missilia sparsit: cf. Calig. 18, 2, sparsit missilia variarum

rerum: Ner. 11, 2, sparsa et populo missilia omnium rerum per omnes
dies: singula cotidie milia avium cuiusque generis, multiplex penus,
tesserae frumentariae, vestis, aurum, argentum, gemmae, margaritae,
tabulae pictae, mancipia, iumenta, atque etiam mansuetae ferae, novissime
naves, insulae ("apartment houses''), agri. Sometimes the gifts themselves, at other times tesserae entitling the recipients to gifts or amusements, were scattered among the people. The first sparsio missilium that
can be dated was that of Agrippa in 33 B.C., when he rained tesserae
upon the heads of the people in the theatre and provided vast quantities
of wares of all kinds to be scrambled for (Dio xlix 43). Statius (S. i 6,
66) mentions Domitian's dives sparsio at the feast in the amphitheatre.

popularia: = sedes populi in theatro (amphitheatro); so equestria (sc.
loca or sedilia) in Calig. 26, 4. This substantival use seems peculiar to
Suetonius; cf. Claud. 25, 4, where the German envoys, having been shown
to the seats of the common people in the theatre (in popularia deducti),
insisted on sitting with the senate in the orchestra, where the Parthian
and Armenian envoys were sitting. For the position of the popularia in
the amphitheatre see below on cuneos.

tesseras: such tokens, billets, or tallies were used for various purposes;
e.g. the tesseraę frumentariae (Aug. 40, 2; Ner. 11, 2) and tesserae nummariae (Aug. 41, 2) for which the poorer classes could get corn or money.
Dio (lxi 18, lxvi 25) describes those distributed by Nero and Titus at their
sparsiones as small wooden balls inscribed with what they could be
exchanged for. The shape and material of the tesserae scattered on such
occasions varied; see Daremberg-Saglio, iii 1936, for illustrations of those
in the form of fish, animals, etc., with a number marked on them. Sometimes they were shaped like coins and were called nomismata; cf. Mart. viii
78, 9, nunc veniunt subitis lasciva nomismata nimbis, | nunc dat spectatas
tessera larga feras.

cuneos: "wedges" or "blocks" of seats. In the amphitheatre the
senators occupied seats on the podium or terrace on the top of the wall
surrounding the arena. Each of the rising divisions of seats (gradus)
above the podium was called a maenianum; the equites sat in the 14 rows
of the first maenianum; in the second were the popularia or seats of the
populus; in the third were wooden benches for the pullati or lower classes.
The lines of seats in the maeniana were divided into blocks (cunei) by
short flights of stairs, to facilitate access. The podium was separated
from the seats of the equites by a wall (balteus) and a passage or
promenade (praecinctio), and each maenianum was separated from that
above it in the same way.
pronuntiavit: = publice promisit; cf. Galb. 16, 1.

plurima et amplissima opera: Eutrop. vii 23, Romae quoque multa
opera fecit: in his Capitolium, et Forum transitorium, Odeum, Divorum
porticus, Iseum, Serapeum, ac stadium: Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 4, multaque
opera inchoata per patrem, vel fratris studio, atque in primis Capitolium
absolvit: Epit. 11, 3, Romae multa aedificia vel coepta vel a fundamentis
construxit: Oros. vii 10, 2, plurimas urbis aedes destructis populi Romani
rebus exstruxit. Martial (ix 3) declares that Olympus would be bankrupt
if the gods tried to pay their debt to Domitian for his magnificent temples;
Jove could not even pay a paltry composition. According to Plutarch
(Poplic. 15) building was merely a disease with Domitian, and the line of
Epicharmus on the ἄσωτος or spendthrift “ Οὐ φιλάνθρωπος τύ γ᾽ ἐσσ᾽· ἔχεις
νόσον· χαίρεις διδούς." might be applied to Domitian in some such way as
this: “ Οὐκ εὐσεβὴς οὐδὲ φιλότιμος τύ γ᾽ ἐσσί· ἔχεις νόσον· χαίρεις οἰκοδομῶν,
ὥσπερ ὁ Μίδας ἐκεῖνος ἅπαντά σοι χρυσᾶ καὶ λίθινα βουλόμενος γίνεσθαι.”
incendio: in 80 A.D., under Titus; see Tit. 8, 3.

Capitolium: the early history of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus
is given on Vitell. 15, 33; for its form and splendour as restored by
Domitian see Jordan Topogr. Rom i 2, 86 sqq. and the illustrations in
Daremberg-Saglio i 903 sqq. The doors were plated with gold, and it was
roofed with gilt tiles. Plutarch (l.c.) says that the gilding alone cost
more than 12,000 talents (about £2,400,000), and he adds the interesting
detail that the columns of Pentelic marble were excellently proportioned
when he saw them at Athens, but that when they were cut and polished
anew at Rome their beauty was impaired by their appearing too slender
for their height.

rursus arserat: Plut. (l.c.), ἅμα τῷ τελευτῆσαι Οὐεσπασιανόν, ἐνεπρήσθη τὸ
Καπιτώλιον. ὁ δὲ τέταρτος οὗτος νεὼς ὑπὸ Δομιτιανοῦ καὶ συνετελέσθη καὶ καθιερώθη.
After the temple had been burned down in 69 A.D. (see Vitell. 15, 3) it
was restored by Vespasian (Vesp. 8, 5), and Plut. says that Vespasian was
luckier than Sulla who died before his temple to Jupiter Capitolinus was
dedicated, whereas Vespasian died before his was destroyed, as it was by
fire immediately after his death. From the Acta Arvalia (C.I.L. vi 2059,
Newton 159) we learn that on Dec. 7, 80 A.D. the Fratres Arvales (who
had to meet in the adjoining temple of Ops since that of Jupiter Capitolinus
had been burned) offered their vows for the restoration and dedication of
the temple by Titus: M. Tittio Frugi, T. Vinicio Iuliano cos., vii Idus
Decembr., in Capitolio in aedem Opis sacerdotes convenerunt ad vota
nuncupando ad restitutionem et dedicationem Capitoli ab Imp. T. Caesare
Vespasiano Aug.

sub titulo tantum suo: in marked contrast to his father Vespasian,
who inscribed on the buildings which he restored merely the names of the
original builders and not his own; Dio lxvi 10 (Zonar. xi 17), τὰ τεμένη
καὶ τὰ δημόσια ἔργα τὰ πεπονηκότα ἀνελάμβανε, καὶ τὰ ἤδη ἐφθαρμένα ἐπανεσκεύαζε,
καὶ συντελουμένοις αὐτοῖς οὐ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπέγραφεν ὄνομα, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῶν πρώτως
δομησαμένων.

aedem Custodi Iovi: as a thankoffering for his escape from the
Capitol when it was stormed by the Vitellians he built in Vespasian's reign a
:

small shrine (sacellum) to Jupiter Conservator on the site of the dwelling
of the aedituus who had sheltered him (see on c. 1, 2), and when he became emperor he also consecrated a vast temple to Jupiter Custos, with an
effigy of himself in the arms (or on the lap) of the god; Tac. H. iii 74,
mox imperium adeptus Iovi Custodi templum ingens seque in sinu dei
sacravit. There are coins of Domitian (from 84 A.D. on) inscribed Iovi
Conservatori, and others (from 86 on) inscribed Iovi Custodi (Eckhel, vi
379, 393; Cohen, i² 430, 432).

forum Nervae: Vespasian's Temple of Peace (Vesp. 9, 1) and the area
surrounding it lay to the S.E. of the Forum Augusti, separated from it by
the street known as the Argiletum, which ran from the Subura to the Forum
Romanum. This portion of the Argiletum was converted by Domitian into
a “forum” called (a) forum Nervae, as it was completed and dedicated
by Nerva in 98; (b) forum Transitorium (or Pervium), on account of the
highway which ran through it; (c) forum Palladium, from the temple of
Minerva built in it; cf. Mart. i 2, 8, Limina post Pacis Palladiumque
forum.

Flaviae templum gentis: on the site of the house where he was born;
see on c. 1, 1.

stadium: Domitian constructed a stadium for foot-races and other
athletic contests to the W. of the Thermae of Nero in the Campus Martius,
near the Pantheon. It held 15,000 spectators, and must have been finished
before 86 A.D. if it is the stadium mentioned in c. 4, 4. After the burning
of the Colosseum in the reign of Macrinus (217-18 A.D.) the stadium was
used for some years for the shows of the amphitheatre (Dio lxxviii 25). It
was restored by Alexander Severus (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 24).
In the
middle of the 4th cent. Ammianus (xvi 10, 14) mentions it and the Odeum
among the “decora urbis aeternae.” For its subsequent history and
remains see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 592 sqq. Julius Caesar had
erected a temporary stadium for athletic contests at his triumph: Iul. 39, 3,
stadio ad tempus exstructo regione Marti Campi; so too Augustus: Aug.
43, 1, (edidit) athletas quoque exstructis in campo Martio sedilibus ligneis.
The stadium connected with the gymnasium of Nero (Ner. 12, 3) which
was destroyed by lightning in 62 was probably on the same site as that
of Domitian.

Odium: this Odium (1) or Odeum (ē) was also in the Campus Martius
between the stadium and the trigarium. It was a roofed theatre for
musical performances, and held an audience of 5000.
The name was
borrowed from the Gr. ᾠδεῖον which denoted a building for the same
purpose, such as that of Pericles at Athens. Dio (lxix 4) mentions among
the works of Trajan an ᾠδεῖον which seems to have been a restoration of
that of Domitian.

naumachiam: for this new basin or lake for the representation of
sea-fights see on c. 4, 2, Edidit navales pugnas
effosso iuxta Tiberim
lacu.

Maximus Circus: see on c. 4, 1.
..

deustis lateribus: the date of this fire is unknown, and it is not
mentioned by any other author. Burn (Rome and the Campagna c. xii)
assumes that it occurred in Domitian's reign and that Domitian rebuilt
the whole Circus with stone taken from his Naumachia. More probably
it was Trajan who used the stone when he restored the Circus with great
magnificence; cf. Plin. Pan. 51, Immensum latus Circi templorum pulchritudinem provocat: digna populo victore gentium sedes, nec minus ipsa visenda
quam quae ex illa spectabuntur, etc.: Dio lxviii 7, οὕτως γάρ που καὶ
μεγαλόφρων καὶ μεγαλογνώμων ἔφυ ὥστε τῷ ἱπποδρόμῳ ἐπιγράψαι ὅτι ἐξαρκοῦντα
αὐτὸν τῷ τῶν Ῥωμαίων δήμῳ ἐποίησεν, ἐπειδὴ διαφθαρέντα πῃ καὶ μείζω καὶ
περικαλλέστερον ἐξειργάσατο.

Chattos: a tribe dwelling about the Taunus mts., their territory
corresponding to the mod. Hesse and part of Bavaria. They had been
defeated by Drusus in 11 B.с., by Germanicus in 14 A.D., and again in
the reign of Claudius (50 A.D.). The occasion of Domitian's expedition
against them in 83 is uncertain (see Vollmer, Introd. to Stat. Silv., p. 44).
There are vague expressions in Frontin. Strateg. i 1, 8, cum Germanos qui
in armis erant vellet opprimere: Stat. S. i 4, 89, Rhenumque rebellem.
Dio (lxvii 5) says the object was to aid the Cherusci, a tribe friendly to
Rome, whose king had been driven out by the Chatti. Domitian marched
north, nominally to hold a census of the two Gauls. Frontinus (ex-governor
of Britain, who served in this campaign) says that he adopted this pretext
lest news of his coming should stir the Germans to a bigger rising
(Strateg. i 1, 8). Frontinus also praises the generalship of Domitian, e.g.
his accustoming his cavalry to fight on foot when the Chatti took to the
forests, and his establishing 120 miles of limites (ii 3, 23; ii, 7; i 3, 10).
No great victory is recorded, and the war seems to have ended by the
granting of a treaty to the Chatti (Stat. S. iii 3, 168, victis parcentia
foedera Chattis). Domitian celebrated a triumph, assumed the title
"Germanicus," let the consulship for 10 successive years be decreed to
him, took the censorship for life, and wore the toga triumphalis as often
as he entered the senate (Dio lxvii 4).
His achievement, though lauded
by Statius (S. i 1, 27, etc.) and Martial (i 4, 3; ii 2, 3; ix 1, 3), is belittled and ridiculed by hostile writers; e.g. Tac. Germ. 37, Germani
triumphati magis quam victi sunt; Tac. Agr. 39; Plin. Pan. 16.
(lxvii 4) says that he never even saw the foe: ἐκστρατεύσας εἰς τὴν Γερμανίαν,
καὶ μηδ᾽ ἑορακώς που πόλεμον, ἐπανῆκε. Modern historians connect Domitian's
campaign with a new plan of frontier defence, the "Limes Germanicus,"
a rampart of earth guarded at intervals by forts protecting the Roman
possessions in the neighbourhood of the Rhine.
This was begun by
Vespasian, and Domitian annexed the territory of the Taunus mts. to the
province of Upper Germany and continued the line of defence between the
Moenus (Main) and the Nicer (Neckar), so as to connect the Moenus and
the Rhine. See Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. 403 sqq.; Mommsen, Prov. Rom.
Emp. i 150 sqq.; Weynand, in Pauly-Wissowa vi 2556 sqq.; Gsell, op. cit.
193 sqq. The most recent account of the Roman frontier fortifications
will be found in Henderson's Five Roman Emperors, cc. v and vi.
..
Dio

Sarmatas: the Sarmatae or Sauromatae dwelt from the Vistula to
the Don, in Poland and Russia. Domitian's punitive expedition against
them lasted 8 months from May 92 to Jan. 93 (Gsell, p. 226). It is not
mentioned by any historian except Eutropius (vii 23, 4) who, as usual,
follows Suetonius: Expeditiones quattuor habuit, unum adversum Sarmatas,
alterum adversum Cattos, duas adversum Dacos. De Dacis Cattisque
duplicem triumphum egit, de Sarmatis solam lauream usurpavit. Multas
tamen calamitates isdem bellis passus est; nam in Sarmatia legio eius cum
duce interfecta est, et a Dacis Oppius Sabinus consularis et Cornelius
Fuscus praefectus praetorio cum magnis exercitibus occisi sunt. Martial
frequently refers to this Sarmatian expedition; e.g. in vii 1 and 2 he
mentions a lorica, or cuirass, made of boars' hoofs (probably Sarmatian
workmanship, see Friedl.), which was taken from a temple of Minerva
at Rome and sent out to be worn by the emperor; in vii 80 he says that
peace has been established: Quatenus Odrysios iam pax Romana triones |
temperat et tetricae conticuere tubae, etc. Statius also lauds Domitian's
victory (S. iii 3, 167 sqq.; iv 3, 153; 7, 49).

legione cum legato simul caesa: this legion was probably v Alaudae
(Parker, Rom. Leg. p. 110; see on Vesp. 8, 2); it has also been identified
with xxi Rapax, which is not mentioned after the time of Domitian
(Schilling, De leg. Rom. i Minervia et xxx Ulpia, p. 24).

in Dacos duas: the chronology and history of Domitian's two
campaigns against the Dacians, whose territory included Roumania, are
obscure (see Vollmer, 48 sqq.; Brandis, in Pauly-Wissowa iv 2248;
Henderson, op. cit. 160 sqq.). Under their king Decebalus (or Diurpaneus)
the Dacians invaded Moesia in the winter of 85 and defeated and slew
Oppius Sabinus, the Roman legatus there. After the death of Sabinus the
emperor took the field and marched to the Danube, but entrusted the
conduct of the war to Cornelius Fuscus, the praetorian prefect.
Fuscus
drove the Dacians out of Moesia, and it was then, apparently, that Domitian
returned to Rome and celebrated a triumph (see on c. 13, 3; cf. Stat. S. iii
3, 118, сит prima truces amentia Dacos | impulit et magno gens est
damnata triumpho). Fuscus next threw a bridge of boats across the
Danube and penetrated into Dacia, but he met with a disastrous defeat
and was himself slain. His successor Julianus again invaded Dacia and
gained a great victory at Tapae in 89. About this time Domitian, after
the suppression of the revolt of L. Antonius in Upper Germany, had
marched from the Rhine to Pannonia to punish the Marcomani and Quadi
for not sending the aid promised to Fuscus against the Dacians; but he
was defeated by them with the aid of the adjoining Sarmatian Iazyges,
and so was ready to grant terms of peace when Decebalus sent envoys to
Pannonia. Domitian placed a diadem on the head of Diegis, brother of
Decebalus, who was the leader of the embassy, as a token that Dacia's
king was now a vassal of Rome. After his return to Rome in '89 Domitian
celebrated a magnificent triumph (see below). The title "Dacicus," which
is only used by Martial in the dedicatory letter to Bk. viii, is a mere
piece of flattery and not an official title (Friedl. ad loc.).

Oppio Sabino consulari: he was consul ordinarius in the early months
of 84 A.D. along with the emperor Domitian, who was consul then for the
tenth time (C.I.L. xiv 245, Dessau 6126).

Cornelio Fusco: appointed procurator of Pannonia by Galba in 69
(Тас. Н. ii 86). He warmly supported the cause of Vespasian, and next
to Antonius Primus had most influence at the councils of Vespasian 's
generals (H. iii 4). He was made commander of the fleet at Ravenna
(H. iii 12), and was voted the insignia praetoria by the senate in Dec. 69
after the victory of the Flavians (H. iv 4). Juvenal (iv 111) mentions
him as one of the consilium hastily summoned to the arx Albana by
Domitian: Et qui vulturibus servabat viscera Dacis | Fuscus, marmorea
meditatus proelia villa. Martial (vi 76) refers to his position as praetorian
prefect charged with Domitian's safety, and talks of his victorious shade
haunting a vassal grove in vanquished Dacia: Ille sacri lateris custos
Martisque togati, | credita cui summi castra fuere ducis, | hic situs est Fuscus.
Licet hoc, Fortuna, fateri: | non timet hostiles iam lapis iste minas; |
grande iugum domita Dacus cervice recepit | et famulum victrix possidet
umbra nemus. For an appreciation of his military ability see Davies,
J.R.S. x 19; Henderson, op. cit. 162.
praefecto cohortium praetorianarum: see on Tit. 4, 2.

varia proelia: varia = vario eventu; cf. Tac. H. v 10, legatum varia
proelia ac saepius adversa excepere. For the disasters to Domitian's armies
cf. Eutrop. vii 23, 4 (quoted above on “Sarmatas"): Tac. Agr. 41, tot
exercitus in Moesia Daciaque et Germania et Pannonia temeritate aut per
ignaviam ducum amissi, tot militares viri cum totis cohortibus expugnati
et capti: Oros. vii 10, 3, Bellum adversum Germanos et Dacos per legatos
gessit pari reipublicae pernicie, cum et in urbe ipse senatum populumque
laniaret et foris male circumactum exercitum adsidua hostes caede conficerent. Nam quanta fuerint Diurpanei, Dacorum regis, cum Fusco duce
proelia, quantaeque Romanorum clades, longo textu evolverem, nisi Cornelius
Tacitus, qui hanc historiam diligentissime contexuit, de reticendo interfectorum numero et Sallustium Crispum et alios auctores quam plurimos
sanxisse et se ipsum idem potissimum elegisse dixisset. Domitianus tamen
pravissima elatus iactantia sub nomine superatorum hostium de exstinctis
legionibus triumphavit. The defeats of Sabinus and Fuscus are also
mentioned in Iordan. Get. xiii 76. Dio (lxvii 6) says that Domitian claimed
the credit of all the successes, none of which was due to him, and blamed
others for reverses incurred in consequence of orders issued by him.
..

duplicem triumphum egit: usually explained as meaning that in 89
Domitian celebrated at the same time a double triumph over the Chatti
who had supported L. Antonius in his revolt (see § 2) and over the Dacians,
this being the triumph dated between Oct. 1, 89 and Sept. 30, 90 by Euseb.-
Hieron., p. 161 Schoene, Domitianus de Dacis et Germanis triumphavit.
Brandis, however, seems right in taking the words to mean that Domitian
twice celebrated a triumph over each of the two: over the Chatti in 83
and 89, and over the Dacians in 86 and 89. Suetonius often uses duplex
in the sense of duo; e.g. Vesp. 4, 2, d. sacerdotium: Ner. 1, 2, d. censura:
Aug. 16, 1, d. naufragium: Aug. 13, 1, bellum duplici proelio transegit,
quorum priore vix.. evaserat. On this view, which is strongly supported
by Janssen, the complete number of Domitian's triumphs is given here; the
two earlier ones (in 83 and 86) are referred to in c. 13, 3, post duos
triumphos transnominavit, where see notes. A colossal equestrian statue
of Domitian was set up in the Forum on his triumphal return in 89 (Stat.
S. i 1). The triumphal games were under the direction of L. Arruntius Stella
(S. i 2, 180), and the cost of the celebration was met by an exaction of
aurum coronarium from the provinces. Dio (lxvii 7) derides the triumphal
procession with its "spoils" supplied from the emperor's palace, and
asserts that the "peace" granted to the Dacians was in reality a humiliating
agreement on Domitian's part to pay a vast sum to Decebalus and to
furnish him with Roman artificers for civil and military purposes. Similarly
Pliny (Pan. 17) contrasts the sham victories of Domitian with the solid
successes of Trajan in his Dacian wars.

lauream Capitolino Iovi rettulit: cf. Ner. 13, 2, where Nero deposits
a laurel wreath in the Capitol (laurea in Capitolium lata) after Tiridates,
king of Armenia, appeared at Rome as a suppliant and had his diadem
restored by the emperor. It was part of the ceremony of a regular (iustus)
triumph that the triumphing general, when the procession reached the
temple of Capitoline Jove, should deposit in the lap of the god the laurel
branch which he bore in his hand and the laurel wreaths with which the
fasces were crowned; cf. Sil. Ital. xv 120, laurumque superbam | in gremio
Iovis excisis deponere Poenis. Furthermore, a laurel wreath was placed in
the lap of the god when news of a victory reached Rome; cf. Plin. N.H. xv
30, laurus.. in gremio Iovis Opt. Max. deponitur quoties laetitiam nova
victoria attulit. Sometimes the wreath was sent from the scene of the
victory; cf. Plin. Pan. 8, allata erat ex Pannonia laurea hanc imperator
Nerva in gremio Iovis collocarat. The poets refer to Domitian's waiving
his claim to a formal triumph over the Sarmatae; e.g. Mart. viii 15, 5, hos
quoque secretos ("suppressed'') memoravit Roma triumphos, | nec minor
ista tuae laurea pacis erat; ix 101, 19, Saepe recusatos parcus duxisse
triumphos | victor Hyperboreo nomen ab orbe tulit: Stat. S. iii 3, 171,
quae (clementia) modo Marcomanos post horrida bella vagosque | Sauromatas
Latio non est dignata triumpho: iv 1, 39, mille tropaea feres, tantum
permitte (i.e. "only accept'") triumphos: | restat Bactra novis, restat
Babylona tributis | frenari, nondum in gremio Iovis Indica laurus.

§ 2. bellum civile: this revolt of L. Antonius is described by Statius
as "civile nefas” (S. i 1, 80); in inscriptions it is called “bellum
Germanicum” (e.g. C.I.L. vi 1347, Dessau 1006).

L. Antonio: L. Antonius Saturninus was military commander in
Upper Germany, and at the end of 88 A.D., acting in concert with some of
the senate, he induced the two legions (xiv Gemina Martia Victrix and xxi
Rapax) in winter-quarters at Moguntiacum (Mainz) to proclaim him
Imperator. He provided himself with funds by seizing the savings of the
legionaries (see c. 7, 3). He was relying on the support of the Germans
beyond the Rhine, who had earlier taken part in the revolt of Civilis,
especially the Chatti and their allies the Usipi. L. Appius Maximus
Norbanus, who in all probability was military commander in Lower Germany
(see Henderson, op. cit. 111), promptly advanced against him and defeated
him in Jan. 89. Domitian had summoned Trajan to march from Spain
over the Pyrenees and Alps (Plin. Pan. 14), and had himself left Rome to
quell the rising before he heard of the victory of Norbanus, and after the
news he continued his march to the Rhine. The officers of the disaffected
legions were executed and many senators were put to death by Domitian.
Cf. Dio lxvii 11 (where Norbanus is praised for burning the captured
correspondence of Saturninus, to save his fellow conspirators): [Aur. Vict.]
Epit. 11, 9, his eius (Domitiani) saevitiis, ac maxime iniuria verborum, qua
scortum vocari dolebat, accensus Antonius, curans Germaniam superiorem,
imperium corripuit. Quo per Norbanum Appium acie strato, Domitianus
longe taetrior, in omne hominum genus, etiam in suos, ferarum more grassabatur. Martial (iv 11) says that Antonius Saturninus wished to emulate
M. Antonius the triumvir: Dum nimium vano tumefactus nomine gaudes, |
et Saturninum te, miser, esse pudet, | impia Parrhasia movisti bella sub
ursa, | qualia qui Phariae coniugis arma tulit, etc. Martial also praises the
loyalty of Norbanus, ix 84, Cum tua sacrilegos contra, Norbane, furores |
staret pro domino Caesare sancta fides, etc.
superioris Germaniae: see on Vitell. 7, 1.

resolutus: ''thawed," a poetical word; cf. Luc. i 219, madidis Euri
resolutae flatibus Alpes: Ov. Trist. iii 10, 13, nix iacet, et iactam ne sol
pluviaeque resolvant, | indurat Boreas perpetuamque facit.

siquidem: "inasmuch as," "since." Suet. uses siquidem (εἴ γε) twenty
times and always with the indic. The causal signification is found at
times in Cic. (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 427) and prevails, almost exclusively,
in post-Aug. writers. Trachmann (op. cit. p. 39) assumes that in our
passage siquidem expresses a doubt: “Suetonius iis, quae addita
'siquidem' particula adiecit, illud praesagium tanquam ex vano haustum
in dubium vocare videtur; but Suetonius is too firm a believer in presages
of every kind to throw any doubt on their reality.

clangores: the regular word for an eagle's screams; cf. Liv. i, 34, S,
aquila cum magno clangore volitans: Cic. carm. frg. 32, 14 (Baehrens),
Iovis satelles (i.e. aquila)
clangorem fundit vastum: Plin. N.H. x 6,
melanaëtos sola aquila sine clangore.

adeo vulgatum est: Plutarch (Aem. Paul. 25), describing the inexplicable way in which the report of the victory of Paulus over Perseus at
Pydna (168 B.C.) suddenly spread at Rome, gives earlier instances of such
strange happenings: (1) the defeat of the Crotoniats by the Locrians at
the Sagras in Bruttium (6 cent. B.C.) known to the Greeks at Olympia on
the same day; (2) the defeat of the Persian fleet by the Greeks at Mycale
in Lydia (479 B.с.) known to the Plataeans on the same day; (3) the defeat
of the Tarquins at Lake Regillus in Latium by the Romans (496 в.с.)
announced at Rome by two mysterious horsemen said to be Castor and
Pollux. He adds that all these stories are confirmed by what happened
in his own day with regard to the report at Rome of this defeat of
L. Antonius: Ὅτε γὰρ ᾿Αντώνιος ἀπέστη Δομετιανοῦ καὶ πολὺς πόλεμος ἀπὸ
Γερμανίας προσεδοκᾶτο, τῆς ῾Ρώμης ταραττομένης ἄφνω καὶ αὐτομάτως ὁ δῆμος ἐξ
αὑτοῦ φήμην ἀνέδωκε νίκης, καὶ τὴν ῾Ρώμην ἐπέδραμε λόγος αὐτόν τε τὸν ᾿Αντώνιον
ἀνῃρῆσθαι καὶ τοῦ σὺν αὐτῷ στρατεύματος ἡττημένου μηδὲν μέρος λελεῖφθαι.
Τοσαύτην δὲ λαμπρότητα καὶ ῥύμην ἡ πίστις ἔσχεν, ὥστε καὶ θῦσαι τῶν ἐν τέλει
πολλούς. Ζητουμένου δὲ τοῦ πρώτου φράσαντος, ὡς οὐδεὶς ἦν, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ λόγος εἰς ἄλλον
· ἐξ ἄλλου διωκόμενος ἀνέφευγε, καὶ τέλος καταδὺς ὥσπερ εἰς πέλαγος ἀχανὲς τὸν
ἄπειρον ὄχλον ἐφάνη μηδεμίαν ἀρχὴν ἔχων βέβαιον, αὕτη μὲν ἡ φήμη ταχὺ τῆς
-πόλεως ἐξερρύη, πορευομένῳ δὲ τῷ Δομετιανῷ μετὰ δυνάμεως ἐπὶ τὸν πόλεμον ἤδη καθ'
·ὁδὸν ἀγγελία καὶ γράμματα φράζοντα τὴν νίκην ἀπήντησεν. Ἡ δ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ
·κατορθώματος (victoriae) ἡμέρα καὶ τῆς φήμης ἐγίνετο, ἐπὶ πλέον ἢ δισμυρίους
σταδίους τῶν τόπων διεστώτων. Ταῦτα μὲν οὐδεὶς ἀγνοεῖ τῶν καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς.

caput adportatum: Dio (lxvii 11) says that Domitian sent the heads
of Antonius and those executed as his accomplices to be exposed on
the Rostra at Rome.
multa in..
habui sane, non

usu novavit: for this constr. cf. Cic. Legg. iii 5, 12, nihil
modo multum, quod putarem novandum in legibus.

sportulas rectarum cenarum: under the early Empire clients, instead of being asked occasionally to a regular dinner (recta cena, see on
Vesp. 19, 1) by their patronus, received from him a portion of food
(sportula) as a daily reward for their attentions. These doles were carried
away in a small basket (sportula, see on sportellae, c. 4, 5); hence the
same name was given to the dole itself. Patrons soon found it more convenient to give in lieu of food a small sum of money (usually 100 quadrantes, less than a shilling). Nero, from motives of economy, substituted
sportulae for publicae cenae (Ner. 16, 2, adhibitus sumptibus modus;
publicae cenae ad sportulas redactae). A publica cena was not a dinner
given at state expense, but one provided either by a magistrate, or by the
emperor, or even by a private person in a public place (in publico), e.g.
the Forum, to which the people or part of the people were invited.
Domitian restored the publicae cenae and abolished the publicae sportulae,
and, presumably, every patron had to furnish a recta cena for his clients;
but the change was disliked by both patrons and clients, and the suppression
of the money sportula did not last more than three or four years. Martial
only mentions it in Bk. iii (published 87/88 A.D.); in his later Books the
money sportula has been restored. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 207 sqq.

gregum: restored by Beroaldus for grecum. The chariot-drivers
(aurigae, agitatores) of each factio formed a grex under the control of
the dominus factionis: cf. Ner. 22, 2, spectaculum multiplicatis missibus
("races") in serum protrahebatur, ne dominis quidem iam factionum
dignantibus nisi ad totius diei cursum greges ducere (i.e. they refused to
bring out their drivers at all unless there was to be a full day's racing).

factiones: companies of contractors who entered into an agreement
with the giver of the games (munerarius, editor spectaculorum) to provide
the chariots, horses, drivers, and all other requisites. Each factio had its
own distinctive colour which was worn by its charioteers and displayed on
its chariots. Everyone at Rome, from the emperor down, became a violent
partizan of one of the different colours.

aurati purpureique: Dio lxvii 4, τοῖς δὲ ἁρματηλάταις δύο γένη ἕτερα, τὸ
μὲν χρυσοῦν, τὸ δὲ πορφυροῦν ὀνομάσας, προσκατέστησε. These two new colours
soon completely disappeared. The "Purple" is once mentioned in Mart. xiv
55 (84/85 A.D.), Proficies nihil hoc, caedas licet usque, flagello, si tibi
purpureo de grege currit equus (this contemptuous reference shows that
the "Purple” found no favour with Domitian, though introduced by him).
The only other mention of the "Purple" is in C.I.L. vi 10062 (Dessau
5282): D. m. Epaphroditus agitator f(actionis) r(ussatae); vicit clxxviii
et ad purpureum liber (i.e. manumissus) vic. viii. Some identify ‘pannus
chelidonius'' in C.I.L. vi 10046 (Dessau 5313) with “pannus purpureus,”
but the reading is uncertain; see Friedl. in Marquardt Staatsv. iii² 518.

panni: pannus (a cloth, garment, or rag) was used specially for the
coloured tunic of the charioteer in the races; cf. Pliny, Ep. ix 6, Quo
magis miror tot milia virorum tam pueriliter identidem cupere currentes
equos, insistentes curribus homines videre. Si tamen aut velocitate
equorum aut hominum arte traherentur, esset ratio non nulla: nunc favent
panno, pannum amant, et si in ipso cursu medioque certamine hic color
illuc, ille huc transferatur, studium favorque transibit, et repente agitatores
illos, equos illos, quos procul noscitant, quorum clamitant nomina, relinquent: Juv. xi 198, Totam hodie Romam circus capit, et fragor aurem |
percutit, eventum ('success'') viridis quo colligo ("infer”) panni.

quattuor pristinas: White (albus), Red (russatus, russeus), Green
(viridis or prasinus, from πράσον a leek), Blue (venetus, see Vitell. 7, 1);
cf. Sidon. carm. xxiii 323, micant colores | albus vel venetus virens rubensque. White and Red were the original colours; Tertull. Spect. 9, ab initio
duo soli fuerunt, albus et russeus. Pliny (N.H. vii 186) quotes from the
acta a notice of the death of one Felix, a driver of the Red factio, on
whose pyre one of his admirers cast himself; this was in the 1st cent.
B.C.
The prasina factio is first mentioned in the reign of Tiberius (C.I.L.
vi 33950) and of Caligula (Suet. Calig. 55; Dio lix 14): the veneta first in
the time of Nero and Vitellius (C.I.L. vi 10055; Suet. Vitell. 7, 1; Dio
lxv 5). Caligula, Nero, Domitian, L. Verus, Commodus, Elagabalus
favoured the "Green"; Vitellius and Caracalla the “Blue.'”

interdixit histrionibus scaenam: cf. Plin. Pan. 46, Obtinuit aliquis
(i.e. Domitian) ut spectaculum pantomimorum populus Romanus tolli
pateretur... Rogatus es tu (i.e. Trajan) quod cogebat alius (i.e. Dom.),
coepitque esse beneficium, quod necessitas fuerat.
Neque enim a te minore
concentu ut tolleres pantomimos, quam a patre tuo (i.e. Nerva) ut restitueret
exactum est. Utrumque recte: nam et restitui oportebat quos sustulerat
malus princeps et tolli restitutos. Under the Empire the word histrio
("actor'") came to be used specially of a pantomimus or dancer. Such
histriones enjoyed extraordinary favour; cf. Tac. Dial. 29, Iam vero
propria et peculiaria huius urbis vitia paene in utero matris concipi mihi
videntur, histrionalis favor et gladiatorum equorumque studia. Besides
public performances in the theatres, the emperors and wealthy families
kept histriones for their private entertainment (cf. Aug. 74). The licence
in which they indulged gave rise to abuses which the emperors made
spasmodic efforts to check. Augustus, though he limited or abolished the
ius virgarum in histriones of the praetors (Aug. 45, Tac. A. i 77), punished
severely their misconduct in private life or on the stage. Tiberius banished
all histriones from Italy (Tac. A. iv 14, cf. Suet. Tib. 37), but Caligula
restored them (Dio lix 2). In 56 Nero again expelled the pantomimi, but
they reappear before 60. Titus refused to countenance his favourite pages
who were the leading pantomimi of the day (Tit. 7, 2). Nerva, at the
request of the people, removed Domitian's ban. Trajan reimposed it, but
withdrew it after his Dacian triumph in 107. Hadrian allowed the imperial
dancers (aulici histriones) to appear on the public stage (Spart. Hadr. 19).
See Friedl., Sitteng. ii10 125 sqq.

castrari mares vetuit: in 82 A.D.; cf. Philostr. vit. Apollon, vi 42,
Δομετιανοῦ δὲ βασιλέως ὑπὸ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον εὐνούχους τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν νομοθετήσαντος.
Dio (lxvii 2) says that he did this as a slur on Titus: καίπερ καὶ αὐτὸς
᾿Εαρίνου τινὸς εὐνούχου ἐρῶν, ὅμως, ἐπειδὴ καὶ ὁ Τίτος ἰσχυρῶς περὶ τοὺς ἐκτομίας
ἐσπουδάκει, ἀπηγόρευσεν ἐπὶ ἐκείνου ὕβρει μηδένα ἔτι ἐν τῇ τῶν ῾Ῥωμαίων ἀρχῇ
ἐκτέμνεσθαι. The reform is praised by Statius (S. iv 3, 13 sqq.) and by
Martial (ii 60, vi 2, etc.). Ammianus (xviii 4, 5) mentions it as a
redeeming feature of Domitian's reign: Horum et similium taedio iuvat
veterem laudare Domitianum, qui, licet patris fratrisque dissimilis
memoriam nominis sui inexpiabili detestatione perfudit, tamen receptissima
inclaruit lege qua minaciter interdixerat ne intra terminos iuris dictionis
Romanae castraret quisquam puerum. Nerva renewed this law, and
Hadrian made offenders against it liable to the penalties of the Lex
Cornelia de sicariis.

mangones: see on Vesp. 4, 3; cf. Mart. ix 6, 4 (referring to this law
of Domitian): Non puer avari sectus arte mangonis | virilitatis damna
maeret ereptae.

pretia moderatus est: presumably lest the dealers, if they were
allowed to ask exorbitant prices for their remaining stock, might be
tempted to break the law (Baumg.-Cr.). For the prices of eunuchs (varying
from about £20 to £4000) see Marquardt, Privatl.2 174.

§ 2. ad: temporal, on the occasion of"; cf. Calig. 51, 1, ad minima
tonitrua et fulgura conivere solebat. See App. i. § 12.

quondam: very frequently used by Suet. in the sense of aliquando;
cf. c. 14, 1: 18, 2: Oth. 3, 2: Vesp. 5, 4: 25: Tit. 8, 1.
edixit: between Oct. 91 and Sept. 92 (Euseb.).

novellaret:
=
novas vites sereret, “plant new vines." The only other
instance cited of the use of this verb is in the Christian writer Paulinus
Nolanus, carm. 21, 659, vitam novellantes Deo, where it is used in a metaphorical sense of a new devotion or consecration. We find the adj. novella
used as an epithet of vitis in Verg. E. iii 11, atque mala vites incidere
falce novellas (cf. Varr. R.R. i 31, 1, novellae vineae); the subst. novelletum, “a vine-nursery," occurs in Dig. xxv 1, 6.
ut in provinciis vina succiderentur: Philostratus (vit. Soph. i 6)
refers to this legislation of Domitian about vines in Asia, and says it was
due to the idea that wine leads to sedition: ἐδόκει τῷ βασιλεῖ μὴ εἶναι τῇ
᾿Ασίᾳ ἀμπέλους, ἐπειδὴ ἐν οἴνῳ στασιάζειν ἔδοξαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξαιρεῖσθαι μὲν τὰς ἤδη
πεφυτευμένας, ἄλλας δὲ μὴ φυτεύειν ἔτι. Again (vit. Apollon. vi 42) he
describes how Apollonius encouraged the Ionians to send an embassy to
Domitian to urge the repeal of this measure on the ground that the
emperor, though he had provided against men being made sterile, was
rendering the earth sterile (τῶν μὲν ἀνθρώπων φειδόμενος, τὴν δὲ γὴν εὐνουχίζων).
The Ionians sent the sophist Scopelianus, who met with such success that
not merely was permission to plant vines granted, but a fine was imposed
on those who did not plant them.

nec exequi rem perseveravit: for nec (= neque vero, neque tamen) cf.
Oth. 1, 1, senator est factus nec praeturae gradum excessit. We may
assume that the petitions of the vine-growers influenced the emperor, but
Suetonius (c. 14, 2) states that it was the boding import of some Greek
verses circulated against him which more than anything else led him to
revoke his order. Statius (S. iv 3, 11) says: qui (i.e. Domitian) castae
Cereri diu negata | reddit iugera sobriasque terras; and Vollmer (ad loc.)
infers that the prohibition of vine-growing must still have had some force
in 95 A.D., the year in which this poem of Statius was written. Rostovtzeff
(Soc. and Econ. Hist. Rom. Emp. p. 189) says that it was apparently
enforced in Africa, to a certain extent in the Danube provinces, in the
north and centre of Gaul, and in part of Spain. On the subject of vineculture in the provinces and the restrictions imposed on it in the interest
of the Italian growers see Marquardt, Privatl.2 p. 446; Mommsen, Prου.
Rom. Emp. i 108. As early as 129 B.C. the planting of the vine and olive
was forbidden in the provinces beyond the Alps (Cic. de rep. iii 9, 16)
and this restriction was not completely removed till the reign of Probus
(276-282 A.D.); cf. Vopisc. Prob. 18, Gallis omnibus et Hispanis ac
Britannis hic permisit ut vites haberent vinumque conficerent.

quaedam ex maximis officiis: important positions in the imperial
household such as ab epistulis, a libellis, a rationibus, a patrimonio, which
were held exclusively by freedmen down to Nero's time. Otho made an
innovation by appointing as his secretary (ab epistulis) the orator Secundus
(Plut. Oth. 9). Vitellius transferred such offices to equites: Tac. H. і 58,
Vitellius ministeria principatus per libertos agi solita in equites Romanos
disponit. An instance of an eques under Vitellius holding posts previously
held by liberti is Propertianus who is described in C.I.L. xi 5028 (Dessau
1447) as "pro(curator) imp(eratoris) a patrim(onio) et heredit (atibus) et
a libell(is)." See Hirschfeld, Kais. Verwaltungsb. p. 112, n. 4. Domitian,
as Suetonius says here, divided the posts between liberti and equites. An
eques so appointed was Cn. Octavius Titinius Capito (friend of the younger
Pliny, cf. Ep. i 17, etc.) who was “procurator) ab epistulis et a patrimonio
(sc. Domitiani),” ‘‘iterum ab epistulis divi Nervae,” and “ab epistulis
tertio imp. Traiani” (C.I.L. vi 798, Dessau 1448). Hadrian, who established a Civil Service at Rome, excluded liberti and confined these offices
to equites; cf. Spart. Hadr. 22, ab epistulis et a libellis primus equites
Romanos habuit (“primus'' is inaccurate, as Mommsen points out,
Staatsr. ii³ 838, n. 2). Domitian in his administration limited in every
way the authority of the senate (cf. Plin. Pan. 62), and gave increased
power to the equites and liberti. He appointed as commander in his Dacian
campaign (c. 6, 1) Cornelius Fuscus who was praefectus praetorio (an
equestrian post, see on Tit. 6, 1). An equestrian procurator of Asia was
commissioned to govern the province in place of the proconsul who had
died (C.I.L. v 875). He included equites as well as senators in his consilium (C.I.L. ix 5420), and so a senator, tried before the imperial consilium, might have equites and not merely his peers as judges. The favour
shown by Domitian to freedmen (cf. Tac. H. i 76, Agr. 41; Plin. Pan. 42,
49, 88) was a reaction from the repressive policy of Titus and Vespasian,
and a reversion to the privileges given to them by Vitellius, Otho, Galba,
Nero, Claudius, and Caligula.

§ 3. geminari castra prohibuit: geminare is used here not in the
sense of duplicare but of coniungere; cf. Hor. A.P. 13, serpentes avibus
geminentur: Stat. S. i 2, 240, dat Iuno verenda | vincula et insigni
geminat Concordia taeda. When several legions were united in the one
camp, the consciousness of their strength often led to mutiny. On the
death of Augustus three legions in Pannonia, which were quartered in the
same summer-camp (aestiva), revolted (Tac. A. i 16), and at the same time
four legions similarly concentrated in Lower Germany conspired to make
Germanicus emperor (A. i 39).

ad signa deponi: each camp had its shrine, usually in the principia
(Oth. 1, 2, n.), in which the ensigns were placed and the imagines of the
emperors were worshipped. This shrine formed an inviolable sanctuary..
In a vault beneath it were deposited the savings of the legionaries which
were kept and administered by the ensign-bearers (signiferi). When the
soldiers received a donativum on the occasion of any special success, etc.,
half of it must be deposited under the protection of the ensigns; cf.
Veget. ii 20, Illud vero ab antiquis divinitus institutum est, ut ex donativo,
quod milites consequuntur, dimidia pars sequestraretur apud signa, et ibidem
ipsis militibus servaretur, ne per luxum aut inanium rerum comparationem
a contubernalibus posset absumi. Miles deinde, qui sumptus suos scit apud
signa depositos, de deserendo nihil cogitat, magis diligit signa, pro illis in
acie fortius dimicat, more humani ingenii, ut pro illis habeat maximam
curam, in quibus suam videt positam esse substantiam. Vegetius says that
each cohort had a sack (follis) in which these sums were placed under the
charge of the signifer.
The evidence of Latin papyri containing military
accounts establishes the fact that the sum credited to a soldier's depositaccount from such irregular donativa was augmented by additions from
his regular pay; the expenses for food, clothing, etc. are deducted from
his stipendium and any surplus is added to his deposit. See Grenfell,
Hunt, and Hogarth, Fayûm Towns and their Papyri pp. 252 sqq.; Reinach,
in Daremberg-Saglio iv 1324 sqq.; Parker, Rom. Legions, 217 sqq.
L. Antonius: see c. 6, 2.

apud duarum legionum hiberna: i.e. the winter-quarters of the 14th
and 21st legions at Moguntiacum (Mainz). The other two legions under
the command of L. Antonius in Upper Germany were the 8th (Augusta),
encamped at Argentoratum (Strassburg), and the 11th (Claudia), encamped
at Vindonissa (Windisch). There does not seem to be any authority for
assuming that they took part in the revolt.

addidit quartum stipendium militi: in 83 A.D., to celebrate his victory
over the Chatti; cf. Zonaras xi 19, καὶ τοῖς στρατιώταις ἐπηύξησε τὴν μισθοφοράν, τάχα διὰ τὴν νίκην· πέντε γὰρ καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα δραχμὰς (= denarios)
ἑκάστου λαμβάνοντος ἑκατὸν ἐκέλευσε δίδοσθαι. From the time of Julius Caesar
payments were made to the soldiers every four months, each payment being
called a stipendium, so that the soldiers got three stipendia each year.
Caesar also raised the pay for the foot-soldier to 225 denarii a year, so
that each stipendium was 75 denarii. The number of stipendia remained
the same under Domitian (as Zon. implies), but he raised each of the
three stipendia to 100 denarii, or a total amount of 300 denarii a year;
this addition to the earlier pay being equivalent to paying a fourth
stipendium of 75 denarii. See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 96.
aureos ternos: = 75 denarii; see on Galb. 20, 2.

ius diligenter et industrie dixit: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 2, ius aequissime dixit; cf. Iul. 43, 1, ius laboriosissime ac severissime dixit: Aug. 33, 1,
ipse ius dixit assidue et in noctem nonnunquam, si parum corpore valeret,
lectica pro tribunali collocata, vel etiam domi cubans: ib. 72, 2, Tibur,
ubi etiam in porticibus Herculis templi persaepe ius dixit. For the civil
and criminal jurisdiction of the emperors in virtue of their imperium see
Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 958 sqq.; Willems, Le Droit Publique Romain
458 sqq.; Greenidge, Roman Public Life 381 sqq.
plerumque
"Ius
..

ordinem: in the early editions the punctuation was
.dixit. Plerumque rescidit''; the punctuation in the text is
that proposed by Burman and adopted by Oudendorp, Ernesti, and the
modern editors; Oudendorp suggested another punctuation “pro tribunali.
Extra ordinem.. rescidit," and Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 981, n. 1) approves
of this, thinking that there is a distinction made between Domitian's own
jurisdiction and the extraordinary supervision which he exercised over the
iudices, partly by admonition and partly by quashing their decisions.

et in Foro: et means in addition to his sittings in his palace and his
arx Albana. Criminal cases, as a rule, were heard by the emperor in his
own house; when he sat in the Forum he nearly invariably heard civil cases
(Mommsen, op. cit. ii³ 965, n. 4; 983, n. 3). Dio frequently mentions the
emperors sitting as judges in the Forum; e.g. lvii 7 (of Tiberius),
ἐπεποίητο βῆμα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἐφ᾽ οὗ προκαθίζων ἐχρημάτιζε : lx 4 (of Claudius),
τὸ μὲν πλεῖστον ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἄλλοθι ἐπὶ βήματος ἐδίκαζε : lxvi 10 (of
Vespasian), ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ πολλάκις ἐδίκαζεν : lxix 7 (of Hadrian), ἐδίκαζε
τότε μὲν ἐν τῷ Παλατίῳ, τότε δὲ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ τῷ τε Πανθείῳ καὶ ἄλλοθι πολλαχόθι,
ἀπὸ βήματος, ὥστε δημοσιεύεσθαι τὰ γιγνόμενα.

pro tribunali: see on Vesp. 7, 2. Magistrates administering justice in
the Forum (Tit. 4, 2) at the place called the Comitium (Dom. 8, 4) sat
on a sella curulis placed on a platform (tribunal, βῆμα).
..

extra ordinem: Domitian may have followed the example of Claudius
in sitting on days usually exempt from legal business: Claud. 14, Ius
laboriosissime dixit, etiam suis suorumque diebus sollemnibus (i.e. anniversaries in his family), nonnumquam festis quoque antiquitus et religiosis.
Nec semper praescripta legum secutus, etc.; but the Princeps always
judged extra ordinem, by cognitio (Tit. 7, 1, n.), the case being decided
either by himself alone or with the assistance of counsellors chosen at his
own discretion, down to the time of the definite organisation of the consilium principis under Hadrian. Bentley proposed to insert et before extra
ordinem.

ambitiosas sententias: verdicts prompted by interested motives, by a
desire to curry favour; cf. Cic. Cluent. 38, 108, quo in reo qui absolvit
ambitiosus existimatur: Ulp. Dig. iv 43, ambitiosa decreta.
centumvirorum: see on Vesp. 10.
reciperatores: see on Vesp. 3.

perfusoriis: “ unsubstantial,”
“unfounded,” "superficial," lit.
"sprinkled on the surface and not sinking deep"; cf. Sen. Ep. 23, 4, haec,
quibus delectatur vulgus, tenuem habent et perfusoriam voluptatem hoc,
de quo loquor, solidum est, et quod plus pateat introrsus. So too the adv.
perfusorie means “vaguely,” “indefinitely"; Ulp. Dig. xliii 24, 5, debebit
..
neque quidem perfusorie, aut obscure, dicere aut denuntiare. In Cic.
Rosc. Amer. 29, 80 there is the phrase aliquem iudicio perfundere, which
Forcellini interprets: iudicii vexationem, ceu aquam, offundere, in ius
vocare, et afficere molestia sistendi se ante iudicem, parandae defensionis,
et causae dicendae; eadem ratione “aspergere alicui molestiam'' dixit Cic.
Q. Fr. ii 10. Halm conjectured pervertere; Trojel pessundare. From
that use of perfundere Ernesti (followed by Baumg.-Cr.) explains perfusoria
assertio here as "ea qua dominus (slave-owner) iustus adducitur per
calumniam litis . . in periculum servi amittendi.”

assertionibus: ‘assertio” tam a servitute in libertatem, quam a libertate in servitutem trahi significat (Priscian iii 365, 9). The word is post-Aug. See on Vesp. 3, ingenuam pronuntiatam, patre asserente. Dio (lxvii
13) mentions that Domitian, as censor, restored to his former owner a slave
who had been illegally declared freeborn and had risen to be a centurion:
Κλαύδιον Πακᾶτον τῷ δεσπότη καίπερ ἑκατονταρχηκότα ἀπέδωκεν, ὅτι ἠλέγχθη
δοῦλος ὤν.
nummarios: = corruptos "bribed," a Ciceronian word.

cum suo consilio: in civil proceedings where the final decision lay
with an individual, either as judge (iudex) or arbitrator (arbiter), he
brought in a consilium of counsellors or assessors (consiliarii, assessores,
cf. Galb. 14, 2) to assist him in arriving at a decision; cf. Cic. Quinct. 2,
10; Q. Rosc. 4, 12; Verr. ii 29, 71; Plin. Εp. v 1; Val. Max. viii 2, 2;
Gell. N.A. xii 13, 2: xiv 2,9. See Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 314.

§ 2. tribunis: the emperor directed the tribunes to bring the indictment for repetundae before the senate, probably because a private accuser
could not bring a charge against a magistrate who was in office (Mommsen,
ii³ 121). The usual procedure in a cognitio senatus was for the accuser to
lodge his complaint with the consuls, and if the case was admitted by
them, the matter came before the senate, which formed the high court of
criminal judicature under the Empire; cf. Tac. A. ii 28, adit consules,
cognitionem senatus poscit: xiii 14, postulatus apud consules a patre interfectae.

sordidum: αἰσχροκερδῆ; cf. Cic. Fam. xiii 36, quosdam sordidos
homines qui Caesaris beneficia vendebant: Plin. Ep. iii 9, 2, proconsulatum
..
non minus violenter quam sordide gesserat. So sordes is used for low
avarice, despicable extortion on the part of a magistrate; e.g. Plin. Ep. ii
12, 4, damnatus sordium: Ven. Sat. Dig. xlviii 11, 6, utque urbani magistratus ab omni sorde se abstineant, neve plus doni muneris in anno accipiant
quam quod sit aureorum centum.

repetundarum: see on Oth. 2, 2.
iudices a senatu petendi: in cases of repetundae or peculatus heard
before the senate, if the accused was convicted the senate did not itself
fix the amount to be refunded (litis aestimatio), but appointed senatorial
iudices or reciperatores (usually 3 or 5) for the purpose. Sometimes the
case was referred directly to such special commissioners; cf. Tac. A. i 74,
de pecuniis repetundis ad reciperatores itum est: Plin. Ep. ii 11, 2, Marius
Priscus omissa defensione iudices petiit; iv 9, 16; vi 29, 10.
provinciarum praesidibus: see on Vesp. 6, 4.

neque modestiores umquam neque iustiores: for modestia see on
Tit. 4, 1. Schiller (Gesch. röm. Kaiserz. i 533) says that Domitian took
as his model Tiberius, whose memoirs were his constant reading (Dom. 20),
and that with the possible exception of Tiberius no emperor kept his magistrates at home and abroad under stricter discipline. Domitian's careful
choice of his officials is praised by Statius, S. v 1, 79: vidit, qui cuncta
suorum | novit et inspectis ambit latus omne ministris. His repression of
the plundering practised by provincial governors is eulogised by Silius
Italicus, Pun. xiv 685: At ni cura viri, qui nunc dedit otia mundo, |
effrenum arceret populandi cuncta furorem, | nudassent avidae terrasque
fretumque rapinae. Baebius Massa, governor of Hispania Baetica, was
prosecuted by Pliny in 93 A.D. on the complaint of the provincials and was
convicted of extortion (Plin. Ep. iii 4, vii 33). This is the only known
case of provincial accusation during his reign. In later times Domitian
was cited as an example of the truth that a bad emperor with good amici
is less injurious than a good emperor with bad amici, Trajan being instanced as a good emperor who incurred odium by entrusting the State to
unprincipled men (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 65). Among those designated to
the consulship by Domitian were Nerva, Trajan, Verginius Rufus, Agricola,
and the grandfather of Antoninus Pius (Duruy, op. cit. iv 697 n.). Pliny
was quaestor in 90, tribune in 92, praetor in 93; Tacitus was praetor in 88
(H. i 1, dignitatem nostram
a Domitiano longius provectam non
abnuerim).

correctione: Tib. 33, si qua in publicis moribus desidia aut mala consuetudine labarent, corrigenda suscepit. After his victory over the Chatti
in 83 A.D. (c. 6, 1) Domitian took the censorship for life, a unique event
in the history of that office; cf. Dio lxvii 4, τιμητὴς δὲ διὰ βίου πρῶτος δὴ
καὶ μόνος καὶ ἰδιωτῶν καὶ αὐτοκρατόρων ἐχειροτονήθη. Martial (vi 4, 1) salutes
him as "censor maxime, principumque princeps"; cf. Quintilian (iv
prooem. 2), Cum vero mihi Domitianus Augustus sororis suae nepotum
delegaverit curam, non satis honorem iudiciorum caelestium intelligam,
nisi ex hoc oneris quoque magnitudinem metiar. Quis enim mihi aut
mores excolendi sit modus, ut eos non immerito probaverit sanctissimus
censor? etc. His censorship is also referred to in Juv. iv 11, Sed nunc de
factis levioribus, et tamen alter | si fecisset idem, caderet sub iudice morum;
in ii 29 sqq. Juvenal bitterly contrasts Domitian's moral ordinances as
censor with his scandalously immoral conduct in relation to his niece Julia
(see c. 22).

in equite: = inter equites; cf. Claud. 25, 4, in senatu (i.e. among the
senators in the orchestra) sedentes. The seats of the knights in the theatre
are called by Suet. equestria (c. 4, 5 n.); cf. Calig. 26, 4, describing how
Caligula, to foment discord between the plebs and the equites, used to have
the tickets for gifts scattered about in the theatre before the appointed
time, in order that the rabble might occupy the equestria and a quarrel
might ensue when the equites claimed their reserved seats. By the lex
Roscia theatralis (67 B.c.) the equites were assigned the 14 rows of seats
in the theatre immediately behind the senators' seats in the orchestra.
Augustus allowed equites who had been impoverished by the civil wars to
sit in the 14 rows, provided that they themselves once had, or their parents
had had, the census equester of 400,000 sesterces (Aug. 40, 1).
Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 534. Any unqualified person occupying the seats
of the equites was liable to a penalty (poena theatralis) and summary
ejection by the attendant (designator theatralis). Such ejections are mentioned by Martial as following Domitian's ordinance (88/89 A.D.); e.g.
▼ 8, Edictum domini deique nostri, | quo subsellia certiora fiunt | et puros
eques ordines recepit, | dum laudat modo Phasis in theatro, | Phasis
purpureis ruber lacernis, | et iactat tumido superbus ore: | “Tandem commodius licet sedere, | nunc est reddita dignitas equestris; | turba non
See
2 N
premimur neque inquinamur”: | haec et talia dum refert supinus, | illas
purpureas et adrogantes | iussit surgere Leitus lacernas.

scripta famosa: libellous verse was punished with the death-penalty
under the xii Tables; cf. Cic. Rep. iv 10, 12, nostrae duodecim tabulae cum
perpaucas res capite sanxissent in his quoque sanciendum putaverunt si
quis occentavisset sive carmen condidisset quod infamiam faceret flagitiumve
alteri: Hor. S. ii 1, 82, si mala condiderit in quem quis carmina, ius est |
iudiciumque (cf. Ep. ii 1, 152); libel and slander against the leading men
of the State were included under maiestas, or treason, by the lex Cornelia
maiestatis of Sulla. A cognitio de famosis libellis was first established by
Augustus; cf. Tac. A. i 72, primus Augustus cognitionem de famosis libellis
specie legis eius (i.e. de maiestate) tractavit, commotus Cassii Severi libidine
qua viros feminasque inlustres procacibus scriptis diffamaverat: Suet.
Aug. 55: Dio lvi 27. Under Tiberius any writings or spoken words which
could be construed as reflecting in any way on the emperor were held to
be maiestas and punishable with death. Mayor, on Juv. i 152, gives many
examples of writers of pasquils and lampoons who were punished by the
emperors.

abolevit: prob. "burned"; cf. Tib. 61, 3, animadversum statim in
auctores scriptaque abolita (= Tac. A. iv 35, libros per aediles cremandos
censuere patres; Dio lvii 24, πρὸς τῶν ἀγορανόμων ἐκαύθη) : Plin. Εp. vii 19,
6, libros [Senecionis] abolitos (= Tac. Agr. 2, in libros [Senecionis]
saevitum ut in comitio et foro urerentur).

quaestorium virum: Caecilius Rufinus; Dio lxvii 13, ἔπραξε δέ τι καὶ ὡς
τιμητὴς (censor) ἀξιόλογον, Καικίλιον γὰρ ῾Ῥουφῖνον ἀπήλασεν ἐκ τοῦ συνεδρίου
(senatu movit) ὅτι ὠρχεῖτο. He is not mentioned elsewhere.
A

gesticulandi: cf. Ner. 42, 2, iocularia carmina lasciveque modulata,
quae vulgo notuerunt, etiam gesticulatus est (i.e. represented in pantomime) :
Petron. Satyr. 36, scissor ("carver") ad symphoniam gesticulatus laceravit
obsonium. The verb is post-Aug.; Cic. uses agere (facere) gestum.
pantomimus in his dances had to depict by his various rhythmical motions
and gestures different characters in different situations, generally of a
passionate and erotic kind; hence such phrases as "speaking hands"
(manus loquacissimae, linguosi digiti, Cassiod. Var. iv 51) and "eloquent
dancing'' (saltare diserte, Tac. Dial. 26). A pantomimus is sometimes
called gesticulator or gesticularius.

movit senatu: movere, eiicere, praeterire (in recitando, i.e. at the public
reading of the list) were the verbs used for the rejection and omission of
senators by the censors. As censor the emperor could remove names from
the senate for moral delinquencies, as was done in the old days by the
ordinary censors at the lectio senatus; moreover, the revision of the lists
of the senate and equites was an admitted right of the Princeps as such;
Dio liii 17, καὶ τοὺς μὲν καταλέγουσι καὶ ἐς τὴν ἱππάδα καὶ ἐς τὸ βουλευτικόν, τοὺς
δὲ καὶ ἀπαλείφουσιν, ὅπως ἂν αὐτοῖς δόξῃ. See Greenidge, op. cit. 347, 374.

probrosis feminis: probrum often means unchastity, lewdness; cf.
Iul. 43, 1, (quoted below): Vitell. 4: Tit. 10, 2: Cic. Phil. ii 38, 99, probri
insimulasti pudicissimam feminam. Dio (lxvii 12) is sarcastic on Domitian,
the adulterer, punishing adultery: συχνοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄνδρες καὶ γυναῖκες τῶν
πλουσίων ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ ἐκολάσθησαν, ὧν ἔνιαι καὶ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐμοιχεύθησαν.

lecticae usum ademit: Julius Caesar prohibited the use of the lectica
by women who had neither husbands nor children and who were under the
age of 45 (Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 137 Schoene); cf. Suet. Iul. 43, 1,
Lecticarum usum, item conchyliatae vestis et margaritarum nisi certis
personis et aetatibus perque certos dies ademit. One restriction on the
use of the lectica was that it was confined to persons of free birth, fòr
Suetonius mentions the “ius vehendi lectica per urbem” as one of the
special privileges granted by Claudius to his freedman Harpocras (Claud.
28). The wives of senators were carried in a canopied lectica closed with
curtains (σκιμπόδιον κατάστεγον, Dio lvii 15).
ius capiendi legata ademit: this penalty was copied from that
imposed on celibates by the lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus of Augustus;
cf. Gaius ii 111, caelibes qui lege Iulia hereditates legataque capere
vetantur.
..

ob reductam uxorem: although Domitian himself had done exactly
the same thing in the case of his wife Domitia (see c. 3, 1).
Julius
Caesar, as a judge, showed a similar moral strictness; cf. Iul. 43, 1,
diremit nuptias praetorii viri, qui digressam a marito post biduum statim
duxerat, quamvis sine probri (= adulterii) suspicione.

erasit iudicum albo: cf. Claud. 16, 2, non modo albo iudicum erasit,
sed in peregrinitatem redegit. The iudices (see on Galb. 14, 3) in a quaestio
were selected from an album compiled by the praetor from those qualified
to serve. The word album (λεύκωμα) was used originally of the white
board or tablet on which magisterial announcements, and especially the
praetor's edict, were published; it then came to be used of any list or
register, e.g. Tac. A. iv 42, albo senatorio erasit: Suet. Ner. 21, 1, nomen
suum in albo profitentium citharoedorum (i.e. the list of competing lyre-players) iussit ascribi.
ex utroque ordine: senatorio et equestri.

lege Scantinia: the lex Scantinia de venere nefanda (anterior to Cicero,
but of uncertain date) punished with a fine of 10,000 sesterces (Quintil. iv
2, 69) unnatural offences against ingenui; cf. Cael. ad Cic. Fam. viii 12, 3;
14, 4: Juv. ii 44: Auson. Epigr. 91 (89), 4: Prudent. Peristeph. x 204.
Domitian himself was not guiltless of such practices; see Stat. S. iii 4, 37.
Dill (Roman Society from Nero to M. Aurelius p. 54) argues that Domitian,
in spite of his own delinquencies, may have been sincere in his censorial
regimen morum: “A voluptuary, with a calm outlook on his time, may
have a wish to restrain vices with which he is himself tainted. A statesman may be a puritan reformer, both in religion and morals, without being
personally severe and devout. Domitian may have had a genuine, if a
pedantic, desire to restore the old Roman tone in morals and religion. He
was, after all, sprung from a sober Sabine stock, although he may have
sadly degenerated from it in his own conduct. And his attempt to reform
Roman society may perhaps have been as sincere as that of Augustus."

incesta Vestalium coercuit: the Vestal virgins were regarded as
daughters of the whole community, and so unchastity in relation to them
was as heinous as incest. Their punishment by Domitian is referred to in
Stat. S. i 1, 35 (on the equestrian statue of the emperor), ipse . . prospectare
videris an tacita vigilet face Troicus ignis | atque exploratas iam laudet
Vesta ministras. Dio (lxvii 3) mentions that during the investigation of
the charges by the pontiffs (under Domitian as Pontifex Maximus) the
2N2
strain of the proceedings was such that one of the pontiffs, Helvius Agrippa,
died suddenly of shock. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vii 6) says that when
news of the fate of the three Vestal virgins reached Ephesus, Apollonius
made a public demonstration against Domitian, praying that as Vesta's
fire was purified, so the Sun might be purified from the unjust murders
with which Domitian was polluting the world.

quoque: even during the censorship of Vespasian and Titus. For
quoque = etiam cf. Vitell. 7, 3, n.
..

priora posteriora: the Vestals (Varronilla and the sisters Oculata)
condemned in the earlier part of Domitian's reign (83/84 A.D.) were simply
sentenced to death and given a choice of deaths; Dio (lxvii 3) says that
Domitian prided himself on his clemency in not burying them alive:
αὐτὸς δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἠγάλλετο, ὅτι τὰς ἀειπαρθένους ὡς ἠνδρωμένας οὐ κατώρυξεν
ἀλλ᾽ ἄλλως ἀποθνήσκειν ἐκέλευσε. Six years later, in the case of Cornelia,
he showed no such clemency.

more veteri: originally the condemned Vestal was beaten to death
with rods, but Tarquinius Priscus introduced an even more awful penalty
which continued in force in later times. The doomed culprit was borne
like a corpse on a litter to the Campus Sceleratus outside the Colline Gate.
She then had to descend into an underground stone cell which was
immediately covered over with earth and she was left to a lingering death,
having been provided with a little food and a lamp. Sometimes she was
