scourged before being buried alive, as in the case of Urbinia (Dion. Hal. ix
40). Cf. Plut. Num. 10, Quaest. Rom. 96; Liv. viii 15, 8: xxii 57, 3;
Dion. Hal. ii 67, viii 8.

§ 4. relegasset: see on Vesp. 15. This was a light penalty compared
with that prescribed by ancient usage for a Vestal's paramours viz. to be
beaten to death with rods while hanging on a cross (Mommsen, Strafr. 919).

Corneliam: Pliny (Ep. iv 11) describes in a spirit of intense hostility
to Domitian the condemnation and execution of Cornelia: Cum Corneliam,
Vestalium maximam, defodere vivam concupisset (Domitianus), ut qui inlustrari saeculum suum eiusmodi exemplis arbitraretur, pontificis maximi
iure seu potius immanitate tyranni, licentia domini, reliquos pontifices non
in Regiam (i.e. the Pontifical palace) sed in Albanam villam convocavit.
Nec minore scelere quam quod ulcisci videbatur absentem inauditamque
damnavit incesti, cum ipse fratris filiam (i.e. Julia, daughter of Titus)
incesto non polluisset solum verum etiam occidisset: nam vidua abortu
periit. Missi statim pontifices qui defodiendam necandamque curarent.
Illa nunc ad Vestam nunc ad ceteros deos manus tendens, multa, sed hoc
frequentissime clamitabat, “me Caesar incestam putat, qua sacra faciente
vicit, triumphavit?”” blandiens haec an irridens, ex fiducia sui an ex contemptu principis dixerit dubium est: dixit, donec ad supplicium, nescio an
innocens, certe tamquam innocens, ducta est. Quin etiam cum in illud
subterraneum cubiculum demitteretur haesissetque descendenti stola, vertit
se ac recollegit, cumque ei carnifex manum daret, aversata est et resiluit
foedumque contagium quasi plane a casto puroque corpore novissima
sanctitate (“with a last display of sanctity'') reiecit, omnibusque numeris
pudoris πολλὴν πρόνοιαν ἔσχεν εὐσχήμων πεσεῖν (Eur. Hec. 569, of Polyxena
slain at Achilles' tomb).

maximam virginem: the “virgo Vestalis maxima'' (Iul. 83, C.I.L. vi
2127, 2129-2146) acquired the title by age; cf. Ov. F. iv 639, natu maxima
virgo: Tac. A. xi 32, virginum Vestalium vetustissima: Dio liv 24,
ἡ πρεσβεύουσα. The Vestals, who were six in number, were chosen between
the ages of six and ten, and must serve for thirty years, after which they
might retire and marry or continue priestesses for life. See Marquardt,
Staatsv. iii² 336 sqq.

repetitam: see on repeti, c. 9, 2.
stupratores virgis

caedi: cf. Cato (Festus p. 241 M.), probrum
virginis Vestalis, ut capite puniretur, vir qui eam incestavisset verberibus
necaretur, lex fixa in atrio Libertatis. Pliny (l.c.) mentions only one of
the alleged paramours of Cornelia as being thus punished: Celer, eques
Romanus, cui Cornelia obiciebatur, cum in Comitio virgis caederetur, in
hac voce perstiterat, “quid feci? nihil feci.” Licinianus (see below) was
threatened with the same penalty. It is doubtful whether Juvenal (iv 8)
means to include Crispinus among the paramours of Cornelia when he says
of him: nemo malus felix, minime corruptor et idem | incestus, cum quo
nuper vittata iacebat | sanguine adhuc vivo terram subitura sacerdos.

in Comitio: cf. Liv. xxii 57, 3, L. Cantilius (a minor pontiff), qui cum
Floronia (Vestali) stuprum fecerat, a pontifice maximo eo usque virgis in
Comitio caesus erat, ut inter verbera expiraret. The Forum Romanum in
its extended sense included the Comitium which originally was separated
from it by the Rostra and lay to the north-western end of it, under the
Capitol, close to the Curia Hostilia. The Comitium was the meeting-place
of the comitia curiata, and in it was the tribunal where the praetor urbanus
administered justice; cf. Varr. L.L. v 155, Comitium ab eo quod coibant
eo comitiis curiatis et litium causâ.

praetorio viro: Valerius Licinianus, whose guilt was very doubtful
according to Pliny (l.c.): Confessus est quidem incestum, sed incertum
utrum quia verum erat an quia graviora metuebat si negasset. Fremebat
enim Domitianus aestuabatque ingenti invidia destitutus (i.e. Domitian
could get no one to support him in his odious conviction of Cornelia and
Celer). Having described the executions of Cornelia and Celer, Pliny
proceeds: Ardebat ergo Domitianus et crudelitatis et iniquitatis infamia.
Arripit Licinianum quod in agris suis occultasset Corneliae libertam (whom
Domitian wanted as a witness). Ille ab iis quibus erat curae praemonetur,
si comitium et virgas pati nollet, ad confessionem confugeret, quasi ad
veniam: fecit. Locutus est pro absente (Liciniano) Herennius Senecio tale
quiddam quale est illud κεῖται Πάτροκλος (the terse words of Antilochus
announcing the death of Patroclus to Achilles, Il. 18, 20). Ait enim “ex
advocato nuntius factus sum: Licinianus recessit" (i.e. he offers no
defence). Gratum hoc Domitiano, adeo quidem ut gaudio proderetur
diceretque "absolvit nos Licinianus” (i.e. by his admission of guilt he
clears me from the imputation of injustice). Domitian allowed Licinianus
to rescue any effects he could before his goods were confiscated, and gave
him an easy place of exile as a reward. Nerva transferred him to Sicily,
where he was a professor of rhetoric at the time Pliny wrote. Henderson,
Five Roman Emperors p. 15, says: “Much pity has recently been lavished
upon the Vestal Cornelia, whom Domitian commanded to be buried alive,
more maiorum, for incest. Pliny indeed inclines to believe her innocent,
and declares that the Emperor condemned her to her ghastly doom unheard. His contemporary Suetonius has no doubt of her guilt, neither did
any later Emperor recall her supposed paramour from exile."

quaestionibus atque tormentis: though a quaestio did not necessarily
involve tormenta, the two generally went together; e.g. Calig. 32, 1, saepe
in conspectu prandentis vel comissantis seriae quaestiones per tormenta
habebantur: Claud. 34, 1, tormenta quaestionum repraesentabat. So
quaestio is used in the sense of tormenta; e.g. Dom. 10, 5, novo quaestionis
genere distorsit: Aug. 19, 2, nihil exprimi quaestione potuit.
•

de semet professo: profiteri indicium was the phrase for turning
informer; Licinianus admitted his own guilt. Suetonius only uses -met
with the reflexive pronoun (cf. sibimet, Vesp. 20).

exilium indulsit: Plin. (l.c.), exilium molle velut praemium dedit. For
the constr., which is post-Aug., cf. Claud. 24, 1, ornamenta consularia procuratoribus indulsit: Dom. 11, 3, ut damnatis liberum mortis arbitrium
indulgeatis: Aug. 41, 1, usum eius (pecuniae) gratuitum iis
indulsit.
§ 5. templo Capitolini Iovis: see c. 5.

inter initia: see on c. 3, 1.
Suetonius is referring to the period
when Domitian, being little more than eighteen years of age, began his
public career at Rome after the victory of Vespasian's forces over the
Vitellians at the end of 69. See c. 1, 3.

ab omni caede abhorrebat: Stahr cites as a parallel the case of
Robespierre, who in his youth could not bear the sight of blood and was
a vehement opponent of the death-penalty.

absente adhuc patre: Vespasian did not arrive at Rome from
Alexandria before the late summer or the autumn of 70.

Vergili versum: Georg. ii 536, Ante etiam sceptrum Dictaei regis
(= Iovis) et ante | impia quam caesis gens est epulata iuvencis, | aureus
hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat. To slay the ox, the fellow-labourer
of the husbandman, was in primitive times an impiety to be punished with
death; cf. Varr. R.R. ii 5, (Bos) socius hominum in rustico opere et Cereris
minister; ab hoc antiqui manus ita abstineri voluerunt, ut capite sanxerint,
siquis occidisset: Cic. N.D. ii 63, 159, quibus (bubus) cum terrae subigerentur fissione glaebarum, ab illo aureo genere, ut poetae loquuntur, vis
nulla umquam afferebatur: “Ferrea tum vero proles exorta repente est |
ausaque funestum prima est fabricarier ensem | et gustare manu vinctum
domitumque iuvencum.” Tanta putabatur utilitas percipi e bubus, ut
eorum visceribus vesci scelus haberetur. (Cicero's verses are a translation
of Arat. Phaen. 129 sqq.) The same view is expressed in Ov. M. xv 120 sqq.;
Plin. N.H. viii 45; Colum. vi praef.

e diverso: = contra, e contrario; cf. Iul. 86, 2, alii e diverso opinantur:
Aug. 27, 2. In Virg., Liv., Vell. Pat., Quintil., etc., ex diverso means
"from the opposite quarter," "on the opposite side," in which sense
Pliny (N.H. iv 9) and Justin (xxx 4, 6) have e diverso, but Pliny elsewhere
(cf. Sillig on N.H. xiv 35) always has e diverso with the same meaning
as it has in Suetonius. See Thes. Ling. Lat. v 1585; Krebs-Schmalz,
Antibarb. i 424.
abstinentiae: see on "abstinuit,” Tit. 7, 3.
§ 2. circa: see on Tit. 4, 3. For prosecutus see on Tit. 2.

sordide: used here of meanness in spending money, as in Ner. 30, 1,
sordidos ac deparcos esse quibus impensarum ratio constaret; in c. 8, 2
it is used of meanness in exacting money.

hereditates
non recepit: legacies from those who had children were
refused also by Hadrian (Spart. Hadr. 18), Antoninus Pius (Capitol. Pius 8),
and Pertinax (id. Pert. 7). Augustus, though valuing highly legacies from
his friends, observed the same rule: Aug. 66, 4, legata vel partes hereditatium, a quibuscumque parentibus relicta sibi, aut statim liberis eorum
concedere, aut si pupillari aetate essent, die virilis togae vel nuptiarum cum
incremento restituere consuerat. The practice of Tiberius is described in
Tac. A. ii 48: neque hereditatem cuiusquam adiit nisi cum amicitia
meruisset: ignotos et aliis infensos eoque principem nuncupantes procul
arcebat. Caligula insisted on being included in wills, and then, when
through terror strangers named him as heir among their intimates, and
parents among their children, he said that they were mocking him by not
dying, and sent poisoned cakes to many (Calig. 38, 2). Nero ordered that
the estates of those who were "ungrateful to their emperor (by leaving
him nothing) should belong to the privy purse (Ner. 32, 2; cf. Tac. A. xiv
31, xvi 11). Domitian in his later days was grasping of legacies and
claimed the estates of total strangers (see c. 12, 2). Tacitus (Agr. 43)
mentions the will of Agricola “quo coheredem optimae uxori et piissimae
filiae Domitianum scripsit," and says that Domitian was pleased by the
compliment, his mind being so blinded by constant flatteries “ut nescireť
a bono patre non scribi heredem nisi malum principem.”

Rusti Caepionis: not mentioned elsewhere. The MSS. have rusci (so
Preud'homme Rusci), but Torrentius rightly introduced Rusti, the form of
the name attested by inscriptions (e.g. C.I.L. vi 2222) in the case of some
others of the gens Rustia.

caverat: cavere or testamento cavere was the regular expression used
of providing for something by will; e.g. Cic. Fin. ii 103, dico magis fuisse
vestrum agere ("to celebrate'") Epicuri diem natalem quam illius testamento cavere ut ageretur.

ut quotannis senatoribus: two interpretations have been suggested,
of which the first seems the more probable: (1) that a sum was to be given
as a New Year's gift (strena) to all the senators every year when they
entered the senate-house for the first time (so Burman and Bremi); (2) that
a sum was to be given to each new senator when he first entered the senate-house (so Baumg.-Cr.). Mommsen (Staatsr. iii³ 895, n. 1) says that though
such gifts were usual in the municipia, Domitian regarded them as lowering
the dignity of the senate at Rome.

praestaret: the usual word for the payment of legacies; so the subst.
praestatio, e.g. Paul. Dig. xxxii 98, heredes legatorum praestatione onerare.

reos, qui apud aerarium pependissent: reos is generally explained
as State debtors, but Casaubon and Ernesti seem right in taking it as
accused persons of any kind; cf. Aug. 32, 2, where Suetonius mentions
the remissions granted by Augustus, which included (1) the burning of
all the records of old debts due to the Treasury: tabulas veterum aerarii
debitorum, vel praecipuam calumniandi materiam, exussit; (2) the striking
out of the names of all those who had long been under accusation without
being tried: diuturnorum reorum et ex quorum sordibus (i.e. the mourning
garb worn by rei) nihil aliud quam voluptas inimicis quaereretur nomina
abolevit, condicione proposita, ut si quem quis repetere vellet, par periculum
poenae subiret (i.e. the reviver of the charge, if he failed in his case, was
to be liable to the same penalty as the accused would have to pay if he
were convicted). The tabulae publicae containing the lists of accused
persons, whose cases had not been tried, but whose names had been given
in to the magistrates, were hung up in the aerarium, which was the
record-office where were lodged all laws, decrees, acta of the magistrates,
etc. (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 546). In the aerarium were also posted the
names of defaulters against whom the Treasury officials were proceeding
to extremes: cf. Claud. 9, 2, ut, cum obligatam aerario fidem liberare non
posset, in vacuum lege praediatoria venalis pependerit sub edicto praefectorum (i.e. the edictum announcing the sale of the securities was hung
in the aerarium). Caligula wiped out arrears of criminal charges which
remained untried when he became emperor: Calig. 15, 4, criminum, si quae
residua ex priore tempore manebant, omnium gratiam fecit. The bona
damnatorum went to the fiscus: see on Vesp. 16, 3.

proximum: proximus was used of what is nearest in time, not merely
in the future, but also in the past (Iul. 83, 1; Aug. 101, 3; Cic. Cat. i 1,
etc.).

repeti: repetere was the term used by the jurists for reviving an
accusation; cf. Aug. 32, 2 (quoted above): Dom. 8, 4, Corneliam
absolutam olim, dein longo intervallo repetitam convictamque. Both repetere
reum and repetere crimen are found.
causam
causâ cadere.
teneret: the regular phrase for winning a case, opp. to

§ 3. scribas quaestorios: see on Vesp. 3. The quaestors referred to
here are primarily those attached to the provincial governors (Mommsen,
Staatsr. i 336, n. 3). Cicero lays great stress on the fact that the old
Romans forbade any buying on the part of provincial governors “quod
putabant ereptionem esse non emptionem, cum venditori suo arbitratu
vendere non liceret” (Verr. ii 4, 5).

Clodiam legem: nothing definite is known of this law. It may have
been one of the many plebiscita of Publius Clodius in his tribuneship,
58 в.с. (Mommsen, l.c.). The old and very improbable view was that it is
the lex Claudia de senatoribus, a plebiscitum of 218 B.c. directed against
trading by senators, which forbade any senator or senator's son to own a
ship of larger cubic capacity than 300 amphorae (Liv. xxi 63); Cicero
says that in his time this law was "antiqua et mortua” (Verr. v 18, 45).

subsiciva: these were oddments of land which were left over when a
territory was portioned out to the colonies of veterans planted in Italy
by Sulla, Julius Caesar, and the early emperors. These oddments had been
usurped by the local communities or neighbouring holders, though they
formed part of the ager publicus, the property of the State. Vespasian
proceeded to reclaim and sell these subsiciva to aid the fiscus, but deputations
came urging the upheaval occasioned by this disturbance of existing
occupations (quassabatur universus Italiae possessor), and Vespasian
suspended the sale; Titus proceeded anew with it, and later Domitian
issued his edict securing possession to the existing occupiers of the subsiciva. For this conversion of these squatters' tenure into proprietorship
see Heitland, Agricola p. 272.

ut usu capta: as if usucapio, or prescriptive right to a property by
undisputed possession for a certain period, were legally possible in the
case of illegal usurpers of State property; cf. Just. Inst. ii 6, 9, res fisci
nostri usucapi non potest.

veteribus possessoribus concessit: this concession is often mentioned
in the extracts from the Gromatici or Agrimensores; e.g. Siculus Flaccus
De condicione agrorum p. 163, Non enim omnis ager centuriatus in assignationem cecidit, sed et multa vacua relicta sunt, quorum ea condicio est,
quae subsicivorum; de quibus Domitianus finem statuit, id est, possessoribus
ea concessit (a centuria was a square of land, 240 rods each way, containing 100 lots, originally of two iugera; any of the ager centuriatus
not assigned would be in the same position as subsiciva): p. 284, quae cum
vel communis iuris, aut publici essent, possessionibus vicinis tunc Domitianus
imperator profudit: Frontinus, De controversiis agrorum p. 54, aeque et
Titus imperator aliqua subsiciva in Italia recollegit: praestantissimus
postea Domitianus ad hoc beneficium procurrit, et uno edicto totius Italiae
metum liberavit: Hyginus, De controv. p. 133, Domitianus per totam Italiam
subsiciva possidentibus donavit, edictoque hoc notum universis fecit. As
early in his reign as July 82 Domitian had decided a dispute about subsiciva on the same principle which he afterwards embodied in his edict
(C.I.L. ix 5420; Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2554). Augustus dealt in the same
way with places in Rome which could not be clearly proved to be public
or private property: Aug. 32, 2, loca in urbe publica iuris ambigui possessoribus adiudicavit.

fiscales calumnias: calumnia, which denoted legal chicanery of any
kind, was specially used of false accusations and vexatious prosecutions;
see Vitell. 7, 2. The delatores (Tit. 8, 5, n.) throve by giving information
about property that might be claimed for the fiscus or imperial money-chest (Vesp. 16, 3, n.), and by promoting accusations which, if successful,
would enable the fiscus to seize the property of the accused. In Ner. 32, 1
Suetonius tells us that Nero resorted to calumniae as a means of raising
money. calumniae also occurred very frequently in connexion with the
aerarium or public treasury; cf. Aug. 32, 2 (quoted above). On the
subject of delationes fiscales and the property which could legally be claimed
by the fiscus see Dig. xlix c. 14, entitled De iure fisci; also Cod. Iust. x 11
(De delationibus) containing rescripts of various emperors on the malpractices of the delatores.

repressit: contrast c. 12, where we find every kind of accusations
by delatores eagerly seized on by Domitian as grounds for his later
extortions. For the attitude of earlier emperors towards delatores see on
Tit. 8, 5.
ferebatur vox eius: Dio (lxvii 1) says that Domitian used the words
in an edict: τῇ δ᾽ αὐτῇ ταύτῃ διανοίᾳ καὶ προέγραψέ ποτε, ὅτι αὐτοκράτωρ ὅταν μὴ
κολάζῃ τοὺς συκοφάντας, αὐτός σφας ποιεῖ τοιούτους. The form of Domitian's
maxim recalls Seneca's Qui non vetat peccare, cum possit, iubet. Another
saying of Domitian's was that those emperors who did not inflict punishment on many were not good emperors, but only fortunate (Dio lxvii 2).
Paridis: see on c. 3, 1.
impuberem: so the Basle ed. of 1533; the MSS. have puberem.

cum maxime: "at that very time"; only here in Suetonius, though
in Tib. 14, 2, Thrasyllum mathematicum.. tum maxime expertus est (= tum
expertus est maxime) there is a variant cum for tum. The words cum
maxime frequently follow tum or nunc to emphasize them; e.g. Cic. Sen. 38,
пипс сит тaxime conficio orationes (= cum maxime conficio orationes,
nunc conficio "the time when I most of all compose is now," Reid ad loc.).
Then cum maxime came to be used absolutely to express tum or nunc in a
more emphatic fashion; so in Cicero, e.g. Verr. iv 38, 82, qui сит топиmenta rerum suarum cum maxime (= nunc) constituat: in Livy, e.g. xxix
17, 20, omnia quae captae urbes patiuntur passi sumus et cum maximé
patimur: in Tacitus, e.g. H. i 29, ut qui adversas res expertus cum maxime
("at this moment'") discam ne secundas quidem minus discriminis habere.
See also Hand Turs. iii 599 sqq., Kühner-Stegmann, ii 480.
Düpow (op.
cit. p. 17) wrongly explains cum maxime aegrum here as meaning "im
höchsten Grade krank."
non absimilis: see on Oth. 1, 2.

Hermogenem Tarsensem: there is no means of fixing this historian;
he may be the Hermogenes (of uncertain date) who wrote a mythological
account of Phrygia of which a few fragments have been preserved (see
Müller, Frag. Hist. Graec. iii 523 sq.). The famous rhetorician Hermogenes
of Tarsus lived later, as he declaimed at the age of 15 before the emperor
M. Aurelius (161-180 A.D.).

figuras: "satirical allusions," "indirect attacks"; see on Vesp. 13,
causidicorum figuras lenissime tulit.

librariis: slaves employed to copy books (scriptor librarius, Hor. A.P.
354).
The author either had a sufficient number of copies produced for
publication by his own librarii, or else he gave his work to an editor who
published it for him. For the different classes of librarii see Marquardt,
Privatl. 825 sqq. Stahr mentions as a parallel to the punishment of the
librarii of Hermogenes the practice which obtains in many modern countries
of punishing the printer as well as the author and publisher of a book
that is condemned.

cruci fixis: cruci figere is post-Aug.; earlier we find cruci suffigere
(Cic., cf. Suet. Iul. 74, 1) and cruci adfigere (Plaut., Liv.). Suetonius also
uses cruce adficere (Galb. 9, 1); in crucem agere (Calig. 12, 2).

patrem familias: a plain, ordinary citizen; cf. Cic. de or. i 132, Sicut
unus paterfamilias (= unus e togatorum numero, i 111) his de rebus loquor:
i 159, effudi vobis omnia quae sentiebam, quae fortasse, quemcumque
patremfamilias adripuissetis ex aliquo circulo, eadem vobis percontantibus
respondisset.

Thraecem murmilloni: for these two kinds of gladiators and their
different equipment see on Tit. 8, 2, where the partiality of Titus for the
Thraeces is described..

munerario: the giver of the munus or gladiatorial show, i.e. Domitian
himself. The point of the remark was that the Thraex, though a match
for the murmillo, was not a match for him when backed by the favour of
Domitian with whom the decision lay. Quintilian (viii 3, 34) says that the
word munerarius was a coinage of Augustus: Quae vetera nunc sunt,
fuerunt olim nova, et quaedam sunt in usu perquam recentia, ut Messala
primus “reatum,””‘“munerarium” Augustus primus dixerunt. Florus (iii
20, 9) has munerator in this sense; later writers use editor.

detractum spectaculis: cf. Calig. 35, 3, hunc spectaculis detractum
repente et in harenam deductum Thraeci comparavit ("matched him
against'"). For spectacula in the sense of subsellia spectatorum cf. Plaut.
Curc. 645, spectacula ruunt: Cic. Sest. 58, 124, ex omnibus spectaculis
plausus est excitatus: Tac. A. xiv 13, exstructos spectaculorum gradus
("tiers"). It was also used = locus quo spectacula eduntur; e.g. Aug.
58, 1, ineunti (Augusto) Romae spectacula.

canibus obiecit: among the offenders whom Caligula threw to the
wild beasts were those who criticized his shows (male de munere suo
opinatos, Calig. 27, 3).

titulo: a label was hung from his neck, like the titulus on the neck
of a slave exposed for sale which stated any special aptitudes, physical
defects, previous misconduct, etc. (cf. Plin. Ep. v 19, Gell. N.A. iv 2,
Prop. iv 5, 51, quorum titulus per barbara colla pependit). Sometimes a
titulus stating his offence was carried before a malefactor as a placard;
cf. Calig. 32, 2, Romae publico epulo servum ob detractam lectis argenteam
laminam carnifici confestim tradidit, ut manibus abscisis atque ante pectus
e collo pendentibus, praecedente titulo qui causam poenae indicaret, per
coetus epulantium circumduceretur.

impie: impietas (ἀσέβεια, Dio) was synonymous with maiestas, lèsemajesté, high treason; cf. Tac. A. vi 47, defertur impietatis in principет.
See on "pietas,” Vitell. 3, 1. Domitian claimed to be a deus (c. 13, 2).
The incident in the amphitheatre is referred to in Plin. Pan. 33 (contrasting
Trajan with Domitian): Iam, quam libera spectantium studia, quam
securus favor! Nemini impietas, ut solebat, obiecta, quod odisset gladiatorem: nemo, e spectatore spectaculum factus, miseras voluptates unco et
ignibus expiavit. Demens ille, verique honoris ignarus, qui crimina
maiestatis in arena colligebat, ac se despici et contemni, nisi etiam
gladiatores eius veneraremur, sibi male dici in illis, suam divinitatem,
suum numen violari interpretabatur:
cum se idem quod Deos, idem
gladiatores quod se putabat.
used the parma or
Martial, to please

parmularius: an adherent of the Thraeces who
parmula, a small round shield (see on Tit. 8, 2).
Domitian, disparages the Thraeces and their infrequent victories: xiv 213,
Haec quae saepe solet vinci, quae vincere raro, | parma tibi scutum
pumilionis erit: ix 68, 7, Mitior in magno clamor furit amphitheatro |
vincenti parmae cum sua turba favet. Marcus Aurelius (Comm. i 5) prides
himself on his impartiality between the two kinds of shield in the arena and
the two colours in the circus, he having been taught to be μήτε πρασιανὸς
(= prasinus “green”) μήτε βενετιανός (= venetus "blue"), μήτε παλμουλάριος (parmularius) ἢ σκούταριος (scutarius, the scutum being carried by
murmillones). Quintilian (ii 11, 2) tells of a rhetorician more interested
in gladiators than in his own art, who, when asked whether he was a
follower of Theodorus or Apollodorus (founders of different schools of
rhetoric), replied that it was the Thraeces whom he followed: Alius percontanti, Theodoreus an Apollodoreus esset? Ego, inquit, parmularius sum.

§ 2. complures senatores interemit: cf. Dio lxvii 3, 11, 12: Eutrop.
vii 23, 2, interfecit nobilissimos e senatu: Oros. vii 10, 2, nobilissimos e
senatu invidiae simul et praedae causa alios palam interfecit alios in
exilium trusit ibique trucidari imperavit: Plin. Pan. 48, domo, quam nuper
illa immanissima belua (Domitian) plurimo terrore munierat, cum nunc
propinquorum sanguinem lamberet, nunc se ad clarissimorum civium strages
caedesque proferret: Juv. iv 151, tempora saevitiae, claras quibus abstulit
urbi | inlustresque animas impune et vindice nullo. Tacitus (Agr. 44) says
that Domitian's savagery reached its climax in the years after Agricola's
death (93 A.D.): postremum illud tempus, quo Domitianus non iam per
intervalla ac spiramenta temporum, sed continuo et velut uno ictu rem
publicam exhausit.

Civicam Cerealem: this is the C. Vettulenus Civica Cerealis mentioned
in a military diploma (Dessau 1995) as legatus of Moesia in 82 A.D. He
was put to death by Domitian while he held the proconsulship of Asia
(c. 88 A.D.); cf. Tac. Agr. 42, where his fate is referred to as furnishing
a warning to Agricola not to accept the proconsulship when his turn came:
Aderat iam annus, quo proconsulatum Africae et Asiae sortiretur, et occiso
Civica nuper nec Agricolae consilium deerat nec Domitiano exemplum (i.e.
a precedent for doing away with Agricola).

Salvidienum Orfitum: consul (suffectus) under the Flavians, year unknown. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vii 8 and 33, viii 7) says that
Apollonius of Tyana, when he appeared before Domitian on the charge
of conspiracy, maintained that Orfitus was just and temperate, averse from
wealth, sluggish by nature, and no more capable of revolutionary designs
than Apollonius' friend Nerva, the future emperor, who also was suspected
by Domitian of intriguing against him. Orfitus and Rufus (who was
alleged to be a fellow-conspirator) were banished to islands. Nerva was
commanded to dwell at Tarentum. Apollonius was acquitted. Ser.
Cornelius Scipio Salvidienus Orfitus, consul in 51, executed by Nero (Ner.
37), was probably the father of the (Ser. Cornelius Scipio) Salvidienus Orfitus
mentioned here; and two consuls of the same name in 110 and 149 were
probably his son and grandson.

Acilium Glabrionem: Manius Acilius Glabrio, who was consul along
with Trajan in 91 A.D.
The same portents appeared to them when they
entered upon the consulship, predicting destruction for Glabrio but empire
for Trajan (Dio lxvii 12). Glabrio's premature death is referred to in
Juv. iv 94 sqq., where he is mentioned as hastening along with his father
(aged about 80) to Domitian's consilium at his Alban fortress: properabat
Acilius | cum iuvene (= filio) indigno, quem mors tam saeva maneret |
et domini gladiis tam festinata. On the occasion of the Iuvenalia Domitian
compelled him, though consul, to fight as a venator against a huge lion
in the amphitheatre at the arx Albana; Glabrio dexterously despatched the
lion, and according to Dio (lxvii 14) it was chiefly Domitian's jealousy of
his skill in the arena which led to his exile and then to his death in 95 A.D.
That Glabrio was also charged with "impiety" in the form of Judaism
or Christianity seems a necessary inference from the words of Dio, who,
after mentioning that several, including Flavius Clemens (see с. 15, 1),
were condemned on this charge, goes on to say: τὸν δὲ δὴ Γλαβρίωνα . . .
κατηγορηθέντα τά τε ἄλλα καὶ οἷα οἱ πολλοὶ καὶ ὅτι καὶ θηρίοις ἐμάχετο, ἀπέκτεινεν.
See von Rohden in Pauly-Wissowa, i 267. Hardy (Studies in Rom. Hist.
p. 67) says: “archaeological discoveries have now established the fact that
the family of the Acilii Glabriones were buried in a crypt, the centre of a
series of catacombs clustered round the tomb of some saint or martyr,
whom, considering the evidence of Dio Cassius, it is not altogether rash
to identify with the Acilius Glabrio of Domitian." Cf. Ramsay, The
Church in the Roman Empire p. 262.
quasi: causal, see on Tit. 5, 1.

molitores rerum novarum: though Suetonius uses the phrase res novas
moliri several times (e.g. Galb. 11, Dom. 7, 3), he only uses the subst.
molitor here; he coins a fem. molitrix in Ner. 35, 4, Antoniam Claudi
filiam quasi molitricem novarum rerum interemit. For molitor cf. Sen.
Tranq. 7, maximorum molitores scelerum: Tac. A. xi 29, Appianae caedis
molitor Narcissus: Cic. Univ. 5, effector mundi molitorque Deus.

Aelium Lamiam: whose wife (Domitia Longina) Domitian took away
and married; see c. 1, 3.

laudanti: Domitian himself may have praised Lamia's voice, or
someone else in the presence of Domitian.

eutacto: i.e. εὐτακτῶ, disciplinam servo, continenter vivo, Venere
abstineo. Gronovius correctly explained the jest of Lamia: "Non mirari
te oportet me bene canere: servo enim disciplinam: et, ut servare possim,
tu fecisti uxore abducta"; he aptly cites Aelian, V.H. iii 30, ᾿Αμοιβεὺς ὁ
κιθαρῳδὸς σωφρονέστατος ἐλέγετο καὶ γυναῖκα ὡραιοτάτην ἔχων μὴ ὁμιλεῖν αὐτῇ.
For εὐτακτεῖν of obeying a trainer's regulations cf. Epictet. Ench. xxix 2,
θέλεις Ὀλύμπια νικῆσαι; . δεῖ σ' εὐτακτεῖν, ἀναγκοτροφεῖν, κ.τ.λ. A trainer
for singing and declamation was called phonascus (φωνασκός), e.g. Aug. 84, 2;
Ner. 25, 3.
μὴ καὶ σὺ γαμῆσαι θέλεις ; : Lamia's first wife had been carried off by
Domitian, and so he sarcastically suggests that Titus, in recommending
him to marry again, was looking forward to carrying off the second wife
as his bride.

§ 3. Salvium Cocceianum: his full name was Lucius Salvius Otho
Cocceianus (C.I.L. vi 2002; Plutarch, Oth. 16, erroneously calls him
Κοκκήιος); he was the son of L. Salvius Otho Titianus, who was brother of
the emperor Otho (see Oth. 1, 3, n.). Tacitus (H. ii 48) describes how Otho
on the eve of his suicide comforted his nephew Salvius Cocceianus, concluding with the words "proinde erecto animo capesseret vitam neu patruum
sibi Othonem fuisse aut oblivisceretur umquam aut nimium meminisset."
Cf. Plut. l.c., Suet. Oth. 10, 2. Cocceianus neglected this wise advice, and
the suspicious mind of Domitian interpreted the nephew's celebrations of
his dead uncle's birthday as a sign that he too was cherishing hopes of
empire.

Othonis imperatoris
diem natalem: April 28; see Oth. 2, 1. The
birthday of Julius Caesar became a State festival after his death (Dio xlvii
18). Dio mentions the celebrations of the birthdays of the emperors
Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Vitellius, Titus, Hadrian, Commodus, Severus,
and Geta; such celebrations being doubtless continued after their death
in so far as they were not specially forbidden. Domitian forbade memorial
games on the birthday of Titus (Dio lxvii 2); so too Caracalla in the case
of Geta (Dio lxxvii 12). See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 268, n. 10.

Mettium Pompusianum: for the different way in which Vespasian
treated Pompusianus and his imperatoria genesis see Vesp. 14. Dio (lxvii
12) says that Domitian first banished him to Corsica and afterwards put
him to death.

quod ferebatur: the indic. is used, though quod circumferret,
quodque..indidisset follows, because it is a compressed form of expression
representing quod, ut ferebatur (ferebant), haberet imperatoriam genesim;
see on quod constabat, Tit. 7, 1. In giving the reasons for the different
executions the construction varies between the indie. (quod dixerat,
quodque responderat, quod celebraverat) and the subjunct. (in this
and the following clauses); the indic. expressing the writer's statements of
facts, the subjunct. expressing the considerations actuating Domitian
(Trachmann, op. cit. p. 26).

depictum orbem terrae in membrana: Dio (lxvii 12) describes the
map which Pompusianus had, not as a portable parchment, but as a painting
on the walls of his bed-chamber (τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐν τοῖς τοῦ κοιτῶνος τοίχοις
εἶχεν ἐγγεγραμμένην). It would be a general map of the world such as
those referred to in Prop. iv 3, 37, Cogor et e tabulis pictos ediscere mundos,
and Vitruv. viii 2, 6, capita fluminum, quae orbe terrarum chorographiis
picta itemque scripta inveniuntur. Maps were frequently painted on
the walls of porticoes; e.g. the map of Italy in the temple of Tellus at
Rome (Varr. R.R. i 2), and the map of the Roman Empire painted (7 A.D.)
in the portico of Polla, sister of Agrippa, at Rome (Plin. N.H. iii 3,
Dio lv 8). Pompusianus was not put to death merely for having a map
in his possession, but for using it to aid his alleged treasonable designs
by studying the points at which the Empire could best be attacked, or by
acquiring a knowledge which would be essential to him when emperor.
contiones. ex Tito Livio: Quintilian praises Livy as “in contionibus
supra quam enarrari potest eloquens” (x 1, 101); he also recommends to
the orator the study of the contiones in the historians (iii 8, 67). Twice
elsewhere Suetonius mentions Livy, telling us that he encouraged the
youthful Claudius to write a history (Claud. 41, 1), and that Caligula
was very near removing his writings and busts from all the libraries,
censuring him as a long-winded and careless historian: ut verbosum in
historia neglegentemque carpebat (Calig. 34, 2).

Magonis et Hannibalis: the Carthaginian general Mago, son of
Hamilcar Barca, was the youngest brother of Hannibal and accompanied
him in the Carthaginian invasion of Italy in 218 B.C. at the beginning of
the second Punic war.

Sallustium Lucullum: the name appears as C. Sallustius Lucullus in
a spurious inscription, Eph. Epigr. vii 1185.* He was one of the successors
of Agricola as legatus of Britain, for the predecessors of Agricola are
named by Tacitus, and so his command must have been at some period
between 84 (when Agricola left Britain) and 96 (when Domitian died).
The reason given by Suetonius for his execution was probably only a
part of a more general charge of inciting the army in Britain to revolt
from Domitian.

lanceas Luculleas: Domitian may have thought that these lances
should have been called after him as head of the army (Bremi). For the
naming of weapons after individuals cf. Δρουσιανὰ ξίφη (Dio lvii 13; see
note on "ferramenta,” Tit. 9, 2). Iphicrates, an Athenian general, invented a new sort of military boots or leggings called after him ᾿Ιφικρατίδες.

Iunium Rusticum: Quintus (?) Iunius Arulenus Rusticus was an unflinching adherent of the Stoic school and a pupil of Thrasea Paetus. As
tribunus plebis in '66 A.D. he wished to use his veto (intercessio) on the
senate's condemnation of Thrasea, but Thrasea forbade him, as it would
not save his life and it would involve the death of Rusticus (Tac. A. xvi 26,
where Rusticus is described as a flagrans iuvenis, actuated “cupidine
laudis''). He was praetor in 69, and was one of the envoys sent by
Vitellius and the senate to the forces of Vespasian which were advancing
on Rome, but they received him with derision and even wounded him (Tac.
H. iii 80; cf. Vitell. 16). In 93 he was condemned by the senate for
treason to Domitian and was executed. The younger Pliny was a warm
admirer of his (see Ep. i 14, ii 18, iii 11). For the difficulty in determining his praenomen see Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 233. Both Tacitus
and Pliny call him Rusticus Arulenus or Arulenus Rusticus or simply
Rusticus.

Paeti Thraseae: P. Clodius Thrasea Paetus, who took the younger
Cato as a model (cf. Plut. Cat. min. 25, 37), put his Stoical principles into
practice by the stubborn opposition which he offered in the senate to Nero's
tyrannous conduct. He was consul (suffectus) in 56. In 63 he was
excluded from the receptions of Nero, and for the next three years he
took no part in public life; his retirement, however, did not placate Nero's
animosity, and in 66, after the conspiracy of Piso and the many executions
which followed it, Nero 'aspired to extirpate Virtue itself” (virtutem ipsam
exscindere concupivit) by putting to death Thrasea Paetus and his friend
Barea Soranus (Tac. A. xvi 21). Thrasea was condemned for treason, and
was only allowed to choose the manner of his death. Tacitus enumerates
the various charges brought against him at his trial; Suetonius (Ner. 37,
1) says that Nero charged him with having a "dour and pedagogic look”
(tristior et paedagogi vultus). The full form of his name was learned
from a tablet found at Pompeii (Mommsen, Hermes xii 128).

Helvidi Prisci: son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus; for his career and
character see on Vesp. 15. If the text here is sound, Suetonius seems
inaccurate in attributing the panegyric on him to Junius Rusticus, for
Tacitus, Pliny, and Dio say that it was composed by Herennius Senecio:
Tac. Agr. 2, Legimus, cum Aruleno Rustico Paetus Thrasea, Herennio
Senecioni Priscus Helvidius laudati essent, capitale fuisse, neque in ipsos
modo auctores, sed in libros quoque eorum saevitum, delegato triumviris
(capitalibus) ministerio ut monumenta clarissimorum ingeniorum in comitio
ac foro urerentur: Plin. Ep. vii 19, cum Senecio reus esset, quod de vita
Helvidi libros composuisset: Dio lxvii 13, τὸν γὰρ δὴ ῾Ρούστικον τὸν ᾿Αρουλῆνον
ἀπέκτεινεν (ὁ Δομιτιανός) ὅτι ἐφιλοσόφει καὶ ὅτι τὸν Θρασέαν ἱερὸν (= sanctissimum, Suet.) ὠνόμαζε, καὶ ῾Ερέννιον Σενεκίωνα... ὅτι τοῦ Πρίσκου τοῦ ῾Ἑλουιδίου
τὸν βίον συνέγραψεν. Macé (Suétone, p. 413) proposed to insert Herennium
Senecionem quod before Helvidi, and to read the pl. edidissent appellassentque, thinking that the copyist jumped from HErennium to HElvidi,
and that later a corrector changed the verbs to the sing. in agreement
with the only subject which was left. Janssen would force the text into
meaning that Rusticus wrote a biography of Thrasea Paetus and not of
Helvidius Priscus, but that in this biography he described both of them
as sanctissimi viri.

philosophos
summovit: Dio (l.c.), ἄλλοι τε ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ταύτης τῆς
κατὰ τὴν φιλοσοφίαν αἰτίας συχνοὶ διώλοντο, καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ πάντες ἐξηλάθησαν
αὖθις ἐκ τῆς ῾Ρώμης: Tac. (l.c.), Scilicet illo igne (i.e. the burning of the
panegyrics on Thrasea Paetus and Helvidius Priscus) vocem populi Romani
et libertatem senatus et conscientiam generis humani aboleri arbitrabantur,
expulsis insuper sapientiae professoribus atque omni bona arte in exilium
acta, ne quid usquam honestum occurreret. This expulsion of philosophers
took place in 93 A.D. Pliny (Ep. iii 11) describes the risks which he as
praetor incurred in that year (cum essent philosophi ab urbe summoti) by
lending aid to the philosopher Artemidorus: atque haec feci, cum septem
amicis meis aut occisis aut relegatis, occisis Senecione, Rustico, Helvidio,
relegatis Maurico, Gratilla, Arria, Fannia, tot circa me iactis fulminibus
quasi ambustus mihi quoque impendere idem exitium certis quibusdam notis
augurarer. Among those banished was Epictetus, "That halting slave,
who in Nicopolis Taught Arrian, when Vespasian's brutal son Cleared
Rome of what most shamed him" (M. Arnold). The Armenian version
of Eusebius (p. 160, Schoene) dates the expulsion correctly in the year
Oct. 92-Sept. 93; Hieronymus puts it two years later (94–95) ‘“Domitianus
rursum philosophos et mathematicos Roma per edictum extrusit," and
mentions an earlier expulsion by Domitian, not known otherwise, in the
year Oct. 88-Sept. 89 ‘mathematicos et philosophos Romanos urbe pepulit,”
which Furneaux-Anderson on Tac. l.c. suggest may arise from a confusion
with the expulsion under Vespasian (see on Vesp. 13) or may indicate
that a number of philosophers and astrologers were charged with complicity
in the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus on the Rhine (Dom. 6, 2).
words ἐξηλάθησαν αὖθις in Dio (l.c.) seem to imply some earlier expulsion
by Domitian, and Janssen surmises that in 88-89 they were expelled from
Rome, in 93-95 from Italy.
The

§ 4. Helvidium filium: this Helvidius (Priscus), whose praenomen and
cognomen do not occur, was a son of Helvidius Priscus (see above) and a
stepson of Fannia. Pliny (Ep. ix 13) says that he lived in retirement
owing to the perils of the times (metu temporum nomen ingens, pares
virtutes secessu tegebat). Pliny speaks of him as consularis and he may
have been consul suffectus in Sept. 87 (Mommsen). When he was accused
by Domitian, the servile senate condemned him and even dragged him to
prison (nostrae duxere Helvidium in carcerem manus, Tac. Agr. 45). After
Domitian's death Pliny impeached Publicius Certus, a senator of praetorian
rank, who had been the principal supporter of the delatores against
Helvidius and had laid violent hands on Helvidius in the senate. Certus
escaped by a death so opportune as to suggest suicide, and Pliny afterwards published his speech de ultione Helvidi, which was modelled on that
of Demosthenes against Meidias (Ep. vii 30, cf. iv 21).
quasi: causal, see on Tit. 5, 1.

scaenico exodio: exodium (ἐξόδιον) denoted an after-piece, especially a
merry farce after a serious play, the actors being called exodiarii; cf. the
Schol. on Juv. iii 175: exodiarius apud veteres in fine ludorum intrabat,
qui ridiculus foret, ut quicquid lacrimarum atque tristitiae, quae exissent
ex tragicis affectibus, huiusce spectaculi risus detergeret. After the disappearance of the old saturae, the Atellanae and mimi were frequently
used for this purpose; hence Atellanicum exodium (Suet. Tib. 45), exodium
Atellanae (Juv. vi 71).

Paridis et Oenones: Oenone, the daughter of the river-god Cebren,
was the first wife of the Trojan Paris and was deserted by him for Helen.
After the capture of Troy and the recovery of Helen by the Greeks Paris
resought Oenone, that she might cure a wound which he had received from
an arrow of Philoctetes. Domitian suspected that his own separation from,
and subsequent reunion with, Domitia (c. 3, 1) and his passion for Julia
(c. 22), wife of Flavius Sabinus (see below), were burlesqued in the farce
of Helvidius. Furthermore, Paris happened to be the name of the paramour
of Domitia.

taxasset: see on retaxare in Vesp. 13.
...

Flavium Sabinum: T. Flavius Sabinus, son of the praefectus urbis
Flavius Sabinus, who was an elder brother of Vespasian (Vesp. 1, 3).
Like his cousin Domitian he escaped from the Capitol when it was stormed
by the Vitellians and his father was captured and slain (Tac. H. iii 69–73;
cf. Dom. 1, 2). Sabinus appears in the consular Fasti as consul ordinarius
for 82 A.D. along with the emperor Domitian, and their names are used
for dating that year in C.I.L. vi 3828, Dessau 6105: Imp. Domitiano
[Aug. viii] T. Flavio Sabi[no cos.] idibus Iu[n]
Presumably, therefore, Sabinus actually held the office at least for the earlier part of 82, so
that if the verbal slip on the part of the herald occurred in 81 when
Sabinus was designated as consul, his execution did not follow immediately
as one might naturally infer from the words of Suetonius. Possibly, as
Gsell (op. cit. 248) and others assume, the contretemps happened in some
later year when Sabinus was designated consul for a second time but
was executed before entering on the office. See Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi
2614 sq. Sabinus was married to Julia, daughter of the emperor Titus,
and on his death Domitian took Julia as his mistress; cf. Philostr. vit.
Apollon. vii 7, Σαβῖνον ἀπεκτονώς, ἕνα τῶν ἑαυτοῦ συγγενῶν, Ἰουλίαν ἤγετο. ἡ δὲ
Ἰουλία γυνὴ μὲν ἦν τοῦ πεφονευμένου, Δομετιανοῦ δὲ ἀδελφιδῆ (“niece”), μία τῶν
Τίτου θυγατέρων. See c. 22.

alterum e patruelibus: the other cousin of Domitian was Flavius
Clemens (c. 15, 1), brother of the Flavius Sabinus mentioned here.

comitiorum consularium die: Tiberius took away from the people the
election of magistrates and transferred it to the senate (Tac. A. i 15, tum
primum e campo comitia ad patres translata sunt). In the days of the
Republic the announcement of the result (renuntiatio) was made by the
magistrate presiding over the comitia or by the voice of a herald (perhaps
by both); cf. Cic. Mur. 1, where Cicero says that he as presiding
consul announced the return of Murena (L. Murenam consulem renuntiavi) :
Gell. xii 8, censores illi voce praeconis renuntiati sunt. Though in
14 A.D. the people were deprived of any active part in the elections, they
20
still assembled as comitia centuriata or tributa to hear the formal announcement of the result of the voting in the senate (Dio lviii 20), and this
custom continued down to the 3rd cent. A.D.

destinatum: for destinare = designare cf. Dom. 15, 1: Tib. 31: Iul. 1,
1; Calig. 12, 1; it is used in this sense by Livy first. On designations to
the consulship under the Empire see Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 588.
=

perperam : imprudenter, per errorem; cf. Plaut. Most. 968, ne ad
alias aedes perperam deveneris: Auct. Bell. Hisp. 12, Tabellarii, qui ad
Pompeium missi erant, perperamque ad castra nostra pervenerant: Varr.
R.R. i 69, perperam facere "to make a mistake."

§ 5. civilis belli: the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus in Upper
Germany (c. 6, 2).
quaestionis: see on c. 8, 4.

immisso per obscaena igne: cf. Apul. Met. vii 28, ardentem titionem
(= facem) gerens mediis inguinibus obtrudit: x 24, titione candenti inter
media femora detruso crudelissime necavit.
manus

nonnullis manus amputavit: cf. Galb. 9, 1, nummulario
amputavit. This verb (= circumsecare, circumcidere) in Cicero means to
prune trees; in the sense of cutting off parts of the body it occurs in
Lucilius, but not in class. Lat.

tribunum: Julius Calvaster; cf. Dio lxvii 11, eἷς δ᾽ οὖν τις νεανίσκος
Ιούλιος Κάλουαστρος κεχιλιαρχηκὼς ἐς βουλείας ἐλπίδα (i.e. he had held the
military tribuneship in the hope of becoming a senator) παραδοξότατα ἐσώθη.
ἐπειδὴ γὰρ πολλάκις κατὰ μόνας συμμεμιχὼς (τῷ ᾿Αντωνίῳ) ἠλέγχετο, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν
ὅπως ἄλλως τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς συνωμοσίας ἀπολύσηται, ἔφη κατ' ἐρωτικὴν χρείαν αὐτῷ
συγγεγονέναι· καὶ γὰρ ἦν οἷος ἐρᾶσθαι δύνασθαι. καὶ ὁ μὲν οὕτως ἀφείθη.

laticlavium: a tribune of senatorial birth and entitled to wear the
tunica laticlavia, for which see on Vesp. 2, 2. The tribunes of the legion
were young men preparing for either a senatorial or an equestrian career.
Those of equestrian birth were called tribuni angusticlavii, e.g. the father
of Suetonius (Oth. 10, 1). A year's service as tribune was sufficient
military qualification for entering on the political cursus honorum of
senators; but those qualifying for the equestrian cursus usually had to
serve as praefectus cohortis, tribunus legionis, and praefectus alae (Parker,
Rom. Legions, p. 189).
culpae: i.e. the guilt of treasonable conspiracy.

impudicos: see on Vesp. 13. In the reign of Claudius, during the
executions which followed the downfall of Messalina in 48 A.D., Caesoninus
escaped the death-penalty by the same shameful defence; cf. Tac. A. xi 36,
Suillio Caesonino et Plautio Laterano mors remittitur, huic ob patrui
egregium meritum: Caesoninus vitiis protectus est, tamquam in illo foedissimo coetu passus muliebria.

callidae inopinataeque saevitiae: Dio lxvii 1, Δομιτιανὸς δὲ ἦν μὲν καὶ
θρασὺς καὶ ὀργίλος, ἦν δὲ καὶ ἐπίβουλος καὶ κρυψίνους, ὥστε ἀφ᾽ ἑκατέρων τῶν μὲν· τὸ
προπετὲς τῶν δὲ τὸ δόλιον ἔχων, πολλὰ μὲν ὥσπερ σκηπτός (instar fulminis)
ὀξέως ἐμπίπτων τισὶν ἐλυμαίνετο, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἐκ παρασκευῆς ἐκακούργει ....
ἐπλάττετο δὲ ἀγαπᾶν ἀεὶ ὃν ἀεὶ μάλιστα ἀποσφάξαι ἤθελεν. The treacherous
smoothness and blandness (like the "placidi pellacia ponti'") of emperors
such as Domitian (and Tiberius) is denounced by Pliny, Pan. 66, Erant
sub oculis naufragia multorum, quos insidiosa tranquillitate provectos
improvisus turbo perculerat. Quod enim tam infidum mare quam blanditiae
principum illorum, quibus tanta levitas (al. lenitas), tanta fraus, ut facilius
esset iratos quam propitios cavere? Cf. also the description in Tac. Agr. 39
of the way in which Domitian "fronte laetus, pectore anxius” disguised
his hatred of Agricola. The gruesome humour he displayed in the treatment of his destined victims is compared by Henderson (Five Roman
Emperors p. 19) with that of Louis XI described in Quentin Durward.

actorem summarum: = actorem in rationibus (C.I.L. v 8237), a steward,
cashier, accountant, who would be a slave or at most a freedman. Sometimes, as here, actor is followed by a defining genitive, cf. actor praedii,
fundi, bonorum, rerum; more frequently it is used absolutely for a
"manager." The varieties of actores are enumerated by Marquardt,
Privatl.2 139; see also Mayor on Plin. Ep. iii 19.

pridie quam: in pre-class. and class. Lat. with perf. indic.; in Livy
and later writers with the subjunct. (always imperf. in Suet., cf.
с. 16, 1).
cruci figeret: see on c. 10, 1.

assidere in toro iuxta: a very high honour; to sit unbidden on an
emperor's seat was to court death: cf. Spart. Hadr. 23, Servianum quasi
adfectatorem imperii
quod in sedili regio iuxta lectum posito sedisset
mori coegit.
..

partibus de cena dignatus est: sending food from the royal table to
absent friends was an honour shown by the Persian kings; cf. Xen.
Anab. i 9, where Cyrus is said to have sent half-eaten geese and half
loaves to his friends. Other references to the custom under Roman emperors
are in Spart. Caracalla 3, fratrem patruelem Afrum, cui pridie partes de
cena miserat, iussit occidi: Capitol. Pertinax 12, amicis si quando de
prandio suo mittere voluit, misit offulas binas, aut omasi partem, aliquando
lumbos gallinaceos. “pars" was the regular word for a "portion" or
"helping" of a dish; cf. Suet. Calig. 18, qua epulatione equiti Romano
contra se hilarius avidiusque vescenti partes suas misit: Petron. Satyr. 33,
ego quidem paene proieci partem meam.

Arrecinum Clementem: Marcus Arrecinus Clemens, brother of Arrecina
Tertulla the first wife of Titus (Tit. 4, 2). He was consul (suffectus) in
73 A.D., and again under Domitian (year uncertain) along with L. Baebius
Honoratus (C.I.L. xii 3637). In 70 A.D. he was appointed by Mucianus to
be prefect of the praetorian guards, an office held by his father under
Caligula; cf. Tac. H. iv 68, Utque Domitiani animum.. deleniret, Arrecinum
Clementem, domui Vespasiani per adfinitatem innexum et gratissimum
202
Domitiano, praetorianis praeposuit, patrem eius sub C. Caesare egregie
functum ea cura dictitans. His appointment to this post was quite exceptional, as he was a senator and not an eques; see on Tit. 6, 1.

emissariis: emissarius meant a scout, spy, or secret agent, especially
for the purpose of securing materials for accusations; cf. Galb. 15, 2, ex
omnibus Neronis emissariis maleficentissimos: Cic. Verr. ii 22, Itaque
apponit, qui petat Veneri Erycinae illam hereditatem. Petit Naevius
Turpio quidam, istius excursor et emissarius, homo omnium ex illo conventu quadruplatorum (= delatorum) deterrimus: v 108, quem iste
in rebus capitalibus in omni calumnia praecursorem habere solebat et
emissarium: Cic. Fam. viii 8, de vi reus a quodam suo emissario Sex.
Tettio factus.
...

simul gestanti: for such gestatio or riding in a litter (the lectica held
two) or carriage see on Vesp. 21. Verbs like gestor and vehor come under
the head of those passives which Kühner-Stegmann (i 105, 108) call
"deponential" passives, differing from ordinary passives in having a
present participle and a gerund; cf. Galb. 8, 1, ne ad gestandum quidem
iter ingressus: Ulp. Dig. vii 8, 12, gestandi ius: Gaius Dig. xl 2, 7, сит
gestandi gratia prodierit: Suet. Claud. 28, lectica per urbem vehendi ius:
Gell. v 6, 27, equo vehens: Cic. Brut. 331, adulescentiam per medias laudes
quasi quadrigis vehentem: Cic. N.D. i 78, Triton natantibus invehens beluis.

§2. contemptius: comparative of contemptim “contemptuously," not
of contempte "contemptibly"; see Thes. Ling. Lat. iv 655.

abuteretur patientia: cf. Cic. Cat. i 1, Quousque tandem abutere,
Catilina, patientia nostra?

tristiorem sententiam: “an especially severe sentence"; cf. Liv. viii
21, 2, interrogatus a quodam tristioris sententiae auctore, quam pоепат
meritos Privernates censeret: Ov. M. xv 43, Tunc quoque sic lata est
sententia tristis, et omnis | calculus inmitem demittitur ater in urnam.
as

non certius atrocis exitus signum: Baumg.-Cr. explains exitus here
“finis vitae, mors," and Rolfe translates "no more certain indication
of a cruel death," but exitus means the "ending" of Domitian's judgement as opp. to principium; cf. Cic. Imp. Pomp. 1, 3, huius orationis
difficilius est exitum quam principium invenire.

more maiorum puniendi condemnarentur: cf. Ner. 49, 12, where Nero
on his flight from Rome learns that he has been condemned by the senate
as a public enemy (hostis) and sentenced to be punished more maiorum;
he inquires the nature of the punishment, and is told "nudi hominis
cervicem inseri furcae, corpus virgis ad necem caedi"; when he hears the
horsemen approaching to arrest him, he stabs himself. Claudius on one
occasion when he was at Tibur wished to witness an antiqui moris supplicium,
but no executioner could be found after the criminals had been tied to
the stake; he sent for one from Rome and continued to wait for him until
nightfall (Claud. 34, 1). On the antiquity of this punishment see Mommsen,
Strafr. 916 sqq. puniendi is the gerund, and more maiorum puniendi = ad
poenam (supplicium) antiqui moris “condemned to the old-fashioned method
of punishing"; for the double gen. with more cf. Cic. Brut. 163, Scaevolae
dicendi elegantia. The gerundive with condemnare is found only in Rufin.
Hist. 5, 1, quem
praeparandum bestiis condemnavit; with damnare in
Ulp. Dig. xlviii 19, 3: 24, 1.

§ 3. intercessit: in virtue of his tribunician power (Tit. 6, 1, n.) the
emperor possessed the right of vetoing a decree of the senate (Mommsen,
Staatsr. ii³ 879). Tacitus mentions two cases of an emperor interposing
his veto where the senate had decreed the punishment "more maiorum'':
A. iv 30, dictis sententiis ut Serenus more maiorum puniretur, quo molliret
invidiam, (Tiberius) intercessit: A. xvi 11, decretum ut more maiorum
punirentur, at Nero mortem sine arbitro (= liberum mortis arbitrium) permittens intercessit. Cf. also A. xiv 48, where Nero hopes for an opportunity
of using his intercessio tribunicia in the event of Antistius being condemned by the senate to this penalty.

ab re: = alienum, lit. "away from the matter in hand," and so "unprofitable" "useless," opposed to in rem or ex re; cf. Aug. 94, 1, non ab re
fuerit subtexere quae ei prius quam nasceretur ... evenerint : Liv. xxxv 32,
non ab re esse Quinctio visum est sociorum aliquos legatos interesse ei
consilio. This use of ab re is nearly confined to negative sentences; see
Kühner-Stegmann, i 493.
pietate: loyalty" to the emperor; see on Vitell. 3, 1: Dom. 10, 1..

difficulter: as though the senators themselves were eager to punish
any alleged maiestas with the severest penalties of the law, and were not
merely obeying the dictates of the tyrant. Tacitus says that Nero spared
the senate the humiliation of his being present to witness them passing
shameful sentences, whereas Domitian loved to be present and to gloat
over their servility: Agr. 45, Nero tamen subtraxit oculos suos iussitque
scelera, non spectavit: praecipua sub Domitiano miseriarum pars erat
videre et aspici, cum suspiria nostra subscriberentur, cum denotandis tot
hominum palloribus sufficeret saevus ille vultus et rubor, quo se contra
pudorem muniebat.

parcetis oculis vestris: parcere oculis meant to avoid unpleasant or
unlawful sights"; cf. Prop. iv 9, 53, parce oculis, hospes, lucoque abscede
verendo: Tibull. i 2, 33, parcite luminibus,
celari vult sua furta Venus.
Contrast pascere oculos in Vitell. 14, 2.
...

intellegent: from the fact that the senate had decreed such a “mild"
penalty.

exhaustus: like Nero; cf. Ner. 32, 1, destitutus atque ita iam exhaustus
et egens ut stipendia quoque militum et commoda (rewards or bounties)
veteranorum protrahi ac differri necesse esset, calumniis rapinisque intendit
animum; also like Caligula; cf. Calig. 38, 1, exhaustus igitur atque egens
ad rapinas convertit animum vario et exquisitissimo calumniarum et
auctionum et vectigalium genere.
stipendio quod adiecerat: see c. 7, 3.

militum numerum deminuere: cf. Zonar. xi 19, μεταμεληθεὶς δὲ τὴν μὲν
ποσότητα (i.e. the amount of pay) οὐκ ἐμείωσε, τὸ δὲ πλῆθος τῶν στρατευομένων
συνέστειλε· καὶ ἑκατέρωθεν μεγάλα τὸ δημόσιον ἔβλαψε, μήθ' ἱκανοὺς τοὺς ἀμύνοντας
αὐτῷ, καὶ τούτους μεγαλομίσθους ποιήσας.

obnoxium se barbaris: obnoxius (= noxae expositus, damno subiectus)
is a favourite word with Suetonius in the sense of "exposed to"; e.g.
Aug. 28, 3, Urbem inundationibus incendiisquc obnoxiam: Tib. 63, 1, contumeliis obnoxius: Tib. 54, 2, omnium criminationibus obnoxios reddidit:
Iul. 45, 2, obtrectatorum iocis obnoxiam expertus calvitii (“baldness'")
deformitatem. He once uses it absolutely in the sense of humilis, demissus,
"subservient”: Tib. 12, 2, non privatum modo, sed etiam obnoxium et
trepidum egit; cf. Cic. ad Brut. i 17, 6, supplex et obnoxius.
neque eo setius: see on Tit. 5, 3.

nihil pensi habuit: cf. Ner. 34, 1, neque in divexanda (matre) quicquam pensi habuit: Sall. Cat. 5, neque id quibus modis assequeretur
quicquam pensi habebat: Liv. xxvi 15, 4, quibus neque quid dicerent neque
quid facerent quicquam pensi fuisset. In these phrases pensum means
what is weighed or considered, and the partitive genitive depends on nihil
or quicquam; in Tac. A. xiii 15, neque fas neque fidem pensi habere, the
gen. is a gen. of price or value (so too in Val. Max. ii 9, 3, non pensi
ducere). See Kühner-Stegmann, i 457, ii 262; Roby Lat. Gr. 1301 (where
it is suggested that Tac. misunderstood the construction of the phrase).

praedaretur omni modo: cf. Pliny's contrast between Domitian and
Trajan, Pan. 41, Nam quid est causae cur aliis quidem, cum omnia raperent
et rapta retinerent, ut si nihil rapuissent, nihil retinuissent, defuerint
omnia: tibi, cum tam multa largiaris et nihil auferas, omnia supersint?
Numquam principibus defuerunt qui fronte gravi et tristi supercilio utilitatibus fisci contumaciter adessent, et erant principes ipsi sua sponte avidi
et rapaces et qui magistris non egerent, plura tamen semper a nobis contra
nos didicerunt.

adversus maiestatem principis: cf. Ner. 32, 2, instituit (Nero) ut
lege maiestatis facta dictaque omnia, quibus modo delator non deesset,
tenerentur. Tacitus (A. iii 38) says that under Tiberius the maiestatis
crimen was the complementum (“makeweight'') omnium accusationum.
The abuse of the charge of maiestas to enrich the Treasury under Domitian
is denounced in Plin. Pan. 42: Locupletabant et fiscum et aerarium non
tam Voconiae et Iuliae leges quam maiestatis singulare et unicum crimen
eorum qui crimine vacarent. Huius tu (i.e. Trajan) metum penitus
sustulisti. For the various offences made indictable under the law of
maiestas see Furneaux, Tac. Ann. Vol. i² p. 141.

§ 2. confiscabantur: = in fiscum redigebantur. The verb confiscare (cf.
publicare, δημεύειν) is first found in Suetonius, either c. acc. pers., e.g.
Calig. 41, 2, duos equites R. locupletes corripi confiscarique iussit (so
Cic. dom. 8, cum lege nefaria Ptolemaeum publicasses), or c. acc. rei, as
here and in Calig. 16, 3, sestertium milies confiscatum; he also uses it of
money kept in the emperor's “fiscus” (Vesp. 16, 3, n.) as opposed to the
“aerarium publicum': Aug. 101, 2, quam summam confiscatam semper
repositamque habuerat.
..

alienissimae hereditates: the estates of those who were in no way
related to the emperor, and to which the fiscus had not the slightest
claim (see on fiscales calumniae, c. 9, 3). Contrast Domitian's earlier
scrupulousness in the matter of inheritances (c. 9, 2). Pliny (Pan. 43)
with epigrammatic neatness and sting describes him as “unus omnium,
nunc quia scriptus, nunc quia non scriptus, heres.”

uno
qui diceret audisse: cf. Calig. 38, 2, testamenta primipilarium,
qui ab initio Tiberi principatus neque illum neque se heredem reliquissent,
ut ingrata rescidit; item ceterorum (testamenta) ut irrita et vana quoscumque quis diceret herede Caesare mori destinasse.

praeter ceteros
acerbissime: for the pleonasm cf. Galb. 9, 1, multo
praeter ceteras altiorem.. crucem: Vitell. 13, 2, famosissima super ceteras
cena.

Iudaicus fiscus: in inscriptions of the early Empire fiscus is thus used
as a name for the imperial exchequer (or central chest) of separate
provinces or finance departments; e.g. fiscus Asiaticus (C.I.L. vi 8570),
Gallicus (vi 5197), frumentarius (vi 544); cf. Suet. Aug. 101, quantum
pecuniae in aerario et fiscis et vectigaliorum residuis. Jewish communities,
wherever they might be situated, were in the habit of levying a didrachm
(half-shekel) each year from every adult male Jew to increase the treasures
of the Temple at Jerusalem. The sums collected were centralised and
exported in gold by trusted agents to Jerusalem (Philo Leg. ad Gaium 23).
This export of gold roused opposition in the Greek towns and also in Italy
where the Roman senate on several occasions forbade all export of gold,
and the propraetor Flaccus confiscated the sums collected for the Temple
by the communities in Asia Minor (Cic. Flac. 28). Julius Caesar issued
edicts, confirmed by Augustus, authorizing anew the sending of these gifts to
Jerusalem from Rome and the provinces, and when the cities of Asia Minor
and Cyrene made a show of opposition, Agrippa intervened in favour of
the Jews (Joseph. Ant. Iud. xvi 16, Phil. Leg. 40). After the fall of
Jerusalem and the destruction of the Temple in 70 A.D. this annual tribute
was transferred to Jupiter Capitolinus and to his earthly representative
the Roman emperor (Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp. ii 217; cf. Dio lxvi 7,
Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 6, 6, Mart. vii 55). All the circumcised were bound
to register their names, and there were procurators to collect this capitation
tax (procuratores ad capitularia Iudaeorum, C.I.L. vi 8604).
abolished the abuses and "delations" connected with it under Domitian,
as is shown by coins of his with the inscription fisci Iudaici calumnia
sublata, but the tax itself was still being levied at the beginning of the
3rd cent.; cf. Orig. Ep. ad Afr. 14, καὶ νῦν ᾿Ιουδαίων τὸ δίδραχμον αὐτοῖς (τοῖς
Ῥωμαίοις) τελούντων. Julian (c. 360 A.D.) forbade exactions from the Jews
and destroyed the fiscal registers of their names (Julian Ep. 23). See
Daremberg-Saglio, iii 625; Hirschfeld, Kais. Verwaltungsb.2 p. 73.
Nerva

ad quem deferebantur: see on Vitell. 14, 4. The delatores (Tit. 8, 5)
gave information to the Treasury officials who controlled the Iudaicus
fiscus of attempts to evade payment by those who could be held liable.

qui vel inprofessi Iudaicam viverent vitam: vel inprofessi is a
correction by I. Fr. Gronovius of velut inprofessi (MG Υδ), veluti professi
(X). Gronovius interprets inprofessi as proselytes who were not of Jewish
extraction and so had not registered themselves on the fiscal register of
Jews, but who observed the Sabbath and various Jewish rites and
purifications; they are here distinguished from those who were born of
Jewish parents but disguised the fact to avoid the tax. Janssen follows
Bremi in taking inprofessi as referring especially to the Christians, the
Jews being referred to in the clause beginning vel dissimulata origine,
while others (e.g. Baumg.-Cr.) think that this latter clause refers to the
Christians, and that the inprofessi are proselytes to Judaism. The adj.
inprofessus is used in post-Aug. writers either in an active (or middle)
sense "not declaring oneself," as here and Dig. xxxix 4, 16, 1, si quis
inprofessus servus fuerit, or passively, e.g. Quintil. in lemm. Decl. 341, res
furtiva inprofessa apud publicanos. The words intra urbem, which are
found in some of the MSS. after Iudaicam, appear in the old editions but
were rightly rejected by Oudendorp as an explanatory gloss.
lemma: qui vel inprofessi Iudaicam viverent vitam

text:
interfuisse memini: the pres. inf. might be expected as in Cic.
Rep. i 23, memini me admodum adulescentulo
perturbari exercitum
nostrum, but there are many instances even in Cicero of the perf. inf.
with memini to express a past event of which one was a witness or contemporary, and it is usual in post-class. Latin (Kühner-Stegmann, i 703).

me adulescentulum: in Ner. 57, 2 Suetonius says that twenty years
after the death of Nero (68 A.D.), "adulescente me,” there arose a false
Nero who won support in Parthia; thus he describes himself as an
adulescens in 88; but it is improbable that he is referring to any earlier
period here, adulescentulus being often a mere synonym of adulescens (e.g.
in Vesp. 8, 3). Bentley would omit me adulescentulum.
consilio: see on c. 8, 1.

circumsectus: = circumcisus, a very rare use, for which the only other
reference in the Thes. Ling. Lat. is Mar. Victorin. in Gal. 5, 12.
For
circumcision as the distinguishing mark of the Jews cf. Tac. H. v 5,
Circumcidere genitalia instituerunt, ut diversitate noscantur. Transgressi
(i.e. proselytes) in morem eorum idem usurpant, nec quicquam prius
imbuuntur quam contemnere deos, exuere patriam, parentes liberos fratres
vilia habere. Other synonyms of circumcisus are recutitus (Pers. v 184)
and verpus (Juv. xiv 104). Horace, Sat. i 9, 70, has curti Iudaei.

§3. iuventa: this poet. form (cf. Dom. 18, 1; Aug. 61, 1; 68) is
used by Livy. Suetonius has iuventus more frequently; he always uses
senecta (not in Cic.), e.g. Galb. 4, 1: 17 (in Tib. 24, 2 senectus occurs in
an utterance of Tiberius).
civilis animi: see on Vesp. 9, 2.

confidens: = audax, impudens, temerarius; cf. Calig. 51, 1, diversissima
in eodem vitia, summam confidentiam et contra nimium metum. As an
adj., confidens is not used in a good sense in any writer between Plautus
and Apuleius; cf. Cic. Tusc. iii 14, Qui fortis est, idem est fidens, quoniam
confidens mala consuetudine loquendi in vitio ponitur, ductum verbum a
confidendo, quod laudis est.

Caenidi: a mistress of Vespasian, who treated her almost as a lawful
wife; see Vesp. 3.

Histria: a peninsula at the north-eastern corner of the Adriatic sea,
running out from the coast of Liburnia between Tergeste (Trieste) and
the Sinus Flanaticus (Gulf of Quarnero).
osculum

offerenti: as though she were the wedded wife of
Vespasian. It was customary at Rome for women to kiss their own
relations and those of their husband as far as the degree of second cousins;
cf. Polyb. in Athen. x 440, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις (τὴν γυναῖκα) φιλεῖν δεῖ τοὺς συγγενεῖς
τοὺς ἑαυτῆς καὶ τοὺς τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἕως ἐξανεψίων (sobrinorum). See Marquardt,
Privatl.2 31.

manum praebuit: sc. osculandam, as a sign of respect due from one
in an inferior station. See on Oth. 6, 2, osculo exceptus.

generum fratris: Flavius Sabinus, married to Julia daughter of Titus;
see c. 10, 4.

albatos
ministros: the imperial attendants (aulici ministri) wore a
white tunic adorned with a border or lace of gold; cf. Amm. Marc. xxxvi
6, 5, tunica auro distincta, ut regius minister: Cod. Iust. xi 9, 2, Nemo vir
auratas habeat aut in tunicis aut in lineis paragaudas (= limbos, i.e.
borders, fringes) nisi in tantummodo quibus hoc propter imperiale ministerium concessum est. Marcus Aurelius allowed the more prominent
citizens to give banquets with the same pomp as himself, and with servants
like his own: Capitol. M. Antoninus 17, 5, Tunc viris clarioribus permisit
ut eodem cultu quo et ipse vel ministris similibus convivia exhiberent.
Οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη: words used by Odysseus in Hom. Il. ii 204.
The rest of this verse and the beginning of the next were quoted by
Caligula at the time when he was claiming absolute monarchy: Calig. 22,
1, Compluribus cognominibus adsumptis-nam et “pius” et “castrorum
filius” et ‘“pater exercituum’”et‘optimus maximus Caesar'' vocabatur—
cum audiret forte reges, qui officii causa in urbem advenerant, concertantes
apud se super cenam de nobilitate generis, exclamavit : Εῖς κοίρανος ἔστω,
εἷς βασιλεύς.

et patri se et fratri imperium dedisse: Martial, in an adulatory poem
(ix 101) on Domitian as the greater Hercules (maior Alcides), praises
him for surrendering a world-empire, which was his own, to his father
Vespasian and for subordinating himself to his elder brother Titus: Solus
Iuleas cum iam retineret habenas, | tradidit inque suo tertius orbe fuit.
Both Vespasian and Titus were absent in the East at the time when the
army of Vespasian under Antonius Primus entered Rome. Domitian
(aged 18) was installed in the Palace and received the title of "Caesar'
as Vespasian's son (see c. 1, 3). He was appointed praetor with consular
power and comported himself with tyrannical arrogance (omnem vim
dominationis licenter exercuit), though the real authority rested with
Mucianus until Vespasian arrived in person.
lemma: et patri se et fratri imperium dedisse

text:
reddidisse: used not only in the sense of giving back, but also of
paying one his due (ἀποδιδόναι).
in reducenda post divortium uxore: see c. 3, 1.

revocatam: so Salmasius for vocatam of the MSS., re- having been
lost by haplography after edicere.

pulvinar: a sacred couch on which the statues of the gods rested,
as distinct from the lectus of a mere mortal. A pulvinar was among the
divine honours bestowed on Julius Caesar (Iul. 76, 1). The imperial box
built by Augustus in the Circus Maximus was also called a pulvinar
(Aug. 45, 1; Claud. 4, 3).

adclamari: this verb is used of cries of disapproval in Cicero; of
cries of approval first in Livy (xxxiv 50). Suetonius uses it in a favourable sense here and in Vitell. 15, 4: Claud. 7; 27, 2; in an unfavourable
sense in Aug. 70, 2; Tib. 52, 3; Galb. 20, 2. So adclamatio favourable
in Iul. 79, 1; Aug. 58, 1; Oth. 6, 3; unfavourable in Dom. 23, 1. See
Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 67.
in amphitheatro epuli die: see on c. 4, 5.

libenter audiit: Statius (Silv. i 6, 84) in his description of a banquet
given by Domitian to the people in the amphitheatre says that the delighted
recipients raised shouts of “dominus" and adds “Hoc solum vetuit licere
Caesar." It would seem therefore that the epulum mentioned by Suetonius
must have been given at a later date when Domitian was less rigorous in
this respect. Cf. Gsell, op. cit. 49, n. 5.

domino: the title "dominus,” which suggested both a slave-master
and a political tyrant, was rejected with loathing by Augustus; cf. Aug.
53, 1, Domini appellationem ut maledictum et obprobrium semper exhorruit.
Cum spectante eo ludos pronuntiatum esset in mimo: “O dominum aequum.
et bonum!" et universi quasi de ipso dictum exultantes comprobassent, et
statim manu vultuque indecoras adulationes repressit et insequenti die
gravissimo corripuit edicto; dominumque se posthac appellari ne a liberis
quidem aut nepotibus suis vel serio vel ioco passus est, atque eius modi
blanditias etiam inter ipsos prohibuit. So too Tiberius: Tib. 27, Dominus
appellatus a quodam denuntiavit ne se amplius contumeliae causa nominaret:
Dio lvii 8, (ὁ Τιβέριος) πολλάκις ἔλεγεν ὅτι δεσπότης (dominus) μὲν τῶν δούλων,
αὐτοκράτωρ (imperator) δὲ τῶν στρατιωτῶν, τῶν δὲ δὴ λοιπῶν πρόκριτος (princeps) εἰμί. Caligula, whom Dio (lix 3) describes as μοναρχικώτατος, claimed
the title of ‘dominus”; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 3, his elatus dominum dici,
atque insigne regni capiti nectere tentaverat. Juvenal (iv 96) uses
“dominus” of Domitian, and Pliny (Pan. 55) says of Trajan in contrast
with him: sedem obtinet principis, ne sit domino locus; cf. ib. 45, scis, ut
sunt diversa natura dominatio et principatus, ita non aliis esse principem
gratiorem quam qui maxime dominum graventur. See below on "dominus
et deus."

feliciter: cf. Claud. 7, adclamante populo: ‘‘Feliciter” partim ‘“patruo
imperatoris, partim “Germanici fratri!”: Petron. Satyr. 50, familia
"Gaio feliciter!'” conclamavit: ib. 60, consurreximus
patri patriae, feliciter!'' diximus.
sed et see on Galb. 4, 1.

Capitolino certamine: see c. 4, 4.
et
"Augusto,

Palfurium Suram: a notorious delator under Domitian; cf. Juv. iv 53,
Si quid Palfurio, si credimus Armillato, | quidquid conspicuum pulchrumque est aequore toto, | res fisci est, ubicumque natat. The Schol. on Juv.
l.c. gives us particulars of his career, on the authority of Marius Maximus
the historian: Palfurius Sura, consularis filius, sub Nerone luctatus est
cum virgine Lacedaemonia in agone (i.e. a public contest): post inde a
Vespasiano senatu motus transivit ad Stoicam sectam, in qua cum praevaleret et eloquentia et artis poeticae gloria, abusus familiaritate Domitiani
acerbissime partes delationis exercuit: quo interfecto, senatu accusante
damnatus est.

de oratoribus: = de numero oratorum (certantium); cf. Ov. Am. iii 3,
46, non de tetricis dicerer esse deus, and other passages cited by KühnerStegmann, i 499. Bremi explains de oratoribus coronatum as propter
victoriam de oratoribus reportatam coronatum (cf. Iul. 11, tropaea Gai
=
Mari de Iugurtha). The contest in which Palfurius was successful is that
described in c. 4, 4, certabant prosa oratione Graece Latineque, where the
"coronae" are also mentioned.

nullo responso dignatus: for this as a sign of arrogance cf. Cicero 's
jesting remark to the jurisconsult Valerius, Fam. i 10, Qui istinc veniunt,
partim te superbum esse dicunt quod nihil respondeas, partim contumeliosum, quod male respondeas; also to another jurisconsult Trebatius, Fam. vii
16, superbiam tuam accusant, quod negent te percontantibus respondere
(resp. meaning "to answer" and "to give counsel's opinion'').
tacere iussit voce praeconis: a precedent followed by Hadrian; cf.
Dio lxix 6, ἦγε δὲ καὶ τὸν δῆμον τῶν Ῥωμαίων ἐμβριθῶς μᾶλλον ἢ θωπευτικῶς, καί
ποτε ἰσχυρῶς αὐτοῦντί τι ἐν ὁπλομαχίᾳ (ludis gladiatoriis) οὔτε ἔνειμε καὶ προσέτι
ἐκέλευσε τοῦτο δὴ τὸ τοῦ Δομιτιανοῦ κηρυχθῆναι “ σιωπήσατε.” οὐκ ἐλέχθη μὲν
γάρ, ὁ γὰρ κῆρυξ ἀνατείνας τὴν χεῖρα καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τούτου ἡσυχάσας, ὥσπερ ἐιώθασι
ποιεῖν (οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁπότε ὑπὸ κηρύγματος σιγάζονται), ἐπειδὴ ἐσιώπησαν, ἔφη
“ τοῦτ᾽ ἐθέλει.”

§2. formalem
epistulam: formalem is explained by Baumg.-Cr. as
“forma sollemni conscriptam, cum formulis titulisque sollemnibus"; by
Forcellini as "quae eadem forma ad plures scribebatur’' (ἐγκύκλιος, α
circular letter). The Thes. Ling. Lat. (vi 1081, 1088) connects formalis
here with forma in its special sense of an emperor's decree or rescript,
which afforded a basis and model for magisterial ordinances. In M the
reading is formaul emdictaret, and Bentley conjectured formulam dictaret
epistula.

dictaret: sc. to his secretary (ab epistulis). The head of the imperial
secretariate under Domitian was Abascantus, and the multitudinous duties
of his office are described by his friend the poet Statius (Silv. v 1, 85 sqq.,
quoted in Introd., p. 11).

dominus et deus: cf. Dio Chrysost. Οr. 45, 1, τὸν ἰσχυρότατον καὶ
βαρύτατον καὶ δεσπότην ὀνομαζόμενον καὶ θεὸν παρὰ πᾶσιν Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις :
Dio Cass. lxvii 5, ἤδη γὰρ καὶ θεὸς ἠξίου νομίζεσθαι, καὶ δεσπότης καλούμενος καὶ
θεὸς ὑπερηγάλλετο. ταῦτα οὐ μόνον ἐλέγετο ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγράφετο: 1xvii 13,
προσκυνήσας (ὁ Κέλσος) αὐτῷ, δεσπότην τε καὶ θεὸν (ἃ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἤδη
προσηγορεύετο) πολλάκις ὀνομάσας, κ.τ.λ.: Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 2, maior
libidinum flagitio ac plus quam superbe utens patribus, quippe qui se
dominum deumque dici coegerit: [id.] Epit. 11, 6, more C. Caligulae
dominum sese deumque dici coegit: Eutrop. vii 23, 2, dominum se et deum
primus appellari iussit: Oros. vii 10, 2, in tantam superbiam prolapsus fuit,
ut dominum sese ac deum vocari scribi colique iusserit. The date at which
Domitian claimed these titles is between Oct. 1, 85 A.D. and Sept. 30, 86
according to Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 161 Schoene. Martial first uses them
of him in Bk. v (89 A.D.) 8, 1, edictum domini deique nostri; contrast
x 72, 3, where on the accession of Trajan he writes: dicturus dominum
deumque non sum |... non est hic dominus sed imperator. Pliny (Pan. 2)
praises Trajan for making no such claim to divinity: Nusquam ut deo,
nusquam ut numini blandiamur: non enim de tyranno, sed de cive, non de
domino, sed de parente loquimur: ib. 52, Tu delubra non nisi adoraturus
intras, tibi maximus honor excubare pro templis, postibusque praetexi.
Sic fit ut tibi di summum inter homines fastigium servent, cum deorum
ipse non appetas. See also note on “domino” above; Mommsen, Staatsr.
ii³ 759.

statuas sibi in Capitolio: cf. Suidas (s.v. Δομετιανός), οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν
ἑτέρων αὐτοῦ γενέσθαι κατὰ τὸ Καπιτώλιον ἀνδριάντων στάσιν ἢ ἐκ χρυσοῦ τε καὶ
ἀργύρου πεποιημένων: Dio lxvii 8, τοσαῦτα δὲ αὐτῷ ἐψηφίσθη, ὥστε πᾶσαν ὀλίγου
δεῖν τὴν οἰκουμένην, τὴν ὑπ᾿ αὐτὸν οὖσαν, εἰκόνων αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀνδριάντων καὶ ἀργυρῶν
καὶ χρυσῶν ἐμπλησθῆναι: Eutrop. vii 23, 2, Nullam sibi nisi auream et
argenteam statuam in Capitolio passus est poni: Plin. Pan. 52, Itaque
tuam (i.e. Trajan's) statuam in vestibulo Iovis Opt. Max. unam alteramve
et hanc aeneam cernimus. At paulo ante aditus omnes, omnes gradus,
totaque area hinc auro, hinc argento relucebat, seu potius polluebatur, cum
incesti principis (i.e. Domitian) statuis permixta deorum simulacra sorderent.
(Pliny goes on to say that the road leading to the Capitol used to be
blocked by the herds of victims intended to honour the hideous effigies of
the tyrant with as much blood as he himself had shed.) Martial, i 70, 5,
refers to the gleaming statues of Domitian on the Palatine: Inde sacro
veneranda petes Palatia clivo, | plurima qua summi fulget imago ducis.
The colossal equestrian statue of Domitian in the Forum, described by
Statius (S. i 1), was of bronze. These statues were all destroyed in the
exultant outburst at his death described in c. 23. On the subject of
imperial statues see Friedlaender, Sitteng. iii¹º 58 sqq.

ponderis certi: Lipsius was the first to suggest that this means
centenum pondus (100 lbs.), the weight mentioned in Stat. S. v 1, 190,
where the dying Priscilla charges her husband Abascantus to set up a
golden image of Domitian on the Capitol: Da Capitolinis aeternum sedibus
aurum, | quo niteat sacri centeno pondere vultus | Caesaris. Vollmer,
however, in his note there, infers that centenum pondus must have exceeded
the weight fixed by Domitian, otherwise Statius would not have mentioned
the weight at all.

Ianos: vaulted passages or open archways were called Iani (or iani);
cf. Cic. N.D. ii 24, 67, principem in sacrificando Ianum esse voluerunt,
quod ab eundo nomen est ductum, ex quo transitiones perviae “iani,”
foresque in liminibus profanarum aedium “ianuae” nominantur. There
were many Iani at Rome; cf. Ov. F. i 257, where the poet addresses the
god Ianus: Cum tot sint Iani, cur stas sacratus in uno? Suetonius
mentions one built by Augustus: Aug. 31, 5, Pompei statuam
marmoreo Iano superposuit. The most famous was the medius Ianus, the
Roman Exchange, in the Forum; on the vexed question whether this was
an arcade or four archways joined in a square (Ianus quadrifrons), and
on the relation between it and the imus and summus Ianus see Jordan,
Topogr. Rom i 2, 214 sqq., and the commentators on Hor. S. ii 3, 18:
Ερ. i 1, 54.
arcus: cf. Plin. Pan. 54, Quasi prolatis imperii finibus nunc ingentes
arcus excessurosque templorum fastigium titulos, nunc menses etiam nec
