hos singulos nomini Caesarum dicabamus. Arches to celebrate victories in
war, and later as a mark of honour, were characteristically Roman structures.
The first recorded instance is that of the three fornices (fornix being the
older Latin term) erected in 196 B.c. by L. Stertinius for victories in
Spain (Liv. xxxiii 27). In 190 B.c. Scipio Africanus built another on
the Clivus Capitolinus, surmounted by seven gilded statues and two figures
of horses (Liv. xxxvii 3). Arches were erected in honour of the Caesars
and the members of the imperial house, not only for military successes
but also for great public works; e.g. the arch in honour of Domitian at
Sinuessa, where the Via Domitia began, mentioned in Stat. S. iv 3, 97,
arcus, belligeris ducis tropaeis | et totis Ligurum nitens metallis, | quantus
nubila qui coronat imbri (i.e. a rainbow). There are still in Rome itself
five arcus triumphales of Drusus, Titus, Septimius Severus, Gallienus, and
Constantine. For illustrations of these, as restored, see Baumeister, Denk.
d. class. Alt. iii 1865 sqq.; Daremberg-Saglio, i 391 sqq.

cum quadrigis: the entablature, resting on columns against the piers
of the arch, was surmounted by an "attica," on the front of which was
the titulus or dedicatory inscription, and on the top of it the statue of the
triumphator, at first on horseback and later standing in a chariot. The
statues of victors standing in their four-horsed chariots above an arcus
triumphalis are mentioned in Prudent. c. Symm. ii 556, Frustra igitur
currus summo miramur in arcu | quadriiugos stantesques duces in curribus
altis | Fabricios, Curios, hinc Drusos, inde Camillos. Juvenal mentions
similar statues set up in the front courts of illustrious Roman houses:
vii 125, huius enim stat currus aeneus, alti | quadriiuges in vestibulis:
viii 3, stantes in curribus Aemilianos. The Arch of Trajan at the entrance
of the Forum Traianum was crowned by a statue of the emperor in a
triumphal chariot drawn by six horses, as is seen from his coins.
regiones urbis: see on c. 1, 1.
cuidam: dat. of agent (App. i. § 3. C. c).

arci: i.e. the Gr. ἀρκεῖ = satis est, a play on the Lat. arci which is
used as the pl. of arcus by Varro (Non. p. 108 Lindsay). With a play on
the word "arch" one might render "Arch-builder, enough!" Bentley
hazarded a conjecture APK (= MCXX), but thinks it more probable
that some Latin word is to be read: Latinum verbum quaerendum, non
Graecum ἀρκεῖ. Nam cum auctor “Graece” dicit, non ponit nisi Latina.
But the practice of Suetonius varies: at times he gives merely a Latin
version of what he says was written or spoken in Greek (e.g. in Ner. 45),
at times he gives the original Greek (e.g. in Claud. 43).

consulatus septemdecim: six in the reign of his father Vespasian,
in the years 71, 73, 75, 76, 77, 79; one with his brother the emperor Titus,
in 80; ten when he himself was emperor, in 82-88 (inclusive), 90, 92, 95.
See also c. 2, 1. After his victory over the Chatti (c. 6, 1) the senate
decreed to Domitian the consulship for ten years, but this sequence was
interrupted in 89. Statius hymns Domitian's 17th consulship in Silv. iv
1, 1, Laeta bis octonis accedit purpura fastis | Caesaris insignemque aperit
Germanicus annum, etc.

text:
septem medios continuavit: in 82-88 A.D. Ausonius, Grat. Act. 6,
speaks loosely of Domitian's 17 consulships as continuous: Scis, imperator
doctissime (i.e. Gratianus), septem ac decem Domitiani consulatus, quos
ille invidia alios provehendi continuando conseruit, ita in eius aviditate
derisos, ut haec eum pagina fastorum suorum, immo fastidiorum, fecerit
insolentem nec potuerit praestare felicem. Pliny (Pan. 58) denounces
these "continuous" consulships: Non te (i.e. Trajan) ad exemplar eius
voco, qui continuis consulatibus fecerat longum quemdam et sine discrimine annum: his te confero, quos certum est, quoties consules fuerunt,
non sibi praestitisse
Contigit ergo privatis aperire annum fastosque
reserare, et hoc quoque redditae libertatis indicium fuit, quod consul alius
quam Caesar esset. Miseros ambitionis, qui ita consules semper ut semper
principes erant!
Quamquam non tam ambitio quam livor et malignitas
videri potest omnes annos possidere summumque illud purpurae decus non
nisi praecerptum praefloratumque transmittere. The flatterer Statius
pretends that the reluctant Domitian was only yielding to an insistent
senate and people: Silv. iv 1, 10, Curia Caesareum gaudet vicisse pudorem;
1, 18, talem (i.e. consul) te cernere semper | mense meo (i.e. January) tua
Roma cupit; 1, 33, flectere (fut.) tamen precibusque senatus | promittes
hunc saepe diem.

text:
quemquam: cf. Iul. 59, 1, ne religione quidem ulla a quoquam incepto
absterritus. Cicero and the writers of his and the Augustan age do not
use quisquam adjectivally except with names of persons or classes; see
Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii³ 505, Tyrrell and Purser on Cic. Att. v 10, 4.
It is found with other nouns in Plaut., Lucr., and post-Aug. writers; e.g.
Tac. Dial. 29, 3, cuiquam ministerio: Quintil. x 2, 6, cuiusquam rei.

text:
plerosque ad Idus usque Ianuarias: a practice condemned by Pliny,
Pan. 65, Quam diversum consuetudine illorum qui pauculis diebus gestum
consulatum, immo non gestum, abiciebant per edictum! An example of
Domitian's resigning the consulship on the Ides (13th) of Jan. is in
92 A.D. when he (for the 16th time) and Q. Volusius Saturninus were
elected on Jan. 1, and on Jan. 13 L. Venuleius Apronianus took Domitian 's
place (C.I.L. xiv 243, Dessau 6126). Caligula held four consulships, one
from the Kalends of July for two months, a second from the Kalends
of Jan. for 30 days, a third up to the Ides of Jan., and the fourth until
Jan. 7 (Calig. 17). Tiberius, when emperor, was thrice consul, once for a
few days, once for 3 months, once until the Ides (15th) of May (Tib. 26).
Augustus held 13 consulships, 5 for the full year, the rest for 9, 6, 4, or
3 months, except the second (33 B.C.) which he held only for a few hours,
resigning it on the Kalends of Jan. (Aug. 26). For the brief tenure of
consulships by private individuals under the Empire see on c. 2, 1.

text:
post autem: for autem placed immediately after the prep. cf. Iul. 46,
post autem pontificatum. This order of words, which is very rare, is found
in Cic. Orat. 154, dicitur cum illis, cum autem nobis non dicitur, sed
nobiscum: N.D. ii 52, Tim. 26, Off. ii 8: Auct. Bell. Afr. 59: Nep.
Eum. 13. Suetonius has autem in the fourth place in Vesp. 22, 1, et
super cenam autem; this is frequent in Plautus, and there are several
instances in Cicero, e.g. Quinct. 44, quid a nobis autem refertur?

text:
Germanici cognomine assumpto: Vollmer (op. cit. p. 45, n. 6) points
out that these words are not to be taken with post duos triumphos (as
Domitian assumed the cognomen of “Germanicus" after the one triumph
of 83), but are introduced to explain why he chose the name "Germanicus''
for September. Gsell (p. 45, n. 4) thinks that the two triumphs mentioned
here are the double triumph of 89 (see on c. 6, 1), and makes Suetonius
guilty of the blunder of asserting that it was not till after this double
triumph that Domitian assumed the cognomen of “Germanicus" and gave
that name to September. The date when he took the cognomen is fixed by
two diplomata militaria (C.I.L. iii pp. 1962, 1963: Dessau, 1996, 1997),
the first dated June 9, 83, in which he is still "Domitianus Augustus,"
and the second dated Sept. 3, 84, in which he appears as "Domitianus
Augustus Germanicus." Also on the coins of 84 he is styled Germanicus,
but not on those of 83. His new title is referred to in Frontin. Strateg. ii
11, 7, Imperator Caesar Augustus Germanicus eo bello quo victis hostibus
cognomen Germanici meruit, etc.: Mart. ii 2, 3, Nobilius (nomen) domito
tribuit Germania Rheno, | et puer hoc dignus nomine, Caesar, eras (cf.
Dom. 2, 1). | Frater Idumaeos meruit cum patre triumphos, | quae datur
ex Chattis laurea, tota tua est: xiv 170, cui nomina Rhenus | vera dedit.

text:
Septembrem et Octobrem
transnominavit: the date of the
renaming of these months is uncertain. Dio (lxvii 4) notices only the
change of October to "Domitianus'' after Domitian's first triumph over
the Chatti. According to Euseb.-Hieron. the changes were made between
Oct. 1, 86 and Sept. 30, 87; but the old names occur in the Acta Arvalia
for 87 (C.I.L. vi 2065). Janssen mentions that “Domitianus” is found
in a Latin papyrus of 88 (Nicole-Morel, P. Gen. Lat. i 8); the first appearance of either of the new names in a Greek papyrus is in 90 (P. Oxyr. ii
p. 164, μηνὸς Δομιτιανοῦ δ'). An inscription of 89 in the Florence Museum
has "Germanicus" for September: exces(sit) viii k[al(endas)] Germ[anic(as)] Saeniano et Blaeso co(n)s(ulibus). Martial and Statius do not
help to fix the date, as the poems in which they refer to the new names
were not published till 94 and 95: Mart. ix 1, 1, Dum Ianus hiemes,
Domitianus autumnos | Augustus annis commodabit aestates, | dum grande
famuli nomen asseret Rheni | Germanicarum magna lux Kalendarum, etc.:
Stat. S. iv 1, 42, nondum omnis honorem | annus habet, cupiuntque decem
tua nomina menses. The months recovered their old names at Domitian's
death; cf. Plut. Num. 19: Macrob. S. i 12, 36, Mensis September principalem sui retinet appellationem, quem Germanici appellatione, Octobrem
vero suo nomine Domitianus invaserat. Sed ubi infaustum vocabulum (i.e.
Domitian's name) ex omni aere vel saxo placuit eradi, menses quoque
usurpatione tyrannicae appellationis exuti sunt: cautio postea principum
ceterorum diri ominis infausta vitantium mensibus a Septembri usque ad
Decembrem prisca nomina reservavit. Tiberius refused to allow the name
"Tiberius" to be given to September and "Livius" to October (Tib. 26).
Nero called April "Neroneus" (Ner. 55). Julius Caesar was honoured
by having Quintilis (July) changed to "Iulius” (Iul. 76), and Augustus
changed Sextilis (August) to "Augustus" (Aug. 31). Commodus (c.
192 A.D.) called all the months by his own names and titles, Amazonius,
Invictus, Felix, Pius, Lucius, Aelius, Aurelius, Commodus, Augustus,
Herculeus, Romanus, Exsuperatorius (Dio lxxii 15). The compound transnominare is first found in Suetonius.

text:
terribilis cunctis et invisus: Eutrop. vii 23, cum ob scelera universis
exosus esse coepisset, interfectus est suorum coniuratione in Palatio: Aur.
Vict. Caes. 11, magis magisque saevitia nimius eoque suspectior etiam suis
libertorum consilio uxore non ignara ... poenas luit.

amicorum libertorumque: Dio (lxvii 15) says that those who planned
and carried out the plot against Domitian were Parthenius (see c. 16, 2)
and Sigerius, who were both Domitian's cubicularii or a cubiculo, Entellus
who was a libellis, and Stephanus a freedman (steward of Domitilla,
Domitian's niece, see c. 17, 1); he also mentions that Norbanus and
Petronius Secundus, praefecti praetorio, were said to have been privy to
the plot.

conspiratione: the reading of YON, adopted by Roth and
Preud 'homme. G has insidiis before amicorum, and this is preferred by
Ihm. The other MSS. omit the substantive on which the genitives depend.

uxoris: Domitia, who lived in continual fear of his vengeance for
her infidelity (c. 3, 1); cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, Igitur metu crudelitatis
et conscientiae suae coniuravere plerique
adscita etiam in consilium
tyranni uxore Domitia, ob amorem Paridis histrionis a Principe cruciatus
formidante. Dio (l.c.) mentions the report (ὡς λέγεται) that she was aware
of the conspiracy: αὐτὸ οὔτε ἡ Δομιτία, ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ, ἠγνόησε . . : ἥ τε γὰρ
Δομιτία ἀεί ποτε ὑπ' αὐτοῦ ἐμισεῖτο, καὶ διὰ τοῦτ᾽ ἐφοβεῖτο μὴ καὶ ἀποθάνῃ.
goes on to say that Domitian kept under his pillow a list of doomed
suspects; while he slept, this was stolen by a page, in whose hands Domitia
found it and communicated the contents to the conspirators.
nec non et: see on Tit. 5, 2.
Chaldaei: see on Vitell. 14, 4.

super cenam: see on Tit. 8, 1.
Dio

fungis: the emperor Claudius was poisoned with a boletus (mushroom)
medicatus (Claud. 44, 2); cf. Tac. A. xii 67, infusum delectabili cibo boleto
venenum: Juv. v 147, boletus (ponetur) domino, sed quales Claudius edit |
ante illum uxoris, post quem nihil amplius edit: Mart. i 20, 4, boletum,
qualem Claudius edit, edas. Nero, who was a party to the poisoning of
Claudius, used afterwards to praise mushrooms as "the food of the
gods" (Ner. 33, 1).
§2. edicti de excidendis vineis: see c. 7, 2.

gratiam faceret: = remitteret; cf. Gell. i 12, gratia Papiae legis per
senatum fit. Sonnenschein, on Plaut. Rud. 1414, shows that the phrase
gratiam facere alicui alicuius rei or de aliqua re means "to renounce
something in favour of someone" and may be used (1) literally "to give
up," or (2) "to let off," e.g. Plaut. Cas. 372, de istac Casina huic nostro
vilico gratiam facias, ‘‘give up"; Rud. 1414, iuris iurandi volo gratiam
facias, "let off"; so in Suet. Tib. 35, 1, equiti Romano iuris iurandi
gratiam fecit: Aug. 17, 2, Bononiensibus gratiam fecit coniurandi cum
tota Italia pro partibus suis (= concessit ut ne coniurarent, coniurare'
remisit, ‘“excused them from joining the general confederation to support
his cause'"): Aug. 38, 3, reddendi equi gratiam fecit eis, qui maiores
annorum quinque et triginta retinere eum nollent (where see Shuckburgh).

sparsi libelli: for this method of defaming an emperor cf. Aug. 55,
Etiam sparsos de se in curia famosos libellos nec expavit et (al. nec)
magna cura redarguit ac ne requisitis quidem auctoribus id modo censuit,
cognoscendum posthac de iis, qui libellos aut carmina ad infamiam cuiuspiam sub alieno nomine edant: Tib. 66, nullo non damnatorum omne probri
genus coram vel per libellos in orchestra (where the senators sat in the
theatre) positos ingerente.

his versibus: these verses are a famous epigram by Evenus of Ascalon,
Anth. Pal. ix 75. The second line is the same as the last line of an
epigram by Leonidas of Tarentum which gives the full fable, Anth. Pal. ix
99, Ἴξαλος εὐπώγων αἰγὸς πόσις ἔν ποθ᾽ ἁλωῇ | οἴνης τοὺς ἁπαλοὺς πάντας ἔδαψε
κλάδους. | τῷ δ᾽ ἔπος ἐκ γαίης τόσον ἄπυε· κεῖρε, κάκιστε, | γναθμοῖς ἡμέτερον κλῆμα
τὸ καρποφόρον· | ῥίζα γὰρ ἔμπεδος οὖσα, πάλιν γλυκὺ νέκταρ ἀνήσει, | ὅσσον
ἐπισπεῖσαι σοί, τράγε, θυομένῳ. This is imitated by Ovid, F. i 355 sqq.,
(caper) quem spectans aliquis dentes in vite prementem | talia non tacito
verba dolore dedit: "Rode, caper, vitem: tamen hinc, cum stabis ad
aram, | in tua quod spargi cornua possit erit." | Verba fides sequitur;
noxae tibi deditus hostis | spargitur affuso cornua, Bacche, mero.
custom of sacrificing to Bacchus the vine-gnawing goat is referred to in
Varr. R.R. i 2; Verg. G. ii 380, non aliam ob culpam Baccho caper
omnibus aris | caeditur.
The
κἄν: a correction by Roth (also in C.I.L. iv 3407, 6) of KAI. Politian
read κήν, which is the form in Anth. Pal. ix 75.
σοί, τράγε : so Roth (and earlier Bentley) from Anth. Pal. for
CΟΙΚΑΡΘΕ (MGLP). Politian, followed by the old editors, read
Καίσαρι. Bücheler conjectured σοί, κάπρε, (“nescio an rectius,” Ihm).
Alexander, op. cit. 28 sqq., defending σοί, κάπρε, (which he proposes independently) says: "Suetonius may have misquoted, particularly in a
place where the Greek τράγε would suggest the Latin caper with a natural
reflex again to the Greek κάπρος, or an alteration in the original may have
been made designedly by those who scattered abroad the defamatory libelli,
to emphasize some point the meaning of which is now obscure."
though the boar (κάπρος) is mentioned as devastating vines (Alexander
cites Psalm 80 and Ov. M. viii 294), the words φάγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν, “eat away
to the root," seem much more appropriate when used of the goat.
But

§ 3. excogitatum: Suetonius is peculiar in using excogitatus (= cogitando inventus, ἐπινενοημένος) in the sense of exquisitus, to denote something carefully devised and distinctive; cf. Calig. 22, 3, templum numini
suo proprium et sacerdotes et excogitatissimas hostias instituit (these
victims including flamingoes, peacocks, guinea-fowl, etc.).
quotiens: see on Galb. 10, 2.

trabeati: the trabea was a variety of toga ornamented with trabes,
bands or stripes, the arrangement of the stripes being uncertain. Three
kinds of trabea were distinguished by Suetonius according to Servius (on
Aen. vii 612): Suetonius in libro de Genere vestium (see Introd. c. iv)
dicit tria esse genera trabearum: unum diis sacratum, quod est tantum de
purpura; aliud regum, quod est purpureum, habet tamen album aliquid;
tertium, augurale, de purpura et cocco. Dion. Hal. (ii 70, vi 13) says that
the trabea of the Salii was bordered with purple and had scarlet παρυφαί
(trabes), while that of the knights was entirely of purple with the same
scarlet παρυφαί. The trabea was worn by the kings at Rome; then by
consuls at the opening of the temple of Janus; by the Salii in their dance
in armour; by knights (trabeata agmina, Stat. S. iv 2, 32), especially on
the occasion of a transvectio or decursio equitum (cf. Tac. A. iii 2);
and by augurs, the Flamen Dialis, and the Flamen Martialis. See
Daremberg-Saglio, v 382; Marquardt, Privatl. 507.

lictores: after his victory over the Chatti in 83 (c. 6, 1) Domitian was
2 P
granted 24 lictors (Dio lxvii 4), and this number may have been continued
under subsequent emperors. Augustus seems to have had 24 lictors down
to 29 B.C.; from then until 23 B.c. he had the 12 consular lictors at Rome,
and until 19 B.C. he had 12 lictors outside Rome as proconsul; in 19 в.с.
he received for ever the right of having 12 lictors on all occasions (Dio liv
10, ταῖς δώδεκα ῥάβδοις ἀεὶ καὶ πανταχοῦ χρῆσθαι). Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. i³
387, ii³ 807; Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2004.
apparitores: this word is more frequently used as a general term
for the public officers attached to, and in immediate attendance upon, the
magistrates at Rome (qui apparent magistratibus), and included the five
classes: scribae, accensi, lictores, viatores, praecones; sometimes it is used
in a more limited sense excluding the lictores (as here and in Val. Max. vii
3, 9), or the scribae (as in Cic. Verr. iii 66, Plut. Cat. min. 16). Mommsen,
op. cit. i 332 sqq.
§ 4. tempore suspecti periculi: i.e. the time foretold by the Chaldaei.

phengite lapide: cf. Plin. N.H. xxxvi 163, Nerone principe in Cappadocia repertus est lapis duritia marmoris, candidus atque translucens etiam
qua parte fulvae inciderant venae, ex argumento phengites (i.e. φεγγίτης
from φέγγος, light, brightness) appellatus. Hoc construxerat (Nero) aedem
Fortunae amplexus aurea domo (i.e. enclosing this temple in the
precincts of his Golden House, see Oth. 7, 1), quare etiam foribus opertis
interdiu claritas ibi diurna erat alio quam specularium modo, tamquam
inclusa luce, non transmissa. In N.H. xxxvi 196 Pliny mentions wallmirrors made from another stone, Obsian or Obsidian, which he describes
as “nigerrimi coloris, aliquando et translucidi, crassiore visu atque in
speculis parietum pro imagine umbras reddente.” Guillaume (in
Daremberg-Saglio, i 176) says that phengites was probably a gypseous
alabaster of a peculiar transparence; Lenz (Mineralogie der alten Griech.
und Römer p. 153) describes it as a colourless calcareous spar. Agricola
(16th cent.), De Natura Fossilium vii 307, considers it a marble; cf.
Chandler, Travels in Greece (1776) с. 63: "The gallery (of the monastery
of St. Luke at Stiris) is illuminated with pieces of the transparent marble
called Phengites, fixed in the wall in square compartments, and shedding
a yellow light." Phengite is a modern name for the species of mica known
as Muscovy-glass. The Greek σεληνίτης or moonstone was used as a material
for windows and so was called φεγγίτης.
•

custodias audiebat: cf. Dio lxvii 12, συνεγίγνετο δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς τοῖς
κατηγορήσουσι καὶ τοῖς καταμαρτυρήσουσι, καὶ συνέπλαττε καὶ συνετίθει πάνθ' ὅσα
λεχθῆναι ἔδει· καὶ πολλάκις καὶ τοῖς δεσμώταις κατὰ μόνας ἐλάλει, τὰ δεσμὰ αὐτῶν
ἐν ταῖς χερσὶ κατέχων, οὔτε γὰρ ἄλλοις τὰ λεχθησόμενα ἐπίστευε, καὶ ἐκείνους καὶ
δεδεμένους ἐδεδίει. Suetonius uses custodiae in the sense of ii qui custodiuntur in Tib. 61, 5, Calig. 27, 1, and similarly the collective singular in
Ner. 31, 3, quod ubique esset custodiae in Italiam deportari praeceperat.
Servius (on Aen. xi 184), noting custodia in the sense of qui custodit,
condemns the passive use : ut hi qui custodiuntur ‘‘custodiae” dicantur,
usurpatum est; unde male est in usu “custodiae audiuntur.” This passive
use occurs in Seneca, Ep. 5, 7, eadem catena et custodiam et militem
copulat: Dial. ix 11, 12, Ptolemaeum inter Gaianas custodias vidimus;
also in Plin. Ep. x 19: Modest. Dig. xlviii 1, 12, praetor custodias auditurus.
For other abstract substantives used in a concrete sense by Suetonius see
App. i. § 2. α.

ne bono quidem exemplo: ablative of manner. Cf. Sen. Ep. 77, 7,
describing how the slaves of the suffering Marcellinus were unwilling to
help him to commit suicide, and a Stoic friend of his pointed out to the
slaves that it was as bad to prevent one's master from killing himself
as it was to kill him (tam mali exempli esse occidere dominum quam
prohibere). See also on Vitell. 10, 1, ut pessimi exempli.

audendam: this reading is found only in some of the later MSS.,
and as a correction in L; audiendam, the reading of the rest, is due to
audiebat at the end of the preceding sentence.

Epaphroditum: first mentioned in Tac. A. xv 55 in connexion with
the discovery of Piso's conspiracy against Nero in 65 A.D. He remained.
faithful to Nero to the end, and was one of the three freedmen who
accompanied him on his last flight from Rome, and when Nero (hearing
that he had been declared a public enemy and sentenced to be scourged
to death) wished to kill himself but lacked strength and courage,
Epaphroditus aided him: cf. Ner. 49, 3, ferrum iugulo adegit iuvante
Epaphrodito a libellis. The Stoic philosopher Epictetus was a slave of
his, and he is probably the Epaphroditus at whose suggestion Josephus
wrote his Jewish Antiquities, and to whom he dedicates his work against
Apion (Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 36).

a libellis: the same office as he had held under Nero, succeeding
Doryphorus who died in 62. The expression a libellis denoted both the
department of petitions and the head of the department. The emperor
Claudius organised the a libellis (ἐπὶ ταῖς βίβλοις) as a distinct office along
with the ab epistulis and a cognitionibus. Under Claudius, as under Nero
and the Flavian emperors, the a libellis were freedmen; Hadrian and his
successors appointed equites. The libelli with which the department dealt
were petitions to the emperor from individuals or communities for benefactions or protection, hearing of cases, relief from imposts, etc. In the
phrases a libellis, ab epistulis, etc., there is an ellipse of servus (or libertus);
cf. Iul. 74, 1, a manu servus (= amanuensis in Tit. 3, 2), the force of a or
ab being "on the side of" "in respect of'" "in the department of"; see
Kühner-Stegmann i 495, where ab epistulis is explained as ein Sklave von
seiten des Briefschreibens.

capitali poena condemnavit: Dio (lxvii 14) says that Domitian first
banished and later (in 95) executed him as a deterrent to his own freedmen. For the rare abl. with condemnare cf. Vitruv. vii praef. 3, non
modo sunt reprehendendi, sed etiam poena condemnandi: Cic. Verr. iii 34,
condemnari quadruplo. Suetonius also uses ad, e.g. Claud. 14, ad bestias
condemnavit, and in, e.g. Tib. 51, 2, uno in antliam ("the treadmill'')
condemnato; in Dom. 11, 1, he has the usual gen. capitis condemnaturus.
post destitutionem: cf. Ner. 40, 1, talem principem paulo minus quattuordecim annos perpessus terrarum orbis tandem destituit.

in adipiscenda morte: cf. Fronto p. 233 N., Quanto quisque eam (sc.
mortem) natu minor adeptus est, tanto beatior . . existimandus est: Carm.
epigr. 466, 2, Quam praemature sim mortis adeptus. Death in Nero's
case was really a boon. adipisci is very rarely used of evils: Cic. Fin. i
32, neque.. quisquam est, qui dolorem amet, consectetur, adipisci velit:
Liv. vi 8, 8: Tac. A. i 74: Apul. Plat. ii 11. Cf. febrim nancisci in
Tit. 10, 1.
2P2

Flavium Clementem: a cousin of Domitian, being son of Vespasian 's
elder brother Flavius Sabinus (Vesp. 1, 3; Dom. 1, 2); he was a brother
of the Flavius Sabinus mentioned in c. 10, 4 as put to death by Domitian.
Hardy (Studies in Rom. Hist. p. 67) points out that Clemens was a possible
danger to Domitian from a political point of view, being the second
personage in the empire as Domitian had no heir of his own.
contemptissimae inertiae: this laziness and apathy, which might have
rendered Domitian inapprehensive of any revolutionary design on his part,
would be urged as a proof that Clemens was a Christian (see below), inactivity and indifference to all public affairs and duties being one of the
charges regularly brought by heathen opponents against the Christians;
cf. Minuc. Oct. 8, 4, latebrosa et lucifuga natio, in publico muta, in angulis
garrula: Tertull. Apol. 42, sed alio quoque iniuriarum titulo postulamur,
et infructuosi in negotiis dicimur (a charge which Tertullian indignantly
refutes; see Mayor ad loc.). Such aloofness from public life and the
interests of their fellow-men formed the charge of "odium humani generis”
for which the Christians were condemned in Nero's reign (Tac. A. xv 44).
The evidence for the alleged general persecution of Christianity by Domitian
is critically examined by Henderson, Five Roman Emperors 45 sqq.

filios: Clemens was married to Flavia Domitilla, a niece of Domitian
(see c. 17, 1), who bore him at least seven children (cf. C.I.L. vi 8942);
one, a daughter whose name is unknown, is mentioned in C.I.L. vi 948.
The two sons referred to by Suetonius were entrusted (about 90 A.D.) to
Quintilian to educate (Quint. iv prooem. 2, quoted on c. 8, 3), and Clemens
secured for Quintilian the ornamenta consularia (Auson. Grat. Act. 31).
These sons' earlier names are unknown; when designated by adoption as
the successors of Domitian their names would be (T. Flavius) Domitianus
and (T. Flavius) Vespasianus; some find a reference to this adoption in
Stat. S. iv 3, 18, qui (i.e. Domitian) genti patriae futura semper | sancit
lumina (but see Vollmer's note).

successores palam destinaverat: by adoption. Such an adoption did
not necessarily follow the legal forms; a public pronouncement by the
emperor in the Forum, the senate, or the camp was sufficient. See on
Galba's adoption of Piso, Galb. 17. There were three other methods used
by the emperors in nominating a successor, though theoretically the constitution did not recognize either heredity or designation: (1) giving a
co-regency (consortium imperii), see on Tit. 9, 3; (2) designating the
intended successor as the emperor's heir; (3) from the time of Hadrian,
bestowing on him the name of "Caesar," see on Dom. 1, 3.

et abolito: sor and Preud'homme; MGX have abolito; Ihm adopts
abolitoque the reading of N.

appellari iusserat: sorN; the other MSS. omit iusserat, and it is
omitted in Ihm's text, appellari being thus left dependent on destinaverat ;
but the passive infin. with destinare is not found in Suetonius and is very
rare elsewhere (Thes. Ling. Lat.). Preud 'homme suggested appellare
(omitting iusserat), and Bentley would read abolito
...
appellans.

Vespasianum: it is a disputed point whether the bronze coins from
Smyrna with a figure of a boy or youth and round it the name Οὐεσπασιανὸς
νεώτερος (Eckhel vi 402, Cohen i² 539) are to be referred to this adopted
son, or to Domitian's own son (mentioned in c. 3, 1) who died young and
whose name is unknown. See Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2623; Gsell,
op. cit. p. 53, n. 3.

ex tenuissima suspicione: Dio (lxvii 14) says that Clemens and his
wife Domitilla were charged with ἀθεότης, i.e. neglect of the gods of the
State, and adoption of the practices of the Jewish faith (which Dio does
not differentiate from Christianity) : κὰν τῷ αὐτῷ ἔτει (95 A.D.) ἄλλους τε
πολλοὺς καὶ τὸν Φλάβιον Κλήμεντα ὑπατεύοντα (consulem), καίπερ ἀνεψιὸν ὄντα
καὶ γυναῖκα καὶ αὐτὴν συγγενῆ ἑαυτοῦ Φλαβίαν Δομιτίλλαν ἔχοντα, κατέσφαξεν ὁ
Δομιτιανός. ἐπηνέχθη δὲ ἀμφοῖν ἔγκλημα ἀθεότητος, ὑφ' ἧς καὶ ἄλλοι ἐς τὰ
τῶν ᾿Ἰουδαίων ἤθη ἐξοκέλλοντες (aberrantes) πολλοὶ κατεδικάσθησαν, καὶ οἱ μὲν
ἀπέθανον, οἱ δὲ τῶν γοῦν οὐσιῶν ἐστερήθησαν, ἡ δὲ Δομιτίλλα ὑπερωρίσθη μόνον ἐς
Πανδατερίαν. Schiller (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i 2, 537, n. 6) and Weynand
(in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2578) less probably explain ἀθεότης as a synonym of
ἀσέβεια (impietas, c. 10, 1, n.) in the sense of lèse-majesté. With regard to
Domitilla's banishment Dio seems to confuse Pandateria with Pontia,
another island in the Tuscan sea, also a place of exile, as Hieron. (Epist.
108, 7) says that Pontia is famous as the place of exile of the Christian
Domitilla; so too Euseb. (Hist. Eccl. iii 18). See note on Domitillae,
c. 17, 1.

tantum non in ipso eius consulatu: Clemens was consul ordinarius
along with Domitian in the latter's 17th consulship in 95 A.D., and probably
held the office till April 30, four months being the usual tenure in
Domitian's reign (Gsell. op. cit. 303). He was put to death in a later
part of that year when, strictly speaking, he was not consul but ex-consul.
Dio (l.c.) and Philostratus (cited below) are inaccurate in saying that he
was consul (ὑπατεύων, ὕπατος) when executed, his real position being ὑπατικός
(consularis); see Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2539. Imhof (Domitianus,
p. 116) holds that Clemens as consul ordinarius retained the title of consul
for the whole year, even though he was succeeded by consules suffecti, and
that he was not put to death till Jan. 96. Gsell makes quite a different
use of the same argument in order to reconcile the statements of Dio and
Suetonius. He thinks that Dio is speaking of Clemens as consul for the
whole of 95, the year of his execution, while Suetonius limits his consulship to the earlier months of that year, when he was actually in office.
lemma: tantum non in ipso eius consulatu

text:
interemit: cf. Eutrop. vii 23, 3, (Domitianus) consobrinos suos (i.е.
Flavius Clemens and Flavius Sabinus) interfecit: Plin. Pan. 48, illa
immanissima belua (i.e. Domitian),
сит propinquorum sanguinem
lamberet.
...
..

quo facto maturavit sibi exitium: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii
25) says that the intention of the gods to depose Domitian from the
presidency of mankind was manifest when he went so far as to slay
Clemens: ἐώθουν οἱ θεοὶ Δομετιανὸν ἤδη τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων προεδρίας. ἔτυχε μὲν
γὰρ Κλήμεντα ἀπεκτονὼς ἄνδρα ὕπατον, κ.τ.λ.

§ 2. continuis octo mensibus: i.e. the eight months preceding his
death on Sep. 18, 96 A.D. Imhof says that they were the eight months
intervening between the execution of Clemens (which, according to his
theory, took place in Jan. 96) and the death of Domitian, and Schiller
takes the same view.

fulgura:
=
fulmina, lightning-flashes that descend and strike, thunderbolts, a use of fulgura found in poetry and post-Aug. prose, e.g. Verg.
G. i 487 (of the portents at Caesar's death), non alias caelo ceciderunt
plura sereno | fulgura. Cf. Galb. 4, 2.

feriat: sc. Iuppiter; cf. Luc. ii 60 (an appeal to Jove), utrasque simul
partesque ducesque
feri: Sen. N.Q. ii 46, quare Iuppiter aut ferienda
transit aut innoxia ferit?

tactum de caelo: cf. Calig. 57, 2, futurae caedis (i.e. the murder of
Caligula) multa prodigia extiterunt Capitolium Capuae de caelo tactum
est, item Romae cella Palatini atriensis; Claud. 46 (among the praesagia
of the death of Claudius), tactum de caelo monumentum Drusi patris:
Galb. 1 (in Nero's last days), tacta de caelo Caesarum aede, capita
omnibus statuis simul deciderunt, Augustique sceptrum e manibus excussum
est. Other instances of this portent are found in Cic. Div. ii 21, 47;
Liv. xxv 7, xxix 14, etc. Seneca, N.Q. ii 49, gives different classifications
of fulmina with their significance as portents.

Capitolium:
=
templum Iovis Capitolini; both it and the templum
Flaviae gentis had been built by Domitian himself (see c. 5).

Palatina domus: Domitian's magnificent restoration of the Palatina
domus (see on Vesp. 25), completed in 92 A.D., was the work of the
architect Rabirius; cf. Mart. vii 56, 1, Astra polumque pia cepisti mente,
Rabiri, | Parrhasiam (= Palatinam) mira qui struis arte domum. The part
of the imperial palace on the Palatine which still exists above ground is
mainly due to this reconstruction under Domitian; see Platner-Ashby,
Topogr. Dict. Rome 158 sqq. Ancient writers give no account of the whole
building, but are lavish in their praises of its splendour; e.g. Mart. viii
36, 1, Regia pyramidum, Caesar, miracula ride; | iam tacet Eoum barbara
Memphis opus: | pars quota Parrhasiae labor est Mareoticus (= Aegyptius)
aulae? | Clarius in toto nil videt orbe dies: Stat. S. iv 2, 18, Tectum
augustum, ingens, non centum insigne columnis, | sed quantae superos
caelumque Atlante remisso | sustentare queant. Stupet hoc vicina
Tonantis | regia teque pari laetantur sede locatum | numina. Cf. also
Plut. Poplic. 15, Philostrat. vit. Apollon. vii 32.
basi: see on Vesp. 23, 3.

statuae triumphalis: probably the colossal equestrian statue (described
in Stat. S. i 1) which was decreed to Domitian by the senate and people
for his victories over the Chatti and Dacians (c. 6, 1).

titulus: this inscription was not carved on the marble base of the
statue, but must have been on a plate of bronze fastened to it. Among
the omens prophetic of the death of Augustus was the blotting out by a
thunderbolt of the letter C from the name Caesar in the inscription on
one of his statues, the haruspices declaring that this foretold that he
would live 100 (C = centum) days and would then become a god, as the
word aesar in Etruscan denoted a god (Aug. 97, 2).

arbor: the cypress-tree which earlier had fallen and risen erect again
as an omen of Vespasian's rise to power (Vesp. 5, 4).

Praenestina Fortuna: at Praeneste (Palestrina) 20 miles E. of Rome
there was a famous temple and oracle of Fortuna primigenia (an epithet
explained as meaning the mother of life or the firstborn daughter of
Jove). Cicero (Div. ii 41, 85) tells the tale of the foundation of the oracle.
A Praenestine, Numerius Suffucius, was bidden by a dream to cleave a
rock, and a great number of wooden lots (sortes), inscribed in antique
characters, fell out, while honey flowed from an olive-tree close by. The
haruspices ordained that the olive-tree should be made into a box, in which
the lots were enclosed, and one was drawn by a child when the oracle was
consulted. Cicero says that in his day only the vulgar had resort to it,
but under the Empire it came into favour again. Tiberius tried to do
away with all oracles near Rome, but desisted through fright at the divine
power of the Praenestine lots, for though he had them conveyed in a sealed
chest to Rome, they could not be found till the chest was taken back to
the temple of Fortuna (Tib. 63). The future greatness of Alexander
Severus was foretold by the Praenestine oracle with a sors bearing the
words of Virgil "si qua fata aspera rumpas, | tu Marcellus eris”
(Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 4). For other references to the oracle see Prop. ii
32, 3: Luc. ii 193: Juv. xiv 88: Sil. Ital. viii 365.

annum novum commendanti: on the Kalends of January Domitian
sent gifts to the goddess and made sacrifice at the temple at Praeneste.
In Rome on that day, in accordance with old Republican usage, there was
a solemn votorum nuncupatio pro incolumitate reipublicae on the Capitol,
and on Jan. 3 vows were offered pro incolumitate principis. As the goddess
Fortuna deserted Domitian, so she had deserted Galba when his doom was
approaching; see Galb. 18, 2.

§ 3. Minervam colebat: for the special honours paid by Domitian
to Minerva, whose son he claimed to be, see on c. 4, 4.

somniavit excedere sacrario: Dio (lxvii 16) gives a different version
of the dream: ἄλλα τε αὐτῷ σημεῖα ἐγένετο, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ ὕπνῳ τόν τε ῾Ρούστικον
(i.e. Junius Rusticus, whom he had put to death, see c. 10, 3) ξίφει προσιέναι
οἱ, καὶ τὴν ᾿Αθηνῶν, ἣν ἐν τῷ κοιτῶνι (cubiculo) ἱδρυμένην εἶχε, τὰ ὅπλα
ἀποβεβληκέναι, καὶ ἐπὶ ἅρματος ἵππων μελάνων ἐς χάσμα ἐσπίπτειν ἔδοξεν.
excedere was the word regularly used of the gods leaving a doomed place;
cf. Tac. H. v 13, Exapertae repente delubri (i.e. the Temple at Jerusalem)
fores, et audita maior humana vox, excedere deos; simul ingens motus
excedentium: Verg. A. ii 351, Excessere omnes, adytis arisque relictis, |
di, quibus imperium hoc steterat.

negantemque: if the reading is sound, Suetonius here combines two
of the constructions which he uses with somniare: the inf. (e.g. Aug. 91, 2,
somniavit queri Capitolinum Iovem) and the pres. ptc. (Galb. 4, 3, somniavit
Fortunam dicentem). He couples the inf. with the passive ptc. (esse
omitted) in Calig. 57, 3, somniavit consistere se in caelo iuxta solium Iovis
impulsumque ab eo dextri pedis pollice et in terras praecipitatum. Roth
and Preud'homme mark a lacuna before negantemque; Stephanus read
negantem; Oudendorp proposed, negantem quoque; P. Thomas would insert
lacrimantem before negantemque.
exarmata. a love: according to the old Greek legend Zeus himself
gave birth to Athena, who sprang fully armed from his head. In Homer
she appears as the protectress of heroes, and in Il. v 736 she is described
as arming herself with the shield (aegis), helmet, and spear of her father
Zeus.
..

perinde quam: this is the only place where Suetonius uses perinde
with quam instead of with ac, atque, ut, ac si, which he has elsewhere.
Tacitus often has perinde . quam, mainly in neg. sentences; see Heraeus
on H. i 30: Draeger, Synt. Tac. 175.

Ascletarionis: this is the reading of all the MSS., but the name is
not found elsewhere. Bentley conjectured Ascleparionis, a correction
suggested also by Kumanudis and approved by Boissevain (on Dio lxvii 16)
who says: "forma ᾿Ασκληταρίων nihili est nec usquam reperitur, ᾿Ασκληπαρίων
redit C.I.A. 3, 3521." Cumont (Catal. codd. astrol. Graec. v p. 205) would
read Asclationis, assuming that the astrologer mentioned by Suetonius is
Asclation, an astrologer cited by Vettius Valens (astrological writer
c. 140 A.D.).

mathematici: see on Vitell. 14, 4. The predictions by astrologers of
Domitian's death are mentioned in c. 14, 1.
delatum: see on Vitell. 14, 4.

hunc sciscitatus est: the acc. with sciscitari (instead of ex or ab)
is first found in Livy; cf. Vitell. 7, 3, Calig. 28.

interfici: Dio (lxvii 16) says that he was sentenced to be burnt
alive, and when this was being done a torrent of rain quenched the pyre:
ἕτερος τέ τις πρότερόν ποτε εἰπὼν αὐτῷ καὶ ὁπότε καὶ ὅπως φθαρήσεται, ἔπειτα
ἐρωτηθεὶς ὁποίῳ αὐτὸς τέλει τοῦ βίου χρήσεται, καὶ ἀποκρινάμενος ὅτι ὑπὸ κυνῶν
ἀναλωθήσεται, ἐκελεύσθη μὲν ζῶν κατακαυθῆναι, καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτῷ προσήχθη. ὑετοῦ
δὲ ἐν τούτῳ πολλοῦ καταρρυέντος ἥ τε πυρὰ ἐσβέσθη καὶ ἐκεῖνον κύνες ὀπίσω τὼ
χεῖρε δεδεμένον καὶ ἐπικείμενον ἐπ' αὐτῆς εὑρόντες διεσπάραξαν.
The burning
alive and the quenching of the pyre by rain are reminiscent of the story
of the deliverance of Croesus when Cyrus ordered him to be placed upon
the pyre (Hdt. i 86 sq.).
temeritatem: see on Tit. 5, 3.

sepeliri: though sepelire denoted more especially inhumation (cf. Cic.
Legg. ii 23, where it is opposed to urere), it was also used of performing
the funeral rites by burning; even humare could be used of burning not
of burying, e.g. Nep. Eumen. 13, Antigonus Eumenem mortuum propinquis
suis sepeliendum tradidit: hi militari honestoque funere . humaverunt,
ossaque eius in Cappadociam deportanda curaverunt.
..

deiecto funere: funus is used vaguely here to include the pyre and the
body placed upon it. Servius has three notes explaining the word: (1) on
Aen. iii 62, proprie “funus” est incensum cadaver; (2) on Aen. ii 539,
“funus” est iam ardens cadaver, quod dum portatur “exequias” dicimus,
crematum iam “reliquias,” conditum iam ‘‘sepulcrum”; (3) on Aen. iii 22,
apparatus mortuorum “funus” dici solet: exstructio lignorum “rogus”:
subiectio ignis “pyra”: crematio cadaveris ‘“bustum”: locus “ustrina”:
operis exstructio “sepulcrum”: nomen inscriptum ‘‘monumentum.”

a mimo Latino: Latinus, an archimimus, is named as a powerful delator
under Domitian by the Schol. on Juv. iv 53, on the authority of the historian
Marius Maximus. Juvenal mentions Latinus as a delator (i 36) and as an
actor (mimus) playing the part of an adulterer concealed in a trunk (vi 44).
Martial refers to his acting (i 4, 5: ii 72, 3: iii 86, 3: 61, 11: xiii 3, 2)
and has one whole epigram (ix 28) in which he combines the praises of
Latinus with those of Domitian his "master" and his "god": Dulce
decus scaenae, ludorum fama, Latinus | ille ego sum plausus deliciaeque
tuae, | qui spectatorem potui fecisse Catonem, | solvere qui Curios Fabriciosque graves. | Sed nihil a nostro sumpsit mea vita theatro, | et sola tantum
scaenicus arte feror: | nec poteram gratus domino sine moribus esse; |
interius mentes inspicit ille deus. | Vos me laurigeri parasitum dicite
Phoebi, Roma sui famulum dum sciat esse Iovis (i.e. Domitian). On the
favour enjoyed by actors, especially mimi or pantomimi, in the imperial
household see Friedl. Sitteng. ii¹º 143 sqq. This is the only passage in
which Suetonius uses mimus for the actor (histrio), elsewhere it denotes
the play or farce (see on Oth. 3, 2); archimimus for a principal actor
occurs in Vesp. 19, 2.

fabulas: "gossip"; cf. Aug. 70, 1, cena eius secretior ("private")
in fabulis fuit ("was a subject of gossip'): Juv. i 145, it nova nec tristis
per cunctas fabula cenas: Plin. Ep. viii 18, habes omnes fabulas urbis.
pridie quam periret: for this constr. see on c. 11, 1.

tubures: Pliny describes these as African apples, more like berries
than apples, of two kinds, one white, the other a deep red. They were
introduced into Italy about 36 A.D., and Martial mentions them as grown
in Italy. Cf. Plin. N.H. xv 47, (māla) peregrina sunt zizypha ("jujubes')
et tubures, quae et ipsa non pridem venere in Italiam, haec ex Africa, illa
ex Syria. Sex. Papinius, quem consulem vidimus, primus utraque attulit,
divi Augusti novissimis temporibus, in castris sata, bacis similiora quam
malis, sed aggeribus praecipua decora, quoniam et in tecta iam silvae
scandunt. Tuberum duo genera: candidum et a colore Syricum dictum:
Mart. xiii 42, Non tibi de Libycis tubures et apyrina (i.e. pomegranates
with soft kernels) ramis, | de Nomentanis sed damus arboribus: xiii 43,
Lecta suburbanis mittuntur apyrina ramis | et vernae ("home-grown'')
tubures. Quid tibi cum Libycis? Harduin explains tubures as nucipersica
"nut-peaches"; Stahr translates it in our passage by "Trüffeln (truffles),
but that would be tubera. The form tubures (not tuberes) is the better
attested in Suetonius, Pliny, and Martial.

luna se in Aquario cruentaret: Domitian was assassinated on Sept. 18,
96 A.D. In that year the moon would enter Aquarius on Sept. 15/16 and leave
it on Sept. 18/19. A red moon usually betokened wind; cf. Arat. Phaen.
784; Verg. Georg. i 431, vento semper rubet aurea Phoebe; Luc. v 549,
ventorumque nota rubuit (luna). Domitian predicted that by reason of his
murder the moon on the morrow would be red with blood. The adjs.
cruentus and sanguineus were used of the heavenly bodies in the sense of
"blood-red," e.g. Sen. N.Q. vii 17, 3, cruenti cometae omen post se futuri
sanguinis ferunt: Verg. Aen. x 273, cometae | sanguinei lugubre rubent:
Ov. Am. ii 1, 23, sanguineae cornua lunae. The ominous significance of the
moon being in Aquarius is perhaps to be deduced from Macrob. Comm. in
Somn. Scip. i 12, Et quia in Leone sunt rudimenta nascendi et quaedam
humanae naturae tirocinia, Aquarius autem adversus Leoni est et illo
oriente mox occidit: ideo, cum sol Aquarium tenet, Manibus parentatur,
utpote in signo quod humanae vitae contrarium vel adversum feratur.
Janssen cites an explanation given by Prof. Van Wageningen: Luna in
Aquario tum erat, cuius tertius decanus est Lunae, cf. Firm. Mat., Math. ii
3: “Aquarii primus decanus Veneris est, secundus Mercurii, tertius
Lunae.'" Decanus autem dicitur in lingua astrologorum qui decem ex
triginta partibus orbis signiferi praeerat. Eadem autem pars Aquarii
arbitrio paret Martis et Saturni stellarum vagarum, cf. Firm. ii 5, 12, qui
dicit etiam “Aquarii dominus est Saturnus.” Hic cum esset omnium
errantium pessimus, iure suspicabatur Domitianus dirum quoddam
exstiturum. Domitian's prediction resembles that of the prophet Joel
(2, 31): “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood,
before the great and terrible day of the Lord be come."
at: see on Vesp. 5, 5.

haruspicem: Dio (lxvii 16) gives the name of the soothsayer as
Larginus Proclus, and says that the death-penalty was postponed in order
that it might be inflicted when Domitian had survived the danger; after
Domitian had been slain, the soothsayer was set free and rewarded by
Nerva with 400,000 sesterces: ὁ δὲ δὴ μάλιστα διὰ πάντων ἄξιον θαυμάσαι ἐστί,
Λαργῖνός τις Πρόκλος, δημοσίᾳ προειπὼν ἐν Γερμανίᾳ ὅτι τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, ἐν ᾗ
ἀπέθανε, τελευτήσει, ἀνεπέμφθη τε ἐς τὴν ῾Ρώμην ὑπὸ τοῦ ἄρχοντος, καὶ ἐσαχθεὶς
πρὸς τὸν Δομιτιανὸν ἔφη καὶ τότε τοῦθ' οὕτως ἕξειν, καὶ καταδικασθεὶς τὴν ἐπὶ

For other predictions of the time of Domitian's death see c. 14, 1.

a change of government; cf. Galb. 8, 2, пес

§ 2. verrucam: “wart'” (ἀκροχορδών), a word familiar from the proverbial expression in Hor. S. i 3, 74, Qui ne tuberibus propriis offendat
amicum | postulat, ignoscet verrucis illius. Serenus Sammonicus (Poet.
Lat. Min. Baehrens iii 158) describes the nature and treatment of verrucae
(Interdum existit turpi verruca papilla, etc.), and the means of stopping
the flow of blood if they burst (Si rupta inmensos fundet verruca cruores,
etc.).

utinam hactenus:
utinam nihil amplius (et gravius) accidat; cf.
Sil. Ital. ix 347, sitque hactenus, oro. The various uses of hactenus are

followed by ut (e.g. Vesp. 13, where see note); he also uses it in Calig. 22, 1,
Hactenus quasi de principe, reliqua ut de monstro narranda sunt ("Thus
far forth as of a prince; now forward relate we must as of a monster"
Holland), and in vit. Ter. 5, 2, Cicero in Limone hactenus ("to this
extent'") laudat (Terentium).

requirenti horas: for the plural cf. Cic. Brut. 54, 200, videt oscitantem
iudicem, loquentem cum altero, nonnumquam etiam circulantem, mittentem
ad horas; Plin. N.H. vii 182 (quoted below): the sing. is used in Hor. S. ii
6, 44, hora quota est?

pro quinta quam metuebat: not merely the day but the very hour
of his death had been predicted to him by the astrologers; see c. 14, 1.

sexta nuntiata est: from the middle of the 2nd cent. B.C. sundials (solaria) and water-clocks (clepsydrae) were in use at Rome, every
wealthy house having special slaves to announce the hours, from whom
the master asked the time; cf. Plin. N.H. vii 182, obiit Cn. Bebius
Tamphilus cum a puero quaesisset horas: Mart. viii 68, 1, horas quinque
puer nondum tibi nuntiat, et tu | iam conviva mihi, Caeciliane, venis:
Juv. x 215, clamore opus est ut sentiat auris, | quem dicat venisse puer,
quot nuntiet horas: Plin. Ep. iii 1, ubi hora balinei nuntiata est: Sen. de
brev. vit. 12, 6, quos quando lavari debeant, quando natare, quando cenare,
alius admonet: Sidon. Ep. ii 9, nuntium per spatia clepsydrae horarum
incrementa servantem. Marquardt, Privatl.2 256 sqq., 788 sqq.

corporis curam: the refreshing of the body by the siesta (meridiatio),
which came at the sixth hour, i.e. noon; cf. Martial (iv 8) on the division
of the hours of the day between social duties, business, and recreation:
Prima salutantes atque altera continet hora, | exercet raucos
causidicos; | in quintam varios extendit Roma labores, | sexta quies lassis,
septima finis erit; etc. Stahr translates our passage, “er eben im Begriff
war sich eilig zum Bade zu begeben," and so Rolfe, he was hastening
to the bath," but the meaning is fixed by Dio lxvii 17, ἀναπαύσεσθαι τὸ
μεθημερινόν, ὥσπερ εἰώθει, ἔμελλε.

Parthenius: freedman and chamberlain of Domitian, who gave him
the high privilege of wearing the sword or dagger (pugio, see on Galb. 11)
which was usually granted only to military officers such as the praefectus
praetorio; cf. Dio lxvii 15, ἐπέθεντο δὲ αὐτῷ (i.e. Domitian) καὶ συνεσκευάσαντο τὴν πρᾶξιν Παρθένιός τε ὁ πρόκοιτος (cubicularius) αὐτοῦ, καίπερ οὕτω
τιμώμενος παρ' αὐτοῦ ὡς καὶ ξιφηφορεῖν, κ.τ.λ. The murder of Domitian secured
the throne for Nerva, but the new emperor was unable to protect Parthenius
and his fellow-conspirators when their punishment was demanded by the
praetorians in 97 A.D., and Parthenius was first mutilated and then slain;
[Aur. Vict.] Epit. 12, 8, demptis prius genitalibus et in os coniectis,
iugulavere. He was a patron of Martial and presented him with a toga
(Mart. viii 28, ix 49); Martial asks him to introduce his books to the
emperor's notice (v 6, xi 1, xii 11), and speaks in extravagant terms of
the poetic talents of Parthenius himself: xii 11, Parthenio dic, Musa, tuo
nostroque salutem: | nam quis ab Aonio largius amne bibit? | Cuius
Pimpleo lyra clarior exit ab antro? | Quem plus Pierio de grege Phoebus
amat? He may be the Parthenius "Aug. libertus a cubiculo” mentioned
in C.I.L. vi 8764 (= Dessau 1736).

cubiculo praepositus: even under the Republic the cubicularii, or
grooms of the bedchamber, filled positions of confidence and exercised.
'great influence; Cicero (Att. vi 2, 5) boasts that he as governor of Cilicia
was not approachable for any purpose through his cubicularii. In the
imperial household the cubicularii were a numerous body of slaves or freedmen with a special commissariat and medical service (see Marquardt,
Privatl.2 144). They were divided into a prima statio and a secunda statio,
but it is doubtful whether these relieved each other on duty, or were distinguished by different degrees of access to the emperor's person as Friedlaender suggests. These two classes were subdivided into decuries (see
Dom. 17, 2), and at their head was a supra cubicularios or praepositus
cubiculo (πρόκοιτος, ὁ ἐπὶ τοῦ κοιτῶνος), always in close attendance on the
emperor and having his ear more than any other man. One of the duties
of a chamberlain was to supervise the introduction of visitors; so Parthenius
announced to Domitian the arrival of Stephanus.
convertit: = ab corporis cura avertit et alii rei intendit (Baumg.-Cr.).

esse qui magnum afferret: i.e. Stephanus, who pretended that he
had a conspiracy to reveal; see c. 17, 1. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25)
says that Stephanus in person accosted Domitian as he was returning from
the law-court and asked him for a private audience, as he had something
important to say; Domitian then took him aside privately into the men's
apartment (ἀνδρών) of the palace, where Stephanus stabbed him.
(lxvii 17) simply says that when Domitian left the court for his midday
rest Parthenius removed the blade of the dagger which was always under
the emperor's pillow, and then introduced Stephanus.

quando et quo modo, id est, lavantemne an cenantem: Burman and
Baumg.-Cr. would delete id est, while Ernesti would change id est to item,
on the ground that lavantemne an cenantem would correspond rather with
quando et quo loco. If change is necessary, quando ex commodo “when
most conveniently'' might be suggested. According to the MSS. Suetonius
several times uses id est or hoc est in giving an explanation or limiting
more definitely a general expression; e.g. Iul. 19, 2, provinciae
negoti, id est, silvae callesque: Aug. 26, 2 magno, id est, septemdecim
annorum intervallo: Aug. 88, orthographiam, id est, formulam rationemque
scribendi a grammaticis institutam: Vesp. 11, neve filiorum familiarum
faeneratoribus exigendi crediti ius umquam esset: hoc est, ne post patrum
quidem mortem. In all such passages editors are naturally inclined to
regard the words introduced by id est or hoc est as mere glosses. But it
must be remembered that Suetonius was a grammaticus, to whom exposition
would become a second nature.

text:
Stephanus: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25) says that this freedman
of Domitilla, who had been signified by the portent of a στέφανος (corona)
surrounding and dimming the orb of the sun, brooded on the murder of
Flavius Clemens, or on the wrongs of the Romans generally, and attacked
Domitian in a spirit worthy of the Athenian champions of liberty (such as
Harmodius and Aristogeiton). The fact which Suetonius mentions, that
Stephanus was to be tried for embezzlement, probably influenced him
much more than any general considerations. Dio (lxvii 18) has a remarkable story that Apollonius of Tyana on the very day and at the very
hour when Domitian was murdered assembled the multitude at Ephesus or
elsewhere and exclaimed “καλῶς, Στέφανε, εὖγε, Στέφανε, παῖε τὸν μιαιφόνον.
ἔπληξας, ἔτρωσας, ἀπέκτειναs." Dio avers that this was so, however in-
credible it may seem (κἂν μυριάκις τις ἀπιστήσῃ). Stephanus himself was
slain by those who rushed in to the aid of Domitian and were not privy
to the plot (Dio c. 17).

Domitillae: Flavia Domitilla, a granddaughter of Vespasian (C.I.L.
vi 948, 8942) and niece of Domitian; her mother Flavia Domitilla, sister
of Domitian, died before the accession of Vespasian (see Vesp. 3), and so
in Philostrat. vit. Apollon. viii 25, where the Domitilla of our passage is
spoken of as a sister of Domitian, ἀδελφιδῆν ‘“niece" must be restored
for ἀδελφήν. Domitilla was wedded to Flavius Clemens, who was put to
death by Domitian, and she herself was banished as a Christian (see c. 15,
1, and note). According to Philostratus she was ordered by Domitian
within a few days after her husband's execution “ ἐς ἀνδρὸς φοιτᾶν” (“to
join her husband in death"; Gsell explains "to wed again"). For her
history and a discussion of the improbable theory that one Flavia Domitilla,
wife of Clemens, was banished for political reasons to Pandateria, and
that another Flavia Domitilla, niece of Clemens (Euseb. Hist. Eccl. iii 18),
was banished as a Christian to Pontia see Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi '2733;
Gsell, op. cit. 298 sqq.; Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 81.

interceptarum: “embezzled," in which sense intervertere (e.g. Vitell.
7, 2) is much more common. Suetonius also uses intercipere of literary
plagiarism; Gramm. 5, commentarios, quorum tamen pars maxima intercepta dicitur. In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 11 we are told (if the reading is
correct) that it was Clodianus (mentioned below by Suet. as a cornicularius)
who was charged with embezzlement: Coniuravere plerique, impulsoribus
Parthenio procurante cubiculum, et Stephano, et tum ob fraudem interceptae pecuniae supplicium suspectante Clodiano (probably et should be
removed before tum and inserted before Clodiano).

sinisteriore: for the comparative cf. Tib. 6, 4, where sinisterior funalis
equus means the trace-horse on the left side as opp. to the dexterior,
the trace-horse on the right; SO in Claud. 7, dexteriore umero:
Galb. 21, in dexteriore latere eius. Suetonius more frequently uses the
positives dexter and sinister. Earlier instances of dexterior and sinisterior
are found in Varr. L.L. ix 34, Galba in Cic. Fam. x 30, 3, Ον. M. ii 138,
vii 241, xii 303, Cels. iv 1, and other passages collected by Neue-Wagener,
Formenlehre ii³ 187.

lanis fasciisque: the bandages may have been rolled round the wool
to keep it in its place, or lanis fasciisque may be a hendiadys for laneis
fasciis "woollen bandages." For fascia "bandage" cf. Galb. 21: Cic.
Brut. 60, 217, devinctus fasciis et multis medicamentis propter dolorem
artuum delibutus. See also on galbeo in Galb. 3, 1.

dolonem: a certain restoration by Ferrarius for dolum or dolo of the
MSS. A dolo was a sword-cane with a blade in it that might be used as
a stiletto (Hesych., δόλωνες· ξιφίδια ἐν ξύλοις ἀποκεκρυμμένα); cf. Claud. 13, 1
(of assassins lying in wait for Claudius), reperti et equestris ordinis duo in
publico cum dolone ac venatorio cultro praestolantes. As a weapon of war
dolo meant a pole with a short iron point, e.g. Aen. vii 664, pila manu
saevosque gerunt in bella dolones, where Servius comments, "dolo est aut
flagellum intra cuius virgam latet pugio; aut, secundum Varronem, ingens
contus cum ferro brevissimo.”
professus conspirationis indicium: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25)
says that what Stephanus revealed to Domitian was that Flavius Clemens
(see c. 15, 1) was not dead as the emperor thought, but was still alive in
a place known to Stephanus, and was planning to attack Domitian.

libellum: for libellus used of a written information lodged by an informer (delator) cf. Plin. Ep. vii 27, nihil notabile secutum, nisi forte,
quod non fui reus: futurus, si Domitianus, sub quo haec acciderunt, diutius
vixisset. Nam in scrinio eius datus a Caro de me libellus inventus est.

attonito suffodit inguina: cf. Philostr., l.c., μέγα δ' αὐτοῦ βοήσαντος περὶ
ὧν ἤκουσε, τεταραγμένῳ προσπεσὼν ὁ Στέφανος καὶ τὸ ξίφος τῆς ἐσκευασμένης
χειρὸς ἀνασπάσας διῆκε τοῦ μηροῦ πρὸς μὲν τὸν αὐτίκα θάνατον οὐ καιρίαν, πρὸς δὲ
τὸν μετὰ ταῦτα οὐκ ἄκαιρον (i.e. the wound was fatal, though not immediately
so): Suidas, δ.υ. Δομετιανόs, says that Domitian was stabbed during his
siesta: Στέφανον
προσπεσόντα Δομετιανῷ καθεύδοντι τὸ μεθημερινὸν πατάξαι
μέν, οὐ μὴν καιρίαν, ἀναπηδήσαντος γοῦν ἐκείνου.
§ 2. Clodianus: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 11 (quoted above on interceptarum); he is not mentioned elsewhere.

cornicularius: a title derived from corniculum, a decoration consisting
of one or two small horns fastened to the side of the helmet, conferred on
soldiers for distinguished service; e.g. Liv. x 44, equites omnes ob insignem
multis locis operam corniculis armillisque argenteis donavit.
Suetonius
(Gramm. 9) tells us that the famous "plagosus" Orbilius gained this distinction when serving in Macedonia. From such distinguished soldiers were
chosen the adjutants attached to the principal officers, and cornicularius
is regularly used for an adjutant. Under the Republic one was attached
to the tribunus militum whose turn it was to command (cf. Val. Max. vi 1,
11), and in inscriptions under the Empire we frequently find references to
the cornicularius of the legates legionis, the tribunus militum, the praefectus praetorio, etc. Civil officials, e.g. the praefectus annonae, when
their departments came to be organised in military form, had their cornicularii; see Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 546. In the Thes. Ling. Lat. our
passage is cited as an instance of cornicularius used de officio civili, but
Clodianus in all probability was attached to one of the praefecti praetorio,
Norbanus and Petronius Secundus, who took part in the conspiracy; see
on c. 14, 1.

Maximus: cf. Dio lxvii 17 (when Domitian was struggling with
Stephanus and had thrown him to the ground), Παρθένιος, δείσας μὴ διαφύγῃ
(ὁ Δομιτιανός), ἐπεισεπήδησεν, ἤ, ὥς γέ τισι δοκεῖ, Μάξιμον ἐξελεύθερον (libertum)
ἐπεισέπεμψε.

Satur: the person denoted by this name (or the variant "Saturius"
read by Roth and Preud'homme) is elsewhere called Sigerus or Sigerius.
Dio mentions Sigerus, a chamberlain (πρόκοιτος), as a prominent conspirator
along with Parthenius (see c. 16, 2), and the two are coupled in Tertull.
Apol. 35, unde qui armati palatium inrumpunt, omnibus tot Sigeriis atque
Partheniis audaciores?; cf. also Mart. iv 78, 8 (addressing a fussy old
fool who is always visiting the Palace and talks of nothing but the
chamberlains): Sigeriosque meros Partheniosque sonas, where Friedlaender
and others prefer the correction Sigerosque, both forms of the name
occurring in inscriptions, “Sigerus" much more frequently.
decurio cubiculariorum: see on c. 16, 2, cubiculo praepositus.

quidam e gladiatorio ludo: this participant in the murder is not
mentioned elsewhere. For the emperor's ludus gladiatorius see on c. 4, 1.

arae: this is Ernesti's correction of curae, and is approved by
*Oudendorp and adopted in their texts by Wolf, Baumg.-Cr., Roth,
Preud 'homme, and Janssen. Burman conjectured cui cura, but this involves
the insertion of et before hoc amplius. C. G. Müller proposed cura, in the
sense of curator. The reading of the MSS., curae assistens, is retained
by Ihm; though it lacks any parallel in Suetonius, it may possibly be
defended by Minuc. Fel. Oct. 26, angelos, id est ministros et nuntios dei
venerationi eius novit adsistere.

Larum cubiculi: there was a shrine for the worship of the Lares
either in or attached to the imperial bedchamber; cf. Aug. 7, 1, where we
read of a bronze statuette of the young Augustus presented by Suetonius
himself to the emperor Hadrian (whose secretary he was) and worshipped
by Hadrian among his Lares: puerilem imagunculam Augusti aeream
quae dono a me principi data inter cubiculi Lares colitur. As loyal citizens
associated the Genius of Augustus with the Lares (cf. Hor. C. iv 5, 31),
and included likenesses of the reigning emperor among the "gods of their
family," so we find the emperors themselves introducing among these gods
the images of those whom they specially revered: cf. Capitol. M. Anton.
Philos. 3, tantum honoris magistris suis (i.e. his teachers of philosophy)
detulit, ut imagines eorum aureas in larario haberet: Lamprid. Alex. Sev.
29, matutinis horis in larario suo in quo et divos principes, sed optimos
electos, et animas sanctiores, in quis Apollonium et Christum, Abraham,
et Orpheum et huiuscemodi ceteros habebat, ac maiorum effigies
divinam faciebat: c. 31, Vergilium autem Platonem poetarum vocabat eiusque imaginem cum Ciceronis simulacro in secundo larario habuit ubi et
Achillis et magnorum virorum. Alexandrum vero Magnum inter optimos
et divos in larario maiore consecravit. The word lararium for a shrine of
the Lares is first used by these Scriptores Historiae Augustae; aedicula is
used earlier, e.g. Petron. Satyr. 29, Juv. viii 111. See also Vitell. 2, 5.

oculos effodere: a very common phrase in Plautus, used also in Cic.,

§ 3. xiv Kal. Octb.: i.e. Sept. 18 (96 A.D.).

anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto: his age at death was 44 years,
10 months, 26 days, as Dio (lxvii 18) states precisely: Δομιτιανὸς δὲ ἔζησε
ἔτη τέσσαρα καὶ τεσσαράκοντα καὶ μῆνας δέκα καὶ ἡμέρας ἓξ καὶ εἴκοσιν. He was
born on Oct. 24, 51 A.D. (see c. 1, 1).

imperii quinto decimo: an inaccurate statement, as strictly speaking
he was in the 16th year of his reign; his dies imperii was Sept. 14, 81 A.D.
(the day after the death of Titus, see Tit. 11) when the senate gave to him
the imperium, the title of "Augustus," and the tribunicia potestas, and
so he had reigned 15 years and 5 days, as Dio correctly calculates:
ἐμονάρχησε δὲ ἔτη πεντεκαίδεκα καὶ ἡμέρας πέντε. Eutropius (vii 23, 6) repeats
the incorrect statement of Suetonius, but Aurelius Victor (Caes. 11, 7)
says: poenas luit quinto et quadragesimo vitae anno, dominationis circiter
quinto decimo.

sandapila: the rude bier on which the bodies of the poor were borne
to burial (the rich being borne on a lectus or lectica funebris); cf. Juv. viii
175, Mart. ii 81, viii 75, 14, ix 2, 12 (in Mart. x 5, 9 it is called Orciniana
sponda). The sandapila was provided with a cheap wooden coffin (capulus)
or shell in which the body was placed; this was spoken of contemptuously
as a "box" (arca), cf. Hor. S. i 8, 8, Luc. viii 736; the arca was not
burned with the body, nor buried with it in cases of interment, but was
used again and again (cf. Val. Max. ii 6, 7). The Schol. on Juv. l.c.
mentions that sandapilae were used for removing slain gladiators from
the amphitheatre; so Aur. Vict. (Caes. 11, 8) says of Domitian: Senatus
gladiatoris more funus ferri (al. efferri), radendumque nomen decrevit.

vispillones: Eutrop. vii 23, 6, funus eius ingenti dedecore per vespillones
exportatum, et ignobiliter est sepultum: Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 163
Schoene, Domitianus occisus in palatio et per vespillones ignobiliter exportatus anno aetatis xxxxv. The vispillones were hireling corpse-bearers who
carried the sandapila (Mart. i 30, 1: 47, 1: ii 61, 3); they were generally
four in number (Mart. viii 75, 9) and were also known as sandapilarii
(Sidon. Apoll. Ep. ii 8). Festus (p. 369 M.) says: vespae et vespillones
dicuntur, qui funerandis corporibus officium gerunt, non a minutis illis
volucribus (wasps, vespae), sed quia vespertino tempore eos efferunt, qui
funebri pompa duci propter inopiam nequeunt. Hi etiam vespullae vocantur.
The form vispillo (not ves-) is supported by the MSS. of Martial and
Suetonius.

exportatum: efferre (ἐξάγειν, ἐκκομίζειν) was the regular word for carrying
out to burial; for exportare cf. Verg. G. iv 255 (of bees), tum corpora
luce carentum | exportant tectis et tristia funera ducunt.

Phyllis: Dio lxvii 18, αὐτοῦ τὸ σῶμα Φυλλὶς ἡ τροφὸς κλέψασα ἔθαψεν.
She is not mentioned elsewhere.

Latina via: this road issued from the Porta Capena along with the
Via Appia, and diverging to the left from it, ran more inland, passing
through the Alban hills and touching Ferentinum, Aquinum, and Casinum,
ending at Casilinum in Campania, where it rejoined the Via Appia. Juvenal
refers to the tombs which lined it and the other great roads leading out
of Rome: i 170, experiar quid concedatur in illos, | quorum Flaminia
tegitur cinis atque Latina; v 55, clivosae veheris dum per monumenta
Latinae.

reliquias intulit: a like regard for the ashes of Nero was shown
by his two nurses: Ner. 50, reliquias Egloge et Alexandria nutrices cum
Acte concubina gentili Domitiorum monumento condiderunt.
templo Flaviae gentis: see c. 1, 1 (also c. 5 and c. 15, 2).

Iuliae: daughter of Titus by his second wife Marcia Furnilla (Tit. 4,
2). Domitian's illicit passion for Julia, which led to her death, is described
in c. 22.
statura fuit procera: see on Galb. 21.

vultu modesto: cf. Tac. H. iv 40, Quo die senatum ingressus est
Domitianus, de absentia patris fratrisque ac iuventa sua (he was aged 18)
pauca et modica disseruit, decorus habitu (“graceful in mien'"); et ignotis
adhuc moribus creba oris confusio pro modestia accipiebatur.

ruborisque pleno: Tacitus (Agr. 45) says that Domitian used this
natural flush as a screen against shame, in that it prevented him showing
the blush of shame: saevus ille vultus et rubor quo se contra pudorem
muniebat; so Pliny, Pan. 48, inveighs against Domitian's “superbia in
fronte, ira in oculis, femineus pallor in corpore, in ore impudentia multo
rubore suffusa.” Blushing was regarded as a sign of gentle breeding;
cf. Plin. Ep. i 14, Est illi (i.e. Acilianus) facies liberalis multo sanguine
multo rubore suffusa, "His countenance is that of a gentleman, the blood
coming readily to his cheeks, which are not seldom suffused with a blush"
20
(Lewis). Seneca, Ep. 11, discourses on blushing and in particular on the
blush of modesty (verecundia) which he describes as “bonum in adulescente
signum''; some men are most dangerous when they redden: quidam (e.g.
Sulla) numquam magis quam cum erubuerint, timendi sunt, quasi omnem
verecundiam effuderint; Pompey was remarkable for extreme mollitia oris;
he blushed in the presence of any gathering. Cf. also Juv. x 300, vultumque modesto | sanguine ferventem.

acie hebetiore: cf. Ner. 51, oculis
hebetioribus. hebes (opp. to
acutus, acer) was used of dim sight; cf. ἀμβλύς, ἀμβλὺ ὁρᾶν, ἀμβλυωπός.
For Suetonius' descriptions of the eyes of the Caesars see on Galb. 21.

decens: the use of decens in the sense of "comely" is poetical (Hor.,
Ov., etc.), and very rare in prose (Plin. Ep. i 21, 2: Quintil. viii 3, 10).

digitos: "toes"; cf. Iul. 61, equo insigni pedibus prope humanis et
in modum digitorum ungulis fissis.

restrictiores: this may mean that the toes were too short or too
bent inward. Pitiscus assumes that Domitian had the claw-like curvature
of the big-toes which disfigured those known as “falcones”; cf. Fest.
p. 88 M., falcones dicuntur, quorum digiti pollices in pedibus intro sunt
curvati, a similitudine falcis.

calvitio deformis: cf. Iul. 45, 2, calvitii deformitas: Apul. Apol. 74,
in pueritia priusquam isto calvitio deformaretur: Petron. Satyr. 108,
deformis praeter spoliati capitis dedecus superciliorum etiam aequalis cum
fronte calvities. Juvenal (iv 37) describes Domitian as the "bald Nero"
in the lines which, according to the Schol. there (differing from the Schol.
on i 1, vii 92, see note on “Paridis” Dom. 3, 1), led to the poet's banishment to Egypt: Cum iam semianimum laceraret Flavius orbem | ultimus
et calvo serviret Roma Neroni; cf. Auson. 257, 12, quem calvum dixit sua
Roma Neronem.

obesitate ventris: cf. Vitell. 17, 2; Ner. 51. Titus also was inclined
to corpulence (Tit. 3, 1).

crurum gracilitate: Nero and Caligula also were spindle-legged: Ner.
51, gracillimis cruribus; Calig. 50, 1, gracilitate maxima cervicis et crurum.
Germanicus, father of Caligula, in his early years had the same defect but
remedied it: Calig. 3, 1, formae minus congruebat gracilitas crurum, sed
ea quoque paulatim repleta assidua equi vectatione post cibum.

remacruerant: the compound remacrescere does not occur elsewhere,
and the prefix re- can only be explained as having an intensive force "to
grow very lean or thin." For a list of similar compounds (e.g. refervescere,
refercire, resciscere) in which re- must be so explained or else regarded as
pleonastic see Roby, Lat. Gramm. § 2103. Bentley and Duker conjectured
emacruerant, Iernstedt longiore macruerant. Marcilius suggested that
gracilitate should be omitted, taking obesitate with crurum as well as with
ventris, and giving to re- the sense of "again." Oudendorp, though preferring emacruerant, explains the reading of the MSS. as meaning “crura
natura quidem gracilia, nihilominus macriora erant facta longa valetudine.”
Bremi takes remacruerant as macruerant.

§2. calvitio ita offendebatur: the sensitiveness of Julius Caesar on the
same subject is well known; Iul. 45, 2, Circa corporis curam morosior, ut
calvitii deformitatem iniquissime ferret, saepe obtrectatorum iocis
obnoxiam expertus. Ideoque et deficientem capillum revocare (“to draw
•
forward'') a vertice adsueverat et ex omnibus decretis sibi a senatu populoque honoribus non aliud aut recepit aut usurpavit libentius quam ius laureae
coronae perpetuo gestandae. Otho had recourse to wearing a wig (Oth.
12, 1.)

in contumeliam suam traheret: the usual phrase is in (ad) contumeliam accipere aliquid; in Aug. 68, populus accepit in contumeliam
eius versum, the meaning is that the people took the verse as a reflection
on Augustus. For trahere in the sense of interpreting cf. Tac. H. ii 20,
ornatum ipsius (ducis) in superbiam trahebant: A. iii 22, quod quidam
ad saevitiam trahebant. Friedlaender notices that Martial's repeated jests
1 baldness (e.g. in v 49, a book dedicated to Domitian) are very strange
in the light of what Suetonius says here.

libello de cura capillorum: nothing more is known of this treatise
by Domitian.
Οὐχ ὁράᾳς, κ.τ.λ.: Hom. Il. xxi 108, part of the reply of Achilles
refusing quarter to Priam's suppliant son Lycaon. The preceding line is
the famous κάτθανε καὶ Πάτροκλος, ὅπερ σέο πολλὸν ἀμείνων, and the succeeding
lines are πατρὸς δ᾽ εἴμ᾽ ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μητηρ· | ἀλλ᾽ ἔπι τοι καὶ ἐμοὶ
θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.

capillorum fata: cf. the little dirge on Hair (capillorum elegidarion)
recited by Eumolpus in Petron. Satyr. 109: Quod solum formae decus est,
cecidere capilli, | vernantesque comas tristis abegit hiemps. | Nunc umbra
nudata sua iam tempora ("the temples'') maerent, | areaque (i.e. the bald
expanse of the head) attritis ridet adulta (so Bücheler for adusta) pilis. |
O fallax natura deûm: quae prima dedisti | aetati nostrae gaudia prima
rapis. Eumolpus adds an epigram in hendecasyllables on the same
theme: -Infelix, modo crinibus nitebas | Phoebo pulchrior et sorore Phoebi
(i.e. the Sun and Moon). | At nunc levior aere vel rotundo | horti tubere
('mushroom'"), quod creavit unda, | ridentes fugis et times puellas. | Ut
mortem citius venire credas, | scito iam capitis perisse partem.

nec gratius quicquam decore nec brevius: for this commonplace cf.
Sall. Cat. 1, 4, formae gloria fluxa atque fragilis est: Ov. A.A. ii 113,
forma bonum fragile est: Sen. Phaedr. 773, res est forma fugax: Nemes.
Ecl. 4, 24, donum forma breve est.
lemma: nec gratius quicquam decore nec brevius

laboris impatiens: cf. Dio lxvii 6, τό τε σῶμα ἄπονος, καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἄτολμος
ἦν. Pliny (Pan. 14) calls Domitian “iners.” Contrast the activity
of Julius Caesar, Iul. 57, laboris ultra fidem patiens erat.

pedibus non temere ambulavit: for non temere see on Tit. 6, 2.
Pliny (Pan. 24) praises Trajan for differing in this respect from his predecessors (especially Domitian): Incedebas pedibus, incedis: laetabaris
labore, laetaris;
nihil in ipso te fortuna mutavit. Liberum est ingrediente per publicum principe subsistere, occurrere, comitari, praeterire:
ambulas inter nos, non quasi < non > contingas, et copiam tui, non ut
imputes, facis... Ante te principes fastidio nostri et quodam aequalitatis
metu usum pedum amiserant. Illos ergo umeri cervicesque servorum super
ora nostra (vehebant), etc. For the practice of Augustus cf. Aug. 53, 2,

In consulatu pedibus fere, extra consulatum saepe adaperta sella per
publicum incessit. Ammianus (xxii 7) says of the emperor Julian:
Humilior princeps. visus est in officio pedibus gradiendo cum honoratis:
quod laudabant alii, quidam ut affectatum et vile carpebant.

in expeditione equo rarius: Trajan on his campaigns led his legions
on foot; cf. Plin. Pan. 14, Cum legiones duceres seu potius (tanta velocitas
erat) raperes, non vehiculum umquam, non equum respexisti. Julius Caesar
generally marched with his soldiers; cf. Iul. 57, in agmine nonnumquam
equo, saepius pedibus anteibat. Tacitus (H. ii 11) says of Otho: Nec illi
segne aut corruptum luxu iter; sed lorica ferrea usus est et ante signa
pedes ire.

lectica vectus est: the lectica was carried on poles (asseres) by six
or eight lecticarii (Oth. 6, 3, n.: Mart. vi 77, 4: ix 2, 11); the emperor's
lecticarii, who formed part of the familia Augusta, are often mentioned in
inscriptions (C.I.L. vi 8872-8875, etc.).
..

armorum nullo studio tenebatur: arma here are the campestria arma
(Hor. A.P. 379), the weapons used in the soldierly exercises in the Campus
Martius, which are referred to e.g. in Aug. 83, Exercitationes campestres
equorum et armorum statim post civilia bella omisit: Hor. Ep. i 18, 52,
Adde virilia quod speciosius arma | non est qui tractet: scis quo clamore
coronae ('ring of spectators'") proelia sustineas campestria: Ov. Tr. iii
12, 19, Usus equi nunc est, levibus nunc luditur armis. By arma in the
strict sense the Romans meant defensive weapons (the scutum, etc.) and
such offensive weapons as were used at close quarters (especially the
gladius); missile weapons were tela not arma, and we find the iaculum
which was used in the exercitationes campestres (cf. Hor. C. i 8) distinguished from the arma in Ov. A.A. iii 383, Sunt illis celeresque pilae,
iaculumque, trochique, | armaque, et in gyros ire coactus equus. Titus was
“armorum et equitandi peritissimus’(Tit. 3, 2).

sagittarum: the use of the bow was not part of the Roman military
training, the bowmen (sagittarii) being supplied by the auxiliaries, mainly
those from Crete and the Balearic isles. Titus, like Domitian, excelled in
bowmanship, slaying 12 of the defenders of Jerusalem with 12 arrows
(Tit. 5, 2). The emperor Julian was destinandi sagittas mire promptus”
(Aur. Vict. Caes. 42, 23), and Honorius also was skilled with the bow (cf.
Claud. iv Cons. Hon. 527 sqq.).

vel praecipuo: Suetonius is very fond of using the intensive vel with
praecipuus, as though it were a superlative adj. like maximus; cf. Aug.
10, 2, quem vel praecipuum adiutorem speraverat: Aug. 32, 2, vel praecipuam calumniandi materiam: Iul. 21: Aug. 29, 1: Claud. 20, 1: Galb.
16, 1; so with the adv., e.g. Vitell. 13, 1, vel praecipue luxuriae
Ner. 22, 1. There are two instances in Tacitus: Dial. 6, vel praecipua
iucunditas est: A. xii 60, сит Marius et Sulla de eo vel praecipuе
bellarent.
deditus:

feras in Albano secessu conficientem: for the venationes in the
amphitheatre attached to Domitian's arx Albana see c. 4,4. Pliny (Pan. 81)
says that Trajan found relaxation in hunting wild beasts in their native
haunts, whereas the beasts on which Domitian showed his skill had their
spirit broken by captivity (domitas fractasque claustris feras).

figentem: the use of figere in the sense of transfigere (of bowmen,
spearmen, etc.) is found in poetry and post-Aug. prose; e.g. Juv. iv 99.
comminus ursos | figebat Numidas, Albana nudus harena | venator: Tac.
A. ii 17, quidam .. admotis sagittariis per ludibrium figebantur.

scopulo: scopulus is a dim. of scopus (σκοπός), a mark or target. The
dim. is not found elsewhere, and Stephanus read scopo, adopted by many
subsequent editors; Roth rightly restored scopulo, which also appears in
the texts of Preud'homme and Ihm. The Greek σκοπός was not naturalised
as a Lat. word, but occurs in its Gr. form in Cic., e.g. Att. viii 11, sed
neutri σκοπός est ille, ut nos beati simus; also in Macrob. Somn. Scip. 4,
somnii mentem, ipsumque propositum, quem Graeci σκοπὸν vocant, tentemus
aperire. For the great number of diminutives in Suetonius see App. i.
§ 1. d.
