dispansam palmam: the accusative has to do double duty with
in and praebentis. For the meaning of palma cf. Isid. Diff. 2, 62, ‘‘palma”
manus est dispansis digitis, sicut et arbor dispansis ramis: Orig. 11, 69,
"palma” est manus expansis digitis, sicut contractis “pugnus” (“fist").
Plautus has the forms dispenno, dispessus (Mil. 360, 1406); Lucretius uses
both dispansus (i 306) and dispessus (ii 1126, Munro; iii 988).

direxit: this, not derexit, is the reading of the better MSS. (Q has
derexerit); M has dirigerent in Claud. 20, 3, but derecta in Calig. 46 and
derecto in Calig. 19, 1. In all four passages Ihm adopts the spelling der-,
in accordance with the commonly accepted view that derigo (which is found
in inscriptions and in the oldest Lat. MSS.) is probably the only genuine
ancient form; see Ribbeck Proleg. ad Verg. 401 sqq., Munro on Lucr. vi
823, the Lexica of Caesar by Meusel and by Menge and Preuss, and the
Thes. Ling. Lat.

per intervalla digitorum: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, Sagittarum tam
doctus fuit ut inter patentes digitos extentae manus viri procul positi
spicula eius transvolarent. Stahr gives a modern parallel to Domitian's
feat:-"Man erzählt Ähnliches von dem bekannten preussischen Prinzen
Louis Ferdinand (der bei Saalfeld blieb), der vielleicht nicht ahnte wer
sein Vorgänger in dieser Art barbarischer Virtuosität war."

liberalia studia.. neglexit: see on "liberales disciplinas,” Galb. 5, 1.
Suetonius has already mentioned (in c. 2, 2) the interest which Domitian
pretended to take in literature, especially poetry, before he became emperor;
for his essays in poetry and the estimate of his poetic talent by other
writers see the note on that passage.
quanquam: see on Galb. 14, 1.

bibliothecas incendio absumptas: the fire referred to is that which
devastated part of Rome in the reign of Titus (see Tit. 8, 3 and notes).
Among the buildings which Dio mentions as destroyed then was the Porticus
Octaviae and the library contained there (τὰ Ὀκταουίεια οἰκήματα μετὰ τῶν
βιβλίων). Macé (op. cit. p. 222) points out that when Suetonius is speaking
of the Palatine library he uses the sing. bibliotheca, but the pl. when he is
speaking of the library in the Porticus Octaviae (this library probably
occupying more than one wing of the rectangular colonnade), and Macé
concludes that it was only the latter library which was restored by Domitian.
Julius Caesar had planned a library at Rome and had commissioned Varro
to procure the books, but the project was cut short by Caesar's death.
Asinius Pollio, out of the spoils of his Illyrian campaigns, founded the
first public library in the Atrium Libertatis on the Aventine, and Augustus
established two others: (1) the bibliothecae Octavianae in the Porticus
Octaviae (named after the sister of Augustus); (2) that in the colonnade
of the temple of Apollo on the Palatine. There was a library in the Palace
of Tiberius (bibliotheca domus Tiberianae), and Tiberius also built a
library, dedicated to the Muses, in connexion with the temple to the deified
Augustus on the slope of the Palatine facing the Capitol. Vespasian
established a library in his temple to Peace (Vesp. 9, 1; cf. Gell. v 21,
xvi 8). These are the only libraries at Rome which we know of as earlier
than the reign of Domitian.

impensissime: this superlative of impense is not found earlier, nor is
impensissimus which Suetonius uses in Tib. 13, 2, impensissimis precibus.
Other superlative adjs., ptcples., or advs. which appear first (if not
exclusively) in Suet. are enixissime (cf. enixius, Galb. 3, 3), animosissime,
criminosissimus (and -e), inaequalissimus, remississimus, diversissime
(diversissimus is common), excogitatissimus, immoderatissimus. Some are
only found in isolated instances outside Suet., e.g. evidentissime, minacissimus, assiduissimus, sollicitissime, persuasissimum, amarissime, reverentissime, notatissimus. See Freund, De Suetonii usu atque genere dicendi
49 sq.

reparare curasset: Duker proposed reparari, but when Suetonius uses
curare in the sense of getting something done by the agency of others, he
regularly joins with it the gerundive and not the acc. and inf. pass. Here
he is emphasizing the personal interest and trouble which Domitian took
in restoring the library or libraries.

exemplaribus undique petitis: the same means as were adopted by
Vespasian in restoring the bronze records destroyed by the burning of
the Capitol; Vesp. 8, 5, aerearumque tabularum tria milia, quae simul conflagraverant, restituenda suscepit undique investigatis exemplaribus.

Alexandream: Ptolemy Philadelphus (king of Egypt, 285-247 в.с.)
collected throughout Greece and Asia a multitude of volumes which he
deposited at Alexandria, the greater number in the library in the Museum,
and the remainder in the library in the Serapeum or temple of Serapis
(Vesp. 7, 1). The Museum library was burnt during the blockade of
Julius Caesar at Alexandria in 47 B.C., and 400,000 volumes are said to
have perished. This loss was partly made good by the transfer to
Alexandria of the 200,000 volumes from the library of the kings of
Pergamum which Antony presented to Cleopatra (Plut. Ant. 58). The
Serapeum library was destroyed under the emperor Theodosius in 389 A.D.
It is uncertain whether Suetonius used the form Alexandrea or Alexandria
for ᾿Αλεξάνδρεια. In 11 places -ia is the better attested; in 6 (including
this) -ea. Here Roth, Preud'homme, and Ihm read eam, but -iam in
Vesp. 7, 1: Tit. 5, 3.

stilo vel necessario: explained by the following sentence; Domitian
would not take the trouble to learn to compose the ordinary epistulae
orationesque et edicta which the emperor usually drafted. Baumg.-Cr.
takes necessario as the adv., but it seems clearly to be the adj.

commentarios et acta Tiberi: commentarii (ὑπομνήματα) here means the
private memoirs written by Tiberius, which are mentioned in Tib. 61, 1,
commentario quem de vita sua summatim breviterque composuit. Similar
memoirs were written by Augustus (Aug. 85, 1), and by Agrippina, mother
of Nero (Tac. A. iv 53). The expression “commentarii principis (principales)" is often used (e.g. in Tac. H. iv 40) in another sense for the
record or register of the acta of the emperor, these including the official
decisions which he gave in matters referred to him (C.I.L. iii 411), privileges
granted by him (Plin. Ep. x 95, 105), and the accusations ordered by him
or brought before him (Suet. Calig. 15, 4: Tac. A. xiii 43). See Introd.
c. iii; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 906.
orationes et edicta: see note on c. 2, 3. For alieno ingenio cf. Tac.
A. xiii 3 on Nero's aliena facundia supplied by Seneca.

sermonis tamen nec inelegantis: nec is generally explained as non,
but this seems quite unsound. In old Lat. there are instances of nec so
used (see Kühner-Stegmann, i 817), but in no other passage of Suetonius
has it this meaning. Alexander (op. cit. p. 13), taking nec here as = non,
cites various passages (e.g. Iul. 78, 2; Calig. 6, 2; Claud. 43; Ner. 26, 1;
34, 4; Oth. 9,3; 12, 2; Dom. 15, 2) in which he says nec carries the
value of non, possibly in all, indubitably in some; but an examination of
these passages shows that in all of them nec is to be taken in the sense
of et non or ne quidem. In our passage some words must have fallen
out before nec inelegantis. Bücheler suggested <nec indiligentis > nec
inelegantis, but more probably the original reading was <nec neglegentis >
nec inelegantis. For neglegens (neclegens) as an epithet of sermo cf.

neglegentem esse sermonem. What is probably a similar corruption occurs

dictorum: “clever sayings” “mots”; cf. Suet. Gramm. 23, dicto non

Maecius: quite unknown, and the MSS. vary in the spelling: M has
maetius (“corr. ex maecius ut vid.," Ihm), and this is read by

subrutilum: “reddish,” ὑπόπυρρον; cf. Plin. N.H. x 8, etc.
similar compounds with the same meaning are subrufus, subrubicundus,
subruber, subrubeus. Suetonius also uses subflavus (Aug. 79, 2: Ner. 51);
subdebilis (Vitell. 17, 2).

incanum: ''with a sprinkling of white hairs"; cf. Gloss. Cyrill. “incanus. σπαρτοπόλιος.”
This adj. is only used in poetry and in post-Aug.
prose.
or

perfusam nivem mulso: mulsum (sc. vinum), “honey-wine"
"mead," was best made by mixing some old rough wine, such as Massic
or Falernian, with new Attic honey; cf. Macrob. Sat. vii 12, 9, illud
proverbium quo utuntur gulones: Mulsum quod probe temperes miscendum
esse novo Hymettio et vetulo Falerno. The blend of snow and mead was
suggested to Domitian's mind by the practice of cooling mead and wine
with snow; cf. Plin. Ep. i 15, where Pliny playfully tells a friend who
had disappointed at dinner that he will have to pay for the fare provided,
and among other items for the "mulsum et nix, nam hanc quoque computabis, immo hanc in primis, quae perit in ferculo." To clarify, as well
as to cool, wine it was strained through a cloth covered with snow; cf.
Mart. viii 45, 3: ix 22, 8, Et faciant nigras nostra Falerna nives.
condicionem principum miserrimam: a saying of Hadrian's also; cf.
Vulc. Gall. Αvid. Cass. 2, where Marcus Aurelius, replying to a letter of
Verus warning him against the treasonable designs of Avidius Cassius,
points out that in cases of treason it is inevitable that even those who have
been proved guilty seem to suffer injustice, and then adds: Scis enim ipse
quid avus tuus Hadrianus dixerit: “misera condicio imperatorum, quibus
de adfectata tyrannide nisi occisis non potest credi.” Eius autem
exemplum ponere malui quam Domitiani, qui hoc primus dixisse fertur.
Tyrannorum enim etiam bona dicta non habent tantum auctoritatis quantum
debent. Dio (liv 15), when mentioning those charged with conspiracy
against Augustus, has a similar reflection on the difficulty of knowing
whether such charges are just or unjust: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ἀκριβῶς τὰ τοιαῦτα τοῖς
ἔξω αὐτῶν οὖσιν εἰδέναι. πολλὰ γὰρ ὧν ἂν ὁ κρατῶν πρὸς τιμωρίαν, ὡς καὶ
ἐπιβεβουλευμένος, ἤτοι δι᾽ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ διὰ τῆς γερουσίας (senatus) πράξῃ,
ὑποπτεύεται κατ᾿ ἐπήρειαν, κἂν ὅτι μάλιστα δικαιότατα συμβῇ, γεγονέναι.
quotiens esset: see on Galb. 10, 2.

alea se oblectabat: Pliny (Pan. 82) contrasts the employment of leisure
by Trajan and by emperors like Domitian: Otio prodimur.
An non
plerique principes hoc idem tempus in aleam, stupra, luxum conferebant,
cum seriarum laxamenta curarum vitiorum contentione supplerent? Diceplaying and gambling were forbidden by law at Rome both under the
Republic and under the Empire, an exception being allowed, by law or by
custom, at the Saturnalia. Repressive laws were quite ineffective, and
Juvenal (i 88) describes the intensity of the gambling fever in his day:
Alea quando | hos animos? neque enim loculis ("purse") comitantibus
itur | ad casum tabulae, posita sed luditur arca (“money-chest'"). The
emperors were notorious gamesters; cf. Aug. 70, 2, (Augustus) notatus est
ut aleae indulgens: 71, 1, aleae rumorem (‘ill-repute'") nullo modo expavit,
lusitque simpliciter et palam oblectamenti causa: Calig. 41, 2, ne ex lusu
quidem aleae compendium spernens (Caligula played at dice in his Alban
villa during his sister Drusilla's funeral, Sen. Cons. ad Polyb. 17, 4):
Claud. 5, ex contubernio sordidissimorum hominum super veterem segnitiae
notam ebrietatis quoque et aleae infamiam subiit; Claud. 33, 2 (quoted
along with Ner. 30, 3 in the notes on Vitell. 4, where Suetonius says
that Vitellius won the intimacy of Claudius and of Nero per aleae studium).

etiam profestis diebus: so too Augustus; cf. Aug. 71, 1, lusit praeterquam Decembri mense (i.e. during the Saturnalia, Dec. 17-23) aliis quoque
festis et profestis diebus. For profesti dies cf. Macrob. Sat. i 16, 2, Numa
ut in menses annum ita in dies mensem quemque distribuit, diesque omnes
aut festos, aut profestos, aut intercisos vocavit: festi dis dicati sunt, profesti hominibus ob administrandam rem privatam publicamque concessi,
intercisi deorum hominumque communes sunt.

lavabat de die: for de die see on de nocte in Vesp. 21; it means
"in full day," before the afternoon has begun. The normal time for
the bath was the 8th-9th hour, i.e. about 2-3 p.m.; cf. Cic. Att. xiii 52,
Inde ambulavit (Caesar) in litore. Post horam viii in balneum: Mart. xi
52, 3, octavam (horam) poteris servare; lavabimur una. But we often
read of bathing about the 5th hour, before the prandium; e.g. Plin. Ep. iii
5, 10 (of the elder Pliny), Post solem (i.e. the apricatio) plerumque frigida
lavabatur, deinde gustabat (i.e. took the prandium) dormiebatque minimum:
Epictet. Diss. i 1, 29, ᾿Αλλὰ ἦλθεν ἡ πεμπτή· ταύτῃ δ' εἰώθει γυμνασάμενος
ψυχρολουτρεῖν : Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 30, Egressus balneas multum lactis et
panis sumebat, ova, deinde mulsum; atque his refectus aliquando prandium
inibat, aliquando cibum usque ad cenam differebat: Juv. xi 204, Iam
nunc in balnea salva | fronte licet vadas, quanquam solida hora supersit |
ad sextam. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 269 sqq.
prandebat ad satietatem: the prandium, the meal between the iantaculum (Vitell. 13, 1, n.) and the cena, was usually taken about the sixth
hour; cf. Aug. 78, 1, post cibum meridianum: Claud. 34, 2, meridie dimisso
ad prandium populo. This midday meal or lunch might be of a very light
nature, as in the case of Augustus, Aug. 76, 1, nos in essedo panem et
palmulas ('dates") gustavimus; cf. Sen. Ep. 83, 6, panis siccus et sine
mensa prandium, post quod non sunt lavandae manus: Hor. S. i 6, 127,
pransus non avide quantum interpellet inani | ventre diem durare.
Generally, however, it was of a more substantial kind with cold or hot
meats, fish, vegetables, fruit, and wine; see the passages quoted by
Marquardt, op. cit. 267. Nero, like Domitian, indulged freely at the
prandium; cf. Tac. A. xiv 2, medio die cum id temporis per vinum et
epulas incalesceret; so too Vitellius (Vitell. 13, 1).
non temere: see on Tit. 6, 2.

super cenam: see on Tit. 8, 1. Pliny (Pan. 49), addressing Trajan,
says that Domitian by his gorging at his lonely lunch had turned this
prandium into a solitaria cena; and so when the regular cena was being
served, the sated tyrant was free to spy on and insult his guests: Non
enim ante medium diem distentus solitaria cena spectator adnotatorque
convivis tuis immines nec ieiunis et inanibus plenus ipse et ructans non tam
adponis quam obicis cibos, quos dedigneris attingere, aegreque perpessus
superbam illam convictus simulationem rursus te ad clandestinam ganeam
occultumque luxum refers.

Matianum malum: the Matian apple is mentioned in Plin. N.H. xv 49
as one of those deriving their names from persons; it was probably called
after C. Matius Calvena, whom Pliny (N.H. xii 13) names as the inventor
of the art of clipping arbours: primus C. Matius ex equestri ordine, divi
Augusti amicus, invenit nemora tonsilia intra hos lxxx annos. This
C. Matius was a friend of Julius Caesar (Iul. 52, 2) and of Cicero (Cic.
Fam. xi 27, 28, etc.); he translated the Iliad into Latin verse, and wrote a
complete account of the art and science of cookery in three books (Colum.
xii 4, 44). Palmer (Introd. to Hor. S. ii 4) argues strongly that the Catius
whose precepts on cookery are given by Horace is C. Matius. The Matianum
malum is also mentioned in Colum. v 10, 19: Macrob. Sat. iii 19, 2 (where
the form used is Mattianum): Athen. iii 82 c, ἐγὼ . . μάλιστα τεθαύμακα τὰ
κατὰ τὴν ῾Ρώμην πιπρασκόμενα μῆλα, τὰ Ματτιανὰ καλούμενα, ἅπερ κομίζεσθαι
λέγεται ἀπό τινος κώμης ἱδρυμένης ἐπὶ τῶν πρὸς ᾿Ακυληίᾳ (Aquileia) ῎Αλπεων.
For the use of apples at dessert (mensae secundae) cf. Hor. S. i 3, 6;
Mart. x 48, 18.

modicam potiunculam: Statius (S. v 1, 121 sqq.) flatteringly alludes
to the abstemiousness of Domitian as a model which Priscilla commended
to her husband Abascantus for imitation: fovet anxia curas | coniugis
hortaturque simul flectitque labores, ipsa dapes modicas et sobria pocula
tradit | exemplumque ad erile (i.e. of Domitian, their lord) monet.

ampulla: the ampulla (λήκυθος) was a narrow-necked vessel with globular
body, principally used for holding oil, but also for vinegar, wine, and
drink of any kind. At times the Romans used to drink out of the ampulla
itself; such a drinking-flask is called ampulla potoria in Mart. xiv 110,
and glass ampullae for this purpose are mentioned in Mart. vi 35, 3, At tu
multa diu dicis vitreisque tepentem | ampullis potas semisupinus aquam.
convivabatur: see on Vesp. 19, 1.

non ultra solis occasum: contrast Nero, Ner. 27, 2, epulas a medio die
ad mediam noctem protrahebat.

comissaretur: the comissatio (κῶμος, κωμάζειν) or drinking revel took
place after the cena, sometimes in the same room, sometimes the diners
went on to another house (e.g. Liv. xl 7, 5: Petron. Satyr. 65). With
their anointed locks wreathed with roses the comissatores drank more
Graeco under the presidency of a magister or arbiter bibendi (Cic. Sen. 14,
46: Hor. C. ii 7, 25), and were entertained by the performances of artistes
of various kinds, the revel being often protracted till midnight or later
(cf. Tit. 7, 1). Vitellius was peculiar in making the comissatio his fourth
great meal for the day (Vitell. 13, 1). See Marquardt, op. cit. 331 sqq.

nihil aliud quam deambulabat: this elliptical mode of expression,
in which a verb of general signification like facere must be supplied out
of a verb of special signification, is found in Nepos (Ages. 4, Tissaphernes
nihil aliud quam bellum comparavit), and is frequent from Livy on.
Suetonius is fond of it; e.g. Aug. 83, nihil aliud quam vectabatur et

deambulabat: Vesp. 5, 2, nec illam quicquam aliud quam cachinasse.
Sometimes nihil aliud quam is used quite adverbially ("only” “merely”),
e.g. Liv. ii 63, hostes, nihil aliud quam perfusis vano timore Romanis,
citato agmine abeunt. Similarly nihil (nec quicquam) amplius quam is
found at times with an ellipse of facere, at times = tantum, tantum modo;
e.g. Tit. 9, 1, nihil amplius quam monuit: Aug. 2, 3, ipse Augustus
nihil amplius quam equestri familia ortum se scribit. Such usages are very
rare in Tacitus (A. iv 34, xiii 40, xv 13, H. ii 91). Cicero in a few instances uses nihil aliud nisi in this way, e.g. Sest. 14, nihil aliud nisi
meum nomen causamque sustinuit; usually he has the fuller form of
expression, e.g. Rosc. Am. 108, nihil aliud fecerunt nisi rem detulerunt.
See Kühner-Stegmann, ii 564.

libidinis nimiae: cf. Dio lxvii 6, ἀσωτότατος καὶ ἀσελγέστατος καὶ πρὸς
γυναῖκας καὶ πρὸς μειράκια ἦν:
Oros. vii 10, 2, libidinis intemperantia quidquid cogitari potest fecit. Suidas describes Domitian as “ἀκρατὴς καὶ
ἀκόλαστος τὰ περὶ τὸ σῶμα, γυναικομανίας καὶ ἀνδρομανίας ἀνάπλεως." For the
genitive of quality cf. Claud. 33, 2, libidinis in feminas profusissimae.

clinopalen: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 7, furens libidine, cuius foedum
exercitium Graecorum lingua κλινοπάλην vocabat. Martial is probably
referring to Domitian's use of the word κλινοπάλη (lectilucta) when in an
ambiguous epigram (xiv 201) he says of a palaestrita or wrestler: Non amo
quod vincat, sed quod succumbere novit | et didicit melius τὴν ἐπικλινοπάλην.
quasi: see on Tit. 5, 3.
develleret: cf. Galb. 22. Marquardt, Privatl.2 787.

nataretque inter
meretrices: Elagabalus indulged in similar
practices: Lamprid. Heliog. 31, in balneis semper cum mulieribus fuit, ita
ut eas ipse psilothro curaret, etc.

Domitiae: Domitia Longina, whom Domitian married after taking
her away from her husband Aelius Lamia (Dom. 1, 3; 10, 2).
palam dilexit: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vii 7, quoted on c. 10, 4)
says that Domitian married (ἤγετο) Julia after he had put her husband
Sabinus to death, but there is no other evidence of this. Dio (lxvii 3) states
that after Domitian had sent away his wife Domitia for intriguing with
the actor Paris (see c. 3, 1) he cohabited more openly with Julia as if
she were a wife (τῇ Ἰουλίᾳ ἀπαρακαλυπτότερον ὡς γαμετῇ συνῴκει), and when
he took back Domitia at the request of the people, he none the less kept
up his illicit relations with Julia (ἐχρῆτο δ᾽ οὐδὲν ἧττον τῇ ᾿Ἰουλίᾳ).

causa mortis: cf. Plin. Ep. iv 11, cum ipse (Domitianus) fratris filiam
incesto non polluisset solum, verum etiam occidisset: nam vidua abortu
periit (the use of vidua, "in her widowhood," shows that she was not
married to Domitian). For the date of her death see on Tit. 4, 2.
=

conceptum a se abigere: conceptum may be either from the subst.
conceptus (coner. fetus, cf. Stat. Th. x 805, quosve ego conceptus aut
quae mala pignora fudi?) or the neut. ptc. used substantivally (cf. Scrib.
Larg. Ep. ad Callist. p. 3, ne praegnanti medicamentum, quo conceptum
excutitur, detur). The Thes. Ling. Lat. (iv 23 and 62) is inconsistent on
the point. The words a se (i.e. Domitian) are to be taken with conceptum;
cf. Colum. vi 37, 10, quae (equa) cum ex asino conceptum edidit. The
usual phrase for forcing birth or procuring abortion is partum abigere;
e.g. Cic. Cluent. 32, partum sibi ipsa. medicamentis abegisset. Juvenal
(ii 29 sqq.) denounces Domitian, who had revived the lex Iulia de adulteriis
et stupro, for his treatment of Julia: Qualis erat nuper tragico pollutus
adulter | concubitu (i.e. Domitian's incest was like that of Oedipus in
Greek tragedy), qui tunc leges revocabat amaras | omnibus atque ipsis
Veneri Martique timendas, | cum tot abortivis fecundam Iulia vulvam |
solveret et patruo (i.e. Domitian) similes effunderet offas. Pliny (Pan. 63)
accuses Domitian of stupra and incestae noctes. Claudius, in order to wed
Agrippina, got a decree passed by the senate legitimizing marriage with a
brother's daughter (Claud. 26, Tac. A. xii 7). Gaius (Inst. i 62) mentions
that this was still in force, though marriage with a sister's daughter was
illegal. Constantine restored the ancient law and prohibited marriage with
a brother's daughter as incestuous.

populus: the ordinary people at Rome had not been affected by the
tyranny of Domitian in the same way as those of higher rank, and moreover the populus under the Empire had come to be absolutely indifferent
to affairs of state; cf. Juv. x 77, populus iam pridem ex quo suffragia
nulli | vendimus, effudit curas; nam qui dabat olim | imperium fasces
legiones omnia, nunc se | continet atque duas tantum res anxius optat, |
panem et circenses.

indifferenter: this post-Aug. adv. is used in the sense of "indiscriminately, by Quintilian (e.g. xi 3, 1, utraque appellatione indifferenter
uti licet) and Gellius (x 24, 8). Suetonius is peculiar in using indifferens
of men in the sense of "careless” “indifferent,” Iul. 53, circa victum
("food") C. Oppius adeo indifferentem (Caesarem) docet; the adj. was
introduced by Cicero (Fin. iii 16) to express the Stoic ἀδιάφορον, i.e.
neutrum, nequè bonum, neque malum.

miles gravissime tulit: for reasons given in Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 9,
Quo moti milites, quibus privatae commoditates dispendio publico largius
procedunt, auctores necis ad supplicium poscere, more suo, seditiosius
coeperunt. Qui vix aegreque per prudentes cohibiti, tandem in gratiam
optimatum convenere. Neque minus per se moliebantur bellum, quod iis
conversum imperium maestitiae erat, ob omissionem praedarum per dona
munifica. Domitian had lavishly increased the soldiers' pay (c. 7, 3).
According to Philostratus (vit. Soph. i 7) the legions on the Danube were
dissuaded from revolting on Domitian's death by the famous Dio
Chrysostom, who had been forced to flee from Italy by Domitian's decree
expelling the philosophers. He used his great eloquence in inveighing
against the dead tyrant, and persuaded the soldiers that they would do
better to obey the senate.

Divum: Domitian was one of the emperors not deified after death;
for such deification see on Vesp. 23, 4.
nisi duces defuissent: the prefects of the praetorians were themselves involved in the conspiracy against Domitian; see on c. 14, 1.

quod paulo post fecit: under Nerva in 97 A.D. the praetorians, led by
their prefect Casperius Aelianus, wreaked vengeance on the assassins, as is
described in [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 12, 7, Cum interfectores Domitiani ad
exitium poscerentur, tantum est consternatus (Nerva) ut neque vomitum,
neque impetum ventris valuerit differre: et tamen vehementer obstitit,
dictitans aequius esse mori quam auctoritatem imperii foedare, proditis
potentiae sumendae auctoribus. Sed milites, neglecto principe, requisitos,
Petronium uno ictu, Parthenium vero, demptis prius genitalibus et in os
coniectis, iugulavere. They even coerced Nerva into publicly returning
thanks to them for slaying “nefandos pessimosque omnium mortalium.”
Dio (lxviii 3) says that Nerva presented his own throat to their swords in
a vain attempt to save Domitian's assassins who had secured the throne
for him. The soldiers similarly avenged the murder of Alexander Severus;
cf. Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 63, mortem eius milites
gravissime tulerunt
atque auctores caedis trucidarunt (one of the many passages in which the
Scriptores Historiae Augustae imitate Suetonius; see Introd. p. 26).

senatus laetatus est: the senate in the later years of Domitian had
been mere slaves of the despot. Marcellus Eprius, the informer against
Thrasea (c. 10, 3), defended himself on the ground that he was but one
member of a senate who had all been slaves together (se unum esse ex
illo senatu qui simul servierit, Tac. H. iv 8). Tacitus (Agr. 45) vividly
describes the dragooning of the senate by the display of armed force
(obsessam curiam et clausum armis senatum), and the way in which he
and his fellow-senators passed servile decrees of condemnation and even
laid violent hands upon members of their own order; see on c. 11, 3.
Hence the frantic exultation at Domitian's death, which Pliny (Pan. 52)
depicts: Iuvabat illidere solo superbissimos vultus, instare ferro, saevire
securibus, ut si singulos ictus sanguis dolorque sequeretur. Nemo tam
temperans gaudii seraeque laetitiae, quin instar ultionis videretur cernere
laceros artus, truncata membra, postremo truces horrendasque imagines
abiectas excoctasque flammis, ut ex illo terrore et minis in usum hominum
ac voluptates ignibus mutarentur.

repleta certatim curia: as on the death of Titus, but for a very
different purpose; see Tit. 11.

adclamationum: see on adclamari, c. 13, 1. Cf. Lamprid. Comm. 18,
adclamationes senatus post mortem Commodi graves fuerunt. Lampridius
fills two chapters with what purport to be the actual outcries of the senate
on that occasion, the following being a portion: "Hosti patriae honores
detrahantur. Parricida trahatur. Hostis patriae, parricida, gladiator in
spoliario lanietur. Hostis deorum, carnifex senatus, qui senatum occidit,
unco trahatur; qui innocentes occidit, unco trahatur; ... qui sanguini
suo non pepercit, unco trahatur;
Gladiatoris et parricidae statuae
detrahantur." (More of these adclamationes of the senate against the
delatores who flourished under Commodus are quoted on Tit. 8, 4.)
clipeos: shields emblazoned with portraits, medallion busts.
Pliny
(N.H. xxxv 3) says that Appius Claudius, consul in 495 B.C., was the first
to hang such shields with portraits of his ancestors in the temple of Bellona.
Macrobius (Sat. ii 3) tells a story about Cicero's witty remark on a shieldbust of his brother Quintus: Cum in ea provincia quam ille rexerat vidisset
clipeatam imaginem eius ingentibus lineamentis usque ad pectus ex more
pictam (erat autem Quintus ipse staturae parvae), ait: Frater meus dimidius
maior est quam totus. We find constant references to such clipei with
portraits of the emperors which were placed in temples or (as here) in the
senate-house (e.g. Mon. Ancyr. 34: Capitol. Anton. Pius 5: Treb. Poll.
Claud. 3).
In Calig. 16, 4 Suetonius mentions that the senate decreed to
Caligula an aureus clipeus which was borne in solemn state to the Capitol
every year by priests attended by senators, with high-born youths and
maidens chanting his praises. For the clipeus decreed to Germanicus after
his death see Tac. A. ii 83.

imagines: those in the senate-house first of all, and then the other
busts and statues were pulled down, and the statues of gold and silver
(c. 13, 2) were melted; cf. Dio lxviii 1, μίσει δὲ τοῦ Δομιτιανοῦ αἱ εἰκόνες αὐτοῦ,
πολλαὶ μὲν ἀργυραῖ, πολλαὶ δὲ καὶ χρυσαῖ οὖσαι, συνεχωνεύθησαν: Plin. Pan. 52,
illae aureae et innumerabiles (statuae) strage et ruina publico gaudio
litaverunt. The colossal equestrian statue of Domitian, the theme of Stat.
S. i 1, was probably destroyed among the rest (see Vollmer ad loc.).
Procopius (6th cent. A.D.) in his Hist. arcana, 8 p. 55 Dind., has a curious
story that the body of Domitian was hewn in pieces, which were collected
and put together by his wife as a model for a bronze statue. This was
set up on the right of the ascent from the Forum to the Capitol and was
the sole existing statue of Domitian in the time of Procopius, who says
that it bore a strange resemblance to Justinian (Friedl., Sitteng. iii¹º 60).
For the destruction of the statues of the fallen great cf. Juv. x 58, descendunt statuae restemque sequuntur |
iam strident ignes, iam follibus
atque caminis | ardet adoratum populo caput, et crepat ingens | Seianus.
Mayor, in his note there, cites many parallels; among the emperors whose
statues were so treated were Caligula, Nero, Vitellius, Commodus, Maximinus,
and Theodosius. In 1878 a mutilated statue, probably of Domitian, was
found in the Tiber.
=

coram: used by Suetonius as adv. (13 times) and prep. (6 times).
As adv., (a) = in conspectu suo, as here and in Vitell. 14, 2, quendam coram
interfici iussit; (b) in conspectu aliorum vel omnium, e.g. Ner. 7, 1,
amitam Lepidam ream testimonio coram afflixit; (c) = in os "to one's
face," e.g. Aug. 13, 2, hunc foedissimo convicio coram prosciderunt. As
a prep. it either precedes or follows its case; e.g. Tib. 62, 2, coram se:
Oth. 1, 2, se coram: Aug. 56, 4, coram iudicibus: Tit. 10, 1, populo coram.
The postposition of coram is not found in class. prose; it occurs most
frequently in Tacitus.

eradendos ubique titulos: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 8, senatus
radendum nomen decrevit: Macrob. Sat. i 12, 37, sed ubi infaustum
vocabulum (Domitiani) ex omni aere vel saxo placuit eradi, menses quoque
usurpatione tyrannicae appellationis (see Dom. 13, 3) exuti sunt: Procop.
1.C., δόγμα ἐγεγόνει τῆς συγκλήτου βουλῆς μηδ' ὄνομα τοῦ βασιλέως τούτου ἐν
γράμμασιν εἶναι, μηδ' εἰκόνα ἡντιναοῦν αὐτοῦ διασώζεσθαι: Euseb. Hist. Eccl.
iii 20, μετὰ δὲ τὸν Δομετιανὸν πεντεκαίδεκα ἔτεσιν ἐπικρατήσαντα, Νέρουα τὴν
ἀρχὴν διαδεξαμένου, καθαιρεθῆναι μὲν τὰς Δομετιανοῦ τιμὰς . . ἡ ῾Ῥωμαίων σύγκλητος
βουλὴ ψηφίζεται. Domitian's name has been erased on extant inscriptions;
see the list in Dessau, Inscr. Lat. Sel. iii 1, 273. Commodus (ob. 192) and
Maximinus (ob. 238) were similarly dishonoured; cf. Lamprid. Comm. 20,
Censeo quae is ob honorem suum decerni coegit abolenda: statuas
abolendas, nomenque ex omnibus privatis publicisque monumentis eradendum:
Capitol. Gord. 9, Appellato igitur Gordiano imperatore, iuvenes, qui auctores
huius facinoris erant, statuas Maximini deiecerunt, imagines perfregerunt,
nomen publicitus eraserunt. Mommsen (Staatsr. iii³ 1190) shows that while
the statues of the enemies of the people were overthrown under the
Republic, the first instance of a name being expunged from the list of
magistrates was that of M. Antonius after the battle of Actium. A
proposal in the senate that the name of Piso (see Vitell. 2, 3) should be
removed from the consular records (nomen Pisonis radendum fastis) was
vetoed by Tiberius (Tac. A. iii 17, 18).
abolendam memoriam: cf. Calig. 60 (after the murder of Caligula),
senatus in asserenda libertate adeo consensit, ut quidam abolendam
Caesarum memoriam ac diruenda templa censuerint: Lamprid. Comm. 19,
parricidae gladiatoris (Commodi) memoria aboleatur: Val. Max. viii 14, 5,
bene consuluerant Ephesii decreto memoriam taeterrimi hominis abolendo.
For the senate's damnatio memoriae and rescissio actorum in the case of
a dead emperor see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 1134. One result of the damnatio
memoriae of Domitian is that comparatively few inscriptions of his reign
have survived. In Rome itself only one has been found (C.I.L. vi 932,
Dessau 246), but a certain number have been preserved in Italy and the
provinces (see Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2542; Gsell, op. cit. 331, n. 3;
Imhof, op. cit. 124). From the very considerable number of Domitian's
coins still extant Gsell (330, n. 2) concludes that it is improbable that the
senate ordered the coins with his name to be melted down, as was done
later with those of Geta (Dio lxxvii 12).
..

§ 2. cornix elocuta est: the crow was reputed to possess the gift of
imitating human speech; cf. Varr. L.L. vi 56: Plin. N.H. x 124, cornix
plura contexta verba exprimens et alia atque alia crebro addiscens (from
which it has been proposed to read cornix for perdix in Stat. S. ii 4, 20,
refert iungens iterata vocabula perdix): Ov. M. ii 547, quem garrula motis |
consequitur pennis, scitetur ut omnia, cornix | auditaque viae causa 'non
utile carpis," | inquit, "iter: ne sperne meae praesagia linguae!” Crows
were among the birds which gave omens by their note (oscines); cf. Paulus
(Fest. p. 197), oscinum tripudium est, quod oris cantu significat quid
portendi; cum cecinit corvus, cornix, noctua, parra, picus: Cic. Ac. ii 128,
cum cornix cecinerit, tum aliquid eam aut iubere aut vetare: Cic. Div. ii 78,
nec (Deiotaro) cornix canere potuit recte eum facere.
ἔσται πάντα καλῶς : cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 13, 10 (praising the virtues
of Trajan), Quae omnia eo maiora visebantur, quo per multos atque atroces
tyrannos perdito atque prostrato statu Romano, in remedium tantorum
malorum divinitus credebatur opportune datus; usque eo, ut adveniens
imperium eius pleraque mirifica denuntiaverint, in quis praecipuum, cornicem
e fastigio Capitolii Atticis sermonibus effatam esse “καλῶς ἔσται.”
..
nec defuit qui.. interpretaretur: cf. Galb. 8, 2: Vesp. 5, 3: Tit. 5, 3.

Tarpeio culmine: cf. Calp. Ecl. 7, 24, spectacula Tarpeium prope
despectantia culmen: Sil. Ital. iii 609, Tarpei culminis ignes: vi 102,
culmina
Tarpeia exosus: x 360, ipse refulgebat Tarpeiae culmine rupis.
On the N. summit of the Mons Capitolinus was the Arx; on the S. summit
the Capitolium or temple of Jupiter. The "Tarpeia rupes" was on the
S.W. slope of the S. summit, and that summit was called the Mons Tarpeius,
though Mons Tarpeius, Arx Tarpeia, and Capitolium are sometimes used
to designate the whole hill, which was more correctly described as “Arx
Capitoliumque."

gibbam: "hunch,” “hump"; the fem. form also in Amm. Marc. xxiii
4; gibbus in Juvenal (vi 109: x 294,309). Suetonius uses the adj. gibber
(Galb. 3, 3) and also has gibberosus in a specimen which he cites of the
caustic utterances of Orbilius ("plagosus''): Gramm. 9, 2, Ac ne principum quidem virorum insectatione abstinuit; siquidem ignotus adhuc cum
iudicio frequenti testimonium diceret, interrogatus a Varrone Murena
diversae partis advocato, quidnam ageret et quo artificio ("profession'')
uteretur, gibberosos se de sole in umbram transferre respondit; quod
Murena gibber erat (see note on Galb. 3, 3).

pone: as a prep. also in Tib. 68, 2 (p. occipitium) and Ner. 51 (p.
verticem); as an adv. in Iul. 20, 1 (lictores p. sequerentur). It is most
frequent in Plautus; only twice in Cicero (Tim. 37 and 48); not in Caesar;
twice in Livy; six times in Tacitus. Quintilian (viii 3, 25) mentions it
among the words by which Virgil gave to his work an air of antiquity.

cervicem: Suetonius uses the sing. in 8 passages, the pl. in 4 (e.g.
Vitell. 17, 1, iniecto cervicibus laqueo). Down to the time of Livy the
sing. is limited to poetry. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 248 sq.

auream: 'somnium hoc Domitiani significabat, a tergo eius, hoc est,
post ipsius obitum, futuros principes optimos, qui aetatem auream orbi
terrarum reducerent” (Beroaldus).
abstinentia: cf. c. 9, 1: 10, 1; see on “abstinuit,” Tit. 7, 3.

moderatione insequentium principum: the mild and beneficent rule
of Domitian's successors, Nerva (96-98) and Trajan (98-116), is attested
by various writers; e.g. Philostr. vit. Apollon. vii 8, ἀρχῇ πρέπειν ἐδόκει
Νέρουας, ἧς μετὰ Δομετιανὸν σωφρόνως ἥψατο : Aur. Vict. Caes. 12, 1, Quid
enim Nerva prudentius magisque moderatum? (Epit. 11, 15, quid enim
Nerva prudentius aut moderatius? quid Traiano divinius? quid praestantius
Hadriano?): Eutrop. viii 1, respublica ad prosperrimum statum rediit bonis
principibus ingenti felicitate commissa; Domitiano enim, exitiabili
tyranno, Nerva successit: Tac. H. i 1, rara temporum (i.e. under Nerva
and Trajan) felicitate, ubi sentire quae velis et quae sentias dicere licet:
Tac. Agr. 3, nunc tandem redit animus; et quamquam primo statim beatissimi saeculi ortu Nerva Caesar res olim dissociabiles miscuerit, principatum
ac libertatem, augeatque cotidie felicitatem Nerva Traianus, nec spem
modo ac votum securitas publica, sed ipsius voti fiduciam ac robur adsumpserit, natura tamen infirmitatis humanae tardiora sunt remedia quam mala:
Florus, praef. 8, sub Traiano principe movet lacertos (populus Romanus),
et praeter spem omnium senectus imperii, quasi reddita iuventute, revirescit.
Gibbon, Decline and Fall c. 3, says: “If a man were called to fix the
period in the history of the world during which the condition of the
human race was most happy and prosperous, he would, without hesitation,
name that which elapsed from the death of Domitian to the accession of
Commodus. The vast extent of the Roman empire was governed by absolute
power, under the guidance of virtue and wisdom. The armies were
restrained by the firm but gentle hand of four successive emperors, whose
characters and authority commanded involuntary respect. The forms of
the civil administration were carefully preserved by Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian,
and the Antonines, who delighted in the image of liberty, and were pleased
with considering themselves as the accountable ministers of the laws. Such
princes deserved the honour of restoring the republic, had the Romans of
their days been capable of enjoying a rational freedom."
